ca_adc_hw_init_periph.brief: Initializes and calibrates the specified ADC hardware peripheral for polling-based operations.

params.name: adc_num
params.desc: The index of the ADC peripheral to initialize (typically 1, 2, or 3 depending on the STM32 model).

params.name: sample_time
params.desc: The sampling time configuration value to be applied to all channels; higher values increase accuracy but decrease conversion speed.

ca_adc_hw_init_periph.returns: Returns true if the ADC was successfully initialized and calibrated, false if the hardware failed to respond (e.g., timeout during calibration or power-up).
ca_adc_hw_init_periph.notes: This function is blocking because it performs hardware polling loops (waiting for voltage regulators or calibration cycles to complete). It is NOT thread-safe and must not be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) due to the potential for long-running loops. Before calling this, ensure the peripheral clock has been enabled via the appropriate clock control function. A common mistake is calling this function multiple times without resetting the peripheral, which may lead to undefined hardware states or calibration errors.
ca_adc_hw_init_periph.usage: This function is intended to be used during the system startup phase or when a specific ADC peripheral is first requested by the application. It is typically called inside a higher-level driver initialization function (like ca_adc_init) that handles clock gating and configuration validation. It should be paired with subsequent functions that trigger conversions and read data registers, ensuring the hardware is in a ready state before any sampling begins.

ca_adc_hw_init_periph_isr.signature: bool ca_adc_hw_init_periph_isr(u8 adc_num, u8 sample_time, ca_adc_isr_cb_t cb)
ca_adc_hw_init_periph_isr.brief: Initializes the ADC hardware peripheral and configures it to trigger an interrupt upon conversion completion.

params.name: adc_num
params.desc: The index of the ADC peripheral (typically 1, 2, or 3 depending on the specific STM32 model). Invalid values return false.

params.name: sample_time
params.desc: The sampling duration configuration for the ADC channels. Must be a valid value supported by the hardware registers.

params.name: cb
params.desc: A function pointer to the callback function that will be executed inside the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) when the conversion finishes.

ca_adc_hw_init_periph_isr.returns: Returns true if the ADC was successfully initialized and the interrupt was enabled. Returns false if the adc_num is out of range, the underlying hardware initialization fails, or the provided callback is invalid.
ca_adc_hw_init_periph_isr.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs hardware-level configuration, including enabling the End-Of-Conversion (EOC) interrupt and setting the NVIC priority. It is not thread-safe and should be called during the system initialization phase before starting any conversions. It must NOT be called from within an ISR itself, as it modifies NVIC settings and peripheral registers that could lead to race conditions or system instability. A common mistake is passing a NULL pointer as the callback, which will cause the system to crash or jump to an invalid memory address when the interrupt fires.
ca_adc_hw_init_periph_isr.usage: This function is used when you need to perform non-blocking ADC conversions, allowing the CPU to execute other tasks while waiting for the hardware to finish sampling. It is typically paired with ca_clock_hw_adc_init to ensure the peripheral clock is running, followed by ca_adc_hw_start_isr to trigger the actual conversion process. Once the conversion completes, the hardware automatically jumps to the provided callback function, where you can read the result using a function like ca_adc_get_value.

ca_adc_hw_irq_handler.brief: Hardware-specific interrupt service routine handler for ADC peripheral completion events.

params.name: adc_num
params.desc: The identifier of the ADC peripheral (e.g., 1, 2, or 3). Must match the hardware configuration limits of the specific STM32 series.

ca_adc_hw_irq_handler.returns: void. This function does not return a value as it is an interrupt handler.
ca_adc_hw_irq_handler.notes: This function is designed to be called exclusively from the hardware interrupt vector table (ISR context). Because it runs in an ISR, it must be extremely fast; performing heavy processing or blocking operations inside the callback will cause system instability or missed interrupts. It is not thread-safe in the sense that it modifies hardware registers directly, but it is re-entrant if the hardware supports multiple ADC instances. A common beginner mistake is to perform long calculations or use blocking RTOS primitives (like mutexes or delays) inside the callback function triggered by this handler, which will crash the system or cause a watchdog reset.
ca_adc_hw_irq_handler.usage: This function is the bridge between the hardware ADC peripheral and your application logic. It is typically invoked by the STM32 vector table when the 'End of Conversion' (EOC) flag is raised by the hardware. You must register a callback function using the appropriate driver initialization function before this handler is triggered, otherwise, the handler will simply exit without notifying your application. It is used in a sequence: initialize the ADC, enable the ADC interrupt in the NVIC, and then this handler will automatically execute every time a conversion finishes.

ca_adc_hw_read.brief: Triggers a single ADC conversion on a specific channel and returns the 12-bit raw digital value.

params.name: adc_num
params.desc: The identifier of the ADC peripheral (e.g., 1, 2, or 3). Must correspond to valid hardware instances defined in the BSP.

params.name: channel
params.desc: The analog input channel index. Must be a valid channel supported by the selected ADC peripheral.

ca_adc_hw_read.returns: A 12-bit unsigned integer (0-4095) representing the converted voltage. Note that this function does not return error codes; it assumes valid hardware state.
ca_adc_hw_read.notes: This function is strictly blocking, meaning the CPU will sit in a 'while' loop waiting for the hardware to finish the conversion. Because it uses a busy-wait loop, it is NOT thread-safe if multiple tasks access the same ADC instance simultaneously, and it must NEVER be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) as it would cause a system hang. Before calling this, ensure the ADC peripheral has been properly initialized via the system clock and GPIO configuration functions. A common beginner mistake is calling this function at a high frequency in a low-priority task, which can starve other tasks of CPU time due to the blocking nature of the hardware wait.
ca_adc_hw_read.usage: This function is typically used for polling-based sensor reading where high-speed, non-blocking asynchronous operation is not required. It is usually paired with an initialization function like 'ca_adc_init_isr' or a generic hardware setup routine that configures the GPIO pins to analog mode. In a typical application, you would call this function periodically within a task loop to sample analog data, process the raw 12-bit value, and then perform control logic based on the result.

ca_adc_hw_start_isr.brief: Triggers an asynchronous ADC conversion on a specific channel without blocking the CPU.

params.name: adc_num
params.desc: The index of the ADC peripheral to use (e.g., 1 for ADC1). Note that some hardware implementations ignore this and always default to ADC1.

params.name: channel
params.desc: The specific analog input channel to sample. Valid values are typically 0-19 depending on the MCU architecture.

ca_adc_hw_start_isr.returns: void. This function does not return a status code; it assumes the hardware is correctly initialized and ready to start.
ca_adc_hw_start_isr.notes: This function is non-blocking and designed to be called from within an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) or a high-priority task. It is not thread-safe by itself, so ensure that no other process is modifying the ADC registers simultaneously. A common beginner mistake is calling this function before the ADC peripheral has been properly clocked and configured, which will result in a hard fault or silent failure. Because it is asynchronous, the function returns immediately after triggering the hardware; you must rely on a separate interrupt handler or callback mechanism to retrieve the conversion result once the hardware sets the End-Of-Conversion (EOC) flag.
ca_adc_hw_start_isr.usage: This function is typically used in a continuous sampling loop or a triggered data acquisition system. It is usually paired with an ADC interrupt handler: you call this function to start the conversion, and when the hardware finishes, the ADC interrupt fires, allowing you to read the result and potentially call this function again to start the next conversion. It is essential for high-performance applications where you cannot afford to wait for the ADC to finish (blocking) while the CPU does other work. In a typical sequence, you initialize the ADC, enable the ADC interrupt, and then call this function to kick off the first conversion.

ca_adc_hw_stop.brief: Safely stops ADC conversions and powers down the hardware peripheral.

params.name: adc_num
params.desc: The index of the ADC peripheral to stop (e.g., 1 for ADC1). Note: Current implementations primarily target ADC1, so this parameter is reserved for future multi-ADC support.

ca_adc_hw_stop.returns: Returns true if the ADC was successfully disabled or was already off. Returns false if the hardware failed to acknowledge the stop command within the internal timeout period.
ca_adc_hw_stop.notes: This function is blocking because it performs a busy-wait loop to ensure the hardware registers (like ADEN or ADSTART) have cleared. It is not thread-safe; if multiple tasks share the same ADC, you must wrap this call in a mutex to prevent race conditions. It is generally not safe to call this from an ISR because the blocking loops could stall the system if the hardware hangs. The most common beginner mistake is calling this while a DMA transfer is still active, which can cause the ADC to lock up or leave the DMA in an inconsistent state; always ensure DMA is stopped before calling this.
ca_adc_hw_stop.usage: This function is used to cleanly shut down the ADC peripheral during system power-down, mode switching, or error recovery. It is the mandatory cleanup step after using functions like ca_adc_init or ca_adc_init_isr. In a typical sequence, you would first stop any active DMA or interrupts, call ca_adc_hw_stop to release the hardware, and then potentially re-initialize the peripheral or enter a low-power sleep mode.

ca_adc_hw_stop_isr.brief: Disables the ADC end-of-conversion interrupt while keeping the peripheral powered and active.

params.name: adc_num
params.desc: The ADC peripheral index (e.g., 1). Note: current implementation ignores this and defaults to ADC1.

ca_adc_hw_stop_isr.notes: This function is non-blocking and safe to call from an ISR. It is designed to silence the interrupt mechanism without powering down the ADC hardware, which is critical if you intend to perform polled reads immediately after. If you were to call a full stop function instead, the ADC would lose its configuration and require a complete re-initialization, causing subsequent reads to return zero or invalid data. A common mistake is calling this when you actually want to power down the peripheral; use ca_adc_stop() for that purpose instead.
ca_adc_hw_stop_isr.usage: This function is typically used when transitioning from an interrupt-driven sampling mode to a polled mode, or when cleaning up after an ISR-based acquisition sequence. It is usually paired with ca_adc_isr_done() to signal that the interrupt-driven phase is complete. The typical sequence is: ca_adc_start_isr() to begin sampling, then ca_adc_hw_stop_isr() to silence the hardware interrupt, followed by ca_adc_isr_done() to finalize the driver state.

ca_adc_init.brief: Initializes the hardware ADC peripheral and configures its sampling parameters.

params.name: cfg
params.desc: Pointer to a configuration structure containing the ADC index (1-3) and the desired sample time. Passing a NULL pointer or an invalid ADC index (outside 1-3) will cause the function to return false immediately.

ca_adc_init.returns: Returns true if the hardware clock and peripheral initialization were successful. Returns false if the input configuration is invalid, the hardware clock fails to initialize, or the peripheral configuration fails.
ca_adc_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs direct hardware register manipulation to set up the ADC clock and peripheral registers. It is not thread-safe, so you must ensure that initialization happens during the system startup phase before any tasks attempt to read from the ADC. It is strictly forbidden to call this from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it performs hardware setup that may take time and is not re-entrant. A common beginner mistake is to call this function multiple times for the same ADC index without checking if it is already initialized, which can lead to unpredictable hardware states or clock configuration conflicts.
ca_adc_init.usage: This function is the mandatory first step in the ADC lifecycle. It is typically called during the system initialization sequence, immediately after hardware clocks are enabled but before any pin-specific configuration (like ca_adc_pin_init) or data acquisition occurs. In a typical application, you define a configuration structure, pass it to this function, and then proceed to configure the specific GPIO pins associated with the ADC channels. If you skip this step, subsequent calls to read ADC values will fail or return garbage data because the peripheral clock will be disabled.

ca_adc_init_isr.brief: Initializes an ADC peripheral in interrupt-driven mode with a user-defined callback function.

params.name: cfg
params.desc: Pointer to a configuration structure containing the ADC number (1-3) and sample time. Must not be NULL.

params.name: cb
params.desc: Function pointer to the callback that will be executed when the ADC conversion completes. Must not be NULL.

ca_adc_init_isr.returns: Returns true if the ADC peripheral was successfully initialized and the interrupt enabled. Returns false if the configuration pointer is NULL, the ADC number is out of range (1-3), the callback is NULL, or the hardware initialization fails.
ca_adc_init_isr.notes: This function is non-blocking and configures the hardware to trigger an interrupt upon conversion completion. It is not thread-safe by itself, so ensure it is called during system initialization or from a controlled task context. A common beginner mistake is passing a NULL callback or an invalid ADC index, which will cause the function to fail immediately. Before calling this, ensure the system clock for the ADC peripheral is managed correctly by the underlying hardware abstraction layer, as this function relies on ca_clock_hw_adc_init to prepare the peripheral.
ca_adc_init_isr.usage: This function is typically used when you need to perform non-blocking ADC sampling, allowing the CPU to perform other tasks while waiting for the hardware conversion to finish. It is usually called once during the setup phase of a specific module or via a CLI command to enable diagnostic monitoring. It is almost always paired with ca_adc_start_isr to trigger the actual conversion process after initialization is complete. Once the conversion finishes, the provided callback is executed, where you would typically read the result and potentially trigger the next conversion.

ca_adc_irq_handler.brief: Dispatches the hardware ADC interrupt to the appropriate caOS driver handler for a specific ADC peripheral.

params.name: adc_num
params.desc: The index of the ADC peripheral (e.g., 1 for ADC1, 2 for ADC2). Must match the hardware peripheral ID defined in your STM32 configuration.

ca_adc_irq_handler.notes: This function is strictly intended to be called from within the STM32 hardware interrupt vector table (the ISR). Because it is an ISR handler, it must execute as quickly as possible to avoid blocking other system interrupts or causing timing jitter in the RTOS scheduler. It is not thread-safe in the sense that it should never be called from a standard task; it is the entry point for the hardware signal itself. A common beginner mistake is to perform heavy processing or blocking operations inside the function called by this handler, which will crash the system or cause missed ADC samples. Ensure that the ADC peripheral has been properly initialized via ca_adc_start_isr before this handler is triggered, otherwise, the hardware may trigger an interrupt for an unconfigured peripheral, leading to undefined behavior.
ca_adc_irq_handler.usage: This function is used exclusively in the STM32 startup or HAL interrupt vector files (e.g., stm32f4xx_it.c). You place it inside the specific ADCx_IRQHandler function generated by the IDE. It acts as the bridge between the raw hardware interrupt and the caOS driver logic. It is typically paired with ca_adc_start_isr, which sets up the GPIO pins and triggers the hardware to begin sampling. Once the hardware completes a conversion, it fires the interrupt, which calls this handler to process the data or signal a waiting task.

ca_adc_isr_done.brief: Signals that an ADC interrupt operation is complete, releasing the ADC peripheral for further use.

params.name: adc_num
params.desc: The ADC peripheral index. Valid values are 1, 2, or 3. Values outside this range are ignored.

ca_adc_isr_done.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe because it performs a simple memory write to a status array. It is specifically designed to be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) context, as it does not use mutexes or any OS primitives that could cause a deadlock or context switch. The most common mistake is passing an invalid ADC index, which results in the function returning immediately without clearing the busy flag, effectively locking the ADC peripheral permanently.
ca_adc_isr_done.usage: This function is used in the final stage of an asynchronous ADC conversion sequence. It is typically called inside the ADC interrupt handler after the conversion result has been retrieved or stored. It pairs with ca_adc_start_isr, which sets the busy flag, and acts as the 'unlock' mechanism so that subsequent calls to ADC functions from tasks or other interrupts can proceed without being blocked by a stale 'busy' state.

ca_adc_pin_init.brief: Configures a specific microcontroller pin to function as an analog input for the ADC peripheral.

params.name: adc_num
params.desc: The identifier of the ADC peripheral (e.g., 1, 2, or 3). Must match the hardware capabilities of your specific STM32 chip.

params.name: channel
params.desc: The specific ADC channel index to be mapped to the pin. Ensure this channel is physically connected to the pin you intend to use according to the datasheet.

ca_adc_pin_init.notes: This function is a hardware abstraction layer (HAL) wrapper that configures the GPIO pin mode to 'Analog'. It is non-blocking and executes quickly, but it is not thread-safe; it should be called during the system initialization phase before the ADC is used for sampling. It is not intended to be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) as it performs hardware register configuration which should be done in a controlled environment. A common beginner mistake is calling this function before initializing the ADC peripheral itself or using an invalid channel/pin combination, which will result in the pin remaining in a digital state or causing unexpected hardware behavior.
ca_adc_pin_init.usage: This function is typically used during the system startup sequence, immediately after calling ca_adc_init(). The standard workflow is: first, define the ADC configuration structure; second, initialize the ADC peripheral with ca_adc_init(); third, call ca_adc_pin_init() to map the physical pin to the ADC channel; and finally, start reading values using ca_adc_read(). It is essential to pair this with the correct hardware pin mapping found in your STM32 reference manual to avoid reading floating or incorrect voltages.

ca_adc_read.brief: Reads the raw digital value from a specific ADC peripheral and channel.

params.name: adc_num
params.desc: The index of the ADC peripheral (e.g., 1, 2, or 3). Must be within the hardware-supported range defined by the MCU datasheet.

params.name: channel
params.desc: The specific input channel index to sample. Must correspond to a pin configured for analog input.

ca_adc_read.returns: Returns a 16-bit unsigned integer representing the raw ADC conversion result (typically 0 to 4095 for a 12-bit ADC).
ca_adc_read.notes: This function is a synchronous, blocking call that waits for the hardware conversion to complete before returning the value. It is generally not thread-safe if multiple tasks access the same ADC peripheral simultaneously, so ensure you have external synchronization if sharing resources. It is typically safe to call from an ISR if the underlying hardware driver supports it, but be aware that blocking in an ISR is bad practice as it stalls the entire system. A common beginner mistake is calling this function without first initializing the GPIO pins and the ADC peripheral using ca_adc_pin_init, which will result in reading garbage data or potentially triggering a hardware fault.
ca_adc_read.usage: This function is used to retrieve analog sensor data, such as voltage levels, potentiometers, or temperature sensors. It is typically used in a periodic loop (e.g., inside a task using ca_os_sleep) to monitor environmental changes over time. The standard workflow involves calling ca_adc_pin_init once during system startup to configure the hardware, followed by repeated calls to ca_adc_read to fetch the current state. It is often paired with mathematical scaling logic to convert the raw 12-bit value into meaningful units like millivolts or physical measurements.

ca_adc_start_isr.brief: Initiates an ADC conversion sequence on a specific hardware peripheral and channel using interrupt-driven mode.

params.name: adc_num
params.desc: The hardware ADC unit index (typically 1, 2, or 3). Must correspond to valid hardware peripherals on the STM32 chip.

params.name: channel
params.desc: The specific analog input channel index to be sampled. Must be a valid channel supported by the selected ADC unit.

ca_adc_start_isr.returns: void. This function does not provide feedback on success or failure, assuming the hardware configuration is valid.
ca_adc_start_isr.notes: This function is non-blocking, meaning it triggers the hardware and returns immediately while the conversion happens in the background. It is designed to be called after the ADC peripheral has been successfully initialized via ca_adc_init_isr. A common beginner mistake is calling this function before initializing the ADC or the GPIO pins, which will result in undefined behavior or hardware faults. Because it relies on interrupts, ensure that the global interrupt vector table is correctly configured and that the callback provided during initialization is ready to handle the incoming data.
ca_adc_start_isr.usage: This function is typically used in a setup sequence where you first initialize the ADC peripheral with a callback function, then configure the specific pin, and finally trigger the start. It is often paired with a stop function (not shown here) to manage power consumption or reconfigure the ADC for different channels. In a typical application, you call this once to begin a continuous sampling process or a single-shot conversion that will be processed asynchronously by your ISR callback.

ca_adc_stop.brief: Safely disables a specific ADC peripheral and releases associated internal resources.

params.name: adc_num
params.desc: The ADC peripheral index to stop. Valid values are 1, 2, or 3. Values outside this range will cause the function to return false immediately.

ca_adc_stop.returns: Returns true if the ADC was successfully stopped, or false if the provided adc_num is invalid or the hardware stop operation failed.
ca_adc_stop.notes: This function is not thread-safe in isolation and relies on internal state management to prevent deadlocks. It is designed to be called from task context to shut down the ADC hardware, ensuring that any pending ISR-based conversions are cancelled before the peripheral is disabled. A common mistake is calling this function while an ADC conversion is still expected to complete, which can lead to inconsistent state if the hardware is powered down abruptly. It is not intended to be called directly from an ISR, as it performs logic that assumes a stable task environment.
ca_adc_stop.usage: Use this function when you need to power down an ADC peripheral to save energy or reconfigure the pins for a different function (like GPIO or DAC). It is typically paired with ca_adc_init or ca_adc_start_isr during the teardown phase of a driver or application lifecycle. Always ensure that any tasks waiting on ADC data are notified or have timed out before calling this, as it effectively kills the active conversion process.

ca_aes_channel_decrypt.signature: i32 ca_aes_channel_decrypt(ca_aes_channel_t *ch, const u8 *cipher, u32 cipher_len, u8 **out, u32 *out_len)
ca_aes_channel_decrypt.brief: Decrypts an AES-GCM encrypted buffer using a secure channel context.

params.name: ch
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized AES channel structure. Must not be NULL.

params.name: cipher
params.desc: Pointer to the raw encrypted data buffer, including nonce, length, ciphertext, and tag.

params.name: cipher_len
params.desc: Total length of the input cipher buffer in bytes. Must be greater than AES_CH_OVERHEAD.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to a buffer pointer that will be allocated by this function to hold the decrypted data.

params.name: out_len
params.desc: Pointer to a variable that will store the length of the decrypted data.

ca_aes_channel_decrypt.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns -1 if any parameter is NULL, if the cipher length is invalid, if memory allocation fails, or if the GCM tag verification fails (indicating data tampering or incorrect key).
ca_aes_channel_decrypt.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses an internal mutex to protect the cryptographic context during the decryption process. It is a blocking function, meaning the calling task will wait if another task is currently using the same channel. It must NOT be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it performs dynamic memory allocation and mutex locking, both of which are forbidden in ISR context. A common mistake is failing to free the memory returned in the 'out' pointer using ca_aes_channel_free (or the appropriate memory deallocator) after processing the decrypted data, which leads to memory leaks.
ca_aes_channel_decrypt.usage: This function is typically used in secure communication protocols where data is received over a network or serial interface. The standard workflow involves: 1) Receiving the encrypted packet, 2) Calling ca_aes_channel_decrypt to verify the integrity and decrypt the payload, 3) Processing the decrypted data, and 4) Freeing the allocated output buffer. It is usually paired with ca_aes_channel_free to prevent memory exhaustion in long-running applications.

ca_aes_channel_deinit.brief: Safely releases and clears all memory resources associated with an AES cryptographic channel.

params.name: ch
params.desc: Pointer to the AES channel structure to be deinitialized. Must not be NULL (though the function handles NULL safely).

ca_aes_channel_deinit.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs memory cleanup by zeroing out sensitive cryptographic contexts before freeing them. It is not thread-safe; you must ensure no other threads are attempting to use the channel while this function is running, typically by holding a mutex or ensuring the task is shutting down. It is strictly forbidden to call this from an ISR because it performs dynamic memory deallocation, which can lead to heap corruption or system crashes. A common beginner mistake is to continue using the channel pointer after calling this function; always set your local channel reference to NULL immediately after deinit to prevent use-after-free bugs.
ca_aes_channel_deinit.usage: This function is used during the teardown phase of a cryptographic service or when a specific secure session is terminated. It is typically called after the channel has been closed and the associated mutex has been released. It is the final step in the lifecycle of an AES channel, following the sequence: initialization (allocation), usage (encryption/decryption), and finally deinitialization to prevent memory leaks and ensure sensitive key material is wiped from RAM.

ca_aes_channel_encrypt.signature: i32 ca_aes_channel_encrypt(ca_aes_channel_t *ch, const u8 *plain, u32 plain_len, u8 **out, u32 *out_len)
ca_aes_channel_encrypt.brief: Encrypts plaintext data using an AES-GCM channel, returning a dynamically allocated buffer containing the nonce, length, ciphertext, and tag.

params.name: ch
params.desc: Pointer to an initialized AES channel structure. Must not be NULL.

params.name: plain
params.desc: Pointer to the raw plaintext data to be encrypted. Must not be NULL.

params.name: plain_len
params.desc: Length of the plaintext in bytes.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to a buffer pointer that will be updated to point to the newly allocated encrypted data. Must not be NULL.

params.name: out_len
params.desc: Pointer to a variable that will store the total length of the allocated encrypted buffer. Must not be NULL.

ca_aes_channel_encrypt.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns -1 if any input parameter is NULL, if memory allocation fails, if key loading fails, or if the encryption process encounters an error.
ca_aes_channel_encrypt.notes: This function is blocking because it uses a mutex to ensure thread-safe access to the AES hardware context. It must NOT be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because mutex operations are not permitted in ISR context and the function performs dynamic memory allocation. The function allocates memory internally for the output buffer; the caller is responsible for freeing this memory using ca_memory_free once the encrypted data has been processed or transmitted. A common mistake is forgetting to free the returned buffer, which will lead to memory leaks in long-running embedded applications.
ca_aes_channel_encrypt.usage: This function is typically used in secure communication tasks where data needs to be encrypted before being sent over a queue or network interface. The standard workflow involves initializing the channel with ca_mutex_init, calling ca_aes_channel_encrypt to prepare the packet, sending the packet via a queue (e.g., ca_queue_static_send), and finally freeing the allocated buffer. It is designed to handle padding automatically, making it easier for developers to encrypt arbitrary lengths of data without manually managing 16-byte alignment requirements.

ca_aes_channel_free.brief: Deallocates memory previously allocated for an AES channel buffer.

params.name: p
params.desc: A pointer to the memory block to be freed. Must be a pointer previously returned by a caOS memory allocation function. Passing NULL is safe and does nothing.

ca_aes_channel_free.notes: This function is a wrapper around the system memory manager. It is non-blocking and thread-safe, meaning it can be called from different tasks without corrupting the heap. However, it is NOT safe to call from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because heap management operations often require mutexes that cannot be acquired in an interrupt context. The most common beginner mistake is 'double-freeing' memory—calling this function twice on the same pointer—which will lead to heap corruption and likely a system crash or hard fault. Always set your pointer to NULL immediately after calling this function to prevent accidental reuse.
ca_aes_channel_free.usage: This function is used to clean up dynamic memory buffers that were allocated to hold encrypted or decrypted data packets. It is typically used in error-handling paths where a transmission fails (e.g., if ca_queue_static_send fails, the buffer is no longer needed) or during the teardown phase of a communication session. It is paired with memory allocation functions; once the data has been successfully sent or processed, the buffer must be freed to prevent memory leaks, which would eventually cause the system to run out of RAM.

ca_aes_channel_init.signature: i32 ca_aes_channel_init(ca_aes_channel_t *ch, ca_aes_mode_t mode, ca_aes_keysize_t keysize, void *ks_handle, ca_aes_iv_gen_cb_t iv_cb, ca_aes_key_ratchet_cb_t ratchet_cb, void *cb_user)
ca_aes_channel_init.brief: Initializes an AES cryptographic channel structure by allocating internal contexts and setting up synchronization primitives.

params.name: ch
params.desc: Pointer to the channel structure to initialize. Must be a valid, non-NULL memory address.

params.name: mode
params.desc: The AES mode of operation (e.g., GCM, CBC).

params.name: keysize
params.desc: The size of the key (e.g., CA_AES_KEY_128, CA_AES_KEY_256).

params.name: ks_handle
params.desc: Pointer to the key storage handle or key material. Must not be NULL.

params.name: iv_cb
params.desc: Optional callback for IV generation. Pass NULL if not required.

params.name: ratchet_cb
params.desc: Optional callback for key ratcheting. Pass NULL if not required.

params.name: cb_user
params.desc: User-defined pointer passed to callbacks.

ca_aes_channel_init.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns -1 if initialization fails, typically due to NULL pointers or memory allocation failure.
ca_aes_channel_init.notes: This function is non-blocking but performs dynamic memory allocation via ca_memory_allocate, meaning it is NOT safe to call from an ISR. It initializes a mutex for thread safety, so it must be called before any other thread attempts to use the channel. A common beginner mistake is failing to check the return value; if memory allocation fails, the channel remains in an uninitialized state, and subsequent operations will cause a system crash or undefined behavior. Ensure the channel structure is not modified by other threads while this function is running.
ca_aes_channel_init.usage: This function is the mandatory first step in the AES channel lifecycle. It is typically called during system startup or when a new secure communication session is established. It pairs with subsequent encryption/decryption functions and should eventually be followed by a cleanup function (if provided by the API) to free the allocated contexts. It is often used in conjunction with keystore services to link a specific key handle to a communication channel.

ca_aes_channel_rotate.brief: Updates an AES channel's cryptographic key by executing a ratchet callback and storing the new key securely.

params.name: ch
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized AES channel structure. Must not be NULL and must have a valid ratchet_cb assigned.

ca_aes_channel_rotate.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns -1 if the channel pointer is invalid, the ratchet callback fails, the key storage access fails, or if the mutex cannot be acquired.
ca_aes_channel_rotate.notes: This function is blocking because it uses a mutex to ensure thread safety during the key rotation process. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because blocking operations are forbidden in ISR context. Before calling this, the channel must be fully initialized with a valid ratchet callback function. A common beginner mistake is failing to check the return value; if the function returns -1, the key was not updated, and the system might be using an outdated or compromised key, which could lead to decryption errors in subsequent operations.
ca_aes_channel_rotate.usage: This function is used in secure communication protocols where 'Perfect Forward Secrecy' is required, meaning keys must be rotated periodically. It is typically called after a specific number of messages have been encrypted or after a time interval has elapsed. It is usually paired with an initialization function that sets up the channel and the ratchet callback, and eventually with a cleanup function when the channel is no longer needed. The workflow is: Initialize channel -> Perform encryption/decryption -> Periodically call ca_aes_channel_rotate -> Destroy channel.

ca_aes_ctx_set_iv.brief: Sets the Initialization Vector (IV) for an AES cryptographic context.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the AES context structure. Must be initialized and configured before use.

params.name: iv
params.desc: Pointer to a 16-byte buffer containing the Initialization Vector. Must not be NULL.

ca_aes_ctx_set_iv.returns: Returns true if the IV was successfully copied into the context, false if the context is invalid, the IV pointer is NULL, or the context has not been configured.
ca_aes_ctx_set_iv.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe provided the context is not being accessed by another task simultaneously. It is safe to call from an ISR, but ensure the context pointer is valid. The most common mistake is passing an uninitialized or unconfigured context, which will cause the function to return false immediately. It does not perform any hardware-specific operations; it merely updates the internal software state of the context structure.
ca_aes_ctx_set_iv.usage: This function is used during the setup phase of an AES operation, typically after the context has been initialized via ca_aes_ctx_setup and before calling encryption or decryption functions like ca_aes_gcm_encrypt. It is essential for maintaining security in modes like GCM or CBC where a unique IV is required for every operation. In a typical sequence, you would enable access to a key slot, set the IV, perform the cryptographic operation, and then lock the slot again.

ca_aes_ctx_setup.signature: bool ca_aes_ctx_setup(ca_aes_ctx_t *ctx, ca_aes_mode_t mode, ca_aes_keysize_t keysize, const u8 *key, const u8 *iv)
ca_aes_ctx_setup.brief: Initializes an AES context structure with the specified mode, key, and initialization vector (IV).

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the AES context structure to be initialized. Must not be NULL.

params.name: mode
params.desc: The AES operation mode (e.g., CA_AES_MODE_ECB, CA_AES_MODE_CBC, CA_AES_MODE_CTR, CA_AES_MODE_GCM).

params.name: keysize
params.desc: The size of the key (CA_AES_KEY_128, CA_AES_KEY_192, or CA_AES_KEY_256).

params.name: key
params.desc: Pointer to the raw key buffer. Must not be NULL.

params.name: iv
params.desc: Pointer to the initialization vector buffer. Required for CBC, CTR, and GCM modes; can be NULL for ECB.

ca_aes_ctx_setup.returns: Returns true if the context was successfully configured, false if parameters are invalid (e.g., NULL pointers, missing IV for required modes, or unsupported key size).
ca_aes_ctx_setup.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs local memory operations to format the key and IV into the context structure. It is thread-safe in the sense that it only modifies the provided local context object, but it does not interact with the hardware AES peripheral directly. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the context pointer is valid and not shared with other tasks without proper synchronization. The most common beginner mistake is passing a NULL pointer for the IV when using modes like CBC or GCM, which will cause the function to return false immediately.
ca_aes_ctx_setup.usage: This function is the mandatory first step before performing any encryption or decryption operations. It is typically used in a sequence: first, you define a local or heap-allocated ca_aes_ctx_t structure, then you call ca_aes_ctx_setup to populate it with your security parameters, and finally, you pass that context to functions like ca_aes_encrypt or ca_aes_decrypt. It is good practice to zero out the key buffer using ca_memzero immediately after calling this function to prevent sensitive data from lingering in memory.

ca_aes_decrypt.signature: bool ca_aes_decrypt(ca_aes_ctx_t *ctx, const u8 *in, u8 *out, u32 len)
ca_aes_decrypt.brief: Decrypts a block of data using the hardware AES engine with thread-safe access.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the AES context structure. Must be initialized and configured before use; passing NULL or an unconfigured context will cause the function to return false.

params.name: in
params.desc: Pointer to the encrypted input buffer. Must not be NULL.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to the destination buffer where decrypted data will be stored. Must not be NULL and must have enough allocated space for 'len' bytes.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the data in bytes. Must be greater than 0 and a multiple of 16 (AES block size). If not a multiple of 16, the function returns false.

ca_aes_decrypt.returns: Returns true if decryption was successful, false otherwise. A false return indicates invalid parameters, unconfigured context, input length not aligned to 16 bytes, or a hardware setup failure.
ca_aes_decrypt.notes: This function is blocking because it uses a mutex to ensure exclusive access to the hardware AES peripheral. It is NOT safe to call this function from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because the mutex lock operation will cause a system hang or crash. You must ensure the context is properly initialized before calling this function. A common mistake is passing a length that is not a multiple of 16, which will cause the function to fail immediately; always ensure your buffers are padded correctly according to the AES standard.
ca_aes_decrypt.usage: This function is used when you need to recover original data from an encrypted buffer using the STM32 hardware acceleration. It is typically used in a sequence: first, you initialize the context, then you call this function to perform the decryption, and finally, you verify the output. It is often paired with ca_aes_encrypt to perform round-trip testing or to process incoming secure data packets. Because it uses a mutex, it is designed to be used in multi-threaded environments where multiple tasks might need to access the AES hardware without corrupting each other's operations.

ca_aes_ecb_selftest.brief: Performs a FIPS-197 AES-256-ECB known-answer self-test to validate the cryptographic backend.
ca_aes_ecb_selftest.returns: Returns a u32 representing the number of failed tests. A return value of 0 indicates that all tests passed successfully.
ca_aes_ecb_selftest.notes: This function is a diagnostic tool used to verify the integrity of the AES implementation. It is not intended for high-frequency use in production loops, as it performs memory-intensive operations and blocking cryptographic calculations. It is thread-safe assuming the underlying AES hardware/software backend is properly initialized. It must NOT be called from an ISR because it performs blocking operations and uses standard output for reporting. The most common mistake is calling this before the system's cryptographic subsystem or memory management has been fully initialized, which will lead to undefined behavior or system crashes.
ca_aes_ecb_selftest.usage: This function is typically used during the system boot sequence or as part of a diagnostic CLI command to ensure the hardware acceleration or software library is functioning correctly. It is often paired with other self-test functions like ca_aes_gcm_selftest or ca_sha256_selftest to provide a comprehensive health check of the security module. Developers should invoke this during the initialization phase of the application to catch hardware faults or configuration errors before the system starts processing sensitive data.

ca_aes_encrypt.signature: bool ca_aes_encrypt(ca_aes_ctx_t *ctx, const u8 *in, u8 *out, u32 len)
ca_aes_encrypt.brief: Encrypts a block of data using the hardware AES engine with thread-safe access.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the AES context structure. Must be initialized and configured before use.

params.name: in
params.desc: Pointer to the input plaintext buffer. Must not be NULL.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to the output buffer where ciphertext will be stored. Must not be NULL.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the data in bytes. Must be a non-zero multiple of 16 (AES block size).

ca_aes_encrypt.returns: Returns true if encryption was successful, false if parameters are invalid, the context is unconfigured, or the hardware processing failed.
ca_aes_encrypt.notes: This function is blocking because it uses a mutex to ensure exclusive access to the hardware AES peripheral. It is thread-safe, meaning multiple tasks can call it, but they will be queued by the mutex. It must NOT be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because mutexes cannot be locked in interrupt context. A common mistake is providing a length that is not a multiple of 16, which will cause the function to return false immediately. Ensure the context is fully initialized before calling this, otherwise the 'configured' check will fail.
ca_aes_encrypt.usage: This function is used when you need to secure data buffers before transmission or storage. It is typically used in a sequence: first, initialize the context with the key, then call ca_aes_encrypt to process the data, and finally use ca_aes_decrypt to verify or retrieve the original data. It is designed to be used in task-level code where you have enough stack space and can afford to wait for the mutex if another task is currently using the AES hardware.

ca_aes_gcm_decrypt.signature: bool ca_aes_gcm_decrypt(ca_aes_ctx_t *ctx, const u8 *aad, u32 aad_len, const u8 *in, u8 *out, u32 len, const u8 tag[AES_GCM_TAG_SIZE])
ca_aes_gcm_decrypt.brief: Decrypts data using AES-GCM and verifies the integrity tag to ensure the data has not been tampered with.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized AES context. Must be configured before use.

params.name: aad
params.desc: Pointer to Additional Authenticated Data. Can be NULL if no AAD is used.

params.name: aad_len
params.desc: Length of the AAD buffer in bytes.

params.name: in
params.desc: Pointer to the encrypted input data buffer.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to the buffer where decrypted data will be stored.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the input/output data in bytes.

params.name: tag
params.desc: The 16-byte authentication tag received with the ciphertext to verify integrity.

ca_aes_gcm_decrypt.returns: Returns true if decryption succeeded and the tag matches (integrity verified). Returns false if the context is invalid, pointers are null, or the tag verification fails.
ca_aes_gcm_decrypt.notes: This function is blocking because it uses a mutex to ensure thread-safe access to the hardware AES peripheral. It must NOT be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because mutexes cannot be acquired in interrupt context. The context must be initialized and configured prior to calling this function, or it will return false immediately. A common mistake is failing to check the return value; if the tag verification fails, the output buffer will contain untrusted data, so you must never process the 'out' buffer if the function returns false.
ca_aes_gcm_decrypt.usage: This function is typically used in secure communication channels or file storage systems where data integrity is as important as confidentiality. It is usually paired with a preceding 'ca_aes_init' and 'ca_aes_ctx_setup' to prepare the context. In a typical workflow, you receive a packet containing the ciphertext and the tag, then call this function to decrypt and verify. If it returns true, the data is safe to use; if false, the system should discard the data and potentially trigger a security alert.

ca_aes_gcm_encrypt.signature: bool ca_aes_gcm_encrypt(ca_aes_ctx_t *ctx, const u8 *aad, u32 aad_len, const u8 *in, u8 *out, u32 len, u8 tag[AES_GCM_TAG_SIZE])
ca_aes_gcm_encrypt.brief: Encrypts data using AES-GCM mode and generates an authentication tag.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to an initialized AES context. Must be configured for GCM mode.

params.name: aad
params.desc: Pointer to Additional Authenticated Data. Can be NULL if aad_len is 0.

params.name: aad_len
params.desc: Length of the AAD in bytes.

params.name: in
params.desc: Pointer to the plaintext buffer. Must be valid if len > 0.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to the output buffer for ciphertext. Must be valid if len > 0.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the plaintext/ciphertext in bytes.

params.name: tag
params.desc: Buffer to store the generated 16-byte authentication tag.

ca_aes_gcm_encrypt.returns: Returns true if encryption and tag generation succeeded, false otherwise (e.g., invalid context, null pointers, or hardware failure).
ca_aes_gcm_encrypt.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses an internal mutex to protect the hardware AES peripheral. It is a blocking function, meaning the calling task will wait if another task is currently using the AES hardware. You must NEVER call this from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because blocking inside an ISR will cause a system crash or deadlock. Ensure the context is fully initialized via ca_aes_ctx_setup before calling this. A common mistake is passing a NULL pointer for the tag buffer or failing to check the return value, which leads to using uninitialized or corrupted ciphertext.
ca_aes_gcm_encrypt.usage: This function is typically used in secure communication protocols to ensure both data confidentiality and integrity. The standard workflow is: first, initialize the context using ca_aes_ctx_setup with the correct key and nonce; second, call ca_aes_gcm_encrypt to process the data; finally, transmit the ciphertext and the generated tag to the receiver. It is often paired with ca_aes_gcm_decrypt on the receiving end to verify the tag and recover the original plaintext. Always ensure that sensitive buffers are cleared using ca_memzero after the operation is complete to prevent data leakage.

ca_aes_gcm_selftest.brief: Performs a self-test of the AES-GCM cryptographic implementation to verify software integrity.
ca_aes_gcm_selftest.returns: Returns 0 if all tests pass, or a non-zero integer representing the count of failed test cases if any errors occur.
ca_aes_gcm_selftest.notes: This function is a diagnostic tool used to ensure the cryptographic implementation is functioning correctly. It is not thread-safe and should not be called from an ISR, as it performs multiple operations and potentially heavy calculations that would block the system. A common mistake is to assume it returns a boolean true/false; it actually returns the number of failures, so a return value of 0 is the only indicator of success. Ensure the system has enough stack space before calling this, as it processes several cryptographic vectors.
ca_aes_gcm_selftest.usage: This function is typically called during the system boot sequence or as part of a diagnostic CLI command to verify the integrity of the crypto library. It is often paired with other self-test functions like ca_sha512_selftest or ca_x25519_selftest to ensure the entire security stack is operational. It is used to validate the environment before the application starts processing real encrypted data, ensuring that the underlying math is correct.

ca_aes_hw_gcm.signature: bool ca_aes_hw_gcm(ca_aes_ctx_t *ctx, bool encrypt, const u8 *aad, u32 aad_len, const u8 *in, u8 *out, u32 len, u8 *tag)
ca_aes_hw_gcm.brief: Performs hardware-accelerated AES-GCM encryption or decryption with authentication tag generation.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized AES context structure containing keys and IV.

params.name: encrypt
params.desc: True for encryption, false for decryption.

params.name: aad
params.desc: Pointer to Additional Authenticated Data (AAD). Can be NULL if aad_len is 0.

params.name: aad_len
params.desc: Length of AAD in bytes.

params.name: in
params.desc: Pointer to input data buffer. Must be valid if len > 0.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to output data buffer. Must be valid if len > 0.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of payload data in bytes.

params.name: tag
params.desc: Pointer to a 16-byte buffer where the authentication tag will be stored.

ca_aes_hw_gcm.returns: Returns true if the operation completed successfully, false if a hardware timeout occurred or parameters were invalid.
ca_aes_hw_gcm.notes: This function is a blocking call that waits for the hardware peripheral to process data. It is NOT thread-safe on its own; it must be protected by a mutex (as seen in the driver layer) to prevent concurrent access to the shared AES hardware registers. It is NOT callable from an ISR because it relies on busy-waiting loops which would hang the system if interrupts are disabled or if the hardware is busy. A common mistake is passing unaligned buffers or invalid pointers, which will cause the hardware to hang or the function to return false due to timeout. Always ensure the context is fully initialized before calling this function.
ca_aes_hw_gcm.usage: This function is used in the high-level AES driver layer to perform authenticated encryption/decryption. It is typically called after the context has been initialized with a key and IV. The standard sequence is: 1) Lock the AES mutex, 2) Call ca_aes_hw_gcm, 3) Unlock the mutex. It is used when data integrity and confidentiality are both required, such as in secure network protocols or encrypted storage. It is the core engine that powers higher-level functions like ca_aes_gcm_encrypt and ca_aes_gcm_decrypt.

ca_aes_hw_init.brief: Initializes the hardware AES cryptographic peripheral by enabling its clock in the RCC register.
ca_aes_hw_init.returns: Returns true if the hardware peripheral was successfully enabled, or false if the hardware is unsupported, disabled in configuration, or unavailable on the specific MCU model.
ca_aes_hw_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a direct register write to the RCC (Reset and Clock Control) unit. It is thread-safe in the sense that it only modifies a peripheral clock register, but it is not intended to be called repeatedly; it should be executed once during system startup. A common beginner mistake is calling this function multiple times or assuming it configures the AES engine's internal registers (like keys or IVs), which it does not. It must be called before any other AES operations are attempted, as accessing the AES peripheral registers without enabling the clock will cause a hard fault or bus error. It is safe to call from an ISR, though typically unnecessary as it is part of the system boot sequence. Note that on some architectures, a read-back of the RCC register is mandatory to ensure the write buffer is drained before subsequent peripheral access.
ca_aes_hw_init.usage: This function is typically called during the system initialization phase, specifically within the higher-level ca_aes_init() function. It acts as the hardware-level prerequisite for the AES driver. You should pair this with other initialization routines to ensure that subsequent cryptographic operations are ready for use. Once initialized, the driver is ready to accept context setups via ca_aes_ctx_setup() and perform encryption or decryption tasks using functions like ca_aes_encrypt or ca_aes_decrypt.

ca_aes_hw_process.signature: bool ca_aes_hw_process(const u8 *in, u8 *out, u32 len)
ca_aes_hw_process.brief: Processes a buffer of data through the hardware AES engine using the currently configured key and mode.

params.name: in
params.desc: Pointer to the input data buffer. Must be aligned to 4-byte boundaries for optimal performance.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to the output buffer where the encrypted/decrypted data will be stored. Must be at least 'len' bytes long.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the data in bytes. Must be a multiple of 16 (AES block size). If not a multiple, the function will fail to process the final partial block.

ca_aes_hw_process.returns: Returns true if the entire buffer was processed successfully, or false if a hardware timeout occurred or the input parameters were invalid.
ca_aes_hw_process.notes: This function is a blocking call that waits for the hardware FIFO to become ready for each 128-bit block. It is not thread-safe on its own; it relies on an external mutex (as seen in the usage context) to prevent multiple tasks from accessing the hardware simultaneously. It is not safe to call from an ISR because it uses a polling loop with a timeout, which could cause significant latency or system hangs if the hardware is busy. A common beginner mistake is passing a length that is not a multiple of 16, which will cause the function to process only complete blocks and potentially leave the output buffer partially unwritten or corrupted.
ca_aes_hw_process.usage: This function is typically used within a higher-level driver wrapper that manages resource locking. The standard sequence is: first, initialize the hardware with 'ca_aes_init', then configure the key and mode using 'ca_aes_ctx_setup', acquire a mutex to ensure exclusive access, call 'ca_aes_hw_process' to perform the actual transformation, and finally release the mutex. It is designed to be called repeatedly for large data streams, provided the mutex is held throughout the entire operation to maintain state consistency.

ca_aes_hw_setup.brief: Configures the hardware AES peripheral with the provided key, IV, and operational mode.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the AES context structure containing the key, IV, and mode settings. Must be initialized before calling this function.

params.name: encrypt
params.desc: Set to true for encryption, false for decryption. Note that decryption may trigger additional key preparation steps.

ca_aes_hw_setup.returns: Returns true if the hardware was successfully configured. Returns false if the mode is unsupported (e.g., GCM), if key preparation fails, or if the hardware is not available on the current platform.
ca_aes_hw_setup.notes: This function is non-blocking but interacts directly with hardware registers, so it is not thread-safe on its own; it must be protected by a mutex if multiple tasks access the AES peripheral. It is generally not safe to call from an ISR because it may perform complex operations like key preparation. A common beginner mistake is failing to check the return value, which leads to processing data with uninitialized or incorrect hardware settings. Ensure the AES peripheral is powered and initialized before calling this function, as it assumes the hardware is ready to accept configuration.
ca_aes_hw_setup.usage: This function is the mandatory setup step before any data processing occurs. It is typically used within a wrapper function that handles mutual exclusion, ensuring that only one task configures and uses the AES engine at a time. The standard sequence is: lock the mutex, call ca_aes_hw_setup, perform the data processing using the hardware-specific processing routine, and finally unlock the mutex. It is never used in isolation; it must always be paired with a processing function to actually perform the cryptographic operation.

ca_aes_init.brief: Initializes the AES hardware peripheral and the internal mutex required for thread-safe cryptographic operations.
ca_aes_init.returns: Returns true if both the mutex and the AES hardware were initialized successfully; returns false if the hardware initialization failed.
ca_aes_init.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called exactly once during the system startup phase, typically before any tasks are created or before any other AES functions are invoked. It is strictly non-blocking and must NOT be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it initializes a mutex, which is a kernel object that requires a running scheduler context. A common mistake is calling this function multiple times or from different tasks; doing so will re-initialize the mutex, potentially causing race conditions or memory corruption if other tasks are already waiting on that mutex.
ca_aes_init.usage: This function is the mandatory entry point for any application requiring AES encryption or decryption. It is typically called during the system initialization sequence, alongside other hardware drivers like RNG, HASH, or Flash. It must be called before any calls to ca_aes_ctx_setup or actual encryption/decryption functions, as those functions rely on the mutex initialized here to prevent concurrent access to the shared AES hardware peripheral.

ca_aes_is_hw.brief: Checks if the current hardware platform supports accelerated AES cryptographic operations.
ca_aes_is_hw.returns: Returns true if hardware-based AES acceleration (CRYP or AES peripheral) is available on the chip, false otherwise.
ca_aes_is_hw.notes: This function is a non-blocking, thread-safe query that reads compile-time definitions. It is safe to call from any context, including ISRs, because it does not perform any I/O or complex logic. It is typically used to decide whether to initialize hardware-accelerated crypto drivers or fall back to software-based implementations. A common mistake is assuming that returning true guarantees the peripheral is currently powered or clocked; you must still call the appropriate initialization functions before attempting to encrypt or decrypt data.
ca_aes_is_hw.usage: This function is used during system configuration or service initialization to determine the optimal security path. It is typically paired with ca_aes_init() to prepare the hardware for use. In a typical sequence, you check this function, and if it returns true, you proceed to call ca_aes_init() and then use functions like ca_aes_encrypt() or ca_aes_decrypt(). If it returns false, the application might need to disable hardware-dependent features or use a software-only library.

ca_arp_avail.brief: Checks if a specific IPv4 address has a corresponding MAC address already resolved in the ARP cache.

params.name: ip
params.desc: The IPv4 address to search for in the ARP table. Must be a valid 32-bit representation of an IP address.

ca_arp_avail.returns: Returns true if the IP address exists in the ARP cache and is associated with a valid MAC address; returns false if the IP is not found or the entry has expired.
ca_arp_avail.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a simple lookup in the internal ARP cache memory. It is thread-safe, meaning it can be called from multiple tasks simultaneously without corrupting the cache data. It is safe to call from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it does not perform any complex operations or wait for hardware responses. The most common mistake is assuming that a 'false' return means the device is offline; it simply means the ARP entry is not currently cached, so you may need to trigger a network request to resolve it.
ca_arp_avail.usage: This function is typically used as a pre-check before attempting to send data to a specific network node to avoid unnecessary ARP resolution delays. It is often paired with ca_arp_find() when you need to retrieve the actual MAC address after confirming its availability. Developers use this in the application layer to verify if a target device is 'known' to the stack before initiating a communication sequence, ensuring that the network stack is ready to transmit packets immediately.

ca_arp_confirm.brief: Updates the ARP cache entry for a specific IP address to mark it as valid and fresh.

params.name: ip
params.desc: The IPv4 address whose ARP cache entry needs to be confirmed or refreshed.

ca_arp_confirm.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses a mutex to protect the internal ARP cache table during write operations. It is not intended to be called from an ISR because it uses mutexes, which can cause blocking and priority inversion. The function first performs a quick read check; if the entry is already valid and recent, it returns immediately to save processing time. A common mistake is calling this function too frequently in a tight loop, which can lead to unnecessary mutex contention and performance degradation in the network stack.
ca_arp_confirm.usage: This function is typically used by the network stack when an ARP reply is received or when a packet is successfully transmitted to a known destination, confirming that the MAC address mapping is still correct. It is often paired with ca_arp_learn when a new mapping is discovered, or ca_arp_lookup when checking if a mapping exists. In a typical lifecycle, the system uses ca_arp_service_init to start the ARP service, then uses ca_arp_confirm to maintain the health of the cache entries during active communication.

ca_arp_del.brief: Removes a specific entry from the ARP cache by its index.

params.name: idx
params.desc: The zero-based index of the active ARP entry to remove. Valid values range from 0 to (ARP_CACHE_SIZE - 1). Providing an index higher than the number of currently active entries will result in a failure.

ca_arp_del.returns: Returns true if the entry at the specified index was found and successfully invalidated. Returns false if the index is out of range or if no active entry exists at that position.
ca_arp_del.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses a mutex to protect the shared ARP cache array from concurrent access. It is a blocking function; if another thread currently holds the mutex, the calling thread will be suspended until the mutex is released. You must NEVER call this function from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because blocking operations are strictly forbidden in ISR context and will cause system instability or hard faults. A common beginner mistake is assuming the index refers to a static memory address rather than the dynamic count of currently active entries.
ca_arp_del.usage: This function is typically used in command-line interfaces (CLI) or network management tasks where a user or system process needs to clear stale or incorrect ARP mappings. It is usually paired with a display function that lists current entries so the user knows which index to target. The typical sequence is: first, call a function to list or iterate through the cache to identify the target index, then call ca_arp_del(idx) to remove it, and finally verify the result via the return boolean to provide feedback to the user.

ca_arp_del_ip.brief: Removes a specific IPv4 address entry from the internal ARP cache table.

params.name: ip
params.desc: The IPv4 address structure to search for and remove. Ensure the structure is correctly populated before calling.

ca_arp_del_ip.returns: Returns true if the IP address was found and successfully removed from the cache, or false if the IP address did not exist in the cache.
ca_arp_del_ip.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses a mutex (s_cache_mtx) to protect the shared ARP cache array from concurrent access. It is a blocking function; if another thread currently holds the mutex, the calling thread will wait until it is released. You must NOT call this function from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because blocking operations are strictly forbidden in ISRs and will cause system instability or deadlocks. A common mistake is assuming the cache is updated instantly across all network tasks; always check the return value to confirm if the entry was actually present before assuming it was deleted.
ca_arp_del_ip.usage: This function is typically used in network management interfaces, such as a Command Line Interface (CLI), to manually clear stale or incorrect ARP entries. It is usually paired with parsing functions like ca_parse_ipv4 to convert user input strings into the required ca_ipv4_t format. In a typical lifecycle, you would use this when a network administrator needs to force a re-discovery of a device's MAC address by clearing its existing ARP mapping, ensuring the system does not use outdated cached information.

ca_arp_dump.brief: Prints the current contents of the ARP cache to the system CLI for debugging purposes.
ca_arp_dump.notes: This function is a blocking operation because it acquires a mutex (s_cache_mtx) to ensure data consistency while reading the cache. It is NOT safe to call from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because mutexes are designed for thread synchronization and can cause the system to hang or trigger an assertion if locked in an ISR context. The function creates a local snapshot of the cache to minimize the time the mutex is held, which is a good practice to prevent blocking other network tasks for too long. A common beginner mistake is calling this function inside a high-frequency loop or an ISR, which will lead to system instability or deadlocks.
ca_arp_dump.usage: This function is intended for diagnostic use, typically triggered by a user command via the Command Line Interface (CLI). It is usually paired with other maintenance functions like ca_arp_flush() or specific entry deletion functions. Developers use this to verify that the network stack is correctly resolving IP addresses to MAC addresses and to check if entries are expiring as expected. It should be invoked only when the user explicitly requests status information, as it performs significant string formatting and output operations that consume CPU cycles.

ca_arp_find.brief: Searches the local ARP cache for a MAC address associated with a specific IPv4 address.

params.name: ip
params.desc: The target IPv4 address to look up in the cache. Must be a valid ca_ipv4_t structure.

params.name: mac_out
params.desc: A pointer to a ca_mac_t structure where the result will be stored if found. Can be NULL if you only want to check existence.

ca_arp_find.returns: Returns true if the IP address exists in the cache and the MAC was successfully copied to mac_out. Returns false if the IP is not found in the cache or if the entry is marked as invalid.
ca_arp_find.notes: This function is blocking because it uses a mutex (ca_mutex_lock) to ensure thread safety while reading the shared ARP cache table. Because it uses a mutex, it must NEVER be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR), as doing so will cause a system deadlock or kernel panic. Before calling this, ensure the network stack and ARP service have been initialized, otherwise the cache will be empty. A common beginner mistake is assuming this function will trigger a network request; it does not. It only checks the local memory table, so if it returns false, you must manually trigger a resolution process like ca_arp_resolve.
ca_arp_find.usage: This function is typically used as the first step in a network communication sequence to avoid unnecessary ARP broadcast traffic. You call it before sending a packet to check if the destination hardware address is already known. If it returns true, you proceed with the transmission using the retrieved MAC. If it returns false, you typically pair it with ca_arp_resolve to perform a network-level lookup, wait for the response, and then proceed with your communication.

ca_arp_flush.brief: Clears all entries in the ARP cache by marking them as invalid.
ca_arp_flush.returns: This function returns void and does not provide a status code.
ca_arp_flush.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses a mutex (s_cache_mtx) to protect the shared ARP cache array during the clearing process. It is a blocking function, meaning if another thread currently holds the mutex, the calling thread will be suspended until the mutex is released. You must NOT call this function from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because blocking operations are strictly forbidden in ISRs and will cause system instability or hard faults. A common mistake is assuming this function resets the hardware network interface; it only clears the software-level mapping table, so the device will need to re-resolve IP-to-MAC addresses via ARP requests after this call.
ca_arp_flush.usage: This function is typically used during network stack resets, interface re-initialization, or when a user explicitly requests a cache clear via a CLI command to resolve connectivity issues caused by stale ARP entries. It is often paired with ca_arp_dump() to verify the state of the cache before and after the flush. In a typical lifecycle, it is called when the network link status changes or when the system detects a potential IP address conflict that requires forcing a fresh ARP discovery cycle.

ca_arp_learn.brief: Updates the ARP cache with a new IP-to-MAC mapping, triggering any pending network tasks waiting for this resolution.

params.name: ip
params.desc: The IPv4 address to associate with the provided MAC address.

params.name: mac
params.desc: The hardware MAC address to be stored in the cache.

ca_arp_learn.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses an internal mutex to protect the ARP cache during write operations. It is a blocking function because it may wait for the cache mutex to become available. You must NEVER call this function from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because blocking in an ISR will cause system instability or a hard fault. The most common beginner mistake is calling this from an Ethernet RX interrupt handler; instead, offload the processing to a task or use a deferred procedure call mechanism.
ca_arp_learn.usage: This function is typically used by the network stack's input processing layer when an ARP reply or a gratuitous ARP packet is received. It is often paired with ca_arp_lookup or ca_arp_find to check if an entry already exists before attempting to learn a new one. In a typical sequence, the system receives a frame, extracts the IP and MAC, and calls ca_arp_learn to update the local routing table, which subsequently allows pending packets (blocked on resolution) to be sent out.

ca_arp_lookup.brief: Attempts to retrieve the MAC address for a given IPv4 address from the ARP cache.

params.name: ip
params.desc: The target IPv4 address to resolve.

params.name: mac_out
params.desc: Pointer to a buffer where the resolved MAC address will be stored. Can be NULL if you only want to check existence.

ca_arp_lookup.returns: Returns true if the MAC address was found in the cache and copied to mac_out. Returns false if the address is not in the cache, triggering an ARP resolution request.
ca_arp_lookup.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it performs a simple cache lookup. It is safe to call from an ISR, but note that it does not wait for the network to respond; it merely initiates an ARP request if the entry is missing. A common mistake is assuming that a 'false' return means the IP is unreachable; it simply means the MAC is not currently cached. You must ensure the ARP service is initialized via ca_arp_service_init before using this function.
ca_arp_lookup.usage: This function is typically used in the network stack's transmission path to map an IP address to a hardware MAC address before sending an Ethernet frame. It is often paired with ca_route_lookup to determine the next-hop IP, followed by ca_arp_lookup to get the destination MAC. If it returns false, the packet should be queued or dropped while the ARP resolution process completes in the background.

ca_arp_resolve.signature: bool ca_arp_resolve(ca_ipv4_t ip, ca_mac_t *mac_out, u32 timeout_ms)
ca_arp_resolve.brief: Resolves an IPv4 address to a MAC address using the ARP protocol with a blocking timeout.

params.name: ip
params.desc: The target IPv4 address to resolve.

params.name: mac_out
params.desc: Pointer to a buffer where the resolved MAC address will be stored. Must be a valid memory address.

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time in milliseconds to wait for the ARP response. Must be greater than the internal ARP retry cycle to avoid race conditions.

ca_arp_resolve.returns: Returns true if the MAC address was successfully resolved and copied to mac_out. Returns false if the resolution failed, the timeout expired, or if no internal ARP slots were available.
ca_arp_resolve.notes: This function is blocking; it will suspend the calling thread until the ARP process completes or the timeout is reached. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it uses mutexes and semaphores that require thread context. A common mistake is providing a timeout that is too short; if the timeout is shorter than the time required for the ARP request/retry cycle, the function will return false even if the device is reachable. Ensure the system network stack is initialized before calling this, as it relies on an internal ARP task to process the request queue.
ca_arp_resolve.usage: This function is typically used when preparing to send an Ethernet frame to a specific IP address. It is often paired with routing functions, such as checking a routing table to find the next hop IP, and then calling this function to resolve that IP into a hardware MAC address. In a typical application flow, you would call this before attempting to transmit data, ensuring the destination hardware address is known. If it returns false, the application should handle the failure by dropping the packet or notifying the user, as communication with that IP is currently impossible.

ca_arp_send_garp.brief: Sends a Gratuitous ARP (GARP) packet to announce the device's IP address on the network.
ca_arp_send_garp.returns: Returns true if the GARP packet was successfully queued for transmission, false if the IP is not set, buffer allocation failed, or the packet construction failed.
ca_arp_send_garp.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it relies on the internal network buffer management system. It is not intended to be called from an ISR because it performs memory allocation via ca_net_buf_alloc. A common beginner mistake is calling this function before the network stack is fully initialized or before the link is confirmed to be up, which will result in the function returning false or the packet being dropped by the hardware. Ensure that the local IP address has been assigned (either via static configuration or DHCP) before calling this, otherwise, the function will immediately return false.
ca_arp_send_garp.usage: This function is typically used during the network initialization sequence to announce the device's presence to other nodes on the local network segment. It is often paired with ca_net_proto_init to set up the stack and ca_eth_link_poll to ensure the physical link is active. Developers call this after the IP address is assigned to prevent IP conflicts and to update the ARP tables of other devices on the network. It is also used when a DHCP lease is renewed or when the network interface is reset to ensure the network topology remains consistent.

ca_arp_service_init.brief: Initializes the ARP service internal structures, mutexes, and semaphores required for network address resolution.

params.name: local_mac
params.desc: The 6-byte hardware MAC address assigned to the device interface. Must be a valid, unique MAC address.

params.name: local_ip
params.desc: The initial IPv4 address for the interface. Can be set to 0.0.0.0 if using DHCP to obtain an address later.
