ca_arp_service_init.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called exactly once during the system initialization phase, typically before the RTOS scheduler starts or before any network tasks are spawned. It performs critical setup of mutexes and semaphores; calling it while the network stack is already active will corrupt the internal state, leading to unpredictable behavior or system crashes. It is strictly forbidden to call this function from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it performs blocking-style initialization operations that are not ISR-safe. A common mistake is to call this function multiple times or after the network stack has already begun processing packets, which will reset the ARP cache and cause active connections to drop.
ca_arp_service_init.usage: This function is the mandatory entry point for the ARP subsystem. It is typically called within the main initialization sequence, often immediately after the Ethernet hardware driver is initialized and the network interface is registered via ca_net_init. It is frequently paired with ca_arp_service_start, which enables the background processing of ARP requests. In dynamic network environments, it is common to initialize the service with a zeroed IP address (0.0.0.0) and later update the IP configuration once a DHCP server provides a valid lease.

ca_arp_service_start.brief: Initializes and launches the background ARP service task within the caOS scheduler.
ca_arp_service_start.notes: This function is non-blocking; it simply registers a new job with the caOS scheduler and returns immediately. It is not thread-safe to call this from an ISR, as it interacts with the OS task management system. You must ensure that the ARP service has been properly initialized (e.g., via ca_arp_service_init) before calling this, otherwise the task may attempt to operate on uninitialized memory or invalid network configurations. A common beginner mistake is calling this function multiple times; doing so will attempt to spawn multiple instances of the ARP task, which will lead to unpredictable network behavior and potential system instability.
ca_arp_service_start.usage: This function is typically called once during the system startup phase inside ca_os_main, alongside other network service starters like DHCP or UDP servers. It acts as the 'enable' switch for the ARP protocol stack, allowing the device to resolve IP addresses to MAC addresses. It is almost always preceded by a configuration step where the local IP and MAC addresses are set, ensuring the ARP service has the necessary identity to communicate on the network. Once started, the ARP service runs as a background task, handling incoming ARP requests and maintaining the ARP cache automatically.

ca_arp_service_update_local_ip.brief: Updates the local IPv4 address used by the ARP service to resolve hardware addresses.

params.name: local_ip
params.desc: A structure containing the 4-byte representation of the new local IP address. Must be a valid IPv4 address; passing an uninitialized or zeroed structure may cause ARP resolution failures.

ca_arp_service_update_local_ip.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately as it performs a simple memory assignment. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs an atomic write to a static variable, but it does not use mutexes, meaning it should be called when the network configuration is stable to avoid race conditions during packet processing. It is safe to call from an ISR, though this is rarely necessary. The most common beginner mistake is calling this function before the ARP service has been initialized or while the network stack is actively processing traffic, which could lead to a momentary inconsistency in ARP replies.
ca_arp_service_update_local_ip.usage: This function is typically used during the network initialization phase or when a DHCP client receives a new IP address lease. It is part of a sequence where the application sets the local IP across multiple layers: first in the core network protocol stack, then in the UDP/TCP server modules, and finally in the ARP service to ensure that outgoing ARP requests use the correct source IP. It is usually paired with functions that configure the network interface to ensure the entire stack is synchronized with the new network identity.

ca_arp_set.brief: Updates or adds an entry in the ARP cache and notifies any tasks waiting for that specific IP address.

params.name: ip
params.desc: The IPv4 address structure to associate with the MAC address. Must be a valid IPv4 representation.

params.name: mac
params.desc: The 6-byte MAC address structure to store in the cache.

ca_arp_set.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses a mutex to protect the internal cache array. It is a blocking operation because it acquires a mutex; therefore, it must NEVER be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR), as this could lead to system deadlocks or crashes. The function implements an LRU (Least Recently Used) replacement policy: if the cache is full and the IP is not found, it overwrites the oldest entry. A common mistake is calling this function from a high-priority interrupt context when processing incoming network packets; ensure that the network stack architecture offloads this to a task context if necessary.
ca_arp_set.usage: This function is the primary mechanism for the network stack to 'learn' the mapping between IP and MAC addresses. It is typically called when an ARP reply is received or when a manual entry is added via a CLI command. It is often paired with ca_sem_post to wake up tasks that were blocked waiting for an ARP resolution to complete. In the network stack lifecycle, it is used during the packet parsing phase to ensure the ARP table remains current, allowing subsequent outgoing packets to be routed correctly without repeated ARP requests.

ca_barrier_init.brief: Initializes a synchronization barrier object that forces a specific number of threads to wait until all have reached a common point.

params.name: b
params.desc: Pointer to the barrier structure to be initialized. Must be allocated in memory accessible by the RTOS.

params.name: count
params.desc: The number of threads that must call the wait function before any are allowed to proceed. Must be greater than 0.

ca_barrier_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs the setup of internal structures like the wait queue and spinlock. It is not thread-safe if called while other threads are actively using the same barrier, so it must be called during the system initialization phase before any worker threads are spawned. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. A common beginner mistake is to initialize the barrier with a count of 0 or to re-initialize it while threads are already blocked on it, which will lead to undefined behavior or system deadlocks.
ca_barrier_init.usage: The barrier is typically used in parallel processing scenarios where multiple worker threads must synchronize their progress before moving to the next phase of a task. You initialize the barrier once during the system setup phase, then pass the pointer to the worker threads. It is usually paired with ca_barrier_wait that threads call to pause execution until the 'count' threshold is met. After the barrier is no longer needed, ensure no threads are still waiting on it before deallocating the memory.

ca_barrier_wait.brief: Synchronizes multiple threads at a specific point by blocking them until a predefined number of threads have arrived.

params.name: b
params.desc: Pointer to an initialized ca_barrier_t structure. Must be properly allocated and initialized via ca_barrier_init before use.

ca_barrier_wait.returns: Returns true only for the last thread that reaches the barrier (the one that triggers the release). Returns false for all other threads that arrive earlier and are subsequently blocked.
ca_barrier_wait.notes: This function is blocking; threads that arrive before the count is met will be suspended and removed from the CPU scheduler until the barrier is released. It is NOT safe to call this function from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it performs thread context switching and blocking operations. The function uses an internal spinlock to ensure thread safety during the increment of the arrival counter. A common beginner mistake is to assume all threads continue execution simultaneously; in reality, the threads are woken up by the scheduler, and their order of resumption depends on the scheduler's priority policy. Ensure the barrier count is correctly set during initialization, otherwise, threads may block indefinitely if the count is never reached.
ca_barrier_wait.usage: The barrier is typically used in parallel processing scenarios where multiple worker threads must complete a specific stage of computation before moving to the next phase. The typical sequence is: initialize the barrier with a specific count using ca_barrier_init, spawn worker threads, have each worker perform its task, and then call ca_barrier_wait. The thread that receives 'true' is often designated as the 'coordinator' to perform cleanup, log progress, or signal a main control thread that the phase is complete. After the barrier is released, all threads proceed to the next block of code, effectively synchronizing the execution flow across the system.

ca_bkp_count.brief: Returns the total number of available hardware backup registers on the current device.
ca_bkp_count.returns: A u32 value representing the count of available backup registers. Returns 0 if the hardware abstraction layer is not initialized or if the device lacks backup register support.
ca_bkp_count.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it typically performs a simple read of a hardware-defined constant or register. It is safe to call from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it does not involve complex OS primitives or blocking operations. The most common beginner mistake is assuming the returned count is zero-indexed; if the function returns 16, the valid register indices are 0 through 15. Always ensure the system hardware abstraction layer is initialized before relying on this value.
ca_bkp_count.usage: This function is used to determine the bounds for data storage in non-volatile backup registers, which persist across system resets. It is typically paired with ca_bkp_write and ca_bkp_read to implement a safe indexing strategy. Developers use it to prevent 'out-of-bounds' access errors when writing status flags or error codes that must survive a reboot. It is often called during system initialization or within an emergency callback (like a watchdog reset handler) to log diagnostic information.

ca_bkp_hw_count.brief: Returns the total number of hardware backup registers available on the current STM32 microcontroller.
ca_bkp_hw_count.returns: An unsigned 32-bit integer representing the count of available backup registers (e.g., 10, 20, or 32 depending on the specific STM32 series).
ca_bkp_hw_count.notes: This function is a hardware abstraction layer (HAL) utility that provides the limit for backup register indexing. It is non-blocking, thread-safe, and safe to call from an ISR because it simply returns a constant value defined at compile-time for the specific target hardware. The most common mistake is assuming a fixed number of registers across different STM32 families; always use this function to determine the limit dynamically rather than hardcoding values like 10 or 32, which will cause out-of-bounds access on different chips.
ca_bkp_hw_count.usage: This function is typically used as a boundary check before performing read or write operations on backup registers. It is usually paired with ca_bkp_read and ca_bkp_write to ensure that the index provided by the application logic does not exceed the physical hardware capacity. By using this function, your code remains portable across different STM32 series (e.g., F1, F4, H7) without requiring manual adjustments to array bounds or loop limits.

ca_bkp_hw_read.brief: Reads a 32-bit value directly from a hardware backup register at the specified index.

params.name: idx
params.desc: The index of the backup register to read. Must be less than the value returned by ca_bkp_count().

ca_bkp_hw_read.returns: The 32-bit value stored in the specified hardware backup register. If the index is out of bounds, the behavior is undefined (typically resulting in a memory access fault).
ca_bkp_hw_read.notes: This function is a low-level hardware abstraction layer (HAL) call and does not perform any bounds checking; it is intended to be called by the higher-level ca_bkp_read() function. It is non-blocking and executes in constant time, making it safe to call from ISRs or critical sections. Because it accesses hardware registers directly, ensure the backup domain is properly initialized and powered before use. A common beginner mistake is calling this function directly instead of using the safer ca_bkp_read() wrapper, which handles index validation.
ca_bkp_hw_read.usage: This function is used to retrieve persistent data stored in the STM32 backup domain, which survives system resets. It is typically used in a sequence where the application first checks the number of available registers using ca_bkp_count(), then reads specific indices to restore system state or configuration flags after a reboot. It is paired with ca_bkp_write() for data persistence and is often used during the system initialization phase to check for 'magic numbers' that indicate if the device has been previously configured.

ca_bkp_hw_sram_open.brief: Initializes the hardware backup SRAM domain and returns a pointer to its base address.
ca_bkp_hw_sram_open.returns: Returns a pointer (u8 *) to the start of the Backup SRAM memory region on success. Returns NULL if the hardware platform does not support Backup SRAM (e.g., F1xx series).
ca_bkp_hw_sram_open.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should be called during system initialization before any tasks attempt to access the backup memory. It performs low-level register manipulation to enable the power and clock domains required for the SRAM to persist data across resets. It is not intended to be called from an ISR, as it performs hardware configuration that should be done in a controlled, synchronous manner. A common mistake is assuming the memory is ready immediately after power-on without calling this function; failing to call it will result in a hard fault or bus error when attempting to access the memory address.
ca_bkp_hw_sram_open.usage: This function is typically used by the internal backup driver to lazily initialize the memory region upon the first request. It is paired with ca_bkp_sram_read and ca_bkp_sram_write to manage persistent data. Developers should check the return value against NULL before dereferencing the pointer to ensure the current hardware target actually supports this feature.

ca_bkp_hw_sram_retain.brief: Enables the backup regulator to maintain power to the Backup SRAM during low-power modes (Standby/VBAT).
ca_bkp_hw_sram_retain.returns: Returns true if the backup regulator is successfully enabled and ready, false if the hardware does not support it or if the regulator failed to stabilize within the timeout period.
ca_bkp_hw_sram_retain.notes: This function is non-blocking in some architectures (U5) but uses a busy-wait loop in others (H7, H5, F4, F7) to verify the regulator's readiness. It is generally thread-safe as it performs atomic register modifications, but it should be called during system initialization before entering low-power states. A common beginner mistake is assuming that calling this function automatically preserves all RAM; it only preserves the specific Backup SRAM region. If the hardware does not support Backup SRAM (like F1), this function will always return false, so always check the return value before assuming data persistence.
ca_bkp_hw_sram_retain.usage: This function is typically used during the system power-up sequence or before entering a deep sleep mode where the main power rail is cut. It is usually paired with ca_bkp_sram_write to store critical data before sleep and ca_bkp_sram_read to retrieve it after a wake-up event. Developers should call this early in the application lifecycle to ensure the hardware state is prepared for potential power loss scenarios.

ca_bkp_hw_sram_size.brief: Returns the total size in bytes of the hardware-specific Backup SRAM available on the current MCU.
ca_bkp_hw_sram_size.returns: Returns a u32 representing the size in bytes. A return value of 0 indicates that the specific MCU model does not have Backup SRAM hardware support.
ca_bkp_hw_sram_size.notes: This function is a hardware abstraction layer (HAL) utility that provides compile-time or platform-specific information about the available non-volatile memory region. It is non-blocking, thread-safe, and safe to call from an ISR because it simply returns a constant value defined by the hardware configuration. The most common mistake is assuming that all STM32 variants have the same amount of Backup SRAM; always check the return value before attempting to allocate or access memory buffers to avoid out-of-bounds access or null pointer dereferences.
ca_bkp_hw_sram_size.usage: This function is typically used during the initialization phase of a driver or a persistent data storage module to determine if the Backup SRAM is available for use. It is often paired with memory management functions to verify if the system can support persistent data retention across resets. Developers use this to dynamically size buffers or to decide whether to fallback to other storage mechanisms like internal Flash or external EEPROM if the returned size is 0.

ca_bkp_hw_write.brief: Unlocks the hardware backup domain and writes a value to a specific backup register index.

params.name: idx
params.desc: The index of the backup register to write. Must be within the valid range defined by the hardware (check ca_bkp_count()).

params.name: value
params.desc: The 32-bit data value to be stored in the register.

ca_bkp_hw_write.notes: This function is a low-level hardware access routine. It performs a 'write-unlock' sequence on the Power Control (PWR) register to allow modification of the backup domain, which is protected by default to prevent accidental corruption. It is not thread-safe; if multiple tasks attempt to write to backup registers simultaneously, you must wrap this call in a mutex or scheduler lock. It is generally safe to call from an ISR, but be aware that it performs a direct register write which is blocking in terms of CPU cycles. The most common mistake is passing an index that exceeds the hardware's available register count, which can lead to memory corruption or hard faults.
ca_bkp_hw_write.usage: This function is typically used to persist small amounts of configuration data or state across system resets. It is usually paired with ca_bkp_read() to retrieve the data after a reboot. In a typical application, you would first verify the index using ca_bkp_count(), then use ca_bkp_write() to save your data. Because the backup domain is battery-backed, this is the standard way to store 'non-volatile' flags that must survive a power cycle without writing to the main Flash memory.

ca_bkp_read.brief: Reads a 32-bit value from the non-volatile backup register at the specified index.

params.name: idx
params.desc: The index of the backup register to read. Must be less than the value returned by ca_bkp_count().

ca_bkp_read.returns: The 32-bit value stored in the backup register if the index is valid; returns 0 if the index is out of range.
ca_bkp_read.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it performs a direct hardware read. It is safe to call from an ISR because it does not involve complex OS primitives or waiting. The most common mistake is assuming that a return value of 0 means the register contains 0; since 0 is also returned for invalid indices, you must ensure your index is always within the bounds provided by ca_bkp_count() before calling this function.
ca_bkp_read.usage: This function is typically used to persist system state across device resets, such as boot flags, error codes, or trial status markers. It is often paired with ca_bkp_write() to update the state and ca_bkp_count() to verify index bounds. In a typical lifecycle, you read the value during system initialization to decide the boot path, and update it during runtime when a state transition occurs (e.g., confirming a firmware update).

ca_bkp_sram_read.signature: bool ca_bkp_sram_read(u32 off, void *dst, u32 len)
ca_bkp_sram_read.brief: Reads a block of data from the Backup SRAM memory area.

params.name: off
params.desc: The starting byte offset within the Backup SRAM to begin reading from.

params.name: dst
params.desc: Pointer to the destination buffer where the read data will be stored. Must not be NULL.

params.name: len
params.desc: The number of bytes to read. The sum of off and len must not exceed the total Backup SRAM size.

ca_bkp_sram_read.returns: Returns true if the read operation was successful. Returns false if the parameters are invalid (e.g., NULL pointer, out-of-bounds access, or if the requested length exceeds the available memory).
ca_bkp_sram_read.notes: This function is a synchronous, blocking operation that copies data directly from the hardware Backup SRAM to your provided buffer. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs a simple memory copy, but it does not implement internal locking for concurrent access to the same memory region; if multiple tasks access the same Backup SRAM offsets, you must manage synchronization externally. It is safe to call from an ISR, as it performs no blocking OS primitives, but keep in mind that large read operations will consume CPU cycles and increase interrupt latency. The most common mistake is failing to check the return value, which leads to processing uninitialized or garbage data when the read fails due to an out-of-bounds offset.
ca_bkp_sram_read.usage: This function is typically used to retrieve persistent configuration data, state flags, or diagnostic logs that must survive a system reset. It is often paired with ca_bkp_sram_size to determine the memory boundaries before reading, and ca_bkp_sram_write to save data. In a typical lifecycle, you would call ca_bkp_sram_size to verify the hardware is available, then perform one or more ca_bkp_sram_read calls to restore the application state during the system initialization phase.

ca_bkp_sram_retain.brief: Checks if the Backup SRAM is configured to retain data during low-power Standby or VBAT modes.
ca_bkp_sram_retain.returns: Returns true if the hardware supports and is configured for SRAM retention, false if the regulator is off or the hardware does not support this feature.
ca_bkp_sram_retain.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe. It does not require complex initialization, but it relies on the underlying hardware support for Backup SRAM. It is safe to call from any context, including ISRs, as it performs a simple register check. A common mistake is assuming that data in Backup SRAM is automatically preserved across all power states; you must verify this function returns true to ensure your data will survive a transition to Standby mode.
ca_bkp_sram_retain.usage: Use this function when your application needs to store critical state information that must persist even if the main power supply is removed or the device enters a deep sleep state. It is typically used in a diagnostic or initialization sequence, often paired with ca_bkp_sram_size to determine how much space is available, and ca_bkp_sram_write or ca_bkp_sram_read to manage the actual data storage.

ca_bkp_sram_size.brief: Returns the total size in bytes of the available Backup SRAM memory.
ca_bkp_sram_size.returns: Returns a u32 representing the size in bytes. Returns 0 if no Backup SRAM is available or if the hardware feature is disabled.
ca_bkp_sram_size.notes: This function is thread-safe and non-blocking. It can be safely called from an ISR, as it simply queries the hardware configuration or a cached size value. The most common mistake is assuming that a non-zero return value guarantees that the memory is currently writable; you must still ensure the Backup SRAM domain is powered and unlocked (via hardware-specific registers) before attempting write operations. It does not perform any initialization itself, but it is often used as a guard condition before calling ca_bkp_sram_write.
ca_bkp_sram_size.usage: Use this function to determine the memory capacity before performing bulk operations like saving system state, logs, or calibration data to the Backup SRAM. It is typically used in a sequence: first check the size with ca_bkp_sram_size, then allocate a buffer if necessary, and finally use ca_bkp_sram_write to commit data. It is essential for writing robust code that adapts to different STM32 variants, some of which may have different Backup SRAM sizes or none at all.

ca_bkp_sram_write.signature: bool ca_bkp_sram_write(u32 off, const void *src, u32 len)
ca_bkp_sram_write.brief: Writes data to the Backup SRAM, handling word-alignment and ECC requirements automatically.

params.name: off
params.desc: The byte offset within the Backup SRAM where writing begins. Must be within [0, ca_bkp_sram_size() - 1].

params.name: src
params.desc: Pointer to the source buffer containing the data to be written. Must not be NULL.

params.name: len
params.desc: Number of bytes to write. The sum of off + len must not exceed the total Backup SRAM size.

ca_bkp_sram_write.returns: Returns true if the write operation was successful. Returns false if parameters are invalid (e.g., NULL pointer, out-of-bounds access, or if Backup SRAM is unavailable).
ca_bkp_sram_write.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should not be called from an ISR. It performs a read-modify-write operation to handle unaligned access, which is critical because Backup SRAM on many STM32 chips (like the H7) uses ECC logic that requires full 32-bit word writes to maintain data integrity. If you attempt to write partial words without this function, a system reset could corrupt the surrounding bytes in the same word. The function is blocking, meaning it will not return until the entire memory copy is complete.
ca_bkp_sram_write.usage: Use this function when you need to persist small amounts of configuration data or state across system resets. It is typically used in conjunction with ca_bkp_sram_size() to verify memory bounds before writing. In a typical lifecycle, you would initialize your data, call ca_bkp_sram_write() to save it, and later use ca_bkp_sram_read() to retrieve it after a reboot. Always ensure the offset and length are validated against the total size to prevent memory corruption.

ca_bkp_write.brief: Writes a 32-bit value to a specific index in the non-volatile backup memory.

params.name: idx
params.desc: The index of the backup register to write. Must be less than the value returned by ca_bkp_count().

params.name: value
params.desc: The 32-bit data to store in the backup register.

ca_bkp_write.returns: Returns true if the write operation was successful (index was valid). Returns false if the index is out of range, indicating the write was ignored.
ca_bkp_write.notes: This function is a wrapper for hardware-specific backup registers, which are typically preserved across system resets. It is not thread-safe by default, so ensure that multiple tasks do not attempt to write to the same index simultaneously without external synchronization. It is generally safe to call from an ISR if the underlying hardware access is atomic, but you should verify your specific hardware implementation. The most common mistake is passing an index that exceeds the hardware limit, which silently fails; always validate your index or use constants defined by the system.
ca_bkp_write.usage: This function is primarily used to persist system state, boot flags, or diagnostic markers that must survive a reboot. It is often paired with ca_bkp_read() to retrieve the stored value upon system startup. In bootloader scenarios, it is used to confirm successful image updates or to signal state transitions between the application and the bootloader. Always check the return value if your application logic depends on the persistence of the data.

ca_blake2s.signature: bool ca_blake2s(ca_blake2s_ctx_t *ctx, u8 *out, u32 outlen, const u8 *in, u32 len, const u8 *key, u32 keylen)
ca_blake2s.brief: Performs a complete BLAKE2s cryptographic hash operation in a single call.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the context structure. Must be allocated and valid.

params.name: out
params.desc: Buffer to store the resulting hash. Must be at least outlen bytes long.

params.name: outlen
params.desc: Desired length of the output hash in bytes.

params.name: in
params.desc: Pointer to the input data to be hashed.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the input data in bytes.

params.name: key
params.desc: Optional key for keyed hashing (HMAC-like). Pass NULL if not used.

params.name: keylen
params.desc: Length of the key. Must be 0 if key is NULL.

ca_blake2s.returns: Returns true if the operation completed successfully, false if the initialization failed (e.g., invalid parameters).
ca_blake2s.notes: This function is a wrapper that performs init, update, and final steps sequentially. It is blocking and performs the entire hash calculation synchronously, so it should not be called from an ISR or a high-priority task if the input data is large, as it will block the scheduler. It is thread-safe only if the provided context pointer is unique to the calling thread. A common mistake is passing an uninitialized or NULL context pointer, which will lead to memory corruption or a system crash.
ca_blake2s.usage: Use this function when you need a quick, one-shot hash of a data buffer without managing the state manually. It is typically used in scenarios where the entire data is available in memory at once, such as verifying a small configuration file or hashing a short message. For streaming data or very large files, you should use the individual ca_blake2s_init, ca_blake2s_update, and ca_blake2s_final functions instead to avoid holding large buffers in memory.

ca_blake2s_final.brief: Finalizes the BLAKE2s hashing process, produces the final digest, and clears the context.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized BLAKE2s context structure. Must not be NULL.

params.name: out
params.desc: Buffer where the final hash digest will be stored. Must be large enough to hold the length specified during initialization.

ca_blake2s_final.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs the final compression of any remaining data in the internal buffer, pads it, and writes the result to the output buffer. It is not thread-safe; you must ensure that no other task or ISR modifies the 'ctx' structure while this function is running. A critical step performed at the end is calling ca_memzero on the context, which securely wipes sensitive data from memory. A common mistake is attempting to call ca_blake2s_update after calling this function without re-initializing the context, which will lead to undefined behavior or corrupted results.
ca_blake2s_final.usage: This function is the final step in the BLAKE2s hashing sequence. The typical workflow is: first, call ca_blake2s_init to set up the context; second, call ca_blake2s_update one or more times to process the input data stream; and finally, call ca_blake2s_final to retrieve the digest and clean up the context. It is essential to use this sequence to ensure the hash is correctly padded and finalized according to the BLAKE2s specification.

ca_blake2s_init.signature: bool ca_blake2s_init(ca_blake2s_ctx_t *ctx, u32 outlen, const u8 *key, u32 keylen)
ca_blake2s_init.brief: Initializes the BLAKE2s hashing context with optional keying and output length parameters.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the context structure to be initialized. Must be allocated memory.

params.name: outlen
params.desc: Desired length of the hash output in bytes. Must be between 1 and 32 (BLAKE2S_OUT_SIZE).

params.name: key
params.desc: Pointer to the secret key buffer. Can be NULL if keylen is 0.

params.name: keylen
params.desc: Length of the key in bytes. Must be between 0 and 32 (BLAKE2S_KEY_SIZE).

ca_blake2s_init.returns: Returns true if initialization is successful, false if parameters are invalid (e.g., outlen is 0, outlen exceeds 32, or key is NULL while keylen > 0).
ca_blake2s_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe provided that the 'ctx' pointer is not accessed by other threads simultaneously. It is safe to call from an ISR, as it performs no blocking operations or OS-level synchronization. The 'ctx' structure must be allocated before calling this function; failing to provide a valid pointer will cause a memory corruption or hard fault. A common mistake is passing an 'outlen' of 0 or exceeding the maximum allowed key/output sizes, which will cause the function to return false immediately.
ca_blake2s_init.usage: This function is the mandatory first step in the BLAKE2s hashing sequence. It is typically followed by one or more calls to ca_blake2s_update to process the data stream, and finally ca_blake2s_final to produce the resulting hash. It is used whenever data integrity or keyed authentication (MAC) is required. In a typical lifecycle, you initialize the context, feed it data, and then finalize it to retrieve the digest.

ca_blake2s_selftest.brief: Executes a comprehensive suite of known-answer tests (KAT) to verify the BLAKE2s cryptographic implementation.
ca_blake2s_selftest.returns: Returns 0 if all tests pass. Returns a non-zero value representing the count of failed test cases if any verification fails or if memory allocation for test contexts fails.
ca_blake2s_selftest.notes: This function is intended for diagnostic and validation purposes during system startup or maintenance. It is not thread-safe and should not be called from an ISR, as it performs heap allocations using ca_memory_allocate and relies on blocking operations. The function requires the caOS memory management system to be initialized. A common mistake is calling this function in a production environment where memory is constrained, as it allocates significant temporary buffers on the heap which are freed before returning.
ca_blake2s_selftest.usage: Use this function during the system initialization phase or via a CLI command to ensure the cryptographic hardware or software implementation is functioning correctly. It is typically paired with ca_memory_init at system startup. In a CLI context, it is invoked to verify integrity after a firmware update or if cryptographic errors are suspected. Always ensure the system has sufficient heap memory available before execution.

ca_blake2s_test_init.brief: Registers the BLAKE2s cryptographic test suite into the system CLI for interactive debugging.
ca_blake2s_test_init.returns: This function returns void and does not provide a status code.
ca_blake2s_test_init.notes: This function is a wrapper that registers a command table to the system Command Line Interface (CLI). It is not thread-safe in the sense that it modifies a global registry, but it is designed to be idempotent; calling it multiple times is a no-op, meaning it will not corrupt the registry if invoked repeatedly. It is not intended to be called from an ISR, as it performs memory-related operations and list management that are not ISR-safe. Ensure that the CLI service is initialized before calling this, otherwise the registration will have no effect.
ca_blake2s_test_init.usage: This function is typically called during the system initialization phase, specifically when setting up diagnostic or test tasks. It is used to expose the BLAKE2s cryptographic primitives to the developer via the serial console, allowing for manual execution of tests or performance checks. It is usually grouped with other *_test_init functions to populate the CLI with all available cryptographic test suites.

ca_blake2s_update.signature: void ca_blake2s_update(ca_blake2s_ctx_t *ctx, const u8 *in, u32 len)
ca_blake2s_update.brief: Updates the BLAKE2s hashing context with a new chunk of input data.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized BLAKE2s context structure.

params.name: in
params.desc: Pointer to the input data buffer to be hashed.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the input data in bytes.

ca_blake2s_update.returns: This function returns void; it updates the internal state of the context directly.
ca_blake2s_update.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs synchronous computation. It is not thread-safe; you must ensure that only one task accesses the specific 'ctx' instance at a time, or protect it with a mutex. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the context is not being accessed simultaneously by a task. The context must be initialized using ca_blake2s_init before calling this function. A common mistake is passing an uninitialized context or a NULL pointer, which will lead to a hard fault or memory corruption.
ca_blake2s_update.usage: This function is used in the middle of a hashing sequence: first initialize the context with ca_blake2s_init, then call ca_blake2s_update one or more times to feed the data, and finally call ca_blake2s_final to retrieve the resulting hash. It is typically used when processing large files or streaming data that cannot fit into a single memory buffer. Always ensure the context is not modified by other threads during the update process.

ca_block_alloc.brief: Allocates a fixed-size memory block from a pre-allocated memory pool.

params.name: bp
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized block pool structure. Must not be NULL and must have been initialized via the appropriate pool creation function.

ca_block_alloc.returns: Returns a pointer to the allocated memory block if successful, or NULL if the pool is empty (no free blocks available).
ca_block_alloc.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses a spinlock to protect the free list during the allocation process. It is safe to call from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it uses a spinlock with interrupt disabling (ca_spinlock_lock_irq). The function is non-blocking; it returns immediately with NULL if no memory is available, rather than waiting for a block to be freed. A common beginner mistake is failing to check if the returned pointer is NULL before dereferencing it, which will cause a hard fault or undefined behavior if the pool is exhausted.
ca_block_alloc.usage: This function is used in scenarios where dynamic memory allocation (like standard malloc) is discouraged due to fragmentation or non-deterministic timing. It is typically used in a producer-consumer pattern where a task requests a block, fills it with data, and then passes it to a queue or another task. It is usually paired with ca_block_free, which returns the block to the pool once the task is finished with it. Before calling this, the pool must be fully initialized to ensure the free list pointers are correctly linked.

ca_block_free.brief: Returns a previously allocated memory block back to the specified block pool for future reuse.

params.name: bp
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized block pool structure. Must not be NULL.

params.name: ptr
params.desc: Pointer to the memory block to be freed. If NULL, the function safely returns without action.

ca_block_free.returns: This function returns void; it does not provide a status code because it is designed to always succeed as long as the pointer belongs to the pool.
ca_block_free.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses a spinlock to protect the internal free list from concurrent access by multiple tasks or interrupts. It is safe to call from an ISR because it uses the 'irq' variant of the spinlock, which disables local interrupts to prevent deadlocks. A common beginner mistake is passing a pointer that was not originally allocated from this specific pool, which will corrupt the free list and cause the system to crash or behave unpredictably during the next allocation. Always ensure the block pool has been properly initialized before calling this function, as using an uninitialized pool will lead to a hard fault.
ca_block_free.usage: This function is used to recycle memory blocks once a task has finished processing data, preventing memory leaks in long-running embedded applications. It is typically paired with a block allocation function (like ca_block_alloc) in a cycle: allocate a block, fill it with data, send it to a queue for processing, and then call ca_block_free once the consumer task is done with the data. It is also used as a fallback mechanism when a message queue is full, allowing the producer to release the memory back to the pool instead of losing the block.

ca_block_pool_free_count.brief: Returns the current number of available (free) memory blocks in a specific block pool.

params.name: bp
params.desc: A pointer to the initialized block pool structure. Must not be NULL.

ca_block_pool_free_count.returns: Returns an unsigned 32-bit integer representing the count of currently free blocks. If the pool is empty, it returns 0.
ca_block_pool_free_count.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes in constant time, making it safe to call from both tasks and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs). It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs a simple read of a variable, but note that the value returned is a 'snapshot'—it may change immediately after the function returns if another task allocates or frees a block. A common mistake is assuming this value remains constant for subsequent logic; always re-read the count if you need to make decisions based on the current availability of memory. Ensure the block pool pointer is valid and initialized before calling, as passing a NULL or uninitialized pointer will cause a hard fault.
ca_block_pool_free_count.usage: This function is primarily used for system monitoring, diagnostics, and debugging purposes rather than for flow control. It is typically paired with 'ca_block_pool_total' to calculate the percentage of memory usage or to log system health statistics to a console or telemetry interface. Developers use it in background tasks or periodic reporting threads to detect memory exhaustion trends before they lead to critical allocation failures in time-sensitive tasks.

ca_block_pool_init.signature: void ca_block_pool_init(ca_block_pool_t *bp, void *buf, u32 buf_size, u32 block_size)
ca_block_pool_init.brief: Initializes a memory pool to manage fixed-size memory blocks for efficient, deterministic allocation.

params.name: bp
params.desc: Pointer to the block pool control structure. Must be allocated in static memory or global scope.

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the raw memory buffer used for the pool. Must be aligned to 4 bytes for optimal performance.

params.name: buf_size
params.desc: Total size of the buffer in bytes. Determines the maximum number of blocks available.

params.name: block_size
params.desc: Size of each individual block. If smaller than 4 bytes, it is automatically padded to 4 bytes.

ca_block_pool_init.returns: void. This function does not return a status code; it assumes valid pointers are provided.
ca_block_pool_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it initializes the internal spinlock. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the buffer memory is already accessible. The function performs 'in-place' initialization, meaning it writes pointers into the provided buffer to link free blocks together; therefore, the buffer must not be used by other parts of the application before this initialization is complete. A common mistake is providing a buffer that is too small to hold even one block, or failing to ensure the buffer is properly aligned, which can lead to hard faults on some ARM Cortex-M architectures.
ca_block_pool_init.usage: This function is typically called during the system startup phase or within a task initialization routine before any memory allocation requests are made. It is the mandatory first step in the lifecycle of a block pool, followed by calls to ca_block_alloc and ca_block_free. It is often paired with static buffer definitions to ensure memory is reserved at compile-time. Once initialized, the pool is ready to be used by other tasks to safely manage fixed-size data structures without the fragmentation risks associated with standard heap allocators.

ca_block_pool_total.brief: Returns the total number of memory blocks available in a specific block pool.

params.name: bp
params.desc: A pointer to the initialized block pool structure. Must not be NULL; passing a NULL pointer will cause a hard fault or undefined behavior.

ca_block_pool_total.returns: Returns a u32 value representing the total capacity of the pool (the number of blocks defined at creation time). This value is constant after the pool is initialized.
ca_block_pool_total.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes in constant time, making it extremely lightweight. It is thread-safe because it only performs a read operation on a structure member that does not change after initialization. It is safe to call from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) or any task context. The most common mistake is passing an uninitialized or NULL pointer to the function, which will lead to a memory access violation. Ensure the block pool has been successfully created before calling this function.
ca_block_pool_total.usage: This function is primarily used for system monitoring, diagnostics, and telemetry. It is typically paired with ca_block_pool_free_count to calculate the percentage of memory usage or to detect potential memory leaks in the application. Developers use it inside logging tasks or status reporting loops to provide visibility into the system's resource consumption. It is usually called after the system initialization phase, once the block pool has been allocated and is ready for use.

ca_boot_confirm.brief: Marks the current firmware image as successfully booted and stable in the bootloader's configuration.
ca_boot_confirm.returns: This function returns void and does not provide a status code.
ca_boot_confirm.notes: This function is used to finalize a 'trial' boot process. If the system is not currently in a trial state (checked via ca_boot_is_trial), the function returns immediately without doing anything. It is not thread-safe in the sense that it should only be called once the application has verified its own health (e.g., network connectivity, sensor initialization). It is not intended to be called from an ISR. The most common mistake is calling this too early, before the application has actually verified that it can perform its primary tasks, which could lead to 'bricking' the device if the new firmware is faulty but marked as confirmed.
ca_boot_confirm.usage: This function is typically used in the main application loop or an initialization task after the system has successfully performed a self-test. It is usually paired with ca_boot_is_trial to ensure the confirmation logic only runs when a new update is being tested. Once ca_boot_confirm is called, the bootloader will consider this image as the 'golden' image and will not attempt to revert to the previous version on the next power cycle.

ca_boot_image_slot.brief: Returns the identifier ('A' or 'B') of the memory slot from which the current application is executing.
ca_boot_image_slot.returns: 'A' if running from slot A, 'B' if running from slot B, or 0 if the execution context does not match a known boot slot.
ca_boot_image_slot.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it performs a simple read of the SCB->VTOR register. It is safe to call from an ISR because it does not involve any OS primitives, locks, or complex logic. The function relies on the bootloader correctly setting the Vector Table Offset Register (VTOR) before jumping to the application. If the application is started via a debugger or a non-standard bootloader that does not configure VTOR as expected, this function will return 0, which may cause logic errors in applications that assume they are always running from a valid slot.
ca_boot_image_slot.usage: This function is typically used during application initialization to determine the current execution context, allowing the firmware to distinguish between slot A and slot B. It is frequently paired with ca_boot_is_trial to verify if the current image is a 'trial' version or a confirmed production image. Developers use it to dynamically locate headers, verify versioning, or decide which backup registers to read for state management.

ca_boot_image_start.brief: Initializes the watchdog and starts a background task to monitor system health during trial mode.
ca_boot_image_start.returns: This function returns void and does not provide a status code.
ca_boot_image_start.notes: This function is intended to be called during the system startup sequence. It checks if the device is in 'trial' mode; if so, it initializes the Independent Watchdog (IWDG) and spawns a background thread to periodically feed it. It is not thread-safe in the sense that it should only be called once during initialization, typically within ca_os_main. A common mistake is calling this function multiple times, which could lead to multiple watchdog-feeding threads competing for resources or re-initializing hardware peripherals incorrectly.
ca_boot_image_start.usage: This function is used in the early stages of the application lifecycle, specifically inside ca_os_main, to ensure the system remains responsive during trial periods. It is typically paired with other service startup functions like ca_arp_service_start or ca_dhcp_service_start. By spawning a dedicated job, it ensures that even if the main application logic hangs, the watchdog is serviced, preventing an unwanted system reset while the trial logic is active.

ca_boot_is_trial.brief: Checks if the current firmware is running in a temporary 'trial' state, typically after an update.
ca_boot_is_trial.returns: Returns true (1) if the system is currently running in a trial mode (waiting for confirmation), and false (0) otherwise.
ca_boot_is_trial.notes: This function is thread-safe and reads from the system's backup registers to determine the boot state. It is non-blocking and can be safely called from any task or ISR. The function relies on the bootloader having correctly set the magic numbers in the backup registers during the boot process. A common mistake is to assume that a 'false' return means the firmware is invalid; it simply means the system is not in a trial state (it is either fully confirmed or not using the trial mechanism).
ca_boot_is_trial.usage: This function is primarily used by the application to decide whether to initialize safety mechanisms like the Independent Watchdog (IWDG). In a typical workflow, the application calls ca_boot_is_trial() at startup; if true, it initializes the watchdog and starts a feeder task. If the application fails to call ca_boot_confirm() before the watchdog expires, the system will reset, allowing the bootloader to revert to the previous stable firmware slot. It is often paired with ca_boot_image_start() to manage the transition from the bootloader to the main application.

ca_boot_receive_update.brief: Downloads a firmware update via TFTP into the inactive flash slot and triggers a system reset to apply it.

params.name: local_mac
params.desc: The MAC address to assign to the TFTP service for receiving the update.

params.name: wait_ms
params.desc: Timeout in milliseconds to wait for the TFTP transfer to complete. Use CA_WAIT_FOREVER to block indefinitely.

ca_boot_receive_update.returns: Returns true if the update was successfully received, verified, and the boot request was queued. Returns false if the device is in a trial state, the TFTP transfer failed, the image header is invalid, or the boot request could not be initiated.
ca_boot_receive_update.notes: This function is a blocking call that manages the entire lifecycle of a firmware update, including network reception and flash writing. It is not thread-safe and must be called from a task context, never from an ISR. Before calling this, ensure the system is not in an unconfirmed trial state, as the function will explicitly refuse to overwrite the current image. A common mistake is calling this function without sufficient free flash space or while the network stack is not yet initialized, which will cause the underlying TFTP service to fail immediately.
ca_boot_receive_update.usage: This function is typically used in a dedicated background task responsible for system maintenance or remote updates. It is often paired with a loop that checks for updates periodically. Once the function returns true, the system will automatically reset into the bootloader to finalize the installation. It is the high-level entry point for the 'A/B' slot update mechanism, abstracting the complexity of TFTP, flash memory management, and bootloader communication.

ca_boot_request_update.brief: Requests a system reboot into the bootloader to perform a firmware update on a specific flash slot.

params.name: slot
params.desc: The target flash slot for the update. Must be either 'A' or 'B'. Any other character will cause the function to return false.

ca_boot_request_update.returns: Returns false if the slot is invalid, if the system is currently in an unconfirmed trial state, or if the backup register write fails. If successful, the function triggers a system reset and does not return.
ca_boot_request_update.notes: This function is a high-level control routine that triggers a system reset; it is not thread-safe in the sense that it alters global system state (backup registers) and halts execution. It must not be called from an ISR because it performs a system reset, which is destructive to the current execution context. A common beginner mistake is calling this function without verifying the integrity of the received update or ignoring the return value, which could lead to a boot loop if the backup register write fails. Ensure that the system is not in a 'trial' state that requires confirmation before attempting an update, as the function will block the request to prevent bricking an unverified installation.
ca_boot_request_update.usage: This function is typically used at the end of a firmware download process (e.g., via TFTP or UART). The typical sequence is: 1) Receive the update data, 2) Verify the data integrity, 3) Call ca_boot_request_update to signal the bootloader to perform the swap/install upon the next reset. It is often paired with ca_os_sleep to ensure communication buffers are flushed before the reset occurs.

ca_bswap16.brief: Swaps the byte order of a 16-bit unsigned integer to convert between little-endian and big-endian formats.

params.name: value
params.desc: The 16-bit value to be byte-swapped. Any valid u16 value is accepted.

ca_bswap16.notes: This function is a highly efficient, non-blocking operation that typically maps to a single CPU instruction (REV16) on ARM Cortex-M processors. It is thread-safe and can be safely called from an ISR because it performs no memory access or OS-level blocking. The most common mistake is using this function on data that is already in the correct host endianness, which will corrupt the data; always verify the source format (e.g., network packets are usually big-endian) before applying the swap.
ca_bswap16.usage: This function is essential when parsing binary protocols or reading hardware registers that do not match the CPU's native endianness. It is typically used in the data-link or application layer when processing raw buffers received from peripherals like SPI, I2C, or Ethernet. You will often see it paired with manual buffer indexing or memory copy operations to ensure that multi-byte fields are correctly interpreted by the application logic.

ca_bswap16_signed.brief: Swaps the byte order of a 16-bit signed integer to convert between Little-Endian and Big-Endian formats.

params.name: value
params.desc: The 16-bit signed integer to be byte-swapped. Any valid i16 value is accepted.

ca_bswap16_signed.returns: The input value with its two bytes swapped. The return type is i16, preserving the signed representation.
ca_bswap16_signed.notes: This function is a static inline helper that performs a byte-swap operation. It is thread-safe and can be safely called from an ISR because it performs a simple register-level manipulation without blocking or accessing shared resources. It is primarily used when communicating with external hardware or network protocols that use a different endianness than the STM32 (which is natively Little-Endian). A common mistake is assuming this function performs a mathematical sign inversion; it only swaps the memory layout of the bytes, not the value's sign.
ca_bswap16_signed.usage: Use this function when receiving 16-bit data from external sensors, network packets, or storage devices that transmit data in Big-Endian format. It is typically used in the data processing stage after receiving raw bytes from a communication peripheral like SPI or UART. It is often paired with ca_bswap32_signed or ca_bswap64_signed when handling larger data structures, and is essential for ensuring data integrity when parsing protocol headers or sensor registers.

ca_bswap32.brief: Swaps the byte order of a 32-bit unsigned integer (Endianness conversion).

params.name: value
params.desc: The 32-bit integer to be byte-swapped. Any 32-bit value is valid.

ca_bswap32.notes: This function is a high-performance utility that typically maps to the hardware 'REV' instruction on ARM Cortex-M processors. It is non-blocking, thread-safe, and can be safely called from an ISR because it performs a simple register-level operation without accessing shared resources or OS primitives. The most common mistake is using this on data that is already in the correct host endianness, which will corrupt the value; always verify if your data source is Big-Endian or Little-Endian before calling this.
ca_bswap32.usage: This function is essential when parsing network protocols or reading binary files from external storage where data is stored in Big-Endian format, but your STM32 is running in Little-Endian mode. It is typically used in a sequence where you read raw bytes from a buffer, assemble them into a u32, and then pass the result through ca_bswap32 to ensure the CPU interprets the bytes correctly. It is often paired with ca_bswap16 or ca_bswap64 depending on the data width being processed, and is frequently used alongside memory management functions like ca_memory_allocate to prepare data structures for network transmission.

ca_bswap32_signed.brief: Swaps the byte order of a 32-bit signed integer to convert between Little-Endian and Big-Endian formats.

params.name: value
params.desc: The 32-bit signed integer value to be byte-swapped. Any 32-bit value is valid.

ca_bswap32_signed.returns: The input value with its bytes reversed (e.g., 0x12345678 becomes 0x78563412).
ca_bswap32_signed.notes: This function is a static inline helper that performs a byte-swap on the underlying bit representation of a signed integer. It is thread-safe and non-blocking because it performs a simple CPU register manipulation without accessing shared resources or OS primitives. It is safe to call from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it does not trigger context switches or wait for locks. The most common mistake is assuming this function performs a mathematical sign inversion; it only affects the memory layout of the bytes, not the numerical sign of the value.
ca_bswap32_signed.usage: This function is typically used when communicating with external hardware or network protocols that use a different endianness than the STM32 (which is Little-Endian). You will often use it when preparing data to be sent via ca_uart_dma_send or ca_net_send, or when parsing incoming data from a buffer received via ca_queue_static_receive. It is essential for ensuring that multi-byte integers are interpreted correctly by both the sender and the receiver.

ca_bswap64.brief: Swaps the byte order of a 64-bit unsigned integer to convert between little-endian and big-endian formats.

params.name: value
params.desc: The 64-bit integer value to be byte-swapped. Any 64-bit value is valid.

ca_bswap64.returns: The byte-swapped 64-bit integer. There are no error conditions as this is a pure mathematical transformation.
ca_bswap64.notes: This function is a non-blocking, thread-safe, and CPU-cycle-efficient operation that performs a direct register manipulation. It is safe to call from an ISR because it does not interact with the OS scheduler, memory, or peripherals. The most common mistake is using this function when the data is already in the correct host endianness, which will result in corrupted data values. Always verify the endianness of your data source (e.g., network packets or external sensors) before applying this swap.
ca_bswap64.usage: This function is typically used when parsing binary protocols or reading raw data from external hardware that uses a different endianness than the STM32 (which is little-endian). It is often paired with memory access functions like ca_memcpy or when reading from communication buffers. You use it to normalize incoming data into the host's native format so that subsequent arithmetic or logic operations work correctly. It is a fundamental building block for network stacks and file system drivers.

ca_bswap64_signed.brief: Converts a 64-bit signed integer between host and network byte order (endianness swap).

params.name: value
params.desc: The 64-bit signed integer to be byte-swapped. Any valid 64-bit signed value is accepted.

ca_bswap64_signed.returns: The byte-swapped 64-bit signed integer. There are no error conditions as this is a pure mathematical transformation.
ca_bswap64_signed.notes: This function is a simple wrapper around ca_bswap64 that casts the result back to a signed type. It is a non-blocking, thread-safe, and pure function, meaning it performs no I/O and does not rely on RTOS state; therefore, it is perfectly safe to call from an ISR or any task context. The most common mistake is assuming this function handles network-to-host conversion automatically based on the CPU architecture; it always performs the swap, so only use it when you know the data is in the opposite endianness of your current system.
ca_bswap64_signed.usage: This function is typically used when processing raw binary data received from external hardware or network protocols that use Big-Endian format (e.g., network packets or specific sensor registers) on a Little-Endian STM32 processor. It is often paired with memory access functions like ca_memcpy or when parsing buffers received via ca_queue_static_receive. You use it to normalize data before performing arithmetic operations or storing it in your application's internal structures.

ca_bus_error_init.brief: Enables the BusFault exception handler in the ARM Cortex-M processor to catch memory access errors.
ca_bus_error_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes almost instantaneously as it only performs a single register write to the System Control Block (SCB). It is thread-safe because it modifies a system-level configuration register that is typically only accessed during the boot sequence. It is not intended to be called from an ISR, as system configuration should be finalized during the initialization phase before the scheduler starts. The most common mistake is calling this function before the system clock or basic hardware abstraction layers are ready, though in this specific case, it is safe to call early in main(). If you fail to call this, the processor might treat bus errors as generic HardFaults, making it significantly harder to debug exactly which memory address caused the crash.
ca_bus_error_init.usage: This function is used exclusively during the system startup sequence, typically inside the main() function before the RTOS scheduler is started. It is usually paired with other hardware protection initializations like ca_mpu_init() and ca_mpu_protect_canary_msp(), which set up memory boundaries and stack overflow protection. By enabling BusFaults, you ensure that if the code attempts to access an invalid memory address or a peripheral that is not responding, the CPU triggers a specific exception handler rather than silently failing or hanging. It is a mandatory step for building robust embedded systems where memory safety and fault detection are critical for long-term stability.

ca_can_deinit.brief: Disables and resets the specified CAN peripheral hardware controller.

params.name: num
params.desc: The index of the CAN peripheral to deinitialize. Must correspond to a valid hardware instance (e.g., 0 for CAN1, 1 for CAN2) defined in the system configuration.

ca_can_deinit.returns: Always returns true. This indicates that the deinitialization command has been issued to the hardware abstraction layer.
ca_can_deinit.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a direct hardware reset of the CAN controller. It is not thread-safe by itself, so ensure no other tasks are attempting to transmit or receive data on the same peripheral instance while this is called. It is generally safe to call from an ISR, but doing so is discouraged as it abruptly terminates communication. The most common beginner mistake is calling this function while the CAN bus is still active, which can lead to bus errors or 'stuck' states on the physical CAN network because the controller stops acknowledging frames mid-transmission.
ca_can_deinit.usage: This function is used during system shutdown, power-saving transitions, or when reconfiguring the CAN peripheral with different baud rates or filters. It is typically paired with an initialization function (e.g., ca_can_init) at the start of the application lifecycle. In a typical sequence, you would stop all application-level CAN processing, call ca_can_deinit to release the hardware resources, and then potentially call the init function again if a hardware reset or reconfiguration is required.

ca_can_hw_deinit.brief: Disables and resets the specified CAN peripheral hardware and its associated clock.

params.name: num
params.desc: The index of the CAN peripheral to deinitialize (e.g., 1 for CAN1, 2 for CAN2). Passing an invalid index will result in the function returning early without performing any action.

ca_can_hw_deinit.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs direct register manipulation to put the CAN peripheral into a reset state and disable its clock. It is not thread-safe; if multiple tasks attempt to deinitialize or initialize the CAN hardware simultaneously, it can lead to race conditions or system instability. It is generally safe to call from an ISR, but you must ensure that no other part of the application is actively using the CAN peripheral, as this will immediately stop all communication and reset the hardware registers. A common beginner mistake is calling this function while a transmission is still in progress, which will cause the hardware to abort the operation abruptly without completing the frame. Furthermore, on some architectures, the clock is only disabled if both CAN instances are inactive, so calling this on one instance may not immediately cut the power to the entire peripheral block if the other instance is still running.
ca_can_hw_deinit.usage: This function is used during the teardown phase of the application lifecycle, such as when shutting down a communication module or reconfiguring the system to save power. It is typically paired with an initialization function (like ca_can_init) to form a complete lifecycle. In the caOS driver architecture, it is called by the higher-level ca_can_deinit function to ensure that the hardware is safely powered down and the clock gate is disabled, preventing unnecessary power consumption when the CAN bus is not in use. Always ensure that any pending messages are handled or discarded before calling this, as the hardware reset will clear all internal buffers and configuration registers.

ca_can_hw_init.brief: Initializes the CAN/FDCAN hardware peripheral with specified baudrate and operating modes.

params.name: cfg
params.desc: Pointer to a configuration structure containing the CAN instance number (1 or 2), desired baudrate, and flags for loopback or silent mode. Must not be NULL.

ca_can_hw_init.returns: Returns true if the hardware successfully entered and exited initialization mode with the new settings. Returns false if the configuration is invalid, the hardware fails to respond to initialization requests, or the baudrate calculation fails.
ca_can_hw_init.notes: This function is blocking because it waits for the hardware to acknowledge the transition into and out of initialization mode using a software timeout loop. It is not thread-safe and should not be called from an ISR, as it performs hardware-level register configuration that expects a stable system state. A common beginner mistake is calling this function multiple times without checking the return value or failing to ensure the system clock (HSE/SystemCoreClock) is correctly configured before initialization, which leads to incorrect baudrate timing. Always ensure the peripheral is not currently in use by another task before re-initializing.
ca_can_hw_init.usage: This function is the primary hardware abstraction layer (HAL) entry point for CAN setup. It is typically called during the system boot sequence or when a specific communication interface needs to be brought online. It is always paired with a higher-level driver function (like ca_can_init) that manages the internal state tracking of active CAN peripherals. You should use this to prepare the peripheral before attempting to send or receive any CAN frames, and pair it with ca_can_deinit if the peripheral needs to be shut down to save power or reconfigured.

ca_can_hw_recv.brief: Reads a single CAN frame from the hardware receive FIFO buffer.

params.name: num
params.desc: The index of the CAN peripheral to read from. Must correspond to a valid, initialized hardware instance.

params.name: frame
params.desc: Pointer to a structure where the received frame data (ID, DLC, data bytes, etc.) will be stored. Must not be NULL.

ca_can_hw_recv.returns: Returns true if a frame was successfully read from the FIFO. Returns false if the FIFO is empty, the peripheral index is invalid, or the hardware instance is not found.
ca_can_hw_recv.notes: This function is non-blocking; it performs an immediate register check and returns false if no data is available, making it suitable for high-frequency polling. It is not inherently re-entrant; if you call this from both a task and an ISR, you must protect the access with a critical section or ensure exclusive ownership. A common beginner mistake is ignoring the boolean return value, which results in the application logic attempting to process garbage data left in the 'frame' structure from previous operations. Ensure the peripheral is initialized via ca_can_init before use, as accessing uninitialized hardware registers will cause a system crash or hard fault.
ca_can_hw_recv.usage: This function is the primary mechanism for retrieving data from the CAN controller's hardware FIFO. It is typically used within a dedicated CAN processing task or an ISR triggered by a CAN receive event. The standard pattern involves calling this function in a loop until it returns false, ensuring the hardware FIFO is completely drained to prevent overflow errors. It is often used in conjunction with ca_can_init during system startup and ca_can_deinit during shutdown.

ca_can_hw_send.brief: Transmits a CAN frame over the specified hardware interface and waits for completion.

params.name: num
params.desc: The index of the CAN peripheral to use. Must correspond to a valid, initialized hardware controller.

params.name: frame
params.desc: Pointer to the structure containing the CAN ID, DLC, data bytes, and flags (IDE/RTR). Must not be NULL.

ca_can_hw_send.returns: Returns true if the frame was successfully transmitted (or acknowledged by the hardware). Returns false if the mailbox is full, the peripheral index is invalid, or the transmission timed out.
ca_can_hw_send.notes: This function is blocking; it enters a busy-wait loop until the hardware confirms the transmission or a timeout occurs. It is NOT thread-safe if multiple threads access the same CAN peripheral simultaneously without external synchronization (like a mutex). Do not call this function from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because the blocking loop will stall the system and potentially cause a watchdog reset. The most common beginner mistake is assuming this function is non-blocking or calling it from an ISR, which leads to system hangs or missed interrupts.
ca_can_hw_send.usage: This function is typically used in the application layer or CLI commands to send data packets over the CAN bus. It is usually preceded by the initialization of the CAN peripheral using ca_can_init and the population of a ca_can_frame_t structure. It is often paired with logic that checks the return value to handle bus congestion or hardware errors, ensuring the system can recover if the CAN bus is saturated or disconnected. After usage, the peripheral may be shut down using ca_can_deinit if it is no longer required.

ca_can_init.brief: Initializes the CAN peripheral hardware and registers the driver configuration within the caOS framework.

params.name: cfg
params.desc: Pointer to a configuration structure containing parameters like CAN instance number, baud rate, and pin mapping. Must not be NULL.

ca_can_init.returns: Returns true if the hardware initialization succeeded and the configuration was stored; returns false if the pointer is NULL, hardware initialization fails, or the CAN instance index is out of bounds.
ca_can_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs low-level hardware setup. It is not thread-safe and should be called during the system initialization phase before any tasks or interrupts attempt to use the CAN bus. It must not be called from an ISR. A common beginner mistake is passing an uninitialized or NULL configuration pointer, which will immediately return false and prevent the CAN peripheral from functioning. Ensure the hardware clocks and GPIOs are configured correctly by the underlying ca_can_hw_init before calling this, as this function relies on that hardware-specific setup.
ca_can_init.usage: This function is typically called once during the system startup sequence, usually within the main initialization routine or a dedicated hardware setup task. It acts as the gateway to the CAN subsystem, pairing with later functions like ca_can_send or ca_can_receive to perform actual data transmission. If the CLI is enabled, it also registers a command-line interface node, allowing developers to debug CAN status via a terminal. Always check the return value; if it returns false, the CAN peripheral is not ready, and attempting to use it will lead to undefined behavior or system crashes.

ca_can_recv.brief: Attempts to retrieve a single CAN frame from the hardware receive buffer for a specific CAN peripheral.

params.name: num
params.desc: The index of the CAN peripheral to read from (e.g., 0 for CAN1, 1 for CAN2). Must correspond to a valid, initialized hardware peripheral.

params.name: frame
params.desc: A pointer to a structure where the received CAN data (ID, DLC, payload) will be stored. Must not be NULL.

ca_can_recv.returns: Returns true if a frame was successfully retrieved from the hardware buffer. Returns false if no frame is available, if the pointer is NULL, or if a hardware error occurred.
ca_can_recv.notes: This function is non-blocking; it checks the hardware status immediately and returns false if the receive buffer is empty, rather than waiting for a message to arrive. It is generally not thread-safe if multiple tasks access the same CAN peripheral simultaneously without external synchronization (like a mutex). Beginners often mistake this for a blocking function that waits for data; if you need to wait for a message, you must implement a polling loop or use an interrupt-driven approach. Ensure the CAN peripheral has been properly initialized via the driver's init function before calling this, otherwise, the hardware access may cause a system fault.
ca_can_recv.usage: This function is typically used inside a periodic task or a dedicated CAN processing thread to poll for incoming messages. It is usually paired with a check for the peripheral's status or called within a loop that processes all pending frames until the buffer is empty. In a standard lifecycle, you initialize the CAN peripheral, enter a loop where you call this function to check for data, process the frame if true, and finally deinitialize the peripheral when the application shuts down.

ca_can_retune.brief: Reinitializes CAN hardware peripherals to match new system clock settings.
ca_can_retune.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a hardware-level reset of the CAN controllers. It is not thread-safe and must not be called from an ISR, as it performs hardware initialization sequences that may take significant time. The primary precondition is that the CAN hardware must have been previously initialized via the standard driver startup sequence. A common beginner mistake is calling this function while CAN messages are actively being transmitted or received; since it re-initializes the hardware registers, any ongoing communication will be abruptly terminated, potentially leading to bus errors or lost frames.
ca_can_retune.usage: This function is used exclusively during power management transitions, specifically when the system clock frequency is scaled up or down to save power. Because the CAN bit timing registers are derived from the peripheral clock (PCLK1), changing the system frequency invalidates the existing baud rate settings. It is typically called in a sequence alongside other 'retune' functions like ca_os_tick_retune and ca_uart_retune immediately after the system clock frequency has been modified by the power management module.

ca_can_send.brief: Transmits a CAN frame through the specified hardware peripheral interface.

params.name: num
params.desc: The index of the CAN peripheral to use. Must correspond to a valid, initialized hardware controller index.

params.name: frame
params.desc: Pointer to the structure containing the CAN message data (ID, DLC, payload). Must not be NULL.

ca_can_send.returns: Returns true if the frame was successfully queued for transmission, false if the pointer is NULL or the hardware failed to accept the frame.
ca_can_send.notes: This function is a wrapper for the hardware-specific transmission routine. It is generally non-blocking, meaning it attempts to place the frame into the hardware transmit mailbox and returns immediately. It is not inherently thread-safe if multiple tasks access the same CAN peripheral simultaneously, so you should use a mutex or semaphore if your application architecture allows concurrent access. A common beginner mistake is passing a pointer to a local stack variable that goes out of scope before the hardware finishes sending, or failing to initialize the CAN peripheral via ca_can_hw_init before calling this function.
