ca_can_send.usage: This function is used in the application layer to send CAN messages to external devices or other microcontrollers on the bus. It is typically used after the system has successfully initialized the CAN hardware using ca_can_hw_init. In a standard workflow, you prepare a ca_can_frame_t structure, populate its fields, and pass it to this function. It is often paired with ca_can_recv to implement full-duplex communication protocols.

ca_caos_config_hash.brief: Calculates a SHA-256 hash of the caOS configuration, excluding the volatile build version field.

params.name: digest
params.desc: Pointer to a buffer of at least 32 bytes where the resulting 32-byte SHA-256 hash will be stored. Must not be NULL.

ca_caos_config_hash.returns: This function does not return a value (void). The hash is written directly into the provided 'digest' buffer.
ca_caos_config_hash.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it performs a read-only operation on a static configuration structure. It is safe to call from an ISR because it performs no I/O or synchronization primitives. The function specifically skips the 'build_ver' field at the start of the configuration struct to ensure the hash remains deterministic across different builds. The most common mistake is providing a buffer smaller than 32 bytes, which will lead to memory corruption, or passing a NULL pointer, which will trigger a hard fault.
ca_caos_config_hash.usage: This function is used to generate a unique fingerprint of the system configuration for integrity checks or version tracking. It is typically called when the system needs to verify that the current configuration matches a known state, such as during a boot-time self-test or when requested by a diagnostic CLI command. It is often paired with hex-encoding logic to display the hash to the user via serial output or stored in non-volatile memory for later comparison.

ca_caos_config_rows.signature: u16 ca_caos_config_rows(const ca_cfg_row_t **os_rows, const ca_cfg_row_t **board_rows, u16 *n_board)
ca_caos_config_rows.brief: Retrieves the configuration table pointers and the count of board-specific rows for the caOS system.

params.name: os_rows
params.desc: Pointer to a pointer that will be updated to point to the internal OS configuration array.

params.name: board_rows
params.desc: Pointer to a pointer that will be updated to point to the board-specific configuration array.

params.name: n_board
params.desc: Pointer to a variable that will be updated with the number of elements in the board configuration array.

ca_caos_config_rows.returns: Returns a u16 representing the total number of elements in the internal OS configuration array.
ca_caos_config_rows.notes: This function is a non-blocking, thread-safe utility that provides metadata about the system configuration tables. It is not intended to be called from an ISR, although it is technically safe as it performs no blocking operations or resource locking. The function relies on static arrays defined within the caOS core; therefore, it must only be called after the system has been initialized. A common mistake is to pass NULL pointers for the parameters, which will cause a hard fault when the function attempts to dereference them to write the results.
ca_caos_config_rows.usage: This function is typically used during the early stages of system startup or during diagnostic routines to inspect the configuration layout. It is often paired with ca_os_configure to verify that the system has loaded the correct configuration tables before starting tasks. Developers use it to dynamically determine the size of configuration arrays, ensuring that subsequent loops or memory operations do not exceed the bounds of the provided tables.

ca_ccm_get_free.brief: Returns the amount of free stack space available for the current task in bytes.
ca_ccm_get_free.returns: A u32 value representing the number of bytes remaining in the current task's stack before it hits the limit. If the stack is exhausted or corrupted, this value may be zero or misleading.
ca_ccm_get_free.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it reads internal task control block (TCB) variables. It is safe to call from an ISR, though it only provides information about the currently executing task context. The most common beginner mistake is assuming this value is static; stack usage changes dynamically as functions are called and local variables are allocated. Always ensure the system is initialized before calling this, as it relies on the internal CCM (Core Coupled Memory) management structures being active.
ca_ccm_get_free.usage: This function is typically used for system monitoring, debugging, or implementing stack overflow protection mechanisms. It is often paired with ca_ccm_get_used to calculate the total stack footprint of a task. Developers use these functions during the development phase to tune stack sizes for specific tasks, ensuring that the allocated memory is sufficient for the worst-case call stack depth without wasting precious RAM.

ca_ccm_get_largest_free.brief: Returns the size in bytes of the largest contiguous free memory block within the CCM arena.
ca_ccm_get_largest_free.returns: Returns a u32 representing the size of the largest available contiguous memory segment in bytes. Returns 0 if no memory is free or if the arena is fully fragmented.
ca_ccm_get_largest_free.notes: This function is thread-safe because it internally disables interrupts to ensure the memory segment list is not modified while being scanned. It is non-blocking in terms of waiting for other tasks, but it does perform a linear scan of all segments, so execution time depends on the number of segments (s_nseg). It is safe to call from an ISR because it manages its own interrupt state, but avoid calling it frequently in high-frequency ISRs to prevent jitter. The most common mistake is assuming that the sum of all free segments equals the largest free segment; always check both total free memory and the largest block before attempting large allocations.
ca_ccm_get_largest_free.usage: This function is typically used for diagnostic purposes or to perform 'pre-flight' checks before attempting to spawn a new task or allocate a large buffer. It is often paired with ca_ccm_get_free to provide a detailed report on memory health, especially when a system is nearing its capacity. Developers use it to decide if a request for a large contiguous block will likely succeed, preventing runtime allocation failures in critical system components.

ca_ccm_get_segments.brief: Returns the total number of memory segments currently managed by the CCM (Core Coupled Memory) allocator.
ca_ccm_get_segments.returns: Returns a u32 representing the count of active memory segments. This value is always non-negative.
ca_ccm_get_segments.notes: This function is a simple getter that returns the internal segment counter. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs a direct read of a variable, but it does not provide a snapshot of the heap state; if other tasks are allocating or freeing memory simultaneously, the returned value may be outdated by the time you use it. It is safe to call from an ISR because it does not involve blocking, mutexes, or complex logic. The most common beginner mistake is assuming this value represents the amount of free memory; it only represents the number of fragmented blocks (segments) currently tracked by the allocator.
ca_ccm_get_segments.usage: This function is typically used for memory diagnostics, debugging, or monitoring heap fragmentation. It is often paired with ca_ccm_get_free and ca_ccm_get_largest_free to assess the health of the memory pool. Developers use it to verify if a series of allocations has caused excessive fragmentation, which might lead to future allocation failures even if total free memory seems sufficient.

ca_ccm_get_used.brief: Returns the number of bytes currently used in the CCM (Core Coupled Memory) stack.
ca_ccm_get_used.returns: Returns a u32 representing the total number of bytes currently occupied by the stack within the CCM memory region.
ca_ccm_get_used.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it performs a simple arithmetic subtraction on internal memory management structures. It is safe to call from an ISR, as it does not involve any OS primitives, mutexes, or complex logic. The function assumes that the CCM memory management system has been correctly initialized by the system startup code. A common mistake is assuming this value represents the 'peak' usage; it only reflects the current stack pointer position relative to the base address, not the maximum depth reached during execution.
ca_ccm_get_used.usage: This function is primarily used for system diagnostics, debugging, and monitoring stack health. It is often paired with ca_ccm_get_free to calculate the total stack size or to verify if a task is approaching a stack overflow condition. Developers typically use this during the development phase to tune stack sizes for specific tasks, ensuring that the allocated memory is sufficient without being excessively wasteful. It is also used in logging routines to report memory pressure to a CLI or remote monitoring interface.

ca_chacha20.signature: void ca_chacha20(ca_chacha20_ctx_t *ctx, u8 *out, const u8 *in, u32 len)
ca_chacha20.brief: Performs ChaCha20 stream encryption or decryption on a buffer using a pre-initialized context.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the ChaCha20 context structure. Must be initialized via ca_chacha20_init or ca_chacha20_init64 before use.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to the output buffer where the processed data will be stored. Can be the same as 'in' for in-place processing.

params.name: in
params.desc: Pointer to the input buffer containing the plaintext or ciphertext to process.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the data to process in bytes. If 0, the function returns immediately without action.

ca_chacha20.returns: void. This function does not return a status code; it assumes the context is valid and the buffers are large enough.
ca_chacha20.notes: This function is synchronous and blocking; it will not return until the entire buffer has been processed. It is not thread-safe if multiple tasks share the same context object, so ensure access is protected by a mutex if necessary. It is generally not recommended to call this from an ISR due to the computational cost of the ChaCha20 block function, which could cause significant jitter. A common mistake is failing to re-initialize the context or using the same nonce/key pair for different data, which breaks the security of the stream cipher.
ca_chacha20.usage: This function is the core engine for ChaCha20 operations. It is typically used after calling ca_chacha20_init to set up the key and nonce. In a typical workflow, you initialize the context, call this function to process your data, and then the function automatically clears sensitive working memory. It is often used as a building block for higher-level protocols like AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) where it generates keystreams for Poly1305 keys or encrypts the actual payload.

ca_chacha20_init.signature: void ca_chacha20_init(ca_chacha20_ctx_t *ctx, const u8 *key, const u8 *nonce, u32 counter)
ca_chacha20_init.brief: Initializes the ChaCha20 cipher context with a key, nonce, and starting counter.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the ChaCha20 context structure to be initialized. Must be allocated and valid.

params.name: key
params.desc: Pointer to the 32-byte secret key. Must be exactly 32 bytes long.

params.name: nonce
params.desc: Pointer to the 12-byte nonce (initialization vector). Must be exactly 12 bytes long.

params.name: counter
params.desc: The initial block counter value, usually 0 for the start of a stream.

ca_chacha20_init.returns: This function returns void and does not provide status codes. It assumes the provided pointers are valid and memory is accessible.
ca_chacha20_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a direct memory initialization of the internal state array. It is thread-safe only if the 'ctx' structure is not shared between concurrent tasks without external synchronization. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the 'ctx' pointer points to memory that is not currently being accessed by another thread. A common beginner mistake is passing a buffer smaller than 32 bytes for the key or 12 bytes for the nonce, which will cause a buffer over-read and lead to unpredictable cryptographic output or memory faults.
ca_chacha20_init.usage: This function is the mandatory first step before performing any encryption or decryption using the ChaCha20 algorithm. It is typically used in a sequence: first, you allocate or declare a 'ca_chacha20_ctx_t' structure, then call 'ca_chacha20_init' to set the key and nonce, and finally call 'ca_chacha20' to process the data. In AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) implementations, it is often used to derive sub-keys or initialize the stream cipher state before passing the context to authentication functions like 'ca_poly1305_init'.

ca_chacha20_init64.signature: void ca_chacha20_init64(ca_chacha20_ctx_t *ctx, const u8 *key, u64 nonce)
ca_chacha20_init64.brief: Initializes a ChaCha20 context with a 256-bit key and a 64-bit nonce for stream encryption.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the ChaCha20 context structure to be initialized. Must be allocated memory.

params.name: key
params.desc: Pointer to a 32-byte (256-bit) array containing the secret key.

params.name: nonce
params.desc: A 64-bit value used as the nonce. This is placed into the state words 14 and 15.

ca_chacha20_init64.returns: void. This function does not return a status code; it assumes the provided pointers are valid.
ca_chacha20_init64.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe provided that the 'ctx' structure is not accessed by other threads simultaneously. It is safe to call from an ISR if the context memory is already allocated and accessible. The most common mistake is passing a 'key' pointer that is not exactly 32 bytes long, which will lead to undefined behavior or weak encryption. Ensure the 'ctx' structure is properly initialized or zeroed before use to avoid garbage data in the state.
ca_chacha20_init64.usage: This function is used when setting up a ChaCha20 stream cipher for encryption or decryption, typically in protocols like WireGuard or custom AEAD implementations. It is the first step in the cryptographic sequence: initialize the context with this function, then call ca_chacha20 to process the data stream. It is often paired with ca_memory_allocate or ca_memory_adopt to manage the context memory lifecycle.

ca_chacha20poly1305_decrypt.signature: bool ca_chacha20poly1305_decrypt(ca_chacha20poly1305_ctx_t *wk, u8 *dst, const u8 *src, u32 src_len, const u8 *ad, u32 ad_len, u64 nonce, const u8 *key)
ca_chacha20poly1305_decrypt.brief: Decrypts and authenticates data using the ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD algorithm with a 64-bit nonce.

params.name: wk
params.desc: Pointer to the context structure used for internal state management.

params.name: dst
params.desc: Buffer where the decrypted plaintext will be stored. Must be at least as large as the ciphertext.

params.name: src
params.desc: Pointer to the input buffer containing the ciphertext followed by the 16-byte authentication tag.

params.name: src_len
params.desc: Total length of the input data (ciphertext + 16-byte tag).

params.name: ad
params.desc: Pointer to the Additional Authenticated Data (AAD) buffer, which is verified but not encrypted.

params.name: ad_len
params.desc: Length of the AAD buffer.

params.name: nonce
params.desc: 64-bit nonce value. Must be unique for every encryption operation performed with the same key.

params.name: key
params.desc: 32-byte secret key buffer.

ca_chacha20poly1305_decrypt.returns: Returns true if the authentication tag is valid and decryption succeeded; returns false if the tag is invalid or the data was tampered with.
ca_chacha20poly1305_decrypt.notes: This function is not thread-safe regarding the context structure; ensure only one task accesses the same 'wk' at a time. It is a synchronous, blocking operation that performs heavy cryptographic calculations, so it should not be called from an ISR. The most common beginner mistake is reusing the same nonce with the same key for different messages, which completely destroys the security of the encryption. Always ensure the 'dst' buffer is large enough to hold the decrypted data, as no bounds checking is performed by the library.
ca_chacha20poly1305_decrypt.usage: Used in secure communication protocols to verify data integrity and confidentiality. It is typically paired with 'ca_chacha20poly1305_encrypt' for symmetric communication. In a typical lifecycle, you initialize the context, perform the decryption, and then check the boolean return value before processing the 'dst' buffer. If the function returns false, you must treat the data as compromised and discard it immediately to prevent processing malicious input.

ca_chacha20poly1305_decrypt_ietf.signature: bool ca_chacha20poly1305_decrypt_ietf(ca_chacha20poly1305_ctx_t *wk, u8 *dst, const u8 *src, u32 src_len, const u8 *ad, u32 ad_len, const u8 *nonce, const u8 *key)
ca_chacha20poly1305_decrypt_ietf.brief: Decrypts and authenticates data using the ChaCha20-Poly1305 IETF construction.

params.name: wk
params.desc: Pointer to the context structure. Must be allocated and valid.

params.name: dst
params.desc: Buffer to store the decrypted plaintext. Must be at least (src_len - 16) bytes.

params.name: src
params.desc: Buffer containing the ciphertext followed by the 16-byte authentication tag.

params.name: src_len
params.desc: Total length of the input (ciphertext + 16-byte tag). Must be >= 16.

params.name: ad
params.desc: Associated Data (AD) buffer for authentication. Can be NULL if ad_len is 0.

params.name: ad_len
params.desc: Length of the Associated Data.

params.name: nonce
params.desc: 12-byte IETF nonce. Must be unique for every encryption operation with the same key.

params.name: key
params.desc: 32-byte secret key.

ca_chacha20poly1305_decrypt_ietf.returns: Returns true if the authentication tag is valid and decryption succeeded. Returns false if the tag is invalid (authentication failure) or if src_len is too small.
ca_chacha20poly1305_decrypt_ietf.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs cryptographic operations in software. It is thread-safe provided that the context 'wk' is not shared between concurrent tasks. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR due to the computational intensity of ChaCha20. The function automatically clears the context 'wk' using ca_memzero before returning to prevent sensitive key material from lingering in memory. A common mistake is providing an incorrect nonce or key, which will result in a failed authentication (false return) even if the ciphertext is technically valid.
ca_chacha20poly1305_decrypt_ietf.usage: This function is used to verify the integrity and confidentiality of received network packets or stored data. It is typically used in a sequence: first, the application receives the encrypted blob, then it calls this function to verify the tag and decrypt the data in one pass. If it returns false, the application must discard the data and never use the 'dst' buffer, as the function clears it to zeros upon failure to prevent data leakage. It is often paired with ca_chacha20poly1305_encrypt_ietf for the corresponding encryption side.

ca_chacha20poly1305_encrypt.signature: void ca_chacha20poly1305_encrypt(ca_chacha20poly1305_ctx_t *wk, u8 *dst, const u8 *src, u32 src_len, const u8 *ad, u32 ad_len, u64 nonce, const u8 *key)
ca_chacha20poly1305_encrypt.brief: Encrypts data using the ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD algorithm with a 64-bit nonce.

params.name: wk
params.desc: Pointer to the encryption context structure. Must be initialized before use.

params.name: dst
params.desc: Buffer to store the encrypted ciphertext and the 16-byte authentication tag.

params.name: src
params.desc: Pointer to the plaintext data to be encrypted.

params.name: src_len
params.desc: Length of the plaintext in bytes.

params.name: ad
params.desc: Additional Authenticated Data (AAD) buffer, which is authenticated but not encrypted.

params.name: ad_len
params.desc: Length of the AAD in bytes.

params.name: nonce
params.desc: 64-bit nonce value. Must be unique for every encryption operation performed with the same key.

params.name: key
params.desc: 32-byte secret key buffer.

ca_chacha20poly1305_encrypt.returns: void. This function does not return a status code; it assumes valid inputs and sufficient buffer sizes.
ca_chacha20poly1305_encrypt.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs the cryptographic operation synchronously. It is not thread-safe if the same context 'wk' is accessed by multiple tasks simultaneously; ensure proper mutex protection if shared. It is generally not recommended to call this from an ISR due to the computational cost of encryption. The most common beginner mistake is reusing the same 'nonce' with the same 'key', which completely destroys the security of the encryption. Ensure the 'dst' buffer is at least 'src_len + 16' bytes long to accommodate the authentication tag.
ca_chacha20poly1305_encrypt.usage: Used for authenticated encryption of data packets, typically in network protocols like WireGuard. It is usually paired with 'ca_chacha20poly1305_decrypt' on the receiving end to verify data integrity and authenticity. The typical sequence is: initialize the context, prepare the key and nonce, call the encrypt function, and then transmit the resulting ciphertext and tag. Always ensure the 'ad' (Additional Authenticated Data) matches exactly on both sides, or decryption will fail.

ca_chacha20poly1305_encrypt_ietf.signature: void ca_chacha20poly1305_encrypt_ietf(ca_chacha20poly1305_ctx_t *wk, u8 *dst, const u8 *src, u32 src_len, const u8 *ad, u32 ad_len, const u8 *nonce, const u8 *key)
ca_chacha20poly1305_encrypt_ietf.brief: Encrypts data using the ChaCha20-Poly1305 IETF authenticated encryption algorithm.

params.name: wk
params.desc: Pointer to the encryption context structure. Must be initialized before use.

params.name: dst
params.desc: Buffer to store the encrypted ciphertext followed by the 16-byte authentication tag.

params.name: src
params.desc: The plaintext data to be encrypted.

params.name: src_len
params.desc: Length of the plaintext in bytes.

params.name: ad
params.desc: Associated Data (AD) that is authenticated but not encrypted.

params.name: ad_len
params.desc: Length of the Associated Data in bytes.

params.name: nonce
params.desc: 12-byte unique nonce for the IETF variant. Must never be reused with the same key.

params.name: key
params.desc: 32-byte secret encryption key.

ca_chacha20poly1305_encrypt_ietf.returns: void. This function does not return a status code; it assumes valid inputs and sufficient buffer space.
ca_chacha20poly1305_encrypt_ietf.notes: This function is not thread-safe if the same context 'wk' is shared across tasks without external synchronization. It is not safe to call from an ISR due to potential execution time and stack usage. The 'dst' buffer must be at least 'src_len + 16' bytes long to accommodate the authentication tag. A common beginner mistake is reusing the same nonce with the same key for different messages, which completely destroys the security of the encryption. Always ensure the context is cleared or re-initialized between different encryption operations to prevent data leakage.
ca_chacha20poly1305_encrypt_ietf.usage: This function is used for secure communication where both confidentiality and integrity are required. It is typically used in a sequence: first, the application prepares the plaintext and associated data, then calls this function to generate the ciphertext and tag, and finally transmits the combined result. It is often paired with 'ca_chacha20poly1305_decrypt_ietf' on the receiving end to verify the tag and recover the original plaintext. Ensure that the 'wk' context is properly allocated, typically in the task's local stack or a dedicated memory block.

ca_chacha20poly1305_selftest.brief: Executes a comprehensive suite of known-answer tests (KAT) to verify the ChaCha20-Poly1305 cryptographic implementation.
ca_chacha20poly1305_selftest.returns: Returns a u32 representing the total number of failed tests. A return value of 0 indicates that all cryptographic operations passed their verification checks.
ca_chacha20poly1305_selftest.notes: This function is intended for diagnostic and validation purposes during development or system startup. It is not thread-safe and performs significant memory allocation via ca_memory_allocate; therefore, it must not be called from an ISR. The function is blocking, as it runs a long sequence of cryptographic operations sequentially. A common mistake is calling this function in a production environment where memory is constrained, as it requires a temporary context buffer that must be successfully allocated to proceed.
ca_chacha20poly1305_selftest.usage: Use this function during the system initialization phase or via a CLI debug command to ensure the cryptographic hardware or software library is functioning correctly. It is typically paired with ca_memory_allocate to create the required context and ca_memory_free to clean up resources after the tests complete. In a production system, you would call this once at boot to verify integrity before enabling secure communication services.

ca_chacha20poly1305_test_init.brief: Registers the ChaCha20-Poly1305 command-line interface (CLI) commands for system testing.
ca_chacha20poly1305_test_init.notes: This function is a wrapper that registers a static command table into the caOS CLI system. It is not thread-safe in the sense that it modifies a global registry, but it is designed to be idempotent; calling it multiple times is a no-op, meaning it will not register the same table twice. It is not intended to be called from an ISR, as it interacts with the CLI registry which is typically managed during system initialization. A common mistake is assuming this function performs the actual cryptographic operation; it only enables the 'chacha' command in the shell for debugging or selftesting purposes.
ca_chacha20poly1305_test_init.usage: This function is typically called during the system boot sequence or within a dedicated initialization task. It is used to expose cryptographic test commands to the user via the serial console. It is often grouped with other initialization functions like ca_sha512_test_init or ca_ed25519_test_init to prepare the full suite of security diagnostic tools before the main application loop starts.

ca_cli_callto_init.brief: Registers the 'callto' command handler into the system CLI interface.
ca_cli_callto_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe because it uses an internal static flag to ensure the registration happens exactly once. It is not intended to be called from an ISR, as it performs memory registration operations that should occur during system initialization. The most common mistake is calling this function before the CLI system itself has been initialized via ca_cli_init, which will result in the registration failing or causing a system fault. Always ensure the CLI subsystem is ready before attempting to register specific command nodes.
ca_cli_callto_init.usage: This function is used to extend the Command Line Interface (CLI) functionality by adding the 'callto' command. It is typically called during the system startup sequence, often wrapped in a macro like EVAL_CLI_CALLTO to ensure it only executes if the feature is enabled in the project configuration. It pairs with ca_cli_init, which must be called first to prepare the CLI infrastructure, and is followed by ca_cli_create_thread to start the CLI processing task.

ca_cli_capture_next.brief: Registers a callback function to process the next line of input received from the CLI.

params.name: fn
params.desc: A pointer to the function that will handle the next CLI input. Must be a valid function pointer or NULL to clear the capture.

ca_cli_capture_next.notes: This function is non-blocking and is intended to change the behavior of the CLI dynamically. It is not thread-safe if multiple tasks attempt to modify the CLI state simultaneously, so ensure it is called within the context of the active CLI task. It is not safe to call from an ISR. The most common beginner mistake is forgetting to clear the capture (setting it to NULL) after the expected input is received, which causes the CLI to keep routing all subsequent input to the same function indefinitely.
ca_cli_capture_next.usage: This function is used to implement interactive CLI flows, such as multi-step configuration wizards or password prompts. It is typically paired with a state machine where the current state determines which function is passed to ca_cli_capture_next. After the captured function processes the input, it should either call ca_cli_capture_next again to continue the sequence or set it to NULL to return the CLI to its default command-parsing mode.

ca_cli_char_class.brief: Classifies a single byte into a command-line category (e.g., command, typo, escape, erase) based on the internal CLI character table.

params.name: byte
params.desc: The raw ASCII or byte value to classify. Valid range is 0-255, though only 0-127 are mapped to specific classes.

ca_cli_char_class.returns: Returns a u8 representing the character class (e.g., CH_CMD, CH_TYPO, CH_ERASE, CH_ESC). Returns CH_NONE if the byte is >= 128.
ca_cli_char_class.notes: This function is a non-blocking, thread-safe lookup table access. It is safe to call from an ISR because it performs no I/O, locking, or complex logic. The primary precondition is that the caOS CLI system must be initialized, though the table itself is static and always available. A common mistake is assuming this function validates input; it only classifies it, so you must still handle unexpected characters or non-printable bytes in your application logic. Because it is a simple array lookup, it is extremely fast and deterministic, making it ideal for high-frequency character processing.
ca_cli_char_class.usage: This function is used to build robust command-line interfaces or network transport parsers that need to distinguish between valid command characters, control sequences, and typos. It is typically used inside a character processing loop where you receive a byte via ca_cli_rx_byte or a UART handler, classify it to determine if it should be buffered or trigger an action (like an escape sequence), and then potentially update the CLI state machine. It ensures that different parts of the system, such as a local console and an SSH transport, share the exact same rules for what constitutes a valid command, preventing inconsistent behavior between different input sources.

ca_cli_create_thread.brief: Initializes and spawns the Command Line Interface (CLI) background task within the RTOS.
ca_cli_create_thread.returns: Returns a u32 task index (handle) representing the created thread, or 0xFFFFFFFF if the CLI module is disabled or the thread creation fails.
ca_cli_create_thread.notes: This function is non-blocking as it merely requests the RTOS scheduler to allocate resources and start the task. It is not thread-safe to call this from an ISR, and it must only be called after the CLI module has been initialized via ca_cli_init. A common beginner mistake is calling this function before initializing the CLI buffers or setting the output sender, which leads to undefined behavior or immediate task crashes. Ensure that the system has enough stack memory available, as the task is created with a minimum of 2048 bytes of stack space.
ca_cli_create_thread.usage: This function is typically used during the system startup phase, usually within the main initialization sequence or a dedicated system configuration task. It is always paired with ca_cli_init to prepare the environment and ca_cli_set_sender to define where the CLI output should be directed. After spawning the thread, you must call ca_cli_register_table to provide the command definitions that the CLI thread will process. Once called, the CLI thread runs in the background at a low priority (CA_TH_LEVEL3), allowing the system to process user commands asynchronously without blocking critical real-time tasks.

ca_cli_data_from_isr.brief: Safely passes incoming data from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) to the CLI processing queue.

params.name: data
params.desc: Pointer to the raw byte array received (e.g., from UART). Must not be NULL.

params.name: len
params.desc: Number of bytes to copy. If greater than the internal buffer size (125 bytes), it will be truncated.

ca_cli_data_from_isr.returns: void. This function does not return a status code; if the queue is full, it increments an internal drop counter.
ca_cli_data_from_isr.notes: This function is specifically designed to be called from within an ISR, such as a UART RX interrupt handler. It is non-blocking, meaning it will not pause the CPU if the queue is full, ensuring the interrupt remains fast and responsive. It is thread-safe regarding the queue interaction, but it uses a shared static buffer (g_isr_buffer), so it cannot be called from multiple different ISRs simultaneously without risking data corruption. The most common mistake is passing a pointer to a local stack variable that goes out of scope or failing to ensure the CLI system is initialized before the interrupt is enabled.
ca_cli_data_from_isr.usage: This function is the bridge between hardware peripherals and the CLI task. It is typically called inside the UART RX interrupt callback after receiving a character or a packet. It pairs with the CLI task's main loop, which uses a function like 'ca_queue_static_receive' to pull the data out of the queue for processing. You should initialize the CLI system using 'ca_cli_init' first, then enable the UART interrupt, and finally call this function inside the ISR to feed the CLI engine.

ca_cli_exec_capture.signature: bool ca_cli_exec_capture(const char *cmd, char *out_buf, u16 buf_size, u32 timeout_ms)
ca_cli_exec_capture.brief: Executes a CLI command and captures its output into a provided buffer instead of the standard console.

params.name: cmd
params.desc: The CLI command string to execute. Must be a null-terminated string.

params.name: out_buf
params.desc: Pointer to the memory buffer where the command output will be stored. Must be at least 2 bytes.

params.name: buf_size
params.desc: Size of the output buffer in bytes. If the command output exceeds this, it will be truncated.

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time in milliseconds to wait for the command to complete before returning failure.

ca_cli_exec_capture.returns: Returns true if the command executed and output was captured successfully within the timeout. Returns false if parameters are invalid, the CLI system is disabled, or the command timed out.
ca_cli_exec_capture.notes: This function is blocking; it suspends the calling thread until the command finishes or the timeout expires. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR because it uses semaphores and thread-level delays. The function internally manages the redirection of stdout, so it is not re-entrant; you cannot call this from two different threads simultaneously. A common mistake is providing a buffer that is too small for the expected output, leading to silent truncation, or setting a timeout that is too short for commands that perform heavy processing or I/O. Ensure the CLI system is initialized via ca_cli_init before calling this.
ca_cli_exec_capture.usage: Use this function when you need to programmatically retrieve the result of a CLI command, such as displaying system status on a web page or logging diagnostic data to a file. It is typically used in a request-response cycle: you call it to trigger a command, wait for the result, and then process the captured string. It pairs with the CLI system's internal state management, automatically restoring the original stdout sender once the capture is complete, ensuring the system returns to its normal state even if the command fails.

ca_cli_exec_capture_stream.signature: bool ca_cli_exec_capture_stream(const char *cmd, sender out_sender, u32 timeout_ms)
ca_cli_exec_capture_stream.brief: Executes a CLI command and redirects its output stream to a specific sender until completion or timeout.

params.name: cmd
params.desc: The CLI command string to execute. Must not be NULL.

params.name: out_sender
params.desc: The destination sender (e.g., a network socket or UART) where the command output will be streamed. Must not be NULL.

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time in milliseconds to wait for the command to finish and the output stream to drain.

ca_cli_exec_capture_stream.returns: Returns true if the command executed and the output stream finished within the timeout period; returns false if the command failed, the timeout expired, or the CLI system is disabled.
ca_cli_exec_capture_stream.notes: This function is blocking and must be called from a task context, never from an ISR. It is thread-safe regarding the CLI state, but users must ensure that the 'out_sender' remains valid for the duration of the call. A common mistake is failing to account for the output drain time; even if the command finishes, the function waits for the stdout queue to empty, so the timeout must be generous enough to cover both execution and transmission latency. It internally manages the CLI output redirection, so it is critical that no other task attempts to modify the CLI sender while this function is active. If the timeout expires, the function still attempts to clean up the redirection, but the caller must handle the potential partial output state.
ca_cli_exec_capture_stream.usage: This function is typically used to bridge CLI output to external interfaces like SSH or HTTP responses. The standard sequence involves: 1) Initializing a mutex to protect the session/response object, 2) Locking the mutex to assign the session, 3) Calling this function to stream the command output, and 4) Locking the mutex again after the function returns to safely clear the session pointer. This ensures that the 'drain' phase of the function completes before the session object is destroyed or reused, preventing dangling pointers and ensuring that the background drain thread has finished accessing the session context.

ca_cli_filtered_count.brief: Returns the total number of CLI input characters that were filtered out by the system.
ca_cli_filtered_count.returns: Returns a u32 value representing the count of characters discarded by the CLI filtering logic. This value is non-negative and increments whenever the CLI subsystem rejects an incoming byte.
ca_cli_filtered_count.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it simply returns the current value of a global counter. It can be safely called from both standard tasks and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs). The primary precondition is that the CLI subsystem must have been initialized via ca_cli_init. A common mistake is assuming this count represents valid commands; it specifically tracks 'filtered' (discarded) data, which is useful for debugging noise on the serial line or identifying malformed input streams.
ca_cli_filtered_count.usage: This function is typically used in diagnostic or monitoring tasks to assess the quality of the serial communication link. It is often paired with ca_cli_stats to provide a comprehensive overview of the CLI subsystem's health. Developers use it to detect if the input buffer is being flooded with unexpected characters or if the CLI parser is rejecting data due to protocol violations.

ca_cli_find.brief: Searches for a command in the CLI command table by its name string.

params.name: word
params.desc: Pointer to the command string to search for. Must be a valid null-terminated string or a valid buffer.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the command string. If the string is null-terminated, this is typically the result of ca_strlen.

ca_cli_find.returns: Returns a pointer to the ca_cli_exec_t structure if the command is found, or NULL if no matching command exists in the registered tables.
ca_cli_find.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it performs a read-only lookup on the internal CLI command table. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the command table has been fully initialized via ca_cli_register_table beforehand. A common mistake is passing an incorrect length or a pointer to a string that is not part of the registered CLI command set, which will result in a NULL return. Always check the returned pointer against NULL before attempting to access the command's execution members to avoid dereferencing a null pointer.
ca_cli_find.usage: This function is typically used within a custom CLI input handler or a stream processor to resolve user input into an executable command. It is often paired with ca_cli_rx_byte to process incoming characters and ca_cli_register_table to populate the searchable command list. Once the command is found, the returned structure is used to trigger the associated function or logic defined in the command table.

ca_cli_get_sender.brief: Retrieves the current sender handle configured for the CLI module.
ca_cli_get_sender.returns: Returns a 'sender' type handle, which is an identifier used by the OS to route messages or responses back to the CLI interface.
ca_cli_get_sender.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it simply returns a stored global variable. It is safe to call from both threads and ISRs, provided the CLI module has been initialized. The most common mistake is assuming the returned sender is valid before calling ca_cli_init; if the CLI is not initialized, the returned handle may be null or invalid, leading to failed message routing in subsequent calls.
ca_cli_get_sender.usage: This function is typically used when you need to send data or status updates back to the CLI console from a background task or a callback. You retrieve the sender handle using this function and then pass it to other caOS communication functions (like message queues or logging) to ensure the output is directed to the active CLI session. It is often paired with ca_cli_set_sender if you need to redirect CLI output to a different destination, such as a remote network socket or a different UART port.

ca_cli_hist_add.brief: Adds a command string to the CLI history buffer for future recall.

params.name: line
params.desc: Pointer to the null-terminated string to store. Must not be NULL or an empty string.

ca_cli_hist_add.notes: This function is not thread-safe; it modifies a global history buffer and index, so it should be called from a single task context or protected by a mutex if accessed concurrently. It is non-blocking and performs a simple memory copy up to the defined CLI buffer size. It is not safe to call from an ISR because it does not implement atomic protection for the shared history indices. A common mistake is passing a pointer to a local stack variable that goes out of scope, or passing a NULL pointer, which the function handles by silently returning.
ca_cli_hist_add.usage: This function is used to populate the command history, typically after a user successfully executes a command via the CLI or an SSH session. It is usually paired with ca_cli_hist_get to retrieve previous commands when the user presses arrow keys. It is typically called after the command has been validated but before the command execution logic completes, ensuring the command is available for immediate recall. Developers should ensure that the string passed is persistent and not a temporary buffer that might be overwritten by other tasks.

ca_cli_hist_count.brief: Returns the current number of commands stored in the CLI history buffer.
ca_cli_hist_count.returns: An unsigned 8-bit integer (u8) representing the total count of command strings currently available in the history buffer. The value ranges from 0 up to the maximum configured history size.
ca_cli_hist_count.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it simply returns a cached counter value. It is safe to call from an ISR, as it performs no complex operations or resource locking. The primary precondition is that the CLI module must be initialized via ca_cli_init before calling this function. A common mistake is assuming the returned value is an index; remember that this is a count, so the valid index range for ca_cli_hist_get is 0 to (ca_cli_hist_count() - 1).
ca_cli_hist_count.usage: This function is typically used to implement command navigation features, such as 'up' and 'down' arrow keys in a terminal or SSH session. It is used to check the boundaries of the history buffer before attempting to retrieve a command with ca_cli_hist_get. Developers use it to prevent out-of-bounds access when iterating through the history stack, ensuring that the navigation pointer stays within the valid range of stored commands.

ca_cli_hist_forget.brief: Wipes sensitive command history entries and the active CLI buffer to prevent unauthorized access.

params.name: prefix
params.desc: The string prefix used to identify sensitive commands in the history. Must not be NULL or empty.

ca_cli_hist_forget.notes: This function is thread-safe because it wraps its internal operations in a critical section using ca_enter_critical and ca_exit_critical. It is designed to be called from task context, but because it uses critical sections, it is safe to call even if interrupts are active. The function iterates through the entire CLI history buffer and clears any entry starting with the provided prefix. A common beginner mistake is passing a NULL or empty string, which the function safely ignores, but this may lead to sensitive data remaining in the history buffer if the developer assumes the wipe was successful. Note that it also clears the active ISR line buffer if the CLI is currently idle, ensuring no residual data remains in RAM.
ca_cli_hist_forget.usage: Use this function immediately after processing a command that contains sensitive information, such as passwords or cryptographic keys. It is typically paired with command execution logic where the input buffer is no longer needed. By calling this, you ensure that if a user presses the 'Up' arrow key on their terminal, the sensitive command is not retrieved from the history buffer. It is part of the security hardening process for CLI-based applications, usually invoked after the command has been parsed and the sensitive data has been moved to a secure, non-volatile or protected memory location.

ca_cli_hist_get.brief: Retrieves a command string from the shared CLI history buffer by its index.

params.name: pos
params.desc: The index of the history entry to retrieve. 0 represents the most recent command, 1 the second most recent, and so on. Must be less than the total number of entries available.

ca_cli_hist_get.returns: A pointer to a null-terminated string containing the command, or NULL if the index is out of bounds or the history is empty.
ca_cli_hist_get.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it provides read-only access to a shared global history buffer. It is safe to call from an ISR, but note that it returns a pointer to internal memory; you should copy this string immediately if you intend to modify it or if the history buffer might be updated by another task. The most common beginner mistake is assuming the returned pointer remains valid indefinitely or attempting to modify the string directly, which would corrupt the shared history for all other CLI sessions.
ca_cli_hist_get.usage: This function is typically used when implementing command-line recall features, such as pressing the 'Up' arrow key in a terminal. It is usually paired with ca_cli_hist_count() to determine the valid range of indices before calling this function. Developers use it to populate a local command buffer (like a session's current line buffer) so the user can edit or re-execute a previously typed command without re-typing it.

ca_cli_init.brief: Initializes the Command Line Interface (CLI) subsystem, allocating internal buffers and setting up the command processing queue.

params.name: buf_size
params.desc: The size in bytes for the CLI input buffer. Values are clamped to CLI_BUFFER_MAX and aligned to DEFAULT_MSG_SIZE. If 0, the CLI remains disabled.

ca_cli_init.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called during the system initialization phase, typically within ca_os_main, before the scheduler starts or before any CLI tasks are spawned. It performs internal memory alignment and static queue initialization; passing a size that results in 0 after alignment will default to the minimum entry size. A common mistake is calling this function multiple times or after the CLI thread has already been created, which can lead to memory corruption or inconsistent state in the command queue. It is not callable from an ISR.
ca_cli_init.usage: The function is the mandatory entry point for the CLI module. It is typically used in a sequence: first, initialize the CLI with ca_cli_init, then configure the output destination with ca_cli_set_sender, register the command table using ca_cli_register_table, and finally spawn the processing thread with ca_cli_create_thread. This sequence ensures that the command parser is fully prepared to handle incoming data from the configured communication interface.

ca_cli_is_enabled.brief: Checks if the Command Line Interface (CLI) system is currently active and ready to process commands.
ca_cli_is_enabled.returns: Returns 'true' if the CLI is enabled and ready to receive input, or 'false' if it is disabled or not yet initialized.
ca_cli_is_enabled.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe because it performs a simple read of a global boolean flag. It is safe to call from both main-line code and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs) because it does not involve complex synchronization primitives like mutexes or semaphores. A common mistake is assuming that 'true' means the CLI is currently idle; it only indicates that the system is enabled. You must ensure that the CLI module has been properly initialized via ca_cli_init before relying on this status, otherwise, it may return a stale or incorrect value.
ca_cli_is_enabled.usage: This function is typically used as a guard clause before attempting to send data to the CLI or before performing heavy operations related to the command parser. It is often paired with initialization functions like ca_cli_init that set the global state and status reporting functions like ca_cli_stats. By checking this status, you prevent the system from attempting to process commands or log output when the CLI is intentionally disabled to save resources or during system shutdown sequences.

ca_cli_line_reset.brief: Resets the internal CLI line buffer, history navigation index, and escape sequence state.
ca_cli_line_reset.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should be called only when the CLI state is known to be stable or when the console is being reclaimed. It resets the global state variables (s_esc, s_hist_nav, g_rx_head) that track the current user input line. It is not intended to be called from an ISR, as it modifies shared console state without locking mechanisms. A common mistake is calling this while a background task is still actively processing or appending to the CLI buffer, which can lead to race conditions or corrupted input state.
ca_cli_line_reset.usage: This function is typically used during console reclamation or when an error occurs that requires clearing the current input line to prevent stale data from being processed. It is often paired with console management functions like console_reclaim or when a task loses ownership of the CLI. It ensures that the next user input starts from a clean slate, preventing the user from accidentally executing partial or corrupted commands left over from a previous session.

ca_cli_register_table.brief: Registers a command table into the system CLI, enabling its commands to be accessible via the console.

params.name: t
params.desc: Pointer to the command table structure. Must not be NULL and must contain a valid 'cmds' pointer.

ca_cli_register_table.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should typically be called during system initialization before the CLI task starts processing input. It is not safe to call from an ISR because it modifies a global linked list without disabling interrupts. A common mistake is passing a pointer to a local (stack-allocated) table, which will cause the CLI to crash or behave unpredictably when it tries to access the table after the function returns. The function is idempotent; if you register the same table pointer multiple times, it will detect the duplicate and ignore subsequent calls, preventing infinite loops in the linked list.
ca_cli_register_table.usage: This function is used to extend the CLI functionality by adding module-specific commands (e.g., crypto, storage, or network diagnostics). It is usually called inside an 'init' function of a specific module, often guarded by a static boolean flag to ensure registration happens exactly once. It pairs with the CLI system initialization; once registered, the commands defined in the table become available for execution via the CLI interface.

ca_cli_rx_byte.brief: Processes a single byte of input for the CLI, handling line buffering, VT100 escape sequences, and command submission.

params.name: ch
params.desc: The raw byte received from a communication interface (UART, USB CDC, etc.). Only the lower 8 bits are used.

ca_cli_rx_byte.notes: This function is the core engine for the CLI input processing. It is not thread-safe and must be called from the context where the data is received (e.g., an ISR or a dedicated communication task). It handles complex state machines like VT100 escape sequences (arrows for history) and backspace logic internally. A common mistake is calling this function from multiple threads simultaneously without external synchronization, which will corrupt the internal line buffer and history state. It is designed to be called for every single byte received, so it should be placed inside the RX callback of your communication driver.
ca_cli_rx_byte.usage: This function is used to bridge raw hardware input to the CLI logic. You typically pair it with a driver initialization function (like ca_lpuart_init or a USB CDC callback) that invokes ca_cli_rx_byte whenever a new byte arrives. It replaces manual buffer management, as it automatically handles line accumulation, echo, and command submission (triggering the STDIN callback when a newline is detected). It is the standard way to feed data into the CLI system after the CLI has been initialized via ca_cli_init.

ca_cli_set_secret_prefix.brief: Sets a secret prefix string that the CLI will ignore when saving commands to history.

params.name: prefix
params.desc: The string literal or buffer to be used as a secret prefix. If NULL, the secret prefix feature is disabled.

ca_cli_set_secret_prefix.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should be called during the initialization phase of your CLI task before the CLI thread starts processing user input. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. The function stores a pointer to the provided string; therefore, you must ensure the memory containing the prefix remains valid and constant for the entire duration of the application. A common mistake is passing a pointer to a local stack variable that goes out of scope, which will cause the CLI to compare incoming commands against garbage memory.
ca_cli_set_secret_prefix.usage: Use this function when you want to prevent sensitive inputs, such as passwords or authentication tokens, from appearing in the CLI command history. It is typically called once during the system setup sequence, immediately after ca_cli_register_table and before the CLI thread begins execution. By setting a prefix, any command starting with that specific string will be treated as 'secret' by the internal history management logic, ensuring it is never logged to the command history buffer. It is usually paired with ca_cli_init and ca_cli_create_thread to secure the CLI session from the start.

ca_cli_set_sender.brief: Configures the output destination (sender) for the Command Line Interface (CLI) system.

params.name: out
params.desc: A handle or identifier representing the output stream (e.g., STDOUT). Passing NULL disables the CLI output.

ca_cli_set_sender.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should be called during the system initialization phase before the CLI thread is started. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. If you pass NULL, the CLI will stop sending data, which is useful for temporarily silencing the interface. The most common mistake is calling this after the CLI thread has already started, which can lead to race conditions where the sender is updated while the CLI is actively trying to write to the previous destination.
ca_cli_set_sender.usage: This function is used during the system boot sequence to bind the CLI to a specific communication channel, such as a UART or USB-CDC interface. It is typically called immediately after ca_cli_init and before ca_cli_create_thread. It is part of the standard initialization pattern: initialize the CLI memory, set the output sender, create the thread, and finally register the command table.

ca_cli_stats.brief: Retrieves current diagnostic statistics for the CLI message queue, including pending items, memory usage, and overflow counts.

params.name: queued
params.desc: Pointer to a variable where the number of messages currently waiting in the queue will be stored. Pass NULL if you do not need this value.

params.name: buffered
params.desc: Pointer to a variable where the total number of bytes currently occupied in the queue buffer will be stored. Pass NULL if you do not need this value.

params.name: dropped
params.desc: Pointer to a variable where the count of messages discarded due to queue overflow will be stored. Pass NULL if you do not need this value.

ca_cli_stats.returns: This function returns void; it provides data via the provided pointers.
ca_cli_stats.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes in constant time, making it safe to call from both standard tasks and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs). It performs direct memory reads of global variables; because it does not use mutexes, the values returned are a 'snapshot' and may be slightly inconsistent if the CLI task is actively modifying the queue at the exact moment of the read. The most common mistake is assuming the returned values are perfectly synchronized with other system events; treat these as diagnostic indicators rather than precise real-time counters. Ensure the CLI system has been initialized via ca_cli_init before calling this, otherwise, the returned statistics will reflect uninitialized memory or zeroed-out global variables.
ca_cli_stats.usage: This function is primarily used for system health monitoring, typically implemented as a 'status' or 'info' command within the CLI itself. Developers use it to detect if the CLI queue is filling up too quickly, which often indicates that the command processing task is blocked, starving, or unable to keep up with incoming data. It is standard practice to pair this with ca_cli_is_enabled() to ensure the subsystem is active before querying. In a typical diagnostic sequence, you would call this periodically from a background monitoring task or a system watchdog to log performance metrics and identify potential bottlenecks in command execution.

ca_cli_typo_count.brief: Returns the total count of typing errors (typos) detected by the CLI subsystem.
ca_cli_typo_count.returns: A 32-bit unsigned integer representing the cumulative number of invalid character sequences or typo events recorded by the CLI since system initialization.
ca_cli_typo_count.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it performs a simple read of a global counter. It is safe to call from both standard tasks and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs). The primary precondition is that the CLI subsystem must have been initialized via ca_cli_init() prior to use. A common mistake for beginners is assuming this counter resets automatically; it does not, so you must track its value over time if you intend to calculate error rates or detect spikes in user input errors.
ca_cli_typo_count.usage: This function is typically used for system diagnostics, telemetry, or monitoring user interaction quality. It is often paired with ca_cli_stats() to provide a comprehensive overview of the console health. Developers use it to determine if a remote user or a local operator is struggling with the interface, allowing the system to trigger alerts or adjust input sensitivity if the typo count exceeds a specific threshold.

ca_clock_hw_adc_init.brief: Enables the hardware clock for a specific ADC peripheral based on the target microcontroller architecture.

params.name: adc_num
params.desc: The index of the ADC peripheral to initialize (typically 1, 2, or 3). Values outside the supported range for the specific MCU will result in no action.

ca_clock_hw_adc_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes extremely quickly, as it only performs register writes to the Reset and Clock Control (RCC) unit. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs atomic-like register modifications, but it is not intended to be called concurrently from multiple threads for the same peripheral. It is safe to call from an ISR, though it is almost exclusively used during system initialization. The most common mistake is calling this function before the system clock tree is stable or attempting to use the ADC peripheral before this function has been called, which will result in a hard fault or a bus error when accessing ADC registers.
ca_clock_hw_adc_init.usage: This function is the mandatory first step in the ADC initialization sequence. It must be called before any other configuration of the ADC registers (such as setting sample times or resolution) because the peripheral registers are inaccessible while the clock is disabled. It is typically called inside the driver's main initialization function, such as ca_adc_init, immediately after validating the peripheral index. It pairs with hardware-specific configuration functions like ca_adc_hw_init_periph to ensure the peripheral is fully powered and ready for operation.

ca_clock_hw_dac_init.brief: Enables the peripheral clock for the DAC hardware module.

params.name: channel
params.desc: The DAC channel index. While the parameter is passed, it is currently ignored by the implementation as the clock enable affects the entire DAC peripheral block.

ca_clock_hw_dac_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs a simple register write, but it is not intended to be called concurrently from multiple tasks or ISRs. The most critical aspect is the mandatory read-back of the RCC register after the write operation; this forces the CPU to complete the bus transaction, preventing an asynchronous BusFault that occurs if the peripheral is accessed before the clock signal has physically propagated through the bus matrix. Beginners often forget this read-back, leading to intermittent, hard-to-debug crashes when the code is optimized.
ca_clock_hw_dac_init.usage: This function is a low-level hardware initialization primitive. It is typically called only once during the system startup or when a specific driver is being initialized. In the caOS driver architecture, it is paired with GPIO initialization and peripheral-specific configuration functions. The standard sequence is: call ca_clock_hw_dac_init, then configure the associated GPIO pins, and finally call the peripheral-specific init function (e.g., ca_dac_hw_init_periph).

ca_clock_hw_deinit.brief: Resets the system clock tree to a safe, low-frequency state (typically HSI/MSIS) and disables PLLs.
ca_clock_hw_deinit.notes: This function is intended for use during system shutdown or before jumping to a new firmware image. It is not thread-safe and must be called when the system is in a controlled state, as it modifies critical clock registers (RCC) and disables caches. It is strictly non-blocking in terms of OS scheduling, but it contains busy-wait loops to ensure hardware stability (e.g., waiting for oscillators to stabilize). It must NOT be called from an ISR, as it performs operations that could interfere with the system's ability to handle interrupts or maintain timing. The most common mistake is calling this while other peripherals or tasks are still actively relying on high-speed clocks or DMA transfers, which will lead to immediate system instability or hard faults.
ca_clock_hw_deinit.usage: This function is typically the final step in the system shutdown sequence, often paired with 'ca_os_end'. It is used to ensure that the hardware is in a predictable, low-power, and low-frequency state before the CPU executes a jump to a bootloader or a different application image. By resetting the clock tree to a default oscillator (like HSI or MSIS) and disabling PLLs, it ensures that the next piece of code running on the processor starts from a known, safe baseline, regardless of the previous configuration.

ca_clock_hw_dma_init.brief: Enables the peripheral clock for a specific DMA controller in the RCC register.

params.name: controller
params.desc: The index of the DMA controller to enable (e.g., 1, 2, or 3). Valid values depend on the specific STM32 series; invalid values are ignored by the switch-case.

ca_clock_hw_dma_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes almost instantaneously. It is thread-safe as it performs a simple bitwise OR operation on the RCC registers, which is atomic on most ARM Cortex-M architectures. It is safe to call from an ISR, though it is typically called during system initialization. The most common mistake is assuming that calling this function is sufficient to use the DMA; you must still configure the DMA streams/channels and interrupts separately. The 'nop' instructions are included to ensure the clock signal has time to propagate through the hardware bus before subsequent configuration registers are accessed.
ca_clock_hw_dma_init.usage: This function is used exclusively during the hardware abstraction layer (HAL) initialization phase, typically inside a driver's init function or the main system startup sequence. It must be called before any attempt to configure DMA registers (like stream settings or interrupt enables), as accessing registers of a peripheral with a disabled clock will result in a bus fault or silent failure. It is usually paired with subsequent calls to configure the specific DMA stream or channel, and it is often called for all available controllers (1, 2, and 3) during the boot process to ensure the entire DMA subsystem is ready for use.

ca_clock_hw_i2c_init.brief: Enables the peripheral clock for the specified I2C hardware module via the RCC register.

params.name: num
params.desc: The I2C peripheral index (e.g., 1, 2, 3, or 4). Must correspond to a valid I2C peripheral available on the specific STM32 MCU model.

ca_clock_hw_i2c_init.returns: void. This function does not return a status code, so it assumes the provided index is valid for the target hardware.
ca_clock_hw_i2c_init.notes: This function is a low-level hardware abstraction layer (HAL) helper. It is non-blocking and executes extremely quickly by performing a direct bitwise OR operation on the RCC (Reset and Clock Control) registers. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs an atomic register write, but it is not intended to be called concurrently from multiple threads or ISRs for the same peripheral. The most common beginner mistake is calling this function before the system clock is properly configured or attempting to initialize an I2C peripheral index that does not exist on the specific MCU variant, which will result in a silent failure or a hard fault if the register address is invalid.
ca_clock_hw_i2c_init.usage: This function is used exclusively during the initialization phase of an I2C peripheral. It is typically called inside the driver's main initialization function (e.g., ca_i2c_init) immediately before configuring the GPIO pins and the I2C peripheral registers themselves. Without calling this function, the I2C peripheral will remain 'dead' because the internal logic gates are not receiving a clock signal, causing any subsequent attempts to write to I2C registers to be ignored or trigger a bus fault.

ca_clock_hw_lptim_init.brief: Initializes the LSI clock source and enables the peripheral clock for a specific Low Power Timer (LPTIM).

params.name: num
params.desc: The index of the LPTIM peripheral to initialize. Currently, only 1 is supported; passing any other value will return false.

ca_clock_hw_lptim_init.returns: Returns true if the clock configuration was successful, or false if the peripheral index is invalid or unsupported by the hardware.
ca_clock_hw_lptim_init.notes: This function is blocking because it waits for the LSI (Low Speed Internal) oscillator to stabilize via a while-loop. It is not thread-safe and should not be called from an ISR, as the wait loop could hang the system if the oscillator fails to start. It must be called before any register-level configuration of the LPTIM peripheral, as the timer will not function without its kernel clock. A common mistake is assuming this function configures the timer's period or interrupts; it only handles the clock tree setup.
ca_clock_hw_lptim_init.usage: This function is used as the first step in the hardware abstraction layer's initialization sequence for the LPTIM. It is typically paired with 'lptim_acquire' to reserve the resource, followed by 'ca_lptim_hw_init' to configure the timer's actual timing parameters and interrupts. If this function fails, the driver must release the resource using 'lptim_release' to prevent locking the peripheral for other tasks.

ca_clock_hw_lse_lock.brief: Locks the system clock (MSI PLL-mode) to the LSE crystal for high-precision timing on supported STM32 families.
ca_clock_hw_lse_lock.returns: Returns true if the system clock was successfully locked to the LSE, or false if the hardware does not support this feature, the LSE is not running, or the lock operation failed.
ca_clock_hw_lse_lock.notes: This function is hardware-specific and only performs an action on families like the STM32U5 that support MSI PLL-mode. It is not thread-safe and should be called during system initialization before the OS scheduler is fully operational. It is a blocking function because it waits for the LSE to stabilize and the PLL to lock. It must NOT be called from an ISR, as it performs busy-waiting loops that could cause system instability or missed interrupts. A common mistake is calling this before the LSE has been properly initialized and enabled in the RCC registers.
ca_clock_hw_lse_lock.usage: This function is typically used during the early boot sequence to improve the accuracy of the system tick. It is usually paired with ca_rtc_get_clk_src() to verify that the LSE is the intended clock source before attempting to lock the system clock to it. Once successfully locked, it is standard practice to call ca_os_tick_retune() to adjust the OS tick frequency to match the new, more precise clock source.

ca_clock_hw_spi_init.brief: Enables the internal RCC clock signal for a specific SPI hardware peripheral.

params.name: num
params.desc: The SPI peripheral index (e.g., 1, 2, or 3). Passing an unsupported number will result in no action being taken.

ca_clock_hw_spi_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes extremely quickly, as it only performs a register write to the Reset and Clock Control (RCC) unit. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs an atomic-like bitwise OR operation on the register, but it does not implement mutexes, so it should be called during the initialization phase before the peripheral is used by multiple tasks. It is safe to call from an ISR, though this is rarely necessary as clock initialization should happen during system startup. The most common beginner mistake is attempting to configure or read/write to SPI registers before calling this function; if the clock is not enabled, the CPU will ignore any writes to the SPI peripheral registers, often leading to a hard fault or silent failure.
ca_clock_hw_spi_init.usage: This function is a mandatory prerequisite for any SPI communication. It is typically called inside the driver initialization sequence, specifically within the 'ca_spi_init' function. The standard sequence is: first, call 'ca_clock_hw_spi_init' to wake up the hardware, then call 'ca_gpio_hw_spi_init' to configure the physical pins, and finally call the peripheral-specific initialization function (e.g., 'ca_spi_hw_init_periph'). Skipping this step is the most frequent cause of 'dead' SPI peripherals that appear configured but never transmit data.

ca_clock_hw_timer_init.brief: Enables the peripheral clock for a specific hardware timer in the STM32 RCC register.

params.name: num
params.desc: The hardware timer index (e.g., 1, 2, 3...). Must match the specific timer available on your target MCU; invalid numbers return false.

ca_clock_hw_timer_init.returns: Returns true if the clock was successfully enabled, or false if the timer index is invalid or unsupported by the current hardware configuration.
ca_clock_hw_timer_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes extremely quickly as it only performs a bitwise OR operation on an RCC register. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs an atomic-like register modification, but it should be called during the initialization phase before the timer is used. It is safe to call from an ISR, though typically you should initialize hardware before enabling interrupts. A common beginner mistake is attempting to configure timer registers (like ARR or PSC) before calling this function; if the clock is not enabled, writing to timer registers will have no effect or cause a hard fault.
ca_clock_hw_timer_init.usage: This function is a mandatory prerequisite for any timer operation. It is typically called inside a driver's initialization sequence, such as ca_timer_init_periodic, immediately after acquiring the timer resource. It acts as the 'power switch' for the peripheral; without it, the timer hardware remains in a reset state and is invisible to the CPU. It is always paired with subsequent hardware-specific configuration functions that set the timer's frequency and mode.

ca_clrex.brief: Clears the exclusive monitor (Load-Link/Store-Conditional) state in the CPU.
ca_clrex.notes: This function is a wrapper for the ARM Cortex-M 'CLREX' instruction. It is used to clear the local exclusive monitor, which is a hardware mechanism used to implement atomic operations like mutexes or semaphores. You must call this if you have performed a 'ca_ldrex' (load-exclusive) but decide not to complete the operation with a 'ca_strex' (store-exclusive), for example, if you detect an error or a condition that makes the write invalid. Failing to clear the monitor can lead to unpredictable behavior in subsequent atomic operations, as the CPU might incorrectly believe an exclusive access is still in progress. It is thread-safe and can be called from both thread mode and ISRs.
ca_clrex.usage: Use this function in low-level synchronization primitives or when implementing custom atomic data structures. It is typically paired with 'ca_ldrex' and 'ca_strex' in a loop. If your logic branches out of the loop before reaching the 'ca_strex' instruction, you must call 'ca_clrex' to reset the monitor state. This ensures that the next atomic operation in the system starts from a clean, predictable state, preventing potential deadlocks or data corruption in multi-threaded environments.

ca_cond_broadcast.brief: Wakes up all tasks currently blocked waiting on the specified condition variable.

params.name: cv
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized condition variable object. Must not be NULL.

ca_cond_broadcast.notes: This function is thread-safe and uses an internal spinlock to protect the wait queue during the broadcast operation. It is non-blocking in the sense that it does not wait for the woken tasks to finish, but it does disable interrupts briefly to ensure atomicity. You must never call this function from an ISR, as it involves scheduler manipulation and potential context switching. A common beginner mistake is assuming that the woken tasks will immediately preempt the current task; in reality, the scheduler decides which task runs next based on priority, so the woken tasks might remain in a 'ready' state for a short time before actually executing.
ca_cond_broadcast.usage: Use this function when a state change occurs that affects multiple waiting tasks, such as a shared resource becoming available or a global flag being updated. It is typically paired with ca_cond_wait, where tasks block until the condition is met. The standard workflow involves locking a mutex, checking the condition, calling ca_cond_wait if the condition is false, and later having another task call ca_cond_broadcast once the condition is satisfied. Unlike ca_cond_signal, which only wakes one task, broadcast is essential for scenarios where multiple consumers need to re-check the state simultaneously after a single event.

ca_cond_init.brief: Initializes a condition variable object to manage thread synchronization and signaling.

params.name: cv
params.desc: A pointer to the condition variable structure that needs to be initialized. Must point to valid, allocated memory.

ca_cond_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs the necessary setup for the internal wait queue and spinlock. It is thread-safe in the sense that it prepares the object for use, but it must be called before any thread attempts to wait on or signal the condition variable. It is safe to call from an ISR context if the memory is already allocated, but typically this is done during system initialization. The most common beginner mistake is attempting to use a condition variable without calling this initialization function first, which leads to undefined behavior because the internal wait queue and spinlock remain in an uninitialized state.
ca_cond_init.usage: This function is used during the system setup phase, typically alongside mutex initialization, to prepare synchronization primitives for producer-consumer patterns. It is almost always paired with ca_cond_wait, ca_cond_signal, or ca_cond_broadcast to manage thread state transitions. You should call this once for every condition variable used in your application before spawning any tasks that might access them. It is part of the standard initialization sequence: define the global variable, call the init function, and then pass the pointer to your task functions.

ca_cond_signal.brief: Wakes up exactly one task currently waiting on the specified condition variable.

params.name: cv
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized condition variable object. Must not be NULL.
