ca_cond_signal.returns: void. This function does not return a status code, as it is designed to be a fire-and-forget notification mechanism.
ca_cond_signal.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, utilizing an internal spinlock to protect the wait queue during the operation. It is safe to call from an ISR because it uses spinlocks with interrupt disabling (irq). The most common beginner mistake is assuming that calling this function guarantees the woken task will run immediately; in reality, the woken task only becomes 'ready' and must still compete for CPU time based on its priority. If no tasks are waiting on the condition variable, the signal is simply lost, which is expected behavior for condition variables.
ca_cond_signal.usage: This function is typically used in producer-consumer patterns to notify a waiting consumer that a resource is available. It is almost always paired with ca_cond_wait or ca_cond_timedwait, which are called by the consumer to block until the signal arrives. The standard sequence is: lock the mutex, modify the shared resource, call ca_cond_signal to wake a waiter, and finally unlock the mutex. Failing to hold the mutex while signaling can lead to race conditions where a task misses the signal entirely.

ca_cond_timedwait.brief: Suspends the current thread until a condition variable is signaled or a timeout expires, while atomically releasing the associated mutex.

params.name: cv
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized condition variable object to wait on.

params.name: mtx
params.desc: Pointer to the mutex that must be held by the caller before calling this function.

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time in milliseconds to wait. If set to 0 (CA_NO_WAIT_TIME), the function returns immediately without waiting.

ca_cond_timedwait.returns: Returns true if the thread was woken up by a signal or broadcast (condition met), or false if the timeout expired or the function was called with a zero timeout.
ca_cond_timedwait.notes: This function is blocking and must only be called from a thread context, never from an ISR. It is thread-safe, but it requires that the caller already owns the mutex passed as an argument; failing to hold the mutex will trigger a system error. The function performs an atomic release of the mutex upon entering the wait state and ensures the mutex is re-acquired before returning to the caller. A common mistake is forgetting that the condition must be re-checked in a loop after this function returns, as spurious wakeups or race conditions might occur between the signal and the thread resuming execution.
ca_cond_timedwait.usage: This function is used to implement producer-consumer patterns or state synchronization where a thread needs to wait for a specific data condition without busy-waiting. It is typically used in a sequence: first, lock the mutex using ca_mutex_lock, then enter a while loop checking the condition, call ca_cond_timedwait inside that loop, and finally process the data once the condition is met. It is always paired with ca_cond_signal or ca_cond_broadcast, which are called by other threads to notify the waiting thread that the state has changed.

ca_cond_wait.brief: Suspends the current thread until a condition variable is signaled, atomically releasing the associated mutex.

params.name: cv
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized condition variable object. Must be initialized via ca_cond_init before use.

params.name: mtx
params.desc: Pointer to the mutex currently held by the calling thread. Must be locked by the caller before invoking this function.

ca_cond_wait.returns: void. This function does not return an error code; if the internal safeguards fail (e.g., the thread does not own the mutex), the system will trigger a safeguard violation.
ca_cond_wait.notes: This function is strictly blocking and must never be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it triggers a context switch. It is thread-safe, but it requires the caller to hold the associated mutex; failing to do so will trigger a safeguard error. The most common beginner mistake is forgetting to wrap the condition check in a 'while' loop; because of spurious wakeups or multiple threads competing for the mutex after a signal, the condition might no longer be true when the thread resumes. Always ensure the mutex is locked before calling this function, as the function will automatically release it upon blocking and re-acquire it before returning to your code.
ca_cond_wait.usage: This function is the standard mechanism for implementing producer-consumer patterns or resource synchronization where a thread needs to wait for a specific state change. It is typically used in a sequence: first, lock the mutex, then enter a 'while' loop checking the condition, call ca_cond_wait inside the loop, and finally perform the protected operation once the condition is met. It is always paired with ca_cond_signal or ca_cond_broadcast, which are called by other threads to wake up the waiting task. Use this to avoid 'busy-waiting' (polling), which wastes CPU cycles and prevents other tasks from executing.

ca_console_getc.brief: Reads a single byte from the console input buffer, blocking until data arrives or the timeout expires.

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Time to wait in milliseconds. Use CA_WAIT_FOREVER to block indefinitely or CA_NO_WAIT_TIME to return immediately if no data is available.

ca_console_getc.returns: Returns the byte (0-255) as an i32 on success. Returns -1 if the timeout expires, if the task does not own the console, or if the operation is interrupted.
ca_console_getc.notes: This function is blocking and must NOT be called from an ISR. It is thread-safe only if the calling task has successfully taken ownership of the console via ca_console_take. A common beginner mistake is calling this function without first verifying ownership with ca_console_is_mine or calling it from an interrupt context, which will cause the system to fail or return -1 immediately. The function uses a semaphore internally to sleep the task while waiting for data, ensuring efficient CPU usage.
ca_console_getc.usage: Typically used in interactive CLI tasks or shell implementations where the system waits for user input. The standard sequence is: 1) Call ca_console_take to claim the console, 2) Loop calling ca_console_getc to process incoming characters, 3) Call ca_console_give to release the console when finished. It is often paired with ca_stdout_put or ca_stdout_echo to provide feedback to the user.

ca_console_give.brief: Releases ownership of the system console, allowing other tasks to access it.
ca_console_give.returns: Returns true if the calling task successfully released the console. Returns false if the calling task did not own the console, meaning the release operation was ignored.
ca_console_give.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe. It is intended to be called by the task that previously acquired the console via ca_console_take. A common mistake is calling this function from a task that does not own the console, which will result in a false return and no action taken. It is not safe to call this from an ISR, as console ownership is tied to task context. Before releasing, ensure all console-related operations are complete, as this function resets the CLI line buffer to prevent data corruption or race conditions with incoming characters.
ca_console_give.usage: Use this function to relinquish control of the console after a sequence of CLI commands or interactive operations is finished. It is typically paired with ca_console_take at the start of a critical console session. The standard pattern is: ca_console_take() -> perform console I/O -> ca_console_give(). If an error occurs during the session (e.g., memory allocation failure), it is good practice to call ca_console_give() before returning to ensure the console is not left locked indefinitely.

ca_console_init.brief: Initializes the internal synchronization primitives required for console operations.
ca_console_init.returns: This function returns void and does not provide a status code.
ca_console_init.notes: This function must be called before any other console-related functions (like ca_console_take or ca_console_rx_byte) are used. It initializes a semaphore and a spinlock, which are essential for thread-safe access to the console buffer. If you fail to call this, the system will likely crash or hang when the first console interrupt occurs because the underlying synchronization objects will be in an uninitialized state. This function is not thread-safe itself and should only be called once during the system startup sequence.
ca_console_init.usage: Use this function during the early initialization phase of your application, typically inside the main function or a dedicated hardware initialization routine. It is mandatory to call this before enabling any UART interrupts that might trigger console input. It is usually paired with ca_uart_init, which handles the physical hardware configuration, while ca_console_init prepares the software-level synchronization layer.

ca_console_is_mine.brief: Checks if the calling task currently holds ownership of the system console.
ca_console_is_mine.returns: Returns true if the calling task is the current owner of the console, false otherwise.
ca_console_is_mine.notes: This function is thread-safe and non-blocking. It is intended to be used to verify if a task has successfully acquired the console via ca_console_take before performing operations that require exclusive access. It is not intended to be called from an ISR, as console ownership is a concept tied to task-level synchronization. A common mistake is to assume that calling this function grants ownership; it only checks the current state. Always ensure ca_console_init has been called during system startup before attempting to use console functions.
ca_console_is_mine.usage: This function is typically used in multi-tasking environments where multiple tasks might attempt to print to or read from the console. A task should first call ca_console_take to request access, then use ca_console_is_mine to verify it has the lock before proceeding with operations like ca_console_getc or custom logging. Once the task finishes its console interaction, it must call ca_console_give to release the resource for other tasks. This pattern prevents interleaved output and ensures data integrity during console communication.

ca_console_rx_byte.brief: Routes an incoming byte to the console buffer or CLI, depending on task ownership.

params.name: ch
params.desc: The raw byte received from a peripheral (UART, USB, etc.). Only the lower 8 bits are used.

ca_console_rx_byte.notes: This function is designed to be called from Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs) or high-priority driver callbacks. It is thread-safe regarding the internal ring buffer, but it relies on the global console state. If the console is currently 'owned' by a specific task, the byte is queued for that task; otherwise, it is passed directly to the CLI handler. A common mistake is calling this before the console system is initialized, which may lead to undefined behavior or null pointer dereferences if the filter or buffer is not set up. It uses non-blocking logic for the buffer insertion to ensure the ISR remains fast.
ca_console_rx_byte.usage: This function is the primary entry point for all character-based input streams (UART, USB CDC, etc.) into the caOS console system. It is typically registered as a callback during driver initialization (e.g., via ca_lpuart_init or similar). It acts as a traffic controller: if a task has taken control of the console (via ca_console_take), the byte is buffered for that task; if the console is free, it is processed by the CLI engine. It is usually paired with ca_console_getc to retrieve the buffered data in the task context.

ca_console_stats.brief: Retrieves the current internal statistics of the console system.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to a structure where the console statistics will be copied. Must not be NULL.

ca_console_stats.returns: This function returns nothing (void). If 'out' is NULL, the function returns immediately without performing any operation.
ca_console_stats.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it performs a simple memory copy of the internal console state structure. It is safe to call from an ISR, although it is rarely useful in that context. The primary precondition is that the console system must have been initialized via ca_console_init before the statistics contain meaningful data. A common beginner mistake is passing a NULL pointer or an uninitialized structure, which can lead to undefined behavior or reading garbage data.
ca_console_stats.usage: This function is typically used for monitoring, debugging, or telemetry purposes to track console activity, such as character counts or error rates. It is often paired with other console functions like ca_console_take to ensure exclusive access before performing operations, or used in a loop to compare state changes over time. Developers use it to verify if the console is receiving data correctly or to diagnose communication bottlenecks in the system.

ca_console_take.brief: Acquires exclusive ownership of the system console for the calling task.

params.name: filter
params.desc: A function pointer used to process incoming characters at the ISR level. If NULL, default handling is applied.

ca_console_take.returns: Returns true if the console was successfully acquired or was already owned by the caller. Returns false if the console is currently held by another active task or if the scheduler is not yet running.
ca_console_take.notes: This function is non-blocking; it immediately returns false if the console is busy, allowing the task to perform other work or retry later. It is thread-safe due to internal spinlock protection, but it cannot be called from an ISR because it relies on task-level ownership tracking. A common beginner mistake is failing to check the return value; if you ignore the false return, your subsequent console operations will fail or behave unpredictably because you do not actually own the resource. Ensure the console is initialized via ca_console_init before attempting to take it.
ca_console_take.usage: This function is used when a task needs exclusive access to the console for interactive operations, such as a CLI session or a REPL. It is typically paired with ca_console_give to release the console once the task is finished. The standard sequence is: call ca_console_take, verify the return value, perform console I/O using ca_console_getc or other console functions, and finally call ca_console_give to allow other tasks to access the console.

ca_cordic_calc.signature: bool ca_cordic_calc(ca_cordic_func_t func, u32 scale, i32 arg1, i32 arg2, i32 *res1, i32 *res2)
ca_cordic_calc.brief: Performs hardware-accelerated mathematical operations using the STM32 CORDIC peripheral.

params.name: func
params.desc: The specific mathematical operation to perform (e.g., SIN, COS, PHASE, SQRT). Must be a valid enum value.

params.name: scale
params.desc: Scaling factor for the result, ranging from 0 to 7. Higher values increase precision for specific operations.

params.name: arg1
params.desc: The primary input argument for the calculation.

params.name: arg2
params.desc: The secondary input argument. If the operation only requires one argument, this value is ignored.

params.name: res1
params.desc: Pointer to store the primary result. Must not be NULL.

params.name: res2
params.desc: Pointer to store the secondary result (if applicable). Can be NULL if the second result is not needed.

ca_cordic_calc.returns: Returns true if the calculation was successful. Returns false if the CORDIC hardware is not initialized, if the function type is invalid, if the scale is out of range (0-7), or if the res1 pointer is NULL.
ca_cordic_calc.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses critical sections to protect the hardware registers during the calculation. It is a blocking function, meaning the calling task will wait until the hardware completes the math operation before returning. It is NOT safe to call this function from an ISR because it uses critical sections that may interfere with system scheduling. Before using this, you must ensure ca_cordic_init() has been called successfully; otherwise, all calls will return false. A common mistake is passing a NULL pointer for res1, which will cause the function to fail immediately.
ca_cordic_calc.usage: This function is used for high-performance trigonometry or square root calculations where CPU cycles are critical. It is typically used in a loop for signal processing or coordinate transformations. The standard workflow is: call ca_cordic_init() during system startup, then call ca_cordic_calc() whenever a math operation is required. It is often paired with higher-level wrappers like ca_cordic_sincos() or ca_cordic_polar() for cleaner code readability.

ca_cordic_hw_calc.signature: void ca_cordic_hw_calc(u32 func, u32 scale, u32 nargs, u32 nres, i32 arg1, i32 arg2, i32 *res1, i32 *res2)
ca_cordic_hw_calc.brief: Performs a low-level CORDIC hardware calculation using fixed-point Q1.31 arithmetic.

params.name: func
params.desc: The CORDIC operation code (e.g., sine, cosine, arctan).

params.name: scale
params.desc: Scaling factor for the CORDIC algorithm.

params.name: nargs
params.desc: Number of input arguments (1 or 2).

params.name: nres
params.desc: Number of expected results (1 or 2).

params.name: arg1
params.desc: First input argument in Q1.31 format.

params.name: arg2
params.desc: Second input argument in Q1.31 format (ignored if nargs=1).

params.name: res1
params.desc: Pointer to store the first result.

params.name: res2
params.desc: Pointer to store the second result (ignored if nres=1).

ca_cordic_hw_calc.returns: This function returns void. It assumes the hardware is available and the caller has already secured exclusive access.
ca_cordic_hw_calc.notes: This function is NOT thread-safe and does not perform any locking internally. It is designed to be called only after the caller has successfully acquired a critical section or mutex to prevent other tasks from corrupting the CORDIC hardware state. It is not safe to call from an ISR unless the hardware is guaranteed to be idle and the lock is held. A common beginner mistake is calling this without wrapping it in ca_enter_critical() and ca_exit_critical(), which leads to race conditions where one task reads the result intended for another task.
ca_cordic_hw_calc.usage: This function is the low-level driver interface used by higher-level math functions like ca_cordic_sincos. It is typically used in a sequence: first, enter a critical section to ensure exclusive hardware access, then call this function to perform the calculation, and finally exit the critical section. It should only be used when you need direct, high-performance access to the CORDIC peripheral and are managing the hardware state manually.

ca_cordic_hw_init.brief: Initializes the CORDIC hardware peripheral by enabling its clock in the RCC register.
ca_cordic_hw_init.returns: Returns true if the CORDIC hardware is present and successfully initialized, false if the current STM32 chip does not support the CORDIC peripheral.
ca_cordic_hw_init.notes: This function is a low-level hardware abstraction layer (HAL) call. It is not thread-safe and should only be called once during the system startup sequence, typically within the board support package (BSP) initialization. It is non-blocking and executes extremely quickly, but it must not be called from an ISR because it performs direct register manipulation that assumes a stable system state. A common mistake is to call this function multiple times or to attempt to use CORDIC functions before verifying the return value of this initialization.
ca_cordic_hw_init.usage: This function is the mandatory prerequisite for all CORDIC operations. It is typically called inside the higher-level ca_cordic_init() function, which sets a static flag (s_cordic_ok) used by subsequent calculation functions like ca_cordic_calc, ca_cordic_sincos, or ca_cordic_polar to ensure the hardware is ready. If this function returns false, the application must avoid calling any CORDIC calculation functions to prevent undefined behavior or bus faults.

ca_cordic_init.brief: Initializes the hardware CORDIC coprocessor if available on the current STM32 chip.
ca_cordic_init.returns: Returns true if the CORDIC hardware is present and successfully initialized; returns false if the hardware is missing or initialization failed.
ca_cordic_init.notes: This function is a hardware abstraction layer (HAL) wrapper. It is not thread-safe in the sense that it should be called once during system startup before any tasks attempt to use CORDIC calculations. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. The most common mistake is failing to check the return value; if you call other ca_cordic_* functions without verifying this initialization, you may trigger a hard fault or receive undefined data because the peripheral registers do not exist on the target silicon.
ca_cordic_init.usage: Use this function during the system configuration phase, typically inside ca_os_configure or early in the main application entry point. It acts as a gatekeeper: if it returns false, the application should gracefully disable features that rely on trigonometric acceleration (like motor control loops or signal processing) to prevent runtime crashes. It is the mandatory prerequisite for all other ca_cordic_* functions.

ca_cordic_polar.signature: bool ca_cordic_polar(i32 x, i32 y, i32 *angle, i32 *modulus)
ca_cordic_polar.brief: Converts Cartesian coordinates (x, y) into polar coordinates (angle, modulus) using the CORDIC hardware peripheral.

params.name: x
params.desc: The X-coordinate in Q31 fixed-point format.

params.name: y
params.desc: The Y-coordinate in Q31 fixed-point format.

params.name: angle
params.desc: Pointer to store the resulting angle (normalized as rad/pi). Must be a valid memory address.

params.name: modulus
params.desc: Pointer to store the resulting magnitude (modulus). Must be a valid memory address.

ca_cordic_polar.returns: Returns true if the calculation completed successfully, false if the input parameters were invalid or the hardware failed to compute.
ca_cordic_polar.notes: This function utilizes the CORDIC hardware accelerator, which is significantly faster than software-based trigonometric calculations. It is thread-safe assuming the underlying hardware peripheral is not being accessed concurrently by another task or ISR. It is non-blocking in the sense that it triggers the hardware and waits for the result, but it should not be called from an ISR unless the hardware is guaranteed to be idle. A common beginner mistake is passing NULL pointers for the output parameters, which will cause a hard fault or memory corruption.
ca_cordic_polar.usage: This function is typically used in signal processing, motor control, or coordinate transformation tasks where Cartesian-to-Polar conversion is required. It is often paired with ca_cordic_calc for more complex operations or ca_cordic_sincos for the inverse operation. Before using this, ensure the CORDIC peripheral has been initialized via the system startup or a specific initialization routine if required by your board configuration.

ca_cordic_sincos.brief: Calculates the sine and cosine of a given angle using the hardware CORDIC peripheral.

params.name: angle
params.desc: The input angle represented in Q31 format, where the full circle (2*pi) is mapped to the range [-1, 1) of the i32 type.

params.name: sin_q31
params.desc: Pointer to an i32 variable where the resulting sine value (in Q31 format) will be stored.

params.name: cos_q31
params.desc: Pointer to an i32 variable where the resulting cosine value (in Q31 format) will be stored.

ca_cordic_sincos.returns: Returns true if the calculation was successful, false otherwise. A false return typically indicates an invalid pointer or a failure in the underlying hardware peripheral communication.
ca_cordic_sincos.notes: This function utilizes the STM32 hardware CORDIC peripheral, which is significantly faster than software-based trigonometric calculations. It is thread-safe, but because it relies on a shared hardware resource, it may block the calling task if the CORDIC unit is currently busy with another operation. It is generally not recommended to call this from an ISR unless the hardware is guaranteed to be idle, as blocking in an ISR is strictly forbidden in RTOS environments. Ensure the CORDIC peripheral is properly initialized before use; failing to do so will result in undefined behavior or incorrect calculations.
ca_cordic_sincos.usage: This function is used in digital signal processing, motor control, or any application requiring fast trigonometric transformations. It is typically used in a loop or a periodic task to update control signals. It is often paired with ca_cordic_polar for coordinate conversions. Before calling this, ensure your application has initialized the necessary hardware resources, and always check the boolean return value to ensure the calculation completed successfully before using the results.

ca_crc32_get.brief: Calculates the CRC32 checksum of a data buffer using the STM32 hardware CRC peripheral.

params.name: buff
params.desc: Pointer to the start of the data buffer. Must be a valid memory address; passing NULL will cause a hard fault.

params.name: size
params.desc: The number of bytes to process. A size of 0 is technically valid but will return the CRC reset value.

ca_crc32_get.returns: Returns a 32-bit unsigned integer representing the calculated CRC checksum.
ca_crc32_get.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses a mutex to protect the shared hardware CRC peripheral. It is a blocking function, meaning the calling task will wait if another task is currently calculating a CRC. You must NEVER call this function from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because the mutex lock will cause a system hang or kernel panic. The most common mistake is passing an unaligned buffer or an incorrect size, which might lead to unexpected results if the hardware peripheral expects specific alignment; however, this implementation handles tail bytes manually to ensure correctness. Ensure the CRC peripheral clock is enabled in your system initialization before calling this function.
ca_crc32_get.usage: Use this function whenever you need to verify data integrity, such as checking if a configuration block in Flash has been corrupted or validating a packet received over a communication interface. It is typically used in a sequence: first, you prepare your data buffer, then you call ca_crc32_get to generate the checksum, and finally, you compare the result against a known good value or store it for later verification. It is often paired with memory management functions to ensure the buffer passed to it remains constant during the calculation process.

ca_crc32_hw_init.brief: Enables the hardware CRC peripheral clock and performs a mandatory bus synchronization read-back.
ca_crc32_hw_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes quickly, but it is not thread-safe if called concurrently from multiple contexts. It must be called before any other interaction with the CRC peripheral registers to ensure the clock is active and the bus write buffer has cleared. The mandatory read-back of the RCC register is critical: without it, the CPU might attempt to access the CRC peripheral before the clock enable signal has propagated, resulting in an asynchronous BusFault. It is intended to be called during system initialization and should not be called repeatedly in a loop.
ca_crc32_hw_init.usage: This function is the first step in the CRC peripheral lifecycle, typically called within a higher-level initialization function like ca_crc32_init. It is used to prepare the hardware for subsequent operations such as calculating checksums. It is usually paired with peripheral-specific register resets (e.g., setting the CRC_CR_RESET bit) and the initialization of synchronization primitives like mutexes to ensure safe access to the shared hardware resource.

ca_crc32_init.brief: Initializes the hardware CRC32 peripheral and its associated software synchronization primitives.
ca_crc32_init.returns: This function returns void and does not provide a status code; it assumes the hardware initialization succeeds.
ca_crc32_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs hardware-level configuration, including clock enabling and peripheral resetting. It is not thread-safe during the initialization phase itself, so it must be called during the system startup sequence before any threads are spawned. It is strictly forbidden to call this from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it initializes a mutex, which is a blocking synchronization primitive that cannot be used in interrupt context. A common beginner mistake is calling this function multiple times or after the OS scheduler has started, which could lead to race conditions or re-initialization of the mutex, potentially causing system instability or deadlocks.
ca_crc32_init.usage: This function is intended to be called exactly once during the system boot-up phase, typically inside the 'ca_os_configure' or main initialization routine. It acts as a prerequisite for any subsequent CRC calculation tasks. It is usually paired with 'ca_mutex_init' (called internally) to ensure that multiple threads can safely share the single hardware CRC peripheral without corrupting each other's calculations. Once initialized, the CRC module is ready to be used by other application threads to verify data integrity.

ca_critical_nesting_level.brief: Returns the current depth of nested critical sections in the system.
ca_critical_nesting_level.returns: Returns a u32 integer representing the current nesting level. A value of 0 indicates that the system is currently outside of any critical section.
ca_critical_nesting_level.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it simply reads a global counter variable. It is safe to call from both task context and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs). The most common mistake is assuming that a non-zero value implies a specific lock is held; this function only tracks the depth of the global interrupt-disable mechanism. If you call this while interrupts are enabled, it will correctly return 0, but it does not provide information about which specific code block initiated the critical section. It is primarily used for debugging, diagnostic logging, or verifying that a function is being called within a protected context.
ca_critical_nesting_level.usage: This function is typically used for system health monitoring or debugging complex synchronization logic where you need to verify if a code path is running with interrupts disabled. It is often paired with ca_enter_critical() and ca_exit_critical() to ensure that state changes are atomic. In advanced scenarios, developers use it to assert that a function is only called when the system is in a 'safe' state, preventing race conditions by checking the nesting level before accessing shared hardware registers or global variables.

ca_dac_comp_init.brief: Initializes the hardware comparator for a specific DAC channel with a defined hysteresis level.

params.name: dac_channel
params.desc: The DAC channel index to configure. Valid values are 1 or 2.

params.name: hyst
params.desc: The hysteresis level to apply. Must be a valid enum value up to CA_DAC_COMP_HYST_HIGH.

ca_dac_comp_init.returns: Returns true if the initialization was successful, false if the channel index or hysteresis value is out of range or if the hardware initialization failed.
ca_dac_comp_init.notes: This function is a wrapper that configures the internal comparator hardware associated with the DAC. It is not thread-safe and should be called during the initialization phase of your application or when reconfiguring the DAC peripheral. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. A common beginner mistake is passing an invalid channel number (e.g., 0 or 3) or an undefined hysteresis enum, which will immediately return false without modifying the hardware state.
ca_dac_comp_init.usage: Use this function when you need to set up a threshold-based trigger using the DAC comparator. It is typically used in a sequence: first call ca_dac_init to prepare the peripheral, then use ca_dac_comp_init to set the hysteresis, and finally use ca_dac_write to set the reference voltage. If you need to stop the comparator later, use ca_dac_comp_stop.

ca_dac_comp_level.brief: Reads the current state of the DAC comparator pin (PB2) relative to the configured threshold.
ca_dac_comp_level.returns: Returns true if the voltage on the comparator pin is above the DAC threshold, and false if it is below.
ca_dac_comp_level.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately by reading the hardware register state. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs a single atomic read of the hardware, but it does not provide any synchronization or debouncing logic. It is safe to call from an ISR, as it does not involve any OS primitives or blocking calls. A common mistake is assuming the signal is noise-free; because this is a raw hardware read, you should implement software filtering or multiple reads if you need to ensure the signal has truly settled.
ca_dac_comp_level.usage: This function is typically used in control loops or calibration routines where you need to determine if an external signal has crossed a specific voltage level defined by the DAC. It is usually paired with ca_dac_comp_init to set up the threshold and hysteresis before polling. In a typical sequence, you call ca_dac_comp_init once during system startup, then periodically call ca_dac_comp_level within a task or a timer-driven loop to monitor the signal state, and finally call ca_dac_comp_stop when monitoring is no longer required.

ca_dac_comp_stop.brief: Stops the DAC comparator hardware operation.
ca_dac_comp_stop.notes: This function immediately halts the DAC comparator peripheral. It is non-blocking and does not return a status, meaning it assumes the hardware is in a state where it can be safely stopped. It is not thread-safe by itself; if multiple tasks access the DAC hardware, you must ensure external synchronization. Do not call this from an ISR unless the underlying hardware driver explicitly supports it, as it may interfere with ongoing peripheral operations. A common mistake is calling this before the comparator has been initialized, which may lead to undefined behavior in the hardware registers.
ca_dac_comp_stop.usage: This function is typically used during the teardown phase of a DAC-based measurement or signal processing task. It is usually paired with ca_dac_comp_init, which sets up the comparator, and is called when the monitoring task is finished or needs to be reset. In a typical lifecycle, you would initialize the DAC and comparator, perform your logic, and then call ca_dac_comp_stop to release the hardware resources or put the peripheral into a low-power state.

ca_dac_hw_comp_init.brief: Initializes the internal hardware comparator to use a DAC channel as a threshold reference.

params.name: dac_channel
params.desc: The DAC channel to use as the reference (1 or 2). Invalid values will cause the function to return false.

params.name: hyst
params.desc: Hysteresis level to apply to the comparator. Valid values depend on the specific MCU hardware capabilities.

ca_dac_hw_comp_init.returns: Returns true if the hardware was successfully configured, false if the hardware does not support this feature or if invalid parameters were provided.
ca_dac_hw_comp_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs direct register manipulation to configure the internal comparator peripheral. It is not thread-safe and should be called during the system initialization phase before the comparator is used. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. A common mistake is assuming this function is available on all STM32 families; always check the specific hardware implementation, as many series (like F1, F4, F7) do not include this hardware comparator block and will return false.
ca_dac_hw_comp_init.usage: This function is used to set up a hardware-based threshold detection system where the DAC output acts as a dynamic reference voltage for the comparator. It is typically paired with ca_dac_init to configure the DAC itself, followed by this function to link the comparator to the DAC output. Once initialized, the application can monitor the threshold state using ca_dac_comp_level and eventually clean up the configuration using ca_dac_comp_stop.

ca_dac_hw_comp_level.brief: Reads the current digital output state of the hardware comparator associated with the DAC.
ca_dac_hw_comp_level.returns: Returns true if the comparator output is high (logic 1), and false if it is low (logic 0) or if the hardware does not support a comparator.
ca_dac_hw_comp_level.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately by reading a hardware register. It is thread-safe as it performs a single atomic read operation, and it is safe to call from an ISR. Note that on many STM32 series (like F1, F4, F7, H5, H7RS), this function will always return false because those specific chips lack the integrated comparator hardware required for this feature. Always verify your target hardware capabilities before relying on this value for control logic, as a false return does not necessarily mean the level is low; it may simply mean the feature is unavailable on your specific MCU.
ca_dac_hw_comp_level.usage: This function is typically used in control loops where the DAC output is being monitored against an external reference voltage via the internal comparator. It is usually called after initializing the comparator with ca_dac_comp_init and before calling ca_dac_comp_stop. It is often used to implement simple threshold detection or 'bang-bang' control logic where the software adjusts the DAC output based on whether the comparator level is high or low.

ca_dac_hw_comp_stop.brief: Disables the hardware comparator associated with the DAC peripheral.
ca_dac_hw_comp_stop.notes: This function is a low-level hardware abstraction that immediately clears the configuration register of the comparator peripheral. It is non-blocking and executes in constant time, making it safe to call from both thread context and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs). However, it does not perform any state checking; calling it when the comparator is already disabled or not present on the specific MCU architecture is harmless but redundant. The primary risk is that it abruptly cuts off the comparator signal, which might cause unexpected behavior in external circuitry or logic that relies on the comparator's output state.
ca_dac_hw_comp_stop.usage: This function is typically used during the teardown phase of a DAC operation or when reconfiguring the analog front-end. It is usually paired with ca_dac_comp_init to stop monitoring or signal generation once the task is complete. In a typical lifecycle, you would initialize the DAC and comparator, perform your operations, and then call this function to ensure the hardware is returned to a safe, idle state, preventing unnecessary power consumption or signal interference.

ca_dac_hw_init_periph.brief: Initializes and enables a specific DAC hardware channel for analog output.

params.name: channel
params.desc: The DAC channel number to initialize. Valid values are 1 or 2. Any other value will cause the function to return false.

ca_dac_hw_init_periph.returns: Returns true if the channel was successfully initialized and enabled, false if the channel index is invalid or the hardware configuration failed.
ca_dac_hw_init_periph.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should be called during the system initialization phase before any DAC write operations occur. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. The function performs direct register manipulation to enable the DAC peripheral; therefore, the system clock and GPIO configuration for the DAC pins must be completed prior to calling this function. A common mistake is attempting to call this function multiple times without checking the return value or failing to initialize the required GPIOs first, which can lead to undefined behavior or silent hardware failure.
ca_dac_hw_init_periph.usage: This function is typically used as the final step in the DAC initialization sequence. The standard workflow involves calling the clock initialization function, then the GPIO configuration function, and finally this function to enable the peripheral. It is often paired with ca_dac_write to output analog signals once the hardware is ready. In systems with CLI support, it is common to track the active status of the DAC channel after a successful call to this function to prevent redundant initializations.

ca_dac_hw_stop.brief: Disables a specific DAC channel by disconnecting its output buffer from the pin.

params.name: channel
params.desc: The DAC channel index to stop. Valid values are 1 or 2. Passing any other value will result in a failure.

ca_dac_hw_stop.returns: Returns true if the channel was successfully disabled, or false if the channel index is invalid or the hardware does not support the operation.
ca_dac_hw_stop.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately by modifying the DAC control register. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs a single atomic register write, but it does not provide synchronization if multiple threads attempt to control the same DAC channel simultaneously. It is safe to call from an ISR, as it does not perform any blocking operations or OS-level synchronization. A common mistake is assuming that calling this function returns the pin to a standard GPIO state; the pin remains in analog mode, so you must manually reconfigure the pin using ca_gpio_configure if you intend to use it for digital I/O after stopping the DAC.
ca_dac_hw_stop.usage: This function is typically used during system shutdown, power-saving transitions, or when reconfiguring a pin for a different peripheral function. It is the counterpart to the initialization sequence and is usually called as part of a cleanup routine to ensure the DAC output is disconnected and the analog buffer is powered down. In the caOS driver architecture, it is often wrapped by a higher-level function (like ca_dac_stop) that also updates internal state tracking variables to prevent further write attempts to a disabled channel.

ca_dac_hw_write.brief: Writes a raw 12-bit digital value to the specified DAC hardware channel.

params.name: channel
params.desc: The DAC channel identifier, typically 1 or 2. Passing an invalid channel index will result in no action taken by the hardware registers.

params.name: val
params.desc: The raw 12-bit value to convert to analog voltage. Valid range is 0 to 4095 (0x0FFF). Values exceeding 4095 will be truncated by the hardware register.

ca_dac_hw_write.returns: void. This function does not return a status code, so it assumes the hardware is already initialized and the parameters are valid.
ca_dac_hw_write.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately by writing directly to the DAC peripheral registers. It is generally thread-safe in the sense that register writes are atomic, but it does not implement any locking mechanisms, so concurrent writes to the same channel from different tasks or ISRs may lead to race conditions. You must ensure that the DAC peripheral is properly configured before calling this function; otherwise, the hardware may not be clocked or configured, and the write will have no effect. A common beginner mistake is assuming this function handles voltage scaling or calibration; it only writes raw bits, so you must perform any necessary math to convert your desired voltage into the 0-4095 range before calling it.
ca_dac_hw_write.usage: This function is used to update the analog output voltage of the DAC peripheral in real-time. It is typically paired with initialization functions like ca_dac_init during system startup. In advanced applications, it is often called inside timer callbacks or periodic tasks to generate waveforms, such as sine waves or ramps, by updating the DAC value at a fixed frequency. It is designed for low-latency updates where the overhead of a full driver stack is not required.

ca_dac_init.brief: Initializes the DAC peripheral hardware, clock, and GPIO pins for a specific channel.

params.name: cfg
params.desc: Pointer to a configuration structure containing the channel number (1 or 2). Must not be NULL.

ca_dac_init.returns: Returns true if the hardware initialization was successful, false if the configuration pointer is NULL, the channel is invalid, or the peripheral hardware failed to initialize.
ca_dac_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs low-level hardware setup, including enabling the peripheral clock and configuring the associated GPIO pins as analog outputs. It is not thread-safe and should be called during the system initialization phase (e.g., inside ca_os_configure) before any write operations are attempted. It must NOT be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it performs hardware configuration that may involve timing-sensitive operations. A common beginner mistake is passing an uninitialized configuration structure or attempting to initialize the same channel multiple times without checking the return value, which can lead to undefined hardware states.
ca_dac_init.usage: This function is the mandatory first step for using the DAC peripheral. It is typically called once during system startup to prepare the hardware. After a successful call, the application can proceed to use functions like ca_dac_write to output analog voltages. If the application requires CLI debugging, this function also handles the registration of the DAC command interface, allowing technicians to monitor or test the DAC state via the console.

ca_dac_stop.brief: Disables a specific DAC channel and resets its internal state.

params.name: channel
params.desc: The DAC channel number to stop. Valid values are 1 or 2. Any other value will cause the function to return false.

ca_dac_stop.returns: Returns true if the channel was successfully stopped, false if the channel index is invalid or the hardware failed to stop.
ca_dac_stop.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should not be called from an ISR. It performs hardware-level operations to disconnect the DAC output buffer from the physical pin, which is critical to prevent electrical contention if you intend to reconfigure the pin as a standard GPIO. Always ensure the DAC has been initialized via ca_dac_init before attempting to stop it. A common mistake is assuming that writing a value of 0 to the DAC is equivalent to stopping it; writing 0 still leaves the output buffer active and connected to the pin, which can interfere with other peripherals sharing that pin.
ca_dac_stop.usage: Use this function when you need to release the DAC hardware, typically during a transition between different peripheral modes (e.g., switching from analog output to digital input/output). It is standard practice to call this before reconfiguring the associated pin using ca_gpio_configure or ca_gpio_init_port to avoid electrical conflicts. It is often paired with ca_dac_init for setup and ca_dac_write for active operation, serving as the cleanup step in the peripheral lifecycle.

ca_dac_write.brief: Writes a 12-bit digital value to the specified DAC channel to generate an analog voltage output.

params.name: channel
params.desc: The DAC channel number. Must be 1 or 2. Values outside this range are ignored by the function.

params.name: val
params.desc: The 12-bit digital value to convert. The function masks this to 0x0FFF (0-4095), so values larger than 4095 are truncated.

ca_dac_write.returns: void. The function does not provide feedback on success or failure, so ensure the channel is valid before calling.
ca_dac_write.notes: This function is a wrapper that handles hardware-specific register writes. It is non-blocking and generally safe to call from most contexts, but it does not perform error checking on the hardware state. A common beginner mistake is assuming the function will return an error if the DAC hardware is not initialized; if you call this before ca_dac_init, the write will likely fail silently or cause undefined behavior. It is not thread-safe if multiple tasks attempt to write to the same channel simultaneously without external synchronization.
ca_dac_write.usage: This function is used to output analog signals, such as generating waveforms or setting reference voltages for sensors. The typical lifecycle involves calling ca_dac_init once during system startup to configure the GPIO pins and DAC peripheral, followed by repeated calls to ca_dac_write whenever the output value needs to change. It is often paired with ADC functions when implementing closed-loop control systems where the DAC output is measured by an ADC input.

ca_dhcp_service_bind.brief: Blocks the calling thread until the DHCP service has successfully acquired an IP address.
ca_dhcp_service_bind.returns: Returns true if the DHCP service is already bound or if the binding completes within the timeout period. Returns false if the timeout expires before the DHCP server provides an IP address.
ca_dhcp_service_bind.notes: This function is a blocking call, meaning the calling thread will be suspended by the RTOS scheduler until the semaphore is released or the timeout occurs. It is NOT safe to call this from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) or from the main network processing task, as doing so will prevent the network stack from receiving the DHCP packets required to complete the binding, leading to a permanent deadlock. Ensure the DHCP service has been started via ca_os_job before calling this. A common beginner mistake is calling this in the same thread that is responsible for processing incoming network packets, which effectively kills the system's ability to communicate.
ca_dhcp_service_bind.usage: Use this function in application-level threads that require a valid IP address before proceeding with network operations like opening sockets or starting a web server. It is typically used after the system has initialized the network interface and started the DHCP job. It pairs with the DHCP service lifecycle: first, the service is started, then the application waits for the binding, and finally, the application proceeds once the function returns true. Never use this in the network processing loop itself; instead, use it in a separate worker thread that waits for the network to be ready.

ca_dhcp_service_bound.brief: Checks if the DHCP client has successfully obtained an IP address and is currently bound to a network lease.
ca_dhcp_service_bound.returns: Returns true if the DHCP client is currently bound to an IP address, false otherwise.
ca_dhcp_service_bound.notes: This function is a non-blocking, thread-safe read of an internal status flag. It is safe to call from both tasks and ISRs because it simply returns the current state of a boolean variable. The most common mistake is assuming that a 'true' result guarantees that the network connection is still physically active; it only indicates that the DHCP lease is valid. Always ensure ca_dhcp_service_init has been called before checking this status, otherwise, the flag will always be false.
ca_dhcp_service_bound.usage: This function is typically used in a polling loop or a state machine to verify network readiness before attempting to perform network-dependent operations like opening a TCP socket or sending data. It is often paired with ca_dhcp_service_start to initiate the process and ca_dhcp_service_get_ip to retrieve the assigned address once this function returns true. In a typical application, you would wait for this to return true before proceeding with higher-level protocols like NTP or HTTP.

ca_dhcp_service_get_dns.brief: Retrieves the current DNS server address assigned by the DHCP service.
ca_dhcp_service_get_dns.returns: Returns an ca_ipv4_t structure containing the 4-byte IP address of the DNS server. If no DNS server has been provided by the DHCP server, the structure will typically contain zeros (0.0.0.0).
ca_dhcp_service_get_dns.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses an internal mutex to protect the shared DHCP lease data during access. It is a blocking call in the sense that it must wait for the mutex to be released by any other task currently modifying the DHCP lease information. You must NEVER call this function from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because the mutex lock operation can block the execution, which is strictly forbidden in ISR context. Ensure the DHCP service has been initialized and started via ca_dhcp_service_init and ca_dhcp_service_start before relying on the returned value.
ca_dhcp_service_get_dns.usage: This function is typically used in diagnostic tasks or CLI interfaces to display the current network configuration to the user. It is often paired with other getters like ca_dhcp_service_get_ip, ca_dhcp_service_get_mask, and ca_dhcp_service_get_gw to provide a complete snapshot of the network interface status. It is commonly called after verifying that the network is ready using ca_dhcp_service_net_ready to ensure the returned data is valid and not stale.

ca_dhcp_service_get_gw.brief: Retrieves the current IPv4 gateway address assigned by the DHCP service.
ca_dhcp_service_get_gw.returns: Returns a ca_ipv4_t structure containing the four bytes of the gateway IP address. If the DHCP service has not yet obtained a lease or is not initialized, the returned structure will contain the default or zeroed values.
ca_dhcp_service_get_gw.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses a mutex (s_lease_mtx) to protect the internal DHCP state variables during the read operation. It is a blocking call in the sense that it must wait for the mutex to be available; therefore, it must NEVER be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine), as blocking in an ISR will cause a system crash or watchdog reset. Ensure that ca_dhcp_service_init has been called successfully before attempting to read network parameters, otherwise, you will receive uninitialized or default data.
ca_dhcp_service_get_gw.usage: This function is typically used in diagnostic tasks or CLI interfaces to display the current network configuration to the user. It is often paired with other getter functions like ca_dhcp_service_get_ip, ca_dhcp_service_get_mask, and ca_dhcp_service_get_dns to provide a complete snapshot of the device's network status. It is usually called after verifying that the network is ready using ca_dhcp_service_net_ready to ensure the returned values are valid and active.

ca_dhcp_service_get_ip.brief: Retrieves the current IPv4 address assigned to the device by the DHCP service.
ca_dhcp_service_get_ip.returns: Returns an ca_ipv4_t structure containing the four bytes of the IP address. If the DHCP service has not yet acquired an address, the returned structure will typically contain zeros (0.0.0.0).
ca_dhcp_service_get_ip.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses a mutex to protect the internal IP variable during access. It is non-blocking in the sense that it does not wait for network activity, but it does perform a mutex lock, so it must NEVER be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine). The DHCP service must be initialized via ca_dhcp_service_init and started via ca_dhcp_service_start before this function will return a valid, non-zero IP address. A common mistake is calling this immediately after system boot without checking if the network is actually ready using ca_dhcp_service_net_ready.
ca_dhcp_service_get_ip.usage: This function is typically used in application tasks or CLI handlers to display or log the device's network identity. It is often paired with ca_dhcp_service_get_mask and ca_dhcp_service_get_gw to retrieve the full network configuration. Developers should use this in a sequence where they first verify the connection status with ca_dhcp_service_net_ready or ca_dhcp_service_bound before attempting to use the IP address for network communication.

ca_dhcp_service_get_mask.brief: Retrieves the current IPv4 subnet mask assigned to the device by the DHCP service.
ca_dhcp_service_get_mask.returns: Returns an ca_ipv4_t structure containing the 4-byte subnet mask. If the DHCP service has not yet acquired a lease, the returned structure will contain the default or uninitialized values (typically 0.0.0.0).
ca_dhcp_service_get_mask.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses a mutex to protect the internal DHCP lease data structure during the read operation. It is a blocking call in the sense that it must wait for the mutex to be available, so it must never be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) as this could cause a system deadlock. Ensure that the DHCP service has been initialized via ca_dhcp_service_init before calling this function, otherwise, you will be reading uninitialized memory. A common mistake is assuming the mask is valid immediately after boot; always verify the network state using ca_dhcp_service_net_ready before relying on the returned mask.
ca_dhcp_service_get_mask.usage: This function is typically used in network diagnostic tasks or CLI interfaces to display the current network configuration to the user. It is often called in a sequence alongside ca_dhcp_service_get_ip, ca_dhcp_service_get_gw, and ca_dhcp_service_get_dns to provide a complete snapshot of the device's network identity. Developers use this to verify that the DHCP handshake was successful and that the assigned subnet mask matches the expected network topology.

ca_dhcp_service_get_ntp_server.brief: Retrieves the NTP server IP address obtained from the DHCP server via Option 42.
ca_dhcp_service_get_ntp_server.returns: An ca_ipv4_t structure containing the NTP server IP address. If no NTP server was provided by the DHCP lease, the address field will be 0.0.0.0.
ca_dhcp_service_get_ntp_server.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses a mutex to protect access to the internal DHCP lease data structure. It is a blocking call because it must acquire a mutex; therefore, it must NEVER be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) or a critical section where blocking is prohibited. A common mistake is assuming the returned IP is always valid; always check if the address is 0.0.0.0 before using it, as the DHCP server might not have provided an NTP option.
ca_dhcp_service_get_ntp_server.usage: This function is typically used during the network initialization phase after a DHCP lease has been successfully acquired. It is usually paired with ca_dhcp_service_bound to ensure the lease is active, and then used to configure the NTP client via ca_ntp_service_set_server. If the returned IP is zero, developers often implement a fallback mechanism, such as using the gateway IP address retrieved via ca_dhcp_service_get_gw.

ca_dhcp_service_get_state.brief: Returns a human-readable string representing the current internal state of the DHCP client service.
ca_dhcp_service_get_state.returns: A pointer to a constant string literal (e.g., "INIT", "BOUND", "UNKNOWN"). This pointer is always valid and never NULL, as it points to static memory defined within the function.
ca_dhcp_service_get_state.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe because it performs a simple read of a state variable without requiring mutex locks. It is safe to call from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) or any task context. The most common mistake is assuming the returned string can be modified; since it points to read-only memory, attempting to write to it will cause a hard fault. Because the state can change asynchronously, the returned string is only a snapshot of the DHCP status at the exact moment the function was called.
ca_dhcp_service_get_state.usage: This function is primarily used for diagnostic purposes, such as logging the network status to a console or a remote monitoring interface. It is typically paired with other DHCP getter functions to provide a full report of the network configuration. Developers use it to verify that the DHCP state machine has successfully reached the 'BOUND' state before attempting to perform network-dependent operations like opening sockets or sending data. It is usually called after the service has been initialized via ca_dhcp_service_init and started via ca_dhcp_service_start.

ca_dhcp_service_init.signature: void ca_dhcp_service_init(ca_mac_t local_mac, ca_dhcp_bound_cb_t on_bound, ca_dhcp_expire_cb_t on_expire)
ca_dhcp_service_init.brief: Initializes the internal DHCP service state, semaphores, and callback functions required for dynamic IP assignment.

params.name: local_mac
params.desc: The unique hardware MAC address of the device. Must be a valid 6-byte array; passing an invalid or zeroed MAC will cause DHCP discovery to fail.

params.name: on_bound
params.desc: Pointer to a callback function executed when an IP address is successfully leased. Cannot be NULL if you need to react to network configuration changes.

params.name: on_expire
params.desc: Pointer to a callback function executed when the DHCP lease expires. Essential for handling network disconnections or re-negotiation.

ca_dhcp_service_init.returns: void. This function does not return a status code, so ensure all parameters are valid before calling.
ca_dhcp_service_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs internal initialization of RTOS primitives like semaphores and mutexes. It is not thread-safe and must be called exactly once during the system startup phase, typically before the RTOS scheduler starts or within the main initialization task. It is strictly forbidden to call this from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it performs memory and synchronization object initialization. A common beginner mistake is calling this function multiple times or after the network stack has already started, which will corrupt the internal state and lead to unpredictable DHCP behavior.
ca_dhcp_service_init.usage: This function is the mandatory first step in the DHCP lifecycle. It is typically paired with ca_dhcp_service_start() to begin the DORA (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge) process. Developers use it to register application-specific callbacks (on_bound/on_expire) that allow the main application to know when the network is ready or when the lease is lost. It is usually called in the system initialization sequence alongside other network services like ca_arp_service_init, ca_ntp_service_init, or ca_dns_service_init to ensure the network stack is fully configured before traffic begins.

ca_dhcp_service_net_ready.brief: Signals the DHCP service that the network interface is initialized and ready to begin the DORA process.
ca_dhcp_service_net_ready.notes: This function is a non-blocking wrapper that interacts with a semaphore to gate the DHCP service state machine. It is thread-safe and can be called from tasks, but it is not intended for use inside an ISR. The function performs a 'trywait' followed by a 'post' to ensure the semaphore state is consistent, effectively acting as a 'gate-opener' for the DHCP task. A common mistake is calling this before the Ethernet link is physically established or before the network stack is fully initialized; doing so will cause the DHCP task to attempt communication on a non-existent link, leading to failed discovery packets.
ca_dhcp_service_net_ready.usage: This function is used as a synchronization trigger in the system startup sequence. It is typically called after the Ethernet link has been verified (e.g., via ca_eth_link_poll) and the network stack is ready to handle UDP traffic on port 68. It pairs with the internal DHCP task loop, which remains blocked until this function is invoked. By calling this, you transition the DHCP service from an idle/waiting state to the active DORA (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge) state, allowing the device to obtain an IP address.

ca_dhcp_service_renew.brief: Triggers a DHCP lease renewal process by sending a renewal event to the DHCP service queue.
ca_dhcp_service_renew.returns: This function returns void and does not provide feedback on whether the renewal request was successfully queued.
ca_dhcp_service_renew.notes: This function is non-blocking because it uses ca_queue_static_trysend, which attempts to place the event in the queue without waiting if the queue is full. It is thread-safe as it relies on the underlying queue implementation, but it is intended to be called from task contexts rather than ISRs, as queue operations can be complex. A mandatory precondition is that the DHCP service must have been initialized and the event queue must be active; otherwise, the event will be silently dropped. The most common beginner mistake is assuming the renewal happens instantly; this function only queues a request, and the actual network transaction will occur later when the DHCP service task processes the event.
ca_dhcp_service_renew.usage: This function is typically used in command-line interfaces (CLI) or system monitoring tasks to manually force the device to request a new IP address or extend its current lease from the DHCP server. It is often paired with network status checks, such as verifying that the link is up before triggering the renewal. In a typical lifecycle, it is called after the system has successfully initialized the network stack and the DHCP service, serving as a diagnostic or recovery tool when the user suspects the current lease is stale or invalid.

ca_dhcp_service_rx_handler.brief: Processes incoming DHCP UDP packets and dispatches events to the DHCP state machine queue.

params.name: udp
params.desc: Pointer to the incoming UDP frame structure. Must be a valid, non-NULL pointer containing valid DHCP protocol data.

params.name: len
params.desc: The length of the UDP payload in bytes. While currently unused in the implementation, it should represent the actual size of the received data.

ca_dhcp_service_rx_handler.returns: void. This function does not return a status code; it performs internal processing and queues events for other tasks to handle.
ca_dhcp_service_rx_handler.notes: This function is designed to be called from the network stack's receive callback context. It is not inherently thread-safe if called concurrently from multiple threads, though it is typically invoked by a single network task. It is non-blocking, as it uses 'ca_queue_static_trysend' to push events to a queue without waiting for space. A common beginner mistake is calling this function with a pointer to invalid memory or failing to free the network buffer after calling this handler, which leads to memory leaks in the network stack. Ensure the network stack is initialized before this handler is triggered.
ca_dhcp_service_rx_handler.usage: This function is the bridge between the raw network stack and the DHCP service logic. It is typically called inside a network packet receive callback after the stack has identified the packet as a DHCP UDP frame. After calling this handler, the developer must call 'ca_net_buf_free' to release the buffer back to the system. It is used in conjunction with 'ca_dhcp_service_bind' to manage the lifecycle of an IP address acquisition, where the handler updates the state machine that 'ca_dhcp_service_bind' is waiting on.

ca_dhcp_service_start.brief: Initializes and launches the background DHCP client task within the RTOS environment.
ca_dhcp_service_start.returns: This function returns void and does not provide a status code; it assumes the OS job scheduler successfully queues the task.
ca_dhcp_service_start.notes: This function is non-blocking as it merely registers a new task with the OS scheduler. It is not thread-safe to call this from an ISR, as it involves memory allocation and scheduler manipulation. You must ensure the network stack and underlying hardware drivers are initialized before calling this, otherwise, the DHCP task will immediately fault upon execution. A common beginner mistake is calling this multiple times; doing so will spawn multiple redundant DHCP client tasks, leading to unpredictable network behavior and potential memory exhaustion. Additionally, the stack size is automatically determined based on the hardware platform to ensure the MPU guard remains aligned; do not attempt to manually override this logic.
ca_dhcp_service_start.usage: This function is typically called once during the system startup sequence inside 'ca_os_main'. It is part of the network initialization phase, usually paired with other service starters like 'ca_arp_service_start', 'ca_dns_service_start', or 'ca_udp_server_start'. Once started, the DHCP service runs autonomously in the background, managing IP address acquisition and lease renewals without further intervention from the main application thread. It is essential that this is invoked before any application logic that requires a valid network configuration.

ca_dma2d_abort.brief: Immediately stops any ongoing DMA2D hardware operation and resets the internal driver state.
ca_dma2d_abort.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs an immediate hardware-level abort of the DMA2D peripheral. It is not thread-safe by itself, so ensure that no other task attempts to initiate a new DMA2D operation while this is executing. It is generally safe to call from an ISR if the hardware state needs to be cleared urgently, but it is primarily intended for task-level error recovery. A common mistake is calling this function without checking if the DMA2D is actually busy, which is harmless but unnecessary; however, failing to call it after a timeout or error will leave the DMA2D driver in a 'busy' state, preventing any subsequent operations from starting.
ca_dma2d_abort.usage: Use this function when a DMA2D operation (like a fill, copy, or blend) takes too long or encounters an error, and you need to force the hardware to stop to regain control. It is typically paired with ca_dma2d_busy() to check if an operation is still running before deciding to abort. In a typical sequence, you might start an operation with a non-blocking call, wait for a specific condition, and if that condition is not met within a timeout, call ca_dma2d_abort() to clean up the driver state before attempting the next operation.

ca_dma2d_blend.signature: bool ca_dma2d_blend(const ca_dma2d_src_t *fg, const ca_dma2d_src_t *bg, const ca_dma2d_dst_t *d, u32 w, u32 h, u32 timeout_ms)
ca_dma2d_blend.brief: Performs a hardware-accelerated alpha blending of two source images into a destination buffer using the DMA2D peripheral.

params.name: fg
params.desc: Pointer to the foreground image source structure containing address, format, and alpha settings.

params.name: bg
params.desc: Pointer to the background image source structure.

params.name: d
params.desc: Pointer to the destination buffer structure defining the target memory area and format.

params.name: w
params.desc: Width of the area to blend in pixels. Must be valid for the hardware constraints.

params.name: h
params.desc: Height of the area to blend in pixels. Must be valid for the hardware constraints.

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time in milliseconds to wait for the DMA2D hardware to complete the operation.

ca_dma2d_blend.returns: Returns true if the blending operation was successfully queued and completed within the timeout. Returns false if parameters are invalid, the hardware is busy, or the operation timed out.
ca_dma2d_blend.notes: This function is blocking; it waits for the DMA2D hardware to finish the transfer before returning. It is not thread-safe by itself, meaning if multiple tasks attempt to use the DMA2D simultaneously, you must protect this call with a mutex or ensure exclusive access. It must NOT be called from an ISR because it performs a blocking wait. Before calling this, ensure the DMA2D peripheral has been initialized via ca_dma2d_init. A common mistake is passing unaligned memory addresses or invalid dimensions that exceed the buffer boundaries, which will cause the function to return false immediately.
ca_dma2d_blend.usage: This function is typically used in graphics rendering pipelines to compose UI elements, such as overlaying icons or text onto a background. It is usually paired with ca_dma2d_init during system startup. In a typical sequence, you define the source and destination structures, call ca_dma2d_blend to perform the hardware operation, and then proceed to the next rendering step. If you need to perform multiple operations, you can check ca_dma2d_busy before initiating a new one to avoid contention.

ca_dma2d_bpp.brief: Returns the number of bits per pixel (BPP) for a given DMA2D color format.

params.name: fmt
params.desc: The DMA2D color format identifier. Must be a valid enum value defined by the driver; passing an out-of-bounds value will result in a return of 0.

ca_dma2d_bpp.returns: The number of bits per pixel (e.g., 8, 16, 24, 32) as a u32. Returns 0 if the format identifier is invalid or out of the supported range.
ca_dma2d_bpp.notes: This function is a simple, thread-safe, non-blocking lookup table accessor. It does not interact with hardware registers, making it safe to call from an ISR or any task context. It does not require the DMA2D peripheral to be initialized. The most common mistake is failing to check for a return value of 0, which leads to division-by-zero errors or incorrect memory allocation sizes when calculating buffer offsets.
ca_dma2d_bpp.usage: This function is essential for calculating memory requirements and pixel offsets in graphics applications. It is typically used during the initialization phase of a graphics task to determine buffer sizes via ca_memory_allocate, or inside custom pixel-processing loops to calculate byte-level pointers. It is frequently used in conjunction with ca_dma2d_copy or ca_dma2d_fill to validate that the provided format is compatible with the intended memory layout before triggering hardware operations.

ca_dma2d_busy.brief: Checks if the DMA2D hardware peripheral is currently performing a data transfer operation.
ca_dma2d_busy.returns: Returns true if the DMA2D engine is busy processing a command, or false if it is idle or the driver is not initialized.
ca_dma2d_busy.notes: This function is non-blocking and provides a snapshot of the hardware state. It is thread-safe in the sense that it reads a volatile hardware status register, but it does not guarantee that the state won't change immediately after the function returns. It is safe to call from an ISR, though typically used in task context to poll for completion before starting a new operation or to verify if an abort was successful. A common beginner mistake is to assume that if this returns false, the memory buffers are immediately safe to modify; always ensure the DMA2D operation has fully completed or been aborted before accessing the target memory.
ca_dma2d_busy.usage: This function is typically used in a polling loop or a conditional check to determine if the DMA2D engine is available for a new task. It is often paired with ca_dma2d_fill, ca_dma2d_copy, or ca_dma2d_blend to check if a previous operation has finished before triggering a new one. In scenarios where a timeout occurs, it is used in conjunction with ca_dma2d_abort to verify that the hardware has successfully stopped its current activity before proceeding with error recovery or re-initialization.

ca_dma2d_convert.signature: bool ca_dma2d_convert(const ca_dma2d_src_t *s, const ca_dma2d_dst_t *d, u32 w, u32 h, u32 timeout_ms)
ca_dma2d_convert.brief: Performs a hardware-accelerated pixel format conversion (PFC) or memory-to-memory copy using the DMA2D peripheral.

params.name: s
params.desc: Pointer to the source configuration structure, defining memory address, format, and alpha blending parameters.

params.name: d
params.desc: Pointer to the destination configuration structure, defining memory address, stride, and output format.

params.name: w
params.desc: Width of the area to process in pixels.

params.name: h
params.desc: Height of the area to process in pixels.

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time in milliseconds to wait for the hardware operation to complete.

ca_dma2d_convert.returns: Returns true if the conversion was successfully queued and completed within the timeout; returns false if parameters are invalid, the hardware is busy, or the operation timed out.
ca_dma2d_convert.notes: This function is blocking; it waits for the DMA2D hardware to finish the transfer before returning. It is not thread-safe by itself, meaning multiple tasks should not access the DMA2D peripheral simultaneously without external synchronization (e.g., ca_dma2d_lock). It must NOT be called from an ISR because it performs blocking waits. Before calling this, ensure the DMA2D peripheral has been initialized via ca_dma2d_init. A common mistake is passing unaligned memory addresses or invalid strides that do not match the hardware requirements of the STM32 DMA2D engine. If the function returns false, the operation did not complete, and the hardware state may be inconsistent.
ca_dma2d_convert.usage: This function is used in graphics rendering pipelines to convert image data from one format (e.g., L8 or RGB565) to another (e.g., ARGB8888) before displaying it on a screen. It is typically used within a protected section: first, call ca_dma2d_lock to ensure exclusive access to the hardware, then perform the conversion, and finally call ca_dma2d_unlock to release the resource for other tasks. It is often paired with ca_dma2d_init during system startup. If the operation fails, developers should use ca_dma2d_errors to diagnose the specific hardware fault.

ca_dma2d_copy.signature: bool ca_dma2d_copy(const ca_dma2d_src_t *s, const ca_dma2d_dst_t *d, u32 w, u32 h, u32 timeout_ms)
ca_dma2d_copy.brief: Copies a rectangular area of pixel data from a source buffer to a destination buffer using the hardware DMA2D engine.

params.name: s
params.desc: Pointer to the source configuration structure containing address, format, and stride. Must not be NULL.

params.name: d
params.desc: Pointer to the destination configuration structure. Must not be NULL and must match the source format.

params.name: w
params.desc: Width of the rectangular area to copy in pixels.

params.name: h
params.desc: Height of the rectangular area to copy in pixels.

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time in milliseconds to wait for the DMA2D hardware to complete the operation.

ca_dma2d_copy.returns: Returns true if the copy operation was successfully initiated and completed within the timeout; returns false if parameters are invalid, formats mismatch, or the hardware operation timed out.
ca_dma2d_copy.notes: This function is blocking; it will wait for the DMA2D hardware to finish the transfer before returning. It is thread-safe regarding the DMA2D peripheral access, but ensure that the source and destination memory buffers are not modified by other tasks while the transfer is in progress. It must NOT be called from an ISR because it relies on blocking synchronization mechanisms.
