ca_exti_hw_tamper_enable.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called during system initialization before any security-critical tasks start. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. The function relies on the RTC peripheral being clocked; if the RTC is not enabled, the function will fail immediately. A common mistake is calling this before the system clock or RTC peripheral has been properly configured, leading to a silent failure where tamper events are never detected.
ca_exti_hw_tamper_enable.usage: This function is typically used in the security initialization phase of the application. It is paired with ca_exti_tamper_enable (which wraps this function with a callback) to register a handler that will be executed when a tamper event occurs. Once enabled, the system will automatically monitor the tamper pin (e.g., PC13 on some models) and trigger the registered callback if a breach is detected. To stop monitoring, use ca_exti_tamper_disable.

ca_exti_init.signature: bool ca_exti_init(u8 port, u8 pin, ca_exti_edge_t edge, ca_exti_cb_t cb)
ca_exti_init.brief: Configures and enables an external interrupt (EXTI) on a specific GPIO pin with a callback function.

params.name: port
params.desc: The GPIO port identifier (e.g., 0 for Port A, 1 for Port B). Must correspond to valid hardware ports.

params.name: pin
params.desc: The pin number (0-15). Values >= 16 are invalid and will cause the function to return false.

params.name: edge
params.desc: The trigger condition: rising edge, falling edge, or both.

params.name: cb
params.desc: A pointer to the function to be executed when the interrupt occurs. Must not be NULL.

ca_exti_init.returns: Returns true if the EXTI was successfully configured, false if the pin index is out of range or the callback pointer is NULL.
ca_exti_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs hardware-level configuration of the EXTI controller and the NVIC (Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller). It is not thread-safe if called simultaneously from multiple tasks, so it should typically be called during system initialization. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. A common beginner mistake is forgetting that the GPIO pin itself must be configured as an input using the appropriate GPIO driver functions before calling this; otherwise, the hardware will not detect the signal changes.
ca_exti_init.usage: This function is used to set up event-driven hardware interactions, such as buttons, sensors, or communication signals that require immediate CPU attention. It is typically paired with GPIO initialization functions to set the pin mode, and often followed by ca_exti_disable() if the interrupt should not trigger immediately upon startup. In a standard lifecycle, you initialize the GPIO, call ca_exti_init to register the callback, and then use ca_exti_enable() or ca_exti_disable() to manage the interrupt state dynamically during runtime.

ca_exti_tamper_disable.brief: Disables the hardware tamper detection mechanism and clears the associated callback.
ca_exti_tamper_disable.returns: This function returns void and does not provide status feedback.
ca_exti_tamper_disable.notes: This function is a wrapper that interacts with hardware registers via ca_exti_hw_tamper_disable (internal) and resets the internal callback pointer. It is not thread-safe by itself; if multiple tasks attempt to enable or disable the tamper feature simultaneously, you should wrap the call in a critical section using ca_enter_critical and ca_exit_critical. It is generally safe to call from an ISR, but ensure that no other task is concurrently modifying the tamper state. A common mistake is calling this function without having previously initialized the EXTI system, which may lead to undefined behavior depending on the underlying hardware state.
ca_exti_tamper_disable.usage: This function is used to deactivate security tamper monitoring, typically when the system enters a maintenance mode or a trusted state where physical intrusion detection is no longer required. It is usually paired with ca_exti_tamper_enable, which is used to arm the system. In a typical lifecycle, you would call ca_exti_init to set up the EXTI pins, then ca_exti_tamper_enable to start monitoring, and finally ca_exti_tamper_disable when the monitoring session is complete or the device is being shut down.

ca_exti_tamper_dispatch.brief: Dispatches the registered tamper callback function when a hardware tamper event occurs.
ca_exti_tamper_dispatch.returns: This function returns void and does not provide a status code.
ca_exti_tamper_dispatch.notes: This function is designed to be called exclusively from within the hardware EXTI interrupt service routine (ISR) responsible for tamper detection. Because it executes inside an ISR, the callback function it triggers must be extremely fast, non-blocking, and must not attempt to acquire mutexes or perform operations that could lead to a deadlock. A common mistake is performing heavy processing or logging inside the callback; keep the logic limited to setting a flag or notifying a high-priority task via a signal or event.
ca_exti_tamper_dispatch.usage: This function is the bridge between the low-level hardware interrupt and your application logic. You typically pair this with ca_exti_tamper_enable to activate the hardware detection and define a callback function that the system will execute when the tamper pin is triggered. It is used in security-critical applications where immediate action, such as clearing sensitive memory or triggering a system reset, is required upon physical intrusion.

ca_exti_tamper_enable.brief: Registers a callback function to be executed when a hardware tamper event is detected.

params.name: cb
params.desc: A pointer to the function to be called upon tamper detection. Must not be NULL.

ca_exti_tamper_enable.returns: Returns true if the tamper interrupt was successfully enabled and the callback registered; returns false if the callback pointer is NULL or if the hardware initialization failed.
ca_exti_tamper_enable.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should be called during system initialization or from a controlled task context. The callback provided will be executed directly within the context of the EXTI interrupt service routine (ISR), meaning it must be extremely fast, must not contain blocking calls (like delays or mutex locks), and should only perform minimal operations like setting a flag or signaling a task. A common beginner mistake is performing heavy processing or logging inside the callback, which can lead to system instability or missed interrupts. Ensure the hardware tamper pins are correctly configured before calling this function.
ca_exti_tamper_enable.usage: This function is typically used in security-sensitive applications to protect sensitive data stored in backup SRAM or internal memory. It is usually paired with ca_exti_tamper_disable to stop monitoring when the system is in a safe state. The typical sequence is: 1) Initialize the system and memory, 2) Define a callback function that clears sensitive data, 3) Call ca_exti_tamper_enable to arm the security mechanism, 4) Call ca_exti_tamper_disable when the system is powered down or entering a maintenance mode.

ca_fat_cat.brief: Reads an entire file from the filesystem into heap memory and displays its contents via hexdump.

params.name: name
params.desc: The null-terminated string path/filename of the file to read. Must be a valid path within the mounted filesystem.

ca_fat_cat.returns: Returns true if the file was successfully read and dumped, false if the file could not be opened, memory allocation failed, or the file size exceeded the available heap safety margin.
ca_fat_cat.notes: This function is blocking and performs dynamic memory allocation on the heap. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR because it uses mutexes (ca_fat_lock) and heap management functions that are not re-entrant. A common mistake is calling this on very large files; the function includes a safety check that prevents allocation if the file size is too close to the current free heap, which will cause the function to return false to protect system stability. Ensure the filesystem is mounted via ca_fat_mount before calling this, or it will fail immediately.
ca_fat_cat.usage: Use this function for debugging or verifying file contents during development. It is typically used in a sequence: first ensure the filesystem is ready with ca_fat_is_mounted, then call ca_fat_cat to inspect a specific file, and finally ensure no other tasks are starving for memory. It is often paired with ca_fat_ls to verify the file exists before attempting to read it.

ca_fat_cd.brief: Changes the current working directory of the FAT filesystem service.

params.name: dir
params.desc: Path string of the target directory. Use ".." for parent, "/" for root, or a folder name. Must be a valid null-terminated string.

ca_fat_cd.returns: Returns true if the directory was successfully changed, false otherwise (e.g., directory not found, filesystem not mounted, or access error).
ca_fat_cd.notes: This function is blocking and thread-safe, as it internally uses a mutex lock to ensure exclusive access to the FAT filesystem state. It must NOT be called from an ISR because it performs blocking operations that could lead to system instability. Before calling this, ensure the FAT service is initialized and mounted; calling this on an unmounted filesystem will trigger an error and return false. A common mistake is passing a NULL pointer or a path that exceeds the maximum path length supported by the underlying FAT driver.
ca_fat_cd.usage: This function is used to navigate the directory structure of an SD card or flash storage managed by the FAT service. It is typically used in a sequence: first, ensure the service is ready with ca_fat_is_mounted, then use ca_fat_cd to navigate to a specific folder, and finally perform file operations like ca_fat_ls, ca_fat_cat, or ca_fat_touch. It is often paired with ca_fat_pwd to verify the current location after a change.

ca_fat_dclose.brief: Closes an open directory handle and releases the associated memory resources.

params.name: d
params.desc: Pointer to the directory handle structure previously returned by ca_fat_dopen. Must not be NULL.

ca_fat_dclose.returns: Returns an i32 representing the FatFs result code (0 for success, non-zero for error). FR_INVALID_OBJECT is returned if the input pointer is NULL.
ca_fat_dclose.notes: This function is blocking as it performs filesystem operations and uses internal mutexes to ensure thread safety. It is NOT callable from an ISR because it performs memory deallocation and filesystem locking. A common mistake is to continue using the directory handle pointer after calling this function, which leads to a dangling pointer and potential system crashes. Always set your pointer to NULL immediately after calling this function to prevent accidental reuse.
ca_fat_dclose.usage: This function is the mandatory cleanup step after finishing directory traversal operations initiated by ca_fat_dopen. It is typically used in a cleanup sequence where you iterate through an array of active directory handles, close each one, and reset the array slot to NULL. It pairs with ca_fat_dopen and ca_fat_dread to ensure that system resources like memory and filesystem locks are returned to the OS.

ca_fat_dopen.brief: Opens a directory on the filesystem to prepare for reading its contents.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to a directory handle pointer. If successful, this will point to a newly allocated directory object.

params.name: path
params.desc: String containing the path of the directory to open (e.g., "/logs"). Must be a valid null-terminated string.

ca_fat_dopen.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns a negative error code (cast from FRESULT) if the path is invalid, the filesystem is not mounted, or memory allocation fails.
ca_fat_dopen.notes: This function performs dynamic memory allocation for the directory handle; if it fails, it returns an error code and does not modify the output pointer. It is thread-safe because it uses internal locking to protect the filesystem state during the operation. It is strictly non-blocking in terms of RTOS scheduling, but it must NOT be called from an ISR because it performs heap allocation and takes a mutex lock. A common mistake is failing to check the return value, which leads to dereferencing a NULL pointer if the directory does not exist or memory is exhausted.
ca_fat_dopen.usage: This function is the mandatory first step when you need to iterate through files in a directory. It is typically used in a sequence: first call ca_fat_dopen to get the handle, then use ca_fat_dread in a loop to retrieve file entries, and finally call ca_fat_dclose to release the memory and close the directory handle. It is often used when building file explorers or log management systems where you need to list files dynamically.

ca_fat_dread.brief: Reads the next entry from an open directory handle.

params.name: d
params.desc: Pointer to an initialized directory handle previously opened with ca_fat_dopen.

params.name: info
params.desc: Pointer to a structure where the file/directory metadata will be stored upon success.

ca_fat_dread.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns a non-zero error code (FRESULT) if the read fails, if the end of the directory is reached, or if the filesystem is inaccessible.
ca_fat_dread.notes: This function is thread-safe as it internally uses ca_fat_lock and ca_fat_unlock to protect the shared filesystem state. It is a blocking operation, meaning the calling task will wait until the filesystem driver completes the read operation. It must NOT be called from an ISR because it attempts to acquire a mutex. A common mistake is failing to check the return value; if the function returns an error, the 'info' structure will not contain valid data, and attempting to use it will lead to undefined behavior.
ca_fat_dread.usage: This function is used to iterate through the contents of a directory. It is typically used in a loop after calling ca_fat_dopen to initialize the directory handle. Once the loop finishes or an error occurs, the directory handle must be released using ca_fat_dclose to prevent memory leaks and resource exhaustion. It is often paired with ca_memory_allocate to provide the 'info' buffer if it is not allocated on the stack.

ca_fat_fclose.brief: Closes an open file handle and releases the associated memory resources.

params.name: f
params.desc: Pointer to the file handle structure previously returned by ca_fat_fopen. Must not be NULL.

ca_fat_fclose.returns: Returns 0 on success, or a negative error code (FRESULT) if the file could not be closed properly.
ca_fat_fclose.notes: This function is blocking as it performs I/O operations to flush file buffers to the storage medium. It is thread-safe because it internally uses ca_fat_lock and ca_fat_unlock to protect the filesystem state. It must NOT be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it performs blocking operations and memory management. A common mistake is to continue using the file pointer after calling this function, which leads to a dangling pointer and memory corruption.
ca_fat_fclose.usage: This function is used to finalize file operations and free up system resources. It is typically called after all read/write operations are complete, or during system shutdown/reset sequences to ensure data integrity. It is always paired with ca_fat_fopen, which allocates the handle. In a typical lifecycle, you open a file, perform operations, and then call ca_fat_fclose to commit changes and deallocate the handle.

ca_fat_fdisk.brief: Creates a new MBR partition table on the storage device, effectively wiping existing data.

params.name: mb
params.desc: Size of the partition in Megabytes. If 0 is passed, it defaults to 64 MB.

ca_fat_fdisk.returns: Returns true if the partition table was successfully written and the card re-initialized, false otherwise.
ca_fat_fdisk.notes: This function is highly destructive as it overwrites the Master Boot Record (MBR) of the storage device. It is a blocking operation that uses internal locks to ensure thread safety, so it must not be called from an ISR. Before calling this, ensure the FAT service is initialized. A common mistake is assuming this function formats the drive; it only creates the partition table. You must follow this with ca_fat_mkfs() to create the filesystem, otherwise, the drive will remain unreadable.
ca_fat_fdisk.usage: This function is used during the initial setup of a storage medium, typically when preparing a new SD card or resetting a corrupted one. It is part of a mandatory sequence: first call ca_fat_fdisk() to define the partition, then ca_fat_mkfs() to format the volume, and finally ca_fat_mount() to make the files accessible. It is often used in factory test routines or system initialization sequences where the storage state must be guaranteed.

ca_fat_fopen.signature: i32 ca_fat_fopen(ca_fat_file_t **out, const char *path, u8 mode)
ca_fat_fopen.brief: Opens a file on the FAT filesystem and returns a handle for subsequent I/O operations.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to a file handle pointer. It will be updated to point to the allocated file object on success.

params.name: path
params.desc: The null-terminated string path of the file to open.

params.name: mode
params.desc: Bitmask defining access mode (e.g., read, write, append). Must be a valid FATFS mode constant.

ca_fat_fopen.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns a negative error code (e.g., FR_INVALID_PARAMETER, FR_NOT_ENOUGH_CORE, or filesystem-specific errors) if the operation fails.
ca_fat_fopen.notes: This function is blocking and performs dynamic memory allocation for the file object; ensure your heap has sufficient space. It is thread-safe due to internal locking, but it must NOT be called from an ISR because it uses mutexes. You must ensure the filesystem is mounted via ca_fat_mount before calling this. A common mistake is failing to check the return value, which leads to dereferencing a NULL pointer if the file fails to open.
ca_fat_fopen.usage: Use this function to initiate file access before performing read or write operations. It is typically paired with ca_fat_fclose to release the allocated memory and close the file handle. In a typical lifecycle, you call ca_fat_fopen, perform operations like ca_fat_fread or ca_fat_fwrite, and finally call ca_fat_fclose to prevent memory leaks.

ca_fat_fread.signature: i32 ca_fat_fread(ca_fat_file_t *f, void *buf, u32 len, u32 *got)
ca_fat_fread.brief: Reads data from an opened file into a provided buffer.

params.name: f
params.desc: Pointer to the file handle structure. Must be previously initialized and opened via ca_fat_fopen.

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the memory buffer where the read data will be stored. Must have enough space to hold 'len' bytes.

params.name: len
params.desc: Number of bytes to attempt to read from the file.

params.name: got
params.desc: Pointer to a variable that will store the actual number of bytes read. Can be NULL if the count is not needed.

ca_fat_fread.returns: Returns an i32 representing the result code (0 usually indicates success). Negative or non-zero values indicate an error (e.g., disk error, file not open).
ca_fat_fread.notes: This function is blocking, meaning the calling task will wait until the file system operation completes. It is thread-safe because it internally uses ca_fat_lock and ca_fat_unlock to protect the file system resource. It must NOT be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it performs blocking operations. The most common beginner mistake is passing an uninitialized or NULL file handle, which will cause a system crash or hard fault.
ca_fat_fread.usage: This function is used to retrieve data from a file on the storage medium. It is typically used in a sequence: first, open the file with ca_fat_fopen, then call ca_fat_fread one or more times to read the content, and finally close the file with ca_fat_fclose. It is often paired with ca_fat_fseek if you need to read from a specific position within the file rather than sequentially.

ca_fat_free.brief: Calculates and prints the total, free, and used space on the currently mounted FAT filesystem.
ca_fat_free.returns: Returns true if the space calculation was successful and printed to stdout; returns false if the filesystem is not mounted or if the underlying FAT driver returns an error.
ca_fat_free.notes: This function is blocking because it performs filesystem operations and uses a mutex lock (ca_fat_lock) to ensure thread safety during the calculation. It must NOT be called from an ISR because it performs blocking I/O and takes a mutex, which would cause a system crash or deadlock. Before calling this, the FAT service must be initialized and a filesystem must be successfully mounted using ca_fat_mount. A common mistake is calling this function immediately after system boot without waiting for the storage media to be ready or mounted.
ca_fat_free.usage: This function is typically used in diagnostic tasks or CLI commands to monitor storage health and capacity. It is usually paired with ca_fat_mount to ensure the filesystem is accessible before requesting space statistics. In a typical lifecycle, you would call ca_fat_mount, then use ca_fat_free to verify available space before performing file write operations, and finally call ca_fat_umount when the storage is no longer needed.

ca_fat_fseek.brief: Moves the read/write pointer of an open file to a specific byte offset.

params.name: f
params.desc: Pointer to the file handle structure, which must have been previously opened via ca_fat_fopen.

params.name: pos
params.desc: The absolute byte position from the start of the file (0 is the beginning).

ca_fat_fseek.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns a non-zero error code (FRESULT) if the operation fails (e.g., invalid file handle, disk error, or seeking beyond file size).
ca_fat_fseek.notes: This function is blocking, meaning the calling task will wait until the file system operation completes. It is thread-safe because it internally uses ca_fat_lock and ca_fat_unlock to protect the file system resource from concurrent access by other tasks. It must NOT be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it performs blocking operations. A common mistake is to assume the file pointer automatically resets after a write or read; you must explicitly use this function to navigate the file.
ca_fat_fseek.usage: Use this function when you need to perform random access on a file, such as reading a specific header or overwriting a specific section of data without rewriting the entire file. It is typically used in a sequence: open the file with ca_fat_fopen, use ca_fat_fseek to navigate to the desired offset, perform read/write operations with ca_fat_fread or ca_fat_fwrite, and finally close the file with ca_fat_fclose.

ca_fat_fsize.brief: Returns the total size of an opened file in bytes.

params.name: f
params.desc: Pointer to an initialized and opened file handle. Must not be NULL.

ca_fat_fsize.returns: Returns the file size as a 32-bit unsigned integer. If the file handle is invalid or the file is not open, the behavior is undefined, typically returning 0.
ca_fat_fsize.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, provided the underlying file system is mounted and the file handle is valid. It is safe to call from an ISR, but ensure the file handle is not being modified by another task simultaneously. The most common beginner mistake is passing a pointer to a file handle that has not been initialized via ca_fat_fopen, which will lead to a memory access violation or incorrect size reporting.
ca_fat_fsize.usage: This function is typically used to determine the buffer size required to read a file's contents or to check if a file is empty before processing. It is often used in a sequence: first, open the file with ca_fat_fopen, then call ca_fat_fsize to get the length, perform operations like ca_fat_fread, and finally close the file with ca_fat_fclose.

ca_fat_fsync.brief: Flushes cached file data to the physical storage medium to ensure data integrity.

params.name: f
params.desc: Pointer to the file handle structure. Must be a valid, previously opened file handle.

ca_fat_fsync.returns: Returns an i32 representing the FRESULT code. 0 (FR_OK) indicates success; any non-zero value indicates a filesystem error (e.g., disk full, hardware failure, or invalid handle).
ca_fat_fsync.notes: This function is blocking, as it must wait for the underlying hardware (SD card or Flash) to complete the write operations. It is thread-safe because it uses internal locking mechanisms (ca_fat_lock/unlock) to prevent concurrent access to the filesystem. It must NOT be called from an ISR, as the blocking nature and mutex usage will cause a system crash or deadlock. A common beginner mistake is to assume that calling ca_fat_fwrite is enough to save data; without calling ca_fat_fsync, data might remain in the internal buffer and be lost if the system loses power.
ca_fat_fsync.usage: Use this function whenever you need to guarantee that data is physically written to the storage, such as after a critical configuration update or before closing a log file. It is typically used in a sequence: ca_fat_fopen to open the file, one or more ca_fat_fwrite calls to write data, ca_fat_fsync to commit the changes to the disk, and finally ca_fat_fclose to release the handle. It is essential for preventing data corruption during unexpected power cycles.

ca_fat_ftell.brief: Returns the current read/write pointer position within an open file.

params.name: f
params.desc: Pointer to the file handle structure previously initialized by ca_fat_fopen. Must not be NULL.

ca_fat_ftell.returns: Returns the current file offset in bytes as a u32. If the file handle is invalid or the file is not open, the behavior is undefined (typically returns 0).
ca_fat_ftell.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it performs a simple read of the internal file pointer structure. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the file handle is valid and the file system is mounted. The most common beginner mistake is calling this function on a file handle that has already been closed via ca_fat_fclose, which will lead to unpredictable results or memory access errors. Always ensure the file is successfully opened before attempting to query its position.
ca_fat_ftell.usage: This function is typically used to track progress during sequential file reads or writes, or to determine the current location before performing a seek operation. It is often paired with ca_fat_fseek to jump to specific locations and ca_fat_fsize to check how much data remains in the file. In a typical lifecycle, you open a file with ca_fat_fopen, perform various read/write operations, use ca_fat_ftell to verify your position, and finally close the file with ca_fat_fclose.

ca_fat_fwrite.signature: i32 ca_fat_fwrite(ca_fat_file_t *f, const void *buf, u32 len, u32 *put)
ca_fat_fwrite.brief: Writes a specified number of bytes from a buffer to an open file handle in the FAT filesystem.

params.name: f
params.desc: Pointer to the file handle structure, which must have been previously opened via ca_fat_fopen.

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the source data buffer containing the bytes to be written.

params.name: len
params.desc: Number of bytes to attempt to write. Must be a valid positive integer.

params.name: put
params.desc: Pointer to a variable where the function will store the actual number of bytes successfully written. Can be NULL if the count is not needed.

ca_fat_fwrite.returns: Returns an i32 representing the result code (0 indicates success, non-zero indicates a FAT filesystem error).
ca_fat_fwrite.notes: This function is blocking, meaning the calling task will wait until the write operation completes or fails. It is thread-safe because it internally uses ca_fat_lock and ca_fat_unlock to manage access to the filesystem resources. It must NOT be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it performs blocking operations. A common mistake is failing to check the return value or the 'put' pointer, which can lead to silent data loss if the disk is full or the file system is corrupted.
ca_fat_fwrite.usage: This function is used to persist data to storage after a file has been opened with ca_fat_fopen. It is typically part of a sequence: open the file, perform one or more write operations, and finally close the file using ca_fat_fclose to ensure data integrity. It is often paired with ca_fat_fseek to position the write pointer or ca_fat_fsync to force a flush of the internal buffers to the physical media.

ca_fat_is_mounted.brief: Checks if the FAT file system is currently mounted and ready for operations.
ca_fat_is_mounted.returns: Returns true if the file system is mounted, false otherwise.
ca_fat_is_mounted.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it simply reads a status flag from the internal FAT service structure. It is safe to call from an ISR, although it is rarely useful to do so since file system operations themselves are generally not ISR-safe. The most common beginner mistake is assuming that a 'true' return value guarantees that a specific file exists or that the SD card is physically present; it only confirms that the software mount process has completed successfully. Always ensure the FAT service has been initialized via ca_fat_service_init before relying on this status.
ca_fat_is_mounted.usage: This function is typically used as a guard clause before performing any file system operations like reading, writing, or listing files. It is standard practice to call this immediately after a user command or a system event to prevent attempting operations on an uninitialized or unmounted drive. It is frequently paired with ca_fat_mount to initialize the drive and ca_fat_umount to safely disconnect it, ensuring the application logic does not crash or hang when the storage medium is removed.

ca_fat_lock.brief: Acquires a recursive mutex to ensure exclusive access to the FAT filesystem service.
ca_fat_lock.returns: This function returns void. It blocks the calling task until the mutex is acquired.
ca_fat_lock.notes: This function is a blocking call; if another task currently holds the lock, the calling task will be suspended by the RTOS scheduler until the lock becomes available. It is not safe to call this function from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because ISRs cannot be suspended. Because it uses a recursive mutex (rmutex), the same task can call this function multiple times without deadlocking itself, provided it calls ca_fat_unlock() an equal number of times. The most common beginner mistake is forgetting to call ca_fat_unlock() in an error path, which will permanently hang all other tasks attempting to access the filesystem.
ca_fat_lock.usage: Use this function whenever you need to perform a sequence of filesystem operations (like opening, reading, and closing a file) that must be treated as an atomic transaction. It is typically used in a pair: call ca_fat_lock() before starting your file operations, and ensure ca_fat_unlock() is called immediately after, even if an error occurs during the process. This prevents data corruption or race conditions when multiple tasks attempt to access the SD card or flash storage simultaneously.

ca_fat_ls.brief: Lists the contents of a specified directory on the FAT filesystem to the standard output.

params.name: dir
params.desc: Path to the directory to list. Pass NULL or an empty string ("") to list the current working directory.

ca_fat_ls.returns: Returns true if the directory was successfully opened and listed, false otherwise (e.g., directory not found, filesystem not mounted, or internal error).
ca_fat_ls.notes: This function is blocking, meaning the calling task will wait until the entire directory content is read and printed. It is thread-safe because it internally uses ca_fat_lock() and ca_fat_unlock() to ensure exclusive access to the filesystem driver. It must NOT be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it performs blocking I/O operations. A common mistake is calling this before the filesystem is initialized or mounted, which will trigger an error message and return false.
ca_fat_ls.usage: This function is typically used for debugging or user interaction to verify the presence of files after creation or before deletion. It is often paired with ca_fat_cd() to navigate the filesystem or ca_fat_touch() to verify that a file was successfully created. In a typical sequence, you would initialize the service with ca_fat_service_init(), mount the drive, perform operations like ca_fat_mkdir() or ca_fat_touch(), and then use ca_fat_ls() to confirm the state of the directory.

ca_fat_mkdir.brief: Creates a new directory on the mounted filesystem.

params.name: dir
params.desc: The path and name of the directory to create. Must be a valid null-terminated string.

ca_fat_mkdir.returns: Returns true if the directory was created successfully, false otherwise (e.g., filesystem not mounted, directory already exists, or disk error).
ca_fat_mkdir.notes: This function is blocking, meaning the calling task will wait until the filesystem operation completes. It is thread-safe because it internally uses ca_fat_lock and ca_fat_unlock to manage access to the shared filesystem resource. You must ensure the filesystem is mounted via ca_fat_mount before calling this; calling it while unmounted will trigger an error. Do not call this function from an ISR, as it performs blocking operations that are not permitted in interrupt context.
ca_fat_mkdir.usage: This function is typically used during filesystem setup or when organizing data logs into specific folders. It is often paired with ca_fat_cd to enter the newly created directory or ca_fat_ls to verify its existence. In a typical workflow, you would initialize the service with ca_fat_service_init, mount the drive, create your directory structure, and finally perform file operations like ca_fat_touch or ca_fat_cat.

ca_fat_mkfs.brief: Formats the storage media with a FAT32 filesystem.
ca_fat_mkfs.returns: Returns true if the formatting process completed successfully, false otherwise. A false return indicates a filesystem error, which can be further investigated using ca_fat_strerror.
ca_fat_mkfs.notes: This function is destructive; it erases all existing data on the partition. It is a blocking operation, meaning the calling task will wait until the format process completes, which can take significant time depending on the storage size. It is not safe to call from an ISR. You must ensure the FAT service is initialized and the partition table has been created via ca_fat_fdisk before calling this. A common mistake is calling this while the volume is still mounted or in use by other tasks, which will lead to unpredictable behavior or errors.
ca_fat_mkfs.usage: This function is typically used during the initial setup of a storage device or when a factory reset is required. It is part of a standard sequence: first, call ca_fat_fdisk to create the partition table, then call ca_fat_mkfs to format the partition, and finally call ca_fat_mount to make the filesystem accessible. It should be used sparingly as it wipes all data on the storage medium.

ca_fat_mount.brief: Mounts the filesystem volume to make it accessible for file operations.
ca_fat_mount.returns: Returns true if the volume was successfully mounted or was already mounted. Returns false if the mount operation failed (e.g., hardware error, invalid filesystem, or unformatted media).
ca_fat_mount.notes: This function is blocking and thread-safe, as it uses internal locking mechanisms to ensure exclusive access to the filesystem driver. It must NOT be called from an ISR because it performs blocking operations and potentially waits for hardware access. Before calling this, ensure the underlying storage driver (e.g., SDIO or QSPI) is initialized. A common mistake is attempting to perform file operations before checking the return value of this function, which will lead to undefined behavior or system crashes.
ca_fat_mount.usage: This function is the entry point for all filesystem activity. It is typically called after hardware initialization and formatting (e.g., ca_fat_fdisk and ca_fat_mkfs) to prepare the volume for use. Once mounted, you can proceed to use functions like ca_fat_mkdir, ca_fat_write_enc, or ca_fat_ls. It is usually paired with ca_fat_umount when the filesystem needs to be safely detached, for example, before entering a low-power sleep mode or removing physical media.

ca_fat_pmkdir.brief: Creates a new directory on the mounted filesystem using a thread-safe wrapper.

params.name: path
params.desc: The null-terminated string representing the path of the directory to create. Must be a valid path string compatible with the underlying FAT filesystem.

ca_fat_pmkdir.returns: Returns an i32 representing the result code. 0 (FR_OK) indicates success. Non-zero values indicate errors (e.g., FR_NOT_ENABLED if the filesystem is not mounted, or standard FatFs error codes like FR_EXIST if the directory already exists).
ca_fat_pmkdir.notes: This function is thread-safe because it internally uses ca_fat_lock() and ca_fat_unlock() to manage access to the shared filesystem resource. It is a blocking function, meaning the calling task will wait until the filesystem mutex is acquired and the operation completes. It must NOT be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because blocking operations are forbidden in interrupt context. A common mistake is calling this before the filesystem has been initialized or mounted, which will result in an FR_NOT_ENABLED error.
ca_fat_pmkdir.usage: This function is typically used in application-level file management tasks, such as setting up directory structures for logging or data storage. It is often paired with ca_fat_mount() during system initialization to ensure the filesystem is ready, and can be used alongside ca_fat_rmdir() or ca_fat_punlink() for filesystem maintenance. In the provided context, it is used as a wrapper for high-level Python-like filesystem interfaces to ensure consistent error handling.

ca_fat_prename.brief: Renames or moves a file or directory on the FAT filesystem.

params.name: from
params.desc: The current path/name of the file or directory. Must be a valid null-terminated string.

params.name: to
params.desc: The new path/name for the file or directory. Must be a valid null-terminated string.

ca_fat_prename.returns: Returns 0 (FR_OK) on success. Returns a non-zero error code (FRESULT) if the operation fails (e.g., file not found, destination exists, or filesystem not mounted).
ca_fat_prename.notes: This function is thread-safe as it internally uses ca_fat_lock and ca_fat_unlock to manage access to the shared filesystem resource. It is a blocking operation, meaning the calling task will wait until the filesystem driver completes the rename process. It must NOT be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it attempts to acquire a mutex, which can lead to system instability or deadlocks. A common mistake is failing to check the return value; if the rename fails (e.g., due to a full disk or invalid path), the original file remains unchanged, and ignoring the error will lead to logic bugs in your application.
ca_fat_prename.usage: Use this function when you need to rename a file or move it to a different directory within the same logical drive. It is typically used in file management tasks, such as updating configuration files or rotating logs. It is often paired with ca_fat_fopen to verify file existence before renaming, or with ca_fat_punlink if you need to replace an existing file. Ensure the filesystem is mounted via ca_fat_mount before calling this, as the function will return FR_NOT_ENABLED otherwise.

ca_fat_pstat.brief: Retrieves file or directory status information from the filesystem.

params.name: path
params.desc: The null-terminated string representing the file or directory path to query.

params.name: info
params.desc: Pointer to a structure where the file metadata (size, attributes, timestamps) will be stored.

ca_fat_pstat.returns: Returns 0 (FR_OK) on success. Returns a non-zero FatFs error code (e.g., FR_NO_FILE, FR_NOT_ENABLED) if the file is not found or the filesystem is not mounted.
ca_fat_pstat.notes: This function is blocking and thread-safe, as it internally uses a mutex to protect the shared filesystem state. It must NOT be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it performs blocking operations and acquires a mutex. Before calling this, ensure the filesystem has been initialized and mounted via the appropriate service functions. A common mistake is passing a NULL pointer for the 'info' structure, which will cause a memory access violation.
ca_fat_pstat.usage: This function is typically used to check if a file exists or to retrieve its size before performing read/write operations. It is often paired with ca_memory_allocate to create the info buffer, followed by a call to ca_fat_pstat, and finally ca_memory_free to release the buffer. It is a standard utility for filesystem management tasks like verifying file existence before opening them with ca_fat_fopen.

ca_fat_punlink.brief: Removes a file or an empty directory from the filesystem.

params.name: path
params.desc: The null-terminated string representing the path to the file or directory to be deleted.

ca_fat_punlink.returns: Returns 0 (FR_OK) on success. Returns a non-zero error code (e.g., FR_NOT_ENABLED, FR_NO_FILE, FR_DENIED) if the operation fails.
ca_fat_punlink.notes: This function is a thread-safe wrapper around the underlying FAT filesystem driver. It uses internal locking (ca_fat_lock/unlock) to ensure that concurrent filesystem access from different tasks does not corrupt the internal state. It is strictly non-blocking in terms of RTOS task suspension, but it will wait for the filesystem mutex to become available. You must NEVER call this function from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it attempts to acquire a mutex, which can lead to a system crash or deadlock. Ensure the filesystem is mounted via ca_fat_mount before calling this, otherwise, it will return FR_NOT_ENABLED.
ca_fat_punlink.usage: This function is typically used in file management tasks where you need to clean up temporary files or remove user-created data. It is often paired with ca_fat_fopen for file creation or ca_fat_pmkdir for directory creation. In a typical lifecycle, you might list files using ca_fat_ls, identify a target, and then call ca_fat_punlink to delete it. It is the standard way to perform 'remove' operations in the caOS filesystem abstraction layer.

ca_fat_pwd.brief: Prints the current working directory path of the FAT filesystem to the standard output.
ca_fat_pwd.returns: Returns true if the current path was successfully retrieved and printed, false if the filesystem is not mounted or an internal FAT error occurred.
ca_fat_pwd.notes: This function is blocking because it acquires a mutex (ca_fat_lock) to ensure thread-safe access to the shared filesystem state. It must NOT be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it performs blocking operations and potentially long-running filesystem I/O. Before calling this, the FAT service must be initialized and mounted; otherwise, it will trigger a 'not_mounted' error. A common mistake is assuming this function returns the path as a string; it does not, it prints the path directly to the system's stdout.
ca_fat_pwd.usage: This function is typically used for debugging or logging purposes to verify the current navigation state within the filesystem hierarchy. It is usually called after successful navigation commands like ca_fat_cd or after creating directories with ca_fat_mkdir to confirm the shell's current context. It is part of the standard filesystem management sequence: initialize the service, mount the drive, navigate using ca_fat_cd, and verify the location with ca_fat_pwd.

ca_fat_read_enc.signature: bool ca_fat_read_enc(u32 key_idx, const char *name, ca_fat_read_cb_t cb, void *user, u32 *total_out)
ca_fat_read_enc.brief: Reads and decrypts a file from the filesystem using a specified cryptographic key.

params.name: key_idx
params.desc: The index of the key stored in the secure keystore to be used for decryption.

params.name: name
params.desc: The null-terminated path/filename of the encrypted file on the storage medium.

params.name: cb
params.desc: A callback function invoked for every decrypted data chunk. Return true to continue reading, false to abort.

params.name: user
params.desc: A pointer to user-defined data passed directly to the callback function.

params.name: total_out
params.desc: Optional pointer to store the total number of decrypted bytes read. Can be NULL.

ca_fat_read_enc.returns: Returns true if the file was read and decrypted successfully. Returns false if the file could not be opened, the decryption failed (e.g., wrong key or corrupted data), or the callback returned false.
ca_fat_read_enc.notes: This function is blocking and performs significant I/O and cryptographic operations; it must never be called from an ISR. It is thread-safe regarding the filesystem access because it internally uses ca_fat_lock and ca_fat_unlock. Before calling this, ensure the filesystem is mounted using ca_fat_is_mounted. A common mistake is passing a NULL callback when the user expects to process data, or failing to check the return value, which leads to ignoring decryption errors or file truncation issues.
ca_fat_read_enc.usage: This function is typically used to retrieve sensitive configuration or data files that are stored in an encrypted format on the SD card or flash. It is usually paired with ca_fat_service_init to prepare the filesystem and potentially ca_fat_write_enc if the application needs to update the encrypted file. The sequence is: verify mount status, call ca_fat_read_enc with a processing callback, and handle the boolean result to confirm data integrity.

ca_fat_rm.brief: Deletes a file from the mounted filesystem by its name.

params.name: name
params.desc: The path/name of the file to delete. Must be a valid string representing a file path within the mounted volume.

ca_fat_rm.returns: Returns true if the file was successfully deleted, false otherwise (e.g., file not found, filesystem not mounted, or permission error).
ca_fat_rm.notes: This function is blocking and thread-safe, as it internally uses a lock to ensure exclusive access to the filesystem. It must NOT be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it performs blocking operations and acquires a mutex. The filesystem must be initialized and mounted via ca_fat_mount before calling this function; otherwise, it will fail. A common mistake is passing a directory path to this function; use ca_fat_rmdir instead for directories.
ca_fat_rm.usage: This function is typically used during file management tasks, such as cleaning up temporary files or removing outdated logs. It is often paired with ca_fat_ls to verify the file exists before deletion, or used in a cleanup sequence after processing data. In a typical lifecycle, you would mount the drive with ca_fat_mount, perform operations, and then use ca_fat_rm to remove specific files before unmounting with ca_fat_umount.

ca_fat_rmdir.brief: Removes an empty directory from the FAT filesystem.

params.name: dir
params.desc: The path string of the directory to remove. Must be a valid path relative to the current working directory or an absolute path.

ca_fat_rmdir.returns: Returns true if the directory was successfully removed, false otherwise (e.g., directory not empty, path does not exist, or filesystem not mounted).
ca_fat_rmdir.notes: This function is blocking, meaning it will wait until the filesystem operation completes before returning. It is thread-safe because it internally uses a lock to prevent concurrent access to the FAT driver. It must NOT be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it performs blocking operations. A common beginner mistake is attempting to remove a directory that still contains files or subdirectories; the underlying FAT driver will reject this, and the function will return false.
ca_fat_rmdir.usage: Use this function when you need to clean up the filesystem structure during runtime. It is typically used after deleting all files inside a directory using ca_fat_rm. It is often paired with ca_fat_cd to navigate to the parent directory before attempting to remove the target folder. Ensure the filesystem is mounted via ca_fat_mount before calling this, otherwise, it will fail.

ca_fat_service_init.brief: Initializes the FAT file system service and registers the CLI command interface.
ca_fat_service_init.notes: This function performs internal memory clearing and initializes a recursive mutex for thread-safe access to the file system. It is not thread-safe to call this function while other FAT operations are in progress, so it must be called during the system boot sequence before any file system tasks are spawned. It is strictly forbidden to call this from an ISR, as it performs initialization tasks that are not ISR-safe. A common mistake is calling this before the underlying hardware driver (like SDIO or Flash) is fully initialized, which will lead to undefined behavior when the file system attempts to mount or access the storage media.
ca_fat_service_init.usage: This function is a mandatory part of the file system initialization sequence. It is typically called after the hardware abstraction layer (e.g., SDIO or Flash drivers) is ready, but before the CLI thread is created or any file system commands are executed. It is often paired with ca_fat_service_set_event_cb to register a callback for file system events, and it must be called after ca_cli_init if the CLI interface is required to interact with the file system.

ca_fat_service_set_event_cb.brief: Registers a callback function to handle FAT filesystem events asynchronously.

params.name: cb
params.desc: A function pointer to the callback routine. Pass NULL to disable the event notification.

ca_fat_service_set_event_cb.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it simply updates a static internal pointer. It is not intended to be called from an ISR, although it is technically safe to do so; however, the callback function itself must be written with extreme caution if triggered from an ISR context. The most common mistake is passing a function pointer that performs heavy processing or blocking operations, which can stall the FAT service or the entire system. Ensure that the FAT service has been initialized via ca_fat_service_init before setting the callback, otherwise, the callback may never be triggered.
ca_fat_service_set_event_cb.usage: This function is used to hook into the FAT filesystem's event system, allowing your application to react to file operations or system events (like media insertion or removal). It is typically called during the system initialization phase, immediately after ca_fat_service_init and before starting the CLI or other tasks that might interact with the filesystem. By registering a callback, you decouple the filesystem driver from your application logic, enabling cleaner event-driven architectures.

ca_fat_statvfs.brief: Retrieves filesystem statistics including cluster size, total capacity, and free space.

params.name: cluster_bytes
params.desc: Pointer to store the size of a cluster in bytes. Pass NULL if not needed.

params.name: total
params.desc: Pointer to store the total number of available clusters. Pass NULL if not needed.

params.name: free_clst
params.desc: Pointer to store the number of free clusters. Pass NULL if not needed.

ca_fat_statvfs.returns: Returns 0 (FR_OK) on success. Returns a non-zero error code (e.g., FR_NOT_ENABLED if the filesystem is not mounted, or other FatFs error codes) on failure.
ca_fat_statvfs.notes: This function is blocking because it must access the underlying storage media, which may take time depending on the hardware interface (SDIO/SPI). It is thread-safe as it internally uses ca_fat_lock and ca_fat_unlock to protect the shared filesystem object. It must NOT be called from an ISR because it performs blocking operations and uses mutexes. Ensure the filesystem is successfully mounted via ca_fat_mount before calling this; otherwise, it will return FR_NOT_ENABLED. A common mistake is assuming the returned values are in bytes; they are in clusters, so you must multiply by the cluster size to get total byte counts.
ca_fat_statvfs.usage: Use this function when you need to monitor disk usage, such as checking if there is enough space before performing a large file write operation. It is typically used in a monitoring task or a CLI command to report system health. It is often paired with ca_fat_mount during initialization and ca_fat_umount during shutdown. In a typical application, you call this to populate a structure representing the filesystem state, similar to the standard POSIX statvfs.

ca_fat_strerror.brief: Converts a numeric FatFS error code into a human-readable string for logging and debugging.

params.name: fr
params.desc: The numeric error code returned by FatFS operations (e.g., FR_OK, FR_NO_FILE). Passing an undefined integer will return 'unknown'.

ca_fat_strerror.returns: A pointer to a constant null-terminated string describing the error. It never returns NULL.
ca_fat_strerror.notes: This function is a simple lookup table and is completely non-blocking, thread-safe, and safe to call from an ISR. It does not perform any hardware I/O or filesystem access, so it has no preconditions other than the FatFS service being initialized. The most common mistake is assuming this function can 'fix' an error; it is strictly for diagnostic reporting. Do not attempt to modify the returned string, as it points to static memory.
ca_fat_strerror.usage: Use this function whenever a FatFS operation (like ca_fat_mount, ca_fat_read_enc, or ca_fat_write_enc) returns a non-zero value. It is typically paired with ca_printf_n or ca_stdout_printf_n to provide meaningful feedback in logs. By converting the raw integer error code into text, you make it significantly easier to diagnose issues like 'no such file' versus 'disk I/O error' during field debugging.

ca_fat_touch.brief: Creates a new empty file on the filesystem if it does not already exist.

params.name: name
params.desc: The path and filename to create. Must be a valid string representing a path within the mounted filesystem.

ca_fat_touch.returns: Returns true if the file was successfully created, false if the file already exists, the filesystem is not mounted, or an I/O error occurred.
ca_fat_touch.notes: This function is blocking, meaning it will pause the execution of the calling task until the filesystem operation completes. It is not safe to call from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it uses internal mutexes (ca_fat_lock) which can cause deadlocks or system crashes if called from an interrupt context. Ensure the filesystem is initialized and mounted via ca_fat_mount before calling this. A common beginner mistake is assuming this function will overwrite an existing file; it will not, as it specifically uses the FA_CREATE_NEW flag, returning false if the file is already present.
ca_fat_touch.usage: Use this function when you need to initialize a new log file or configuration file on the SD card or flash storage. It is typically used in a sequence where you first verify the filesystem state with ca_fat_is_mounted, then create the file with ca_fat_touch, and subsequently open it for writing using other filesystem functions. It is often paired with ca_fat_ls to verify the file creation or ca_fat_rm if you need to clean up the file later.

ca_fat_trylock.brief: Attempts to acquire the FAT filesystem lock without blocking the calling task.
ca_fat_trylock.returns: Returns true if the lock was successfully acquired, false if the lock is already held by another task.
ca_fat_trylock.notes: This function is non-blocking, meaning it returns immediately regardless of whether the lock is available. It is thread-safe and intended for scenarios where you prefer to skip an operation rather than waiting for the filesystem to become free. It must not be called from an ISR, as mutex operations are designed for task-level synchronization. A common mistake is failing to call ca_fat_unlock() after a successful trylock, which will permanently lock the filesystem and cause all other tasks to hang.
ca_fat_trylock.usage: Use this function in non-critical background tasks, such as logging or telemetry, where you want to avoid stalling the system if the filesystem is busy with a high-priority operation. It is typically used in a pattern where you check the return value: if true, you perform the file operation (e.g., ca_fat_write_enc) and then immediately release the lock; if false, you simply drop the data or retry later. This prevents low-priority tasks from blocking the entire system when the FAT service is under heavy load.

ca_fat_umount.brief: Safely unmounts the currently mounted FAT filesystem volume.
ca_fat_umount.returns: Returns true if the filesystem was successfully unmounted or was already unmounted. Returns false if an internal error occurs during the unmount process.
ca_fat_umount.notes: This function is thread-safe and uses internal locking to ensure that filesystem operations are not interrupted during the teardown process. It is a blocking function, meaning the calling task will wait until the internal cleanup (closing files, flushing buffers) is complete. It must NOT be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it performs blocking operations. A common beginner mistake is to attempt to call this function while other tasks are still actively reading or writing to the filesystem, which can lead to data corruption or incomplete file writes; ensure all application-level file handles are closed before calling this.
ca_fat_umount.usage: This function is typically used during system shutdown or when a storage medium (like an SD card) needs to be safely removed. It is the final step in the filesystem lifecycle, following the sequence: ca_fat_service_init -> ca_fat_mount -> [file operations] -> ca_fat_umount. It is often paired with ca_fat_is_mounted to check the status before attempting the unmount, ensuring the system state is consistent.

ca_fat_unlock.brief: Releases the internal mutex lock protecting the FAT filesystem service.
ca_fat_unlock.notes: This function is used to release a recursive mutex that prevents multiple tasks from accessing the FAT filesystem simultaneously. It is not thread-safe to call this from an ISR, as mutexes are intended for task-level synchronization. A common beginner mistake is to forget to call this after a 'ca_fat_lock()', which results in a permanent deadlock where no other task can ever access the filesystem again. Always ensure that every lock operation has a corresponding unlock operation, even in error-handling paths.
ca_fat_unlock.usage: This function is used in a 'lock-process-unlock' pattern to ensure data integrity during filesystem operations. You typically call 'ca_fat_lock()' before performing a sequence of operations like 'f_open', 'f_read', or 'f_write', and then call 'ca_fat_unlock()' immediately after the work is done. It is essential to use this when multiple tasks might attempt to read or write to the SD card or flash memory simultaneously, as it prevents file corruption and race conditions.

ca_fat_work_buf.brief: Retrieves the pointer to the internal shared working buffer used by the FAT filesystem service.

params.name: size
params.desc: Optional pointer to a variable where the function will store the size of the buffer in bytes. Pass NULL if the size is not needed.

ca_fat_work_buf.returns: A pointer (u8 *) to the internal static working buffer. This pointer is never NULL as it points to a statically allocated memory area within the FAT service.
ca_fat_work_buf.notes: This function is not thread-safe on its own; it provides access to a shared global resource. You MUST call ca_fat_lock() before accessing the buffer and ca_fat_unlock() immediately after you are finished to prevent data corruption from other tasks. This function is non-blocking and can be called from an ISR, but since the buffer is shared, using it in an ISR is highly discouraged as it would require locking mechanisms that are not ISR-safe. The most common mistake is accessing the buffer without holding the FAT lock, which leads to race conditions where multiple tasks overwrite the same memory area.
ca_fat_work_buf.usage: This function is used when you need a temporary scratchpad memory area to perform raw data operations, such as preparing a block of data to be written to the SD card or reading a sector. It is typically used in a sequence: first, call ca_fat_lock() to gain exclusive access, then call ca_fat_work_buf() to get the pointer, perform your data manipulation (e.g., using ca_memcpy), and finally call ca_fat_unlock() to release the resource for other tasks.

ca_fat_write_enc.signature: bool ca_fat_write_enc(u32 key_idx, const char *name, const u8 *buf, u32 len)
ca_fat_write_enc.brief: Writes data to a file on the FAT filesystem after encrypting it using a specified AES key.

params.name: key_idx
params.desc: The index of the AES key to use for encryption. Must correspond to a valid key stored in the system keystore.

params.name: name
params.desc: The null-terminated string representing the file path/name on the FAT filesystem.

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the source data buffer to be encrypted and written.

params.name: len
params.desc: The length of the data in bytes. Must be greater than 0.

ca_fat_write_enc.returns: Returns true if the file was successfully created, encrypted, and written to the disk. Returns false if the filesystem is not mounted, the key is invalid, the disk is full, or any I/O error occurs.
ca_fat_write_enc.notes: This function is blocking and performs multiple disk I/O operations, so it should never be called from an ISR. It is thread-safe because it internally uses ca_fat_lock() to ensure exclusive access to the filesystem during the write process. A common mistake is calling this function before the filesystem is initialized or mounted, which will result in an immediate failure. Ensure the buffer provided is valid for the entire duration of the call, as the function processes data in chunks.
ca_fat_write_enc.usage: This function is typically used in the application layer to securely store sensitive configuration or data logs on an SD card or flash storage. It is usually preceded by ca_fat_mount() to ensure the storage is ready. After the write operation, the system automatically closes the file handle, so no manual close is required by the user. It is often paired with ca_fat_read_enc() to retrieve and decrypt the data later.

ca_fb_blit.signature: i32 ca_fb_blit(ca_fb_t fb, i32 x, i32 y, i32 w, i32 h, const void *src, u32 src_stride)
ca_fb_blit.brief: Copies a rectangular block of pixel data from a source buffer into a framebuffer.

params.name: fb
params.desc: The handle to the target framebuffer.

params.name: x
params.desc: The horizontal starting coordinate in the framebuffer.

params.name: y
params.desc: The vertical starting coordinate in the framebuffer.

params.name: w
params.desc: The width of the rectangle to copy.

params.name: h
params.desc: The height of the rectangle to copy.

params.name: src
params.desc: Pointer to the source pixel data buffer. Must not be NULL.

params.name: src_stride
params.desc: The number of bytes per row in the source buffer. Must account for the full width of the source image, not just the blit width.

ca_fb_blit.returns: Returns the total number of pixels copied on success, 0 if the rectangle is fully clipped out or src is NULL, or -1 if the framebuffer handle is invalid or the framebuffer becomes inaccessible during the operation.
ca_fb_blit.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses internal scheduler locking to protect the framebuffer access. It is a blocking operation because it performs memory copies and waits for scheduler access; therefore, it must NEVER be called from an ISR. A common beginner mistake is passing an incorrect stride or unaligned buffer, which can lead to memory corruption or visual artifacts. Ensure the framebuffer is properly initialized via ca_fb_create before attempting to blit to it. Because it locks the scheduler during each row copy, it may introduce latency in high-frequency real-time tasks.
ca_fb_blit.usage: This function is typically used in GUI rendering loops or display drivers to update specific regions of the screen. It is often paired with ca_fb_create for initialization and ca_fb_destroy for cleanup. In a typical workflow, you would calculate the area to update, prepare the pixel buffer, call ca_fb_blit to push the data, and then signal the display hardware that the frame is ready. It is frequently used inside display flush callbacks where the GUI library provides a buffer that needs to be copied into the system's active framebuffer.

ca_fb_clear.brief: Fills the entire framebuffer with a single solid color.

params.name: fb
params.desc: The handle to the framebuffer object. Must be a valid, initialized handle obtained from ca_fb_create.

params.name: color
params.desc: The color value to fill the screen with. The format depends on the framebuffer's pixel depth and palette configuration.

ca_fb_clear.returns: Returns the total number of pixels written (width * height) on success. Returns -1 if the framebuffer handle is invalid or if the operation fails.
ca_fb_clear.notes: This function is a wrapper around ca_fb_fill_rect that targets the entire screen area. It is not inherently thread-safe; if multiple tasks access the same framebuffer, you must use a mutex or ca_fb_take to prevent visual corruption or race conditions. It is a blocking operation, meaning the task will wait until the fill command is processed. Do not call this from an ISR, as it may involve blocking synchronization primitives that are forbidden in interrupt context. A common beginner mistake is passing an uninitialized or NULL framebuffer handle, which will cause the function to return -1 immediately.
ca_fb_clear.usage: Use this function to reset the display state or clear the screen before drawing a new frame. It is typically used in the initialization phase of a UI task or during a screen refresh cycle. It is often paired with ca_fb_create to set up the buffer, ca_fb_set_palette to define the colors, and ca_fb_fill_rect for drawing specific shapes or text on top of the cleared background. It is also used to prepare the canvas before performing complex blitting operations with ca_fb_blit.

ca_fb_create.signature: ca_fb_t ca_fb_create(u16 width, u16 height, ca_fb_fmt_t fmt, u8 buffers)
ca_fb_create.brief: Allocates and initializes a new framebuffer resource in shared memory.

params.name: width
params.desc: Horizontal resolution in pixels. Must be greater than 0.

params.name: height
params.desc: Vertical resolution in pixels. Must be greater than 0.

params.name: fmt
params.desc: Pixel format. Must be CA_FB_FMT_L8 or CA_FB_FMT_RGB565.

params.name: buffers
params.desc: Number of buffers. Must be 1.

ca_fb_create.returns: Returns a valid ca_fb_t handle (a non-zero identifier) on success, or CA_FB_NONE if allocation fails, parameters are invalid, or the maximum number of framebuffers has been reached.
ca_fb_create.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses internal scheduler locking to protect the framebuffer registry. It is NOT callable from an ISR because it performs dynamic memory allocation via ca_memory_allocate_shared, which is blocking and non-deterministic. The function initializes the memory with a default palette and clears the pixel data to zero. A common mistake is failing to check if the returned handle is CA_FB_NONE, which will lead to invalid operations when passing the handle to other ca_fb_* functions. Always ensure the system has enough heap available before calling this, as it allocates a significant block of memory.
ca_fb_create.usage: This function is typically called during system initialization or when a specific display task starts. It is the mandatory first step in the framebuffer lifecycle: create -> use (e.g., ca_fb_fill_rect, ca_fb_set_pixel) -> destroy (ca_fb_destroy). It is often paired with ca_fb_info to verify the allocation succeeded or to retrieve dimensions before drawing operations. If the application needs to switch display modes, it should destroy the old framebuffer before creating a new one to prevent memory leaks.

ca_fb_destroy.brief: Destroys a framebuffer object and releases its associated memory back to the system.

params.name: fb
params.desc: The handle of the framebuffer to be destroyed. Must be a valid handle previously returned by ca_fb_create.

ca_fb_destroy.returns: Returns true if the framebuffer was successfully found, retired, and its memory freed. Returns false if the framebuffer handle is invalid, if the calling task does not own the framebuffer, or if the memory deallocation fails.
ca_fb_destroy.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses internal scheduler locking to safely access the framebuffer registry. It is NOT callable from an ISR because it performs memory management operations that may block. The function ensures that only the owner of the framebuffer (or a task with no owner assigned) can destroy it, preventing accidental resource cleanup by unrelated tasks. A common mistake is attempting to use the framebuffer handle after calling this function; always set your handle variable to a null or invalid state immediately after destruction to avoid use-after-free bugs.
ca_fb_destroy.usage: This function is typically used during the teardown phase of a service or task lifecycle. It is paired with ca_fb_create (initialization) and ca_fb_take (to claim ownership). In a typical sequence, a task creates a framebuffer, performs drawing operations, and finally calls ca_fb_destroy when the task is shutting down or the display resource is no longer required, ensuring no memory leaks occur in the system heap.

ca_fb_fill_rect.signature: i32 ca_fb_fill_rect(ca_fb_t fb, i32 x, i32 y, i32 w, i32 h, u32 color)
ca_fb_fill_rect.brief: Fills a rectangular area of a framebuffer with a specific color, handling clipping automatically.

params.name: fb
params.desc: Handle to the target framebuffer, obtained via ca_fb_create.

params.name: x
params.desc: Starting X coordinate (top-left corner). Can be negative for clipping.

params.name: y
params.desc: Starting Y coordinate (top-left corner). Can be negative for clipping.

params.name: w
params.desc: Width of the rectangle. Values <= 0 result in no operation.

params.name: h
params.desc: Height of the rectangle. Values <= 0 result in no operation.

params.name: color
params.desc: The color value to fill. If the framebuffer uses 1 byte per pixel, only the lowest 8 bits are used.

ca_fb_fill_rect.returns: Returns the total number of pixels modified (n * rows) on success, 0 if the rectangle is outside the clipping area or has invalid dimensions, or -1 if the framebuffer handle is invalid or was destroyed during the operation.
ca_fb_fill_rect.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses internal scheduler locks to protect the framebuffer access. It is NOT callable from an ISR because it performs blocking operations and scheduler locking. The function performs automatic clipping, meaning if your rectangle extends beyond the framebuffer boundaries, it will only draw the visible portion. A common mistake is assuming the function is atomic; while it locks the scheduler, it does so per-row, meaning other tasks might preempt it between rows if the framebuffer is large. Ensure the framebuffer handle is valid before calling; if the handle is invalidated by another task (e.g., via ca_fb_destroy), the function will return -1.
ca_fb_fill_rect.usage: This function is the primary primitive for drawing operations in caOS. It is typically used after initializing a framebuffer with ca_fb_create. It is often paired with ca_fb_clear (which calls this with full dimensions) or used in loops to draw lines, borders, or UI elements. In a typical lifecycle, you create the buffer, perform multiple fill operations to compose your frame, and then potentially swap or display the buffer.

ca_fb_get.brief: Retrieves a direct read-only pointer to the raw pixel buffer of a framebuffer.

params.name: fb
params.desc: The handle of the framebuffer to access. Must be a valid handle previously returned by ca_fb_create.

ca_fb_get.returns: A pointer to the constant pixel data (const u8*) if the handle is valid, or NULL if the handle is invalid or the framebuffer does not exist.
ca_fb_get.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses internal scheduler locking to ensure the framebuffer handle remains valid during the lookup. It is non-blocking in terms of waiting for hardware, but it must NOT be called from an ISR because it invokes scheduler locking primitives. The most common mistake is assuming the returned pointer remains valid indefinitely; if another task calls ca_fb_destroy on this handle, the pointer becomes dangling and will cause a memory fault if accessed. Always ensure the framebuffer lifecycle is managed correctly within your task.
ca_fb_get.usage: This function is typically used when you need to perform direct memory operations on the framebuffer, such as passing the buffer address to a DMA controller or a hardware-accelerated drawing engine. It is usually paired with ca_fb_create during initialization and ca_fb_destroy during cleanup. In a typical workflow, you call ca_fb_get to obtain the base address, verify it against expected geometry using ca_fb_info, and then use it for direct memory access or as a source for DMA operations.

ca_fb_get_pixel.signature: i32 ca_fb_get_pixel(ca_fb_t fb, i32 x, i32 y)
ca_fb_get_pixel.brief: Retrieves the color value of a specific pixel from a framebuffer.

params.name: fb
params.desc: The handle to the framebuffer object, previously initialized via ca_fb_create.

params.name: x
params.desc: The horizontal coordinate (column). Must be >= 0 and less than the framebuffer width.

params.name: y
params.desc: The vertical coordinate (row). Must be >= 0 and less than the framebuffer height.

ca_fb_get_pixel.returns: Returns the color value as an i32 if successful. Returns -1 if the coordinates are out of bounds, the framebuffer handle is invalid, or the framebuffer is not initialized.
ca_fb_get_pixel.notes: This function is thread-safe because it internally uses ca_os_sched_lock and ca_os_sched_unlock to protect the framebuffer memory access. It is a blocking operation because it waits for the scheduler lock, meaning it must NEVER be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) as this could cause a system deadlock. A common beginner mistake is assuming the function will handle out-of-bounds coordinates gracefully; it will simply return -1. Always ensure your framebuffer is properly initialized and that your coordinates are within the bounds retrieved via ca_fb_info before calling this function.
ca_fb_get_pixel.usage: This function is used in graphics rendering loops or UI logic to inspect the current state of a pixel before performing a conditional update. It is typically paired with ca_fb_create during the initialization phase and ca_fb_set_pixel when you need to modify the pixel color based on its current value. It is often used in conjunction with ca_fb_info to retrieve the width and height of the buffer to ensure that the x and y parameters remain within valid bounds during runtime.

ca_fb_info.brief: Retrieves metadata and memory access details for a specific framebuffer handle.

params.name: fb
params.desc: The handle of the framebuffer to query. Must be a valid handle previously created or obtained.

params.name: info
params.desc: Pointer to a structure where the framebuffer details (base address, dimensions, format) will be stored. Must not be NULL.

ca_fb_info.returns: Returns true if the framebuffer was found and the info structure was successfully populated. Returns false if the handle is invalid, the framebuffer does not exist, or the info pointer is NULL.
ca_fb_info.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses internal scheduler locking to ensure the framebuffer state remains consistent during the copy operation. It is a blocking operation because it must wait for the scheduler lock, so it must NEVER be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine). A common mistake is passing a NULL pointer for the info structure, which will immediately return false without modifying any memory. Always ensure the framebuffer handle is still valid before using the returned base address, as the framebuffer could be destroyed by another task.
ca_fb_info.usage: This function is typically used when a task needs to perform direct memory operations on the framebuffer, such as calculating a CRC, performing image processing, or streaming the screen content over a network (e.g., VNC). It is usually called after obtaining a handle via ca_fb_create or ca_fb_take. It is often paired with direct memory access to the 'base' address provided in the info structure, followed by operations that might involve ca_dma2d_copy or similar hardware acceleration functions.

ca_fb_mark_dirty.signature: i32 ca_fb_mark_dirty(ca_fb_t fb, i32 x, i32 y, i32 w, i32 h)
ca_fb_mark_dirty.brief: Marks a rectangular region of a framebuffer as modified, triggering a refresh for that area.

params.name: fb
params.desc: The handle to the framebuffer object to be updated.

params.name: x
params.desc: The top-left X coordinate of the dirty rectangle.

params.name: y
params.desc: The top-left Y coordinate of the dirty rectangle.

params.name: w
params.desc: The width of the dirty rectangle.

params.name: h
params.desc: The height of the dirty rectangle.

ca_fb_mark_dirty.returns: Returns the total number of pixels marked as dirty (n * rows) on success, 0 if the rectangle is outside the clipping area, or -1 if the framebuffer handle is invalid.
ca_fb_mark_dirty.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses internal scheduler locking to protect the framebuffer's dirty state. It is NOT callable from an ISR because it performs scheduler operations (locking). The framebuffer must be initialized via ca_fb_create before calling this. A common mistake is passing coordinates that exceed the framebuffer dimensions; while the function handles clipping internally, it is more efficient to calculate valid coordinates beforehand to avoid unnecessary processing.
ca_fb_mark_dirty.usage: This function is used in graphics applications to notify the system that a specific portion of the screen has changed and needs to be redrawn. It is typically called after drawing operations like ca_fb_fill_rect or ca_fb_set_pixel. It is often paired with ca_fb_take_dirty, which is used by the display driver or a background task to retrieve and process the accumulated dirty regions for screen updates.

ca_fb_present.brief: Signals that a frame buffer is complete and ready to be displayed or copied to the output device.

params.name: fb
params.desc: The handle to the frame buffer object previously created via ca_fb_create.
