ca_fb_present.returns: Returns true if the frame buffer was successfully marked as ready and the copy process was triggered. Returns false if the handle is invalid or the frame buffer is not configured for double-buffering.
ca_fb_present.notes: This function is non-blocking but performs internal scheduling locks to ensure thread safety during the state update. It is NOT callable from an ISR because it performs internal scheduling operations. The function assumes the frame buffer has been properly initialized; calling it with an uninitialized or destroyed handle will result in a return value of false. A common beginner mistake is calling this function too frequently (e.g., inside every pixel-drawing loop) instead of once per completed frame, which wastes CPU cycles and may cause flickering or incomplete frame rendering.
ca_fb_present.usage: This function is the final step in a rendering pipeline. Typically, you initialize a frame buffer with ca_fb_create, perform drawing operations using functions like ca_fb_fill_rect or ca_fb_blit, and finally call ca_fb_present to commit the changes to the display. It is often used in a loop where the application calculates the next frame, draws it, and then calls this function to signal the hardware or the display driver that the buffer is ready for swapping or transmission.

ca_fb_set_palette.signature: bool ca_fb_set_palette(ca_fb_t fb, u16 first, u16 count, const u32 *rgb)
ca_fb_set_palette.brief: Updates a range of entries in the framebuffer's color palette.

params.name: fb
params.desc: The handle of the framebuffer to modify.

params.name: first
params.desc: The starting index in the palette (0 to CA_FB_PALETTE_SIZE - 1).

params.name: count
params.desc: Number of palette entries to update. Must not cause (first + count) to exceed the palette size.

params.name: rgb
params.desc: Pointer to an array of 32-bit color values (0xRRGGBB format). Must not be NULL.

ca_fb_set_palette.returns: Returns true if the palette was successfully updated. Returns false if the input pointer is NULL, if the index range is out of bounds, or if the framebuffer handle is invalid.
ca_fb_set_palette.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses internal scheduler locking to protect the framebuffer structure during the update. It is not intended to be called from an ISR because it performs a loop that could take significant time depending on the 'count' parameter, which would violate real-time constraints. A common mistake is passing an index range that exceeds the hardware-defined palette size, which will cause the function to fail immediately by returning false. Ensure the framebuffer handle is valid and initialized before calling this function, as the function performs a lookup that will fail if the handle is stale or uninitialized.
ca_fb_set_palette.usage: This function is used to dynamically change the color mapping of a framebuffer, typically for effects like color cycling, fading, or remapping indexed colors to specific RGB values. It is usually called after the framebuffer has been created with ca_fb_create and before or during the rendering loop. It is often paired with ca_fb_info to verify the 'palette_gen' counter, which increments every time the palette is updated, allowing the system to track if a redraw is necessary. It is typically used in a sequence: initialize the framebuffer, set the desired palette, and then perform drawing operations like ca_fb_clear or ca_fb_fill_rect.

ca_fb_set_pixel.signature: i32 ca_fb_set_pixel(ca_fb_t fb, i32 x, i32 y, u32 color)
ca_fb_set_pixel.brief: Sets the color of a single pixel at the specified (x, y) coordinates within a framebuffer.

params.name: fb
params.desc: The handle to the initialized framebuffer object. Must be a valid handle returned by ca_fb_create.

params.name: x
params.desc: Horizontal coordinate. Must be within [0, width-1]. Values outside this range result in no operation.

params.name: y
params.desc: Vertical coordinate. Must be within [0, height-1]. Values outside this range result in no operation.

params.name: color
params.desc: The color index or value to write to the pixel. The interpretation depends on the framebuffer's pixel format.

ca_fb_set_pixel.returns: Returns 1 if the pixel was successfully set (within bounds), or 0 if the coordinates were outside the framebuffer boundaries.
ca_fb_set_pixel.notes: This function is a wrapper around ca_fb_fill_rect and is generally non-blocking, though it depends on the underlying framebuffer driver implementation. It is not explicitly guaranteed to be thread-safe; if multiple tasks access the same framebuffer, you should protect access using a mutex or scheduler lock. Do not call this from an ISR unless the underlying driver is specifically documented as ISR-safe. A common beginner mistake is passing negative coordinates or coordinates exceeding the framebuffer dimensions, which will silently fail (return 0) rather than crashing, but can lead to unexpected visual results.
ca_fb_set_pixel.usage: Used for drawing individual points, lines, or custom shapes on a display buffer. It is typically used after calling ca_fb_create to initialize the buffer and before any display refresh or swap operation. It is often paired with ca_fb_get_pixel to verify state or perform read-modify-write operations. In a typical lifecycle, you initialize the framebuffer, perform multiple calls to ca_fb_set_pixel or ca_fb_fill_rect to compose your image, and then trigger the hardware update.

ca_fb_take.brief: Attempts to acquire exclusive ownership of a framebuffer resource for the calling task.

params.name: fb
params.desc: The handle of the framebuffer to be acquired. Must be a valid handle previously created via ca_fb_create.

ca_fb_take.returns: Returns true if the task successfully became the owner (or was already the owner), false if the framebuffer is already owned by another task, the handle is invalid, or the calling task context is invalid.
ca_fb_take.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it uses internal scheduler locking to ensure atomic access to the framebuffer's ownership slot. It cannot be called from an ISR because it relies on the calling task's handle (ca_os_self_handle). A common beginner mistake is assuming that calling this function automatically waits for the resource; it does not. If it returns false, the task must either retry later or handle the failure gracefully, as the resource is currently busy. Always ensure the task is properly initialized before calling this, as an invalid task handle will cause the function to return false immediately.
ca_fb_take.usage: This function is used to claim exclusive access to a framebuffer before performing operations like drawing or clearing. It is typically used in a pattern where a task first calls ca_fb_take to secure the resource, then performs operations like ca_fb_fill_rect or ca_fb_set_pixel, and finally maintains ownership for the duration of a specific service lifecycle. It is often paired with ca_fb_info to verify the framebuffer dimensions before allocating local buffers for processing. If the task fails to take the framebuffer, it should not attempt to draw, as the memory might be owned by another task, leading to race conditions or memory corruption.

ca_fb_take_dirty.signature: bool ca_fb_take_dirty(ca_fb_t fb, u32 *map, u32 words)
ca_fb_take_dirty.brief: Retrieves and clears the 'dirty' region map of a framebuffer to identify which parts of the screen need updating.

params.name: fb
params.desc: The framebuffer handle to query. Must be a valid, initialized handle.

params.name: map
params.desc: Pointer to a buffer where the dirty bits will be ORed. Must not be NULL.

params.name: words
params.desc: Size of the provided map buffer in 32-bit words. Must be >= the internal dirty map size.

ca_fb_take_dirty.returns: Returns true if the dirty map was successfully retrieved and cleared, false if the framebuffer is invalid, the map pointer is NULL, or the provided buffer is too small.
ca_fb_take_dirty.notes: This function is non-blocking but uses a scheduler lock to ensure atomic access to the framebuffer's internal state, so it is not safe to call from an ISR. It is thread-safe regarding other tasks accessing the same framebuffer. The most common mistake is providing a 'map' buffer that is too small for the framebuffer's resolution, which will cause the function to return false without updating the map. Ensure the framebuffer is initialized via ca_fb_create before use.
ca_fb_take_dirty.usage: This function is typically used in display-streaming tasks (like VNC or remote UI updates) to determine which parts of the screen have changed since the last frame. It is usually called in a loop: first, check if the framebuffer is still valid using ca_fb_info, then call ca_fb_take_dirty to get the changes, and finally process those changes (e.g., sending pixel data over a network). It pairs with ca_fb_create for initialization and ca_fb_destroy for cleanup.

ca_flash_erase_range.brief: Erases a specified range of flash memory, handling sector boundaries and partial sector modifications automatically.

params.name: addr
params.desc: The starting memory address in the flash peripheral to begin erasing.

params.name: len
params.desc: The number of bytes to erase. Must be greater than zero.

ca_flash_erase_range.returns: Returns true if the entire requested range was successfully erased (or modified). Returns false if the operation failed, memory allocation failed, or if the input length is zero.
ca_flash_erase_range.notes: This function is a blocking operation, meaning the CPU will wait until the hardware flash controller completes the erase cycles before returning. It is NOT thread-safe and must not be called from an ISR, as it performs dynamic memory allocation (ca_memory_allocate) which is forbidden in interrupt contexts. A common mistake is passing an address or length that exceeds the physical flash boundaries, which may lead to undefined behavior or hardware faults. Always ensure the flash is not being read by other tasks during this operation, as erasing causes the memory to return 0xFF and may crash code executing from the same flash bank.
ca_flash_erase_range.usage: Use this function when you need to clear configuration data, logs, or firmware update slots stored in internal flash. It is typically used in a sequence: first, ensure the system is in a safe state, then call ca_flash_erase_range to clear the target area, and finally use ca_flash_hw_write to store new data. It is designed to handle partial sector erasures by performing a read-modify-write cycle, which is essential when your data structure is smaller than the hardware's minimum erase sector size.

ca_flash_erase_sector.brief: Erases a specific flash memory sector starting at the provided address.

params.name: addr
params.desc: The starting memory address of the flash sector to be erased. Must be a valid sector boundary address defined in the MCU datasheet; providing an invalid or non-aligned address will result in a hardware error.

ca_flash_erase_sector.returns: Returns true if the sector was successfully erased, or false if the operation failed due to hardware protection, invalid address, or timeout.
ca_flash_erase_sector.notes: This function is a blocking operation, meaning the CPU will wait until the flash hardware completes the erase cycle before returning control to your code. It is not thread-safe by default, so you must ensure that no other task attempts to access the flash memory while an erase is in progress. It is generally not safe to call this from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because the long execution time of an erase cycle will block all other interrupts, potentially causing system instability. A common beginner mistake is failing to unlock the flash peripheral before calling this function or attempting to erase a sector that contains critical code currently being executed.
ca_flash_erase_sector.usage: This function is typically used during firmware updates, configuration storage, or data logging where old data must be cleared before writing new information. It is almost always paired with a preceding 'ca_flash_unlock' call (if required by the hardware) and followed by a 'ca_flash_write' operation to store new data. After the write operation is complete, it is standard practice to call 'ca_flash_lock' to prevent accidental corruption of the flash memory during normal system operation.

ca_flash_erase_sector_irq.brief: Erases a specific flash memory sector using an interrupt-driven approach to avoid blocking the CPU.

params.name: addr
params.desc: The starting memory address of the flash sector to be erased. Must be a valid sector boundary address defined in the STM32 datasheet.

ca_flash_erase_sector_irq.returns: Returns true if the sector was erased successfully. Returns false if the flash driver is not initialized, the hardware could not be unlocked, or if an error occurred during the erase operation.
ca_flash_erase_sector_irq.notes: This function is blocking because it uses ca_sem_wait to pause the calling thread until the hardware interrupt signals that the erase is complete. It is NOT safe to call this function from an ISR because it waits on a semaphore, which would cause a system deadlock or kernel panic. Before calling this, you must ensure the flash driver has been initialized via the internal setup routine. A common beginner mistake is calling this function repeatedly in a tight loop without checking the return value, which can lead to system instability if the flash hardware is busy or locked.
ca_flash_erase_sector_irq.usage: This function is typically used when performing firmware updates or saving configuration data to non-volatile memory. It is part of a sequence: first, the driver is initialized, then ca_flash_erase_sector_irq is called to clear the memory, followed by a write operation. It is designed to be used in task-level code where the developer wants to offload the long-running erase process to the hardware interrupt controller, allowing the RTOS to switch to other tasks while the flash hardware works in the background.

ca_flash_erase_sector_num.brief: Erases a specific flash memory sector by its index number.

params.name: sector
params.desc: The index of the flash sector to erase. Must be a valid sector index supported by the hardware; invalid indices will cause the function to return false.

ca_flash_erase_sector_num.returns: Returns true if the sector was successfully erased, or false if the sector index is invalid, the flash hardware could not be unlocked, or the erase operation failed.
ca_flash_erase_sector_num.notes: This function is a blocking operation, meaning the CPU will wait until the flash hardware completes the erase cycle before returning. It is not thread-safe by itself, so you must ensure that no other task attempts to access the flash while this function is running. It is strictly forbidden to call this from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because the blocking nature will stall the entire system and potentially cause a watchdog reset. A common beginner mistake is forgetting that flash memory must be erased before it can be written to; attempting to write to a non-erased sector will result in corrupted data.
ca_flash_erase_sector_num.usage: This function is typically used during configuration storage or firmware updates where you need to clear a specific memory region before writing new data. It is usually paired with ca_flash_hw_unlock() and ca_flash_hw_lock() to manage write protection, and followed by ca_flash_hw_write() to commit new data. In a typical workflow, you call this to prepare the sector, verify the success, and then proceed to write your data buffer to the now-blank memory area.

ca_flash_get_error.brief: Retrieves the current error code status of the flash memory peripheral.
ca_flash_get_error.returns: Returns a 32-bit unsigned integer representing the error state. A return value of 0 typically indicates 'no error' (success), while any non-zero value corresponds to a specific hardware or driver error code defined in the flash driver header.
ca_flash_get_error.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes extremely quickly as it simply reads a global variable. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs an atomic read of a 32-bit value, making it safe to call from both standard tasks and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs). The most common beginner mistake is assuming that calling this function clears the error; it does not. You must ensure that the flash driver has been properly initialized via ca_flash_init before relying on this value, as an uninitialized driver might return garbage data or a stale error code from a previous boot cycle.
ca_flash_get_error.usage: This function is typically used as a diagnostic tool after performing flash operations like ca_flash_write or ca_flash_erase_sector. You should call it immediately after a flash function returns an error status to determine the specific cause of the failure, such as a protection violation or a timeout. It is often paired with functions like ca_flash_write or ca_flash_erase_sector to verify the integrity of the operation. In a robust system, you would use this in an error-handling block to decide whether to retry the operation or enter a safe state.

ca_flash_get_num_sectors.brief: Returns the total number of flash memory sectors available on the current STM32 device.
ca_flash_get_num_sectors.returns: Returns a 16-bit unsigned integer representing the total count of flash sectors. This value is constant for a specific microcontroller model and will never return an error code or NULL.
ca_flash_get_num_sectors.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes almost instantaneously as it simply reads a hardware-defined constant. It is thread-safe and can be safely called from both main-line code and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs) because it performs no complex operations or resource locking. The most common mistake is assuming the sector count is the same across different STM32 families; always use this function to query the hardware dynamically rather than hardcoding values. Ensure the flash driver is initialized before calling this, although in most caOS implementations, this is a static hardware mapping that is available immediately upon system boot.
ca_flash_get_num_sectors.usage: This function is typically used during the initialization phase of an application to determine the boundaries of the flash memory layout. It is frequently paired with ca_flash_get_sector_addr and ca_flash_get_sector_size to iterate through all available sectors for tasks like clearing configuration data, performing firmware updates, or managing a file system. By using this function, your code remains portable across different STM32 chips, as the loop bounds will automatically adjust to the specific hardware's memory map.

ca_flash_get_sector_addr.brief: Retrieves the starting memory address of a specific flash sector.

params.name: sector
params.desc: The index of the flash sector to query. Must be less than the value returned by ca_flash_get_num_sectors().

ca_flash_get_sector_addr.returns: Returns the 32-bit absolute memory address (u32) of the requested sector. Returns 0 if the sector index is invalid or out of range.
ca_flash_get_sector_addr.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it performs a simple lookup in the hardware configuration table. It is safe to call from an ISR because it does not involve complex logic or waiting for hardware peripherals. The most common mistake is passing a sector index that exceeds the total number of available sectors, which will return 0 and potentially cause a crash if the result is used as a pointer without validation. Always ensure the flash driver is initialized before calling this function, as the underlying hardware mapping might not be populated otherwise.
ca_flash_get_sector_addr.usage: This function is typically used during the initialization phase of a storage module or before performing read/write operations to calculate the target memory offset. It is almost always paired with ca_flash_get_sector_size() to verify that the data being written fits within the sector boundaries. Developers use it to map logical sector numbers to physical memory addresses, allowing the application to perform direct memory access or pass addresses to low-level flash programming functions.

ca_flash_get_sector_size.brief: Retrieves the total byte size of a specific flash memory sector.

params.name: sector
params.desc: The index of the flash sector to query. Must be a value between 0 and (ca_flash_get_num_sectors() - 1). Providing an out-of-bounds index may lead to undefined hardware behavior or return 0.

ca_flash_get_sector_size.returns: Returns the size of the sector in bytes as a u32. Returns 0 if the sector index is invalid or if the hardware driver fails to retrieve the information.
ca_flash_get_sector_size.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it performs a simple read operation from the hardware configuration table. It is safe to call from an ISR because it does not involve complex synchronization or waiting for hardware peripherals. The most common mistake is assuming all flash sectors have the same size; on many STM32 microcontrollers, sectors at the beginning of the memory map are often smaller than those at the end. Always verify the sector size before performing write operations to prevent buffer overflows or writing into adjacent memory regions.
ca_flash_get_sector_size.usage: This function is typically used during the initialization or validation phase of a flash storage routine to ensure that the data being written fits within the allocated sector. It is almost always paired with ca_flash_get_sector_addr to determine the starting memory address and the available capacity of the target region. Developers use this to perform bounds checking before calling erase or write functions, ensuring that the application does not corrupt critical data stored in other sectors.

ca_flash_hw_erase_sector.brief: Erases a specific flash memory sector containing the provided address.

params.name: addr
params.desc: The memory address located within the sector to be erased. Must be a valid flash memory address; passing an invalid or out-of-bounds address may cause hardware errors or system instability.

ca_flash_hw_erase_sector.returns: Returns true if the sector was erased successfully, or false if a hardware error occurred during the operation.
ca_flash_hw_erase_sector.notes: This function is strictly blocking, meaning the CPU will wait until the flash hardware completes the erase cycle before returning. It is not thread-safe; if multiple tasks attempt to access the flash simultaneously, you must protect this call with a mutex or semaphore. Do not call this function from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because the blocking wait will hang the system and potentially cause a watchdog reset. A common beginner mistake is assuming the flash is ready for immediate writing after this function returns without checking the return value for errors.
ca_flash_hw_erase_sector.usage: This function is typically used during firmware updates, configuration storage, or data logging where existing flash data must be cleared before writing new information. It is usually paired with a write function (like ca_flash_write) in a sequence: first, verify the address, then call this erase function, and finally perform the write operation. Always ensure the flash is unlocked using ca_flash_unlock before calling this function, as the hardware will ignore erase commands if the protection bits are set.

ca_flash_hw_irq_disable.brief: Disables hardware interrupts related to Flash memory operations.
ca_flash_hw_irq_disable.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately by modifying the Flash control registers. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs a direct bitwise operation on the hardware register, but it does not provide synchronization between tasks. It is safe to call from an ISR, as it only performs a register write. The most common mistake is forgetting to re-enable interrupts after a critical Flash operation, which will cause the system to hang or fail to signal the completion of subsequent Flash writes or erasures.
ca_flash_hw_irq_disable.usage: This function is used to prevent the Flash controller from triggering interrupts during sensitive operations, such as finalizing a write sequence or locking the peripheral. It is typically called as part of a cleanup sequence after a Flash operation has finished or failed. It is almost always used immediately before 'ca_flash_lock' to ensure the peripheral is in a safe, quiescent state before releasing control to other tasks.

ca_flash_hw_irq_enable.brief: Enables hardware interrupts for Flash operations (End of Operation and Error) for a specific memory address.

params.name: addr
params.desc: The target memory address in the Flash peripheral. On some architectures (like H7), it determines which bank's interrupt register is modified; on others, it is ignored.

ca_flash_hw_irq_enable.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately by modifying hardware registers. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs an atomic register write, but it does not manage synchronization; you must ensure that the Flash peripheral is unlocked before calling this. It is safe to call from an ISR, but typically it is called from a task context before initiating a long-running Flash operation. A common beginner mistake is calling this without first enabling the global NVIC interrupt for the Flash peripheral, which would result in the hardware triggering the interrupt but the CPU never executing the handler.
ca_flash_hw_irq_enable.usage: This function is used as a prerequisite for asynchronous (interrupt-driven) Flash operations like erasing or writing. It is typically paired with a sequence: first, you unlock the Flash hardware, then you call this function to enable the interrupt, and finally, you trigger the operation (e.g., ca_flash_hw_start_erase_irq). After triggering the operation, you usually wait on a semaphore (ca_sem_wait) to block the task until the interrupt handler signals that the operation is complete. Failing to call this function before starting an interrupt-driven operation will cause the system to hang indefinitely on the semaphore wait.

ca_flash_hw_irq_handler.brief: Handles hardware-specific Flash interrupts by clearing status flags and returning error codes.
ca_flash_hw_irq_handler.returns: A 32-bit bitmask representing hardware-specific flash errors (e.g., protection, programming, or sequence errors). A return value of 0 indicates no errors were detected.
ca_flash_hw_irq_handler.notes: This function is designed to be called exclusively from within a hardware Interrupt Service Routine (ISR). It is not thread-safe and must never be called from a standard task context, as it directly manipulates hardware registers to acknowledge and clear interrupt flags. A common mistake is failing to realize that this function clears the hardware status registers; if you call it manually outside the ISR, you will lose the ability to detect the actual interrupt event. It is non-blocking and executes very quickly, which is critical for maintaining system responsiveness during flash operations.
ca_flash_hw_irq_handler.usage: This function is the core component of the Flash driver's interrupt management strategy. It is typically invoked inside the global 'FLASH_IRQHandler' function, which the CPU automatically triggers when a flash operation completes or fails. After calling this function, the driver usually updates a global error variable and signals a semaphore (using 'ca_sem_post') to notify a waiting task that the flash operation has finished. This sequence allows the system to perform other tasks while the slow flash hardware is busy, ensuring efficient CPU utilization.

ca_flash_hw_lock.brief: Re-enables write protection on the internal Flash memory controller.
ca_flash_hw_lock.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately by setting the hardware lock bit in the Flash control register. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs a single atomic register write, but it does not provide mutual exclusion; if two tasks call this simultaneously, they may interfere with the flash state. It is safe to call from an ISR, though typically you should only lock flash from the same task that performed the write operation. The most common beginner mistake is forgetting to call this after a write or erase operation, leaving the flash memory vulnerable to accidental corruption by stray pointers or software bugs.
ca_flash_hw_lock.usage: This function is used to finalize flash memory operations by re-enabling hardware write protection. It is typically used in a 'sandwich' pattern: first, call the unlock function to gain write access, perform the necessary write or erase operations, and finally call this lock function to secure the memory. It is essential to call this immediately after the flash operation completes to maintain system integrity and prevent unintended data modification during normal application execution.

ca_flash_hw_num_sectors.brief: Returns the total number of physical flash memory sectors available on the current MCU.
ca_flash_hw_num_sectors.returns: A 16-bit unsigned integer representing the total count of flash sectors. The value is hardware-dependent and reflects the specific memory layout of the STM32 chip being used.
ca_flash_hw_num_sectors.notes: This function is non-blocking, thread-safe, and safe to call from an ISR because it performs a simple register read or returns a constant value. It does not require any prior initialization of the flash peripheral, making it safe to call during early system startup. A common mistake is assuming that all STM32 chips have the same number of sectors; always use this function to query the hardware dynamically rather than hardcoding values in your application logic. If you hardcode sector counts, your code will break when ported to a different STM32 series or even a different density variant of the same series.
ca_flash_hw_num_sectors.usage: This function is typically used as a boundary check before performing flash erase or write operations to ensure the application does not attempt to access memory outside the valid range. It is usually paired with ca_flash_get_sector_addr and ca_flash_get_sector_size to iterate through the flash memory map. Developers use it to dynamically calculate the last available sector (e.g., for configuration storage) to ensure they do not overwrite the application code area, which is a critical safety practice to prevent bricking the device.

ca_flash_hw_nvic_enable.brief: Configures and enables the Flash memory interrupt in the Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller (NVIC).
ca_flash_hw_nvic_enable.returns: This function returns void and does not provide feedback on success or failure.
ca_flash_hw_nvic_enable.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes extremely quickly as it only writes to NVIC registers. It is thread-safe in the sense that NVIC register access is atomic, but it should typically be called only once during system initialization. It is safe to call from an ISR, though it is almost exclusively used during the driver setup phase. The most common beginner mistake is calling this function before the system clock or peripheral clocks are properly initialized, which can lead to unpredictable behavior if the NVIC peripheral is not yet accessible. Always ensure this is called as part of the driver's initialization sequence to prevent the CPU from ignoring Flash completion or error events.
ca_flash_hw_nvic_enable.usage: This function is a mandatory step in the initialization sequence of the Flash driver. It is typically called within a higher-level initialization function like 'ca_flash_irq_init' to prepare the hardware to signal the CPU when a Flash operation (like erase or write) completes or encounters an error. By setting the priority to 6, it ensures that Flash events are handled with a specific urgency relative to other system interrupts. It is always paired with the setup of synchronization primitives, such as semaphores, which are used to block the calling task until the interrupt handler signals that the hardware operation is finished.

ca_flash_hw_sector_addr.brief: Calculates the absolute memory address of a specific flash sector based on the hardware architecture.

params.name: sector
params.desc: The zero-based index of the flash sector. Valid values range from 0 to (ca_flash_hw_num_sectors() - 1). Providing an index outside this range will result in an invalid address return.

ca_flash_hw_sector_addr.returns: Returns the 32-bit absolute memory address (u32) of the start of the requested sector. Returns 0U if the sector index is out of bounds or invalid for the specific hardware platform.
ca_flash_hw_sector_addr.notes: This function is non-blocking, thread-safe, and can be safely called from an ISR because it performs simple arithmetic or array lookups without accessing hardware registers or waiting for flash operations. It does not require any initialization beyond the standard system boot. The most common mistake is assuming that sector sizes are uniform across all STM32 families; always use this function to resolve addresses rather than hardcoding offsets, as the memory map changes significantly between F1, F4, H7, and U5 series. If you receive 0U, it indicates a logic error in your code where you are attempting to access a non-existent sector.
ca_flash_hw_sector_addr.usage: This function is typically used as a foundational step before performing low-level flash operations like erasing or writing data. It is usually paired with ca_flash_hw_num_sectors() to validate the sector index before calling functions like ca_flash_erase_sector_num(). Developers use it to calculate pointers for memory-mapped access or to verify that a data structure fits within a specific flash boundary. It acts as an abstraction layer, allowing your application code to remain portable across different STM32 microcontrollers.

ca_flash_hw_sector_size.brief: Returns the size in bytes of a specific flash memory sector.

params.name: sector
params.desc: The index of the flash sector to query. Must be less than the total number of sectors returned by ca_flash_hw_num_sectors().

ca_flash_hw_sector_size.returns: Returns the size of the sector in bytes as a u32. Returns 0 if the sector index is out of bounds or invalid for the specific hardware.
ca_flash_hw_sector_size.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes in constant time, making it safe to call from both main threads and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs). It is thread-safe because it performs a read-only operation on hardware-defined constants or lookup tables. The most common mistake is passing a sector index that exceeds the hardware limit, which will return 0; always validate your index against ca_flash_hw_num_sectors() before performing calculations to avoid logic errors in memory management.
ca_flash_hw_sector_size.usage: This function is typically used during the initialization phase of a storage driver or when calculating memory offsets for writing data to flash. It is frequently paired with ca_flash_hw_num_sectors() to iterate through all available memory blocks and ca_flash_hw_sector_addr() to determine the starting memory address of a specific sector. Developers use this to ensure they do not overflow a sector boundary when writing data, as flash memory must be erased in whole-sector chunks.

ca_flash_hw_start_erase_irq.brief: Initiates a non-blocking flash sector erase operation and triggers an interrupt upon completion.

params.name: addr
params.desc: The starting memory address of the flash sector or page to be erased. Must be aligned to the hardware-specific sector/page boundary.

ca_flash_hw_start_erase_irq.returns: Always returns true in current implementations, indicating the hardware command sequence has been successfully triggered.
ca_flash_hw_start_erase_irq.notes: This function is non-blocking regarding the actual erase time, meaning it returns immediately after starting the hardware peripheral. It is not thread-safe; you must ensure that no other flash operations occur simultaneously, typically by using a mutex or semaphore to guard the flash peripheral. It is generally not intended to be called directly from an ISR, as it relies on the system's ability to handle the subsequent completion interrupt. A common beginner mistake is failing to call the corresponding 'irq_enable' function before this, which results in the system hanging indefinitely because the completion interrupt is never triggered or handled.
ca_flash_hw_start_erase_irq.usage: This function is used in asynchronous flash management workflows where the CPU should perform other tasks while the hardware erases memory. It is typically used in a sequence: first, unlock the flash and enable interrupts via 'ca_flash_hw_irq_enable', then call this function to start the erase, and finally wait for completion using a semaphore like 'ca_sem_wait'. After the semaphore is released by the ISR, you must disable interrupts and lock the flash to ensure system stability.

ca_flash_hw_start_write_irq.signature: u32 ca_flash_hw_start_write_irq(u32 addr, const u8 *buf, u32 remaining)
ca_flash_hw_start_write_irq.brief: Initiates a non-blocking hardware flash write operation for a single memory word/block.

params.name: addr
params.desc: The target memory address in the flash peripheral. Must be correctly aligned according to the specific MCU architecture (e.g., 4-byte alignment for H7/U5/H5).

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the source data buffer containing the bytes to be written.

params.name: remaining
params.desc: The number of bytes left to write. The function will pad the remainder of the hardware write unit with 0xFF if this value is smaller than the hardware's native write unit size.

ca_flash_hw_start_write_irq.returns: Returns the number of bytes consumed (the hardware write unit size, e.g., 2, 4, 16, or 32 bytes). Returns 0 if the operation could not be initiated.
ca_flash_hw_start_write_irq.notes: This function is intended to be used as part of an asynchronous write sequence. It is blocking in the sense that it waits for the flash peripheral to be ready (wait_bsy) before starting, but it does not wait for the actual write to complete; instead, it triggers a hardware interrupt (IRQ) upon completion. It is generally thread-safe if protected by a semaphore or mutex, but it is not intended to be called directly from an ISR unless the system design explicitly allows nested flash operations. The most common beginner mistake is failing to wait for the completion semaphore after calling this function, which leads to race conditions where the next write starts before the previous one has finished, causing data corruption or hardware errors.
ca_flash_hw_start_write_irq.usage: This function is the core engine for writing data to flash in chunks. It is typically used inside a loop that iterates through a large data buffer, calling this function to write one 'unit' at a time. It must be paired with a synchronization mechanism (like a semaphore) to wait for the 'End of Operation' (EOP) interrupt to signal that the hardware is ready for the next chunk. The typical sequence is: 1) Initialize flash/unlock, 2) Loop through data, 3) Call ca_flash_hw_start_write_irq, 4) Wait on a semaphore, 5) Check for errors, 6) Repeat until finished, 7) Disable IRQs and lock flash.

ca_flash_hw_unlock.brief: Removes the hardware write-protection from the internal Flash memory controller.
ca_flash_hw_unlock.returns: Returns true if the Flash controller is successfully unlocked (or was already unlocked), and false if the unlock sequence failed or the controller remains locked.
ca_flash_hw_unlock.notes: This function is non-blocking in terms of RTOS scheduling, but it interacts directly with hardware registers that may be busy. It is thread-safe only if the application ensures no other task or ISR attempts to modify Flash registers simultaneously. It is generally safe to call from an ISR, but you must ensure the Flash is not currently busy with a write or erase operation, as the hardware will ignore the unlock keys if the BUSY flag is set. A common beginner mistake is calling this function without checking if the Flash is busy, or forgetting to call the corresponding lock function immediately after the write operation is complete, which leaves the memory vulnerable to accidental corruption.
ca_flash_hw_unlock.usage: This function is used as a mandatory precursor to any write or erase operation on the internal Flash memory. In a typical sequence, you first verify the Flash is idle, call ca_flash_hw_unlock(), perform your write or erase operation, and then immediately call the lock function to restore protection. It is typically paired with ca_flash_hw_lock() to ensure the 'unlocked' state is as short-lived as possible, minimizing the risk of stray pointers or software bugs corrupting the firmware or configuration data stored in Flash.

ca_flash_hw_write.signature: bool ca_flash_hw_write(u32 addr, const u8 *buf, u32 len)
ca_flash_hw_write.brief: Writes a block of data to the internal flash memory at a specified address.

params.name: addr
params.desc: The target memory address in the internal flash. Must be aligned to the hardware-specific write unit (e.g., 16 or 32 bytes) depending on the MCU series.

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the source data buffer. Must not be NULL.

params.name: len
params.desc: Number of bytes to write. If the length is not a multiple of the hardware write unit, the function pads the remaining bytes with 0xFF.

ca_flash_hw_write.returns: Returns true if the write operation completed successfully, false if a hardware error occurred or parameters were invalid.
ca_flash_hw_write.notes: This function is strictly blocking, meaning the CPU will wait until the flash hardware completes the write cycle before returning. It is NOT thread-safe; you must ensure that no other task or interrupt attempts to access the flash controller simultaneously. It is not safe to call this from an ISR because the blocking nature will cause significant latency and potential system instability. Before calling this, you must ensure the flash is unlocked (via ca_flash_unlock) and the target memory sector has been erased. A common beginner mistake is attempting to write to a flash address that has not been erased, which will result in a hardware error or corrupted data.
ca_flash_hw_write.usage: This function is used for persistent data storage, such as saving configuration parameters, calibration data, or security keys. The typical sequence is: 1) Unlock the flash controller, 2) Erase the target sector using ca_flash_erase_sector, 3) Call ca_flash_hw_write to store the data, and 4) Lock the flash controller to prevent accidental writes. It is often paired with ca_flash_unlock and ca_flash_lock to ensure the write operation is performed within a protected window.

ca_flash_init.brief: Initializes the flash driver's Command Line Interface (CLI) integration.
ca_flash_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe because it uses a static flag to ensure the CLI registration happens exactly once. It is not intended to be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) as it interacts with the CLI subsystem which is designed for task-level execution. The mandatory precondition is that the CLI system must be initialized before this function is called; otherwise, the registration will fail or cause undefined behavior. A common beginner mistake is calling this function multiple times in different parts of the code; while the static flag prevents duplicate registration, it is best practice to call it only once during the system startup sequence to keep the code clean and predictable.
ca_flash_init.usage: This function is used exclusively to expose flash-related diagnostic commands to the system's Command Line Interface. It is typically called during the early system initialization phase, immediately after the OS starts but before the main application tasks begin. It is often paired with other hardware-specific initialization functions like ca_flash_irq_init() to ensure the driver is fully prepared for operation. By calling this during the startup sequence, you ensure that developers can debug or inspect flash memory status via the serial console as soon as the system is powered on.

ca_flash_irq_init.brief: Initializes the internal semaphore and NVIC interrupts required for asynchronous Flash operations.
ca_flash_irq_init.returns: This function returns void and does not provide a status code, as it performs internal system setup.
ca_flash_irq_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and is intended to be called during the system configuration phase. It is not thread-safe in the sense that it should only be called once during initialization; calling it from multiple threads simultaneously could lead to race conditions on the global flag 'g_flash_irq_ready'. It is strictly forbidden to call this from an ISR, as it performs OS-level resource allocation (semaphore initialization). A common mistake is calling this before the hardware abstraction layer or the OS kernel is fully initialized, which will lead to a hard fault when the NVIC tries to enable interrupts for an unconfigured peripheral.
ca_flash_irq_init.usage: This function is used to prepare the Flash driver to operate in interrupt-driven mode rather than polling mode. It is typically called inside 'ca_os_configure' or during the early stages of the main application setup, immediately after 'ca_flash_init'. By initializing the semaphore 'g_flash_sem', it allows the system to block a task while waiting for a Flash operation to complete, effectively yielding CPU time to other threads. It must be called before any attempt to perform asynchronous Flash read/write operations that rely on interrupt completion signals.

ca_flash_lock.brief: Locks the internal Flash memory controller to prevent accidental write or erase operations.
ca_flash_lock.returns: This function returns void and does not provide a status code, as locking the hardware is considered an atomic and guaranteed operation.
ca_flash_lock.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately by setting the lock bit in the Flash Control Register. It is thread-safe in the sense that it simply writes to a hardware register, but it does not provide mutual exclusion; if two tasks call this simultaneously, the hardware state remains locked. It is safe to call from an ISR, though rarely necessary. The most common beginner mistake is forgetting to call this after a write operation, which leaves the Flash memory vulnerable to accidental corruption from stray pointers or software bugs. Always ensure that you call this immediately after your write or erase sequence is complete to maintain system integrity.
ca_flash_lock.usage: This function is used as the final step in a Flash memory modification sequence. Typically, you follow a strict pattern: first call ca_flash_unlock to enable write access, perform your data write or sector erase operations, and finally call ca_flash_lock to re-enable the hardware protection. It is paired with ca_flash_unlock and functions like ca_flash_erase_sector or other write-related functions. Failing to lock the flash after use is a significant security and stability risk, as it allows any erroneous code execution to potentially overwrite your application code or configuration data.

ca_flash_unlock.brief: Unlocks the internal flash memory controller to allow write or erase operations.
ca_flash_unlock.returns: Returns true if the flash controller was successfully unlocked, or false if the operation failed (e.g., due to hardware protection or invalid state).
ca_flash_unlock.notes: This function is a non-blocking wrapper that interacts directly with the hardware registers to disable write protection. It is not thread-safe by itself; if multiple tasks attempt to modify flash simultaneously, you must wrap this call in a mutex or semaphore to prevent data corruption. It is generally safe to call from an ISR, but you must ensure that no other task is currently performing a flash operation, as the hardware state is global. A common beginner mistake is forgetting to call ca_flash_lock() after the write operation is complete, which leaves the flash memory vulnerable to accidental corruption by stray pointers or software bugs.
ca_flash_unlock.usage: This function is the mandatory first step in any flash programming sequence. You typically call it immediately before performing a write or erase operation, and it is almost always paired with ca_flash_lock() to restore the protection state once the task is finished. In a typical workflow, you would initialize the flash driver, call ca_flash_unlock(), perform your data write, and then immediately call ca_flash_lock() to ensure system stability. If you fail to unlock the flash before writing, the hardware will ignore your commands, and the data will not be saved.

ca_flash_write.signature: bool ca_flash_write(u32 addr, const u8 *buf, u32 len)
ca_flash_write.brief: Writes a block of data to the internal flash memory at a specified address.

params.name: addr
params.desc: The starting memory address in the flash where writing should begin. Must be aligned according to the hardware requirements (e.g., 4-byte alignment).

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the source data buffer. Must not be NULL.

params.name: len
params.desc: The number of bytes to write. Must be greater than 0.

ca_flash_write.returns: Returns true if the write operation was successful, false if the input parameters are invalid (NULL pointer or zero length) or if the hardware write operation failed.
ca_flash_write.notes: This function is a wrapper around hardware-specific flash operations and is typically blocking, meaning the CPU will wait until the flash controller completes the write cycle. It is generally not thread-safe by itself; if multiple tasks attempt to write to flash simultaneously, you must protect this call with a mutex or semaphore to prevent data corruption. Do not call this from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) unless the underlying hardware driver explicitly supports it, as flash operations are slow and will block the system, potentially causing missed interrupts. A common beginner mistake is attempting to write to a flash sector without erasing it first, which will result in a failed write or corrupted data because flash memory can only transition bits from 1 to 0.
ca_flash_write.usage: This function is used for persistent data storage, such as saving configuration parameters or calibration values that must survive a power cycle. It is typically used in a sequence: first, you must call ca_flash_erase_sector to clear the target memory area, then call ca_flash_write to store the new data. It is often paired with a verification step where the written data is read back to ensure integrity. In a typical application, this is called during system initialization or when a user triggers a 'Save Settings' command.

ca_flash_write_irq.signature: bool ca_flash_write_irq(u32 addr, const u8 *buf, u32 len)
ca_flash_write_irq.brief: Writes data to flash memory using an interrupt-driven approach to avoid blocking the CPU during hardware operations.

params.name: addr
params.desc: The starting memory address in the flash to write to. Must be aligned according to hardware requirements.

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the source data buffer. Must not be NULL and must contain at least 'len' bytes.

params.name: len
params.desc: The number of bytes to write. Must be greater than 0.

ca_flash_write_irq.returns: Returns true if the entire buffer was written successfully, false if the operation failed, the input parameters were invalid, or the flash hardware reported an error.
ca_flash_write_irq.notes: This function is blocking because it uses ca_sem_wait to wait for the hardware interrupt to signal completion of each write chunk. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR because it relies on a semaphore to synchronize with the flash hardware interrupt. Before calling this, ensure the flash driver is initialized and the global ready flag is set. A common mistake is passing a buffer that is not valid for the entire duration of the write, or failing to check the return value, which leads to silent data corruption if the flash write fails.
ca_flash_write_irq.usage: This function is typically used when updating configuration parameters or logging data to non-volatile memory without freezing the entire system. It is usually paired with a preceding check of the flash status and followed by a verification step to ensure data integrity. In the typical lifecycle, you initialize the flash driver, call ca_flash_write_irq to commit data, and then perform any necessary cleanup or state updates. It is designed for scenarios where the CPU should perform other tasks while the hardware handles the slow flash programming process.

ca_fmac_flags.brief: Retrieves the current status and error flags from the FMAC (Filter Math Accelerator) hardware.
ca_fmac_flags.returns: Returns a 32-bit unsigned integer representing the hardware status flags. Returns 0 if the FMAC peripheral is not initialized or currently inactive.
ca_fmac_flags.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it performs a simple read of the internal hardware state. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the FMAC peripheral has been previously initialized via ca_fmac_init. The most common mistake is calling this function before initializing the FMAC or after calling ca_fmac_stop, which will result in a return value of 0, potentially masking actual hardware errors if the user assumes 0 means 'success'.
ca_fmac_flags.usage: This function is typically used immediately after a data processing operation (like ca_fmac_run) to verify if the hardware encountered any overflow, underflow, or configuration errors during the calculation. It is part of the standard FMAC lifecycle: initialize with ca_fmac_init, start the operation with ca_fmac_start, process data with ca_fmac_run, check the result status with ca_fmac_flags, and finally clean up with ca_fmac_stop. It acts as a diagnostic tool to ensure the integrity of the mathematical operations performed by the accelerator.

ca_fmac_hw_flags.brief: Reads the hardware status flags (Saturation, Overflow, Underflow) from the FMAC peripheral.
ca_fmac_hw_flags.returns: A bitmask of flags: CA_FMAC_SAT (saturation), CA_FMAC_OVFL (overflow), or CA_FMAC_UNFL (underflow). Returns 0 if no flags are set or if the hardware platform does not support FMAC (e.g., F1xx, F4xx, F7xx, H7xx).
ca_fmac_hw_flags.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a direct read of the hardware status register. It is thread-safe for reading, but it does not provide any locking mechanism for the peripheral itself, meaning other tasks could potentially modify FMAC settings simultaneously. It is safe to call from an ISR because it does not involve OS primitives or blocking waits. A common mistake is failing to check if the FMAC peripheral is actually enabled or initialized before calling this, as reading registers on an unclocked or uninitialized peripheral can lead to unpredictable behavior or hard faults on some STM32 architectures.
ca_fmac_hw_flags.usage: This function is used to monitor the health and accuracy of mathematical operations performed by the FMAC unit. It is typically called after a calculation sequence, such as after ca_fmac_run, to verify if the result is valid or if numerical errors occurred. It is intended to be used in conjunction with the higher-level ca_fmac_flags() wrapper, which handles the internal state check (s_fmac_ok) to ensure the peripheral is ready before accessing the hardware registers directly.

ca_fmac_hw_init.brief: Initializes the hardware FMAC (Filter Math Accelerator) unit by enabling its clock and resetting the peripheral.
ca_fmac_hw_init.returns: Returns true if the FMAC hardware is present and successfully initialized, or false if the specific MCU model does not support the FMAC peripheral.
ca_fmac_hw_init.notes: This function is a low-level hardware abstraction layer (HAL) call. It is non-blocking and executes quickly, but it is not thread-safe; it must be called during the system initialization phase before any tasks attempt to use the FMAC. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. A common mistake is assuming that all STM32 chips have an FMAC unit; always check the return value to ensure the hardware is actually available before proceeding with filter operations.
ca_fmac_hw_init.usage: This function is typically called once during the system boot sequence or driver initialization phase. It is paired with the higher-level ca_fmac_init function, which acts as a wrapper to store the initialization status in a static variable. Once ca_fmac_hw_init returns true, the application can safely proceed to call ca_fmac_start to configure filters and ca_fmac_run to process data.

ca_fmac_hw_param.signature: void ca_fmac_hw_param(u32 func, u32 p, u32 q, u32 r)
ca_fmac_hw_param.brief: Configures the FMAC hardware parameters and triggers a processing operation.

params.name: func
params.desc: The specific FMAC function to execute (e.g., FMAC_LOAD_X1, FMAC_LOAD_X2). Must be a valid constant defined in the FMAC driver header.

params.name: p
params.desc: Primary parameter value, typically representing buffer sizes or coefficient counts.

params.name: q
params.desc: Secondary parameter value, often used for additional coefficient counts or state offsets.

params.name: r
params.desc: Tertiary parameter value, used for specific hardware configuration flags or additional offsets.

ca_fmac_hw_param.returns: void. This function does not return a status code; it writes directly to the hardware register.
ca_fmac_hw_param.notes: This function is a low-level hardware abstraction. It is non-blocking and executes immediately by writing to the FMAC peripheral registers. It is thread-safe only if the FMAC peripheral is not being accessed by multiple tasks simultaneously; ensure you have exclusive access to the FMAC hardware before calling this. It is generally safe to call from an ISR if the hardware is dedicated to that context, but be aware that it does not perform any validation on the parameters. The most common beginner mistake is passing incorrect buffer sizes or function codes that do not match the hardware's current state, which can lead to undefined behavior or hardware faults. Note that on some platforms (f1xx, f4xx, f7xx, h7xx), this function is a no-op, meaning it does nothing; always check your target hardware implementation.
ca_fmac_hw_param.usage: This function is used to prepare the FMAC hardware for signal processing tasks. It is typically called after initializing the peripheral with ca_fmac_init and before starting the processing loop with ca_fmac_run. It is often paired with low-level hardware write operations to load coefficients or data into the FMAC buffers. The sequence is usually: initialize the peripheral, set parameters via this function, write the required data, and finally trigger the processing run.

ca_fmac_hw_run.signature: u32 ca_fmac_hw_run(const i16 *in, i16 *out, u32 len)
ca_fmac_hw_run.brief: Processes a stream of audio samples through the hardware FMAC (Filter Math Accelerator) unit.

params.name: in
params.desc: Pointer to the input buffer containing raw audio samples. Must not be NULL.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to the output buffer where processed samples will be stored. Must not be NULL.

params.name: len
params.desc: Number of samples to process. Valid values are > 0.

ca_fmac_hw_run.returns: Returns the number of samples successfully processed and written to the output buffer. If the return value is less than 'len', it indicates a hardware stall or timeout occurred during processing.
ca_fmac_hw_run.notes: This function is a blocking, polled implementation that waits for the hardware registers to clear before feeding new data. It is NOT thread-safe and must not be called from an ISR, as it uses a spin-loop (FMAC_SPIN_MAX) to wait for hardware readiness. Before calling this, the FMAC peripheral must be initialized via ca_fmac_init and started via ca_fmac_start. A common beginner mistake is passing a NULL pointer or failing to verify that the FMAC is actually running, which will cause the function to return 0 immediately. On some hardware platforms (f1xx, f4xx, f7xx, h7xx), this function is a stub that returns 0, meaning the hardware does not support FMAC operations.
ca_fmac_hw_run.usage: This function is typically used in a dedicated processing task or a high-priority loop where audio filtering is required. The standard sequence is: call ca_fmac_init to configure the filter coefficients, call ca_fmac_start to enable the hardware, and then repeatedly call ca_fmac_run within a loop to process incoming audio buffers. Once processing is complete or the task is shutting down, call ca_fmac_stop to safely disable the peripheral. Always check the return value against 'len' to ensure the hardware kept up with the data stream.

ca_fmac_hw_setup.signature: void ca_fmac_hw_setup(u32 x1_base, u32 x1_size, u32 x2_base, u32 x2_size, u32 y_base, u32 y_size, bool clip)
ca_fmac_hw_setup.brief: Configures the FMAC (Filter Math Accelerator) hardware buffer layout and clipping settings.

params.name: x1_base
params.desc: Base address offset for the X1 input buffer.

params.name: x1_size
params.desc: Size of the X1 input buffer.

params.name: x2_base
params.desc: Base address offset for the X2 coefficient buffer.

params.name: x2_size
params.desc: Size of the X2 coefficient buffer.

params.name: y_base
params.desc: Base address offset for the Y output buffer.

params.name: y_size
params.desc: Size of the Y output buffer.

params.name: clip
params.desc: If true, enables output clipping to prevent overflow.

ca_fmac_hw_setup.returns: void. This function does not return a status code; it assumes the hardware is accessible.
ca_fmac_hw_setup.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs direct register writes to the FMAC peripheral. It is NOT thread-safe; you must ensure no other task or ISR is accessing the FMAC registers simultaneously. It must be called while the FMAC is in a stopped state (START bit = 0), as the buffer registers are locked during operation. A common beginner mistake is calling this while the FMAC is actively processing data, which will result in undefined hardware behavior or corrupted filter outputs. Note that on some platforms (e.g., F1xx, F4xx, F7xx, H7xx), this function is a no-op, so always check your target hardware capabilities.
ca_fmac_hw_setup.usage: This function is the primary configuration step for the FMAC peripheral. It is typically called after initializing the FMAC hardware and before loading coefficients or starting the processing loop. The standard sequence is: 1) Call ca_fmac_init to prepare the peripheral, 2) Call ca_fmac_hw_setup to define the memory layout for input/output buffers, 3) Load coefficients using hardware-specific write functions, and 4) Call ca_fmac_start to begin processing. It is used to define the memory map for the filter's circular buffers, ensuring the hardware knows exactly where to read input samples and where to store the resulting filtered data.

ca_fmac_hw_stop.brief: Immediately halts the FMAC (Filter Math Accelerator) hardware peripheral.
ca_fmac_hw_stop.notes: This function is a low-level hardware abstraction that directly clears the START bit in the FMAC peripheral register. It is non-blocking and executes almost instantaneously, but it does not wait for any ongoing hardware calculations to finish; it simply cuts off the operation. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs a single atomic register write, but it should not be called from an ISR unless you are certain the hardware state is consistent. The most common beginner mistake is calling this function without first ensuring the system is in a state where an abrupt stop is safe, potentially leaving the FMAC in an undefined state for subsequent operations.
ca_fmac_hw_stop.usage: This function is typically used as part of a clean-up or error-handling sequence to ensure the FMAC is not processing data when it shouldn't be. It is usually paired with ca_fmac_init for setup and ca_fmac_start or ca_fmac_run to initiate processing. In a typical application, you would call ca_fmac_stop when a task is being suspended, when a calculation is aborted by the user, or during a system reset sequence to ensure the hardware is idle before re-initialization.

ca_fmac_hw_write.brief: Writes a sequence of 16-bit data words into the FMAC hardware peripheral.

params.name: data
params.desc: Pointer to the array of 16-bit values to write. If NULL, the function writes zeros to the hardware.

params.name: n
params.desc: Number of 16-bit words to write. Must match the expected hardware buffer size.

ca_fmac_hw_write.notes: This function performs direct memory-mapped I/O writes to the FMAC peripheral. It is non-blocking and executes synchronously, meaning the CPU remains occupied until the entire loop completes. It is NOT thread-safe; if multiple tasks or an ISR and a task attempt to write to the FMAC simultaneously, the hardware state will be corrupted. It is callable from an ISR, but keep in mind that long loops will block other interrupts, potentially causing system latency. The most common beginner mistake is providing an incorrect 'n' value, which leads to buffer underflows or overflows in the FMAC registers, resulting in incorrect filter output or hardware stalls.
ca_fmac_hw_write.usage: This function is used during the configuration phase of the FMAC peripheral to load coefficients or initial state data. It is typically called after initializing the peripheral and setting the required parameters (e.g., filter length). The typical sequence is: call 'ca_fmac_init' to prepare the hardware, use a function to set the specific FMAC parameters (like buffer size and operation mode), call 'ca_fmac_hw_write' to load the data, and finally trigger the processing with 'ca_fmac_start'.

ca_fmac_init.brief: Initializes the Filter Math Accelerator (FMAC) hardware peripheral.
ca_fmac_init.returns: Returns true if the FMAC hardware is present and successfully initialized, false otherwise.
ca_fmac_init.notes: This function is a hardware abstraction layer (HAL) wrapper that checks for the existence of the FMAC peripheral on the specific STM32 chip being used. It is not thread-safe and must be called during the system initialization phase before any other FMAC operations are attempted. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. The most common mistake is failing to check the return value; if the function returns false, any subsequent calls to FMAC functions will likely result in undefined behavior or hard faults because the hardware registers do not exist on that specific silicon.
ca_fmac_init.usage: This function is typically called once during the system startup sequence, usually inside the ca_os_configure function. It acts as a gatekeeper: if it returns false, the application should gracefully disable features that rely on the FMAC (like digital filtering or signal processing) to prevent system crashes. It is often paired with ca_cordic_init to verify that all required math acceleration hardware is available before the main application logic starts.

ca_fmac_run.signature: u32 ca_fmac_run(const i16 *in, i16 *out, u32 len)
ca_fmac_run.brief: Processes a buffer of audio samples through the hardware FMAC (Filter Math Accelerator) unit.

params.name: in
params.desc: Pointer to the input buffer containing raw audio samples. Must not be NULL.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to the output buffer where filtered samples will be stored. Must not be NULL.

params.name: len
params.desc: Number of samples to process. Must be greater than 0.

ca_fmac_run.returns: Returns the number of samples successfully processed. If the return value is less than the requested 'len', it indicates a hardware stall or an error condition.
ca_fmac_run.notes: This function is a wrapper for the hardware FMAC peripheral and is not thread-safe; ensure that only one task accesses the FMAC at a time. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. Before calling this, the FMAC must be initialized and started using the appropriate configuration functions. A common beginner mistake is passing NULL pointers or failing to check the return value, which leads to silent data processing failures if the hardware stalls.
ca_fmac_run.usage: This function is used in a processing loop to stream audio data through a filter. The typical sequence is: 1) Initialize the FMAC hardware, 2) Start the FMAC, 3) Call ca_fmac_run repeatedly in a loop to process chunks of data, 4) Check the return value to ensure all samples were processed, 5) Stop the FMAC when finished. It is often paired with ca_fmac_flags to retrieve status information after the processing is complete.

ca_fmac_start.brief: Initializes and starts the FMAC hardware peripheral with the provided filter coefficients and state.

params.name: f
params.desc: Pointer to a filter structure containing coefficients (b, a), lengths (nb, na), gain, and clipping settings. Must not be NULL, and internal pointers (b, a) must be valid.

ca_fmac_start.returns: Returns true if the hardware was successfully configured and started. Returns false if the hardware is already running, the input structure is invalid, coefficients are missing, or the filter parameters exceed hardware limits.
ca_fmac_start.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must not be called from an ISR. It performs blocking hardware register writes to configure the FMAC peripheral. Before calling this, you must ensure ca_fmac_init() has been called successfully. A common mistake is passing a filter structure where the number of feedback coefficients (na) is greater than or equal to the feedforward coefficients (nb), or failing to check the return value, which leads to silent failures if the hardware is busy or parameters are out of range.
ca_fmac_start.usage: This function is the entry point for digital signal processing using the FMAC peripheral. It is typically used in a sequence: first, call ca_fmac_init() during system startup; then, call ca_fmac_start() to load a specific filter configuration; perform processing using ca_fmac_run() in a loop; and finally, call ca_fmac_stop() to release the hardware for other tasks or different filter configurations.

ca_fmac_stop.brief: Stops the hardware FMAC (Filter Math Accelerator) unit and updates the internal state.
ca_fmac_stop.returns: This function returns void and does not provide a status code.
ca_fmac_stop.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should not be called from an ISR unless the system design guarantees no concurrent access to the FMAC hardware. It is a non-blocking function that immediately triggers the hardware stop sequence and updates the internal 's_fmac_running' flag. A common beginner mistake is to call this function while an asynchronous DMA transfer is still active, which can lead to unpredictable hardware states; always ensure the hardware is idle or the operation is complete before calling this. It requires that the FMAC module has been previously initialized via ca_fmac_init.
ca_fmac_stop.usage: This function is used to gracefully terminate an FMAC operation, typically after a processing loop finishes or when an error occurs during data calculation. It is almost always paired with ca_fmac_run to ensure the hardware is released and the internal state is reset to a non-running condition. In a typical workflow, you would initialize the module, perform one or more runs, and then call ca_fmac_stop to ensure the peripheral is safely disabled, preventing potential resource conflicts with other tasks.

ca_gpio_configure.signature: bool ca_gpio_configure(ca_gpio_port_t port, ca_gpio_pin_t pin, ca_gpio_mode_t mode, ca_gpio_otype_t otype, ca_gpio_speed_t speed, ca_gpio_pull_t pull, u8 af)
ca_gpio_configure.brief: Configures the electrical and functional parameters of a specific STM32 GPIO pin.

params.name: port
params.desc: The GPIO port identifier (e.g., CA_GPIO_PORT_A). Must be a valid port defined in the hardware abstraction layer.

params.name: pin
params.desc: The specific pin number (e.g., CA_GPIO_PIN_0). Must be a valid pin index for the selected port.

params.name: mode
params.desc: Operating mode: Input, Output, Analog, or Alternate Function (AF).

params.name: otype
params.desc: Output type: Push-Pull or Open-Drain.

params.name: speed
params.desc: Slew rate/speed setting: Low, Medium, High, or Very High.

params.name: pull
params.desc: Internal resistor configuration: No pull, Pull-up, or Pull-down.

params.name: af
params.desc: Alternate Function index (0-15). Only relevant if mode is set to CA_GPIO_MODE_AF.

ca_gpio_configure.returns: Returns true if the configuration was applied successfully, or false if the hardware configuration failed (e.g., invalid parameters or hardware error).
ca_gpio_configure.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes quickly. It is not inherently thread-safe; if multiple tasks attempt to modify the same port's configuration registers simultaneously, you may experience race conditions that lead to undefined pin states. While it is technically callable from an ISR, it is strongly discouraged to perform hardware configuration inside an interrupt; keep ISRs short and fast. The most common beginner mistake is failing to call ca_gpio_init_port() before this function, which leaves the peripheral clock disabled, causing the configuration to fail or the pin to remain unresponsive.
ca_gpio_configure.usage: This function is used to prepare pins for specific hardware tasks, such as driving LEDs, setting up communication lines (SPI/UART), or configuring external sensors. It is typically used in a strict sequence: first, enable the port clock using ca_gpio_init_port(), then apply the electrical settings with ca_gpio_configure(), and finally set the initial logic state using ca_gpio_write(). It is frequently paired with peripheral initialization functions to ensure the physical pins are correctly mapped to the internal hardware logic before the peripheral starts operation.

ca_gpio_get_io_port.brief: Retrieves the base memory address (pointer) of the STM32 GPIO peripheral register block for a given port.

params.name: port
params.desc: An enumeration representing the GPIO port (e.g., GPIOA, GPIOB). Must be a valid member of the ca_gpio_port_t enum defined in the system headers.

ca_gpio_get_io_port.returns: Returns a pointer to the GPIO_TypeDef structure (the hardware register map) if the port is valid. Returns NULL if the provided port identifier is invalid or not supported by the current MCU configuration.
ca_gpio_get_io_port.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it only performs a lookup in a static mapping table. It is safe to call from an ISR because it does not perform any I/O operations or OS synchronization primitives. The most common mistake is failing to check the returned pointer for NULL before dereferencing it, which will cause a HardFault if the port is invalid. Ensure the GPIO peripheral clock is enabled via the system clock configuration before attempting to read or write to the registers returned by this function.
ca_gpio_get_io_port.usage: This function is typically used as the first step when performing low-level GPIO manipulation or when building custom drivers that require direct register access. It is often paired with ca_gpio_init_port to ensure the hardware is ready, followed by direct register access or ca_gpio_write/ca_gpio_read functions. Use this when you need to bypass standard abstraction layers for performance-critical tasks or to access specific register bits (like MODER or PUPDR) not exposed by higher-level APIs.

ca_gpio_hw_adc_pin_init.brief: Configures a specific microcontroller pin to operate in analog mode for ADC input.

params.name: adc_num
params.desc: The index of the ADC peripheral. Currently unused in implementation, but should be provided as the target ADC unit index.

params.name: channel
params.desc: The specific channel number corresponding to the physical pin to be configured for analog input.

ca_gpio_hw_adc_pin_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs direct register manipulation to set the GPIO mode to analog. It is not thread-safe by itself, but since it is typically called during system initialization before the RTOS scheduler starts, this is usually acceptable. It is safe to call from an ISR if the hardware allows, but it is strongly discouraged to reconfigure pins while an ADC conversion is actively running, as this can lead to undefined electrical behavior or hardware faults. The most common mistake is calling this function multiple times for the same channel or failing to ensure the GPIO clock is enabled before calling this, which may result in the pin configuration being ignored.
ca_gpio_hw_adc_pin_init.usage: This function is a low-level hardware abstraction layer (HAL) call used during the system startup phase. It is typically invoked by the higher-level 'ca_adc_pin_init' function to prepare the physical hardware before any ADC readings are attempted. You should call this once during your driver initialization sequence, pairing it with subsequent calls to ADC configuration functions to ensure the pin is ready to receive analog signals before the ADC peripheral is enabled.

ca_gpio_hw_configure.signature: bool ca_gpio_hw_configure(ca_gpio_port_t port, ca_gpio_pin_t pin, ca_gpio_mode_t mode, ca_gpio_otype_t otype, ca_gpio_speed_t speed, ca_gpio_pull_t pull, u8 af)
ca_gpio_hw_configure.brief: Configures the hardware registers of a specific GPIO pin to set its mode, speed, pull-up/down, and alternate function.

params.name: port
params.desc: The GPIO port identifier (e.g., CA_GPIO_PORT_A). Must be a valid port supported by the MCU.

params.name: pin
params.desc: The pin number (0-15). Values outside this range may cause undefined behavior or register corruption.

params.name: mode
params.desc: The operating mode: Input, Output, Analog, or Alternate Function.

params.name: otype
params.desc: Output type: Push-Pull or Open-Drain. Only relevant when mode is Output or AF.

params.name: speed
params.desc: Output speed configuration. Affects signal slew rate and power consumption.

params.name: pull
params.desc: Internal pull-up, pull-down, or no-pull resistor configuration.

params.name: af
params.desc: Alternate Function index (0-15). Only used if mode is set to GPIO_MODE_AF.

ca_gpio_hw_configure.returns: Returns true if the configuration was applied successfully. Returns false if the port initialization failed (e.g., clock enable error) or if the port pointer is invalid (NULL).
ca_gpio_hw_configure.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs direct register manipulation. It is not inherently thread-safe; if multiple tasks attempt to configure the same port simultaneously, you may corrupt the register state. While it can be called from an ISR, it is strongly recommended to perform all GPIO configurations during system initialization to avoid race conditions.
