The most common beginner mistake is assuming the configuration succeeded without checking the return value; if the hardware clock for the port is not enabled, the register writes will be ignored by the MCU, leaving the pin in its default reset state.
ca_gpio_hw_configure.usage: This function is the low-level hardware abstraction layer (HAL) used by the higher-level ca_gpio_configure function. It is typically invoked during the system startup sequence or when a peripheral (like a UART or SPI bus) is being initialized. It must always be preceded by a successful call to ca_gpio_init_port to ensure the peripheral clock is active, otherwise, the register writes will have no effect. It is the foundation for all GPIO operations, including reading inputs, toggling outputs, and setting up complex alternate functions.

ca_gpio_hw_dac_init.brief: Configures the specific GPIO pin for DAC operation by setting it to analog mode.

params.name: channel
params.desc: The DAC channel number. Valid values are 1 (maps to PA4) or 2 (maps to PA5).

ca_gpio_hw_dac_init.notes: This function is a low-level hardware abstraction layer (HAL) helper. It is not thread-safe and must not be called from an ISR, as it performs register-level configuration that should be done during system initialization. It is non-blocking and assumes the GPIO clock has already been enabled for Port A. A common mistake is calling this function before the system clock or GPIO peripheral clocks are initialized, which will result in the configuration being ignored or causing a hard fault.
ca_gpio_hw_dac_init.usage: This function is intended to be used exclusively within the DAC driver initialization sequence. It is typically called by ca_dac_init immediately after the hardware clock for the DAC peripheral is enabled, but before the DAC peripheral itself is configured. It ensures the physical pin is disconnected from digital logic and set to high-impedance analog mode to prevent signal interference.

ca_gpio_hw_i2c_init.brief: Configures the specific GPIO pins for I2C communication in Alternate Function Open-Drain mode.

params.name: num
params.desc: The I2C peripheral index (typically 1 to 4). Must match the hardware capabilities of the specific STM32 series being used.

params.name: alternate
params.desc: Selects the pin mapping pair. 0 is the default. On some families (like F1xx), this is ignored; on others, it selects specific alternate pin configurations.

ca_gpio_hw_i2c_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately. It is not thread-safe by itself, but since it is typically called during the system initialization phase before the RTOS scheduler starts, this is rarely an issue. It is not intended to be called from an ISR, as GPIO configuration is a setup task. The most common beginner mistake is calling this function without ensuring the corresponding GPIO clock has been enabled, or attempting to use an I2C index that does not exist on the specific MCU variant, which will result in no signal on the pins. Note that on some architectures like F1xx, the function ignores the Alternate Function index parameter as it is implicitly tied to the peripheral clock, whereas on H7xx/H5xx/U5xx/F4xx/F7xx it explicitly sets the AF mode.
ca_gpio_hw_i2c_init.usage: This function is a mandatory step in the I2C initialization sequence. It is always called by the high-level driver 'ca_i2c_init' immediately after enabling the peripheral clock and before configuring the I2C peripheral registers. You should never call this function manually in your application code; instead, rely on the 'ca_i2c_init' function to handle the full hardware setup sequence (Clock -> GPIO -> Peripheral). It is part of the low-level hardware abstraction layer (HAL) that ensures the physical pins are correctly routed to the I2C controller.

ca_gpio_hw_init_port.brief: Enables the peripheral clock for a specific GPIO port in the RCC register.

params.name: port
params.desc: The identifier for the GPIO port (e.g., CA_GPIO_PORT_A). Must be a valid enum value supported by the specific MCU architecture.

ca_gpio_hw_init_port.returns: Returns true if the clock was successfully enabled for the requested port. Returns false if the port identifier is invalid or unsupported by the current hardware configuration.
ca_gpio_hw_init_port.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes in constant time. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs a simple bitwise OR operation on the RCC register, but it should be called during the initialization phase of your application before any other GPIO configuration functions are invoked. It is safe to call from an ISR, though typically you should initialize hardware before enabling interrupts. The most common mistake is attempting to configure GPIO pins (like setting mode or speed) before calling this function; if the clock is not enabled, the CPU will ignore any writes to the GPIO registers, leading to silent failures where your pins do not behave as expected. The function includes a mandatory read-back of the RCC register to ensure the write operation completes before subsequent peripheral access, preventing potential BusFaults on high-speed STM32 architectures.
ca_gpio_hw_init_port.usage: This function is the mandatory first step in the GPIO initialization sequence. It is typically called inside a driver's 'init' function or during system startup before configuring pin modes, pull-up/pull-down resistors, or output speeds. It is usually paired with ca_gpio_configure to set the pin's electrical properties. You must ensure this is called once per port; calling it multiple times is harmless due to the bitwise OR operation, but failing to call it will result in the peripheral being effectively 'dead' to the processor.

ca_gpio_hw_spi_init.brief: Configures the physical GPIO pins for a specific SPI peripheral instance.

params.name: num
params.desc: The SPI peripheral index (typically 1, 2, or 3). Must match the hardware capabilities of the specific MCU.

params.name: alternate
params.desc: If true, selects the alternative pin mapping for the SPI peripheral; if false, uses the default pin mapping.

ca_gpio_hw_spi_init.returns: void. This function does not return a status code, so it assumes the provided parameters are valid for the current hardware target.
ca_gpio_hw_spi_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately. It is not thread-safe by itself, but it is typically called during the system initialization phase before the RTOS scheduler starts or during driver setup, so concurrency is rarely an issue. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. A common mistake is assuming that setting 'alternate' to true works on all MCUs; always check the datasheet or the specific implementation file for your MCU, as some SPI instances may not support alternate mappings. On F1xx series, this function also handles complex AFIO register remapping, which can inadvertently disable JTAG/SWD debug pins if not handled carefully.
ca_gpio_hw_spi_init.usage: This function is a mandatory step in the SPI initialization sequence. It is called by the high-level 'ca_spi_init' function after enabling the peripheral clock and before configuring the actual SPI peripheral registers. You should use it whenever you need to switch between different physical pin layouts on the PCB, such as when the default pins are already occupied by other peripherals like an Ethernet controller or an SD card slot. It is strictly a hardware-level setup function and should not be called repeatedly during runtime.

ca_gpio_init_port.brief: Initializes the hardware clock and base configuration for a specific GPIO port.

params.name: port
params.desc: The identifier for the GPIO port (e.g., CA_GPIO_PORT_A). Must be a valid port defined in the hardware abstraction layer.

ca_gpio_init_port.returns: void. This function does not return a status code, but it logs an error to the system output if the hardware initialization fails.
ca_gpio_init_port.notes: This function is non-blocking and is intended to be called during the system initialization phase. It is not thread-safe; it should be called once per port during startup to avoid redundant hardware clock configuration. It is not safe to call from an ISR because it performs logging and potential CLI registration, which are not ISR-safe operations. A common mistake is calling this function repeatedly inside a main loop; this is unnecessary and can lead to performance overhead or unexpected hardware state resets. Always ensure the system clock for the GPIO peripheral is enabled before attempting to use specific pins.
ca_gpio_init_port.usage: This function is the mandatory first step when preparing a GPIO port for use. It is typically followed by ca_gpio_configure to set specific pin modes (input/output/AF) and then by read/write operations. In complex drivers like SPI or Timers, it is used to prepare the port before configuring the specific pins required for the peripheral's Chip Select or signal lines. It acts as a gatekeeper to ensure the hardware peripheral is powered and ready for pin-level configuration.

ca_gpio_read.brief: Reads the current logic level (0 or 1) of a specific GPIO pin.

params.name: port
params.desc: The GPIO port identifier. Must be a valid port initialized in the system.

params.name: pin
params.desc: The pin number (0-15). Values outside this range will cause incorrect bit shifting.

ca_gpio_read.returns: Returns 1 if the pin is HIGH, 0 if the pin is LOW. Returns 0 if the port handle is invalid (NULL).
ca_gpio_read.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a direct, atomic read of the STM32 Input Data Register (IDR). It is safe to call from both tasks and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs) because it does not rely on OS primitives that might block. You must ensure the GPIO port has been initialized via ca_gpio_init_port and configured as an input via ca_gpio_configure before reading; otherwise, the hardware may not be clocked or the pin mode may be incorrect. A common beginner mistake is forgetting to configure the internal pull-up or pull-down resistors, causing the pin to 'float' and return random values when nothing is connected to it.
ca_gpio_read.usage: This function is used to sample the state of digital inputs such as buttons, switches, or communication lines. It is typically used in a sequence: first, initialize the hardware with ca_gpio_init_port and ca_gpio_configure, then periodically call ca_gpio_read within a task loop or a CLI command handler to monitor the signal. It is often used in conjunction with ca_gpio_write to implement bit-banging protocols or to verify the state of an output pin that is being driven by the MCU.

ca_gpio_toggle.brief: Inverts the current logic state of a specific GPIO pin (High to Low, or Low to High).

params.name: port
params.desc: The GPIO port identifier. Must be a valid port returned by the system configuration.

params.name: pin
params.desc: The specific pin number (0-15). Must be within the valid range for the selected port.

ca_gpio_toggle.returns: void. This function does not return a status code; if an invalid port is provided, the function silently returns without performing any action.
ca_gpio_toggle.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes very quickly by writing directly to the BSRR (Bit Set/Reset Register) of the STM32. It is thread-safe because the BSRR register is atomic, meaning you can safely call this from both the main loop and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs) without worrying about race conditions on the pin state. A common beginner mistake is assuming the function will work if the GPIO port has not been initialized; always ensure ca_gpio_init_port has been called for the specific port before attempting to toggle pins. Because it reads the ODR (Output Data Register) to determine the current state, it is strictly intended for pins configured as outputs; toggling an input pin will not produce the expected result.
ca_gpio_toggle.usage: This function is typically used for visual debugging (blinking LEDs), generating square waves for timing analysis, or signaling error states in real-time. It is often paired with ca_gpio_read to verify the state after a toggle or used inside periodic timer callbacks to create heartbeat signals. In a typical application lifecycle, you would first call ca_gpio_init_port to configure the pin direction, then use ca_gpio_toggle within a loop or ISR to change the state, and finally use ca_gpio_read if you need to synchronize your software logic with the physical pin state.

ca_gpio_write.signature: void ca_gpio_write(ca_gpio_port_t port, ca_gpio_pin_t pin, u8 state)
ca_gpio_write.brief: Sets the logic level (high or low) of a specific GPIO pin on the STM32 hardware.

params.name: port
params.desc: The identifier for the GPIO port. Must be a valid port identifier recognized by the system.

params.name: pin
params.desc: The pin number (0-15) to be controlled. Ensure the pin is configured as an output before writing.

params.name: state
params.desc: The desired logic level: 1 (or non-zero) for high, 0 for low.

ca_gpio_write.returns: void. This function does not return a status code; if the port identifier is invalid (resulting in a NULL pointer from ca_gpio_get_io_port), the function silently returns without performing any action.
ca_gpio_write.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes extremely quickly because it writes directly to the BSRR (Bit Set/Reset Register) of the STM32. It is thread-safe because BSRR operations are atomic, meaning you can safely call this from different threads or even from an ISR without worrying about race conditions on the pin state. A common beginner mistake is calling this function before initializing the GPIO port via ca_gpio_init_port or configuring the pin via ca_gpio_configure; if the hardware clock for the port is not enabled, the write operation will have no effect. Always ensure the peripheral is initialized before attempting to write to it.
ca_gpio_write.usage: This function is the primary way to control external hardware like LEDs, relay drivers, or chip-select lines for communication protocols like SPI. It is typically used in a three-step sequence: first, initialize the port using ca_gpio_init_port; second, configure the pin mode as output using ca_gpio_configure; and finally, use ca_gpio_write to set the state. In communication drivers, it is frequently used to set a chip-select pin high to deselect a device or low to initiate a transaction. It is also used in system management, such as pulling a PHY reset pin low to force a network interface to restart.

ca_hash_compute.signature: bool ca_hash_compute(ca_hash_algo_t algo, const u8 *data, u32 len, u8 *digest, u32 *digest_len)
ca_hash_compute.brief: Performs a complete one-shot cryptographic hash calculation using the hardware accelerator.

params.name: algo
params.desc: The specific hashing algorithm to use (e.g., CA_HASH_ALGO_SHA256). Must be a valid enum value supported by the hardware.

params.name: data
params.desc: Pointer to the input buffer containing the data to be hashed. Must not be NULL.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the input data in bytes. Must be greater than 0.

params.name: digest
params.desc: Pointer to the output buffer where the resulting hash will be stored. Must be large enough to hold the digest and not NULL.

params.name: digest_len
params.desc: Pointer to a variable that receives the actual length of the generated digest. Must not be NULL.

ca_hash_compute.returns: Returns true if the hash calculation completed successfully, false otherwise. A false return indicates invalid input pointers, hardware initialization failure, or an unsupported algorithm.
ca_hash_compute.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses a mutex to protect the hardware peripheral, ensuring that multiple tasks do not corrupt the hashing process. It is a blocking function, meaning the calling task will wait (sleep) if another task is currently using the hardware accelerator. You must NEVER call this function from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because blocking operations are strictly forbidden in ISRs and will cause system instability or deadlocks. Before calling this, ensure ca_hash_init() has been called during system startup, otherwise the hardware mutex and peripheral will not be ready.
ca_hash_compute.usage: This function is typically used for one-shot hashing operations where the entire data block is available in memory. It is often paired with ca_hash_init() during the system boot sequence to prepare the hardware. In a typical workflow, you allocate a buffer for the digest, call ca_hash_compute, and then verify the return value before using the digest data. It is commonly used in security services, such as verifying file integrity, generating key fingerprints, or performing iterative hashing for password derivation.

ca_hash_ctx_final.brief: Completes a hashing operation, retrieves the final digest, and releases the hardware context.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the hash context structure. Must be initialized and currently in a 'started' state.

params.name: digest
params.desc: Buffer where the resulting hash bytes will be stored. Must be large enough to hold the algorithm's output.

params.name: digest_len
params.desc: Pointer to a variable that will receive the actual length of the generated digest in bytes.

ca_hash_ctx_final.returns: Returns true if the hash was successfully finalized and the digest was written. Returns false if any input pointer is NULL, if the context was not previously started, or if the hardware operation failed.
ca_hash_ctx_final.notes: This function is blocking because it uses a mutex to ensure exclusive access to the hardware hashing engine. It is thread-safe, meaning multiple threads can attempt to use different contexts, but they will wait for the mutex if the hardware is busy. It must NOT be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because the mutex lock will cause a system hang or kernel panic. A common mistake is failing to check the return value; if the function returns false, the digest buffer will contain invalid data, and the context remains in an inconsistent state.
ca_hash_ctx_final.usage: This function is the final step in the hashing lifecycle: init -> update (one or more times) -> final. It is used to extract the result after all data chunks have been processed. It pairs with ca_hash_ctx_update to finalize the calculation and automatically cleans up the internal hardware state, allowing other threads to use the hashing engine for their own operations.

ca_hash_ctx_free.brief: Releases the heap-allocated buffer and resets the hash context structure.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the hash context structure. Must be a valid pointer or NULL.

ca_hash_ctx_free.notes: This function is safe to call multiple times on the same context because it checks if the buffer is already NULL. It is not thread-safe; ensure no other task is accessing the context while this function is running. It is not intended to be called from an ISR as it performs heap memory management. The most common mistake is attempting to use the context structure after calling this function without re-initializing it via ca_hash_ctx_init.
ca_hash_ctx_free.usage: This function is used to clean up resources after a hashing operation is complete or if an error occurs during processing. It is typically the final step in the lifecycle of a hash context: ca_hash_ctx_init -> ca_hash_ctx_update -> ca_hash_ctx_final -> ca_hash_ctx_free. By calling this, you prevent memory leaks in the system heap, which is critical in long-running embedded applications.

ca_hash_ctx_init.brief: Initializes a hash context structure to prepare for cryptographic operations.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the context structure to be initialized. Must not be NULL.

params.name: algo
params.desc: The hashing algorithm to use (e.g., CA_HASH_ALGO_SHA256). Must be a valid enum value supported by the hardware.

ca_hash_ctx_init.returns: Returns true if the context was successfully initialized, false if the provided pointer is NULL.
ca_hash_ctx_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe because it only modifies the local memory structure provided by the caller. It is safe to call from an ISR, as it does not perform any hardware I/O or OS synchronization primitives. The most common mistake is passing an uninitialized or NULL pointer, which will cause the function to return false and potentially lead to a crash if the caller ignores the return value. Always ensure the context structure is allocated in a scope that remains valid for the duration of the hashing process.
ca_hash_ctx_init.usage: This function is the mandatory first step in the hashing lifecycle. It is typically used at the start of a task loop or before a specific data processing block to reset the state of the hash engine. It is always followed by calls to update functions (like ca_hash_ctx_update) to feed data into the engine, and eventually a finalization function to retrieve the digest. By using a context-based approach, you can maintain multiple independent hashing operations simultaneously in different tasks without them interfering with each other.

ca_hash_ctx_update.signature: bool ca_hash_ctx_update(ca_hash_ctx_t *ctx, const u8 *data, u32 len)
ca_hash_ctx_update.brief: Updates a hash calculation context with a new chunk of data, managing hardware state transitions automatically.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the hash context structure. Must be initialized via a constructor function before use.

params.name: data
params.desc: Pointer to the buffer containing the data to be hashed. Must not be NULL.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the data buffer in bytes. Must be greater than zero.

ca_hash_ctx_update.returns: Returns true if the data was successfully processed and the context saved. Returns false if the input parameters are invalid, the hardware fails to start, or the mutex cannot be acquired.
ca_hash_ctx_update.notes: This function is blocking because it uses a mutex to ensure exclusive access to the shared hardware hash engine. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because mutexes cannot be locked in interrupt context. The function handles context switching automatically: if it is the first call, it initializes the hardware; otherwise, it restores the previous state from the context structure. A common mistake is passing a NULL pointer or a zero length, which will cause the function to return false immediately without processing any data. Always ensure the context structure is not modified by other threads while this function is executing.
ca_hash_ctx_update.usage: This function is used to process data in chunks, which is essential when the total data size is too large to fit in memory or arrives in fragments from a network or peripheral. It is typically used in a sequence: first, the context is initialized, then 'ca_hash_ctx_update' is called one or more times to feed the data, and finally 'ca_hash_ctx_final' is called to retrieve the resulting hash digest. It is designed to be thread-safe, allowing multiple tasks to perform hashing operations concurrently by serializing access to the underlying hardware registers.

ca_hash_hw_csr_count.brief: Returns the number of Context Save/Restore (CSR) registers available in the hardware HASH peripheral.
ca_hash_hw_csr_count.returns: Returns an unsigned 32-bit integer representing the count of CSR registers. Returns 0 if the hardware does not support HASH or if the peripheral is not enabled in the current build configuration.
ca_hash_hw_csr_count.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it simply reads a constant or a hardware-defined value. It is safe to call from an ISR because it does not perform any complex operations or wait for hardware flags. A common beginner mistake is assuming that every STM32 chip has a HASH peripheral; always check the return value, as it will be 0 on platforms like the H747 or F1xx where HASH is not implemented. Ensure the HASH driver is properly initialized via ca_hash_hw_init before relying on this count for context management.
ca_hash_hw_csr_count.usage: This function is primarily used during the initialization phase of a HASH context structure. It is typically called inside a setup function to determine how many registers need to be saved or restored when performing a context switch or pausing a long-running hash operation. By pairing this with the context structure initialization, the driver ensures that the software knows exactly how much memory is required to preserve the state of the HASH engine. It acts as a hardware abstraction layer (HAL) bridge, allowing the higher-level software to remain portable across different STM32 families.

ca_hash_hw_digest.brief: Finalizes the hardware hash calculation and retrieves the resulting digest into a provided buffer.

params.name: digest
params.desc: Pointer to the destination buffer where the calculated hash will be stored. Must be large enough to hold the result (e.g., 32 bytes for SHA256).

params.name: digest_len
params.desc: Pointer to a variable that will be updated with the actual length of the generated digest in bytes.

params.name: algo
params.desc: The hashing algorithm used (e.g., CA_HASH_ALGO_SHA1, CA_HASH_ALGO_SHA256). Must match the algorithm initialized at the start.

ca_hash_hw_digest.returns: Returns true if the digest was successfully calculated and read within the timeout period. Returns false if the hardware timed out waiting for the calculation to complete or if an unsupported algorithm was requested.
ca_hash_hw_digest.notes: This function is blocking; it enters a busy-wait loop (polling) until the hardware sets the DCIS flag or the timeout expires. It is not thread-safe on its own and should be protected by a mutex if multiple tasks access the hardware. Do not call this from an ISR, as the busy-wait loop will block the CPU and prevent other interrupts from being serviced. A common mistake is failing to ensure the hardware peripheral is properly initialized and fed with data before calling this function, which will result in an invalid or incomplete digest.
ca_hash_hw_digest.usage: This function is the final step in the hashing sequence: initialization (ca_hash_hw_start), data processing (ca_hash_hw_feed), and finally retrieval (ca_hash_hw_digest). It is typically used within a wrapper function that manages a mutex to ensure exclusive access to the hardware peripheral. Once this function returns true, the digest buffer is ready for use, and the hardware is typically ready for the next hashing operation.

ca_hash_hw_feed.brief: Transfers raw data bytes into the hardware HASH peripheral's data input register.

params.name: data
params.desc: Pointer to the buffer containing the data to be hashed. Must be a valid memory address; passing NULL will cause a hard fault.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the data in bytes. Can be any value, but the function handles non-word-aligned lengths by padding the final word.

ca_hash_hw_feed.notes: This function is a low-level driver routine that writes directly to the HASH peripheral's data register (DIN). It is non-blocking in terms of RTOS scheduling, but it is synchronous in execution, meaning the CPU will stay inside this function until all data is copied to the hardware. It is not thread-safe on its own; you must ensure that access to the HASH peripheral is protected by a mutex or semaphore before calling this. It is generally safe to call from an ISR if the hardware is not being accessed by a task simultaneously, but this is highly discouraged as it can lead to race conditions. A common mistake is calling this function without first initializing the HASH peripheral or starting the algorithm, which will result in the data being written to an unconfigured or disabled hardware block.
ca_hash_hw_feed.usage: This function is used in the middle of a hashing operation sequence. The typical workflow is: 1) Acquire a mutex to ensure exclusive access to the HASH hardware, 2) Call a function to initialize/start the specific algorithm (e.g., SHA-256), 3) Call ca_hash_hw_feed to push the data payload into the hardware, 4) Call ca_hash_hw_digest to retrieve the final result, and 5) Release the mutex. It is strictly a data-transfer function and does not manage the state machine of the HASH peripheral itself.

ca_hash_hw_init.brief: Initializes the hardware HASH peripheral by enabling its clock in the RCC register.
ca_hash_hw_init.returns: Returns true if the hardware peripheral is successfully enabled and available on the current MCU; returns false if the peripheral is missing, disabled in configuration, or unsupported on the specific chip.
ca_hash_hw_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes very quickly as it only performs a register write to the Reset and Clock Control (RCC) unit. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs a simple atomic-like write, but it is not intended to be called repeatedly; it should be called once during system startup. It is safe to call from an ISR, but there is no logical reason to do so, as hardware initialization should happen during the system boot phase. The most common mistake is assuming this function configures the HASH algorithm settings; it only powers the hardware block. If you call this and it returns false, your application must handle the error immediately, as subsequent calls to HASH functions will likely fail or cause a hard fault if they attempt to access unclocked registers.
ca_hash_hw_init.usage: This function is the mandatory first step in the HASH driver lifecycle. It is typically called inside the higher-level 'ca_hash_init' function, which also initializes the mutexes required to protect the peripheral from concurrent access by multiple threads. You should always check the return value of this function before proceeding to any data processing tasks. It is paired with subsequent configuration and computation functions; if this returns false, the driver is effectively dead for that session.

ca_hash_hw_restore_ctx.signature: void ca_hash_hw_restore_ctx(const u32 *csr, u32 count, u32 cr)
ca_hash_hw_restore_ctx.brief: Restores the internal state of the hardware HASH peripheral from a previously saved buffer.

params.name: csr
params.desc: Pointer to an array containing the saved HASH Context Swap Registers (CSR). Must point to a valid memory block of at least 'count' size.

params.name: count
params.desc: The number of registers to restore. This must match the hardware-specific count used during the save operation.

params.name: cr
params.desc: The saved value of the Control Register (CR), which defines the HASH configuration and state.

ca_hash_hw_restore_ctx.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately by writing directly to hardware registers. It is thread-safe only if the caller ensures that no other task or ISR is accessing the HASH peripheral simultaneously, as the HASH hardware is typically a shared resource. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the hardware is not currently busy with another operation. A common mistake is passing an incorrect 'count' or a stale buffer, which will result in corrupted hash calculations without triggering an explicit error. Note that on some STM32 families (like F1, F4, F7), this function is a no-op because the hardware does not support context switching; always verify your target architecture's capabilities.
ca_hash_hw_restore_ctx.usage: This function is used to implement 'context switching' for HASH operations, allowing the system to pause a long-running hash calculation, perform other tasks, and resume later. It is typically used in a sequence: first, the context is saved using a corresponding save function, then the hardware is used for other tasks, and finally, this function is called to restore the state before calling 'ca_hash_hw_feed' to continue processing data. It is essential for multi-threaded environments where multiple data streams need to be hashed concurrently using the same hardware peripheral.

ca_hash_hw_save_ctx.brief: Saves the current internal state of the hardware HASH peripheral into a buffer for later resumption.

params.name: csr
params.desc: Pointer to an array where the HASH Context Swap Registers (CSR) values will be stored. Must be large enough to hold 'count' elements.

params.name: count
params.desc: The number of CSR registers to read from the hardware. This value is hardware-specific and must match the peripheral's register count.

params.name: cr
params.desc: Pointer to a variable where the HASH Control Register (CR) state will be saved.

ca_hash_hw_save_ctx.returns: This function returns void and does not provide status codes. It assumes the hardware is accessible and the pointers provided are valid.
ca_hash_hw_save_ctx.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately by reading hardware registers. It is thread-safe only if the caller ensures exclusive access to the HASH peripheral, typically via a mutex, before calling this function. It is generally safe to call from an ISR, provided the hardware is not currently being accessed by a lower-priority task. A common beginner mistake is providing a buffer that is too small for the 'count' parameter, which will cause a memory corruption (buffer overflow). Always ensure the HASH peripheral clock is enabled and the peripheral is initialized before attempting to save its context.
ca_hash_hw_save_ctx.usage: This function is used in multi-tasking environments where a long-running HASH operation needs to be paused to allow other tasks to use the hardware. It is typically used in a sequence: first, the task locks a mutex, performs some data processing using ca_hash_hw_feed, calls ca_hash_hw_save_ctx to preserve the state, and then unlocks the mutex. Later, when the task resumes, it restores the saved registers back into the hardware before continuing the calculation. This pattern allows the system to share a single hardware HASH engine across multiple threads without losing data integrity.

ca_hash_hw_set_nblw.brief: Configures the number of valid bits in the final partial word of a hash data block.

params.name: valid_bytes
params.desc: Number of valid bytes in the last word (0 to 3). A value of 0 indicates the last word is empty or fully processed.

ca_hash_hw_set_nblw.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a direct hardware register write to the HASH peripheral's STR (STRategy/STatus) register. It is not thread-safe; it must be called while the HASH peripheral is locked by a mutex or within a critical section to prevent race conditions between multiple tasks. It is generally not safe to call from an ISR unless the HASH peripheral is exclusively managed by that ISR. The most common mistake is passing a value greater than 3, which may corrupt the register bits or cause undefined hardware behavior depending on the specific STM32 series.
ca_hash_hw_set_nblw.usage: This function is used exclusively during the finalization phase of a hash calculation. It is called after all full 32-bit words have been fed into the hardware using ca_hash_hw_feed, but before triggering the final digest calculation. It informs the hardware exactly how many bytes of the final, potentially partial, word should be included in the hash computation. It is typically paired with ca_hash_hw_feed and followed by a function that triggers the final digest calculation.

ca_hash_hw_start.brief: Initializes the hardware cryptographic engine to begin a new hashing session with a specified algorithm.

params.name: algo
params.desc: The hashing algorithm to use (e.g., CA_HASH_ALGO_SHA1, CA_HASH_ALGO_SHA256). Must be a supported enum value; passing an unsupported or invalid algorithm will cause the function to return false.

ca_hash_hw_start.returns: Returns true if the hardware was successfully configured for the requested algorithm, or false if the algorithm is unsupported or the hardware initialization failed.
ca_hash_hw_start.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately by writing to the hardware control registers. It is generally thread-safe only if protected by a mutex, as the underlying hardware peripheral is a shared resource; calling this from multiple threads simultaneously without synchronization will corrupt the hashing state. It is safe to call from an ISR only if the hardware peripheral is not being used by the main thread, but this is strongly discouraged due to the risk of race conditions. A common mistake is failing to check the return value; if the hardware is not initialized or the algorithm is unsupported, proceeding to feed data will result in undefined behavior or silent failure.
ca_hash_hw_start.usage: This function is the entry point for any hashing operation and must be called before feeding data into the engine. It is typically used within a wrapper function that manages a mutex to ensure exclusive access to the hardware. The standard sequence is: lock the mutex, call ca_hash_hw_start, feed the data using ca_hash_hw_feed, retrieve the result with ca_hash_hw_digest, and finally unlock the mutex.

ca_hash_init.brief: Initializes the internal HASH hardware peripheral and its associated thread-safety mutex.
ca_hash_init.returns: Returns true if both the mutex and the hardware peripheral were initialized successfully; returns false if the hardware initialization failed.
ca_hash_init.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called exactly once during the system startup phase, typically within ca_os_main or a configuration routine. It is strictly non-blocking and must NOT be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it initializes a mutex, which is a kernel object intended for task-level synchronization. A common beginner mistake is calling this function multiple times or from different tasks; doing so will re-initialize the mutex, potentially causing race conditions or memory corruption if other tasks are already waiting on that mutex.
ca_hash_init.usage: This function is the mandatory entry point for any cryptographic operations involving hashing. It is typically paired with ca_hash_compute, which performs the actual data processing. In a standard application lifecycle, you call this during the system initialization phase (before starting any worker tasks) to ensure the hardware is ready and the synchronization primitive is allocated. If this function returns false, the application should enter a safe state or halt, as subsequent calls to hash functions will likely lead to undefined behavior or hardware faults.

ca_hchacha20.signature: void ca_hchacha20(ca_chacha20_ctx_t *wk, u8 *out, const u8 *key, const u8 *nonce)
ca_hchacha20.brief: Derives a subkey and nonce from a master key and nonce using the HChaCha20 function.

params.name: wk
params.desc: Pointer to the ChaCha20 context structure used for internal state calculations. Must be initialized or cleared before use.

params.name: out
params.desc: Buffer of at least 32 bytes where the derived 256-bit subkey and 64-bit nonce will be stored.

params.name: key
params.desc: Pointer to the 256-bit master key (32 bytes).

params.name: nonce
params.desc: Pointer to the 128-bit nonce (16 bytes).

ca_hchacha20.returns: void. This function does not return a status code; it performs the derivation and clears the context buffer internally.
ca_hchacha20.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a deterministic cryptographic transformation. It is thread-safe provided that the 'wk' context pointer is not shared between concurrent tasks without external synchronization (like a mutex). It is safe to call from an ISR, but be aware that it performs a significant amount of computation (20 rounds of ChaCha20), which may impact interrupt latency. The most common mistake is passing an uninitialized or NULL context pointer, which will lead to a memory access violation or corrupted output.
ca_hchacha20.usage: This function is primarily used in XChaCha20-based constructions to derive a subkey from a long-term key and a large nonce. It is typically called during the initialization phase of an encryption or decryption session. Developers should ensure the 'wk' context is properly allocated, often using ca_memory_allocate or as part of a larger structure, and that the 'out' buffer is large enough to hold the 32-byte result. It is often paired with ca_memcpy to move the derived subkey into a specific encryption context.

ca_hexdump.brief: Prints a formatted hexadecimal and ASCII memory dump to the system standard output.

params.name: ptr
params.desc: Pointer to the start of the memory buffer to be dumped. Must be a valid memory address accessible by the CPU.

params.name: size
params.desc: The total number of bytes to display. If the size is not a multiple of 16, the final line will be padded accordingly.

ca_hexdump.notes: This function is a blocking utility that formats and sends data to the system output stream. It is not thread-safe if multiple tasks attempt to print simultaneously, as it may result in interleaved or garbled output. It is strictly forbidden to call this function from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it performs blocking I/O operations which can cause system instability or deadlocks. A common beginner mistake is passing an uninitialized pointer or a pointer to memory that is not currently mapped, which will trigger a HardFault exception.
ca_hexdump.usage: This function is primarily used for debugging hardware drivers (like QSPI, SDIO, or Flash) to verify that data read from peripherals matches expected values. It is typically used in a sequence where a buffer is allocated, data is read into that buffer via a hardware driver function, the buffer is inspected using ca_hexdump, and finally, the buffer is released using ca_memory_free. It is an essential tool for verifying data integrity during communication protocol development or file system debugging.

ca_hexdump_u32.brief: Prints a formatted hexadecimal dump of a memory block containing 32-bit unsigned integers to the standard output.

params.name: ptr
params.desc: A pointer to the starting memory address of the data to be dumped. Must be a valid, aligned memory address; passing a NULL pointer will cause a hard fault.

params.name: size
params.desc: The number of 32-bit words to read and print. Ensure this value does not exceed the allocated buffer size to avoid reading out-of-bounds memory.

ca_hexdump_u32.returns: This function returns void and does not provide a status code, meaning it cannot signal if the memory read was successful or if the output buffer was full.
ca_hexdump_u32.notes: This function is non-blocking in terms of RTOS task scheduling, but it performs synchronous string formatting and output operations, which can be slow if the output device (e.g., UART) is busy. It is NOT safe to call from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it uses internal string buffers and standard output functions that likely rely on mutexes or shared resources. A common beginner mistake is passing an uninitialized pointer or a size that is too large, which can lead to reading sensitive system memory or triggering a memory protection fault. Always ensure the memory region pointed to by 'ptr' is accessible and within the bounds of your allocated heap or static memory.
ca_hexdump_u32.usage: This function is primarily used for debugging and diagnostic purposes to inspect the contents of memory buffers, configuration structures, or peripheral registers in real-time. It is typically called during the development phase when you need to verify that data processing algorithms are producing the expected results in memory. It is often paired with initialization functions that allocate memory or configure hardware, and it is used before or after data processing steps to verify state changes. In a production environment, these calls should be wrapped in preprocessor macros (e.g., #ifdef DEBUG) to ensure they are removed from the final binary to save execution time and memory.

ca_hkdf_sha256.signature: bool ca_hkdf_sha256(ca_hmac_sha256_ctx_t *ctx, const u8 *salt, u32 salt_len, const u8 *ikm, u32 ikm_len, const u8 *info, u32 info_len, u8 *out, u32 out_len)
ca_hkdf_sha256.brief: Derives a cryptographically strong key from input material using the HKDF-SHA256 algorithm (RFC 5869).

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to a pre-allocated HMAC context. Must not be NULL.

params.name: salt
params.desc: Optional salt value. If NULL or length is 0, a default zero-filled salt is used.

params.name: salt_len
params.desc: Length of the salt buffer in bytes.

params.name: ikm
params.desc: Input Keying Material. Must not be NULL if ikm_len > 0.

params.name: ikm_len
params.desc: Length of the IKM buffer in bytes.

params.name: info
params.desc: Optional application-specific context/info string. Can be NULL.

params.name: info_len
params.desc: Length of the info buffer in bytes.

params.name: out
params.desc: Buffer to store the derived key. Must not be NULL.

params.name: out_len
params.desc: Desired length of the output key. Must be > 0 and <= HKDF_SHA256_MAX_OUT.

ca_hkdf_sha256.returns: Returns true if the key derivation succeeded, false if any input validation failed (e.g., NULL pointers, invalid lengths).
ca_hkdf_sha256.notes: This function is blocking and performs multiple HMAC operations, which can be computationally expensive depending on the output length. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR because it performs heap-like operations or uses shared context buffers that are not re-entrant. The provided 'ctx' is used as a workspace and is wiped internally, so do not expect it to retain state after the call. A common beginner mistake is passing an uninitialized or NULL context pointer, which will immediately trigger a return of false.
ca_hkdf_sha256.usage: Use this function when you need to expand a short, low-entropy secret into a longer, cryptographically strong key for encryption or authentication. It is typically used in secure communication protocols (like TLS or custom pipes) to derive session keys from a master secret. The standard sequence is: allocate the context (often via ca_memory_allocate), call ca_hkdf_sha256 to generate the key, and then free the context memory once the operation is complete.

ca_hmac_blake2s.signature: void ca_hmac_blake2s(ca_hmac_blake2s_ctx_t *ctx, u8 *out, const u8 *key, u32 keylen, const u8 *in, u32 len)
ca_hmac_blake2s.brief: Computes a BLAKE2s-based HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) in a single operation.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the HMAC context structure. Must be allocated and valid.

params.name: out
params.desc: Buffer to store the resulting HMAC tag. Must be at least 32 bytes.

params.name: key
params.desc: Pointer to the secret key data.

params.name: keylen
params.desc: Length of the secret key in bytes.

params.name: in
params.desc: Pointer to the input message data to be authenticated.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the input message in bytes.

ca_hmac_blake2s.returns: This function returns void. It assumes the provided pointers are valid and the context is properly initialized.
ca_hmac_blake2s.notes: This function is a convenience wrapper that performs the full HMAC sequence: initialization, data processing, and finalization. It is not thread-safe if multiple tasks share the same context pointer simultaneously. It is not intended to be called from an ISR because cryptographic operations can be computationally expensive and may block the system for too long. A common mistake is passing an uninitialized or NULL context pointer, which will cause a memory access violation (hard fault).
ca_hmac_blake2s.usage: Use this function when you have the entire message available in memory and want to generate an authentication tag quickly. If the message is too large to fit in memory or arrives in chunks, you should instead use the individual functions: ca_hmac_blake2s_init, followed by multiple calls to ca_hmac_blake2s_update, and finally ca_hmac_blake2s_final. This function is typically used in security protocols to verify data integrity and authenticity.

ca_hmac_blake2s_final.brief: Finalizes the HMAC-BLAKE2s calculation, writes the result to the output buffer, and clears the context.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the HMAC context structure previously initialized with ca_hmac_blake2s_init.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to a buffer where the resulting HMAC tag will be stored. Must have enough space for the output size.

ca_hmac_blake2s_final.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs the final cryptographic operations, including the second pass of the HMAC algorithm. It is not thread-safe; you must ensure that no other task or ISR accesses the same context object while this function is executing. A critical security feature is that it calls ca_memzero on the context structure before returning, which wipes sensitive key material from memory. The most common mistake is passing an uninitialized or already-finalized context, which will lead to undefined behavior or incorrect HMAC tags.
ca_hmac_blake2s_final.usage: This function is the final step in the HMAC-BLAKE2s sequence. It is typically used after calling ca_hmac_blake2s_init to set the key and one or more calls to ca_hmac_blake2s_update to process the data stream. Once this function is called, the context is wiped and cannot be reused for further updates; you must call ca_hmac_blake2s_init again if you wish to start a new HMAC calculation.

ca_hmac_blake2s_init.brief: Initializes the HMAC-BLAKE2s context with a provided key to prepare for message authentication.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the HMAC context structure. Must be allocated and valid.

params.name: key
params.desc: Pointer to the secret key buffer. Can be NULL if keylen is 0.

params.name: keylen
params.desc: Length of the key in bytes. If greater than the block size, the key is hashed first.

ca_hmac_blake2s_init.notes: This function is not thread-safe; you must ensure that the context structure is not accessed by multiple tasks simultaneously. It is not intended to be called from an ISR because it performs memory operations and internal hashing that may take significant time. Before calling this, ensure the context pointer is valid and the key buffer is accessible. A common mistake is passing an uninitialized or stack-allocated context that is not properly cleared, leading to unpredictable HMAC results.
ca_hmac_blake2s_init.usage: This function is the mandatory first step in the HMAC-BLAKE2s sequence. It is typically followed by one or more calls to ca_hmac_blake2s_update to process the message data, and finally by ca_hmac_blake2s_final to produce the authentication tag. Use this when you need to verify data integrity or authenticity using a shared secret key.

ca_hmac_blake2s_update.brief: Updates the HMAC-BLAKE2s context with a new chunk of input data.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the HMAC context structure initialized by ca_hmac_blake2s_init.

params.name: in
params.desc: Pointer to the buffer containing the data to be hashed.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the input data in bytes.

ca_hmac_blake2s_update.notes: This function is not thread-safe; you must ensure that no other task or ISR accesses the same context object simultaneously. It is a non-blocking operation that processes the input data immediately. You must call ca_hmac_blake2s_init before calling this function, otherwise, the internal state will be invalid and the resulting HMAC will be incorrect. A common mistake is passing a NULL pointer or an uninitialized context, which will lead to a hard fault or memory corruption.
ca_hmac_blake2s_update.usage: This function is used to process data in chunks, which is essential when the input message is too large to fit into memory at once. It is typically used in a sequence: first call ca_hmac_blake2s_init to set the key, then call ca_hmac_blake2s_update one or more times to feed the data, and finally call ca_hmac_blake2s_final to retrieve the resulting MAC. It is the standard way to compute HMACs for streaming data or large files.

ca_hmac_sha256.signature: void ca_hmac_sha256(ca_hmac_sha256_ctx_t *ctx, const u8 *key, u32 key_len, const u8 *data, u32 len, u8 mac[HMAC_SHA256_SIZE])
ca_hmac_sha256.brief: Computes a full HMAC-SHA256 message authentication code in a single operation.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the HMAC context structure. Must be allocated and valid.

params.name: key
params.desc: Pointer to the secret key buffer.

params.name: key_len
params.desc: Length of the secret key in bytes.

params.name: data
params.desc: Pointer to the input data buffer to be authenticated.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the input data in bytes.

params.name: mac
params.desc: Output buffer of 32 bytes to store the resulting HMAC.

ca_hmac_sha256.returns: void. If ctx is NULL, the function returns immediately without performing any operation.
ca_hmac_sha256.notes: This function is a wrapper that performs initialization, data processing, and finalization in one go. It is non-blocking and thread-safe provided that the 'ctx' structure is not shared between concurrent tasks without external synchronization. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR if the underlying implementation uses locks or shared resources that could cause deadlocks. A critical detail is that this function wipes the 'ctx' structure after completion, meaning you cannot perform incremental updates after calling this; if you need to process data in chunks, use the individual init/update/final functions instead. The most common mistake is passing an uninitialized or NULL context pointer, which will lead to a silent failure or a system crash.
ca_hmac_sha256.usage: Use this function when you have all your data available in a single contiguous buffer and do not need to stream it. It is typically used for generating authentication tags for network packets, verifying file integrity, or deriving keys in protocols like HKDF. In a typical sequence, you declare a context variable, pass it to this function, and then immediately use the resulting 'mac' buffer. If you are building a protocol that requires multi-part hashing (e.g., hashing a header and then a body), do not use this function; instead, use ca_hmac_sha256_init, followed by multiple calls to ca_hmac_sha256_update, and finally ca_hmac_sha256_final.

ca_hmac_sha256_final.brief: Finalizes an HMAC-SHA256 calculation, writes the result to a buffer, and wipes the context for security.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the HMAC context structure initialized by ca_hmac_sha256_init. Must not be NULL.

params.name: mac
params.desc: Output buffer of size 32 bytes where the final HMAC digest will be stored.

ca_hmac_sha256_final.returns: void. The function does not return a status code; it assumes the context is valid and the output buffer has sufficient space.
ca_hmac_sha256_final.notes: This function is blocking as it performs the final hashing operations. It is not thread-safe if multiple tasks access the same context object simultaneously. It is not safe to call from an ISR because it performs multiple internal hashing steps that may take significant time. A critical security feature of this function is that it calls ca_memzero on the context structure after completion; this prevents sensitive key material from remaining in RAM. The most common mistake is attempting to use the context object again after calling this function; since the context is wiped, any subsequent call to ca_hmac_sha256_update will result in undefined behavior or a crash.
ca_hmac_sha256_final.usage: This function is the final step in the HMAC-SHA256 lifecycle. The typical sequence is: 1) Initialize the context with ca_hmac_sha256_init, 2) Feed data into the context using one or more calls to ca_hmac_sha256_update, and 3) Call ca_hmac_sha256_final to retrieve the result and securely clear the memory. It is used whenever you need to verify data integrity or authenticate a message using a shared secret key.

ca_hmac_sha256_init.signature: void ca_hmac_sha256_init(ca_hmac_sha256_ctx_t *ctx, const u8 *key, u32 key_len)
ca_hmac_sha256_init.brief: Initializes the HMAC-SHA256 context with a provided key for secure message authentication.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the HMAC context structure to be initialized. Must be allocated memory.

params.name: key
params.desc: Pointer to the secret key buffer. Can be NULL if key_len is 0.

params.name: key_len
params.desc: Length of the key in bytes. If greater than 64 (SHA256 block size), the key is hashed first.

ca_hmac_sha256_init.returns: void. This function does not return a status code; it assumes the provided pointers are valid.
ca_hmac_sha256_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs purely computational operations, making it safe to call from ISRs or tasks. It is not thread-safe if multiple tasks share the same context object simultaneously; ensure each task uses its own context instance. The function handles key preprocessing (hashing long keys and padding) as per RFC 2104. A common mistake is passing an uninitialized or NULL context pointer, which will cause a memory access violation. Always ensure the context structure is allocated before calling this function.
ca_hmac_sha256_init.usage: This function is the mandatory first step in the HMAC-SHA256 sequence. It is typically followed by one or more calls to ca_hmac_sha256_update to process the message data, and finally ca_hmac_sha256_final to retrieve the resulting MAC. It is used in security protocols, such as KDF (Key Derivation Functions) or message integrity checks, to prepare the internal state with the secret key.

ca_hmac_sha256_update.brief: Updates the HMAC-SHA256 calculation with a new chunk of input data.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the HMAC context structure. Must be initialized via ca_hmac_sha256_init before use.

params.name: data
params.desc: Pointer to the buffer containing the data to be processed.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the data buffer in bytes.

ca_hmac_sha256_update.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs the hashing operation synchronously on the current thread. It is not thread-safe; you must ensure that the same context is not accessed by multiple tasks simultaneously. It is generally not recommended to call this from an ISR due to the computational cost of SHA256, which could cause jitter in real-time tasks. The most common mistake is passing an uninitialized context or a NULL pointer, which will lead to a hard fault or memory corruption.
ca_hmac_sha256_update.usage: This function is used in the middle phase of an HMAC calculation. The typical sequence is: 1) call ca_hmac_sha256_init to set up the key, 2) call ca_hmac_sha256_update one or more times to process the message data, and 3) call ca_hmac_sha256_final to retrieve the resulting MAC. It is used when the data to be authenticated is too large to fit in a single buffer or arrives in fragments (e.g., streaming data over a network).

ca_hmac_sha384_ctx.signature: void ca_hmac_sha384_ctx(ca_sha512_ctx_t *work, const u8 *key, u32 key_len, const u8 *data, u32 len, u8 *mac)
ca_hmac_sha384_ctx.brief: Computes an HMAC-SHA384 message authentication code using a provided SHA512 context.

params.name: work
params.desc: Pointer to a pre-allocated SHA512 context structure used as a workspace for the HMAC calculation.

params.name: key
params.desc: Pointer to the secret key buffer.

params.name: key_len
params.desc: Length of the secret key in bytes.

params.name: data
params.desc: Pointer to the input data buffer to be authenticated.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the input data in bytes.

params.name: mac
params.desc: Pointer to the output buffer where the resulting 48-byte HMAC-SHA384 tag will be stored.

ca_hmac_sha384_ctx.returns: void. This function does not return a status code; it assumes valid pointers and sufficient buffer sizes are provided.
ca_hmac_sha384_ctx.notes: This function is synchronous and blocking; it performs multiple hashing passes and will hold the CPU until the calculation is complete. It is not thread-safe if the same 'work' context is shared across multiple tasks simultaneously, so ensure each task uses its own context or protect access with a mutex. It is generally safe to call from an ISR if the stack size is sufficient, but because it performs heavy cryptographic operations, it is strongly discouraged to call it from high-frequency interrupts as it will cause significant jitter. The most common beginner mistake is providing a 'work' context that is not properly aligned or is being modified by another function (like a concurrent SHA512 update) during the HMAC process.
ca_hmac_sha384_ctx.usage: This function is used to verify data integrity and authenticity in network protocols (like TLS) or secure storage. It is typically used in a sequence where the developer first prepares the key and data, then calls this function to generate the tag. It is often paired with ca_memset to clear sensitive key material from the stack after the operation is complete to prevent memory leakage. In a typical application, you would initialize your context, call this function to compute the MAC, and then immediately clear the buffers containing the key and intermediate hashes.

ca_http_resp_bad_request.brief: Sends a standard HTTP 400 Bad Request response to the client.

params.name: r
params.desc: A pointer to the HTTP response handle. Must be a valid, initialized response object; passing a NULL pointer will cause a system crash.

ca_http_resp_bad_request.returns: This function returns void and does not provide a status code; it assumes the underlying network stack handles the transmission successfully.
ca_http_resp_bad_request.notes: This function is a blocking call that prepares and sends the HTTP header and body over the network. It is not thread-safe if multiple tasks attempt to write to the same response handle simultaneously, so ensure only one task manages a specific response object. It must not be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it performs blocking I/O operations which are forbidden in ISR context. The most common beginner mistake is calling this function after the response has already been partially sent or closed, which leads to corrupted HTTP streams or memory access violations.
ca_http_resp_bad_request.usage: This function is used within HTTP request handlers when the incoming request is malformed, missing required parameters, or fails validation logic. It is typically called during the request parsing phase, immediately after detecting an error, to terminate the request cycle gracefully. It is often paired with ca_http_resp_begin to initialize the response structure and is followed by a return statement to exit the handler function, preventing further processing of the invalid request.

ca_http_resp_begin.signature: void ca_http_resp_begin(ca_http_response_t *r, u16 status, const char *content_type)
ca_http_resp_begin.brief: Initializes an HTTP response buffer by writing the status line, headers, and a placeholder for the content length.

params.name: r
params.desc: Pointer to the response structure. Must be pre-allocated and valid; passing a NULL pointer will cause a system crash.

params.name: status
params.desc: The HTTP status code (e.g., 200, 404). Only specific codes have defined reason phrases; others default to 'OK'.

params.name: content_type
params.desc: A string representing the MIME type (e.g., 'text/html', 'application/json'). Must be a null-terminated string.

ca_http_resp_begin.returns: void. This function does not return a status code, so it assumes the buffer has sufficient space to hold the headers.
ca_http_resp_begin.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs direct memory operations on the provided buffer. It is not thread-safe if multiple tasks access the same response object simultaneously, so ensure the response object is owned by the current task. It is not safe to call from an ISR because it performs string operations and memory writes that are not atomic. A common beginner mistake is failing to ensure the response buffer is large enough to hold the headers plus the body; if the buffer is too small, the headers will be truncated, resulting in an invalid HTTP response that the client will reject.
ca_http_resp_begin.usage: This function is the mandatory first step when generating an HTTP response in a handler function. It is typically followed by calls to write the actual body content and finally, the response is sent over the network. It pairs with functions like ca_http_resp_write to populate the body and relies on the internal state of the ca_http_response_t structure to track where the content length needs to be patched later. Use this whenever you need to start a new HTTP transaction in response to a client request.

ca_http_resp_begin_chunked.brief: Initializes an HTTP response using chunked transfer encoding, allowing data to be sent in multiple parts without knowing the total size beforehand.

params.name: r
params.desc: Pointer to the HTTP response structure. Must be initialized and valid.

params.name: status
params.desc: HTTP status code (e.g., 200, 404, 400). Only specific codes like 200, 400, 404, 405 are explicitly mapped to reason strings.

params.name: content_type
params.desc: String defining the MIME type (e.g., "text/plain", "application/json").

ca_http_resp_begin_chunked.returns: void. This function does not return a status code; it assumes the response structure is valid and memory is available for appending headers.
ca_http_resp_begin_chunked.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called within the context of a single HTTP request handler. It is strictly non-blocking as it only appends data to the internal response buffer. It must NOT be called from an ISR, as it performs string operations and memory management that are not ISR-safe. The most common mistake is calling this function after the response headers have already been sent or using an uninitialized response pointer, which will lead to memory corruption or system crashes.
ca_http_resp_begin_chunked.usage: Use this function when the total size of the HTTP response body is unknown at the start of the request, such as when streaming data from a sensor or generating a large log file on the fly. It is typically the first function called in a request handler, followed by multiple calls to ca_http_resp_write to send the actual data chunks. After all chunks are sent, the connection is typically closed or finalized by the underlying HTTP service logic.

ca_http_resp_flush.brief: Flushes the HTTP response staging buffer to the network, handling chunked encoding if enabled.

params.name: r
params.desc: Pointer to the HTTP response structure. Must be initialized via ca_http_resp_begin or ca_http_resp_begin_chunked.

ca_http_resp_flush.returns: Returns true if the data was successfully sent or if there was nothing to flush. Returns false if the underlying TCP transmission failed or if the response state is already marked as failed.
ca_http_resp_flush.notes: This function is blocking as it relies on ca_tcp_send, which waits for network transmission. It is not thread-safe and must not be called from an ISR, as it performs network I/O operations. The function automatically manages the transition from header transmission to body chunking; once the headers are flushed, the internal buffer pointers are reset. A common mistake is calling this function after the connection has been closed or after a previous call has already returned false, which will simply return the current failure state.
ca_http_resp_flush.usage: This function is used to push accumulated data from the HTTP response buffer to the client. It is typically called after one or more calls to ca_http_resp_write or ca_http_resp_puts to ensure the data is actually transmitted over the wire. In a typical request-response cycle, you initialize the response with ca_http_resp_begin_chunked, write data, call ca_http_resp_flush to send chunks, and finally close the connection or finish the response.

ca_http_resp_not_found.brief: Sends a standard HTTP 404 Not Found error response to the client.

params.name: r
params.desc: Pointer to the HTTP response handle. Must be a valid, initialized response object; passing a NULL pointer will cause a system crash.

ca_http_resp_not_found.notes: This function is a wrapper that simplifies sending a 404 error by calling ca_http_resp_begin and ca_http_resp_puts internally. It is not thread-safe if multiple tasks attempt to write to the same response handle simultaneously, so ensure the handle is owned by the current task. It is strictly non-blocking in terms of logic, but it relies on the underlying network stack's buffer availability; if the network buffer is full, it may wait until space is available. Do not call this from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) as it performs heap or buffer operations that are not ISR-safe.
ca_http_resp_not_found.usage: Use this function in your HTTP request handler logic whenever a client requests a resource (like a file or API endpoint) that does not exist on the device. It is typically called after parsing the incoming request path and determining that no matching route is found. It is designed to be the final action for that specific request, effectively terminating the response cycle with a standard error message. You should pair this with your routing logic to ensure that valid requests are handled normally and invalid ones are gracefully rejected with this function.

ca_http_resp_puti.brief: Converts an unsigned 32-bit integer to its string representation and appends it to an HTTP response buffer.

params.name: r
params.desc: Pointer to the HTTP response object. Must be a valid, initialized handle.

params.name: v
params.desc: The unsigned 32-bit integer value to be appended to the response.

ca_http_resp_puti.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a local stack-based conversion of the integer before calling the internal append function. It is not thread-safe if multiple tasks attempt to write to the same response object simultaneously, so ensure the response object is owned by the calling task. It is generally not recommended to call this from an ISR because it performs memory operations and string manipulation that could be time-consuming. A common mistake is passing a NULL pointer for the response object, which will cause a hard fault or memory corruption when the function attempts to access the object members.
ca_http_resp_puti.usage: This function is used during the construction of HTTP responses, typically within a web server callback or a network service task. It is used to dynamically inject numeric data, such as status codes, content lengths, or sensor readings, into the HTTP payload. It is typically paired with ca_http_resp_begin to start the response, followed by a sequence of ca_http_resp_puts and ca_http_resp_puti calls to build the body, and finally finished by the internal response transmission logic.

ca_http_resp_puts.brief: Appends a null-terminated string to an HTTP response buffer if the response is not header-only.

params.name: r
params.desc: Pointer to the active HTTP response object. Must be initialized via ca_http_resp_begin before use.

params.name: s
params.desc: The null-terminated C-string to append. Must not be NULL.

ca_http_resp_puts.returns: This function returns void and does not provide an error code. If the string is empty, it effectively does nothing.
ca_http_resp_puts.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a memory copy into the internal response buffer. It is not thread-safe; you must ensure that only one task accesses the specific response object at a time. It is generally not recommended to call this from an ISR because it performs string length calculation and memory operations which can be unpredictable in timing. A common beginner mistake is passing a NULL pointer or a string that is not null-terminated, which will cause the internal ca_strlen to read past the buffer and trigger a hard fault.
ca_http_resp_puts.usage: This function is used during the body generation phase of an HTTP response. It is typically called after ca_http_resp_begin has initialized the response headers and before the response is finalized. It is often paired with ca_http_resp_puti to construct dynamic JSON or HTML content. You should use this when you have static text or pre-formatted strings to send to the client, ensuring the response object remains valid throughout the entire sequence.

ca_http_resp_write.signature: void ca_http_resp_write(ca_http_response_t *r, const char *s, u16 len)
ca_http_resp_write.brief: Appends a specific length of data to the body of an HTTP response buffer.

params.name: r
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized HTTP response object. Must not be NULL.

params.name: s
params.desc: Pointer to the data buffer to be written. Must be a valid memory address.

params.name: len
params.desc: Number of bytes to copy from the source buffer. Ensure this does not exceed the remaining buffer capacity.

ca_http_resp_write.returns: void. This function does not return a status code, so it assumes the buffer has sufficient space.
ca_http_resp_write.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a memory copy into the internal response buffer. It is not thread-safe if multiple tasks access the same response object simultaneously, so ensure the response object is owned by the current task handler. It is strictly forbidden to call this from an ISR, as it performs memory operations that are not re-entrant. A common beginner mistake is passing a length that exceeds the pre-allocated buffer size, which will cause a buffer overflow or silent data truncation. Always ensure the response object has been properly initialized via ca_http_resp_begin before calling this function.
ca_http_resp_write.usage: This function is used within HTTP request handler callbacks to populate the payload of the response. It is typically called after ca_http_resp_begin, which sets up the HTTP headers and status codes. You use this function when you have a specific block of data, such as a pre-compiled HTML page or a binary payload, that needs to be sent to the client. It is often paired with ca_http_resp_puts if you are sending null-terminated strings, but ca_http_resp_write is preferred for binary data or when the exact length is already known to avoid unnecessary string scanning.

ca_http_serve_connection.brief: Processes an incoming HTTP request on a connection and handles the corresponding response lifecycle.

params.name: c
params.desc: Pointer to the connection structure containing pre-allocated RX/TX buffers and response state. Must be valid and initialized.

params.name: io
params.desc: Pointer to the I/O interface structure containing the transport-specific send/recv functions (e.g., TCP or TLS).

ca_http_serve_connection.returns: void. This function does not return a status code; it handles errors internally by closing the connection or setting the 'failed' flag in the response structure.
ca_http_serve_connection.notes: This function is blocking and performs multiple network read operations until the full HTTP request is received or a timeout occurs. It is NOT thread-safe for the same connection object; you must ensure only one task processes a specific connection at a time. It cannot be called from an ISR because it performs blocking I/O operations. A common mistake is passing a connection structure with insufficient buffer sizes (HTTP_REQ_BUF_SIZE/HTTP_RESP_BUF_SIZE), which will cause the request to be truncated or the response to fail. Ensure the underlying transport (TCP/TLS) is already established before calling this.
ca_http_serve_connection.usage: This function is the core engine for HTTP services. It is typically called immediately after a connection is accepted (e.g., via ca_tcp_accept). It automates the parsing of headers, waiting for the request body if necessary, and invoking the application-level routing logic. After this function returns, the caller should close the transport connection (e.g., ca_tcp_close or ca_tls_close) to release resources.

ca_http_service_start.signature: void ca_http_service_start(const ca_http_route_t *routes, u8 count, u16 port)
ca_http_service_start.brief: Initializes and launches the background HTTP server task with a defined routing table and port.

params.name: routes
params.desc: Pointer to an array of route structures defining URL paths and their associated callback functions. Must remain valid for the lifetime of the HTTP service.

params.name: count
params.desc: The number of elements in the routes array. Ensure this matches the actual array size to prevent out-of-bounds access.

params.name: port
params.desc: The TCP port to listen on. If set to 0, the system defaults to the standard HTTP port (usually 80).

ca_http_service_start.notes: This function is non-blocking; it spawns a background RTOS task and returns immediately. It is not thread-safe if called simultaneously from multiple contexts, though it contains a guard to prevent multiple starts. It must not be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) as it performs OS task creation. A common mistake is passing a local (stack-allocated) array for the routes parameter; since the HTTP task runs in the background, the array must be defined as 'static' or global to ensure it persists after the calling function returns.
ca_http_service_start.usage: This function is typically called during the system initialization phase or after network configuration (e.g., DHCP assignment) is complete. It is the entry point for enabling web-based management or telemetry on the device. It is often paired with network stack initialization functions like 'ca_arp_service_update_local_ip' to ensure the device has a valid IP address before the server begins listening for incoming connections.

ca_http_update_local_ip.brief: Updates the local IPv4 address stored within the HTTP service module.

params.name: ip
params.desc: A structure containing the four bytes of the new IPv4 address. Ensure the address is valid and formatted correctly before passing.

ca_http_update_local_ip.notes: This function is a simple memory assignment and is non-blocking, meaning it executes almost instantaneously. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs a single atomic write, but it does not include internal mutex protection, so you should avoid calling it while the HTTP service is actively processing requests to prevent race conditions. It is safe to call from an ISR, but it is typically used in the main application thread during network configuration changes. A common mistake is calling this function before the HTTP service has been initialized, which may lead to the IP being overwritten or ignored when the service eventually starts.
ca_http_update_local_ip.usage: This function is used primarily during network initialization or when a DHCP lease is renewed or changed. It is typically paired with other network service update functions like ca_arp_service_update_local_ip to ensure all protocol layers are synchronized with the new IP address. You should call this after receiving a new IP from a DHCP server but before calling ca_http_service_start to ensure the HTTP server binds to the correct interface address.
