A common beginner mistake is forgetting to check the return value; if the timer is already busy, the function will return false, and subsequent calls to start or stop the timer will fail or cause undefined behavior. Ensure the callback function is kept short and efficient, as it typically executes in a high-priority context.
ca_lptim_init_periodic.usage: This function is used to set up periodic tasks, such as blinking an LED, polling a sensor, or triggering a state machine update at regular intervals. It is typically used in a sequence: first, call ca_lptim_init_periodic to configure the hardware, then call ca_lptim_start to begin the counting process. Once the task is complete, you must call ca_lptim_stop followed by ca_lptim_deinit to release the hardware resource back to the system. It is often paired with ca_os_sleep to wait for a specific number of timer events to occur in the main application loop.

ca_lptim_is_busy.brief: Checks if a specific Low Power Timer (LPTIM) peripheral is currently allocated or in use by the system.

params.name: num
params.desc: The index of the LPTIM peripheral to check. Valid values are 1 up to LPTIM_MAX. Values outside this range are treated as 'busy' to prevent invalid hardware access.

ca_lptim_is_busy.returns: Returns true if the LPTIM is currently busy, reserved, or if the provided index is invalid. Returns false if the LPTIM is available for use.
ca_lptim_is_busy.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it performs a simple bitwise read on a static status variable. It is safe to call from an ISR because it does not involve complex logic or waiting. The most common mistake is assuming that 'false' means the hardware is powered on; this function only checks the software allocation status. Always ensure the LPTIM driver has been initialized before relying on this status, as an uninitialized driver might report an incorrect state.
ca_lptim_is_busy.usage: This function is primarily used as a guard clause before attempting to configure or start an LPTIM peripheral. It is typically paired with initialization functions like ca_lptim_init_periodic to ensure you do not overwrite an active timer configuration. In power management contexts, it is used to verify if the LPTIM is already claimed by another task or wake-up routine, preventing resource conflicts when the system attempts to enter low-power sleep modes.

ca_lptim_start.brief: Starts a previously initialized Low Power Timer (LPTIM) peripheral.

params.name: num
params.desc: The index of the LPTIM peripheral to start. Must correspond to a valid hardware timer index previously initialized via ca_lptim_init_periodic or similar.

ca_lptim_start.returns: Returns true if the timer was successfully started. Returns false if the timer is not in a busy/initialized state or if the hardware start command failed.
ca_lptim_start.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a quick check to ensure the timer is in a valid state before triggering the hardware. It is thread-safe assuming the underlying hardware registers are protected, but it is generally not intended to be called from an ISR unless specified by the architecture. A common beginner mistake is calling this function before initializing the timer; if the timer has not been initialized, ca_lptim_is_busy will return false, and the start command will be ignored. Always ensure the timer is properly configured with a callback before calling start to avoid unexpected behavior when the timer expires.
ca_lptim_start.usage: This function is used to trigger the countdown or periodic firing of a timer after it has been fully configured. It is typically used in a sequence: first, you initialize the timer with a period and a callback function using ca_lptim_init_periodic, then you call ca_lptim_start to begin the operation. Once the task is complete, you must call ca_lptim_stop to halt the timer and ca_lptim_deinit to release the hardware resources for other parts of the application. It is essential to pair this with stop and deinit to prevent resource leaks or unintended timer interrupts.

ca_lptim_stop.brief: Stops a running Low Power Timer (LPTIM) instance identified by its index.

params.name: num
params.desc: The index of the LPTIM peripheral to stop. Must be a valid index previously initialized via ca_lptim_init_periodic or similar functions.

ca_lptim_stop.returns: Returns true if the timer was successfully stopped. Returns false if the timer was not currently running (not busy) or if the hardware stop operation failed.
ca_lptim_stop.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately. It is generally thread-safe, but you must ensure that no other task is attempting to re-initialize or modify the same timer index simultaneously. A common beginner mistake is calling this function on a timer that has already been stopped or never started, which will return false; always check the return value if your application logic depends on the timer state. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the underlying hardware driver implementation is also ISR-safe, though typically this is used in task-level code to manage periodic events.
ca_lptim_stop.usage: Use this function when you need to halt a periodic task or a one-shot timer before it expires. It is typically used in a lifecycle sequence: first, you initialize the timer with a callback using ca_lptim_init_periodic, start it with ca_lptim_start, perform your timed operations, and finally call ca_lptim_stop to prevent further interrupts. After stopping, you should call ca_lptim_deinit if you no longer need the timer resource, ensuring proper cleanup of the hardware peripheral.

ca_lptim_wake_active.brief: Returns a bitmask identifying which LPTIM instances are currently configured to trigger a system wake-up from low-power modes.
ca_lptim_wake_active.returns: A 32-bit integer where each bit position corresponds to an LPTIM instance index (e.g., bit 0 for LPTIM1). If a bit is set (1), that specific timer is active and configured to wake the MCU; if clear (0), it is not.
ca_lptim_wake_active.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it performs a read-only operation on the internal state of the LPTIM driver. It is safe to call from an ISR, as it does not involve mutexes or complex synchronization primitives. The most common mistake is assuming that a set bit implies the timer is currently running; it only confirms that the timer is 'in use' and has the 'wake' flag enabled. Ensure the LPTIM driver is initialized before calling this, otherwise, the returned mask will always be zero.
ca_lptim_wake_active.usage: This function is primarily used by the Power Management module (PWR) before entering low-power states like Sleep or Stop. It allows the system to determine if it needs to configure specific EXTI lines or power-domain settings to ensure the LPTIM can actually trigger a wake-up event. It is typically paired with other 'wake_active' functions from different peripherals (like ca_lpuart_wake_active) to build a comprehensive wake-up configuration mask before the CPU executes the low-power entry sequence.

ca_lpuart_configure_gpio.brief: Configures the LPUART TX and RX pins to their required Alternate Function (AF) mode for hardware communication.

params.name: alternate_gpio
params.desc: A boolean flag where true (1) selects the alternate pin mapping (if supported by the hardware) and false (0) selects the default pin mapping.

ca_lpuart_configure_gpio.returns: Returns true (1) if the GPIO configuration was successful, or false (0) if the hardware initialization failed.
ca_lpuart_configure_gpio.notes: This function is a wrapper for the low-level hardware initialization of the LPUART pins. It is non-blocking and executes quickly, but it is not thread-safe if called simultaneously from multiple tasks, though it is typically only called during system startup. It is generally not safe to call from an ISR because it interacts with the GPIO peripheral registers which may require clock enabling or other shared resource access. The most common beginner mistake is calling this function before the GPIO peripheral clock has been enabled in the RCC registers, which will result in the configuration being ignored or the system hanging.
ca_lpuart_configure_gpio.usage: This function is used during the system initialization phase to prepare the physical pins for serial communication. It is typically called inside ca_lpuart_init or during the early system boot sequence before the LPUART peripheral is enabled. It pairs with other initialization functions like ca_lpuart_init to ensure the hardware is ready to receive or transmit data. If you need to override the default pin mapping or perform custom hardware setup, you call this function explicitly before starting the UART communication tasks.

ca_lpuart_deinit.brief: Safely shuts down the LPUART peripheral and resets its internal driver state.
ca_lpuart_deinit.returns: Returns true if the LPUART was successfully deinitialized. Returns false if the LPUART was already inactive (s_in_use is false), indicating an attempt to deinitialize an uninitialized or already closed peripheral.
ca_lpuart_deinit.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a clean teardown of the hardware and software state. It is not thread-safe by itself, so ensure no other tasks are attempting to transmit or receive data while this is called. It is generally not safe to call this from an ISR unless you are certain no other thread is accessing the LPUART. The most common beginner mistake is calling this function without checking the return value or calling it while an active communication process is still pending, which can lead to data loss or undefined behavior in the application logic.
ca_lpuart_deinit.usage: This function is used to release the LPUART hardware resources when they are no longer needed, typically to save power or to reconfigure the peripheral for a different communication mode. It is the counterpart to the initialization function and should be called as part of a clean shutdown sequence or before entering a deep sleep mode where the peripheral must be disabled. It is typically paired with a preceding initialization call and ensures that the internal callback pointer (s_on_rx) and usage flags are reset to prevent dangling pointers or accidental re-entry.

ca_lpuart_dispatch.brief: Processes incoming LPUART data by draining the hardware buffer and triggering the registered callback.
ca_lpuart_dispatch.notes: This function is designed specifically to be called from the LPUART1_IRQHandler. It is non-blocking in the sense that it only processes data currently present in the hardware FIFO; once the FIFO is empty, it returns immediately. It is not thread-safe on its own, but since it is intended for an ISR context, it relies on the hardware's atomic nature. A common beginner mistake is calling this function from the main loop instead of the ISR, which prevents the system from reacting to incoming data in real-time. Another critical error is failing to ensure the callback function (s_on_rx) is registered before the interrupt is enabled, which would lead to a null pointer dereference.
ca_lpuart_dispatch.usage: This function is the bridge between the hardware interrupt and your application logic. You typically use it by placing it inside the LPUART1_IRQHandler function in your STM32 family-specific file. It is used in conjunction with a registration function (like a hypothetical 'ca_lpuart_set_rx_callback') that defines what the system should do with the received byte. The typical sequence is: initialize the LPUART peripheral, register your callback function, enable the LPUART interrupt in the NVIC, and then let this function handle the data flow automatically whenever the hardware signals a receive event.

ca_lpuart_hw_deinit.brief: Performs a complete hardware shutdown of the LPUART peripheral, including disabling interrupts, clearing registers, and gating clocks.
ca_lpuart_hw_deinit.returns: This function returns void and does not provide feedback on the success of the hardware operations.
ca_lpuart_hw_deinit.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately. It is safe to call from an ISR, but you must ensure that no other tasks are attempting to read or write to the LPUART registers simultaneously, as this function performs a hard reset of the peripheral state. A common mistake is calling this function while a DMA transfer or an interrupt-driven transmission is still in progress, which will result in truncated data and potentially leave the hardware in an inconsistent state. Always ensure the higher-level driver logic has stopped all communication before invoking this hardware-level cleanup.
ca_lpuart_hw_deinit.usage: This function is used as the final step in the LPUART lifecycle, typically when the peripheral is no longer needed or the system is entering a low-power state. It is paired with ca_lpuart_init to ensure the hardware is returned to a clean, power-efficient state. In the caOS driver architecture, it is called by the wrapper function ca_lpuart_deinit, which manages the internal software state flags (like s_in_use) before triggering this hardware-specific cleanup. You should use this whenever you need to release the LPUART resource to save power or reconfigure the pins for a different function.

ca_lpuart_hw_gpio_init.brief: Configures the physical microcontroller pins for LPUART communication by setting them to the correct Alternate Function mode.

params.name: alternate_gpio
params.desc: If true, selects the secondary pin mapping (e.g., PB6/PB7 on H7). If false, uses the default pin mapping. Note that on many MCUs (U5, H5), this parameter is ignored as only one mapping exists.

ca_lpuart_hw_gpio_init.returns: Returns true if the GPIO configuration was successful or if the hardware supports LPUART. Returns false if the specific microcontroller model does not support LPUART or if the hardware configuration failed.
ca_lpuart_hw_gpio_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately. It is not thread-safe in the sense that it modifies hardware registers directly; therefore, it should only be called during the system initialization phase before the scheduler starts or before the LPUART peripheral is used. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. A common beginner mistake is to call this function multiple times or while the LPUART is already transmitting/receiving data, which can cause glitches on the communication lines or unexpected peripheral behavior. Ensure that the system clock for the GPIO port is enabled before calling this, as the underlying ca_gpio_configure function assumes the peripheral clock is active.
ca_lpuart_hw_gpio_init.usage: This function is used exclusively during the hardware abstraction layer (HAL) initialization sequence for the LPUART peripheral. It is typically called inside ca_lpuart_init to prepare the physical pins (TX and RX) before the UART registers are configured for baud rate and parity. You should never call this function manually in your application code; instead, rely on the driver's initialization sequence. It pairs with ca_lpuart_init to ensure the hardware is ready for data transfer.

ca_lpuart_hw_init.brief: Initializes the Low-Power UART (LPUART) hardware peripheral with specific baud rate and wake-up capabilities.

params.name: baud
params.desc: The desired communication speed in bits per second. Must be non-zero and satisfy the hardware constraint: 3 * baud <= clock_frequency <= 4096 * baud.

params.name: wake
params.desc: If true, enables the LPUART to wake the MCU from low-power sleep modes (Stop mode) upon receiving data.

ca_lpuart_hw_init.returns: Returns true if the hardware was successfully configured and the receiver is ready. Returns false if the baud rate is invalid, the clock constraints are not met, or the hardware platform does not support LPUART.
ca_lpuart_hw_init.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called during system initialization or from a single control task. It is a blocking function because it waits for the HSI clock to stabilize and for the LPUART receiver to acknowledge readiness (REACK). It must NOT be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) due to these blocking loops. A common mistake is failing to verify the return value; if the baud rate is too high or low for the current clock source, the function will fail, and proceeding as if it succeeded will lead to silent communication errors. Additionally, ensure that the system clock configuration is stable before calling this, as it relies on the HSI clock being available.
ca_lpuart_hw_init.usage: This function is part of the low-level driver initialization sequence. It is typically called by a higher-level driver wrapper (like ca_lpuart_init) after GPIO pins have been configured via ca_lpuart_configure_gpio. It is used to prepare the peripheral for asynchronous data reception and to configure the NVIC interrupts. It should be paired with a corresponding de-initialization function (ca_lpuart_deinit) to disable interrupts and clocks when the peripheral is no longer needed, ensuring power efficiency and preventing dangling interrupts.

ca_lpuart_hw_put.brief: Transmits a string of data over the LPUART peripheral using blocking polling mode.

params.name: message
params.desc: A pointer to a structure containing the data buffer and its size. Must not be NULL and must contain a valid size; passing an uninitialized structure will lead to undefined behavior.

ca_lpuart_hw_put.returns: Returns the number of bytes successfully transmitted (equal to message->size). Returns 0 if the hardware is not supported, if the peripheral is not in use, or if the input is invalid.
ca_lpuart_hw_put.notes: This function is strictly blocking, meaning the CPU will sit in a 'while' loop waiting for the hardware transmit buffer to empty for every single byte. Because it uses polling, it is thread-unsafe; if two tasks call this simultaneously, the output will be garbled. It is generally safe to call from an ISR, but doing so is strongly discouraged because the blocking nature will stall the entire system and potentially cause missed interrupts or watchdog resets. Ensure the LPUART peripheral is fully initialized via ca_lpuart_init before calling this, otherwise, the CPU may hang indefinitely in the wait loop.
ca_lpuart_hw_put.usage: This function is typically used for low-level debugging or system logging where simplicity is preferred over performance. It is usually called after a successful ca_lpuart_init sequence. In the caOS architecture, it is wrapped by ca_lpuart_put, which adds a safety check for the peripheral state. It is the standard way to send data to a console or CLI interface when the system is in a state where interrupts are not yet enabled or when immediate, synchronous output is required.

ca_lpuart_hw_recv.brief: Polls the LPUART hardware for a single received byte and clears overrun errors.

params.name: rx_data
params.desc: Pointer to a memory location where the received byte will be stored. Must be a valid, non-NULL address.

ca_lpuart_hw_recv.returns: Returns 0 if a byte was successfully read from the hardware buffer. Returns -1 if no data is available (RX buffer empty) or if the hardware is not initialized.
ca_lpuart_hw_recv.notes: This function is non-blocking; it checks the hardware status register immediately and returns control to the caller. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs atomic register reads, but it should not be called from multiple threads simultaneously to avoid race conditions on the hardware state. A critical feature is the automatic handling of the Overrun Error (ORE) flag: if the hardware detects that data was lost because the buffer wasn't read fast enough, this function clears the error bit so that future reception can continue. A common mistake is ignoring the return value and assuming the data in 'rx_data' is valid even when the function returns -1.
ca_lpuart_hw_recv.usage: This function is typically used inside a polling loop or a high-frequency timer callback to drain the LPUART hardware FIFO. It is usually paired with 'ca_lpuart_hw_init' to prepare the peripheral and is called within a dispatcher function like 'ca_lpuart_dispatch' to process incoming bytes. By calling it in a 'while' loop, you ensure that all pending bytes in the hardware buffer are processed before returning to the main task loop.

ca_lpuart_init.signature: bool ca_lpuart_init (u32 baud, ca_lpuart_rx_cb_t on_rx, bool wake, bool alternate_gpio)
ca_lpuart_init.brief: Initializes the Low Power UART (LPUART) peripheral with a specific baud rate, callback function, and wake-up capability.

params.name: baud
params.desc: The desired communication speed in bits per second. Must be greater than 0; passing 0 will cause the function to fail immediately.

params.name: on_rx
params.desc: A pointer to the callback function that will be executed whenever data is received. This function must be defined by the user.

params.name: wake
params.desc: A boolean flag indicating if the LPUART should be capable of waking the system from low-power sleep modes upon receiving data.

params.name: alternate_gpio
params.desc: A boolean flag to select between default or alternate GPIO pin mapping for the LPUART peripheral.

ca_lpuart_init.returns: Returns true if the initialization was successful and the peripheral is ready for use. Returns false if the peripheral is already in use, the baud rate is invalid, GPIO configuration fails, or the hardware initialization fails.
ca_lpuart_init.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should be called during the system initialization phase before starting the RTOS scheduler or enabling interrupts. It is strictly non-blocking, meaning it returns immediately after attempting to configure the hardware. It is not safe to call this function from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it performs hardware setup that may involve shared resource access. A common beginner mistake is calling this function multiple times without checking the return value or attempting to re-initialize while the peripheral is already active, which will result in a false return. Always ensure the peripheral is properly shut down using ca_lpuart_deinit before attempting to re-initialize it with different parameters.
ca_lpuart_init.usage: This function is typically used at the very beginning of the application lifecycle to prepare the serial communication interface. It is usually paired with a callback function that handles incoming data packets. After calling ca_lpuart_init, the system expects the LPUART to be ready to trigger the provided callback whenever bytes arrive. It is the mandatory first step before any other LPUART operations like ca_lpuart_put or ca_lpuart_dispatch can be performed, ensuring the hardware pins and internal registers are correctly configured for the specific baud rate.

ca_lpuart_is_busy.brief: Checks if the LPUART peripheral is currently occupied by an ongoing transmission or reception process.
ca_lpuart_is_busy.returns: Returns 'true' if the LPUART is currently in use (busy), and 'false' if it is idle and ready for a new operation.
ca_lpuart_is_busy.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it simply reads a static boolean flag. It is safe to call from both main-loop tasks and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs). The most common beginner mistake is assuming that a 'false' return guarantees the peripheral is powered or configured; you must ensure the LPUART driver has been initialized via ca_lpuart_init before checking this status. If you ignore this check and attempt to start a new transfer while the peripheral is busy, you will likely overwrite the internal buffer or trigger a hardware error, leading to corrupted data or a system hang.
ca_lpuart_is_busy.usage: This function is typically used as a guard clause before initiating a new communication sequence to prevent resource contention. In a standard workflow, you call this function to verify the peripheral is free, then proceed to trigger a transmission using ca_lpuart_put. It is frequently paired with ca_lpuart_wake_active to determine if the peripheral is not only busy but also currently holding the system in a wake state. It is also used in power management logic to determine if the MCU can safely enter a low-power sleep mode without aborting an active serial transaction.

ca_lpuart_put.brief: Sends a string message through the LPUART peripheral if the driver is initialized.

params.name: message
params.desc: A pointer to the null-terminated string to be transmitted. Must not be NULL.

ca_lpuart_put.returns: Returns the number of bytes successfully queued for transmission (u16). Returns 0 if the driver is not initialized (s_in_use is false) or if the provided message pointer is NULL.
ca_lpuart_put.notes: This function is a wrapper that checks the internal state of the LPUART driver before attempting hardware access. It is not thread-safe by itself, so ensure that multiple tasks do not attempt to write to the LPUART simultaneously without external synchronization like a mutex. It is generally not safe to call this from an ISR unless the underlying ca_lpuart_hw_put implementation is specifically designed for non-blocking, re-entrant operation. The most common beginner mistake is calling this function before the LPUART driver has been properly initialized, which will result in a silent failure (returning 0) because s_in_use remains false.
ca_lpuart_put.usage: This function is typically used in the application layer to send logs, debug information, or command responses to a terminal or external device. It is usually paired with an initialization function that sets s_in_use to true. In a typical workflow, you initialize the peripheral, wait for the system to be ready, and then call this function whenever you need to output data. It is often used as the backend for system console or CLI (Command Line Interface) implementations where the application needs to communicate with a human operator.

ca_lpuart_std_cli.brief: Initializes the Low-Power UART (LPUART) peripheral specifically to act as a Command Line Interface (CLI) input.

params.name: alternate_gpio
params.desc: If true, configures the LPUART to use the secondary (alternate) pin mapping; if false, uses the default pin mapping.

ca_lpuart_std_cli.returns: Returns true if the LPUART peripheral was successfully initialized and configured for CLI operation, or false if the initialization failed (e.g., invalid baud rate or hardware resource conflict).
ca_lpuart_std_cli.notes: This function is a high-level wrapper that configures the LPUART hardware to route incoming bytes directly to the system CLI parser. It is not thread-safe and must be called during the system initialization phase before the RTOS scheduler starts. It is strictly non-blocking, but it relies on the underlying hardware being ready; calling it while the LPUART is already active or without proper GPIO configuration will lead to undefined behavior. A common mistake is calling this function multiple times or from within an ISR, which can corrupt the peripheral state or cause a system hang.
ca_lpuart_std_cli.usage: This function is typically used during the early boot sequence in the main initialization routine to set up the debug console. It is usually paired with ca_lpuart_configure_gpio() to ensure the physical pins are mapped correctly before the peripheral is enabled. Once initialized, the system expects the LPUART to handle incoming characters automatically via the internal callback, allowing the developer to interact with the system via a terminal emulator connected to the board.

ca_lpuart_wake_active.brief: Checks if the LPUART peripheral is currently initialized and configured to act as a system wake-up source.
ca_lpuart_wake_active.returns: Returns 1 if the LPUART is both active and configured for wake-up functionality, otherwise returns 0.
ca_lpuart_wake_active.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it only performs a read operation on internal static status flags. It is safe to call from an ISR, though it is primarily intended for power management logic in the main thread. A common mistake is assuming this function checks if the LPUART is currently receiving data; it only checks the configuration state set during initialization. You must ensure the LPUART driver has been initialized via its setup function before relying on this value, otherwise, it will always return 0.
ca_lpuart_wake_active.usage: This function is typically used by the Power Management (PWR) module before the MCU enters a low-power sleep mode. It allows the system to dynamically determine if the LPUART should be included in the wake-up interrupt mask. It is usually paired with initialization functions that set the wake-up flag and is checked during the transition to deep sleep to ensure the system can be awakened by incoming serial traffic.

ca_mdns_service_bind.brief: Registers the mDNS service to listen for incoming UDP packets on the standard mDNS port.
ca_mdns_service_bind.returns: Returns true if the UDP port was successfully bound to the mDNS handler, or false if the port is already in use or the network stack failed to allocate the socket.
ca_mdns_service_bind.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs the low-level registration of the mDNS protocol handler with the network stack. It is not thread-safe in the sense that it should only be called once during the system initialization phase; calling it multiple times may lead to resource exhaustion or undefined behavior in the network stack. It cannot be called from an ISR because it involves memory allocation and internal mutex locking within the network stack. A common beginner mistake is calling this before the network interface is initialized or before the underlying network stack is ready, which will cause the function to return false.
ca_mdns_service_bind.usage: This function is typically used during the system startup sequence after the network stack has been initialized via ca_net_proto_init. It is paired with the mDNS service lifecycle: first, the service is bound using this function, then the system waits for the network link to be established, and finally, the service is notified that the network is ready via ca_mdns_service_net_ready. It is essential to ensure that the MDNS_PORT is not already occupied by another service, otherwise, the binding will fail silently or return false.

ca_mdns_service_init.brief: Initializes the mDNS service internal structures, semaphores, and CLI interface.

params.name: local_mac
params.desc: The hardware MAC address of the device. Must be a valid 6-byte array structure.

params.name: hostname
params.desc: A null-terminated string representing the device name (e.g., 'my-device'). Must not exceed the internal buffer size.

ca_mdns_service_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs internal memory setup for the mDNS stack. It is not thread-safe and must be called during the system initialization phase before the RTOS scheduler starts or before any network tasks are spawned. It is strictly forbidden to call this from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) as it performs semaphore initialization and potential CLI registration. A common beginner mistake is calling this function multiple times or after the network stack has already started, which can lead to memory corruption or inconsistent state in the semaphore handles.
ca_mdns_service_init.usage: This function is the mandatory first step in the mDNS lifecycle. It is typically called in the main initialization sequence alongside other network services like DHCP and ARP. It must be followed by a call to ca_mdns_service_start() to actually begin network operations. By initializing the semaphores here, it ensures that the background tasks responsible for handling mDNS queries and announcements have the necessary synchronization primitives ready before the network interface becomes active.

ca_mdns_service_net_ready.brief: Signals the mDNS service that the network interface is configured and ready to begin service announcements.

params.name: local_ip
params.desc: The IPv4 address assigned to the device. Must be a valid, non-zero IP address obtained via DHCP or static configuration.

ca_mdns_service_net_ready.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, designed to be called once the network stack has successfully acquired an IP address. It updates the internal state of the mDNS module and triggers the semaphore that controls the announcement cycle. It is not intended to be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it performs semaphore operations that could lead to undefined behavior if the scheduler is not ready. A common mistake is calling this function before the network stack is fully initialized or before an IP address has been assigned, which results in the mDNS service attempting to announce an invalid or null IP address.
ca_mdns_service_net_ready.usage: This function is typically used in the network initialization sequence, specifically after a DHCP lease is granted or a static IP is applied. It acts as the 'go' signal for the mDNS module to start broadcasting its presence on the local network. It is usually paired with ca_mdns_service_bind() which sets up the UDP socket. In a typical application, you would call ca_mdns_service_bind() during system startup, and then call ca_mdns_service_net_ready() only after the network link is confirmed and an IP address is assigned.

ca_mdns_service_rx_handler.brief: Processes incoming mDNS UDP packets to detect queries targeting the device's hostname.

params.name: udp
params.desc: Pointer to the raw UDP frame structure extracted from the network buffer. Must be a valid, non-NULL pointer to a properly formatted UDP packet.

params.name: len
params.desc: The total length of the UDP payload in bytes. While passed to the function, it is currently ignored in the implementation.

ca_mdns_service_rx_handler.returns: void. This function does not return a status code; it performs internal state updates via semaphores if a matching query is found.
ca_mdns_service_rx_handler.notes: This function is designed to be called from the network stack's receive context. It is thread-safe regarding semaphore operations, but it assumes the mDNS service has been properly initialized with a valid hostname. A common mistake is calling this function before the network stack is fully initialized or with a pointer that does not point to a valid UDP frame, which will cause memory access violations. Because it uses semaphore operations, ensure that the internal semaphores are correctly initialized before any packets are processed, otherwise the system may hang or trigger an assertion failure.
ca_mdns_service_rx_handler.usage: This function is the entry point for mDNS query processing within the caOS network stack. It is typically invoked by the low-level network driver or the buffer management layer immediately after a UDP packet is received and identified as an mDNS packet. It works in tandem with 'ca_net_buf_free' to ensure memory is released after processing, and it signals an internal semaphore to wake up the mDNS background task, which then prepares and sends the appropriate response. It is part of the standard lifecycle: init -> bind -> start -> rx_handler.

ca_mdns_service_start.brief: Initializes and launches the mDNS background service task in the RTOS scheduler.
ca_mdns_service_start.returns: This function returns void; it does not provide feedback on whether the task creation succeeded or failed.
ca_mdns_service_start.notes: This function is non-blocking as it merely registers a new task with the RTOS scheduler. It is not thread-safe to call this from an ISR, as it involves memory allocation and scheduler manipulation. You must ensure that the underlying network stack and hardware drivers are initialized before calling this, otherwise, the mDNS task will immediately crash or hang. A common beginner mistake is calling this function multiple times during runtime; since it spawns a new thread each time, this will quickly exhaust your system memory and lead to a stack overflow or system instability.
ca_mdns_service_start.usage: This function is typically called once during the system initialization phase, usually inside the main entry point or a dedicated network configuration routine. It is part of the standard service startup sequence, often paired with other network services like DHCP or ARP to establish connectivity. Once started, the mDNS task runs autonomously in the background, handling incoming UDP queries and responding to service discovery requests without further intervention from the main application loop.

ca_measure_start.brief: Captures the current system runtime tick count to a provided memory address for performance profiling.

params.name: p_start
params.desc: A pointer to a 32-bit unsigned integer where the current system runtime value will be stored. Must not be NULL.

ca_measure_start.returns: void. The function does not return a status code; it directly modifies the memory location pointed to by p_start.
ca_measure_start.notes: This function is non-blocking and extremely fast, as it simply reads a global counter maintained by the scheduler. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs a single atomic read of the runtime variable, making it safe to call from both tasks and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs). The most common mistake is passing a NULL pointer, which the function handles safely by doing nothing, but this will result in your timing variable remaining uninitialized. Ensure the variable passed is accessible in the scope where you intend to calculate the duration, as it will be overwritten with the start timestamp.
ca_measure_start.usage: This function is used exclusively for benchmarking and profiling the execution time of code blocks or functions. It is always used in a pair with ca_measure_stop, where ca_measure_start captures the 'before' timestamp and ca_measure_stop calculates the difference between the current time and that stored timestamp. You typically initialize a local u32 variable, pass its address to this function before your target code, and then pass the same address to the stop function to update the variable with the elapsed time.

ca_measure_stop.brief: Calculates the elapsed time in system ticks between a start point and the current moment.

params.name: p
params.desc: A pointer to a variable that previously stored the start timestamp via ca_measure_start. Must not be NULL.

ca_measure_stop.returns: This function returns void. The result of the calculation is written directly into the memory address pointed to by p.
ca_measure_stop.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes very quickly, making it safe to use in most contexts. It is thread-safe provided that the variable pointed to by p is not accessed by other tasks simultaneously. It is safe to call from an ISR, but be aware that the accuracy depends on the system tick frequency. The most common beginner mistake is passing a NULL pointer or a pointer that was not initialized by ca_measure_start, which will result in an incorrect calculation or a memory access violation. Always ensure the variable passed is declared as volatile to prevent the compiler from optimizing away necessary memory updates.
ca_measure_stop.usage: This function is used for profiling code execution time or measuring the duration of specific tasks within the RTOS. It is always used in a pair: first, you call ca_measure_start to capture the initial system runtime, then you execute the code block you wish to measure, and finally, you call ca_measure_stop to overwrite the initial value with the calculated delta. It is typically used during the debugging or optimization phase of development to identify bottlenecks in your application logic.

ca_memcmp.signature: signed int ca_memcmp(const void *ptr1, const void *ptr2, unsigned int count)
ca_memcmp.brief: Compares two memory blocks byte-by-byte for equality or difference.

params.name: ptr1
params.desc: Pointer to the first memory block. Must not be NULL.

params.name: ptr2
params.desc: Pointer to the second memory block. Must not be NULL.

params.name: count
params.desc: Number of bytes to compare. If 0, the function returns 0 immediately.

ca_memcmp.returns: Returns 0 if the blocks are identical. Returns a non-zero value if a difference is found (the difference between the first non-matching bytes). Returns -1 if ptr1 is NULL, or -2 if ptr2 is NULL.
ca_memcmp.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes synchronously, meaning it consumes CPU cycles proportional to the 'count' parameter. It is thread-safe as it does not modify any global state or shared resources, only reading from the provided pointers. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the memory addresses are valid and accessible. The most common beginner mistake is passing an incorrect 'count' value, which can lead to reading past the end of a buffer (buffer over-read) if the pointers are not pointing to sufficiently large memory regions.
ca_memcmp.usage: Use this function whenever you need to verify data integrity, such as checking if a received network packet matches an expected header, or validating that decrypted data matches the original plaintext. It is frequently paired with cryptographic functions like 'ca_aes_gcm_decrypt' to verify success, or with binary data buffers where you need to ensure exact content matching. Unlike standard string functions, it does not stop at a null terminator, making it ideal for binary data or fixed-length structures where you must compare the entire length specified.

ca_memcpy.signature: void *ca_memcpy(volatile void *dest, const void *src, unsigned int count)
ca_memcpy.brief: Copies a specified number of bytes from a source memory area to a destination memory area.

params.name: dest
params.desc: Pointer to the destination memory buffer. Must be large enough to hold 'count' bytes. If NULL, the function returns immediately without performing any copy.

params.name: src
params.desc: Pointer to the source memory buffer. Must contain at least 'count' bytes. If NULL, the function returns immediately without performing any copy.

params.name: count
params.desc: The number of bytes to copy. A value of 0 results in no operation.

ca_memcpy.returns: Returns the original 'dest' pointer. If either 'dest' or 'src' is NULL, it returns the 'dest' pointer unchanged.
ca_memcpy.notes: This function is a non-blocking, synchronous byte-by-byte copy utility. It is thread-safe in the sense that it does not modify global state, but it is NOT re-entrant if the same memory regions are accessed by other threads simultaneously. It is safe to call from an ISR because it does not use OS primitives, locks, or blocking delays. A common beginner mistake is failing to ensure the destination buffer is large enough to hold the data, which leads to buffer overflows and memory corruption. Unlike standard C 'memcpy', this implementation does not handle overlapping memory regions; if 'src' and 'dest' overlap, the data will be corrupted.
ca_memcpy.usage: Used extensively for preparing data structures, serializing buffers, or populating communication packets. It is typically used in a sequence where a buffer is allocated, populated using one or more 'ca_memcpy' calls to assemble different fields (like IVs or headers), and then passed to a hardware peripheral or crypto engine. It is frequently paired with buffer management logic where you calculate offsets (e.g., 'buffer + offset') to concatenate multiple data segments into a single contiguous memory block.

ca_memcpy_u16.signature: void* ca_memcpy_u16(volatile u16 *dest, const u16 *src, u32 count)
ca_memcpy_u16.brief: Copies a specified number of 16-bit words from a source memory address to a destination memory address.

params.name: dest
params.desc: Pointer to the destination memory buffer. Must be a valid, non-NULL address. If NULL, the function returns immediately without performing any copy.

params.name: src
params.desc: Pointer to the source memory buffer. Must be a valid, non-NULL address. If NULL, the function returns immediately.

params.name: count
params.desc: The number of 16-bit elements (u16) to copy. A value of 0 results in no operation.

ca_memcpy_u16.returns: Returns the original 'dest' pointer. If either 'dest' or 'src' is NULL, it returns the original 'dest' pointer unchanged, effectively doing nothing.
ca_memcpy_u16.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes synchronously, meaning the CPU will stay in this function until the entire copy is complete. It is thread-safe in the sense that it does not rely on global state, but it does not provide any protection against race conditions if another thread or ISR modifies the source or destination buffers while the copy is in progress. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the memory addresses are accessible. A common beginner mistake is passing the count in bytes instead of 16-bit words, which will result in only half the data being copied or potential buffer overflows if the count is misinterpreted.
ca_memcpy_u16.usage: This function is typically used for high-performance memory transfers between buffers, such as moving data from a peripheral's memory-mapped buffer to a local application buffer. It is often used in drivers or communication stacks where data alignment is guaranteed to be 16-bit or 32-bit. Developers use this when they need a faster alternative to the standard C 'memcpy' that is specifically optimized for 16-bit word alignment and potentially 32-bit word access patterns on STM32 hardware. It is usually called after a buffer has been allocated or a DMA transfer has completed, ensuring that the data is ready to be processed by the application logic.

ca_memcpy_u32.signature: void* ca_memcpy_u32(volatile u32 *dest, const u32 *src, u32 count)
ca_memcpy_u32.brief: Optimized memory copy function that transfers data in 32-bit chunks for improved performance.

params.name: dest
params.desc: Pointer to the destination memory area. Must be 32-bit aligned; passing an unaligned address may cause hardware faults on some ARM Cortex-M cores.

params.name: src
params.desc: Pointer to the source memory area. Must be 32-bit aligned.

params.name: count
params.desc: Number of 32-bit words to copy. If the total data size is not a multiple of 4 bytes, the remaining bytes must be handled separately.

ca_memcpy_u32.returns: Returns the updated destination pointer (dest + count), pointing to the address immediately following the last copied word. If either pointer is NULL, it returns the original destination pointer without performing any copy.
ca_memcpy_u32.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes synchronously, meaning the CPU will wait until the copy is complete before moving to the next instruction. It is thread-safe only if the memory regions being accessed are not modified by other threads or ISRs simultaneously. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the pointers are valid and aligned. The most common beginner mistake is passing a byte count instead of a word count, or providing unaligned pointers, which can lead to hard faults or data corruption on architectures that strictly enforce alignment.
ca_memcpy_u32.usage: Use this function when you need to move large blocks of data, such as network packets or flash memory buffers, where performance is critical. It is typically used in a sequence where you first calculate the number of 32-bit words (data_len >> 2), call this function to handle the bulk of the data, and then use a simple loop to copy any remaining bytes (data_len & 3). It is often paired with memory allocation functions like ca_memory_allocate to prepare destination buffers before processing data.

ca_memmap_get.brief: Retrieves the system memory map, providing addresses and sizes of available memory regions.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to an array of ca_mem_range structures where the memory map will be stored. Must be large enough to hold CA_MEMMAP_MAX entries. Passing NULL will result in an immediate return of 0.

ca_memmap_get.returns: Returns the number of memory regions successfully populated in the provided array. Returns 0 if the input pointer is NULL or if no memory regions are defined.
ca_memmap_get.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it simply copies pre-defined hardware constants into the provided buffer. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the buffer passed is not being accessed by another task simultaneously. The most common mistake is providing a pointer to an array smaller than CA_MEMMAP_MAX, which will cause a buffer overflow if the system has more regions than the array can hold. Ensure the array is allocated in a scope that remains valid during the function call.
ca_memmap_get.usage: This function is typically used for system diagnostics, debugging, or CLI commands that need to report the memory layout to the user. It is often paired with CLI output functions to display the start address, end address, and size of each memory block. It is usually called after the system has initialized, as it relies on the hardware-specific memory configuration defined during the board bring-up phase.

ca_memmove.signature: void *ca_memmove(volatile void *dest, const void *src, unsigned int count)
ca_memmove.brief: Safely copies a block of memory between potentially overlapping source and destination buffers.

params.name: dest
params.desc: Pointer to the destination memory area. Must be a valid, writable memory address.

params.name: src
params.desc: Pointer to the source memory area. Must be a valid, readable memory address.

params.name: count
params.desc: Number of bytes to copy. If 0, the function returns immediately without action.

ca_memmove.returns: Returns the original 'dest' pointer. If 'dest' or 'src' are NULL, or 'count' is 0, it returns 'dest' without performing any copy.
ca_memmove.notes: Unlike ca_memcpy, this function is specifically designed to handle cases where the source and destination memory regions overlap. It automatically detects the overlap direction and copies data either forward or backward to prevent data corruption during the transfer. This function is not inherently thread-safe if multiple tasks modify the same memory regions simultaneously; ensure you use synchronization primitives like ca_mutex if concurrent access is possible. It is safe to call from an ISR, but keep in mind that large copy operations will block the CPU and increase interrupt latency, which can negatively impact real-time performance. A common mistake is passing an uninitialized pointer or a pointer to a memory region that has already been freed via ca_memory_free, which will lead to a hard fault.
ca_memmove.usage: Use this function whenever you need to shift data within a buffer or move data between buffers that might share the same memory space. It is commonly used in protocol stacks or data processing pipelines where a buffer needs to be 'compacted' by moving remaining data to the start of the array after a portion has been consumed. It is often paired with ca_memory_allocate to prepare the destination buffer or used in conjunction with ca_os_sched_lock to ensure the memory move operation completes atomically without task preemption. Always ensure the memory region is valid using ca_memory_check before performing operations on dynamic buffers.

ca_memory_adopt.brief: Transfers ownership of a shared memory block to the current task.

params.name: p
params.desc: Pointer to the memory block to adopt. Must be a valid pointer previously allocated via ca_memory_allocate_shared.

ca_memory_adopt.returns: Returns true if the memory block was successfully adopted by the current task, false if the pointer is invalid, outside heap bounds, or not currently in a BUSY state.
ca_memory_adopt.notes: This function is thread-safe and uses internal locking to safely update the memory block's owner metadata. It is NOT callable from an ISR because it interacts with the scheduler to identify the current task context. The most common mistake is passing a pointer that was not allocated via ca_memory_allocate_shared or attempting to adopt memory that has already been freed. If you fail to adopt a shared block, the system may leak memory or trigger an error when the original owner attempts to free it.
ca_memory_adopt.usage: Use this function when a task receives a pointer to a shared memory buffer from another task or a service (e.g., via a queue). By calling ca_memory_adopt, the receiving task becomes the new 'owner' of that memory, allowing it to safely free the memory later using ca_memory_free. This is essential in producer-consumer patterns where the producer allocates the buffer and the consumer takes responsibility for its lifecycle.

ca_memory_allocate.brief: Allocates a block of memory from the system heap.

params.name: size
params.desc: The number of bytes requested. Must be greater than 0. The system will align this value and enforce a minimum block size.

ca_memory_allocate.returns: Returns a pointer to the allocated memory block on success. Returns NULL if the heap is not initialized, if there is insufficient memory, or if the heap structure is corrupted.
ca_memory_allocate.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses an internal spinlock to protect the heap structure. It is NOT callable from an ISR because it may block while waiting for the spinlock. You must ensure ca_memory_init has been called during system startup before using this function. A common mistake is failing to check the returned pointer for NULL; always verify the pointer before dereferencing it to avoid hard faults. If the allocation fails, the system may trigger a corruption report if the heap integrity check fails.
ca_memory_allocate.usage: Use this function whenever you need dynamic memory for buffers, context structures, or temporary data that does not fit on the stack. It is typically paired with ca_memory_free to release the memory once the task is complete. In a typical lifecycle, you allocate the memory, perform your operations (like reading from flash or decrypting data), and then free the memory to prevent leaks. Always handle the NULL return case by cleaning up any previously allocated resources and exiting the current operation gracefully.

ca_memory_allocate_shared.brief: Allocates a block of memory from the shared heap, accessible by multiple tasks.

params.name: size
params.desc: The number of bytes to allocate. Must be greater than 0. If 0 is passed, behavior is implementation-defined but typically returns NULL.

ca_memory_allocate_shared.returns: A pointer (void *) to the allocated memory block on success, or NULL if the allocation fails (e.g., out of memory or heap fragmentation).
ca_memory_allocate_shared.notes: This function is thread-safe and manages memory from a global shared pool. It is NOT callable from an ISR because it may block the calling task while waiting for heap access or performing memory compaction. Always check if the returned pointer is NULL before dereferencing it to avoid hard faults. A common beginner mistake is assuming the memory is zero-initialized; it is not, so you must manually clear it if needed using ca_memzero.
ca_memory_allocate_shared.usage: Use this function when you need to share data structures (like buffers or configuration objects) between different tasks that do not have a private memory pool. It is typically used in the initialization phase of a task or service. It is paired with ca_memory_free to release the memory back to the system once the task is finished with the resource. For debugging, you can use ca_memory_get_avail_memory to monitor heap usage before and after allocation.

ca_memory_canary_high.brief: Returns the memory address of the high-side heap integrity canary.
ca_memory_canary_high.returns: A constant pointer (const u32 *) to the memory location where the high-side canary value is stored. This pointer is never NULL if the memory system is initialized.
ca_memory_canary_high.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it simply returns a static memory address. It is safe to call from an ISR, though typically it is used by the scheduler or diagnostic tasks. The canary is a specific memory pattern used to detect buffer overflows; if the value at this address changes, it indicates that a task has written past its allocated memory block. Beginners often mistake this for a function that checks the memory; it does not, it only provides the address of the marker. Use ca_memory_check_canary() to actually verify the integrity.
ca_memory_canary_high.usage: This function is primarily used by the system diagnostic routines to report the location of corrupted memory during a heap fault. It is typically paired with ca_memory_canary_low() to provide a full range of the corrupted area to the developer via ca_stdout_printf_n(). It is part of the internal memory protection mechanism that runs periodically or upon detection of a system instability to help identify which memory region was compromised.

ca_memory_canary_low.brief: Returns the memory address of the low-side heap integrity canary buffer.
ca_memory_canary_low.returns: A constant pointer (const u32 *) to the start of the low-side canary memory area. This pointer is never NULL as it points to a statically allocated internal buffer.
ca_memory_canary_low.notes: This function is non-blocking, thread-safe, and can be safely called from an ISR. It provides read-only access to the internal canary array used by the heap manager to detect buffer overflows. The most common mistake is attempting to write to the memory pointed to by this function; doing so will corrupt the heap integrity mechanism and trigger false positives in the system's safety checks. It is intended for diagnostic and reporting purposes only, and you must never modify the contents of the returned memory address.
ca_memory_canary_low.usage: This function is primarily used by the system's safety monitoring tasks to report the location of memory corruption when a canary check fails. It is typically paired with ca_memory_canary_high to provide a full range of the corrupted memory area in logs. Developers use it within error-handling routines, often alongside ca_memory_check_canary to verify heap health and ca_memory_restore_canary to reset the markers after a detected violation. It is part of the diagnostic sequence: check -> report -> restore.

ca_memory_check.brief: Performs a comprehensive integrity check of the heap memory management system.

params.name: r
params.desc: Pointer to a structure where diagnostic results are stored. If NULL, a local stack variable is used, but results will be lost after the function returns.

ca_memory_check.returns: Returns true if the memory chain is intact, canaries are valid, and available memory matches expectations. Returns false if any check fails or if the memory system is not initialized.
ca_memory_check.notes: This function is blocking because it acquires a spinlock to ensure a consistent snapshot of the heap metadata. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR because it uses spinlocks that could cause deadlocks if the interrupted task already holds the lock. The function requires that the memory system has been previously initialized via ca_memory_init. A common mistake is assuming this function is lightweight; it traverses the entire memory chain, so calling it frequently in a high-frequency loop will significantly degrade system performance.
ca_memory_check.usage: This function is typically used for system health monitoring or debugging memory corruption issues. It is often paired with ca_memory_init during system startup to verify the heap state, or called periodically by a watchdog task to detect buffer overflows or heap metadata corruption. If it returns false, developers should use ca_memory_list to inspect the heap state and identify which task or operation caused the corruption. It is the primary tool for verifying that heap metadata has not been overwritten by illegal memory access.

ca_memory_check_canary.brief: Verifies the integrity of the heap memory by checking predefined canary values and block metadata.
ca_memory_check_canary.returns: Returns true if the heap memory is intact (or not yet initialized). Returns false if any canary value has been overwritten or if the heap block metadata is corrupted.
ca_memory_check_canary.notes: This function is a critical diagnostic tool for detecting buffer overflows or memory corruption. It is non-blocking and performs a read-only check, making it safe to call from most contexts. However, because it iterates through the entire canary array and validates block metadata, it can be computationally expensive; calling it inside a high-frequency ISR is discouraged as it may cause jitter. A common beginner mistake is to assume this function 'fixes' the memory; it only detects corruption. If it returns false, the heap is already compromised, and you must either trigger a system reset or use a recovery function to restore the markers.
ca_memory_check_canary.usage: This function is typically used in the idle task or a dedicated system monitor task to perform background health checks. It is often paired with ca_memory_restore_canary to attempt a recovery if corruption is detected. In a robust system, you would call this before performing sensitive memory operations or as part of a watchdog-like monitoring loop to ensure that no task has performed an out-of-bounds write that would otherwise go unnoticed until a hard fault occurs.

ca_memory_dump.brief: Prints a formatted hexadecimal and ASCII memory dump to the standard output for debugging purposes.

params.name: p
params.desc: The starting memory address to dump. The function will automatically align this address to an 8-byte boundary.

params.name: lines
params.desc: The number of 16-byte rows to display. A value of 1 prints 16 bytes, 2 prints 32 bytes, and so on. The maximum supported value is 4095.

ca_memory_dump.returns: This function returns void and does not provide a status code. If the memory system is not initialized, the function returns silently without printing anything.
ca_memory_dump.notes: This function is intended strictly for debugging and development. It is not thread-safe and relies on the global state of the memory manager; if the memory manager has not been initialized, the function will trigger a safety handler and return. It is a blocking operation because it writes to the output stream, meaning it will pause the execution of the current task until the data is sent. Do not call this function from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) as it may cause system instability or deadlocks due to the blocking nature of the output stream. A common mistake is passing an invalid or unmapped memory address, which could lead to a HardFault if the underlying memory access attempts to read protected or non-existent memory regions.
ca_memory_dump.usage: Use this function during the development phase to inspect the contents of buffers, structures, or peripheral registers when you suspect data corruption or incorrect initialization. It is typically used after a memory allocation via 'ca_memory_allocate' or a data reception process to verify that the expected values are present in RAM. It is often paired with 'ca_stdout_put_n' for logging headers and is usually wrapped in conditional compilation flags (like ENABLE_LOG) to ensure it is stripped out of production builds to save performance and memory. It is the standard way to visualize raw memory state when 'ca_memory_check' indicates a potential corruption.

ca_memory_dump_avail.brief: Prints a detailed diagnostic report of the heap memory status to the standard output.
ca_memory_dump_avail.returns: This function returns void and does not provide a status code.
ca_memory_dump_avail.notes: This function is non-blocking but performs extensive string formatting and serial output, making it unsuitable for use inside high-frequency Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs) where timing is critical. It requires the memory system to be initialized; if called before 'ca_memory_init', it will trigger a safety handler and return immediately. The function performs a full heap integrity check, including canary validation and block chain verification, which is computationally expensive. A common beginner mistake is calling this function repeatedly in a tight loop, which will flood the serial output and significantly degrade system performance.
ca_memory_dump_avail.usage: This function is used as a primary diagnostic tool for heap health monitoring, typically triggered by a CLI command or a system watchdog task. It is used to verify that memory allocation is behaving as expected, checking for corruption in the heap chain or canary patterns. Developers use this in conjunction with 'ca_memory_list' to inspect specific allocations or 'ca_scheduler_dump_task' to correlate memory usage with active tasks. It is the standard way to confirm if a system crash was caused by memory exhaustion or heap corruption.

ca_memory_free.brief: Releases a previously allocated memory block back to the system heap, optionally wiping the data for security.

params.name: p
params.desc: Pointer to the memory block to be freed. Must be a pointer previously returned by ca_memory_allocate. Passing NULL is safe and returns false.

params.name: freed_size
params.desc: Optional pointer to a variable where the function will store the size of the freed block. Pass NULL if you do not need this information.

params.name: wiped
params.desc: If true, the function overwrites the memory with zeros before releasing it. Use this for sensitive data like cryptographic keys.

ca_memory_free.returns: Returns true if the memory block was successfully identified and freed. Returns false if the pointer is invalid, the memory system is uninitialized, or the pointer is outside the managed heap range.
ca_memory_free.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses an internal spinlock to protect the heap structure. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR because it uses spinlocks that disable interrupts, which can cause system instability or deadlocks if called from a high-priority context. The function is blocking; it must traverse the heap metadata to update block status, so execution time depends on heap fragmentation. A common beginner mistake is passing a pointer that was not allocated by ca_memory_allocate (e.g., a stack variable or a static buffer), which will trigger a memory error log and return false. Always ensure the memory system is initialized before calling this.
ca_memory_free.usage: This function is the standard way to prevent memory leaks in long-running embedded applications. It is typically used in a cleanup pattern: after a task completes, or when an error occurs during initialization, you must free any buffers allocated during the setup phase. It is often paired with ca_memory_allocate in a 'try-allocate-then-free-on-error' pattern to ensure that if a complex operation fails halfway through, the system does not leak memory. In driver development, it is used to release temporary buffers used for DMA or flash operations once the data transfer is complete.

ca_memory_free_all_owned_by.brief: Automatically releases all memory blocks currently held by a specific task.

params.name: task_slot
params.desc: The unique identifier (slot) of the task whose memory needs to be reclaimed. Must be a valid task slot index.

ca_memory_free_all_owned_by.returns: Returns a u32 representing the total number of memory blocks successfully freed. Returns 0 if no memory was allocated by the task or if the memory system is not initialized.
ca_memory_free_all_owned_by.notes: This function is designed for emergency cleanup and task termination. It is thread-safe and uses internal spinlocks to protect the memory heap, but it is intended to be called by the scheduler or system manager during task teardown. Because it modifies the memory list structure, it performs a restart-scan, meaning it is not an O(1) operation and can take longer depending on the number of blocks to free. Do not call this from a standard application task unless you are intentionally cleaning up a child process or a failed task, as it will forcefully reclaim memory without notifying the owner. It is safe to call from ISR context because it uses spinlocks with interrupt disabling.
ca_memory_free_all_owned_by.usage: This function is typically used in the scheduler's task-deletion sequence. When a task is terminated (e.g., due to a watchdog timeout or explicit exit), the system calls this to prevent memory leaks. It is usually paired with ca_os_task_slot to identify the task and is invoked before the task structure is unlinked from the scheduler's run queues. It ensures that resources are returned to the heap before the task slot is marked as available for reuse.

ca_memory_get_avail_memory.brief: Returns the total amount of free memory currently available in the system heap.
ca_memory_get_avail_memory.returns: Returns the number of bytes currently available as a u32. Returns 0 if the memory manager has not been initialized yet.
ca_memory_get_avail_memory.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses a spinlock to protect the global memory variable during access. It is non-blocking in the sense that it does not wait for external hardware, but it does briefly disable interrupts to ensure data consistency. You can safely call this from an ISR or a task, but avoid calling it in a tight loop inside a high-frequency interrupt as the spinlock overhead could impact system timing. The most common mistake is assuming this value remains constant; in a dynamic system, memory is constantly being allocated and freed, so treat this value as a snapshot rather than a guarantee for future allocations.
ca_memory_get_avail_memory.usage: This function is primarily used for system monitoring, diagnostics, and debugging purposes. It is typically paired with ca_memory_get_total_size() to calculate memory utilization percentages or to check if enough heap space remains before performing a large dynamic allocation. Developers use it in telemetry tasks or CLI commands to report system health to the user. It should only be called after the system memory manager has been initialized, otherwise, it will return 0, which might be misinterpreted as an 'out of memory' condition.

ca_memory_get_end_address.brief: Retrieves the absolute end address of the managed memory heap area.
ca_memory_get_end_address.returns: Returns a pointer (u32*) to the end of the memory heap if initialized, or NULL if the memory system has not been initialized yet.
ca_memory_get_end_address.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses a spinlock to protect the global memory boundary variable during access. It is non-blocking in the sense that it does not wait for external hardware, but it does disable interrupts briefly to ensure atomicity, making it safe to call from both standard tasks and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs). A common mistake is assuming the returned address is always valid without checking for NULL; if the memory subsystem failed to initialize or was not started, dereferencing the returned NULL pointer will trigger a HardFault. Always verify the return value before performing pointer arithmetic or memory boundary checks.
ca_memory_get_end_address.usage: This function is typically used by system diagnostic tasks or memory management routines to calculate the total size of the heap or to perform bounds checking on dynamic allocations. It is often paired with ca_memory_get_start_address() to define the full memory range. Developers use this during system startup or when implementing custom memory monitoring tools to ensure that pointers do not exceed the allocated heap boundaries, preventing buffer overflows or memory corruption.

ca_memory_get_start_address.brief: Retrieves the base memory address of the managed heap or memory pool.
ca_memory_get_start_address.returns: Returns a pointer to the start of the memory region (u32*) if initialized, or NULL if the memory system has not been initialized yet.
ca_memory_get_start_address.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses a spinlock to protect the internal pointer variable during access. It is non-blocking in the sense that it does not wait for a task to finish, but it does disable interrupts briefly via ca_spinlock_lock_irq, so it is safe to call from an ISR, though it should be used sparingly to avoid latency. A common mistake is assuming the returned pointer is always valid without checking for NULL; if the memory system failed to initialize, dereferencing the returned NULL pointer will cause a HardFault. Always ensure the memory subsystem is fully initialized before calling this, as the function relies on the internal state of the memory manager.
ca_memory_get_start_address.usage: This function is typically used by system-level drivers or diagnostic tools that need to perform bounds checking or memory mapping verification. It is often called after the system boot sequence, specifically after the memory manager has been initialized via ca_memory_init. Developers use it to calculate offsets or verify if a specific memory address falls within the managed heap range. It is frequently paired with ca_memory_get_end_address to define the boundaries of the heap, ensuring that pointers being passed to hardware peripherals or DMA controllers are within the valid, managed memory space.

ca_memory_get_task_usage.brief: Calculates the total amount of heap memory currently allocated by a specific task.

params.name: task_slot
params.desc: The unique slot index of the task to query. Must be a valid index assigned by the scheduler; passing an invalid index will return 0 as no blocks will match.

ca_memory_get_task_usage.returns: Returns the total number of bytes (payload only) currently held by the specified task. Returns 0 if the memory system is not initialized or if the task has no active memory allocations.
ca_memory_get_task_usage.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses a spinlock to protect the heap structure during traversal. It is non-blocking in terms of waiting for other tasks, but it does disable interrupts via ca_spinlock_lock_irq to ensure data consistency. Do not call this function from an ISR, as the spinlock mechanism is intended for thread-level synchronization and may cause system instability or deadlocks if invoked from an interrupt context. A common beginner mistake is to call this function frequently in a high-priority loop, which can significantly increase system jitter due to the time spent traversing the entire heap list while interrupts are disabled.
ca_memory_get_task_usage.usage: This function is primarily used for system monitoring, debugging, and diagnostic reporting. It is typically called by a system monitor task or a shell command handler that iterates through the task list to display resource usage statistics. You would use this in conjunction with task management functions to print memory footprints during runtime, helping you identify memory leaks or tasks that are consuming more heap than expected. It is usually paired with scheduler inspection functions to correlate task status with memory consumption, often invoked when a user requests a system status dump via a CLI or debug interface.

ca_memory_get_total_memory.brief: Returns the total amount of heap memory managed by the caOS memory allocator in bytes.
ca_memory_get_total_memory.returns: Returns the total memory size in bytes as a u32. Returns 0 if the memory manager has not been initialized yet.
ca_memory_get_total_memory.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses a spinlock to protect the internal memory variable during access. It is safe to call from both standard tasks and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs) because it uses a spinlock that disables interrupts (ca_spinlock_lock_irq). The function is non-blocking in the sense that it does not wait for other tasks to finish, but it will briefly stall the CPU to acquire the lock. A common mistake is assuming this value represents 'free' memory; this function specifically returns the 'total' capacity, not the currently available space. Always ensure the system has reached the initialization phase before relying on this value, as it will return 0 if called too early during the boot sequence.
ca_memory_get_total_memory.usage: This function is typically used during system diagnostics, boot-up logging, or health monitoring to report the hardware capabilities to the user via a console or debug interface. It is often paired with other system information functions like ca_os_clock_get_freq() to provide a snapshot of the system state. Developers use it to verify that the memory heap was configured correctly during the linker script setup or initialization phase. It is rarely used in the main control loop of an application, as the total memory size is usually a static constant determined at compile time.

ca_memory_get_total_size.brief: Returns the total size of the managed heap memory in bytes.
ca_memory_get_total_size.returns: Returns the total memory size as a u32 integer. Returns 0 if the memory system has not been initialized yet.
ca_memory_get_total_size.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses a spinlock to protect access to the global memory boundaries. It is safe to call from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it uses a spinlock that disables interrupts (ca_spinlock_lock_irq), preventing deadlocks or race conditions during the calculation. The most common mistake is assuming this function returns 'available' memory; it only returns the static total capacity defined at system startup. If you call this before the memory manager is initialized, you will receive 0, which might lead to division-by-zero errors if you use this value to calculate percentages without checking for zero first.
ca_memory_get_total_size.usage: This function is typically used for system diagnostics, telemetry, or monitoring tasks to report memory health. It is often paired with ca_memory_get_avail_memory() to calculate the current memory utilization percentage. Developers use this in a sequence: first, verify the system is initialized, then fetch the total size, fetch the available size, and finally perform arithmetic to determine how much heap is currently consumed by the application.

ca_memory_info.brief: Retrieves and logs diagnostic metadata for a specific heap memory block.

params.name: p
params.desc: A pointer to the payload area of a memory block previously allocated by the system. Must be within the heap range; passing NULL or an address outside the heap will trigger an audit log error.

ca_memory_info.returns: void. This function does not return a value; it outputs diagnostic information directly to the system stdout.
ca_memory_info.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses a spinlock to protect the heap metadata during inspection. It is non-blocking in the sense that it does not wait for other tasks, but it does disable interrupts briefly via ca_spinlock_lock_irq to ensure data consistency. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the spinlock is not held elsewhere, though it is primarily intended for debugging tasks. A common mistake is passing a pointer that has already been freed or a pointer that does not point to the start of an allocated block, which will cause the function to report an invalid header or block status.
