ca_memory_info.usage: Use this function during development or troubleshooting to inspect the state of specific memory allocations. It is typically used when a system behaves unexpectedly, such as when a memory leak is suspected or when a task is crashing due to memory corruption. You would pair this with ca_memory_dump_avail to get a global view of memory, then use ca_memory_info to drill down into the specific block causing issues. It is not intended for production runtime logic, but rather as a diagnostic tool to verify ownership and block integrity.

ca_memory_init.brief: Initializes the system heap memory manager, setting up memory blocks, canaries, and internal tracking structures.

params.name: heap_start
params.desc: Pointer to the beginning of the memory region reserved for the heap. Must be aligned according to system requirements.

params.name: heap_end
params.desc: Pointer to the end of the memory region reserved for the heap.

ca_memory_init.returns: void. If the provided memory range is too small to hold the required metadata and canaries, it prints an error and leaves the heap uninitialized.
ca_memory_init.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called exactly once during the system boot sequence before any memory allocation occurs. It is strictly non-reentrant and must NOT be called from an ISR. The function performs critical setup, including placing 'canaries' (sentinel values) at the boundaries of the heap to detect buffer overflows; if these canaries are corrupted later, the system may trigger a fault. A common beginner mistake is attempting to allocate memory before calling this function or providing a memory range that overlaps with the stack or static data sections.
ca_memory_init.usage: This is a foundational initialization function used during the early boot phase of the application. It is typically called immediately after hardware-level initializations (like MPU or bus error handlers) and before the scheduler or any task-based memory allocation begins. It pairs with subsequent calls to ca_memory_allocate to manage dynamic memory throughout the application lifecycle.

ca_memory_list.brief: Prints a detailed report of the current heap memory allocation status to the standard output.
ca_memory_list.returns: This function returns void; it does not provide a status code. If the memory system is not initialized, it prints an error message to stdout and returns immediately.
ca_memory_list.notes: This function is a diagnostic tool that performs a blocking operation by acquiring a spinlock to ensure the memory list remains consistent while traversing the linked list of blocks. Because it uses a spinlock with interrupt disabling, it is technically safe to call from an ISR, but it is highly discouraged because printing to stdout is a slow, blocking operation that will cause significant system jitter. The function requires that the memory manager has been previously initialized via ca_memory_init; if called before initialization, it prints a warning. A common mistake is calling this function frequently in a high-frequency loop, which will cause the system to hang or miss real-time deadlines due to the time taken to format and transmit the string data over the serial interface.
ca_memory_list.usage: This function is primarily used for debugging and system monitoring during development to detect memory leaks or fragmentation issues. It is typically triggered by a user command via a Command Line Interface (CLI) or a diagnostic task. It is usually paired with other system diagnostic functions like ca_os_clock_dump or ca_os_banner to provide a full snapshot of the system state. Developers use it to verify that memory blocks are being correctly allocated and freed by checking the 'Free Memory' and 'Busy Memory' statistics printed at the end of the list.

ca_memory_reserve_secret.brief: Reserves a specific, fixed memory region for sensitive data to prevent the heap manager from overwriting it.

params.name: size
params.desc: Pointer to a variable where the reserved size will be stored. Can be NULL if the size is not needed by the caller.

ca_memory_reserve_secret.returns: Returns a void pointer to the start of the reserved secret memory area, or NULL if the reservation failed or the area is not defined.
ca_memory_reserve_secret.notes: This function is intended to be called only during the system boot sequence before the heap is fully utilized. It is idempotent, meaning calling it multiple times has no additional effect after the first successful reservation. It is not thread-safe in the sense that it modifies global state, but it uses internal locking mechanisms to ensure the heap range is protected during the reservation process. Do not call this from an ISR, as it performs heap management operations that are not re-entrant.
ca_memory_reserve_secret.usage: This function is used to 'carve out' a piece of RAM that the OS heap manager must ignore, typically for security-sensitive data like encryption keys or tamper-sensitive buffers. It is usually called immediately after system initialization but before any application tasks start allocating memory. By reserving this range, you ensure that the heap allocator never places dynamic objects in this specific memory address, preventing accidental corruption or exposure of sensitive data.

ca_memory_restore_canary.brief: Resets the heap memory integrity markers (canaries) to their default safe values.
ca_memory_restore_canary.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should be used with extreme caution. It is intended for system recovery after a memory corruption event has been detected. It does not repair the corrupted memory itself; it only resets the 'canary' markers so that future corruption can be detected again. Calling this function while the heap is actively being accessed by other tasks will lead to race conditions and unpredictable system behavior. It is not safe to call from an ISR, as it performs a non-atomic loop over the heap metadata.
ca_memory_restore_canary.usage: This function is typically used by the system's error-handling or watchdog routines after a memory violation has been identified. It is often paired with functions like ca_memory_check_canary to verify if a corruption occurred. Once the system logs the error and potentially resets the affected task, this function is called to 're-arm' the detection mechanism. It is part of the system's self-healing infrastructure rather than standard application logic, and should only be invoked when the system is in a controlled state.

ca_memory_secret.brief: Retrieves the base address and size of the system's reserved secure memory area.

params.name: size
params.desc: Pointer to a 32-bit variable where the function will store the size of the secret area. If NULL, the size is not returned.

ca_memory_secret.returns: Returns a void pointer to the start of the secret memory area. Returns NULL if no secret area has been reserved or initialized.
ca_memory_secret.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it simply returns a pointer to a pre-allocated static memory region. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the memory area has been initialized during system startup. The most common mistake is failing to check if the returned pointer is NULL before accessing it, which will trigger a HardFault if the memory region is not mapped or reserved. Ensure that the system has successfully called the initialization routine that reserves this area before attempting to use it.
ca_memory_secret.usage: This function is typically used in security-sensitive contexts, such as storing cryptographic keys or sensitive configuration data that must be protected. It is often paired with memory protection unit (MPU) configurations to ensure the area is restricted. Developers use it during the system boot sequence to verify if a secure storage area is available before initializing key management services. It is commonly used in conjunction with memory management functions to ensure the application does not overwrite this reserved space.

ca_memset.signature: void *ca_memset(volatile void *dest, unsigned char value, unsigned int count)
ca_memset.brief: Fills a block of memory with a specific byte value.

params.name: dest
params.desc: Pointer to the memory block to be filled. Must not be NULL.

params.name: value
params.desc: The byte value to set. Every byte in the range will be set to this value.

params.name: count
params.desc: Number of bytes to set. If 0, the function does nothing.

ca_memset.returns: Returns the original 'dest' pointer on success, or NULL if the 'dest' pointer provided was NULL.
ca_memset.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes synchronously in the caller's context. It is thread-safe only if the memory region being modified is not accessed by other threads or ISRs simultaneously. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the memory address is valid and not currently locked by another process. A common beginner mistake is passing an incorrect 'count', which can lead to buffer overflows if the value exceeds the allocated memory size, or passing a NULL pointer without checking the return value. The implementation uses word-aligned optimization for performance, so it is highly efficient for large memory blocks.
ca_memset.usage: Used primarily for clearing buffers (setting to 0) before use, initializing structures to a known state, or filling buffers with dummy data (like 0x5A for testing or 0xFF for SPI read-only operations). It is typically used during the initialization phase of a driver or service to ensure no garbage data remains in memory. It is often paired with memory allocation functions like ca_memory_allocate or used before passing a structure to a peripheral driver to ensure all fields are properly zeroed out.

ca_memset_u16.signature: void* ca_memset_u16(volatile u16 *dest, u16 value, u32 count)
ca_memset_u16.brief: Efficiently fills a block of 16-bit memory locations with a specific 16-bit value using 32-bit word alignment.

params.name: dest
params.desc: Pointer to the start of the memory block to be filled. Must be a valid, non-NULL memory address.

params.name: value
params.desc: The 16-bit pattern to write into each memory location.

params.name: count
params.desc: The number of 16-bit elements to fill. A value of 0 results in no operation.

ca_memset_u16.returns: Returns the original pointer to the destination memory block (dest) on success, or NULL if the input pointer is invalid.
ca_memset_u16.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes synchronously, meaning the CPU will remain occupied until the memory fill is complete. It is thread-safe in the sense that it does not rely on global state, but it does not provide mutual exclusion; if two threads write to the same memory area simultaneously, data corruption will occur. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the destination memory is not being accessed by other tasks or interrupts at the same time. The most common beginner mistake is passing an uninitialized or NULL pointer, which will trigger the safety check and return NULL, potentially causing a crash if the return value is not checked before use.
ca_memset_u16.usage: This function is typically used to clear buffers, initialize arrays, or reset hardware-mapped memory regions to a default state. It is often paired with memory allocation routines or used during system initialization to ensure that peripheral buffers or data structures start with known values. Because it uses 32-bit word-aligned writes internally, it is significantly faster than a standard byte-by-byte loop, making it ideal for high-performance applications where large blocks of memory must be cleared quickly, such as clearing a frame buffer or a large communication packet buffer.

ca_memset_u32.signature: void* ca_memset_u32(volatile u32 *dest, u32 value, u32 count)
ca_memset_u32.brief: Efficiently fills a block of 32-bit memory locations with a specific value.

params.name: dest
params.desc: Pointer to the start of the memory block to be filled. Must be 32-bit aligned.

params.name: value
params.desc: The 32-bit pattern to write into each memory location.

params.name: count
params.desc: Number of 32-bit words to write. If 0, the function does nothing.

ca_memset_u32.returns: Returns a pointer to the memory address immediately following the last written word. Returns NULL if the input pointer 'dest' is NULL.
ca_memset_u32.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes synchronously, meaning it will hold the CPU until the entire memory block is filled. It is thread-safe in the sense that it does not rely on global state, but it is not atomic; if another thread or an ISR modifies the memory while this function is running, the result will be inconsistent. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the memory being accessed is not currently being used by another process. The most common beginner mistake is passing a byte-count instead of a word-count, or providing an unaligned pointer, which can trigger a HardFault on some ARM Cortex-M architectures.
ca_memset_u32.usage: This function is typically used for bulk memory initialization, such as clearing buffers, zeroing out thread control blocks (TCB), or filling stack memory with a 'magic pattern' to detect stack overflows later. It is often paired with manual byte-level handling for the 'tail' of a buffer if the total size is not a multiple of 4 bytes. In a typical lifecycle, you would allocate a memory block, use ca_memset_u32 to initialize it to a known state, and then proceed to populate it with application-specific data.

ca_memzero.brief: Sets a specified block of memory to zero bytes.

params.name: dest
params.desc: Pointer to the memory block to be cleared. Must be a valid, writable memory address.

params.name: count
params.desc: Number of bytes to set to zero. Must not exceed the allocated size of the destination buffer.

ca_memzero.returns: Returns the original pointer to the destination memory block (dest).
ca_memzero.notes: This function is a wrapper around ca_memset and is non-blocking, meaning it executes synchronously and returns immediately after the memory is cleared. It is thread-safe provided that no other thread or ISR is accessing the same memory region simultaneously, as concurrent access during a zeroing operation will lead to race conditions. It is safe to call from an ISR because it does not perform any OS-level blocking or context switching. The most common beginner mistake is passing an incorrect 'count' value, such as using sizeof() on a pointer instead of the struct or array it points to, which results in partial clearing or buffer overflows.
ca_memzero.usage: This function is primarily used for security-sensitive operations, such as clearing cryptographic keys or sensitive buffers before they are freed or reused, to prevent data leakage. It is also used during object initialization to ensure that structures start in a clean, predictable state (all zeros) before fields are populated. In a typical lifecycle, you would use ca_memzero immediately after allocating a buffer to avoid garbage data, or immediately before freeing a buffer that contained sensitive information. It is frequently paired with ca_memcpy when moving data and then sanitizing the source buffer.

ca_message_count.brief: Returns the current number of messages stored in the specified message buffer.

params.name: mb
params.desc: Pointer to the message buffer structure. Must be a valid, initialized pointer; passing NULL will result in a return value of 0.

ca_message_count.returns: Returns an unsigned 16-bit integer representing the count of messages currently in the buffer. Returns 0 if the buffer is empty or if the provided pointer is NULL.
ca_message_count.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes in constant time, making it safe to call from both standard tasks and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs). It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs a simple read of a structure member, but be aware that the returned value may become stale immediately after the function returns if another task or interrupt adds or removes messages. A common beginner mistake is assuming the count remains constant while performing subsequent operations; always re-check the count or use appropriate synchronization primitives if you need to ensure the buffer state does not change during a critical sequence.
ca_message_count.usage: This function is typically used for monitoring the health and load of a communication channel or task queue. It is frequently paired with ca_message_space_available to calculate buffer utilization percentages or to decide if it is safe to push a new message without overflowing. Developers use it in a polling loop or a diagnostic task to print status updates to the console, ensuring that the system is not hitting its message capacity limits during high-traffic periods.

ca_message_destroy.brief: Safely deallocates the internal memory buffer of a message queue and resets its control structure.

params.name: mb
params.desc: Pointer to the message buffer structure to be destroyed. Must be a valid, previously initialized pointer; passing NULL is safe but does nothing.

ca_message_destroy.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses a spinlock to protect the internal state during the cleanup process. It is safe to call from an ISR because it uses the IRQ-safe variant of the spinlock, which disables interrupts to prevent deadlocks. The most common mistake is attempting to use the message buffer after calling this function; since the internal buffer is freed and set to NULL, any subsequent attempt to send or receive messages will fail or cause a system crash. Always ensure that no other tasks are currently blocked on this buffer before destroying it, as the function does not explicitly wake up or notify waiting tasks.
ca_message_destroy.usage: This function is typically used during the teardown phase of a system component or when a dynamic communication channel is no longer needed to reclaim heap memory. It is the final step in the lifecycle of a ca_message_buffer_t, following the initialization sequence (where the buffer was created and allocated). You should pair this with the initial creation function to prevent memory leaks in long-running embedded applications. It is often called during system shutdown routines or when reconfiguring peripheral drivers that rely on message passing.

ca_message_init.brief: Initializes a message buffer structure by allocating memory and setting up synchronization primitives.

params.name: mb
params.desc: Pointer to the message buffer control block. Must not be NULL.

params.name: size
params.desc: Total size in bytes to allocate for the buffer. Must be at least CA_MSG_HEADER_SIZE + 1.

ca_message_init.returns: Returns true if the buffer was successfully allocated and initialized; returns false if the pointer is NULL, the size is insufficient, or the heap allocation fails.
ca_message_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs heap allocation via ca_memory_allocate, so it must be called before the RTOS scheduler starts or during system initialization. It is not thread-safe to call this on an already initialized buffer, as it will overwrite existing pointers and cause memory leaks. It is not safe to call from an ISR because heap allocation is generally non-deterministic and may be blocked by other tasks. The most common beginner mistake is failing to check the return value, which leads to a NULL pointer dereference when the system later attempts to write to the unallocated buffer.
ca_message_init.usage: This function is the mandatory first step when setting up inter-task communication via message buffers. It is typically called in the main initialization sequence before spawning tasks with ca_os_job. Once initialized, the buffer is used by producer tasks to send data and consumer tasks to receive data. It is usually paired with a cleanup function (if available) to free the heap memory when the buffer is no longer needed, ensuring no memory fragmentation occurs over the system's lifecycle.

ca_message_init_static.brief: Initializes a static message buffer structure for inter-task communication.

params.name: mb
params.desc: Pointer to the message buffer control structure. Must be a valid memory address.

params.name: buffer
params.desc: Pointer to the raw byte array used as the storage area. Must be large enough to hold data plus headers.

params.name: size
params.desc: Total size of the buffer in bytes. Must be greater than CA_MSG_HEADER_SIZE.

ca_message_init_static.returns: void. If parameters are invalid (NULL pointers or insufficient size), the function returns immediately without initializing the buffer.
ca_message_init_static.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it initializes the internal spinlock. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the memory passed is not currently being accessed by another task. A common beginner mistake is providing a buffer size that is too small; if the size is less than CA_MSG_HEADER_SIZE + 1, the buffer will be unusable, and the function will silently fail. Always ensure the buffer memory is statically allocated (e.g., global or static array) to prevent it from going out of scope, as the RTOS will continue to reference this memory address for the lifetime of the buffer.
ca_message_init_static.usage: This function is the mandatory first step before any message passing can occur. It is typically called during system initialization or driver setup to prepare a communication channel between tasks. You pair this with other message functions like sending or receiving data. Once initialized, the buffer remains ready for use until the system is reset or the buffer is explicitly re-initialized. It is essential to ensure that the buffer memory is not modified by other parts of the application while the message buffer is active.

ca_message_is_empty.brief: Checks if the specified message buffer contains zero messages.

params.name: mb
params.desc: Pointer to the message buffer structure. Must be a valid, initialized pointer.

ca_message_is_empty.returns: Returns true if the buffer is empty or if the provided pointer is NULL. Returns false if there is at least one message currently stored in the buffer.
ca_message_is_empty.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes in constant time, making it safe to call from both standard tasks and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs). It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs a simple read of the internal message counter, but be aware that the buffer state might change immediately after the function returns if another task is writing to it. A common beginner mistake is assuming that if this returns true, the buffer will remain empty for subsequent operations; always use this only for status checks or logic branching, not for synchronization. Ensure the message buffer has been properly initialized via the system's setup functions before passing it here, as passing an uninitialized pointer will lead to undefined behavior.
ca_message_is_empty.usage: This function is typically used in monitoring loops or before attempting to read data from a buffer to avoid unnecessary processing. It is often paired with 'ca_message_count' to get the exact number of items or 'ca_message_space_available' to check if there is room to write new data. In a typical producer-consumer pattern, a consumer task might call this to decide whether to enter a low-power sleep state or to process pending messages. It is also frequently used in diagnostic routines to print the current system status to a console or log file.

ca_message_peek_size.brief: Returns the size of the next pending message in the buffer without removing it from the queue.

params.name: mb
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized message buffer structure. Must not be NULL.

ca_message_peek_size.returns: Returns the size of the next message in bytes (u16). Returns 0 if the buffer is empty, if the pointer is NULL, or if no message is currently available.
ca_message_peek_size.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe because it uses an IRQ-safe spinlock to protect the internal buffer state during the read operation. It is safe to call from an ISR, but keep in mind that frequent calls in high-frequency interrupts can introduce latency. The most common beginner mistake is assuming that a non-zero return value guarantees that a subsequent receive operation will succeed; if another task or interrupt receives the message between your 'peek' and your 'receive', the buffer might become empty. Always check the return value of your subsequent receive operation to handle race conditions.
ca_message_peek_size.usage: This function is typically used in a consumer task to decide if a buffer has enough data to process or to pre-allocate a memory buffer of the correct size before calling the actual retrieval function. It is usually paired with 'ca_message_receive' in a loop where the consumer waits for a specific message size or simply checks for pending work. By using this, you avoid removing data from the queue prematurely, which is useful when you need to inspect the message header or size before committing to a full read operation.

ca_message_receive.signature: u16 ca_message_receive(ca_message_buffer_t *mb, void *data, u16 max_len, u32 timeout_ms)
ca_message_receive.brief: Retrieves a message from a message buffer, blocking the current task if the buffer is empty until data arrives or a timeout occurs.

params.name: mb
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized message buffer handle. Must not be NULL.

params.name: data
params.desc: Pointer to the destination buffer where the received message will be copied. Must not be NULL.

params.name: max_len
params.desc: The maximum number of bytes to copy into the destination buffer. Must be greater than 0.

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Wait time in milliseconds. Use 0 for non-blocking, or 0xFFFFFFFF for infinite wait.

ca_message_receive.returns: Returns the number of bytes copied into the data buffer (0 to max_len). Returns 0 if the buffer is empty after the timeout expires or if input parameters are invalid.
ca_message_receive.notes: This function is blocking, meaning the calling task will be suspended if no data is available, allowing other tasks to run. It is thread-safe due to internal spinlocks, but it must NEVER be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it contains blocking logic and sleep calls. A common beginner mistake is passing a timeout of 0 and expecting the task to wait for data; if the buffer is empty, it will return immediately. Ensure the message buffer is properly initialized before calling this function, otherwise, the system may crash due to a NULL pointer dereference or invalid memory access.
ca_message_receive.usage: This function is typically used in a producer-consumer pattern where a task waits for data sent by another task or an ISR. It is usually paired with a message buffer initialization function at system startup. In the main loop of a consumer task, you call this function to block until work is available, process the data, and then loop back to wait for the next message. It is the standard way to synchronize data flow between tasks without busy-waiting, which saves CPU cycles and power.

ca_message_receive_isr.brief: Reads a message from a message buffer specifically designed for use within Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs).

params.name: mb
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized message buffer structure. Must not be NULL.

params.name: data
params.desc: Pointer to the destination buffer where the received message will be copied. Must have enough space to hold the message.

params.name: max_len
params.desc: The maximum number of bytes to copy into the destination buffer. Must be greater than 0.

ca_message_receive_isr.returns: Returns the actual number of bytes copied into the destination buffer. Returns 0 if the buffer is empty, if parameters are invalid (NULL pointers), or if max_len is 0.
ca_message_receive_isr.notes: This function is explicitly designed to be safe for calling from within an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it uses spinlocks that disable interrupts, preventing race conditions between the main thread and the hardware interrupt. It is non-blocking, meaning it will return immediately even if no data is available, which is critical for maintaining low latency in interrupt handlers. A common beginner mistake is passing a destination buffer that is too small for the incoming message, which can lead to data truncation or memory corruption if the underlying msgbuf_read_msg implementation does not handle bounds checking correctly. Always ensure the message buffer has been properly initialized before calling this function, as passing an uninitialized pointer will cause a system crash.
ca_message_receive_isr.usage: This function is typically used in high-frequency data acquisition scenarios where hardware peripherals (like UART or SPI) trigger an interrupt upon receiving a packet. It is usually paired with a producer function that writes to the buffer from the main loop or another task. The standard sequence involves the hardware interrupt firing, the ISR calling this function to drain the message buffer into a local variable, and then processing that data immediately or signaling a task to handle it. It is the primary mechanism for moving data from the hardware-facing interrupt context into the application-facing processing logic without risking data corruption.

ca_message_reset.brief: Clears all data and resets the internal pointers of a message buffer to an empty state.

params.name: mb
params.desc: A pointer to the message buffer structure to be reset. Must be a valid, initialized pointer; passing NULL will result in a silent return.

ca_message_reset.returns: This function returns void and does not provide a status code.
ca_message_reset.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses a spinlock to protect the internal buffer variables during the reset process. It is non-blocking in the sense that it does not wait for other tasks, but it will briefly disable interrupts to acquire the spinlock, so it should not be called in time-critical sections. It is safe to call from an ISR because it uses the 'irq' variant of the spinlock functions. The most common mistake is calling this function on a buffer that has not been initialized yet, which will lead to a crash when the function attempts to access the uninitialized spinlock member.
ca_message_reset.usage: Use this function when you need to flush a message buffer, such as during a system re-initialization, a manual user command via CLI, or when recovering from a buffer overflow error. It is typically used to clear stale data before starting a new communication sequence or after a communication timeout. It is often paired with the initialization function that sets up the buffer structure, and it is frequently triggered by administrative tasks or error-handling routines to ensure the buffer starts from a clean, predictable state.

ca_message_send.signature: bool ca_message_send(ca_message_buffer_t *mb, const void *data, u16 len, u32 timeout_ms)
ca_message_send.brief: Sends a data packet to a message buffer, blocking the calling task until space is available or the timeout expires.

params.name: mb
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized message buffer handle. Must not be NULL.

params.name: data
params.desc: Pointer to the memory buffer containing the data to send. Must not be NULL.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the data in bytes. Must be greater than 0 and fit within the buffer's remaining capacity.

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time to wait in milliseconds. Use 0 for non-blocking, or 0xFFFFFFFF for infinite wait.

ca_message_send.returns: Returns true if the message was successfully copied into the buffer. Returns false if the buffer is full after the timeout, if parameters are invalid, or if the message size exceeds the buffer capacity.
ca_message_send.notes: This function is blocking, meaning the calling task will pause execution if the buffer is full until space becomes available or the timeout is reached. It is thread-safe due to internal spinlocks, but it must NOT be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it uses ca_os_sleep() which triggers a context switch. A common beginner mistake is passing a timeout of 0 and expecting the system to wait, or failing to check the boolean return value, which leads to silent data loss when the buffer is full. Ensure the message buffer is properly initialized before calling this function, otherwise, the system will likely crash due to a NULL pointer dereference.
ca_message_send.usage: This function is typically used in producer-consumer patterns where one task generates data and another processes it. It is usually paired with ca_message_receive() on the consumer side. The typical workflow involves initializing the buffer once at system startup, then calling ca_message_send() inside a loop or event-driven task to pass data packets. If the return value is false, the application should implement a retry strategy or log an error, as it indicates the consumer task is not processing data fast enough to keep up with the producer.

ca_message_send_isr.signature: bool ca_message_send_isr(ca_message_buffer_t *mb, const void *data, u16 len)
ca_message_send_isr.brief: Sends a message to a message buffer specifically from within an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR).

params.name: mb
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized message buffer handle. Must not be NULL.

params.name: data
params.desc: Pointer to the memory buffer containing the data to send. Must not be NULL.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the data in bytes. Must be greater than 0.

ca_message_send_isr.returns: Returns true if the message was successfully written to the buffer and any waiting task was signaled. Returns false if the buffer is full, parameters are invalid, or the write operation failed.
ca_message_send_isr.notes: This function is designed exclusively for use inside Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs) because it uses spinlocks that disable interrupts to ensure thread safety without causing deadlocks. It is non-blocking, meaning it will return immediately if the buffer is full rather than waiting for space. A common beginner mistake is calling this function from a standard task context instead of the non-ISR version; while it might work, it is inefficient and ignores the specific synchronization requirements of the RTOS. Always ensure the message buffer is properly initialized before calling this, or the system will likely crash due to a null pointer dereference.
ca_message_send_isr.usage: This function is typically used in hardware interrupt handlers, such as a UART RX interrupt or a timer callback, to pass data from the hardware peripheral to a processing task. It is usually paired with a 'receive' function in the task context, where the task waits for data to arrive. The typical sequence is: the ISR triggers, it calls ca_message_send_isr to push data into the buffer, and the RTOS scheduler then wakes up the task that was blocked waiting for that specific message buffer.

ca_message_space_available.brief: Returns the number of bytes currently available for writing in a message buffer.

params.name: mb
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized message buffer structure. Must not be NULL.

ca_message_space_available.returns: Returns the number of free bytes (u32) remaining in the buffer. Returns 0 if the provided pointer is NULL or if the buffer is completely full.
ca_message_space_available.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes in constant time, making it safe to call from both standard tasks and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs). It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs a simple read operation, but be aware that the returned value may become stale immediately if another task or interrupt writes to the buffer simultaneously. A common beginner mistake is assuming the returned value guarantees that a subsequent write operation will succeed; if an interrupt occurs between checking the space and performing the write, the buffer might fill up, leading to a failed write operation. Always ensure the buffer has been properly initialized before passing the pointer to this function.
ca_message_space_available.usage: This function is typically used as a guard check before attempting to send data into a message buffer to prevent buffer overflow or blocking. It is frequently paired with functions like 'ca_message_send' or 'ca_message_peek_size' to manage data flow dynamically. In a typical application, you would call this in a loop to monitor buffer health or to decide if a task should yield execution until more space becomes available. It is essential for implementing flow control in producer-consumer patterns where the producer must not overwhelm the consumer.

ca_modbus_disconnect.brief: Gracefully terminates an active Modbus TCP connection and updates the internal connection status.
ca_modbus_disconnect.returns: This function returns void and does not provide feedback on the success of the underlying TCP closure.
ca_modbus_disconnect.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a clean shutdown of the TCP socket associated with the Modbus service. It is not thread-safe by itself; if multiple tasks access the Modbus state, you must ensure external synchronization to prevent race conditions where the connection status is checked while it is being closed. It is generally safe to call from an ISR, but be aware that the underlying ca_tcp_close might involve complex stack operations that could be heavy for high-frequency interrupts. The most common beginner mistake is calling this function without checking if the connection is already closed, or assuming that calling this immediately frees up resources for a new connection before the TCP stack has finished its handshake process.
ca_modbus_disconnect.usage: This function is used to manually drop a Modbus connection, typically during a system shutdown sequence, a network error recovery routine, or when switching between different Modbus masters. It is usually paired with a connection check function like ca_modbus_is_connected to ensure the state is consistent before attempting to reconnect. In a typical lifecycle, you would initialize the service, use ca_modbus_is_connected to verify the link, and call ca_modbus_disconnect when the communication session is finished or when a timeout occurs to prevent resource leakage in the TCP stack.

ca_modbus_is_connected.brief: Checks if the Modbus TCP service currently has an active network connection.
ca_modbus_is_connected.returns: Returns true if the Modbus TCP connection is established and active, false if the connection is down or not yet initialized.
ca_modbus_is_connected.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it simply reads a boolean flag maintained by the internal service state. It is safe to call from both main-loop tasks and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs) because it performs a simple memory read without waiting for hardware or mutexes. A common beginner mistake is to assume that a 'true' return value guarantees that the remote server is still responding to data requests; this function only confirms that the TCP socket layer is up. Always ensure the Modbus service has been initialized via ca_modbus_service_init before relying on this status, otherwise, it will return false by default.
ca_modbus_is_connected.usage: This function is primarily used in a 'watchdog' pattern within the main application loop to monitor connection health. It is typically paired with ca_modbus_service_init to trigger a reconnection attempt if the connection drops due to network instability or server timeouts. By checking this status periodically, you can implement robust recovery logic that attempts to re-initialize the service only when necessary, preventing unnecessary resource allocation while the connection is already healthy.

ca_modbus_read_coils.signature: bool ca_modbus_read_coils(u16 addr, u16 count, u8 *out)
ca_modbus_read_coils.brief: Sends a Modbus Function Code 01 request to read the status of multiple coils from a remote device.

params.name: addr
params.desc: The starting address of the first coil to read. Must be a valid address supported by the slave device.

params.name: count
params.desc: The number of coils to read. Must be between 1 and 2000 inclusive.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to a buffer where the coil data will be stored. Must be large enough to hold (count + 7) / 8 bytes.

ca_modbus_read_coils.returns: Returns true if the request was successful and the response was validated; returns false if the parameters are invalid, the transaction fails, or the received data is incomplete.
ca_modbus_read_coils.notes: This function is blocking, meaning the calling task will wait until the Modbus transaction completes or times out. It is not thread-safe if multiple tasks attempt to access the same Modbus bus simultaneously, so ensure you have a mutex or task-level synchronization if your application is multi-threaded. It must NOT be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it performs blocking I/O operations. A common beginner mistake is providing an 'out' buffer that is too small for the requested 'count', which will cause a memory corruption (buffer overflow) when the function copies the received data.
ca_modbus_read_coils.usage: This function is used in Modbus master applications to poll the status of digital outputs or flags from a slave device. It is typically used in a periodic task loop after the Modbus service has been initialized. It is often paired with other Modbus functions like ca_modbus_write_coil or ca_modbus_read_registers to perform full device monitoring. Before calling this, ensure the communication interface (e.g., RS485/UART) is properly initialized and the slave device is online.

ca_modbus_read_holding_regs.signature: bool ca_modbus_read_holding_regs(u16 addr, u16 count, u16 *out)
ca_modbus_read_holding_regs.brief: Sends a Modbus Function Code 03 request to read a sequence of holding registers from a remote device.

params.name: addr
params.desc: The starting register address to read. Must be a valid address supported by the target Modbus slave device.

params.name: count
params.desc: Number of registers to read. Must be between 1 and 125 inclusive, as per Modbus protocol limits.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to an array where the retrieved register values will be stored. Must be large enough to hold 'count' elements.

ca_modbus_read_holding_regs.returns: Returns true if the transaction was successful and data was parsed correctly. Returns false if the input parameters are invalid, the transaction fails (e.g., timeout or communication error), or the slave returns an insufficient byte count.
ca_modbus_read_holding_regs.notes: This function is blocking, meaning the calling task will wait until the Modbus transaction completes or times out. It is not thread-safe if multiple tasks attempt to access the Modbus bus simultaneously; ensure you have a mutex or semaphore protecting the bus access if your application is multi-threaded. It must NOT be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it performs blocking I/O operations. A common beginner mistake is providing an 'out' buffer that is smaller than the 'count' requested, which will cause a buffer overflow and memory corruption.
ca_modbus_read_holding_regs.usage: This function is typically used in a periodic task to poll sensor data or configuration registers from a Modbus slave device. It is usually paired with other Modbus functions like 'ca_modbus_write_single_reg' to manage device state. Before calling this, ensure the Modbus communication interface is initialized. It is standard practice to check the boolean return value; if it returns false, the application should handle the communication error, perhaps by logging the failure or attempting a retry after a short delay.

ca_modbus_service_init.signature: void ca_modbus_service_init(ca_ipv4_t server_ip, u16 server_port, ca_ipv4_t local_ip, ca_mac_t local_mac, u8 unit_id)
ca_modbus_service_init.brief: Initializes the internal Modbus TCP service state, configures network parameters, and prepares synchronization primitives.

params.name: server_ip
params.desc: The IPv4 address of the remote Modbus server (PLC or gateway). Must be a valid network-order structure.

params.name: server_port
params.desc: The TCP port number for the Modbus service, typically 502.

params.name: local_ip
params.desc: The static IPv4 address assigned to the STM32 device.

params.name: local_mac
params.desc: The unique MAC address of the device's network interface.

params.name: unit_id
params.desc: The Modbus slave/unit identifier (1-247). Use 0xFF for broadcast if supported.

ca_modbus_service_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs internal memory clearing and synchronization object initialization. It is NOT thread-safe; it must be called during the system startup phase before any Modbus communication tasks are spawned. If called while a connection is active, it will forcefully close the existing TCP handle, which may lead to unexpected behavior if other tasks are currently using the socket. A common beginner mistake is calling this function multiple times during runtime; this will reset the internal state, clear the transaction ID counter, and potentially cause memory leaks or race conditions if the RTOS tasks are not suspended first.
ca_modbus_service_init.usage: This function is the mandatory entry point for the Modbus stack. It is typically called once during the system initialization sequence, immediately after the network interface is brought up but before the Modbus polling task starts. It is usually followed by a call to ca_modbus_service_net_ready() to signal the stack that the network layer is prepared to establish the TCP connection. It pairs with the internal state management to ensure that the mutexes and semaphores required for thread-safe access to the Modbus buffer are correctly allocated.

ca_modbus_service_net_ready.brief: Initializes and triggers the TCP connection process for the Modbus service.
ca_modbus_service_net_ready.returns: Returns true if the TCP connection handle was successfully allocated (handle != 0xFFU), otherwise returns false if the connection request failed.
ca_modbus_service_net_ready.notes: This function is non-blocking; it initiates the TCP handshake process but does not wait for the connection to be established. It is not thread-safe and should not be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) as it performs memory operations and handle allocation. A common mistake is calling this function repeatedly in a loop without checking if a connection is already active, which can lead to resource exhaustion or multiple overlapping connection attempts. Ensure that the Modbus service has been fully initialized via ca_modbus_service_init before calling this, otherwise, the internal configuration structure 's' will contain invalid data.
ca_modbus_service_net_ready.usage: This function is typically used during the system startup phase or within a state machine that manages network recovery. It is the bridge between the static configuration (IP, MAC, Port) and the active network stack. It is usually paired with ca_modbus_service_init to set up parameters, and the resulting connection status is monitored via the callback functions (on_tcp_connected, on_tcp_closed) provided in the configuration structure. In a robust application, you would call this once at boot, and then again only if the 'on_tcp_closed' callback indicates that the connection has been lost.

ca_modbus_write_multiple_regs.signature: bool ca_modbus_write_multiple_regs(u16 addr, const u16 *values, u16 count)
ca_modbus_write_multiple_regs.brief: Sends a Modbus Function Code 16 request to write a block of multiple holding registers to a remote device.

params.name: addr
params.desc: The starting register address on the target device. Must be a valid address supported by the slave.

params.name: values
params.desc: Pointer to an array of 16-bit values to be written. Must not be NULL.

params.name: count
params.desc: Number of registers to write. Must be between 1 and 123 inclusive.

ca_modbus_write_multiple_regs.returns: Returns true if the transaction was successfully initiated and completed, false if parameters are invalid, the buffer size is exceeded, or the underlying transaction failed.
ca_modbus_write_multiple_regs.notes: This function is blocking, meaning the calling task will wait until the Modbus transaction completes or times out. It is not safe to call this function from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it relies on task-level synchronization and blocking mechanisms. Before calling this, ensure the Modbus communication stack is initialized and the target device is reachable. A common mistake is passing a 'count' that exceeds the Modbus protocol limit of 123 registers or providing a NULL pointer, both of which will cause the function to return false immediately without attempting communication.
ca_modbus_write_multiple_regs.usage: This function is used when you need to update a contiguous block of configuration parameters or status registers on a remote Modbus slave device in a single atomic operation. It is typically used in a sequence where you first verify the connection, prepare an array of data, and then call this function to commit the changes. It is often paired with other Modbus functions like 'ca_modbus_read_holding_regs' to verify the write operation by reading the values back, or used within a state machine that manages periodic device configuration updates.

ca_modbus_write_single_reg.brief: Sends a Modbus Function Code 06 request to write a single 16-bit register to a remote device.

params.name: addr
params.desc: The 16-bit address of the Modbus register to be written. Must be a valid register address defined by the slave device's memory map.

params.name: value
params.desc: The 16-bit data value to be stored in the specified register.

ca_modbus_write_single_reg.returns: Returns true if the transaction was successfully sent and acknowledged by the slave device; returns false if the transaction failed, timed out, or received an error response.
ca_modbus_write_single_reg.notes: This function is blocking, meaning the calling task will wait until the Modbus transaction completes or times out. It is not thread-safe if multiple tasks attempt to access the Modbus bus simultaneously; you must ensure external synchronization (like a mutex) if your application has multiple tasks communicating over the same bus. It is strictly forbidden to call this from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it performs blocking I/O operations. A common beginner mistake is assuming the write is successful just because the function was called; you must always check the boolean return value to handle communication errors or slave exceptions.
ca_modbus_write_single_reg.usage: This function is used in industrial automation contexts to update configuration parameters, setpoints, or control flags on remote Modbus slaves. It is typically used within a control loop or a state machine after the Modbus service has been initialized. It is often paired with other Modbus functions like ca_modbus_read_input_regs or ca_modbus_read_holding_regs to verify the state of the device before and after the write operation. In a typical sequence, you would initialize the communication interface, perform a read to check the current status, perform the write using this function, and then verify the change.

ca_mpu_add_region.signature: int ca_mpu_add_region(u32 addr, u32 size, u16 mode)
ca_mpu_add_region.brief: Configures and enables a Memory Protection Unit (MPU) region to restrict or grant access to a specific memory address range.

params.name: addr
params.desc: The starting memory address for the region. Note that the hardware often requires this to be aligned to the size of the region.

params.name: size
params.desc: The size of the memory block in bytes. The MPU will automatically round this up to the nearest power-of-two (minimum 32 bytes).

params.name: mode
params.desc: Access permissions: MPU_ACCESS_RDONLY (read-only), MPU_ACCESS_NONE (no access), or MPU_ACCESS_RDWR (read-write).

ca_mpu_add_region.returns: Returns the assigned region index (0 to N) on success, or -1 if no MPU regions are available or an error occurred.
ca_mpu_add_region.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes very quickly, but it is not inherently thread-safe; if multiple tasks attempt to configure MPU regions simultaneously, you must protect this call with a mutex. It is generally safe to call from an ISR, but be aware that modifying MPU settings while the CPU is executing code in that memory area can trigger a MemManage fault. The most common beginner mistake is failing to check the return value; if you run out of MPU regions, the function returns -1, and ignoring this will lead to silent failures where your memory protection is not actually active.
ca_mpu_add_region.usage: This function is used to enforce memory safety by isolating sensitive data (like cryptographic keys or stack areas) from unauthorized access. It is typically called during system initialization or when a module is being set up. You would pair this with other MPU management functions to track how many regions are currently in use and to ensure you do not exceed the hardware's physical limit of available MPU slots.

ca_mpu_dump_regions.brief: Prints the current configuration of all enabled Memory Protection Unit (MPU) regions to the system console.
ca_mpu_dump_regions.notes: This function is a diagnostic tool that iterates through the hardware MPU registers to display memory access permissions, base addresses, and sizes. It is non-blocking and performs read-only operations on the MPU registers, making it safe to call from most contexts, though it is primarily intended for debugging via CLI. It is not thread-safe in the sense that if another task modifies MPU settings while this function is iterating, the output may be inconsistent. The most common mistake is assuming this function will 'fix' memory issues; it only reports the current state, it does not validate if the configuration is logically correct for your application.
ca_mpu_dump_regions.usage: This function is typically used during the development and debugging phase to verify that memory protection regions (like stack guards or peripheral access restrictions) are configured as expected. It is commonly invoked via a CLI command (e.g., 'mpu') when a MemManage fault occurs or when verifying system initialization. It is often paired with other diagnostic functions like 'ca_scheduler_dump_task' to correlate memory layout with task-specific stack usage.

ca_mpu_first_free_region.brief: Finds the index of the first MPU region that is currently disabled.
ca_mpu_first_free_region.returns: Returns the index (0 to N-1) of the first available MPU region, or the total number of regions if all are currently enabled.
ca_mpu_first_free_region.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes very quickly by iterating through the hardware MPU registers. It is thread-safe in the sense that it only reads hardware state, but it does not reserve the region; you must immediately follow this with a call to configure the region to prevent race conditions. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided you are not modifying MPU registers elsewhere simultaneously. A common mistake is assuming that finding a free region guarantees it is safe to use; you must always verify the memory address range does not overlap with existing critical system regions.
ca_mpu_first_free_region.usage: This function is typically used during system initialization or when dynamically creating memory-protected tasks. It is usually paired with ca_mpu_get_total_regions to check for availability, followed by ca_mpu_update_region to actually enable and configure the found slot. It is essential for managing hardware resources when you need to isolate specific memory areas for security or stability.

ca_mpu_get_available_regions.brief: Returns the count of MPU regions that are currently disabled and available for configuration.
ca_mpu_get_available_regions.returns: Returns a u32 integer representing the number of free MPU slots. Returns 0 if all hardware MPU regions are currently in use.
ca_mpu_get_available_regions.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes quickly, making it safe to call from most contexts. However, it is not inherently thread-safe; if another task or an interrupt modifies MPU registers while this function is iterating through them, the returned count might be inconsistent. It is callable from an ISR, but be aware that it performs a loop over hardware registers, which adds a small amount of latency. A common beginner mistake is assuming that having 'available' regions means they are automatically configured; this function only reports availability, it does not reserve or allocate the regions for you.
ca_mpu_get_available_regions.usage: This function is typically used during system initialization or when dynamically creating memory-protected tasks to ensure there is enough hardware capacity before attempting to configure a new MPU region. It is usually paired with functions that configure specific MPU regions, such as ca_mpu_add_region or ca_mpu_update_region. By checking availability first, you prevent 'silent' failures where a new memory protection rule fails to apply because the hardware limit was reached. It acts as a safety gate to verify that your application's memory protection strategy fits within the physical constraints of the specific STM32 microcontroller being used.

ca_mpu_get_busy_regions.brief: Returns the count of MPU regions currently allocated and in use by the system.
ca_mpu_get_busy_regions.returns: Returns an unsigned 32-bit integer representing the number of MPU regions currently occupied. A return value of 0 indicates that no MPU regions are currently reserved by the OS.
ca_mpu_get_busy_regions.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes in constant time, making it safe to call from both thread mode and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs). It is thread-safe as it performs a simple arithmetic calculation based on internal state variables. The primary precondition is that the MPU subsystem must be initialized via ca_mpu_init() before calling this function, otherwise, the returned values may be undefined or zero. A common beginner mistake is assuming that this function returns the total number of available hardware slots; instead, it specifically returns the count of slots already taken, which is useful for monitoring memory protection resource exhaustion.
ca_mpu_get_busy_regions.usage: This function is typically used for system diagnostics, debugging, or resource management when you need to verify if there are enough free MPU slots remaining before attempting to configure a new memory region. It is often paired with ca_mpu_get_available_regions() to perform a 'pre-flight check' before calling functions like ca_mpu_add_region(). By monitoring the busy count, developers can prevent system crashes caused by attempting to configure more regions than the hardware supports, which is a critical limitation on STM32 microcontrollers.

ca_mpu_get_total_regions.brief: Retrieves the total number of configurable memory protection regions supported by the hardware MPU.
ca_mpu_get_total_regions.returns: An unsigned 32-bit integer representing the count of available MPU regions (typically 8 or 16 depending on the specific STM32 silicon).
ca_mpu_get_total_regions.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes in constant time by reading directly from the MPU_TYPE register. It is thread-safe and can be safely called from both main-line code and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs) because it performs a simple read operation without modifying any system state. The most common mistake is assuming a fixed number of regions across different STM32 families; always use this function to query the hardware dynamically rather than hardcoding values like 8 or 16. There are no mandatory preconditions other than the MPU hardware being present on the chip.
ca_mpu_get_total_regions.usage: This function is typically used during system initialization or when implementing dynamic memory management schemes that require partitioning memory into protected segments. It is often paired with functions that configure specific regions, such as ca_mpu_add_region or ca_mpu_update_region, to ensure the application does not attempt to configure a region index that exceeds the hardware's physical limit. By using this function, your code becomes portable across different STM32 series, as it automatically adapts to the specific MPU capabilities of the target microcontroller.

ca_mpu_init.brief: Initializes the Memory Protection Unit (MPU) to enable hardware-based memory access control and stack overflow protection.
ca_mpu_init.returns: void. This function does not return a status code; if the hardware lacks an MPU, it silently returns without performing any configuration.
ca_mpu_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and must be called during the early system boot sequence before the RTOS scheduler starts. It is not thread-safe and should never be called from an ISR, as it modifies critical system registers that control CPU exception behavior. A common mistake is calling this function after memory allocation or task creation has already begun, which can lead to unpredictable behavior if the MPU configuration conflicts with existing memory usage. Always ensure this is one of the first hardware initialization steps to guarantee that subsequent memory operations are protected by the MPU's fault-detection logic.
ca_mpu_init.usage: This function is used exclusively during the system startup phase, typically inside the main() function before the RTOS scheduler is initialized. It is part of a mandatory sequence: first, the MPU is initialized with ca_mpu_init(), then specific memory regions (like the stack canary) are protected using functions like ca_mpu_protect_canary_msp(), and finally, the memory heap and scheduler are initialized. This order ensures that the system is fully protected before any user tasks or dynamic memory allocations are created.

ca_mpu_protect_canary_msp.brief: Configures the MPU to make the Main Stack Pointer (MSP) canary memory region read-only to detect stack overflows.

params.name: canary_addr
params.desc: The memory address of the canary value. Must be 32-byte aligned. Passing 0 disables the protection.

ca_mpu_protect_canary_msp.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes very quickly, but it is not thread-safe; it should only be called during system initialization before the scheduler starts. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. The most common mistake is providing an address that is not 32-byte aligned, which will cause the MPU to misconfigure the region, potentially leading to unexpected MemManage faults. Always ensure the address provided is the start of the reserved canary area defined in your linker script.
ca_mpu_protect_canary_msp.usage: This function is used during the early boot sequence of the RTOS, immediately after the MPU hardware is initialized via ca_mpu_init(). It is typically called before memory heap initialization and scheduler startup to ensure that the stack integrity monitoring is active before any tasks are created. It pairs with ca_mpu_init() to set up the hardware and precedes ca_bus_error_init() to ensure that if a violation occurs, the system can handle the resulting fault gracefully.

ca_mpu_protect_canary_psp_end.brief: Configures an MPU region to make a specific memory area read-only, typically used to protect stack canary values from accidental corruption.

params.name: canary_addr
params.desc: The base memory address of the canary. Must be 32-byte aligned. Passing 0 disables the protection region.

ca_mpu_protect_canary_psp_end.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes very quickly as it directly writes to the MPU hardware registers. It is thread-safe in the sense that it modifies a specific MPU region reserved for the canary, but it must be used carefully during context switches. It is callable from an ISR, but typically it is used by the kernel scheduler. The most common mistake is providing an address that is not 32-byte aligned, which will cause the MPU to mask the lower bits and potentially protect the wrong memory area. Always ensure the MPU is enabled in the system configuration before calling this, otherwise, the settings will have no effect.
ca_mpu_protect_canary_psp_end.usage: This function is used by the RTOS kernel to implement stack overflow detection. It is typically called during a context switch or task initialization sequence. The standard workflow is: first, disable the protection by passing 0 to update the canary value, then perform the write operation to the memory, and finally call the function again with the new address to re-enable the read-only protection. This ensures that the canary value remains immutable during normal task execution, triggering a MemManage fault if any code attempts to overwrite it.

ca_mpu_protect_canary_psp_start.brief: Configures the MPU to make a 32-byte memory region read-only, typically used to protect stack canary values.

params.name: canary_addr
params.desc: The memory address of the canary. Must be 32-byte aligned. Passing 0 disables the protection region.

ca_mpu_protect_canary_psp_start.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes very quickly, but it is not thread-safe; if multiple tasks or an ISR attempt to modify MPU settings simultaneously, the system state will become corrupted. It is intended to be called from privileged code during task context switching or initialization. The most common mistake is providing an unaligned address, which will cause the MPU to mask the address incorrectly, potentially protecting the wrong memory area. Always ensure the MPU is enabled in the system configuration before calling this, as it only configures a specific region, not the MPU hardware itself.
ca_mpu_protect_canary_psp_start.usage: This function is used by the kernel scheduler to implement stack overflow detection. It is typically used in a 'disable-modify-enable' pattern: first, call with 0 to disable protection so the kernel can write the canary pattern into the stack; second, perform the write operation; third, call with the actual address to lock the region as read-only. This ensures that if a task accidentally writes into its own stack canary area, the CPU triggers a MemManage fault, allowing the system to catch the overflow immediately.

ca_mpu_region_covers.signature: bool ca_mpu_region_covers(u16 region, u32 addr, u32 size)
ca_mpu_region_covers.brief: Checks if a specific MPU region is enabled and overlaps with a given memory range.

params.name: region
params.desc: The index of the MPU region to check (e.g., 0 to 7 or 0 to 15 depending on the MCU).

params.name: addr
params.desc: The starting memory address of the range to verify.

params.name: size
params.desc: The size in bytes of the memory range to verify.

ca_mpu_region_covers.returns: Returns true if the region is enabled and the specified range overlaps with the region's memory span; returns false otherwise.
ca_mpu_region_covers.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe regarding the MPU hardware state, as it saves and restores the MPU region index (RNR) on newer architectures. It is safe to call from an ISR, but be aware that it performs direct hardware register access, which is fast but requires the MPU to be initialized. A common beginner mistake is assuming the function checks if the entire range is contained within the region; it only checks for any overlap. Always ensure the 'region' index provided is within the valid range supported by your specific STM32 hardware.
ca_mpu_region_covers.usage: This function is typically used for safety checks, such as verifying if a buffer or a stack area conflicts with protected memory regions. It is often paired with ca_mpu_add_region or ca_mpu_update_region during system initialization to validate configuration. In runtime, it is used to perform sanity checks before memory operations to ensure that critical system areas, like stack canaries, are not being inadvertently overwritten by user code.

ca_mpu_region_is_reserved.brief: Checks if a specific MPU region index is reserved by the OS kernel.

params.name: idx
params.desc: The index of the MPU region to check. Valid values are 0 to (total available MPU regions - 1).

ca_mpu_region_is_reserved.returns: Returns true if the index is reserved for internal OS use, false if it is available for user-defined memory protection.
ca_mpu_region_is_reserved.notes: This function is a non-blocking, thread-safe helper that performs a simple bounds check against the internal OS configuration. It is safe to call from both task context and ISRs because it does not perform any hardware access or complex logic. The most common mistake is assuming that a 'false' return means the region is currently unused; it only means the region is not reserved by the kernel. You must still verify if the region is already in use by the application using other MPU management functions like checking the busy regions list.
ca_mpu_region_is_reserved.usage: This function is typically used during system initialization or when dynamically configuring memory protection for specific tasks. It is usually paired with ca_mpu_first_free_region to find a valid slot for a new memory protection rule. Developers use this to ensure they do not accidentally overwrite critical kernel memory regions when calling ca_mpu_add_region or ca_mpu_update_region. It is part of the standard MPU setup sequence: init -> check availability -> add region.

ca_mpu_update_region.signature: int ca_mpu_update_region(u16 region_index, u32 addr, u32 size, u16 mode)
ca_mpu_update_region.brief: Configures a specific Memory Protection Unit (MPU) region to enforce access permissions and memory boundaries.

params.name: region_index
params.desc: The specific MPU slot to configure. Must be less than the value returned by ca_mpu_get_total_regions().

params.name: addr
params.desc: The starting memory address for the region. Note that the hardware may force alignment based on the size.

params.name: size
params.desc: The size of the memory region in bytes. The hardware will round this up to the nearest power of 2.

params.name: mode
params.desc: Access permission constant: MPU_ACCESS_RDONLY, MPU_ACCESS_NONE, or MPU_ACCESS_RDWR.

ca_mpu_update_region.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns -1 if the region_index is invalid (out of bounds).
ca_mpu_update_region.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately. It is thread-safe in the sense that it modifies hardware registers directly, but you must ensure that no other task or ISR attempts to modify the same MPU region simultaneously, as this would cause a race condition. It is safe to call from an ISR, but be aware that changing memory protections while the CPU is executing code in that region can trigger an immediate MemManage fault. A common beginner mistake is providing an unaligned address or a size that is not a power of 2; while the function handles the math, the resulting memory coverage might be larger than expected, potentially overlapping with other critical memory areas.
ca_mpu_update_region.usage: This function is typically used during system initialization or when switching security contexts (e.g., before accessing sensitive data like cryptographic keys). It is often paired with ca_mpu_get_total_regions() to ensure the index is valid before attempting configuration. Developers use this to create 'sandboxes' in memory, ensuring that specific tasks or drivers cannot write to memory they don't own. It is standard practice to call this whenever a memory buffer's lifecycle changes, such as locking a key storage area after a write operation is complete.

ca_mqtt_disconnect.brief: Gracefully terminates an active MQTT session and closes the underlying TCP connection.
ca_mqtt_disconnect.returns: This function returns void and does not provide feedback on whether the disconnection packet was successfully acknowledged by the server.
ca_mqtt_disconnect.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a 'best-effort' shutdown by sending a DISCONNECT packet before closing the socket. It is not thread-safe; if multiple tasks attempt to manage the MQTT state simultaneously, you may encounter race conditions where the connection state flags become inconsistent. It is strictly forbidden to call this from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it relies on TCP stack operations that require task context. A common beginner mistake is calling this function without checking if the connection is actually active, or assuming that calling this immediately frees up all network resources, whereas the underlying TCP stack might still be performing a graceful FIN handshake.
ca_mqtt_disconnect.usage: Use this function when you need to shut down the MQTT client, such as during a system power-down sequence, a network interface reset, or when transitioning to a low-power state. It is typically used to clean up the connection state before the application enters a state where the network is no longer required. In a robust application, you should call this before re-initializing the network stack or when the application logic determines that the MQTT broker is no longer needed, ensuring that the server is notified of the client's departure rather than just timing out.

ca_mqtt_is_connected.brief: Checks if the MQTT client is currently connected to the broker.
ca_mqtt_is_connected.returns: Returns true if the MQTT client is connected (s.mqtt_up is set), and false if the client is disconnected or the service is not initialized.
ca_mqtt_is_connected.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it simply reads a boolean flag from the internal service state. It is safe to call from both tasks and Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs) because it performs a simple memory read without acquiring mutexes or waiting for hardware. A common mistake is assuming that a 'true' return value guarantees that the network socket is still healthy; the flag only reflects the last known state of the MQTT session. If the network cable is unplugged or the router drops the connection, this flag might remain true until the next keep-alive timeout or TCP error occurs, so always pair this with logic that handles communication timeouts.
ca_mqtt_is_connected.usage: This function is primarily used in the main application loop or a dedicated network management task to monitor the health of the MQTT connection. It is typically used as a guard condition before attempting to publish data to ensure the message is not lost. It is frequently paired with ca_mqtt_service_init() to trigger a reconnection sequence when the connection is lost, and it is often used alongside ca_os_tick_ms() to implement non-blocking reconnection intervals, preventing the system from flooding the broker with connection requests during a network outage.

ca_mqtt_ping.brief: Sends an MQTT PINGREQ packet to the broker to maintain the connection alive.
ca_mqtt_ping.returns: This function returns void and does not provide feedback on whether the packet was successfully sent or if the network connection is failing.
ca_mqtt_ping.notes: This function is non-blocking and relies on the underlying ca_tcp_send function to handle the transmission. It is not thread-safe if called simultaneously from multiple tasks, though it is typically only called by the MQTT management task. It cannot be called from an ISR because it performs network operations that require a stable stack and OS context. A common mistake is calling this function before the MQTT service is initialized or while the connection is down; the function internally checks the s.mqtt_up flag to prevent sending packets on a dead socket, but it does not attempt to reconnect automatically.
ca_mqtt_ping.usage: This function is used as a heartbeat mechanism to prevent the MQTT broker from closing the connection due to inactivity. It is typically called within a periodic loop inside an MQTT management task, paired with a timer check to ensure the ping is sent at the required interval (e.g., every 30-60 seconds). It is usually used in conjunction with ca_mqtt_is_connected to verify the link status before attempting to send data, and it relies on the TCP handle initialized during the MQTT service startup sequence.

ca_mqtt_publish.signature: bool ca_mqtt_publish(const char *topic, const u8 *payload, u16 len)
ca_mqtt_publish.brief: Publishes a message to a specific MQTT topic over an established TCP connection.

params.name: topic
params.desc: The MQTT topic string. Must be a null-terminated C string. Invalid if NULL or if the resulting packet exceeds MQTT_TX_BUF_SIZE.

params.name: payload
params.desc: Pointer to the data buffer to be sent. Can contain binary data or text.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the payload in bytes. Must not cause the total packet size to exceed MQTT_TX_BUF_SIZE.

ca_mqtt_publish.returns: Returns true if the packet was successfully formatted and passed to the TCP stack, false otherwise. A false return indicates the MQTT service is not up, the packet is too large, or the underlying TCP send operation failed.
ca_mqtt_publish.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called from a single task context to avoid race conditions on the internal transmission buffer. It is not callable from an ISR because it performs memory operations and relies on the TCP stack which is likely blocking or requires task-level synchronization. The function performs a bounds check against MQTT_TX_BUF_SIZE; if your topic and payload combined exceed this limit, the function will silently fail, so always verify your data size before calling. A common beginner mistake is assuming this function guarantees delivery; it only confirms that the packet was handed off to the TCP layer, not that the broker received it.
ca_mqtt_publish.usage: This function is used after the MQTT service has been initialized and the TCP connection is established. It is typically called within a main application loop or a dedicated telemetry task to send sensor data or status updates to a broker. It is usually paired with a connection check (to ensure s.mqtt_up is true) and follows a sequence of: initialize network, connect TCP, perform MQTT handshake, and then repeatedly call ca_mqtt_publish to send data.

ca_mqtt_service_init.signature: void ca_mqtt_service_init(ca_ipv4_t broker_ip, u16 broker_port, ca_ipv4_t local_ip, ca_mac_t local_mac, const char *client_id, ca_mqtt_connected_cb_t on_connected, ca_mqtt_message_cb_t on_message, ca_mqtt_disconnected_cb_t on_disconnected)
ca_mqtt_service_init.brief: Initializes the MQTT service state and registers callback functions for connection events.

params.name: broker_ip
params.desc: The IPv4 address of the MQTT broker.

params.name: broker_port
params.desc: The TCP port of the MQTT broker (e.g., 1883).

params.name: local_ip
params.desc: The local IPv4 address assigned to the device.

params.name: local_mac
params.desc: The local MAC address of the network interface.

params.name: client_id
