ca_rtc_hw_get_src.brief: Reads the current RTC clock source configuration from the hardware backup domain registers.
ca_rtc_hw_get_src.returns: Returns a ca_rtc_clk_src_t enum value: CA_RTC_CLK_LSE (external crystal), CA_RTC_CLK_LSI (internal low-speed oscillator), CA_RTC_CLK_HSE (external high-speed oscillator), or CA_RTC_CLK_AUTO (no source configured, indicating a cold boot).
ca_rtc_hw_get_src.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it performs a simple read of the RCC backup domain register. It is safe to call from an ISR because it does not involve any waiting, mutexes, or complex logic. The backup domain is a special area of the STM32 that persists through system resets (but not power-off), allowing the RTC to maintain its configuration across warm reboots. A common mistake is assuming the RTC is ready just because a source is returned; this function only reports the hardware register state, not the operational status or stability of the clock source.
ca_rtc_hw_get_src.usage: This function is typically used during the system initialization phase, specifically within the RTC driver's startup sequence. It is called to determine if the RTC was already running before the current reset, which helps the system decide whether to re-initialize the clock or trust the existing configuration. It is usually paired with ca_rtc_clock_init to perform conditional hardware setup based on the detected source.

ca_rtc_hw_get_sub.brief: Reads the current RTC date, time, and sub-second fraction in a single atomic-like operation.

params.name: dt
params.desc: Pointer to a structure where the date and time (year, month, day, hour, minute, second) will be stored.

params.name: sub
params.desc: Pointer to store the current sub-second value (fraction of a second).

params.name: sub_div
params.desc: Pointer to store the divisor used for the sub-second calculation (PREDIV_S + 1).

ca_rtc_hw_get_sub.returns: Returns true if the hardware registers were read successfully, false if the RTC is not synchronized or if any pointer is NULL.
ca_rtc_hw_get_sub.notes: This function is not thread-safe by itself; it relies on hardware-level register locking (reading SSR locks TR and DR) to ensure the time components belong to the same instant. It is generally safe to call from tasks, but avoid calling it from high-priority ISRs if the RTC synchronization wait (rtc_wait_sync) takes too long, as this could block the system. The most common mistake is failing to check the return value; if the RTC is not initialized or the clock is not running, the function will return false and the data in 'dt' will be invalid.
ca_rtc_hw_get_sub.usage: Use this function when you need high-precision timestamps, such as logging events with sub-second accuracy or calculating time intervals between tasks. It is typically used after the RTC has been initialized via ca_rtc_init. You would pair this with your own logic to convert the 'sub' and 'sub_div' values into milliseconds or microseconds for display or storage. Always ensure the RTC is ready before calling this, as it is a prerequisite for the hardware registers to contain valid, stable data.

ca_rtc_hw_init.brief: Initializes the Real-Time Clock (RTC) hardware peripheral with a specific clock source.

params.name: src
params.desc: The clock source to use: CA_RTC_CLK_LSE (External 32kHz crystal), CA_RTC_CLK_LSI (Internal low-speed RC), or CA_RTC_CLK_HSE (High-speed external divided).

ca_rtc_hw_init.returns: Returns true if the RTC was successfully initialized and the clock source stabilized. Returns false if the clock source failed to start (timeout) or if the hardware configuration sequence failed.
ca_rtc_hw_init.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called during system initialization before any other RTC operations. It performs hardware-level register manipulation, including unlocking the backup domain and configuring the prescalers. It is a blocking function because it waits for the selected clock source to become ready (LSERDY/LSIRDY flags). Do not call this from an ISR. A common mistake is failing to provide a stable clock source (e.g., missing crystal for LSE), which will cause the function to return false after the timeout period.
ca_rtc_hw_init.usage: This function is the mandatory first step for using the RTC peripheral. It is typically called once during the system boot sequence or hardware abstraction layer initialization. After a successful call, you can proceed to use other RTC functions like ca_rtc_set or ca_rtc_calibrate. It should be paired with the appropriate clock source selection based on your board's hardware design.

ca_rtc_hw_lse_on.brief: Enables or disables the Low-Speed External (LSE) crystal oscillator without modifying the RTC clock source configuration.

params.name: on
params.desc: Set to true to enable the LSE oscillator, false to disable it.

ca_rtc_hw_lse_on.returns: Returns true if the LSE oscillator is stable and ready (LSERDY bit set), false otherwise.
ca_rtc_hw_lse_on.notes: This function is non-blocking; it initiates the hardware request and immediately returns the current status of the LSE oscillator. It is thread-safe regarding the register access sequence but does not implement internal software delays, meaning the caller must poll the return value to verify if the crystal has started. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the hardware-specific power/backup domain registers are already accessible. A common mistake is assuming the LSE is ready immediately after calling this function with 'true'; you must implement a timeout loop to wait for the return value to become true.
ca_rtc_hw_lse_on.usage: This function is typically used during the RTC initialization sequence to prepare the clock source before the RTC peripheral is fully configured. It is usually paired with a polling loop that checks the return value against a system timer to ensure the crystal has stabilized within a reasonable timeframe. If the function fails to return true within the expected timeout, the application should abort the RTC initialization to prevent system hangs. It is often followed by a call to initialize the RTC peripheral itself if the LSE is confirmed ready.

ca_rtc_hw_set.brief: Updates the hardware Real-Time Clock (RTC) registers with the provided date and time structure.

params.name: dt
params.desc: Pointer to a structure containing the date and time values (hour, min, sec, year, month, day, wday). Must not be NULL.

ca_rtc_hw_set.returns: Returns true if the RTC registers were successfully updated, false if the input pointer is NULL or if the hardware failed to enter initialization mode.
ca_rtc_hw_set.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should be protected by a mutex if multiple tasks attempt to access the RTC simultaneously. It is a blocking operation because it waits for the hardware to enter and exit initialization mode, which can take several clock cycles. It must NOT be called from an ISR because it performs blocking operations and potentially locks/unlocks hardware resources. A common beginner mistake is passing an uninitialized or NULL structure, which will cause the function to return false or write garbage data to the RTC registers.
ca_rtc_hw_set.usage: This function is typically used during system startup to synchronize the RTC with an external time source (like an NTP server) or when the user manually updates the system time via a CLI. It is usually paired with ca_rtc_init to ensure the peripheral is ready before setting the time. In a typical sequence, you would call ca_rtc_init, then populate a ca_rtc_dt_t structure, and finally call ca_rtc_set to commit the values to the hardware.

ca_rtc_hw_set_alarm.signature: bool ca_rtc_hw_set_alarm(u8 alarm_id, const ca_rtc_alarm_t *alarm, ca_rtc_alarm_cb_t cb)
ca_rtc_hw_set_alarm.brief: Configures a hardware RTC alarm with a specific callback function to be executed when the alarm triggers.

params.name: alarm_id
params.desc: The alarm identifier, typically CA_RTC_ALARM_A or CA_RTC_ALARM_B. Must match the hardware capabilities of the specific STM32 series.

params.name: alarm
params.desc: Pointer to a structure containing the alarm time settings (hours, minutes, seconds, etc.). Must not be NULL.

params.name: cb
params.desc: The function pointer to be called when the alarm event occurs. Can be NULL if no callback is required.

ca_rtc_hw_set_alarm.returns: Returns true if the alarm was successfully configured, false if the hardware timed out waiting for the RTC registers to become writable or if input parameters were invalid.
ca_rtc_hw_set_alarm.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be protected by a mutex or critical section if multiple tasks access the RTC simultaneously. It performs blocking operations while waiting for the RTC hardware synchronization flags (e.g., ALRAWF/ALRBWF), meaning it should never be called from an ISR. Before calling this, ensure the RTC peripheral has been properly initialized via ca_rtc_init. A common beginner mistake is assuming the alarm will trigger immediately if the time is set in the past, or failing to check the return value, which leads to silent failures if the RTC hardware is busy or locked. Note that on some older hardware like F1xx, the alarm functionality is limited and may not support callbacks.
ca_rtc_hw_set_alarm.usage: This function is used to schedule periodic or one-shot events based on the real-time clock. It is typically paired with ca_rtc_init to set up the peripheral, followed by ca_rtc_set_alarm to define the trigger time. If the alarm is no longer needed, it should be disabled or cleared using ca_rtc_clear_alarm to prevent unwanted interrupts or callback executions. It is the standard way to implement wake-up events or scheduled tasks in the system.

ca_rtc_hw_set_prescaler.brief: Configures the RTC prescaler dividers to define the internal clock frequency for timekeeping.

params.name: div_a
params.desc: Asynchronous prescaler divider. Valid range: 1 to 128.

params.name: div_s
params.desc: Synchronous prescaler divider. Valid range: 1 to 32768.

ca_rtc_hw_set_prescaler.returns: Returns true if the prescalers were successfully updated, false if parameters are out of range or hardware initialization failed.
ca_rtc_hw_set_prescaler.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called when the RTC is in a state that allows configuration (typically during initialization). It is not callable from an ISR because it involves blocking operations and hardware register locking/unlocking sequences. A common mistake is providing values that result in an invalid clock frequency or exceeding the hardware's 20-bit register limit on older F1xx series, which will cause the function to return false immediately. Always ensure the RTC clock source is stable before calling this, as the hardware requires a specific sequence to enter 'init mode' to modify these registers.
ca_rtc_hw_set_prescaler.usage: This function is used during the early system boot phase or when recalibrating the RTC clock source (e.g., switching from LSE to LSI). It is typically paired with other RTC initialization functions to set up the time base before enabling alarms or reading the current time. In a typical sequence, you would call this to define the clock frequency, then proceed to set the initial date/time or start the RTC counter.

ca_rtc_init.brief: Initializes the Real-Time Clock (RTC) peripheral and configures its clock source.

params.name: src
params.desc: The clock source to drive the RTC. Use CA_RTC_CLK_AUTO to let the kernel decide based on boot configuration, or specify CA_RTC_CLK_LSE or CA_RTC_CLK_LSI.

ca_rtc_init.returns: Returns true if the RTC hardware was successfully initialized, false otherwise (e.g., hardware failure or clock source calibration error).
ca_rtc_init.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called during the system initialization phase, typically before the RTOS scheduler starts. It is not intended to be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR). If the CLI is enabled in the project configuration, this function registers the RTC command-line interface node. A common mistake is calling this function multiple times or after the RTC has already been used by other tasks, which may lead to unexpected hardware state resets or loss of time synchronization.
ca_rtc_init.usage: This function is used at the very beginning of the application, usually inside the main initialization sequence before starting any tasks. It is typically paired with other hardware initialization functions like ca_pwr_init. Once initialized, the RTC is used to set the system time or configure alarms using ca_rtc_set and ca_rtc_set_alarm. It is often called with CA_RTC_CLK_AUTO to ensure the system uses the most accurate available clock source (LSE if present, otherwise LSI).

ca_rtc_lse_start_ms.brief: Returns the time in milliseconds taken by the LSE (Low Speed External) crystal to start during system power-up.
ca_rtc_lse_start_ms.returns: Returns a non-negative integer (>= 0) representing the startup time in milliseconds if the LSE successfully started. Returns a negative value (< 0) if the LSE failed to start, was not used, or if the RTC is currently running on a different clock source (like LSI).
ca_rtc_lse_start_ms.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it simply returns a cached value calculated during the early boot phase. It is safe to call from an ISR, although it is typically used during system initialization or diagnostic reporting. The most common beginner mistake is assuming this function triggers the LSE startup; it does not. The LSE startup process is handled automatically by the system clock initialization sequence (ca_rtc_clock_init). If you call this before the RTC subsystem has finished its initialization, the returned value may not reflect the final status.
ca_rtc_lse_start_ms.usage: This function is primarily used for diagnostic purposes to verify hardware health and clock stability. It is typically called after ca_rtc_clock_init has been executed to check if the 32.768 kHz crystal is functioning correctly. Developers use it to decide whether to log a warning about slow crystal startup or to confirm that the system is running on the high-precision LSE clock rather than the less accurate internal LSI oscillator. It is often paired with ca_rtc_get_clk_src to determine the current RTC clock source before interpreting the startup time.

ca_rtc_lsi_hz.brief: Returns the current calibrated frequency of the LSI (Low Speed Internal) oscillator in Hertz.
ca_rtc_lsi_hz.returns: Returns a u32 value representing the frequency in Hz. Returns 0 if the LSI is not calibrated, if the RTC is not using the LSI clock source, or if the calibration process has not yet completed.
ca_rtc_lsi_hz.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it simply returns a cached value stored in a global variable. It is safe to call from an ISR. The value is only accurate if the system has performed a calibration routine (typically involving the SysTick or a stable reference clock) during the RTC initialization phase. If the RTC is configured to use LSE (External Crystal) or HSE, this function will return 0, as the LSI is not the active timebase. A common mistake is assuming this function triggers a new measurement; it does not, it only reports the last known calibrated value stored in the system state.
ca_rtc_lsi_hz.usage: This function is typically used in diagnostic routines or system status reports to verify the accuracy of the RTC when an external crystal (LSE) is unavailable. It is usually called after the RTC has been initialized via ca_rtc_init. Developers use it to decide whether to apply software compensation to timekeeping or to inform the user via CLI that the RTC is running on an uncalibrated, nominal LSI frequency. It is often paired with ca_rtc_get_clk_src to confirm the clock source before interpreting the frequency value.

ca_rtc_set.brief: Updates the internal Real-Time Clock (RTC) hardware with the provided date and time structure.

params.name: dt
params.desc: Pointer to a structure containing the date and time fields (year, month, day, hour, min, sec, wday). Must not be NULL.

ca_rtc_set.returns: Returns true if the RTC hardware was successfully updated, false if the input pointer is NULL or the hardware update failed.
ca_rtc_set.notes: This function is a wrapper that interacts directly with the RTC peripheral hardware. It is not inherently thread-safe if multiple tasks attempt to write to the RTC simultaneously, so ensure synchronization (e.g., using a mutex) if your application design allows concurrent access. It is generally non-blocking, but it relies on the underlying hardware driver being initialized via ca_rtc_init first. A common beginner mistake is passing an uninitialized or partially filled structure, which can lead to invalid time values being written to the hardware registers; always ensure all fields, especially the day of the week (wday), are set to valid ranges.
ca_rtc_set.usage: This function is typically used during system startup to set the initial time from a source like an NTP server or user input, or during runtime to adjust the clock. It is often paired with ca_rtc_init for setup and ca_rtc_get to verify the time after setting. In a typical sequence, you initialize the RTC, populate the ca_rtc_dt_t structure with current values, call ca_rtc_set, and then optionally configure alarms using ca_rtc_set_alarm to trigger periodic tasks.

ca_rtc_set_alarm.signature: bool ca_rtc_set_alarm(u8 alarm_id, const ca_rtc_alarm_t *alarm, ca_rtc_alarm_cb_t cb)
ca_rtc_set_alarm.brief: Configures a hardware RTC alarm to trigger a callback function at a specific time.

params.name: alarm_id
params.desc: The identifier of the alarm to set. Must be either CA_RTC_ALARM_A or CA_RTC_ALARM_B.

params.name: alarm
params.desc: Pointer to a structure containing the target time and match flags. Must not be NULL.

params.name: cb
params.desc: The function pointer to execute when the alarm triggers. Can be NULL if no callback is needed.

ca_rtc_set_alarm.returns: Returns true if the alarm was successfully configured, false if the alarm_id is invalid, the alarm pointer is NULL, or the hardware failed to set the alarm.
ca_rtc_set_alarm.notes: This function is a non-blocking wrapper that interacts with the STM32 RTC hardware registers. It is thread-safe in the sense that it uses underlying hardware locks, but it should be called after the RTC has been initialized via ca_rtc_init. A common mistake is failing to set the match flags (e.g., match_sec, match_min) correctly in the ca_rtc_alarm_t structure, which results in the alarm never triggering or triggering at the wrong time. Note that the callback function is executed in an interrupt context (ISR), so it must be kept extremely short and should not perform blocking operations like waiting for semaphores or performing heavy calculations.
ca_rtc_set_alarm.usage: This function is typically used to schedule wake-up events or periodic tasks based on the real-time clock. It is often paired with ca_rtc_init to prepare the hardware, and ca_rtc_clear_alarm to disable the alarm once it has served its purpose. In power-sensitive applications, it is frequently used before calling ca_pwr_enter to ensure the system wakes up from a low-power state at a specific time. Always ensure the RTC clock source is stable before setting alarms to avoid unexpected behavior.

ca_rtc_to_net.brief: Reads the hardware RTC and returns it as a standard Unix timestamp (seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC), the inverse of ca_rtc_from_net.
ca_rtc_to_net.returns: Unix seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC (the RTC's 2000-based calendar plus RTC_UNIX_2000 = 946684800), so a value of at least 946684800. Returns 0U if the RTC cannot be read or holds an invalid date (month outside 1-12, day 0, year past 2099).
ca_rtc_to_net.notes: The RTC calendar covers 2000-2099 and is taken as UTC: the result is a real Unix time, directly comparable with the value an NTP client hands to ca_rtc_from_net, with no offset to add. The weekday stored in the RTC is ignored; the date alone decides. It calls ca_rtc_get, which waits for the RTC shadow registers to synchronise, so call it from a task, not from an ISR. Concurrent calls only read the RTC and do not interfere. A 0U return means 'no valid time', never a date: test for it before using the value. On the bench: the CLI command 'rtc unix' prints this value with the calendar it came from.
ca_rtc_to_net.usage: This function is typically used when you need to timestamp log entries, network packets, or security events. It is often paired with ca_rtc_get to validate the hardware state before conversion. In a typical workflow, you would call ca_rtc_get to ensure the clock is running, then call ca_rtc_to_net to get a numeric value for easy comparison or transmission over a network protocol like NTP or MQTT.

ca_rwlock_init.brief: Initializes a Read-Write lock structure to manage concurrent access to shared resources.

params.name: rw
params.desc: Pointer to the rwlock object to be initialized. Must point to valid, allocated memory.

ca_rwlock_init.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called before any other ca_rwlock_* function is used. It resets the internal reader count, clears the writer status, and initializes the internal wait queues and spinlock. It is strictly intended for initialization and must NOT be called while other tasks are attempting to acquire or release the lock, as this would corrupt the internal state. This function is not designed to be called from an ISR; it should be called during system startup or task initialization.
ca_rwlock_init.usage: Use this function when you have a shared resource (like a configuration table or a data buffer) that is read frequently by many tasks but written to only occasionally. It is typically paired with ca_rwlock_read_lock/unlock and ca_rwlock_write_lock/unlock to enforce data integrity. In a typical lifecycle, you declare the lock variable, call ca_rwlock_init once, and then pass the pointer to the various tasks that need to synchronize access to the protected resource.

ca_rwlock_owner_died.brief: Checks if the owner of a read-write lock died while holding it, indicating a potential resource inconsistency.

params.name: rw
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized read-write lock object. Must not be NULL.

ca_rwlock_owner_died.returns: Returns true (non-zero) if the previous owner of the lock died while holding it, otherwise returns false (zero).
ca_rwlock_owner_died.notes: This function is used for error recovery in systems where tasks might crash while holding synchronization primitives. It is thread-safe and non-blocking, as it simply reads a status flag maintained by the lock's internal state. It is safe to call from an ISR, though typically used in task context to decide if a resource needs to be reset or re-initialized. A common beginner mistake is to ignore the return value; if this returns true, the system state associated with the lock may be corrupted, and the application should perform a cleanup or re-initialization before attempting to use the lock again.
ca_rwlock_owner_died.usage: This function is typically used in a recovery loop or a diagnostic task. When a task detects that a critical resource is locked but the owner is no longer active, it calls this function to confirm the 'owner died' state. It is often paired with other recovery functions to reset the lock or the protected resource. In a typical sequence, you would: 1) Detect a timeout or error on a lock, 2) Call this function to verify if the owner died, 3) If true, perform necessary cleanup, and 4) Re-initialize or release the lock to restore system operation.

ca_rwlock_owner_gone.brief: Cleans up and releases all Read/Write locks held by a task that is terminating or crashing.

params.name: ctx
params.desc: Pointer to the thread context of the task being terminated. Must be a valid pointer; NULL is ignored.

ca_rwlock_owner_gone.notes: This function is designed for internal OS use during task cleanup. It iterates through all RW locks currently held by the task and releases them to prevent system deadlocks. It is not thread-safe if called manually outside the scheduler's cleanup sequence, as it relies on internal task state. It is not callable from an ISR. The most common mistake is attempting to call this manually for a task that is still running; this will corrupt the lock state and likely cause a system crash.
ca_rwlock_owner_gone.usage: This function is used by the OS scheduler when a task is being destroyed or has encountered a fatal error. It ensures that if a task was holding a read lock or a write lock, those locks are released so other tasks waiting on them can proceed. It is typically paired with ca_mutex_owner_gone to ensure all synchronization primitives are cleaned up when a thread context is freed.

ca_rwlock_read_lock.brief: Acquires a read lock on a read-write lock, allowing multiple readers but blocking writers.

params.name: rw
params.desc: Pointer to the read-write lock structure. Must not be NULL. Invalid if the lock is not initialized or has been corrupted.

ca_rwlock_read_lock.returns: This function does not return a value. It blocks until the read lock is acquired or an error occurs.
ca_rwlock_read_lock.notes: This function is blocking: it will wait indefinitely if a writer holds the lock or if a writer is waiting. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR. It is not thread-safe if the same lock is accessed by multiple threads without proper synchronization. The function assumes the lock is properly initialized before use. Common mistake: calling this function without initializing the rwlock structure first.
ca_rwlock_read_lock.usage: Used in scenarios where multiple threads need to read shared data concurrently, such as reading configuration data or lookup tables. It pairs with ca_rwlock_read_unlock() to release the lock. Typically used in long-running tasks that read data without modifying it.

ca_rwlock_read_unlock.brief: Releases a read lock on a read-write lock, allowing other readers or writers to proceed.

params.name: rw
params.desc: Pointer to the read-write lock structure. Must not be NULL. Passing NULL will cause a crash.

returns.desc: Function does not return a value. It only modifies internal state.

notes.desc: This function is NOT blocking. It immediately decrements the reader count and may wake up a writer if this was the last reader.
Function is thread-safe. It uses a spinlock internally to protect access to shared data.
Not callable from interrupt service routines (ISR). It uses spinlocks that may not be safe in ISR context.
The calling thread must have previously acquired a read lock using ca_rwlock_read_lock(). Otherwise, behavior is undefined.

Calling this function without first acquiring a read lock leads to incorrect reader count and potential deadlock or undefined behavior. Also, calling it more times than locking leads to negative reader counts.

usage.context: Reading shared data in a multi-threaded environment
usage.description: Used after completing a read operation on shared data protected by a read-write lock. Ensures other readers can proceed and potentially allows writers to acquire the lock if no readers remain.
Used in performance-sensitive code where read operations are frequent and write operations are rare. Helps avoid unnecessary blocking of writers.

example.comments: This example shows a typical read operation on a shared configuration structure. The lock is acquired before reading and released after, allowing other readers to proceed.
In this example, a task reads from a shared memory region protected by a read-write lock. After completing the read, it releases the lock so other readers or writers can proceed.

ca_rwlock_write_lock.brief: Acquires exclusive write access to a read-write lock, blocking if another writer or readers hold the lock.

params.name: rw
params.desc: Pointer to the read-write lock structure. Must not be NULL. Invalid if the lock is not initialized or has been corrupted.

returns.desc: Function does not return a value. It blocks until write access is granted.

notes.desc: This function blocks the calling thread until it can acquire exclusive write access. It will not return until no other threads are reading or writing.
Yes, but only when used correctly with proper initialization and matching unlock calls.
No. This function is not safe to call from an interrupt service routine (ISR). It may block and is not designed for interrupt context.
The rw lock must be initialized before calling this function. The scheduler must be running (not in idle context).
Calling this function without a matching ca_rwlock_write_unlock() leads to deadlock. Using it in an ISR causes undefined behavior.

usage.description: Used when a thread needs to modify shared data that other threads may be reading or writing. Ensures no readers or writers are active before granting access.
Used to update configuration tables or structures that are accessed by multiple threads. Guarantees atomicity of the update.
Used in tasks that perform write operations to shared memory regions, ensuring exclusive access during the write cycle.

example.comment: This example shows how to use ca_rwlock_write_lock() to safely update a configuration table. The lock ensures that no readers or other writers can access the data during the update.

ca_rwlock_write_unlock.brief: Releases a write lock on a read-write lock, allowing other readers or writers to proceed.

params.name: rw
params.desc: Pointer to the read-write lock structure. Must not be NULL. Passing NULL will cause a crash.

returns.desc: Function does not return a value. It simply releases the lock.

notes.desc: This function is NOT blocking. It immediately releases the lock and may wake up waiting threads.
Function is thread-safe as long as the rw pointer is valid and no other thread is modifying the same lock concurrently.
Not callable from interrupt service routines (ISR). It uses spinlocks that are not safe in ISR context.
The calling thread must already hold the write lock. If not, behavior is undefined and may lead to deadlock or corruption.
Calling this function without holding the write lock, or calling it multiple times without matching locks, leads to undefined behavior.

usage.context: After completing a write operation on shared data
usage.description: Used to release a write lock acquired earlier using ca_rwlock_write_lock(). Typically used in a critical section where data is being modified.

usage.context: In multi-threaded applications with shared resources
usage.description: Paired with ca_rwlock_write_lock() to protect write access to shared data structures, ensuring exclusive access during writes.

code: ca_rwlock_write_lock(&rw_cfg);  // Acquire write lock before modifying config
ca_rwlock_write_unlock(&rw_cfg);  // Release write lock after modification
ca_stdout_printf_n("CFG update v%u (reads so far: %u)", seq, reads_ok);
example.comment: Example shows a typical use case where a configuration is updated with a write lock, then unlocked after modification.

code: ca_rwlock_write_lock(&s_rw);  // Acquire write lock before modifying data
if ((i & 3U) == 3U) ca_os_yield();  // Optional yield for fairness
ca_rwlock_write_unlock(&s_rw);  // Release write lock after modification
example.comment: Another example where a data array is modified under a write lock, then unlocked.

ca_safeguard_failed.signature: void ca_safeguard_failed(const char *cond_str, const char *msg, const char *file, u32 line)
ca_safeguard_failed.brief: Triggers a system-wide fatal error handler to safely halt execution when an invariant or critical condition is violated.

params.name: cond_str
params.desc: A string literal describing the condition that failed (e.g., "ptr != NULL").

params.name: msg
params.desc: Optional additional context or error message; can be NULL.

params.name: file
params.desc: The source filename where the failure occurred, usually passed via the __FILE__ macro.

params.name: line
params.desc: The line number where the failure occurred, usually passed via the __LINE__ macro.

ca_safeguard_failed.returns: This function never returns. It either triggers an SVC exception to perform a controlled system shutdown or enters an infinite loop (HALT) if the OS is not running or if called from an ISR.
ca_safeguard_failed.notes: This function is the ultimate 'panic' mechanism. It is not thread-safe in the sense that it stops the entire system, but it is designed to be called from any context. If called from an ISR or before the scheduler starts, it disables interrupts and enters an infinite loop to prevent further system corruption. The most common beginner mistake is using this for recoverable errors; only use this for unrecoverable state corruption where continuing execution would be dangerous. It is mandatory that the system is in a state where it can at least attempt to log the error before halting.
ca_safeguard_failed.usage: Use this function to enforce critical system invariants that, if broken, would lead to undefined behavior or hardware damage. It is typically wrapped in a macro (e.g., #define ASSERT(cond) if(!(cond)) ca_safeguard_failed(#cond, NULL, __FILE__, __LINE__)) to automatically capture the file and line information. It is used during development to catch logic errors early and in production to ensure the system enters a safe state rather than operating with corrupted data.

ca_safeguard_reset.brief: Clears the internal safeguard recursion flag to allow future fault handling.
ca_safeguard_reset.returns: This function returns void and has no return value.
ca_safeguard_reset.notes: This function is used to reset a global flag that prevents the system from entering a recursive loop if a fault occurs while already processing another fault. It is not thread-safe in the sense that it modifies a global variable, but it is intended to be called by the scheduler during task recovery. If you fail to call this after a task has been safely restarted or cleaned up, the system will permanently block any future safeguard triggers, effectively disabling the OS's ability to handle subsequent crashes. It is not intended to be called from an ISR, as it is a management function for the scheduler's internal state.
ca_safeguard_reset.usage: This function is strictly used within the OS kernel's fault management logic. You will typically see it called inside the scheduler's fault handling routine, specifically after a task has been successfully reset or removed following a crash. It acts as a 'gatekeeper' reset; by clearing the flag, you signal to the OS that the previous error state has been resolved and the system is ready to monitor for new faults again. It is usually paired with logic that performs task cleanup or stack restoration.

ca_sai_errors.brief: Retrieves the current accumulated error status of the SAI (Serial Audio Interface) peripheral.
ca_sai_errors.returns: A 32-bit unsigned integer representing a bitmask of error flags (CA_SAI_ERR_*). A return value of 0 indicates no errors have been detected.
ca_sai_errors.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it simply reads an internal status variable. It is safe to call from both tasks and ISRs. The function internally triggers a hardware error check if the SAI interface is active (s_sai_fs != 0), meaning it performs a read-modify-write operation on the error register. A common mistake is to ignore the return value or fail to mask out expected transient errors (like underruns during stream stops) when evaluating system health.
ca_sai_errors.usage: This function is typically used in the main monitoring loop or a diagnostic task to verify the health of the audio stream. It is often paired with ca_sai_stream_start to begin operations and ca_sai_stop to end them. Developers use it to decide whether to restart the audio peripheral or report a system failure to the user via CLI or logs. It is frequently combined with bitwise operations to ignore specific, non-critical errors like underruns (CA_SAI_ERR_UDR) that occur naturally during stream termination.

ca_sai_fs.brief: Returns the actual configured sample rate of the SAI (Serial Audio Interface) peripheral.
ca_sai_fs.returns: Returns a u32 representing the sample rate in Hz. Returns 0 if the SAI peripheral has not been initialized or is currently in an error state.
ca_sai_fs.notes: This function is a non-blocking getter that provides the current hardware state. It is thread-safe as it simply reads a static variable updated during the initialization phase. It is safe to call from an ISR, although it is typically used in CLI or monitoring tasks to verify hardware configuration. A common beginner mistake is to assume the returned value is always the requested frequency; always check for 0 to ensure the hardware initialization was successful before attempting to process audio data.
ca_sai_fs.usage: This function is used to verify the operational status of the audio hardware. It is typically called after the system initialization sequence (where ca_sai_init would have been invoked) to confirm that the SAI peripheral is running at the expected frequency. It is often paired with ca_sai_errors to provide a complete diagnostic report in a CLI interface or system health monitor.

ca_sai_hw_dma_bind.brief: Retrieves the hardware-specific DMA stream and request mapping for the SAI peripheral.

params.name: tx_flat
params.desc: Pointer to store the TX DMA stream/channel index. Set to -1 if any channel is acceptable.

params.name: tx_req
params.desc: Pointer to store the TX DMA request mapping ID.

params.name: rx_flat
params.desc: Pointer to store the RX DMA stream/channel index. Set to -1 if any channel is acceptable.

params.name: rx_req
params.desc: Pointer to store the RX DMA request mapping ID.

ca_sai_hw_dma_bind.returns: Returns true if the hardware supports DMA for SAI and the mapping was successfully populated. Returns false if DMA is not supported on the current hardware or if the configuration is unavailable.
ca_sai_hw_dma_bind.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it only performs memory writes based on static hardware definitions. It is safe to call from an ISR, though it is typically used during peripheral initialization. The most common mistake is failing to check the return value; if it returns false, the subsequent DMA channel allocation functions will fail, potentially leaving the system in an inconsistent state. Always ensure the pointers passed are valid memory addresses to avoid hard faults.
ca_sai_hw_dma_bind.usage: This function is used during the SAI driver initialization sequence to determine which DMA resources are physically wired to the SAI peripheral. It is typically called before ca_dma_free_channel or ca_dma_free_channel_index to reserve the specific hardware streams required for audio data transfer. By abstracting the hardware-specific DMA mapping, it allows the higher-level SAI driver to remain portable across different STM32 families.

ca_sai_hw_dma_count_div.brief: Returns the divisor factor required to normalize DMA remaining count to word units based on the hardware architecture.
ca_sai_hw_dma_count_div.returns: Returns 4 for GPDMA-based systems (H5/U5) where DMA counts bytes, and 1 for older architectures (F1/F4/F7) where DMA counts data elements (words).
ca_sai_hw_dma_count_div.notes: This function is a hardware abstraction layer (HAL) helper. It is non-blocking, thread-safe, and safe to call from an ISR. It is mandatory to use this when calculating stream positions or buffer offsets in DMA-based SAI transfers to ensure the logic remains portable across different STM32 families. The most common mistake is hardcoding a division by 4 or 1, which will cause buffer pointer arithmetic errors when porting code between different STM32 series.
ca_sai_hw_dma_count_div.usage: This function is used exclusively within the SAI driver's streaming logic. It is typically paired with ca_dma_get_remaining() to convert the raw DMA counter into a meaningful number of audio words. By dividing the raw DMA count by the result of this function, the application can accurately track how many samples have been processed, allowing for correct synchronization between the audio buffer and the DMA hardware.

ca_sai_hw_dr.brief: Returns the memory address of the SAI hardware data register for the specified direction.

params.name: rx
params.desc: If true, returns the address of the receiver (Block B) data register. If false, returns the address of the transmitter (Block A) data register.

ca_sai_hw_dr.returns: A volatile pointer to the hardware data register (DR) on supported platforms, or NULL if the hardware abstraction layer does not support direct register access for the current target.
ca_sai_hw_dr.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it simply returns a constant memory address mapped to the peripheral. It is safe to call from an ISR. The primary risk is passing this address to a DMA controller on a platform where the SAI peripheral is not supported (returning NULL), which would cause a null pointer dereference or invalid DMA configuration. Always ensure the SAI peripheral is initialized before attempting to use its data register address.
ca_sai_hw_dr.usage: This function is used to provide the destination or source address to DMA transfer functions, such as ca_dma_copy_target. It is typically used in the sequence: stop the SAI peripheral, clear any pending errors, obtain the data register address, and then configure the DMA channel to stream data directly to or from that register. It is essential for high-speed audio processing where CPU-based data copying would be too slow.

ca_sai_hw_errors.brief: Retrieves and clears hardware-level Serial Audio Interface (SAI) error flags.
ca_sai_hw_errors.returns: A bitmask of error flags (u32). Returns 0 if no errors occurred. Specific flags include CA_SAI_ERR_UDR (underrun), CA_SAI_ERR_OVR (overrun), CA_SAI_ERR_AFS (audio frame synchronization error), and CA_SAI_ERR_LFS (late frame synchronization error).
ca_sai_hw_errors.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs direct register access to the SAI hardware. It is thread-safe in the sense that it reads and clears hardware registers atomically, but it should be called periodically to ensure errors are captured before they are overwritten by subsequent events. A common mistake is to ignore the return value; since the function clears the hardware error flags upon reading, calling it without storing the result means the error information is lost forever. It is safe to call from an ISR, but typically it is called from a background task or a monitoring thread.
ca_sai_hw_errors.usage: This function is used to monitor the health of the SAI peripheral during audio streaming. It is typically paired with ca_sai_xfer or other data transfer functions. The standard workflow involves calling this function periodically (e.g., inside a system tick or a dedicated monitoring task) to check if the hardware has encountered synchronization or buffer issues. If a non-zero value is returned, the application should log the error or trigger a recovery sequence, such as resetting the SAI peripheral.

ca_sai_hw_get.brief: Reads a single 32-bit data word from the SAI Block B hardware FIFO.

params.name: w
params.desc: Pointer to a 32-bit variable where the retrieved data word will be stored. Must be a valid memory address.

ca_sai_hw_get.returns: Returns true if a word was successfully read from the FIFO, or false if the FIFO was empty.
ca_sai_hw_get.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a direct hardware register read. It is thread-safe in the sense that it accesses hardware registers, but it does not implement software-level locking; if multiple tasks access the SAI hardware simultaneously, you must protect this call with a mutex or scheduler lock. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the SAI hardware is already initialized and active. A common beginner mistake is ignoring the return value; if you call this when the FIFO is empty, the pointer 'w' will not be updated, and your application logic may process stale or uninitialized data.
ca_sai_hw_get.usage: This function is typically used in a polling loop to drain the SAI receive FIFO during manual (non-DMA) data transfers. It is usually paired with 'ca_sai_hw_put' to handle full-duplex communication. The standard sequence is: initialize the SAI peripheral, enter a loop that checks for data availability using this function, process the received word, and finally call 'ca_sai_hw_stop' once the transfer is complete to flush the hardware buffers.

ca_sai_hw_init.signature: u32 ca_sai_hw_init(u32 fs_hz, u32 bits, ca_sai_proto_t proto)
ca_sai_hw_init.brief: Initializes the Serial Audio Interface (SAI) hardware peripheral for digital audio streaming.

params.name: fs_hz
params.desc: Target sampling frequency in Hertz (e.g., 44100, 48000). Use 0 to disable the SAI peripheral.

params.name: bits
params.desc: Data word length in bits. Valid values are 16, 24, or 32.

params.name: proto
params.desc: Audio protocol type (e.g., CA_SAI_MSB, CA_SAI_SPDIF). Determines clocking and data alignment.

ca_sai_hw_init.returns: Returns the actual achieved sampling frequency in Hz as a u32. Returns 0 if the initialization failed (e.g., unsupported clock configuration or invalid parameters).
ca_sai_hw_init.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called during system initialization or when the audio stream is stopped. It is not callable from an ISR because it performs complex clock calculations and hardware register configuration. The function handles clock tree setup, GPIO pin configuration, and block synchronization (Master TX/Slave RX). A common mistake is calling this function while an active DMA transfer is running, which will cause hardware instability or corrupted audio; always ensure the SAI is stopped first.
ca_sai_hw_init.usage: This function is the primary entry point for configuring the SAI hardware. It is typically used in a sequence: first, call ca_sai_stop() to ensure the hardware is idle, then call ca_sai_hw_init() to apply new settings, and finally use ca_sai_stream_start() to begin data transmission. It is often paired with ca_sai_xfer() or ca_sai_xfer_dma() for actual data movement.

ca_sai_hw_put.brief: Writes a single 32-bit data word into the SAI hardware transmit FIFO.

params.name: w
params.desc: The 32-bit data word to be transmitted. The value is placed directly into the SAI Data Register (DR).

ca_sai_hw_put.returns: Returns true if the word was successfully written to the FIFO. Returns false if the FIFO is full, indicating the hardware cannot accept more data at this moment.
ca_sai_hw_put.notes: This function is non-blocking; it checks the hardware status register and returns immediately. It is thread-safe in the sense that it interacts with hardware registers, but it does not implement software locking, so concurrent access from multiple tasks to the same SAI block must be managed by the caller. It is safe to call from an ISR if the hardware is already initialized. The most common beginner mistake is ignoring the return value: if you call this in a loop without checking for 'false', you will lose data because the FIFO will overflow silently.
ca_sai_hw_put.usage: This function is used to manually feed the SAI peripheral when not using DMA. It is typically used in a loop to pre-fill the FIFO before calling ca_sai_hw_start, and then periodically called within a processing loop to keep the FIFO fed while data is being consumed. It is often paired with ca_sai_hw_start to initiate the transmission and ca_sai_hw_stop to halt the peripheral.

ca_sai_hw_start.brief: Activates the SAI hardware blocks to begin audio data transmission and reception.

params.name: dma
params.desc: If true, enables DMA mode for data transfer; if false, manual polling (CPU-driven) is used.

ca_sai_hw_start.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called only after the SAI hardware has been fully configured via the initialization sequence. It performs a critical hardware operation: it flushes the RX FIFO and enables the SAI blocks in a specific order (Slave B then Master A) to ensure synchronization. It is not intended to be called from an ISR, as it performs register-level hardware orchestration that expects a stable system state. A common mistake is calling this before the TX FIFO has been pre-filled with initial data, which can lead to underrun errors or silent failure to start the audio stream.
ca_sai_hw_start.usage: This function is the final step in the SAI startup sequence. Typically, you first initialize the SAI hardware, then pre-fill the TX FIFO with initial audio samples to prevent immediate underrun, and finally call this function to trigger the hardware clock and data flow. It is usually paired with a loop that monitors the FIFO status or uses DMA interrupts to keep the buffers fed while the audio stream is active.

ca_sai_hw_stop.brief: Stops the SAI hardware blocks and flushes their internal FIFOs.
ca_sai_hw_stop.notes: This function is non-blocking in the sense that it does not wait indefinitely; it uses a spin-loop (SAI_STOP_SPIN) to wait for the hardware to finish the current audio frame before disabling the blocks. It is not thread-safe, meaning you must ensure no other task or interrupt is attempting to configure the SAI registers simultaneously. It is generally safe to call from an ISR, but be aware that the spin-loop consumes CPU cycles, which could delay other high-priority tasks. The most common beginner mistake is calling this function while a DMA transfer is still active without first ensuring the DMA channel is properly stopped or aborted, which can lead to unpredictable hardware states.
ca_sai_hw_stop.usage: This function is used to cleanly shut down the Serial Audio Interface (SAI) peripheral, typically before reconfiguring the audio parameters or when stopping audio playback. It is usually paired with ca_sai_hw_init for setup and ca_sai_hw_start to begin the data flow. In a typical sequence, you call ca_sai_hw_stop to ensure the hardware is in a known idle state, clear any pending error flags using ca_sai_errors, and then proceed to fill the FIFOs or re-initialize the peripheral for the next audio session.

ca_sai_init.brief: Initializes the SAI (Serial Audio Interface) hardware peripheral with the specified sample rate, bit depth, and protocol.

params.name: cfg
params.desc: Pointer to a configuration structure containing fs_hz (4000-192000), bits (16, 24, or 32), and proto (CA_SAI_MSB or similar). Must not be NULL.

ca_sai_init.returns: Returns the actual configured sample rate in Hz as a u32. Returns 0 if the configuration is invalid, out of range, or if the hardware failed to initialize.
ca_sai_init.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should be called during the system initialization phase before starting audio processing tasks. It is a blocking call because it interacts directly with hardware registers to set up clocks and pins. Do not call this from an ISR. A common mistake is passing a NULL pointer or an unsupported sample rate, which will cause the function to return 0 immediately without configuring the hardware.
ca_sai_init.usage: This function is the entry point for audio hardware setup. It is typically used in a sequence: first, define the configuration structure, then call ca_sai_init to apply settings, and finally use ca_sai_stream_start to begin data transfer. If the return value is 0, the application should halt or enter an error state, as audio processing cannot proceed without a valid hardware clock.

ca_sai_stop.brief: Stops the Serial Audio Interface (SAI) hardware and associated DMA transfers.
ca_sai_stop.notes: This function is a wrapper that safely halts the SAI peripheral and, if enabled, the DMA controller. It is not thread-safe and should not be called from an ISR, as it performs hardware-level operations that may involve blocking or synchronization. A common mistake is calling this function while the SAI is still actively processing data without waiting for the current buffer to finish, which can lead to incomplete data frames or hardware state inconsistencies. Ensure that any higher-level application logic has finished processing or flushing the audio buffers before invoking this stop command.
ca_sai_stop.usage: This function is typically used at the end of an audio processing task or when a measurement cycle is complete. It is usually paired with 'ca_sai_init' for setup and 'ca_sai_stream_start' for beginning the audio flow. In a typical sequence, you would stop the stream, perform final data calculations or checks, and then call 'ca_sai_stop' to put the hardware into a low-power or idle state to prevent unnecessary resource consumption.

ca_sai_stream_pos.brief: Returns the current read position (index) of the active SAI DMA stream.
ca_sai_stream_pos.returns: Returns a u32 representing the current word index (0 to words-1) being processed by the DMA. Returns 0 if the stream is not active or if the DMA has not yet started processing.
ca_sai_stream_pos.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it performs a simple calculation based on the current DMA register state. It is safe to call from an ISR, as it does not perform any complex synchronization or blocking operations. The function relies on the internal state set by a previous call to ca_sai_stream_start (not listed in the catalog, but implied by the implementation). A common mistake is calling this function before initializing the SAI stream, which will result in a return value of 0, potentially leading to logic errors if the application assumes the stream is active.
ca_sai_stream_pos.usage: This function is typically used in real-time audio or signal processing applications to monitor the progress of a circular DMA buffer. It is used to determine how much data has been processed or to synchronize application logic with the hardware's current position in the buffer. It is usually called periodically within a task loop or after a delay to check if the DMA has advanced, often paired with ca_os_sleep or ca_os_delay to pace the monitoring frequency.

ca_sai_stream_start.signature: bool ca_sai_stream_start(const i32 *tx, i32 *rx, u32 words)
ca_sai_stream_start.brief: Starts a continuous, circular full-duplex SAI (Serial Audio Interface) data stream using DMA.

params.name: tx
params.desc: Pointer to the memory buffer containing audio data to be transmitted. Must be valid and aligned for DMA access.

params.name: rx
params.desc: Pointer to the memory buffer where received audio data will be stored. Must be valid and aligned for DMA access.

params.name: words
params.desc: The number of 32-bit words per circular buffer cycle. Must be greater than 0.

ca_sai_stream_start.returns: Returns true if the DMA channels were successfully bound and the SAI hardware started streaming. Returns false if the SAI is not initialized, buffers are NULL, the count is zero, the system is already streaming, or DMA binding fails.
ca_sai_stream_start.notes: This function is non-blocking; it configures the DMA and SAI hardware to run in the background. It is not thread-safe and should not be called from an ISR. Before calling this, the SAI peripheral must be initialized via ca_sai_init. A common mistake is passing buffers that are not properly aligned or are located in memory regions inaccessible to the DMA controller. If the function returns false, the streaming state remains unchanged, and no hardware resources are locked.
ca_sai_stream_start.usage: This function is used to initiate high-speed, continuous audio data exchange. It is typically paired with ca_sai_stream_pos to monitor the current buffer index during processing. The typical lifecycle is: initialize the SAI peripheral, allocate buffers, call ca_sai_stream_start, perform processing in a loop while checking the stream position, and eventually stop the stream using ca_sai_hw_stop.

ca_sai_xfer.signature: u32 ca_sai_xfer(const i32 *tx, i32 *rx, u32 words, u32 timeout_ms)
ca_sai_xfer.brief: Performs a synchronous, polled full-duplex SAI (Serial Audio Interface) data transfer.

params.name: tx
params.desc: Pointer to the buffer containing data to transmit. Must not be NULL.

params.name: rx
params.desc: Pointer to the buffer where received data will be stored. Must not be NULL.

params.name: words
params.desc: Number of 32-bit words to exchange. Must be greater than 0.

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time in milliseconds to wait for the transfer to complete.

ca_sai_xfer.returns: Returns the number of words successfully received. Returns 0 if the SAI is not initialized, if pointers are NULL, or if the transfer fails/times out.
ca_sai_xfer.notes: This function is blocking, meaning the calling task will wait inside the function until the transfer completes or the timeout expires. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR because it relies on polling the hardware status and system ticks. Before calling this, ensure the SAI peripheral has been successfully initialized via ca_sai_init. A common mistake is providing a buffer that is too small for the requested number of words, which will lead to memory corruption. Always verify the return value matches the requested 'words' count to ensure the transfer was successful.
ca_sai_xfer.usage: This function is used for synchronous audio data exchange where the application needs to wait for the hardware to finish processing before proceeding. It is typically used in a sequence: first, initialize the SAI peripheral with ca_sai_init, then prepare the transmit data, call ca_sai_xfer to perform the exchange, and finally check the results. It is often paired with ca_os_tick_64_ms to manage timing or ca_sai_errors to diagnose hardware issues if the transfer count is lower than expected.

ca_sai_xfer_dma.signature: bool ca_sai_xfer_dma(const i32 *tx, i32 *rx, u32 words, u32 timeout_ms)
ca_sai_xfer_dma.brief: Performs a simultaneous full-duplex audio data transfer using DMA for both SAI transmit and receive channels.

params.name: tx
params.desc: Pointer to the buffer containing audio data to be transmitted. Must not be NULL.

params.name: rx
params.desc: Pointer to the buffer where received audio data will be stored. Must not be NULL.

params.name: words
params.desc: Number of 32-bit audio samples to transfer. Must be greater than 0.

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time in milliseconds to wait for the DMA transfer to complete.

ca_sai_xfer_dma.returns: Returns true if the transfer completed successfully within the timeout, false otherwise. Returns false if parameters are invalid, if the SAI is currently streaming, or if DMA binding/transfer fails.
ca_sai_xfer_dma.notes: This function is blocking; it will suspend the calling task until the DMA transfer finishes or the timeout expires. It is not safe to call from an ISR because it relies on blocking wait mechanisms. Before calling this, ensure the SAI hardware is properly initialized. A common mistake is passing a buffer that is too small for the requested number of words, which will lead to memory corruption. Always check the return value; if it returns false, the transfer did not complete, and the hardware state may need to be reset.
ca_sai_xfer_dma.usage: This function is used for high-performance, full-duplex audio streaming where CPU intervention per sample is undesirable. It is typically used in a loop or a dedicated audio processing task. The sequence is: initialize the SAI and DMA subsystems, allocate buffers, call this function to perform the transfer, and process the received data. It is often paired with ca_sai_init for setup and ca_memory_allocate for buffer management.

ca_scheduler_check_all_canaries.brief: Checks all task stacks for corruption using canary values in an MPU-enabled system.
ca_scheduler_check_all_canaries.returns: This function does not return a value (void). However, it prints diagnostic messages to stdout indicating whether each task's stack is OK or corrupted.
ca_scheduler_check_all_canaries.notes: This function is NOT blocking; it iterates through the task list and prints results immediately. It is NOT thread-safe because it iterates over global task structures; if tasks are created or destroyed during execution, it could lead to inconsistent data or crashes. It must NOT be called from an ISR because it performs I/O operations (ca_stdout_printf_n) which are not re-entrant or safe in interrupt context. It requires the MPU (Memory Protection Unit) to be enabled (__MPU_PRESENT must be defined). A common beginner mistake is assuming this function fixes corruption; it is purely diagnostic and only reports the state of the stack canaries at the moment of execution.
ca_scheduler_check_all_canaries.usage: This function is used during system debugging to identify stack overflows or memory corruption issues. It is typically triggered via a CLI command (e.g., 'canary') to inspect the health of all running tasks. It is often used in conjunction with ca_mpu_dump_regions to verify if memory protection is correctly configured and with ca_memory_get_task_usage to correlate stack usage with potential corruption. It is intended for post-mortem analysis or periodic health checks during development.

ca_scheduler_dump_all_tasks.brief: Prints a formatted list of all registered tasks and their current status to the system output.

params.name: mode
params.desc: Bitmask defining the level of detail. Use specific flags to show CPU registers, stack usage, or task integrity. A value of 0 typically provides a summary, while higher values increase verbosity.

ca_scheduler_dump_all_tasks.notes: This function is intended for debugging and system monitoring. It is not thread-safe and should not be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it performs multiple blocking I/O operations via ca_stdout_printf_n. The function iterates through the internal task list; if the scheduler is in an inconsistent state or if memory corruption has occurred, this function may trigger a hard fault. Always ensure the system is initialized before calling this. A common beginner mistake is calling this function while the scheduler is under heavy load, which can cause significant jitter or output buffer overflows.
ca_scheduler_dump_all_tasks.usage: This function is typically used within a Command Line Interface (CLI) or a diagnostic task to inspect system health. It is often paired with ca_scheduler_update_all_stack_usage to ensure the stack usage data is current before printing. Developers use this to verify that all tasks are running as expected, check for stack overflows, or identify which task is currently active during a system hang. It is usually invoked manually by a user via a CLI command to troubleshoot specific task behavior.

ca_scheduler_dump_task.brief: Prints detailed diagnostic information about a specific task to the standard output.

params.name: index
params.desc: The unique identifier (index) of the task in the system task list. Must be a valid index within the range of allocated tasks.

params.name: mode
params.desc: Bitmask flags (e.g., DUMP_TASK_HDR, DUMP_TASK_REG, DUMP_TASK_ADDR, DUMP_TASK_STACK, DUMP_TASK_STATS) determining which sections of the task context to print.

ca_scheduler_dump_task.returns: Returns true if the task was found and successfully dumped, false if the index is invalid, the task slot is empty, or the task's memory integrity (canary) is corrupted.
ca_scheduler_dump_task.notes: This function is non-blocking but performs multiple I/O operations via ca_stdout_printf_n, which may involve internal mutexes; therefore, it is NOT safe to call from an ISR. It is not strictly thread-safe regarding the task list, meaning if a task is deleted or a slot is reused while this function is running, the output might be inconsistent or reflect a partial state. The function relies on ca_os_task_snapshot to capture the task state safely, but the caller must ensure the system is stable. The most common beginner mistake is assuming the task exists without checking the return value, or calling this function inside a high-frequency loop, which will flood the serial output and potentially cause system latency.
ca_scheduler_dump_task.usage: This function is typically used in CLI interfaces or diagnostic shells to inspect the state of a specific thread when a system fault or unexpected behavior occurs. It is often paired with ca_scheduler_dump_all_tasks for a global view or used after a system crash to identify which task caused a memory fault or stack overflow. Developers use it to verify task priorities, stack usage, and register values during live debugging sessions. It is usually invoked after parsing a user command via ca_strtol to identify the target task index, and it is often used in conjunction with ca_scheduler_size to ensure the index is within bounds.

ca_scheduler_get_context_from_idx.brief: Retrieves a pointer to a thread's context structure by its index in the scheduler's task list.

params.name: idx
params.desc: The index of the thread in the global task list. Must be less than the total number of active threads. Invalid values (e.g., out-of-bounds index) will cause the function to return NULL.

ca_scheduler_get_context_from_idx.returns: Returns a pointer to a valid ca_thread_context_t structure on success, or NULL if the index is out of bounds, the scheduler is not initialized, or the task list is inaccessible.
ca_scheduler_get_context_from_idx.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a direct lookup in the internal task list. It is not inherently thread-safe; if the task list is being modified (e.g., tasks being created or destroyed) while this function is called, you may receive a stale or invalid pointer. While it can be called from an ISR, you must ensure that the task list structure is not being mutated by the scheduler at that exact moment. The most common mistake is failing to check the returned pointer for NULL before dereferencing it, which will trigger a HardFault if the index provided was invalid.
ca_scheduler_get_context_from_idx.usage: This function is typically used when you need to perform operations on a specific task that is not the currently running one, such as sending notifications, inspecting stack usage, or managing priority inheritance. It is often paired with ca_scheduler_size() to iterate through all existing tasks in the system. In a typical lifecycle, you would use this to locate a target task's handle or context, then use that context to perform administrative tasks like checking stack health or modifying thread parameters.

ca_scheduler_get_current_context.brief: Returns a pointer to the internal control structure of the currently executing task.
ca_scheduler_get_current_context.returns: A pointer to the ca_thread_context_t structure of the active task, or NULL if the scheduler is not running or the function is called from an interrupt context where no task is active.
ca_scheduler_get_current_context.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it simply reads a global pointer maintained by the scheduler. It is safe to call from any context, but you must handle the NULL return case, which indicates that the system is either in the pre-scheduler initialization phase or currently executing inside an ISR. A common beginner mistake is assuming this function will always return a valid pointer; always check for NULL before dereferencing the result to avoid a HardFault.
ca_scheduler_get_current_context.usage: This function is primarily used to identify the 'owner' of a resource or to determine if the current execution flow is allowed to perform blocking operations. It is frequently paired with ca_os_task_slot to map the current task to a fixed index for resource tracking, such as memory allocation ownership or event waiting. You will typically see it used in drivers or system services to decide whether to perform a blocking wait (if in a task) or a busy-spin (if in an ISR or early boot).

ca_scheduler_get_current_task_id.brief: Returns the unique index identifier of the task currently executing on the CPU.
ca_scheduler_get_current_task_id.returns: Returns a u32 representing the task index (0 to N-1). Returns 0xFFFFFFFF if no task is currently running (e.g., called before the scheduler starts or during early system initialization).
ca_scheduler_get_current_task_id.notes: This function is thread-safe and non-blocking. It is safe to call from both task context and ISRs, as it simply reads the global pointer to the current task structure. A common beginner mistake is assuming this function will always return a valid ID; always check for the 0xFFFFFFFF error code before using the result as an index into task arrays or lookup tables. It does not require any specific initialization beyond the OS scheduler being active.
ca_scheduler_get_current_task_id.usage: This function is primarily used for task-specific resource management, such as identifying which task owns a specific memory block, logging task-specific debug information, or implementing task-aware synchronization primitives. It is frequently paired with ca_scheduler_get_task_name to provide human-readable logs, or used in conjunction with ca_memory_get_task_usage to monitor stack or heap consumption per task. In complex systems, it helps differentiate between multiple tasks accessing the same shared resource (like a message buffer or stream) to ensure proper ownership tracking.

ca_scheduler_get_next_wait.brief: Retrieves the next task in a wait queue chain, used to traverse or remove tasks from a linked list of waiting threads.

params.name: task
params.desc: Pointer to the current task in the wait queue. Must be a valid pointer to a task context, or NULL if the queue is empty.

returns.value: Pointer to the next task in the wait queue
returns.meaning: The function returns the next task in the chain, allowing traversal or removal of tasks from the queue.
Returned when the input task is the last in the queue, or if the input task is NULL (queue is empty).

notes.content: This function does not block; it simply returns the next pointer in a linked list.
It is safe to call from both thread and ISR contexts, as it only reads memory.
It is not thread-safe if the queue is modified concurrently by another thread or ISR.
The function assumes that the input 'task' is a valid node in a wait queue and that the 'next' field is properly initialized.
Common mistake: Using the returned pointer without checking if it's NULL before dereferencing.

usage.content: Used to traverse a wait queue, such as in event or semaphore handling, to find the next waiting task.
Used to remove a task from a wait queue by updating the links of the previous task.
Used in debugging or validation functions to check if a specific task is in a wait queue.

ca_scheduler_get_runtime_total.brief: Returns the total CPU cycles consumed by the currently running task.
ca_scheduler_get_runtime_total.returns: Returns a u32 value representing the total CPU cycles accumulated by the task. Returns (u32)-1 if no task is currently running (e.g., called from an invalid context).
ca_scheduler_get_runtime_total.notes: This function is thread-safe and non-blocking. It reads the DWT->CYCCNT register to calculate the time spent in the current slice. It is safe to call from a task, but calling it from an ISR is generally discouraged as it relies on the 'g_current_task' pointer, which may not be meaningful depending on the interrupt context. The function uses a 'do-while' loop to ensure that the read operation is atomic relative to context switches; if a PendSV interrupt occurs during the read, the function detects the inconsistency and retries. A common mistake is assuming this value represents wall-clock time; it represents CPU cycles, which depend on the current system clock frequency.
ca_scheduler_get_runtime_total.usage: This function is primarily used for performance profiling and task monitoring. It is typically paired with ca_measure_start and ca_measure_stop to calculate the execution time of a specific code block. By capturing the total runtime before and after a critical section, developers can determine how many CPU cycles a specific algorithm or task consumes. It is often used in conjunction with ca_scheduler_dump_task or similar diagnostic tools to identify tasks that are hogging the CPU.

ca_scheduler_get_task_name.brief: Retrieves the name of a task given its index in the task list.

params.name: idx
params.desc: Index of the task in the global task list. Must be a valid index (0 to MAX_TASK - 1). Invalid indices will cause the function to return NULL.

ca_scheduler_get_task_name.returns: Returns a pointer to a null-terminated string containing the task name if the index is valid. Returns NULL if the index is out of bounds, the task slot is empty, or the task context is uninitialized.
ca_scheduler_get_task_name.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes in constant time as it performs a direct lookup in the internal task list. It is safe to call from an ISR because it only performs a read operation on the task list structure. However, it is not inherently thread-safe; if another thread modifies the task list (e.g., creating or deleting tasks) while this function is reading, you might get inconsistent results. The most common mistake is failing to check the returned pointer for NULL before attempting to use it, which will cause a hard fault if you try to dereference it.
ca_scheduler_get_task_name.usage: This function is primarily used for diagnostic purposes, such as logging, error reporting, or building system monitors. It is typically paired with ca_scheduler_get_current_task_id() to identify the caller during a system fault or within a CLI command. Developers also use it in loops to iterate through all possible task slots to count active tasks or display a system task snapshot. It is essential for human-readable debugging, as it maps numeric task IDs to meaningful string identifiers defined during task creation.

ca_scheduler_init.brief: Initializes the RTOS scheduler, task management structures, and the idle task.
ca_scheduler_init.returns: Returns true if the task manager and scheduler structures were successfully initialized, false otherwise.
ca_scheduler_init.notes: This function is not blocking and must be called exactly once during system startup before any other tasks are created. It is not thread-safe and must never be called from an ISR, as it performs critical memory setup and disables interrupts to ensure atomicity. A common mistake is attempting to call this function after the scheduler has already started or failing to ensure the linker memory regions (like the TLB area) are correctly defined, which will trigger a hard-coded infinite loop if the task array exceeds the allocated space. It must be called after memory initialization but before any application tasks are spawned.
ca_scheduler_init.usage: This function is the cornerstone of the OS boot sequence. It is typically called immediately after low-level hardware and memory initialization (like ca_memory_init) but before any application-level tasks are defined via ca_os_job. It prepares the internal task array and the idle task, which acts as the system fallback when no other tasks are ready to run. It is often followed by ca_os_tick_calibrate to ensure timing accuracy before the scheduler is fully engaged.

ca_scheduler_is_valid_context.brief: Verifies if a given task ID (thid) corresponds to a currently active and valid task context in the scheduler.

params.name: thid
params.desc: The unique task identifier to validate. Must be a value previously assigned by the OS during task creation.

ca_scheduler_is_valid_context.returns: Returns true if the thid is valid and currently managed by the scheduler, false otherwise (e.g., if the task has been destroyed or the ID is out of range).
ca_scheduler_is_valid_context.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, meaning it can be called safely from multiple tasks simultaneously. It is generally safe to call from an ISR, provided the underlying task manager structures are not being modified by the scheduler at that exact moment. The most common mistake is passing an uninitialized or stale thid that was previously used by a task that has already been terminated, which will return false even if the ID was once valid.
ca_scheduler_is_valid_context.usage: This function is typically used as a safety check before performing operations on a specific task, such as signaling, suspending, or querying memory usage. It is often paired with ca_os_thid_from_handle to verify that a handle still points to a valid, living task before attempting to interact with it. Use this to prevent 'dangling' references when managing dynamic task lifecycles in your application.

ca_scheduler_manage_fault.brief: Handles task faults by either restarting or removing the faulty task, and optionally calling an emergency handler.
ca_scheduler_manage_fault.returns: This function does not return directly; it triggers a context switch to either restart the task, remove it, or switch to the idle task. A return value is not applicable here.
ca_scheduler_manage_fault.notes: This function is NOT blocking; it performs immediate actions and then lets the SVC handler perform a context switch. It is NOT thread-safe because it modifies global state (e.g., g_current_task). It is callable from an ISR context, but only if the fault is handled in a way that does not cause further issues. It assumes that a valid task context exists or that the system is in a state where a fault can be handled. Common mistakes include calling this function without ensuring that the fault context is valid or not handling the case where no task is active. It is critical to understand that this function does not return to the caller; it forces the scheduler to re-evaluate the system state, effectively terminating the current execution flow of the faulted task.
ca_scheduler_manage_fault.usage: This function is used in low-level fault handlers (like HardFault, MemManage, or BusFault) to manage task-level errors. It is typically called after a fault is detected and the CPU state is captured, but before the final context switch is performed. It works by inspecting the 'fault_type' flags of the current task to decide whether to trigger an emergency callback, restart the task, or permanently remove it from the scheduler's list. It is usually paired with functions like ca_os_remove_job_handle or task-specific cleanup routines to ensure system stability after a crash.

ca_scheduler_sched_info.brief: Prints scheduler performance statistics including CPU usage, task switching, and idle time.
ca_scheduler_sched_info.returns: None. This function only prints debug information to stdout.
ca_scheduler_sched_info.notes: This function is NOT blocking. It is NOT thread-safe because it accesses internal static variables that track system state; if called from multiple threads simultaneously, the statistics will be corrupted. It CAN be called from an ISR, but it is designed for diagnostic CLI output, not for high-frequency control loops. It requires the OS to be running and the scheduler to be initialized. The most common beginner mistake is calling it only once; the function calculates 'deltas' between calls, so the first call will always print a message indicating that the window has just started, and only subsequent calls will provide actual performance data.
