params.desc: Buffer to store the generated HELLO packet. Must be at least CA_SP_LINK_HELLO_SIZE bytes.

params.name: cap
params.desc: Capacity of the 'out' buffer in bytes. Must be >= CA_SP_LINK_HELLO_SIZE.

params.name: out_len
params.desc: Pointer to store the actual number of bytes written to 'out'.

ca_sp_link_hello.returns: CA_SECURE_PIPE_OK on success, CA_SECURE_PIPE_ERR if parameters are invalid or internal crypto fails, CA_SECURE_PIPE_SIZE if the buffer capacity is insufficient.
ca_sp_link_hello.notes: This function is blocking because it uses a mutex to protect the link state during the cryptographic operations. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because mutexes cannot be locked in interrupt context. The link must be fully initialized via ca_sp_link_init before calling this. A common mistake is providing a buffer smaller than CA_SP_LINK_HELLO_SIZE, which will immediately return an error; always ensure your buffer is sized correctly using the provided constant.
ca_sp_link_hello.usage: This function is the core of the secure handshake process. It is typically used in a sequence: first, the initiator calls it with 'reply' set to false, then the peer calls ca_sp_link_accept to process the packet, followed by the peer calling this function with 'reply' set to true to complete the handshake. It is used in conjunction with ca_net_buf_alloc to prepare the network packet buffer before sending the generated HELLO data over the wire.

ca_sp_link_init.signature: i32 ca_sp_link_init(ca_sp_link_t *l, u8 role, const char *password, const char *name)
ca_sp_link_init.brief: Initializes a secure communication link context by deriving cryptographic keys from a password and name.

params.name: l
params.desc: Pointer to the link structure to initialize. Must be allocated and not already initialized.

params.name: role
params.desc: The role of the device in the link (1 or 2). Determines key derivation direction.

params.name: password
params.desc: Secret string used for key derivation. Must be within CA_SP_LINK_SECRET_MIN and CA_SP_LINK_SECRET_MAX length.

params.name: name
params.desc: Identifier string used as salt for key derivation. Must be within valid length limits.

ca_sp_link_init.returns: CA_SECURE_PIPE_OK (0) on success, or CA_SECURE_PIPE_ERR (-1) if parameters are invalid, memory allocation fails, or key derivation fails.
ca_sp_link_init.notes: This function is blocking because it performs heavy cryptographic operations (PBKDF2/HKDF) which consume significant CPU cycles. It is not thread-safe for the same link structure, so ensure no other task accesses 'l' during initialization. It must NOT be called from an ISR because of the blocking nature and memory allocation requirements. A common mistake is passing a password or name that is too short or too long, which will cause the function to return an error immediately. Always ensure the 'l' structure is zeroed or previously deinitialized before calling this.
ca_sp_link_init.usage: This function is the mandatory first step in establishing a secure pipe. It is typically used during system startup or when a new connection is requested. It is paired with ca_sp_link_deinit to clean up resources. In a typical sequence, you allocate the link structure, call ca_sp_link_init, and then proceed to use other functions like ca_sp_link_hello or ca_sp_link_open to establish the actual communication.

ca_sp_link_is_up.brief: Checks if a secure pipe link is fully initialized and currently active.

params.name: l
params.desc: Pointer to the secure pipe link structure. Must be a valid, initialized pointer.

ca_sp_link_is_up.returns: Returns true if the link is both ready and up; returns false if the pointer is NULL, the link is not ready, or the link is down.
ca_sp_link_is_up.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it performs a simple read of internal status flags. It is safe to call from an ISR because it does not attempt to acquire mutexes or perform I/O operations. The most common mistake is assuming that a 'true' return value guarantees the link will remain up indefinitely; in a multi-threaded environment, the link status could change immediately after the function returns. Always ensure the link structure has been properly initialized via ca_sp_link_init before calling this function to avoid undefined behavior.
ca_sp_link_is_up.usage: This function is typically used as a guard clause before performing secure communication operations like sealing or unsealing data. It is often paired with ca_sp_link_init during the setup phase and ca_sp_link_accept during the handshake process. Developers use it to verify the health of the connection before attempting to send data, preventing errors that would occur if the pipe were disconnected or uninitialized. It is also used in monitoring loops to decide if a re-keying process is necessary via ca_sp_link_need_rekey.

ca_sp_link_need_rekey.brief: Checks if a secure pipe link requires a re-keying operation based on message count or session duration.

params.name: l
params.desc: Pointer to the secure pipe link structure. Must be a valid, initialized pointer; passing NULL will result in a safe return of false.

ca_sp_link_need_rekey.returns: Returns true if the link is active and either the message threshold (CA_SP_LINK_REKEY_MSGS) or the time threshold (CA_SP_LINK_REKEY_MS) has been exceeded. Returns false if the link is not up, not ready, or if the thresholds have not been met.
ca_sp_link_need_rekey.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it performs a read-only check on the link structure. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the pointer passed is valid and the link structure is not being modified concurrently by another task. The function relies on the system tick (ca_os_tick_ms), so it assumes the OS clock is correctly initialized. A common mistake is to assume this function performs the re-keying itself; it does not. It is purely a status check used to trigger a re-keying logic flow elsewhere in your application.
ca_sp_link_need_rekey.usage: This function is typically used in the main loop of a communication task to monitor the health and security status of a secure pipe. It is usually paired with ca_sp_link_is_up to verify the connection state before checking for re-keying requirements. When this function returns true, the application should initiate a new handshake or re-keying sequence (e.g., calling a function to send a new HELLO packet) to maintain secure communication. It is part of the lifecycle management of a secure pipe, following the sequence: ca_sp_link_init -> [data exchange] -> ca_sp_link_need_rekey -> [re-keying logic] -> ca_sp_link_deinit.

ca_sp_link_open.signature: i32 ca_sp_link_open(ca_sp_link_t *l, const u8 *aad, u32 aad_len, const u8 *in, u32 len, u8 *out, u32 cap, u32 *out_len)
ca_sp_link_open.brief: Decrypts and verifies an incoming secure pipe packet using AES-GCM.

params.name: l
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized secure pipe link structure.

params.name: aad
params.desc: Additional Authenticated Data buffer; must be non-NULL if aad_len > 0.

params.name: aad_len
params.desc: Length of AAD; must not exceed CA_SP_LINK_AAD_MAX.

params.name: in
params.desc: Pointer to the encrypted input buffer (wire format).

params.name: len
params.desc: Total length of the input buffer including header and tag.

params.name: out
params.desc: Buffer to store the decrypted plaintext.

params.name: cap
params.desc: Capacity of the output buffer; must be at least the size of the decrypted data.

params.name: out_len
params.desc: Pointer to store the actual length of the decrypted data.

ca_sp_link_open.returns: CA_SECURE_PIPE_OK on success. Returns CA_SECURE_PIPE_ERR for invalid parameters or malformed packets, CA_SECURE_PIPE_NOT_UP if the link is not established, CA_SECURE_PIPE_REPLAY if the packet counter is invalid, CA_SECURE_PIPE_DECRYPT if authentication fails, or CA_SECURE_PIPE_SIZE if the output buffer is too small.
ca_sp_link_open.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses an internal mutex to protect the link state and replay window. It is a blocking function because it performs cryptographic operations and mutex acquisition; therefore, it must NEVER be called from an ISR. The link must be fully initialized via ca_sp_link_init and established before calling this. A common mistake is providing an output buffer smaller than the actual payload size, which triggers a CA_SECURE_PIPE_SIZE error, or failing to check the return value, which could lead to processing uninitialized or zeroed memory.
ca_sp_link_open.usage: Used in secure communication protocols to process incoming encrypted frames. It is typically paired with ca_sp_link_seal on the sender side. The standard sequence is: initialize the link, wait for the connection to be established, and then call this function in a loop to process incoming data packets. It is often used in conjunction with network receive buffers to verify data integrity and authenticity before passing the payload to the application layer.

ca_sp_link_seal.signature: i32 ca_sp_link_seal(ca_sp_link_t *l, const u8 *aad, u32 aad_len, const u8 *plain, u32 len, u8 *out, u32 cap, u32 *out_len)
ca_sp_link_seal.brief: Encrypts and authenticates a plaintext buffer into a secure wire-format packet for transmission.

params.name: l
params.desc: Pointer to the initialized secure pipe link handle.

params.name: aad
params.desc: Additional Authenticated Data buffer; can be NULL if aad_len is 0.

params.name: aad_len
params.desc: Length of AAD; must not exceed CA_SP_LINK_AAD_MAX.

params.name: plain
params.desc: Pointer to the plaintext data to be encrypted.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of plaintext; must be > 0 and <= 0xFFFF.

params.name: out
params.desc: Output buffer where the sealed packet is written.

params.name: cap
params.desc: Capacity of the output buffer; must be large enough to hold header, padded data, and tag.

params.name: out_len
params.desc: Pointer to store the final size of the generated packet.

ca_sp_link_seal.returns: CA_SECURE_PIPE_OK on success. Returns CA_SECURE_PIPE_ERR for invalid parameters or crypto failure, and CA_SECURE_PIPE_NOT_UP if the link is not established. Returns CA_SECURE_PIPE_SIZE if the output buffer capacity is insufficient.
ca_sp_link_seal.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses an internal mutex to protect the link state and transmission counter. It is a blocking function because it performs cryptographic operations and mutex locking, so it must NOT be called from an ISR. The link must be fully initialized and in an 'up' state before calling this. A common mistake is providing an output buffer that is too small; always ensure the buffer size accounts for the header, padding (to 16-byte alignment), and the AES-GCM tag size.
ca_sp_link_seal.usage: Used in secure communication protocols to prepare data for transmission over an untrusted medium. It is typically used in a sequence: first, the link is initialized with ca_sp_link_init, then the connection is established, and finally, this function is called to seal data before sending it via a transport layer (like UART or Ethernet). It is the counterpart to ca_sp_link_open, which is used by the receiver to decrypt and verify the packet.

ca_spdifrx_channel_status.brief: Captures a complete S/PDIF Channel Status (CS) block from the incoming stream.

params.name: cs
params.desc: Pointer to a buffer of at least CA_SPDIFRX_CS_BYTES size to store the received status data.

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time in milliseconds to wait for a complete, valid block to be received.

ca_spdifrx_channel_status.returns: Returns CA_SPDIFRX_CS_BYTES (the number of bytes) if a full block was successfully captured, or 0 if the operation timed out, the input pointer was NULL, or the hardware failed to synchronize.
ca_spdifrx_channel_status.notes: This function is blocking; it will pause the calling task until a full S/PDIF block is received or the timeout expires. It is not safe to call from an ISR because it relies on time-based waiting and hardware state management. The function requires the S/PDIF hardware to be initialized and running. A common mistake is providing a buffer smaller than CA_SPDIFRX_CS_BYTES, which will cause memory corruption, or setting a timeout too short to capture the full block, which occurs at a specific rate depending on the audio sample frequency.
ca_spdifrx_channel_status.usage: This function is typically used during the initialization or diagnostic phase of an audio application to verify the source configuration (e.g., sample rate, copyright bits, or audio format). It is usually paired with ca_spdifrx_init to set up the hardware, followed by this function to read the metadata, and finally ca_spdifrx_read_dma to begin streaming the actual audio data. It is essential to clear the buffer before calling this function to ensure that old data does not persist if the capture fails.

ca_spdifrx_errors.brief: Retrieves the current error status flags from the SPDIF receiver peripheral.
ca_spdifrx_errors.returns: A 32-bit unsigned integer representing a bitmask of error flags (CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_*). A return value of 0 indicates no errors are currently detected.
ca_spdifrx_errors.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it simply reads a cached status variable updated by the SPDIF hardware interrupt service routine (ISR). It can be safely called from both task context and ISRs. The most common mistake is assuming that calling this function clears the errors; it does not. The error flags are typically latched by the hardware or the driver's ISR, and you must ensure your application logic handles these flags immediately after reading them to prevent missing transient error states.
ca_spdifrx_errors.usage: This function is used to monitor the health of the SPDIF digital audio input stream. It is typically called after synchronization functions like ca_spdifrx_sync or data retrieval functions like ca_spdifrx_channel_status to verify that the operation completed without hardware errors (such as parity errors, buffer overflows, or loss of lock). In a typical audio processing loop, you would pair this with your data acquisition logic to decide whether to process the received audio buffer or discard it due to corruption.

ca_spdifrx_fs.brief: Returns the sampling frequency (fs) of the SPDIF receiver measured during the last synchronization or measurement cycle.
ca_spdifrx_fs.returns: Returns a 32-bit unsigned integer representing the frequency in Hz. A return value of 0 indicates that no valid signal is currently detected or no measurement has been performed yet.
ca_spdifrx_fs.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it simply returns a cached value stored in a static variable. It is safe to call from an ISR, although the value returned may be stale if the hardware state has changed since the last measurement. It does not trigger a new hardware measurement; it only reports the result of the most recent one. A common mistake is assuming this function will actively wait for a signal or perform a fresh measurement; if you need an up-to-date value, you must ensure a measurement function (like the one that updates the internal state) has been called previously.
ca_spdifrx_fs.usage: This function is typically used in diagnostic CLI commands or monitoring tasks to report the current status of the audio input. It is often paired with functions that perform the actual hardware synchronization and measurement, such as those that wait for a sync lock and then trigger a frequency calculation. In a typical sequence, the system initializes the SPDIF hardware, waits for a valid signal, performs a measurement, and then this function is used to retrieve that result for display or logic decisions.

ca_spdifrx_hw_dma_bind.brief: Retrieves the hardware-specific DMA stream and request ID required for SPDIFRX data transfers.

params.name: flat
params.desc: Pointer to store the DMA stream/channel index. Set to -1 if the hardware supports dynamic routing (e.g., via DMAMUX).

params.name: req
params.desc: Pointer to store the hardware-specific DMA request ID required by the peripheral to trigger DMA transfers.

ca_spdifrx_hw_dma_bind.returns: Returns true if the hardware configuration is valid and parameters were successfully populated. Returns false if DMA is not supported on the current platform or the configuration is unavailable.
ca_spdifrx_hw_dma_bind.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it only performs a memory write based on compile-time constants or hardware-specific logic. It is safe to call from an ISR, though it is typically used during the driver initialization phase. The most common mistake is assuming that the returned 'flat' index is always a valid DMA stream index; on some platforms (like H7), it returns -1, which indicates that the caller must use a dynamic DMA channel allocation function rather than a hardcoded index. Always check the return value before attempting to use the 'flat' or 'req' values to configure the DMA controller.
ca_spdifrx_hw_dma_bind.usage: This function is used exclusively during the initialization of the SPDIFRX driver to prepare the DMA subsystem. It is typically called before requesting a DMA channel from the system pool. The standard sequence is: call ca_spdifrx_hw_dma_bind to get the requirements, then pass those values to ca_dma_free_channel_index or ca_dma_free_channel to reserve the hardware resource, and finally call ca_dma_set_request to link the peripheral to the DMA controller.

ca_spdifrx_hw_dr.brief: Returns the memory-mapped address of the SPDIFRX Data Register (DR) for direct hardware access.
ca_spdifrx_hw_dr.returns: Returns a volatile pointer to the SPDIFRX->DR register if supported by the hardware, or NULL if the hardware does not support direct access or DMA operations are disabled.
ca_spdifrx_hw_dr.notes: This function provides a raw pointer to the hardware register. It is non-blocking and thread-safe in the sense that it only returns a constant memory address. It is safe to call from an ISR, but you must never write to this pointer directly unless you are performing manual register manipulation, which is discouraged in favor of higher-level caOS drivers. The most common beginner mistake is assuming this function will work on all STM32 variants; always check if the returned pointer is NULL before dereferencing it, as many STM32 series do not implement the SPDIFRX peripheral.
ca_spdifrx_hw_dr.usage: This function is primarily used to provide the hardware source or destination address to the DMA controller. In a typical workflow, you initialize the SPDIFRX peripheral, clear any pending data using a loop with ca_spdifrx_hw_get, and then pass the result of ca_spdifrx_hw_dr to ca_dma_copy_target to set up a high-speed data transfer from the peripheral to memory. It is the bridge between the low-level hardware register and the caOS DMA abstraction layer.

ca_spdifrx_hw_flags.brief: Reads and clears the current SPDIFRX hardware status flags and error conditions.
ca_spdifrx_hw_flags.returns: A bitmask (u32) representing current hardware states (e.g., CA_SPDIFRX_HW_SYNCD) and error conditions (e.g., CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_PAR). Returns 0 if no flags are set.
ca_spdifrx_hw_flags.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes quickly by reading the hardware status register and immediately writing to the interrupt flag clear register. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs an atomic read-modify-write on the hardware registers, but it should be used carefully in multi-threaded environments to avoid missing transient error flags. It is safe to call from an ISR, as it does not involve any OS primitives or blocking operations. The most common beginner mistake is ignoring the returned flags; you must check these bits to detect stream synchronization issues or data corruption (like parity or overrun errors) that require a peripheral reset.
ca_spdifrx_hw_flags.usage: This function is typically used in a polling loop or an error-handling routine to monitor the health of the SPDIF stream. It is often called after initializing the peripheral with ca_spdifrx_hw_state to verify that the hardware has successfully locked onto the incoming signal. In a typical sequence, you would call it periodically to check for errors, and if a critical error (like a timeout or sync loss) is detected, you would use ca_spdifrx_hw_state to reset the peripheral and attempt to re-synchronize.

ca_spdifrx_hw_get.brief: Reads a single data word from the SPDIFRX hardware buffer if available.

params.name: w
params.desc: Pointer to a 32-bit variable where the received data word will be stored. Must be a valid memory address.

ca_spdifrx_hw_get.returns: Returns true if a word was successfully read from the hardware register (RXNE flag was set). Returns false if the hardware buffer is empty (RXNE flag is 0), in which case the value at *w remains unchanged.
ca_spdifrx_hw_get.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a direct register read. It is thread-safe in the sense that it only accesses the hardware register, but it does not implement any internal locking; if multiple tasks call this simultaneously, you may experience data corruption or race conditions. It is safe to call from an ISR because it does not wait for hardware or use OS primitives. The most common beginner mistake is ignoring the return value; if you do not check the boolean result, you might process 'junk' data or stale values when the hardware has not actually received a new frame.
ca_spdifrx_hw_get.usage: This function is typically used in a polling loop or within an interrupt service routine to drain the SPDIFRX hardware FIFO. It is often paired with ca_spdifrx_hw_state to manage the peripheral's lifecycle (init -> state(enable) -> loop(get) -> state(disable)). It is essential for clearing the hardware buffer during initialization or after a synchronization error to ensure that subsequent reads start from a clean state.

ca_spdifrx_hw_get_cs.brief: Reads the raw Channel Status (CS) register from the SPDIFRX peripheral if data is available.

params.name: csr
params.desc: Pointer to a 32-bit variable where the raw register value will be stored. Must be a valid memory address.

ca_spdifrx_hw_get_cs.returns: Returns true if the register was read successfully (CSRNE flag was set). Returns false if no new Channel Status data is available (CSRNE = 0).
ca_spdifrx_hw_get_cs.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a direct hardware register read. It is thread-safe only if the hardware access is not interrupted by other tasks modifying the same peripheral registers. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the hardware is already initialized. The most common beginner mistake is ignoring the return value; if you call this when the peripheral has no new data, the pointer 'csr' will not be updated, potentially leaving you with stale or uninitialized data.
ca_spdifrx_hw_get_cs.usage: This function is typically used during the initialization or synchronization phase of the SPDIFRX driver to clear out old, irrelevant data from the hardware buffers. It is often paired with 'ca_spdifrx_hw_get' in a 'while' loop to flush the hardware state before starting a new stream. It is part of the low-level hardware abstraction layer (HAL) and should be used when you need to inspect the raw Channel Status bits (such as User bits or Channel Status bits) directly from the hardware register.

ca_spdifrx_hw_init.brief: Initializes the SPDIFRX hardware peripheral, configures clocks, GPIOs, and sets the receiver to idle state.
ca_spdifrx_hw_init.returns: Returns the configured SPDIFRX clock frequency in Hz as a u32. Returns 0 if the hardware is not supported on the current chip, if the clock configuration fails, or if the peripheral is disabled.
ca_spdifrx_hw_init.notes: This function is a low-level hardware abstraction layer (HAL) driver. It is not thread-safe and must be called during the system initialization phase before any SPDIFRX data processing tasks are started. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. A common mistake is calling this function multiple times without proper de-initialization, which may lead to redundant clock configuration or GPIO conflicts. It assumes the system clock tree is already in a state where the required peripheral clocks can be derived.
ca_spdifrx_hw_init.usage: This function is the mandatory first step in the SPDIFRX driver lifecycle. It is typically called by the higher-level 'ca_spdifrx_init' function to prepare the hardware registers and pins. Once initialized, the application can proceed to use 'ca_spdifrx_sync' to wait for incoming data streams or 'ca_spdifrx_read' to capture audio frames. It should be paired with a corresponding stop or de-init sequence if the peripheral needs to be power-cycled or reconfigured.

ca_spdifrx_hw_state.brief: Configures the SPDIFRX hardware peripheral state and DMA mode.

params.name: en
params.desc: Peripheral state: 0 for IDLE, 1 for SYNC, 3 for RECEIVE.

params.name: dma
params.desc: True to enable DMA transfer, false to disable it.

ca_spdifrx_hw_state.notes: This function directly modifies the SPDIFRX control register. It is not thread-safe; if multiple tasks access the SPDIFRX peripheral, you must wrap calls in a critical section or mutex. It is not intended to be called from an ISR unless you are certain no other context is modifying the peripheral state simultaneously. A common mistake is calling this while a DMA transfer is active without first stopping the DMA, which can lead to hardware state corruption or unexpected interrupts.
ca_spdifrx_hw_state.usage: This function is used to transition the SPDIFRX peripheral between operational modes, such as resetting to IDLE before re-initialization or switching to RECEIVE mode after synchronization. It is typically paired with functions that drain the hardware buffers (like reading remaining data) to ensure a clean state before changing the mode. It is part of the low-level driver sequence: init -> sync -> state change -> data processing.

ca_spdifrx_hw_width5.brief: Reads the SPDIFRX hardware register to get the measured width of 5 symbols in clock periods.
ca_spdifrx_hw_width5.returns: Returns a 32-bit unsigned integer representing the number of SPDIFRX_CLK periods measured over 5 symbols. Returns 0 if the hardware is not initialized, not supported on the current chip, or if no signal is currently being detected.
ca_spdifrx_hw_width5.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes in constant time as it performs a direct register read from the SPDIFRX peripheral. It is thread-safe in the sense that it only performs a read operation, but it should only be called after the SPDIFRX peripheral has been properly initialized. It is safe to call from an ISR, as it does not involve any OS primitives or blocking mechanisms. The most common beginner mistake is assuming this value is a constant frequency; it is a dynamic measurement that changes based on the incoming audio stream's sample rate, so it must be sampled periodically to calculate the actual frequency.
ca_spdifrx_hw_width5.usage: This function is used in the context of digital audio signal processing to determine the sample rate of an incoming SPDIF stream. It is typically paired with a local clock reference to calculate the actual sampling frequency (Fs) by comparing the measured symbol width against the expected ideal width. Developers usually call this within a periodic task or a monitoring function to detect changes in the audio source's sample rate, often following an initialization sequence involving ca_spdifrx_init.

ca_spdifrx_init.brief: Initializes the SPDIFRX hardware peripheral and returns the detected clock frequency in Hz.
ca_spdifrx_init.returns: Returns the detected clock frequency as a u32 value in Hz. Returns 0 if the initialization failed or if the clock detection was unsuccessful.
ca_spdifrx_init.notes: This function is a non-blocking wrapper that resets internal state variables and triggers the hardware-level initialization. It is not thread-safe; ensure that only one task manages the SPDIFRX peripheral at a time to avoid race conditions. It is not intended to be called from an ISR, as it may involve hardware setup delays. A common beginner mistake is to ignore the return value; if it returns 0, the peripheral is not ready, and attempting to use it will lead to undefined behavior or system hangs.
ca_spdifrx_init.usage: This function is typically used during the system startup or peripheral configuration phase. It is usually called after initializing related hardware, such as the SAI (Serial Audio Interface), because the SPDIFRX often shares the same clock source (like the PLLI2S on STM32 F4/F7 series). The typical sequence is: initialize the SAI, call ca_spdifrx_init, verify the returned clock frequency is non-zero, and then proceed to start the audio stream.

ca_spdifrx_read.signature: u32 ca_spdifrx_read(u32 *w, u32 words, u32 timeout_ms)
ca_spdifrx_read.brief: Reads a specified number of words from the SPDIF receiver using a polled approach with a timeout.

params.name: w
params.desc: Pointer to the buffer where the received data will be stored. Must not be NULL.

params.name: words
params.desc: Number of 32-bit words to read. Must be greater than 0.

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time in milliseconds to wait for the requested number of words before aborting.

ca_spdifrx_read.returns: Returns the number of words successfully read (0 to 'words'). A return value of 0 indicates either a timeout, an invalid parameter, or a hardware error during synchronization.
ca_spdifrx_read.notes: This function is blocking; it will keep the CPU busy in a loop until the requested data is received or the timeout expires. It is NOT thread-safe and must not be called from an ISR, as it relies on system ticks and hardware state management. Before calling this, ensure the SPDIF hardware has been properly initialized. A common mistake is providing a buffer that is too small for the requested number of words, which will cause memory corruption, or setting a timeout that is too short for the incoming data rate, leading to frequent read failures.
ca_spdifrx_read.usage: This function is typically used in a polling loop to capture a specific burst of audio data or status frames from the SPDIF interface. It is usually paired with ca_spdifrx_errors() to check for data corruption after the read attempt and ca_spdifrx_init() for initial setup. In a typical sequence, you would initialize the hardware, call this function to fill a buffer, check the error status, and then process the data.

ca_spdifrx_read_dma.signature: bool ca_spdifrx_read_dma(u32 *w, u32 words, u32 timeout_ms)
ca_spdifrx_read_dma.brief: Reads a block of data from the S/PDIF receiver using DMA with a timeout.

params.name: w
params.desc: Pointer to the destination buffer where the received 32-bit words will be stored. Must be valid and large enough to hold 'words' count.

params.name: words
params.desc: Number of 32-bit words to read. Must be greater than 0.

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time in milliseconds to wait for the data transfer to complete.

ca_spdifrx_read_dma.returns: Returns true if the transfer completed successfully within the timeout. Returns false if the input parameters are invalid, the hardware fails to sync, the DMA transfer fails, or the timeout expires.
ca_spdifrx_read_dma.notes: This function is blocking; it will suspend the calling task until the DMA transfer finishes or the timeout occurs. It is not safe to call this function from an ISR because it relies on OS-level timing and synchronization primitives. Before calling this, ensure the S/PDIF hardware is initialized and the DMA channel is properly configured. A common mistake is providing a buffer that is too small for the requested number of words, which will lead to memory corruption, or failing to check the return value, which leaves the application unaware of potential data loss or hardware sync errors.
ca_spdifrx_read_dma.usage: This function is typically used in a data acquisition loop where high-throughput audio or digital data is expected from an S/PDIF source. It is usually paired with a preceding check of the S/PDIF status or channel status to ensure the signal is valid. After the function returns, the application should verify the data integrity (e.g., checking for errors via ca_spdifrx_errors) and then process the buffer. It is often used in a sequence: initialize hardware, enter a loop to read blocks via DMA, process the data, and finally stop the hardware when the task is complete.

ca_spdifrx_stop.brief: Stops the SPDIF receiver hardware and releases associated DMA resources.
ca_spdifrx_stop.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a clean shutdown of the SPDIF peripheral. It is not thread-safe; if multiple tasks access the SPDIF hardware, you must wrap this call in a mutex or scheduler lock to prevent race conditions. It is generally not safe to call this from an ISR because it may trigger DMA abort sequences that require task-level context. The most common mistake is calling this function while a DMA transfer is still being processed by another task, which can lead to inconsistent hardware states or memory corruption if the DMA buffer is freed immediately after.
ca_spdifrx_stop.usage: Use this function when you need to stop audio streaming or reconfigure the hardware pins for a different purpose. It is typically paired with ca_spdifrx_init at the start of a session and ca_spdifrx_read_dma during active operation. In a typical lifecycle, you call this to halt the peripheral, then proceed to reconfigure GPIOs or power down the clock tree to save energy or switch modes.

ca_spdifrx_sync.brief: Synchronizes the SPDIF receiver with an incoming audio stream and measures the sample rate.

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time in milliseconds to wait for a valid SPDIF signal lock. A value of 0 means no wait (immediate return).

ca_spdifrx_sync.returns: Returns the measured sample rate (fs) in Hz as a u32. Returns 0 if no valid stream is detected within the timeout period or if the hardware is not initialized.
ca_spdifrx_sync.notes: This function is a blocking call; it will pause the execution of the calling task until the signal is locked or the timeout expires. It is not thread-safe and must not be called from an ISR, as it relies on OS timing mechanisms. Before calling this, ensure the SPDIF hardware has been initialized via the appropriate hardware setup function. A common beginner mistake is setting the timeout too low for the incoming signal to stabilize, resulting in a false 0 return even when a valid cable is connected.
ca_spdifrx_sync.usage: This function is typically used in audio processing tasks to verify the presence and quality of an incoming digital audio signal before starting a data stream. It is usually paired with ca_spdifrx_errors to check for signal integrity and ca_spdifrx_channel_status to retrieve metadata. The typical sequence is: initialize hardware, call ca_spdifrx_sync to lock the clock, check for errors, and then proceed to read data or configure downstream audio peripherals.

ca_spi_cs_assert.brief: Activates the Chip Select (CS) pin for a specific SPI peripheral to initiate communication.

params.name: spi_num
params.desc: The SPI peripheral index (1-based). Must be within the range [1, SPI_MAX_NUM]. Values outside this range are ignored.

ca_spi_cs_assert.returns: void. No status is returned; if an invalid index is provided, the function returns silently without performing any action.
ca_spi_cs_assert.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately by writing to the GPIO register configured for the CS pin. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs a single atomic GPIO write, but it does not provide mutual exclusion for the SPI bus itself; if multiple tasks access the same SPI bus, you must use a mutex to prevent data corruption. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the underlying GPIO driver is also ISR-safe. The most common mistake is calling this function without having first initialized the SPI peripheral and the associated GPIO pin via ca_spi_init, which results in the CS pin remaining in an undefined or inactive state.
ca_spi_cs_assert.usage: This function is used to signal the start of a SPI transaction to a slave device. It is typically called immediately before sending or receiving data (e.g., via ca_spi_dma_xfer or ca_spi_xfer). The standard sequence is: ca_spi_cs_assert() -> [perform data transfer] -> ca_spi_cs_deassert(). It is essential to ensure that the CS pin is correctly configured in the SPI initialization structure so that the driver knows which GPIO port and pin to toggle.

ca_spi_cs_deassert.brief: Deasserts (sets to high) the Chip Select (CS) pin for a specific SPI peripheral.

params.name: spi_num
params.desc: The SPI peripheral index (1-based). Must be between 1 and SPI_MAX_NUM. Values outside this range are ignored.

ca_spi_cs_deassert.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately by writing to the GPIO pin configured as CS. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs a single atomic GPIO write, but it does not provide mutual exclusion for the SPI bus itself; you must ensure no other task is using the bus simultaneously. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the underlying GPIO driver is also ISR-safe. The most common mistake is calling this before the SPI peripheral has been initialized via ca_spi_init, which results in the function operating on uninitialized or default GPIO settings.
ca_spi_cs_deassert.usage: This function is used to signal the end of a SPI transaction to a slave device. It is typically called after a data transfer function (like ca_spi_dma_xfer or ca_spi_xfer) to release the bus. The standard sequence is: ca_spi_cs_assert(n) -> [perform data transfer] -> ca_spi_cs_deassert(n). It is only effective if the SPI peripheral was configured with 'manage_cs' enabled during initialization.

ca_spi_dma_read.signature: u16 ca_spi_dma_read(u8 spi_num, u8 *buf, u16 len)
ca_spi_dma_read.brief: Reads a specified number of bytes from an SPI peripheral using DMA.

params.name: spi_num
params.desc: The index of the SPI peripheral to use (e.g., 0, 1). Must correspond to a hardware instance initialized via ca_spi_init_dma.

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the memory buffer where the received data will be stored. Must be large enough to hold 'len' bytes.

params.name: len
params.desc: Number of bytes to read. Must be greater than 0.

ca_spi_dma_read.returns: Returns a status code (u16). Typically, 0 indicates success, while non-zero values indicate an error (e.g., peripheral busy, invalid parameters, or DMA transfer failure).
ca_spi_dma_read.notes: This function is a wrapper around ca_spi_dma_xfer and is non-blocking, meaning it initiates the DMA transfer and returns immediately while the hardware handles the data movement in the background. It is not safe to call from an ISR unless the underlying driver explicitly supports it, and it requires the SPI peripheral to have been previously initialized with ca_spi_init_dma. A common mistake is to modify or free the 'buf' memory before the DMA transfer has completed, which leads to data corruption; always ensure the transfer is finished before accessing the buffer.
ca_spi_dma_read.usage: This function is used when high-throughput data reception is required without stalling the CPU. It is typically used in a sequence: first, initialize the SPI peripheral with ca_spi_init_dma, then assert the Chip Select line using ca_spi_cs_assert, call ca_spi_dma_read to fetch the data, and finally deassert the Chip Select line using ca_spi_cs_deassert once the transfer is confirmed complete.

ca_spi_dma_write.signature: u16 ca_spi_dma_write(u8 spi_num, const u8 *buf, u16 len)
ca_spi_dma_write.brief: Transmits a buffer of data over SPI using DMA without receiving data.

params.name: spi_num
params.desc: The index of the SPI peripheral to use (e.g., 0, 1, 2). Must match the hardware configuration.

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the data buffer to be sent. Must be a valid memory address and remain unchanged until the transfer completes.

params.name: len
params.desc: Number of bytes to transmit. A value of 0 will result in no action.

ca_spi_dma_write.returns: Returns the number of bytes requested to be sent (len) upon successful initiation. If the SPI peripheral is busy or the DMA channel fails to initialize, it may return 0 or an error code depending on the underlying driver implementation.
ca_spi_dma_write.notes: This function is a wrapper around the DMA transfer mechanism and is typically blocking until the transfer is queued or completed, depending on the driver's internal implementation. It is not safe to call from an ISR unless the driver explicitly supports it, as it may involve waiting for hardware flags. A common beginner mistake is to modify or free the 'buf' memory immediately after calling this function; because DMA operates independently of the CPU, the buffer must remain valid until the hardware has finished shifting all bits out. Ensure the SPI peripheral has been initialized via ca_spi_init and ca_spi_init_dma before calling this function.
ca_spi_dma_write.usage: This function is used when you need to send command sequences or data packets to an external SPI device (like a display or sensor) efficiently without consuming CPU cycles during the transmission. It is typically used in a sequence: first, assert the Chip Select (CS) line using ca_spi_cs_assert, then call ca_spi_dma_write to send the payload, and finally deassert the CS line using ca_spi_cs_deassert once the transfer is confirmed complete. It is the standard way to perform high-speed SPI output in a multitasking RTOS environment.

ca_spi_dma_xfer.signature: u16 ca_spi_dma_xfer(u8 spi_num, const u8 *tx, u8 *rx, u16 len)
ca_spi_dma_xfer.brief: Performs a full-duplex SPI data transfer using DMA, blocking the calling task until completion.

params.name: spi_num
params.desc: The index of the SPI peripheral to use. Must correspond to a valid, initialized SPI instance.

params.name: tx
params.desc: Pointer to the buffer containing data to send. If NULL, the function performs a read-only operation by sending dummy 0xFF bytes.

params.name: rx
params.desc: Pointer to the buffer where received data will be stored. If NULL, the function performs a write-only operation.

params.name: len
params.desc: Number of bytes to transfer. Must be greater than 0.

ca_spi_dma_xfer.returns: Returns the number of bytes transferred (len) on success, or 0 if the parameters are invalid or the DMA transfer failed to initialize.
ca_spi_dma_xfer.notes: This function is blocking; it puts the calling task into a wait state until the DMA hardware signals completion via interrupts. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR because it relies on task-level synchronization (ca_dma_wait). Before calling this, ensure the SPI peripheral has been initialized via ca_spi_init. A common mistake is passing buffers that are not properly aligned or are located in memory regions inaccessible to the DMA controller (e.g., certain stack locations or non-DMA-capable SRAM).
ca_spi_dma_xfer.usage: This function is the primary way to perform high-speed SPI communication in caOS. It is typically used in a sequence: first, initialize the SPI peripheral with ca_spi_init, then prepare your data buffers, and finally call ca_spi_dma_xfer to perform the transaction. It is often paired with ca_spi_cs_assert and ca_spi_cs_deassert to manage the Chip Select line manually if the hardware does not handle it automatically.

ca_spi_hw_dma_bind.signature: bool ca_spi_hw_dma_bind(u8 spi_num, i16 *rx_flat, u16 *rx_req, i16 *tx_flat, u16 *tx_req)
ca_spi_hw_dma_bind.brief: Retrieves the hardware-specific DMA stream and request identifiers required to configure a SPI peripheral for DMA transfers.

params.name: spi_num
params.desc: The SPI peripheral index (e.g., 1, 2, or 3). Must correspond to valid hardware instances.

params.name: rx_flat
params.desc: Pointer to store the RX DMA stream/channel index. Returns -1 if the system allows dynamic allocation.

params.name: rx_req
params.desc: Pointer to store the RX DMA request/channel selection ID required by the DMA controller.

params.name: tx_flat
params.desc: Pointer to store the TX DMA stream/channel index. Returns -1 if the system allows dynamic allocation.

params.name: tx_req
params.desc: Pointer to store the TX DMA request/channel selection ID required by the DMA controller.

ca_spi_hw_dma_bind.returns: Returns true if the SPI index is valid and parameters were successfully populated. Returns false if the spi_num is invalid or unsupported.
ca_spi_hw_dma_bind.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it performs simple memory writes based on constant lookup tables. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the pointers passed are valid. It does not initialize the DMA hardware itself; it only provides the necessary configuration data. The most common mistake is failing to check the boolean return value, which leads to using uninitialized or garbage values for DMA configuration, potentially causing hard faults or peripheral lockups.
ca_spi_hw_dma_bind.usage: This function is typically used during the initialization phase of a SPI driver. It is called before requesting a DMA channel from the OS allocator. The sequence is: 1) Call ca_spi_hw_dma_bind to get the hardware requirements. 2) Use the returned 'flat' values with ca_dma_free_channel or ca_dma_free_channel_index to reserve the hardware resources. 3) Pass the 'req' values to the DMA controller configuration registers. This ensures that the driver respects hardware-specific constraints and avoids conflicts with other peripherals like UARTs.

ca_spi_hw_dma_finish.brief: Finalizes a DMA-based SPI transfer by waiting for hardware completion and resetting the peripheral to an idle state.

params.name: spi_num
params.desc: The index of the SPI peripheral to finalize (e.g., 0, 1, 2).

params.name: rx_en
params.desc: Set to true if RX was enabled during the transfer, false for TX-only. This helps the driver decide whether to clear RX FIFO/OVR flags.

ca_spi_hw_dma_finish.notes: This function is blocking; it polls hardware status registers (like EOT or BSY) until the SPI peripheral has finished shifting all bits. It is NOT thread-safe and must not be called from an ISR, as it contains busy-wait loops that could hang the system if the hardware fails to signal completion. A common beginner mistake is calling this function before the DMA transfer has actually finished or while the SPI peripheral is still actively communicating, which can lead to data corruption or unexpected hardware faults (like Mode Faults). Ensure the DMA transfer is fully completed or aborted before invoking this cleanup routine.
ca_spi_hw_dma_finish.usage: This function is used as the final step in a DMA-based SPI communication sequence. It is typically called after the DMA transfer has been triggered and verified, or in an error-handling block if the DMA setup fails. It pairs with functions like ca_spi_dma_xfer or manual DMA configuration to ensure the SPI peripheral is returned to a clean, idle state, preventing the bus from being locked or left in an inconsistent configuration for the next transaction.

ca_spi_hw_dma_kick.brief: Triggers the hardware SPI DMA transfer process by enabling the peripheral and starting the clock.

params.name: spi_num
params.desc: The index of the SPI peripheral to trigger. Must be a valid index previously initialized by the system.

ca_spi_hw_dma_kick.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs direct register manipulation to initiate hardware-level data movement. It is not thread-safe and must not be called from an ISR unless the system design guarantees that no other task is accessing the same SPI peripheral registers simultaneously. The most common mistake is calling this function before the DMA channels and SPI peripheral have been fully configured, which will result in a hardware fault or an incomplete transfer. Ensure that the SPI peripheral is in the correct state (e.g., chip select asserted) before invoking this, as the transfer starts immediately upon execution.
ca_spi_hw_dma_kick.usage: This function is the final step in the SPI DMA transmission sequence. It is typically used after the DMA channels have been configured and the SPI peripheral has been prepared for data exchange. It is almost always followed by a call to ca_dma_wait to block the current task until the hardware transfer completes, ensuring data integrity before the next operation or before deasserting the chip select line.

ca_spi_hw_dma_prepare.signature: void ca_spi_hw_dma_prepare(u8 spi_num, u16 len, bool rx_en)
ca_spi_hw_dma_prepare.brief: Prepares the SPI hardware for a DMA-based transfer by configuring registers and clearing error flags.

params.name: spi_num
params.desc: The index of the SPI peripheral to configure (e.g., 0, 1, 2).

params.name: len
params.desc: The number of data frames to transfer. On newer hardware (v3), this sets the TSIZE register; on older hardware, it is ignored.

params.name: rx_en
params.desc: Set to true to enable DMA reception (RXDMAEN), false to disable it.

ca_spi_hw_dma_prepare.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called from a single task or protected by a mutex if multiple tasks access the same SPI peripheral. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. The function performs low-level register manipulation to clear error flags like MODF (Mode Fault) and OVR (Overrun), which are critical because if these flags remain set, the SPI peripheral will refuse to act as a Master, causing the DMA transfer to hang indefinitely. A common beginner mistake is calling this function while the SPI peripheral is already enabled (SPE=1); always ensure the peripheral is in a safe state before calling this to avoid configuration errors.
ca_spi_hw_dma_prepare.usage: This function is used as the first step in the SPI DMA transfer sequence. It is typically called after initializing the SPI peripheral via ca_spi_init_dma and before starting the actual DMA transfer using ca_dma_copy_target. The standard sequence is: 1) Call ca_spi_cs_assert to select the slave, 2) Call ca_spi_hw_dma_prepare to configure the hardware, 3) Start the DMA transfer, 4) Wait for completion, and 5) Call ca_spi_cs_deassert to release the slave.

ca_spi_hw_dma_rx_addr.brief: Returns the memory-mapped address of the SPI peripheral's RX data register for DMA operations.

params.name: spi_num
params.desc: The index of the SPI peripheral (e.g., 0 for SPI1, 1 for SPI2). Must be a valid index supported by the hardware configuration.

ca_spi_hw_dma_rx_addr.returns: A volatile pointer to the hardware RX data register (DR or RXDR). Returns NULL if the spi_num is invalid, though implementation-specific behavior may vary.
ca_spi_hw_dma_rx_addr.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it simply performs a pointer calculation based on the peripheral base address. It is safe to call from an ISR because it does not perform any I/O or synchronization. The primary purpose is to provide the DMA controller with the source or destination address for hardware-accelerated data transfers. A common mistake is passing an uninitialized or out-of-bounds spi_num, which will result in a pointer to an invalid memory location, likely causing a HardFault when the DMA attempts to access it.
ca_spi_hw_dma_rx_addr.usage: This function is used exclusively in the context of setting up DMA-based SPI transfers. It is typically called immediately before configuring the DMA channel to point to the SPI peripheral's data register. It is almost always paired with ca_dma_copy_target or similar DMA configuration functions to establish the link between the peripheral hardware and system memory. The sequence is: prepare the SPI peripheral for DMA, retrieve the register address, configure the DMA channel, and finally trigger the transfer.

ca_spi_hw_dma_tx_addr.brief: Returns the memory-mapped address of the SPI peripheral's transmit data register for DMA operations.

params.name: spi_num
params.desc: The index of the SPI peripheral (e.g., 0, 1, 2). Must be a valid index configured in the system.

ca_spi_hw_dma_tx_addr.returns: A volatile pointer to the hardware register (e.g., DR, TXDR) used by the DMA controller to push data into the SPI peripheral. Returns NULL if the spi_num is invalid or the peripheral is not initialized.
ca_spi_hw_dma_tx_addr.notes: This function is a low-level hardware abstraction layer (HAL) utility. It is non-blocking and thread-safe as it only performs a pointer calculation based on the peripheral base address. It is safe to call from an ISR because it does not perform any complex logic or synchronization. The most common mistake is passing an invalid spi_num, which will lead to a hard fault when the DMA controller attempts to access an invalid memory address. Always ensure the SPI peripheral is initialized before requesting its DMA address.
ca_spi_hw_dma_tx_addr.usage: This function is used exclusively to configure DMA transfers for SPI communication. It is typically called immediately before invoking ca_dma_copy_target to set the destination address for a memory-to-peripheral (M2P) transfer. The standard sequence is: 1) Initialize SPI and DMA, 2) Call ca_spi_hw_dma_tx_addr to get the register address, 3) Pass that address to ca_dma_copy_target, and 4) Trigger the transfer using a hardware-specific kick function.

ca_spi_hw_init_periph.signature: bool ca_spi_hw_init_periph(u8 num, ca_spi_br_t br, u8 cpol, u8 cpha)
ca_spi_hw_init_periph.brief: Initializes the SPI peripheral hardware in Master mode.

params.name: num
params.desc: The SPI peripheral index (e.g., 1, 2, 3). Must correspond to a valid hardware instance.

params.name: br
params.desc: Baud rate prescaler value. Must be a valid enum or integer supported by the hardware.

params.name: cpol
params.desc: Clock Polarity: 0 for low level when idle, 1 for high level when idle.

params.name: cpha
params.desc: Clock Phase: 0 for first clock transition capture, 1 for second clock transition capture.

ca_spi_hw_init_periph.returns: Returns true if the peripheral was successfully initialized, false otherwise (e.g., invalid peripheral index).
ca_spi_hw_init_periph.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs low-level register configuration. It is NOT thread-safe and must not be called from an ISR. Before calling this, you must ensure the peripheral clock and GPIO pins are already configured using the appropriate hardware initialization functions. A common mistake is failing to clear the Mode Fault (MODF) flag on newer STM32 series (H7/H5/U5), which prevents the SPI from enabling; this function handles that sequence internally, so do not attempt to re-initialize registers manually after calling this.
ca_spi_hw_init_periph.usage: This function is typically called during the system startup phase or when reconfiguring a communication bus. It is part of the initialization sequence: first, initialize the system clocks and GPIOs, then call this function to set up the SPI hardware, and finally proceed to use functions like ca_spi_xfer or ca_spi_dma_xfer for data transmission. It is paired with the driver-level configuration logic to ensure the SPI bus is ready for master-mode operations.

ca_spi_hw_init_periph_slave.signature: bool ca_spi_hw_init_periph_slave(u8 num, u8 cpol, u8 cpha, u16 frame_size, ca_spi_slave_cb_t cb)
ca_spi_hw_init_periph_slave.brief: Initializes an SPI peripheral in slave mode with interrupt-driven data reception.

params.name: num
params.desc: The SPI peripheral index (typically 1, 2, or 3 depending on the MCU).

params.name: cpol
params.desc: Clock polarity: 0 for low level when idle, 1 for high level when idle.

params.name: cpha
params.desc: Clock phase: 0 for first clock transition capture, 1 for second.

params.name: frame_size
params.desc: Expected packet size in bytes. Values > 0 and <= SPI_DEF_PKT_SIZE are accepted.

params.name: cb
params.desc: Callback function pointer triggered when data is received. Pass NULL to disable interrupts.

ca_spi_hw_init_periph_slave.returns: Returns true if the peripheral was successfully initialized, false if the index is invalid or hardware configuration failed.
ca_spi_hw_init_periph_slave.notes: This function is non-blocking and configures the hardware registers to act as a passive slave. It is not thread-safe; ensure it is called during system initialization before any SPI communication occurs. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. A common mistake is passing an invalid SPI index or failing to provide a valid callback, which leaves the peripheral in a state where it cannot signal the application about incoming data. On some older hardware (F4xx), the function performs a specific sequence of reading registers to clear stale flags; failing to initialize correctly can lead to interrupt loops that starve other system tasks like USB.
ca_spi_hw_init_periph_slave.usage: This function is used when the device acts as a peripheral (slave) to an external master (e.g., a sensor or another MCU). It is typically called during the system boot sequence or driver initialization phase. It is often paired with GPIO configuration functions to set up the pins (MOSI, MISO, SCK, NSS) and is the prerequisite for the hardware to start responding to the master's clock signals.

ca_spi_hw_recv_handler.brief: Low-level SPI interrupt handler for slave mode to process incoming bytes and trigger callbacks.

params.name: num
params.desc: The SPI peripheral index (e.g., 1 for SPI1, 2 for SPI2). Must be within the valid range defined by the hardware abstraction layer.

ca_spi_hw_recv_handler.notes: This function is designed to be called exclusively from the hardware SPI interrupt service routine (ISR). It is not thread-safe and must never be called from a standard task context. Because it runs in an ISR, it must be extremely fast; avoid heavy processing inside the callback triggered by this function. A common mistake is failing to ensure the SPI peripheral is properly initialized via ca_spi_init before the interrupt is enabled, which will lead to accessing null or unconfigured hardware registers.
ca_spi_hw_recv_handler.usage: This function is the backbone of slave-mode SPI communication in caOS. It is typically invoked inside the system's SPIx_IRQHandler. It automatically manages the internal receive buffer and, once a full frame (as defined by the system configuration) is received, it executes a registered callback function to notify the application layer that data is ready for processing.

ca_spi_hw_slave_sync.brief: Resets and re-aligns the SPI slave hardware to recover from framing errors or overrun conditions.

params.name: num
params.desc: The SPI peripheral index (typically 1 to 3). Values outside this range are ignored.

ca_spi_hw_slave_sync.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a low-level hardware reset of the SPI peripheral by toggling the SPE (SPI Enable) bit. It is designed to be called when the slave detects a desynchronization, such as missing a clock edge or encountering an overrun error that halts communication. It is not thread-safe and should be used with caution; it is typically called from an interrupt context (like an EXTI pin handler) or a high-priority task when the SPI state machine is known to be stalled. A common beginner mistake is calling this during an active transfer, which will immediately abort the transaction and potentially corrupt the data stream.
ca_spi_hw_slave_sync.usage: This function is used in slave-mode SPI configurations to ensure the peripheral is ready for the next frame. It is typically paired with ca_spi_init during system startup and is invoked inside an interrupt service routine triggered by the Chip Select (CS) pin falling edge. By calling this, the driver ensures that any 'phantom' clock pulses or previous errors are cleared, effectively 're-arming' the slave to start fresh on the next incoming byte.

ca_spi_hw_slave_sync_pending.brief: Checks if a byte was already waiting in the SPI slave hardware buffer at the start of the last synchronization.

params.name: num
params.desc: The SPI peripheral index (typically 1 to 3 depending on the STM32 series).

ca_spi_hw_slave_sync_pending.returns: Returns 1 if a byte was pending (indicating a potential overrun or late synchronization), and 0 otherwise.
ca_spi_hw_slave_sync_pending.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it simply reads a status flag maintained by the driver. It is intended to be used in the context of SPI slave communication where timing is critical. The most common beginner mistake is ignoring the return value; if this returns 1, it means the master sent data before the slave was ready, which usually implies the slave's processing loop is too slow or the SPI interrupt priority is too low. It does not perform any hardware interaction itself, so it can be safely called from both tasks and ISRs.
ca_spi_hw_slave_sync_pending.usage: This function is typically used immediately after calling ca_spi_slave_sync() to verify the integrity of the incoming data frame. In a high-speed slave implementation, you pair it with ca_spi_slave_sync() to detect if the master started transmitting before the slave had finished clearing the previous frame. If it returns 1, the system should increment an error counter or trigger a re-synchronization logic to handle the data overrun.

ca_spi_hw_slave_tx_fill.brief: Preloads the SPI slave transmit FIFO with a specific byte to be sent back to the master upon reception.

params.name: num
params.desc: The SPI peripheral index (typically 1 to 3 depending on the MCU model). Values outside this range are ignored.

params.name: fill
params.desc: The byte to transmit on MISO. If 0, no data is preloaded, effectively disabling the auto-response behavior.

ca_spi_hw_slave_tx_fill.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs direct register access to the SPI peripheral. It is not thread-safe; if multiple tasks access the same SPI peripheral, you must ensure synchronization using other caOS primitives. It is safe to call from an ISR, but it is primarily intended for initialization or configuration phases. A common mistake is calling this function while the SPI peripheral is actively transferring data, which may lead to unexpected data being sent or FIFO corruption. Always ensure the SPI peripheral is properly initialized via ca_spi_init before calling this function.
ca_spi_hw_slave_tx_fill.usage: This function is used when the device acts as an SPI slave and needs to provide a constant 'dummy' or 'status' byte back to the master for every byte the master sends. It is typically called during the SPI configuration sequence, immediately after ca_spi_init, to ensure the hardware is ready to respond to the very first clock pulse from the master. It is often paired with an interrupt-driven mechanism where the IRQ handler continues to top up the FIFO after the initial byte is consumed.

ca_spi_hw_stop.brief: Safely disables an SPI peripheral by stopping transfers, clearing interrupts, and draining the FIFO.

params.name: num
params.desc: The SPI peripheral index (e.g., 1, 2, 3). Must correspond to a valid, initialized SPI hardware instance.

ca_spi_hw_stop.returns: Returns true if the peripheral was successfully stopped within the timeout period, false if the operation timed out or the peripheral index is invalid.
ca_spi_hw_stop.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should not be called from an ISR. It performs a 'graceful' shutdown by suspending active transfers and draining the hardware FIFO to prevent stale data from triggering interrupts after the peripheral is disabled. A common mistake is calling this while a DMA transfer is still active without waiting for the DMA to finish, which can lead to unpredictable hardware states. Always ensure the SPI is not in use by other tasks before calling this, as it forces the peripheral into a disabled state (SPE=0).
ca_spi_hw_stop.usage: Use this function when you need to reconfigure the SPI bus, enter a low-power mode, or shut down a communication channel. It is typically used in the teardown sequence of a driver: first, stop the peripheral with this function, then update any internal state tracking (like a global 'active' bitmask), and finally perform any necessary GPIO re-configuration. It is the mandatory counterpart to the initialization sequence.

ca_spi_hw_xfer.signature: bool ca_spi_hw_xfer(u8 num, u8 data, u8 *rx)
ca_spi_hw_xfer.brief: Performs a full-duplex SPI transfer of a single byte with a built-in timeout mechanism.

params.name: num
params.desc: The index of the SPI peripheral to use. Must correspond to a valid, initialized SPI hardware instance.

params.name: data
params.desc: The byte to transmit over the MOSI line.

params.name: rx
params.desc: Pointer to a memory location where the received byte from the MISO line will be stored. Must be a valid, non-NULL pointer.

ca_spi_hw_xfer.returns: Returns true if the transfer completed successfully within the timeout period. Returns false if the operation timed out, if a hardware error (like MODF) occurred, or if the SPI peripheral was disabled.
ca_spi_hw_xfer.notes: This function is blocking, meaning the calling task will wait in a loop until the hardware completes the transfer or the timeout expires. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR because it relies on system ticks and blocking loops. Before calling this, ensure the SPI peripheral has been properly initialized via the hardware abstraction layer. A common beginner mistake is to call this function without first asserting the Chip Select (CS) pin, which will result in the peripheral waiting indefinitely or receiving garbage data.
ca_spi_hw_xfer.usage: This function is the low-level building block for all SPI communication in caOS. It is typically used by higher-level drivers to implement byte-by-byte transmission. In a typical sequence, you would first call a function to assert the CS pin, then call ca_spi_hw_xfer one or more times to exchange data, and finally call a function to deassert the CS pin. It is often paired with ca_os_delay_ms if you need to implement a specific protocol timing requirement between bytes.

ca_spi_init.brief: Initializes the SPI hardware peripheral and configures its GPIO pins and operating mode.

params.name: cfg
params.desc: Pointer to a configuration structure containing SPI number (1-3), master/slave mode, clock polarity/phase, and GPIO settings. Must not be NULL.

ca_spi_init.returns: Returns true if the initialization was successful, false if the configuration pointer is invalid, the SPI number is out of range, or the hardware peripheral failed to initialize.
ca_spi_init.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should be called during the system initialization phase before any SPI communication tasks are started. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. The function handles clock enabling, GPIO pin multiplexing, and peripheral register setup. A common mistake is passing a NULL pointer or an uninitialized configuration structure, which will cause the function to return false immediately. If 'manage_cs' is set to true, the function also configures the Chip Select pin as an output and sets it to a high idle state.
ca_spi_init.usage: This function is the mandatory first step for any SPI communication. It is typically called once during system startup or task initialization. After calling ca_spi_init, you can proceed to use other SPI functions like ca_spi_xfer or ca_spi_dma_write. If you are using the CLI, this function also registers the SPI interface for debugging purposes if the feature is enabled.

ca_spi_init_dma.brief: Initializes a SPI peripheral for DMA-based data transfers.

params.name: cfg
params.desc: Pointer to a configuration structure containing SPI parameters (port number, master/slave mode, etc.). Must not be NULL and must specify master mode.

ca_spi_init_dma.returns: Returns true if the SPI peripheral was successfully initialized and DMA channels were bound and configured. Returns false if the configuration is invalid, the SPI port is already in use, no free DMA slots are available, or hardware binding fails.
ca_spi_init_dma.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should be called during system initialization before starting tasks. It is not callable from an ISR because it performs memory and resource allocation. It requires that the underlying SPI hardware is already clocked and that the DMA controller is available. A common beginner mistake is attempting to call this function multiple times for the same SPI port without checking if it is already initialized, or failing to verify the return value, which leads to silent failures in communication.
ca_spi_init_dma.usage: This function is used to prepare a SPI peripheral for high-performance, non-blocking data transfers. It is typically called once during the system startup phase, immediately after defining the configuration structure. It must be paired with subsequent calls to ca_spi_dma_xfer or ca_spi_dma_write/read to actually perform data operations. It is essential to ensure that the SPI port is not already registered in the system's internal DMA table before calling this function.

ca_spi_read_buf.signature: u16 ca_spi_read_buf(u8 spi_num, u8 *buf, u16 len)
ca_spi_read_buf.brief: Reads a specified number of bytes from an SPI peripheral by performing a dummy write for each byte.

params.name: spi_num
params.desc: The index of the SPI peripheral to read from. Must correspond to a previously initialized SPI port.

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the buffer where the received data will be stored. Must have enough allocated space for 'len' bytes.

params.name: len
params.desc: Number of bytes to read. A value of 0 results in no operation.

ca_spi_read_buf.returns: void. This function does not return status codes; it assumes the hardware transfer succeeds.
ca_spi_read_buf.notes: This function is blocking, meaning the CPU will wait for the SPI hardware to complete the transfer of every single byte before returning. It is not thread-safe by itself; if multiple tasks access the same SPI peripheral, you must protect this call with a mutex. It is not safe to call from an ISR because the blocking nature will stall the system interrupt latency. A common beginner mistake is providing a buffer pointer that is too small for the requested length, which will cause a memory corruption (buffer overflow).
ca_spi_read_buf.usage: This function is typically used in a master-slave communication sequence where the master needs to pull data from a slave device. It is usually paired with ca_spi_cs_assert to select the slave, followed by ca_spi_read_buf to perform the transaction, and finally ca_spi_cs_deassert to release the bus. It is often used in polling-based communication loops where the application logic waits for a specific signal or state before initiating the read.

ca_spi_recv_handler.brief: Handles incoming SPI data processing, typically triggered by an interrupt service routine (ISR).

params.name: spi_num
params.desc: The index of the SPI peripheral to handle. Must be a valid index within the range [1, SPI_MAX_NUM].

ca_spi_recv_handler.returns: void. This function does not return a value.
ca_spi_recv_handler.notes: This function is designed to be called from within an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) context to process hardware-level SPI events. It is not thread-safe in the sense that it should only be invoked by the specific hardware interrupt associated with the SPI peripheral. A common mistake is calling this function from a standard task context instead of the ISR, which can lead to race conditions or improper handling of hardware flags. Ensure the SPI peripheral has been properly initialized using ca_spi_init before this handler is ever triggered.
ca_spi_recv_handler.usage: This function is the bridge between the hardware SPI interrupt and the caOS driver layer. It is typically registered as the callback for the SPI interrupt vector. When the hardware signals that data has been received, the ISR calls this function to clear flags and move data into internal buffers. It is often used in conjunction with ca_spi_read_buf or ca_spi_dma_read to retrieve the processed data after the handler has performed the necessary low-level maintenance.

ca_spi_slave_sync.brief: Resets the SPI slave state machine to ensure frame alignment at the start of a transmission.

params.name: spi_num
params.desc: The SPI peripheral index (1 to SPI_MAX_NUM). Values outside this range are ignored.

ca_spi_slave_sync.notes: This function is designed to be called from an EXTI (External Interrupt) handler triggered by the SPI Chip Select (CS) pin falling edge. It is not thread-safe in the sense that it must be called in the context of the hardware event to be effective. If you fail to call this, the SPI slave may remain misaligned if the master starts transmitting mid-frame, or it may remain locked in an error state (like an overrun) on certain hardware versions. The most common mistake is calling this from a standard task instead of the CS interrupt, which misses the critical timing window required to reset the hardware state before the first clock pulse arrives.
ca_spi_slave_sync.usage: This function is used exclusively in SPI slave mode implementations. It is typically paired with an EXTI configuration that detects the CS pin state change. The sequence is: 1) Initialize the SPI peripheral using ca_spi_init, 2) Configure the CS pin as an input with an EXTI interrupt using ca_exti_init, 3) Inside the EXTI ISR, call ca_spi_slave_sync to clear the hardware state, and 4) Proceed to handle the data transfer using ca_spi_recv_handler or similar.

ca_spi_stop.brief: Disables a specific SPI peripheral and clears its internal active status in the OS.

params.name: spi_num
params.desc: The SPI peripheral index to stop. Valid values are 1, 2, or 3. Values outside this range will cause the function to return false immediately.

ca_spi_stop.returns: Returns true if the SPI peripheral was successfully stopped and the internal state updated. Returns false if the provided spi_num is invalid or if the underlying hardware stop operation fails.
ca_spi_stop.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should not be called from an ISR. It performs a hard stop on the SPI peripheral, meaning any ongoing DMA transfers or communication will be abruptly terminated. You must call ca_spi_init() again before attempting to use the SPI peripheral after calling this function, as the internal configuration state is cleared. A common mistake is calling this function while a DMA transfer is still in progress, which can leave the hardware in an inconsistent state.
ca_spi_stop.usage: This function is typically used during system shutdown, power-saving modes, or when reconfiguring the SPI bus for a different protocol. It is usually paired with ca_spi_init() for setup and is often called after ensuring all SPI-related tasks have been parked or suspended using ca_os_sleep() or similar synchronization primitives. It ensures that the CLI and DMA drivers no longer attempt to access the peripheral, preventing potential system crashes or memory corruption.

ca_spi_write_buf.signature: u16 ca_spi_write_buf(u8 spi_num, const u8 *buf, u16 len)
ca_spi_write_buf.brief: Transmits a buffer of data over a specified SPI peripheral.

params.name: spi_num
params.desc: The index of the SPI peripheral to use (e.g., 0, 1). Must correspond to a peripheral initialized via ca_spi_init.

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the memory buffer containing the data to be sent. Must not be NULL.

params.name: len
params.desc: Number of bytes to transmit from the buffer. A value of 0 results in no action.

ca_spi_write_buf.notes: This function is a blocking call; it will not return until every byte in the buffer has been processed by the hardware. It is not thread-safe by itself, meaning if multiple tasks access the same SPI peripheral, you must protect this call with a mutex or semaphore. It is generally not safe to call this from an ISR because the blocking nature will stall the system interrupt latency. Ensure the SPI peripheral is properly initialized with ca_spi_init before calling this function, or the system may hang or trigger a hardware fault.
ca_spi_write_buf.usage: This function is typically used to send command sequences or data frames to external SPI peripherals like sensors, displays, or flash memory. The standard workflow involves: 1) Initializing the SPI bus with ca_spi_init, 2) Asserting the Chip Select (CS) line using ca_spi_cs_assert, 3) Calling ca_spi_write_buf to send the payload, and 4) Deasserting the CS line with ca_spi_cs_deassert. It is often paired with ca_spi_read_buf when full-duplex communication is required.

ca_spi_xfer.brief: Performs a full-duplex SPI transfer by sending one byte and receiving one byte simultaneously.

params.name: spi_num
params.desc: The index of the SPI peripheral to use (e.g., 0, 1, 2). Must match the hardware configuration initialized by ca_spi_init.

params.name: data
params.desc: The byte of data to transmit over the MOSI line.

ca_spi_xfer.returns: Returns the byte received from the MISO line during the transfer. There is no error code returned; the function assumes the hardware is ready.
ca_spi_xfer.notes: This function is a blocking call, meaning the CPU will wait until the entire byte has been shifted out and the corresponding byte has been shifted in before returning. It is generally not safe to call this from an ISR unless the underlying hardware driver explicitly supports it, as blocking in an ISR can crash the system. Ensure that ca_spi_init has been called for the specific spi_num before use. A common beginner mistake is to call this function without asserting the Chip Select (CS) pin first using ca_spi_cs_assert, which will result in the peripheral ignoring the data.
ca_spi_xfer.usage: This function is the fundamental building block for SPI communication. It is typically used in a sequence: first, call ca_spi_cs_assert to select the target device, then call ca_spi_xfer one or more times to exchange data, and finally call ca_spi_cs_deassert to release the bus. For larger data transfers, developers often wrap this in a loop or use ca_spi_write_buf, but ca_spi_xfer remains the core mechanism for synchronous byte-level interaction.

ca_spinlock_cooperative_init.brief: Initializes a cooperative spinlock structure to the free state.

params.name: lock
params.desc: Pointer to the spinlock structure to initialize. Must not be NULL.

ca_spinlock_cooperative_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a simple memory write followed by a Data Memory Barrier (__DMB) to ensure the initialization is visible to all CPU cores. It is safe to call from any context, including ISRs, though it is typically called during system startup. The most common beginner mistake is failing to initialize the lock before passing it to lock or trylock functions, which leads to undefined behavior as the 'key' will contain random garbage memory. Always ensure the memory address provided is valid and not currently being accessed by other tasks during the initialization phase.
ca_spinlock_cooperative_init.usage: This function is the mandatory first step when using a cooperative spinlock.
