ca_strtol_index.usage: This function is primarily used in CLI (Command Line Interface) parsing to extract numerical parameters from user input strings. It is typically used in a sequence: first, locate the start of a token using ca_skip_sp, then call ca_strtol_index to extract the value, and finally use the returned 'index' to advance the pointer for the next token. It is often paired with ca_strncmp to identify commands and ca_stdout_printf_n to report errors if the conversion fails or the value is out of range.

ca_sw_timer_count_active.brief: Returns the total number of software timers currently in the RUNNING state.
ca_sw_timer_count_active.returns: An unsigned 8-bit integer (u8) representing the count of active timers. Returns 0 if no timers are currently running or if the timer system is not initialized.
ca_sw_timer_count_active.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes in constant time relative to the maximum number of timers defined in the system (CA_TIMER_MAX). It is thread-safe as it performs a read-only iteration over the global timer array. It can be safely called from an ISR, though it is primarily intended for monitoring tasks. A common mistake is assuming this returns the total number of created timers; it specifically filters for those that are both 'active' and in the 'CA_TIMER_RUNNING' state, ignoring stopped or expired timers.
ca_sw_timer_count_active.usage: This function is typically used in diagnostic or monitoring tasks to provide system health feedback. It is often paired with ca_sw_timer_get_state or ca_sw_timer_get_remaining to provide a detailed overview of the system's background activity. Developers use it to verify that periodic tasks are correctly scheduled and that one-shot timers have not unexpectedly stopped, often printing the result via ca_stdout_printf_n for debugging purposes.

ca_sw_timer_create.signature: ca_sw_timer_handle_t ca_sw_timer_create(u32 period_ms, ca_sw_timer_mode_t mode, ca_timer_callback_t callback, void *arg)
ca_sw_timer_create.brief: Allocates and initializes a software timer object for periodic or one-shot tasks.

params.name: period_ms
params.desc: Timer duration in milliseconds. Must be greater than 0.

params.name: mode
params.desc: Operation mode: CA_TIMER_PERIODIC (restarts automatically) or CA_TIMER_ONESHOT (runs once).

params.name: callback
params.desc: Function pointer to be executed when the timer expires.

params.name: arg
params.desc: Optional pointer to data passed to the callback function.

ca_sw_timer_create.returns: Returns a valid ca_sw_timer_handle_t (index + 1) on success, or CA_TIMER_INVALID if the system is not initialized, the period is 0, or no free timer slots are available.
ca_sw_timer_create.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses a spinlock to protect the internal timer array during allocation. It is non-blocking, meaning it returns immediately after finding a slot. You must call ca_sw_timer_init() before using this function, otherwise it will always return CA_TIMER_INVALID. A common mistake is forgetting to check if the returned handle is CA_TIMER_INVALID before passing it to ca_sw_timer_start(), which can lead to undefined behavior or system crashes.
ca_sw_timer_create.usage: This function is typically used during the initialization phase of a module or task to reserve a timer resource. It is part of a lifecycle: first, create the timer with this function, then start it using ca_sw_timer_start(), and finally, if the timer is no longer needed, release the slot using ca_sw_timer_delete(). It is commonly used for background tasks like LED blinking, periodic sensor polling, or implementing timeouts for communication protocols.

ca_sw_timer_delete.brief: Permanently removes a software timer from the system, freeing its slot for future use.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The unique identifier returned by ca_sw_timer_create. Must be a valid handle; CA_TIMER_INVALID or out-of-bounds values will cause the function to return false.

ca_sw_timer_delete.returns: Returns true if the timer was successfully deactivated and removed. Returns false if the handle is invalid, the timer was already inactive, or the software timer system was not initialized.
ca_sw_timer_delete.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses internal spinlocks to protect the timer array during modification. It is non-blocking, meaning it will return immediately after updating the timer's internal state. You must ensure that the timer handle is not used again after calling this function, as it will no longer point to a valid, active timer. A common mistake is attempting to delete a timer that has already been deleted or was never created, which will result in a false return value.
ca_sw_timer_delete.usage: Use this function when a periodic or one-shot timer is no longer needed to prevent unnecessary processing overhead. It is typically used in the cleanup phase of a task or when a specific application state (e.g., a timeout monitor) is exited. It is usually paired with ca_sw_timer_create at the start of a process and called before the associated task or module is destroyed or re-initialized.

ca_sw_timer_detach.brief: Detaches a software timer from its owner task, preventing the system from automatically managing or reclaiming it.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The handle of the timer to detach. Must be a valid handle returned by ca_sw_timer_create. Passing CA_TIMER_INVALID or an out-of-bounds index will result in failure.

ca_sw_timer_detach.returns: Returns true if the timer was successfully detached, false if the handle is invalid, the timer is already inactive, or the system timer service is not initialized.
ca_sw_timer_detach.notes: This function is thread-safe and uses internal spinlocks to protect the timer registry. It is not intended to be called from an ISR because it performs internal locking operations that could lead to deadlocks or system instability. The primary purpose of detaching is to 'orphan' a timer so that it persists even if the task that created it terminates or is destroyed. A common mistake is to detach a timer and then lose the handle, which makes it impossible to stop or delete the timer later, leading to a resource leak.
ca_sw_timer_detach.usage: Use this function when you need a timer to outlive the task that initialized it, such as a background periodic task or a driver-level timer that must continue running after a CLI command or setup task finishes. It is typically used in the sequence: ca_sw_timer_create -> ca_sw_timer_detach -> ca_sw_timer_start. Once detached, the timer is no longer tied to the lifecycle of the creator, meaning the system will not automatically clean it up if the creator task exits.

ca_sw_timer_get_remaining.brief: Retrieves the remaining time in milliseconds for a specific software timer.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The handle of the timer to query. Must be a valid handle returned by ca_sw_timer_create. Passing CA_TIMER_INVALID or an out-of-bounds value will result in a return of 0.

ca_sw_timer_get_remaining.returns: Returns the remaining time in milliseconds if the timer is active. Returns 0 if the timer is inactive, not initialized, or if the provided handle is invalid.
ca_sw_timer_get_remaining.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it performs a simple read operation on the internal timer structure. It can be safely called from an ISR, provided the timer system has been initialized via ca_sw_timer_init. A common mistake is assuming that a return value of 0 implies the timer has expired; it could also mean the timer was never started or has been stopped. Always verify the timer state using ca_sw_timer_get_state if you need to distinguish between an expired timer and an inactive one.
ca_sw_timer_get_remaining.usage: This function is typically used for monitoring or diagnostic purposes within a task loop. It is often paired with ca_sw_timer_get_state to provide a full status report of the system's background tasks. Developers use it to check how much time is left before a periodic or one-shot event triggers, allowing for dynamic adjustments to application logic or UI updates based on the remaining duration.

ca_sw_timer_get_state.brief: Retrieves the current operational state of a software timer.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The unique identifier returned by ca_sw_timer_create. Must be a valid handle; CA_TIMER_INVALID or values exceeding CA_TIMER_MAX will result in an error state.

ca_sw_timer_get_state.returns: Returns a ca_sw_timer_state_t enum value. CA_TIMER_RUNNING indicates the timer is active and counting down. CA_TIMER_STOPPED indicates the timer is either inactive, has expired, or the handle provided was invalid.
ca_sw_timer_get_state.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, making it safe to call from multiple tasks. It is not intended for use inside Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs) unless explicitly documented as such by the OS architecture, though it is generally safe as it performs a simple memory read. The most common beginner mistake is failing to check if the timer handle is valid before calling this function, or assuming that a 'STOPPED' state implies the timer was never started rather than having simply finished its cycle.
ca_sw_timer_get_state.usage: This function is typically used in monitoring loops or diagnostic tasks to check the health or progress of background processes. It is usually paired with ca_sw_timer_create during system initialization, and then used periodically within a while(1) loop alongside ca_sw_timer_get_remaining to display system status or trigger conditional logic based on whether a specific task's timer is still active.

ca_sw_timer_init.brief: Initializes the software timer system and spawns the background daemon task.
ca_sw_timer_init.returns: Returns true if the system was successfully initialized or was already initialized. Returns false if the internal daemon task could not be created.
ca_sw_timer_init.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called once during system startup before any other timer operations are performed. It initializes the internal timer structures and creates a dedicated daemon task that manages the timing logic; if this task fails to start, the timer system will not function. It is not callable from an ISR. A common mistake is attempting to create or start timers before calling this initialization function, which will lead to undefined behavior or system instability.
ca_sw_timer_init.usage: This function is the mandatory entry point for the software timer subsystem. It is typically called once in the main initialization sequence of the application, before any calls to ca_sw_timer_create or ca_sw_timer_start. It pairs with the rest of the timer API to ensure that the background daemon is running to process timer expirations and execute callbacks.

ca_sw_timer_reset.brief: Resets a software timer's remaining time to its original period without changing its running or stopped state.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The unique identifier of the timer to reset. Must be a valid handle returned by ca_sw_timer_create. Passing CA_TIMER_INVALID or a value out of range will cause the function to return false.

ca_sw_timer_reset.returns: Returns true if the timer was successfully reset. Returns false if the timer system is not initialized, the handle is invalid, or the timer is not currently active (not created/already deleted).
ca_sw_timer_reset.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses internal spinlocks to protect the timer structure during the update. It is non-blocking, meaning it will not put the calling task into a wait state. While it can technically be called from an ISR, it is generally intended for task-level logic. The most common mistake is assuming this function starts a stopped timer; it only resets the countdown value. If the timer is currently stopped, it will remain stopped with the period reloaded, and if it is running, it will continue running from the full period duration.
ca_sw_timer_reset.usage: Use this function when you need to restart a timeout period for an active timer, such as a watchdog-style heartbeat or a command-timeout mechanism. It is typically used in a sequence: first, create the timer with ca_sw_timer_create, then start it with ca_sw_timer_start, and use ca_sw_timer_reset whenever the event associated with the timer occurs to prevent it from expiring. It is often paired with ca_sw_timer_stop if the monitoring logic needs to be suspended entirely.

ca_sw_timer_set_period.brief: Updates the interval period of an existing software timer without resetting its current countdown.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The unique identifier of the timer to modify. Must be a valid handle returned by ca_sw_timer_create and not CA_TIMER_INVALID.

params.name: period_ms
params.desc: The new duration in milliseconds. Must be greater than 0.

ca_sw_timer_set_period.returns: Returns true if the period was successfully updated, false if the handle is invalid, the timer is inactive, the period is 0, or the timer system is not initialized.
ca_sw_timer_set_period.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses internal spinlocks to protect the timer structure during the update. It is non-blocking, meaning it returns immediately after updating the internal configuration. Crucially, it does not reset the 'remaining_ms' counter; the new period will only take effect starting from the next cycle of the timer. A common mistake is assuming the timer will immediately restart or reset its current countdown upon calling this function, which is not the case.
ca_sw_timer_set_period.usage: This function is typically used in dynamic applications where the frequency of a periodic task needs to change based on system state (e.g., increasing a polling rate when a sensor detects activity). It is used after the timer has been created with ca_sw_timer_create and started with ca_sw_timer_start. It is often paired with ca_sw_timer_get_state to ensure the timer is active before attempting to modify its period.

ca_sw_timer_start.brief: Starts a previously created software timer, enabling it to begin counting down its period.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The unique identifier returned by ca_sw_timer_create. Must be a valid handle (not CA_TIMER_INVALID) and within the range [1, CA_TIMER_MAX].

ca_sw_timer_start.returns: Returns true if the timer was successfully started. Returns false if the system is not initialized, the handle is invalid, or the timer is not in an active state.
ca_sw_timer_start.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses internal spinlocks to protect the timer state during the update. It is non-blocking, meaning it returns immediately after updating the timer's internal state. You must ensure the timer has been created via ca_sw_timer_create before calling this; attempting to start an uninitialized or deleted timer will fail. A common mistake is forgetting to check the return value, which can hide errors if the timer handle was already invalidated or if the system timer module failed to initialize. Note that this function is not intended to be called from an ISR, as it uses spinlocks that may conflict with system-level locking mechanisms.
ca_sw_timer_start.usage: This function is typically used to trigger periodic tasks or one-shot delays in the background. It is usually paired with ca_sw_timer_create during system initialization to allocate the timer, and ca_sw_timer_stop or ca_sw_timer_delete when the task is no longer needed. In a typical workflow, you create the timer once, then call ca_sw_timer_start whenever you need to restart the countdown, such as resetting a watchdog-style timer or re-triggering a periodic sensor sampling task.

ca_sw_timer_stop.brief: Stops a running software timer, preventing its callback from executing.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The unique identifier of the timer to stop. Must be a valid handle returned by ca_sw_timer_create. Passing CA_TIMER_INVALID or an out-of-bounds index will result in failure.

ca_sw_timer_stop.returns: Returns true if the timer was successfully stopped. Returns false if the handle is invalid, the timer was not active, or the timer system is not initialized.
ca_sw_timer_stop.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses a spinlock to protect the internal timer state during the update. It is non-blocking, meaning it returns immediately after updating the state. While it is technically safe to call from an ISR due to the spinlock implementation, it is generally recommended to use it from task context to manage application-level logic. A common mistake is attempting to stop a timer that has already expired or was never started, which will return false; always check the return value if your logic depends on the timer being successfully halted.
ca_sw_timer_stop.usage: This function is used to cancel pending periodic or one-shot events before they trigger. It is typically paired with ca_sw_timer_start to manage state machines or timeout mechanisms. In a typical lifecycle, you create a timer with ca_sw_timer_create, start it when an operation begins, and call ca_sw_timer_stop if the operation completes early or is aborted by the user, preventing the callback from firing unexpectedly.

ca_syslog_dropped.brief: Returns the total count of syslog messages that failed to be queued due to a full buffer.
ca_syslog_dropped.returns: Returns a u32 value representing the cumulative number of dropped syslog messages since system boot or last reset.
ca_syslog_dropped.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it simply returns the current value of a static counter. It is safe to call from both tasks and ISRs. The counter increments only when the syslog queue is full and a 'trysend' operation fails. A high or rapidly increasing value indicates that the syslog service is unable to process logs as fast as they are being generated, suggesting a need to increase the queue size or optimize the logging frequency. The most common mistake is assuming this value resets automatically; it is a cumulative counter that persists until the system is rebooted.
ca_syslog_dropped.usage: This function is typically used for system health monitoring and diagnostics. It is often called within a periodic status report task or a CLI command handler to provide visibility into system performance. Developers use it to verify if the logging subsystem is keeping up with the application's demand, often pairing it with other diagnostic functions like ca_net_stats to get a complete picture of system stability. It is typically used in a sequence where the developer checks the network status, then checks the syslog drop count to see if the logging backend is saturated.

ca_syslog_send.brief: Sends a log message to the system logging service queue for remote transmission.

params.name: severity
params.desc: The priority level of the log (e.g., SYSLOG_SEV_INFO, SYSLOG_SEV_ERROR). Must be a valid severity constant defined in the system headers.

params.name: msg
params.desc: Pointer to the null-terminated string to be logged. If NULL, the function returns immediately without action.

ca_syslog_send.returns: void. This function does not return a status code; if the internal queue is full, the message is silently dropped and the internal drop counter is incremented.
ca_syslog_send.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it uses a try-send mechanism on the internal queue. It is safe to call from tasks, but be cautious when calling from high-frequency ISRs as it performs string copying which consumes CPU cycles. The function requires the syslog service to be initialized via ca_syslog_service_init before use. A common mistake is assuming the message is delivered immediately; because it uses a queue, the message is only buffered and will be sent later by the syslog background task.
ca_syslog_send.usage: Used to report system events, errors, or status updates to a remote syslog server. It is typically used after the network stack is ready (ca_syslog_service_net_ready). The standard lifecycle involves initializing the service at startup, setting the server address with ca_syslog_service_set_server, and then calling ca_syslog_send whenever an event occurs. If you notice logs are missing, check ca_syslog_dropped to see if the queue is overflowing.

ca_syslog_service_init.signature: void ca_syslog_service_init(ca_ipv4_t server_ip, ca_mac_t local_mac, u8 facility)
ca_syslog_service_init.brief: Initializes the internal configuration for the Syslog logging service.

params.name: server_ip
params.desc: The IPv4 address of the remote Syslog server. Must be a valid structure containing the server's IP.

params.name: local_mac
params.desc: The MAC address of the local network interface. Used for identifying the source of logs.

params.name: facility
params.desc: The Syslog facility code (e.g., SYSLOG_FAC_LOCAL0) defining the category of the application logs.

ca_syslog_service_init.returns: This function returns void and does not provide a status code.
ca_syslog_service_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs internal variable initialization, including setting up a mutex for configuration thread-safety. It is not intended to be called from an ISR, as it performs mutex initialization which is not ISR-safe. The most common mistake is calling this function before the network stack or the OS scheduler is fully prepared, or attempting to send logs before the service has been properly initialized. Ensure that the provided IP and MAC structures are correctly populated before passing them to this function.
ca_syslog_service_init.usage: This function is typically called during the system startup phase, immediately after network hardware initialization but before the main application loop begins. It is part of the standard initialization sequence: ca_dhcp_service_init -> ca_syslog_service_init -> ca_syslog_service_start. It must be called once to prepare the internal state before any calls to ca_syslog_send are made. If the system requires dynamic reconfiguration of the Syslog server, this function may be called again, provided the application logic handles the potential race conditions.

ca_syslog_service_net_ready.brief: Signals to the syslog service that the network interface is initialized and ready for transmission.
ca_syslog_service_net_ready.notes: This function is a non-blocking, thread-safe flag setter. It is designed to be called once the network stack has successfully acquired an IP address or established a link. It is safe to call from an ISR, as it only performs a simple boolean assignment. The most common mistake is calling this before the network stack is actually ready, which may cause the syslog task to attempt sending packets over an uninitialized interface, leading to dropped logs or system instability.
ca_syslog_service_net_ready.usage: This function is used in the initialization sequence of network-dependent services. It is typically called after the network stack (e.g., DHCP or static IP configuration) has confirmed a valid connection. It acts as a gatekeeper, ensuring that the syslog task does not attempt to transmit data until the underlying network hardware and protocol stack are fully operational. It is usually paired with ca_syslog_service_start to initialize the task and then this function to enable its network-dependent operations.

ca_syslog_service_set_server.brief: Updates the destination IPv4 address for the Syslog service and resets the cached MAC address.

params.name: server_ip
params.desc: The target IPv4 address of the Syslog server. Ensure this is a valid network-byte-order address.

ca_syslog_service_set_server.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses a mutex to protect the internal configuration variables. It is a blocking function because it waits to acquire the mutex, so it must NEVER be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine). A common mistake is calling this function before the Syslog service has been initialized, which may lead to undefined behavior or race conditions if the service is already attempting to send logs. Always ensure the network stack is ready before updating the server address.
ca_syslog_service_set_server.usage: This function is typically used during system configuration or when a user changes the Syslog server destination via a CLI command. It is usually paired with ca_syslog_service_init to set up the service, and ca_syslog_send to transmit logs. By setting the internal MAC cache to false, it forces the network stack to perform a new ARP resolution for the new IP address, ensuring that logs are routed correctly to the updated server.

ca_syslog_service_start.brief: Initializes and launches the background task responsible for sending system logs to a remote server.
ca_syslog_service_start.returns: This function returns void and does not provide a status code; it assumes the underlying task creation will succeed.
ca_syslog_service_start.notes: This function is non-blocking as it merely registers a new task with the RTOS scheduler. It is not thread-safe to call this from an ISR, as it involves memory allocation and task list management within the kernel. Before calling this, you must ensure the system memory and the syslog service have been initialized via ca_syslog_service_init. A common beginner mistake is calling this function multiple times during runtime, which may lead to multiple instances of the syslog task competing for resources or causing memory leaks.
ca_syslog_service_start.usage: This function is typically called during the system startup phase inside ca_os_main, alongside other network service starters like ca_arp_service_start and ca_dhcp_service_start. It is part of the initialization sequence that prepares the device for network communication. Once started, the syslog task runs independently in the background, waiting for log messages to be sent via ca_syslog_send. It is rarely called again unless the service needs to be explicitly restarted after a critical failure.

ca_system_banner.brief: Prints the system identification banner and hardware status information to the configured stdout.

params.name: arg
params.desc: Reserved for future use. Pass NULL as it is currently ignored by the implementation.

ca_system_banner.returns: Always returns 0. The return value is currently unused.
ca_system_banner.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should not be called from an ISR. It performs blocking operations (via ca_os_sleep) when using UART to ensure the transmission buffer is not overwhelmed. A common mistake is calling this function before the stdout subsystem (UART or USB CDC) has been fully initialized, which will result in silent failure or garbled output. When using USB CDC, the function checks for a connection; if the host has not opened the terminal, it exits immediately to prevent data loss, relying on the CDC event handler to trigger a reprint later.
ca_system_banner.usage: Used primarily during system boot to display firmware version, MCU details, and hardware health metrics. It is also invoked dynamically by the USB CDC event handler when a terminal connection is established to ensure the user sees the banner upon opening the serial port. It pairs with stdout initialization functions and relies on system status functions like ca_os_clock_get_freq and ca_memory_get_total_memory to gather its report data.

ca_task_set_emergency_exec.signature: bool ca_task_set_emergency_exec(ca_task_handle_t h, ca_emergency_fn_t func, u32 emerg_param)
ca_task_set_emergency_exec.brief: Registers a callback function to be executed when a task encounters a critical failure or emergency state.

params.name: h
params.desc: The handle of the target task. Must be a valid handle obtained from ca_os_task_handle or similar.

params.name: func
params.desc: A pointer to the function to execute. Must match the required signature for emergency handlers.

params.name: emerg_param
params.desc: A user-defined 32-bit value passed to the emergency function when triggered.

ca_task_set_emergency_exec.returns: Returns true if the emergency handler was successfully registered, false otherwise (e.g., invalid handle, task not found, or task memory corrupted).
ca_task_set_emergency_exec.notes: This function is thread-safe and uses internal interrupt disabling to ensure atomic updates to the task control block. It is safe to call from an ISR because it manages its own critical section by disabling interrupts, but it is generally intended for task-level configuration. A common mistake is passing an uninitialized or NULL handle, which will cause the function to return false. The function performs a sanity check on the task's internal 'canary' value; if the task memory is corrupted, the function will refuse to register the handler to prevent unpredictable behavior.
ca_task_set_emergency_exec.usage: This function is typically used during the system initialization phase or when a task is dynamically created to define a 'last resort' recovery routine. It is often paired with task creation logic to ensure that if a task crashes or hits a hardware fault (like a divide-by-zero), the system can execute a cleanup routine before the OS handles the fault. It is a critical component of the system's self-healing strategy, allowing developers to define task-specific recovery logic that runs before a potential system reset.

ca_task_swap_param.brief: Swaps the current task's primary parameter (p1) with its emergency parameter (emerg_param).
ca_task_swap_param.returns: This function returns nothing (void). If no task is currently running (g_current_task is NULL), the function performs no operation.
ca_task_swap_param.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes in constant time. It is thread-safe because it only modifies the context of the currently executing task, but it must NOT be called from an ISR because the global 'g_current_task' pointer is only valid within the context of a running task. The primary purpose is to allow a task to temporarily switch its operational data pointer during an emergency or error-handling routine. A common beginner mistake is assuming this function automatically handles the logic of the task; it only swaps the pointers, so the task code itself must be written to check which parameter is currently active or handle the data accordingly.
ca_task_swap_param.usage: This function is used to implement a 'fail-safe' or 'emergency' mode within a task without needing to stop or restart the task. It is typically used in a sequence where the task initializes an emergency buffer, performs normal work, and then calls this function when a fault is detected to switch to a recovery buffer. It is often paired with ca_task_set_emergency_exec during the task setup phase to ensure the emergency parameter is valid before the swap is ever triggered.

ca_tcp_abort.brief: Immediately terminates a TCP connection by sending a RST packet and freeing the associated resources.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The connection identifier (1 to TCP_MAX_CONN). Passing 0 or an invalid handle results in no action.

ca_tcp_abort.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it uses an internal mutex to protect the connection state. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR because it attempts to acquire a mutex. Unlike ca_tcp_close(), which performs a graceful shutdown (FIN handshake), ca_tcp_abort() forces an immediate closure by sending a TCP RST (Reset) packet. This is essential when a connection is stuck in a non-established state (like SYN_SENT) where a graceful close would be ignored by the stack. A common beginner mistake is calling this function while the connection is still being processed by other tasks, which can lead to race conditions if the handle is not properly cleared or invalidated immediately after the call.
ca_tcp_abort.usage: Use this function when you need to forcefully reset a connection, such as during error recovery, service restarts, or when a peer becomes unresponsive. It is typically used in the cleanup phase of a service lifecycle, often paired with ca_memset to clear the service structure after the connection is aborted. It is the standard way to ensure that a stale PCB (Protocol Control Block) does not linger in the system memory or on the network wire, which would otherwise cause issues like phantom connections or resource exhaustion.

ca_tcp_accept.brief: Blocks the calling task until a new TCP connection request arrives on the specified listening handle.

params.name: listen_handle
params.desc: The handle returned by a previous call to ca_tcp_listen. Must be in the range [1, TCP_MAX_LISTEN].

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time in milliseconds to wait for a connection. Use 0 for non-blocking polling or a large value (e.g., CA_WAIT_FOREVER) for indefinite blocking.

ca_tcp_accept.returns: Returns a valid connection handle (non-zero) if a connection is successfully established. Returns 0 if the timeout expires, the handle is invalid, or the listener is not in blocking mode.
ca_tcp_accept.notes: This function is blocking and relies on semaphore waiting mechanisms, meaning it must only be called from a task context; it is NOT thread-safe to call from an ISR. The function internally manages a queue of connection requests and automatically filters out 'stale' handles (connections that closed or were recycled before the task could process them). A common beginner mistake is assuming that a non-zero return value guarantees an active connection; always verify the connection state or handle potential immediate closure. Ensure the listener is properly initialized via ca_tcp_listen before calling this function, and remember that the returned handle is owned by the calling task until explicitly closed.
ca_tcp_accept.usage: This function is the entry point for TCP server applications. It is typically used inside a continuous loop within a dedicated server task. The standard lifecycle involves: 1) Initializing the listener with ca_tcp_listen, 2) Calling ca_tcp_accept to block until a client connects, 3) Performing data exchange using functions like ca_tcp_send or ca_tcp_recv, and 4) Releasing the connection handle using ca_tcp_close. In multi-threaded environments, this function allows the server to remain idle without consuming CPU cycles until a client arrives.

ca_tcp_close.brief: Gracefully terminates an established TCP connection by sending a FIN packet.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The connection identifier returned by ca_tcp_accept or ca_tcp_connect. Passing 0 or an invalid handle results in an immediate return.

ca_tcp_close.returns: void. This function does not provide feedback on whether the FIN packet was successfully transmitted or acknowledged by the peer.
ca_tcp_close.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses an internal mutex to protect the connection state. It is NOT callable from an ISR because it performs blocking operations, including mutex locking and ca_os_sleep. The function initiates a graceful shutdown by attempting to send a FIN packet; if the driver ring is full, it will retry for a limited number of attempts. A common mistake is assuming the connection is closed immediately upon return; the TCP stack still needs to process the handshake completion in the background. If the handle is stale or the connection has already been closed/reassigned to a new session, the function safely ignores the request to prevent tearing down the wrong connection.
ca_tcp_close.usage: Use this function when you are finished with a TCP session to allow the remote peer to close its side cleanly. It is typically called after completing a transaction, such as sending an HTTP response or finishing an iperf test. It is the standard cleanup function paired with ca_tcp_accept or ca_tcp_connect. If you need to force-close a connection regardless of the state (e.g., during a hard error or timeout), use ca_tcp_abort instead.

ca_tcp_connect.brief: Initiates a TCP connection to a remote host and returns a handle for subsequent communication.

params.name: cfg
params.desc: Pointer to a configuration structure containing local/remote IP, ports, and optional callback functions. Must not be NULL.

ca_tcp_connect.returns: Returns a non-zero handle (1 to TCP_MAX_CONN) on success. Returns 0U if the connection fails, the configuration is invalid, or no connection slots are available.
ca_tcp_connect.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses internal mutexes to manage connection slots. It is NOT callable from an ISR because it performs blocking operations (like ARP resolution and semaphore waiting). If 'on_connected' is NULL in the configuration, the function will block the calling thread until the connection is established or the timeout expires. A common mistake is failing to check the returned handle for 0U, which leads to passing an invalid handle to subsequent functions like ca_tcp_send or ca_tcp_close. Always ensure the network stack is initialized before calling this. Note that if the connection fails, the slot is not reserved, so calling ca_tcp_close on a 0 handle is a logic error.
ca_tcp_connect.usage: Typically used in network service tasks (e.g., MQTT, Modbus) to establish a client-side connection. The sequence starts by populating the configuration struct, calling ca_tcp_connect, and checking the returned handle. If successful, the handle is stored and used for data exchange; finally, the connection is terminated using ca_tcp_close when the service shuts down or encounters a fatal error. If the connection is not established, you must not call ca_tcp_close, as the slot may not be fully allocated or may have been recycled by the stack for other purposes.

ca_tcp_is_connected.brief: Checks if a TCP connection handle is active, established, or in a half-closed state with pending data.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The connection identifier returned by ca_tcp_connect or ca_tcp_accept. Passing 0 or an invalid handle returns false.

ca_tcp_is_connected.returns: Returns true if the connection is ESTABLISHED, or if it is in CLOSE_WAIT with unread data remaining in the buffer. Returns false if the handle is invalid, the connection is fully closed, or the state is not ready for data processing.
ca_tcp_is_connected.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it performs a read-only check on the internal PCB (Protocol Control Block) structure. It is safe to call from an ISR, though it is primarily intended for use within application tasks. A critical nuance is that it returns true during the CLOSE_WAIT state if data is still queued; this prevents data loss by allowing the application to drain the receive buffer before finally closing the connection. The most common beginner mistake is to ignore the return value and attempt to call ca_tcp_recv on a closed handle, which will fail or return invalid data.
ca_tcp_is_connected.usage: This function is the standard guard for TCP communication loops. It is used to verify that a socket is ready for data exchange after a connection attempt (ca_tcp_connect) or an incoming request (ca_tcp_accept). It is typically placed at the start of a 'while' loop to ensure the connection is still alive before calling ca_tcp_recv. When the function returns false, the application should stop processing, perform any necessary cleanup, and call ca_tcp_close to release the handle back to the system.

ca_tcp_listen.brief: Initializes a TCP passive socket to listen for incoming connection requests on a specific port.

params.name: cfg
params.desc: Pointer to a configuration structure containing the local IP, port, and optional callback functions. Must not be NULL.

ca_tcp_listen.returns: Returns a non-zero handle (1 to TCP_MAX_LISTEN) on success, which is used to identify this listener in subsequent calls. Returns 0 if no free slots are available, if the port is already held by a live task, or if the input configuration is invalid.
ca_tcp_listen.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses an internal spinlock to manage access to the listener table. It is non-blocking and does not perform network I/O itself; it merely registers the intent to listen. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR because it performs internal locking and potential memory management. A common mistake is failing to check the return value for 0, which leads to passing an invalid handle to subsequent functions like ca_tcp_accept, causing the application to fail silently. Additionally, the function includes a 'reaper' mechanism: if it detects a listener slot associated with a task that is no longer alive, it will automatically reclaim that slot for the new request.
ca_tcp_listen.usage: This function is the mandatory first step in creating a TCP server. It is typically called once during service initialization to reserve a port. After obtaining a valid handle, the application enters a loop calling ca_tcp_accept to wait for incoming clients. When the service is no longer needed, the handle should be released using ca_tcp_unlisten to free the slot for other services.

ca_tcp_peer.brief: Retrieves the remote IP address and port associated with an active TCP connection handle.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The unique identifier of the TCP connection. Must be a valid handle returned by a previous connection or acceptance operation.

params.name: ip
params.desc: Pointer to a structure where the remote IPv4 address will be stored. Can be NULL if the IP is not needed.

params.name: port
params.desc: Pointer to a variable where the remote port number will be stored. Can be NULL if the port is not needed.

ca_tcp_peer.returns: Returns true if the handle is valid and the connection is active (ESTABLISHED or CLOSE_WAIT with pending data). Returns false if the handle is invalid, the connection is closed, or the handle is not active.
ca_tcp_peer.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses an internal mutex to protect the TCP control block list. It is non-blocking, meaning it will return immediately after checking the internal state. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR because it attempts to lock a mutex, which can lead to system deadlocks or crashes. The most common mistake is passing an uninitialized handle or a handle that has already been closed via ca_tcp_close(), which will result in a false return value.
ca_tcp_peer.usage: This function is typically used after a connection has been established to identify the remote peer for logging, security filtering, or session management. It is often paired with ca_tcp_connect() or a server-side accept mechanism. Developers use it to extract connection metadata before performing data transfers or when handling connection-specific events in a multi-client application.

ca_tcp_recv.signature: bool ca_tcp_recv(u8 handle, u8 *buf, u16 buf_len, u16 *out_len, u32 timeout_ms)
ca_tcp_recv.brief: Reads incoming TCP data from a specific connection handle into a provided buffer with a timeout.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The connection identifier returned by ca_tcp_accept or ca_tcp_connect. Must be a valid, active handle.

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the destination buffer where received data will be stored. Must not be NULL.

params.name: buf_len
params.desc: Size of the destination buffer in bytes.

params.name: out_len
params.desc: Pointer to a variable that will store the actual number of bytes copied. Can be NULL.

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time in milliseconds to wait for data. Use 0 for non-blocking polling.

ca_tcp_recv.returns: Returns true if data was successfully copied to the buffer. Returns false if the connection is closed, the handle is invalid, the timeout expires, or the buffer pointer is NULL.
ca_tcp_recv.notes: This function is blocking and thread-safe; it suspends the calling task until data is available or the timeout expires. It MUST NOT be called from an ISR because it uses mutexes and semaphores that require task context. A critical detail is that the function re-validates the handle after waiting; this prevents 'use-after-free' bugs where a connection slot is recycled for a new peer while the task was waiting. A common mistake is assuming that a wake-up implies data is ready; always check the return value and handle the case where the connection was closed during the wait. If the function returns false, it may have internally released a semaphore post if data was still present, ensuring that subsequent calls do not hang indefinitely.
ca_tcp_recv.usage: This function is the primary way to consume data from an established TCP stream. It is typically used in a loop within a dedicated communication task, following a successful ca_tcp_accept or ca_tcp_connect. It is often paired with ca_tcp_send to implement request-response protocols. If the function returns false, the application should verify the connection status using ca_tcp_is_connected and potentially call ca_tcp_close to clean up resources. Because the function manages internal ring buffers, it is essential to call it frequently enough to prevent the TCP receive window from filling up, which would otherwise stall the remote sender.

ca_tcp_send.signature: i32 ca_tcp_send(u8 handle, const u8 *data, u16 len)
ca_tcp_send.brief: Sends a buffer of data over an established TCP connection handle.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The TCP connection identifier. Must be a valid handle returned by ca_tcp_accept or ca_tcp_connect.

params.name: data
params.desc: Pointer to the data buffer. Must not be NULL.

params.name: len
params.desc: Number of bytes to send. Must be greater than 0.

ca_tcp_send.returns: Returns CA_TCP_SENT (1) when the WHOLE buffer was queued for transmission. Returns CA_TCP_RETRY (0) when there were not enough inflight slots or buffers for the whole buffer: nothing was sent, send the same data again after ca_tcp_wait_writable(). Returns CA_TCP_GONE (-1) when the handle is stale or the connection is not ESTABLISHED, or when len needs more than TCP_MAX_INFLIGHT segments.
ca_tcp_send.notes: All or nothing: the data is cut into segments of min(MSS, MTU - 40), one inflight slot each, and the call either queues every segment or none. A queued segment that the peer window or the driver cannot take now leaves on the next ACK or timer tick, invisibly to the caller; the call never waits for the peer's ACK. Uses an internal mutex: never call it from an ISR. ALWAYS compare the result with CA_TCP_SENT: 'if (!ca_tcp_send(...))' is wrong because CA_TCP_GONE is -1 and !(-1) is 0, and 'return ca_tcp_send(...)' in a bool function turns -1 into true.
ca_tcp_send.usage: Call it from a task on a handle from ca_tcp_connect() or ca_tcp_accept(). On CA_TCP_RETRY wait for room with ca_tcp_wait_writable() and send the same buffer again; on CA_TCP_GONE stop using the handle and close it.

ca_tcp_service_start.brief: Initializes the TCP/IP stack services, registers the TCP timer task, and optionally enables the CLI interface.
ca_tcp_service_start.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called during the system initialization phase, typically inside ca_os_main before starting other network-dependent tasks. It performs internal memory and protocol binding, so calling it multiple times or after the network stack is already active may lead to undefined behavior or memory leaks. It is not callable from an ISR because it spawns OS tasks and performs heap allocations. The most common mistake is calling this function before the underlying network hardware or memory manager has been initialized.
ca_tcp_service_start.usage: It is used as a mandatory entry point for any application requiring TCP communication. It is typically paired with ca_arp_service_start and ca_dhcp_service_start to ensure the full network stack is ready. Once called, the system is prepared to handle TCP connections, and the developer can proceed to use functions like ca_tcp_listen or ca_tcp_connect to establish communication channels.

ca_tcp_unlisten.brief: Stops a TCP listening socket and releases the associated resources.

params.name: listen_handle
params.desc: The handle returned by a previous call to ca_tcp_listen. Valid range is 1 to TCP_MAX_LISTEN. Passing 0 or an invalid handle results in no action.

ca_tcp_unlisten.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses a spinlock to protect the internal listen table. It is non-blocking, meaning it will return immediately after updating the internal state. It is safe to call from an ISR because it uses an IRQ-safe spinlock (ca_spinlock_lock_irq). The most common mistake is failing to call this function after a connection is accepted or when a service is shutting down, which leads to resource leaks where the TCP port remains occupied and unavailable for future use. Always ensure the handle is set to 0 after calling this function to prevent accidental double-unlistening.
ca_tcp_unlisten.usage: This function is used to clean up after a TCP server has finished its task or when a listening socket needs to be reconfigured. It is typically paired with ca_tcp_listen during initialization and called before the application exits or when the network configuration changes. In a standard server loop, you call ca_tcp_listen to start, wait for a client, and then ca_tcp_unlisten to stop accepting new connections once the service is no longer needed. It is also used to free up a port before re-binding it to a different IP address or configuration, ensuring that the network stack does not keep stale listening state active.

ca_tcp_wait_writable.brief: Blocks the calling task until the TCP connection buffer has space to send data or the timeout expires.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The connection identifier. Must be a valid, active handle previously opened by the network stack.

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time in milliseconds to wait. Use 0 for non-blocking check, or a specific value for a timed block.

ca_tcp_wait_writable.returns: Returns true if a transmission slot is available, false if the timeout expired, the handle is invalid, or the connection is no longer active.
ca_tcp_wait_writable.notes: This function is blocking and must only be called from a task context, never from an ISR. It uses an internal semaphore to suspend the task, which is efficient as it consumes no CPU cycles while waiting. A critical detail is that the handle must be re-validated after the wait; because the task was suspended, another task might have closed the connection or changed the state of the handle. The most common mistake is assuming the connection is still valid after the function returns true without checking ca_tcp_is_connected, which can lead to sending data into a closed or reset socket. Additionally, because the internal semaphore is shared, the function re-resolves the handle after every wake-up to ensure the connection state is still current.
ca_tcp_wait_writable.usage: This function is used for flow control in network applications to prevent buffer overflows when the network stack is busy or the peer is slow. It is typically used in a loop: first, call ca_tcp_wait_writable to ensure the stack can accept data, then verify the connection status with ca_tcp_is_connected, and finally perform the data transmission using ca_tcp_send. This sequence ensures that your application respects the underlying network constraints and handles connection drops gracefully. It is essential to pair this with a retry mechanism or a timeout check to prevent the application from hanging indefinitely if the network link is lost.

ca_temp_dts_present.brief: Checks if the internal Digital Temperature Sensor (DTS) is available on the current hardware.
ca_temp_dts_present.returns: Returns true if the DTS is present and initialized, false otherwise.
ca_temp_dts_present.notes: This function is a non-blocking, thread-safe status check that simply returns a cached boolean value. It is safe to call from any context, including ISRs, because it does not perform hardware I/O or wait for sensor measurements. The most common mistake is assuming that this function triggers a measurement; it does not. You must call this before attempting to read the DTS to avoid reading invalid or uninitialized data on hardware variants that lack the sensor.
ca_temp_dts_present.usage: This function is typically used as a guard clause in initialization routines or CLI commands to ensure hardware compatibility. It is usually paired with ca_temp_read_dts() in a sequence where you first verify presence, then perform the actual measurement. By checking this first, you prevent your application from attempting to access registers or memory regions that do not exist on specific STM32 chip variants.

ca_temp_hw_convert.brief: Converts raw ADC values from the internal temperature sensor and VREFINT into a calibrated temperature in degrees Celsius.

params.name: ts_raw
params.desc: The raw 12-bit or 16-bit ADC value read from the internal temperature sensor channel.

params.name: vrefint_raw
params.desc: The raw 12-bit or 16-bit ADC value read from the internal VREFINT channel, used to compensate for supply voltage fluctuations.

ca_temp_hw_convert.returns: Returns an i32 representing the temperature in degrees Celsius. If the hardware calibration data is missing or the ADC readings are invalid (e.g., zero), the result may be mathematically incorrect or represent a default error state depending on the specific MCU implementation.
ca_temp_hw_convert.notes: This function is a pure mathematical calculation and is non-blocking, thread-safe, and safe to call from an ISR. It relies on factory-programmed calibration values stored in the MCU's system memory (e.g., TS_CAL1_ADDR). A common beginner mistake is passing zero or uninitialized ADC values to this function, which will lead to division-by-zero errors or nonsensical temperature outputs. Always ensure the ADC peripheral is fully initialized and the conversion has completed before reading the raw values.
ca_temp_hw_convert.usage: This function is typically used as the final step in a temperature acquisition sequence. It is paired with ca_temp_read_raw() (or direct ADC reads) to obtain the raw data, which is then passed to this function to produce a human-readable value. It is usually called within a periodic task or a sensor polling loop after the ADC has finished sampling both the temperature and VREFINT channels.

ca_temp_hw_dts_alarm.signature: void ca_temp_hw_dts_alarm(u32 raw_hot, u32 raw_cold, bool hot_on, bool cold_on, ca_temp_alarm_cb_t cb)
ca_temp_hw_dts_alarm.brief: Configures hardware temperature thresholds and an interrupt callback for the Die Temperature Sensor (DTS).

params.name: raw_hot
params.desc: Raw sensor count threshold for the hot alarm (triggers when temperature is at or below this value).

params.name: raw_cold
params.desc: Raw sensor count threshold for the cold alarm (triggers when temperature is at or above this value).

params.name: hot_on
params.desc: Enable the hot alarm interrupt.

params.name: cold_on
params.desc: Enable the cold alarm interrupt.

params.name: cb
params.desc: Function pointer to be called when an alarm triggers. Pass NULL to disable all alarms.

ca_temp_hw_dts_alarm.notes: This function is non-blocking and interacts directly with hardware registers. It is not thread-safe; if multiple tasks attempt to configure the alarm simultaneously, the behavior is undefined. It is intended to be called from a task context, but it internally manages NVIC settings to ensure the interrupt is configured correctly. A common mistake is passing invalid raw values that exceed the hardware register capacity, or failing to realize that the callback executes within the context of the DTS interrupt service routine (ISR). Keep the callback execution time extremely short to avoid blocking other system interrupts.
ca_temp_hw_dts_alarm.usage: This function is used to monitor die temperature without polling. It is typically paired with a conversion function like ca_temp_hw_dts_raw() to translate human-readable temperature values into hardware-specific counts. The sequence is usually: calculate thresholds, call this function to arm the hardware, and then handle the resulting event in the provided callback. To stop monitoring, call this function again with cb set to NULL.

ca_temp_hw_dts_centi.brief: Converts raw digital temperature sensor (DTS) counts into temperature in centi-degrees Celsius.

params.name: raw
params.desc: The raw frequency count obtained from the DTS hardware. A value of 0 is invalid and indicates a sensor error or uninitialized state.

ca_temp_hw_dts_centi.returns: Returns the temperature in centi-degrees Celsius (e.g., 2500 for 25.00°C) as an i32. Returns CA_TEMP_NO_DTS if the input is 0, if the sensor hardware is missing, or if calibration data (ramp/offset) is invalid.
ca_temp_hw_dts_centi.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it performs pure mathematical calculations based on hardware registers. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the hardware registers are accessible. It is mandatory that the system clock is initialized before calling this, as the calculation depends on the current CPU frequency. A common beginner mistake is passing a raw value of 0 without checking, which will result in an error return code rather than a valid temperature.
ca_temp_hw_dts_centi.usage: This function is typically used in a periodic task or a monitoring loop to convert raw sensor data into human-readable units. It is usually paired with a sampling function that reads the hardware register, followed by an averaging filter to reduce noise. The sequence is: sample the raw value, validate the result, pass it to this function, and then use the resulting centi-degree value for thermal management or logging.

ca_temp_hw_dts_init.brief: Initializes the internal Digital Temperature Sensor (DTS) hardware if available on the current STM32 chip.
ca_temp_hw_dts_init.returns: Returns true if the DTS was successfully initialized and is ready for use. Returns false if the hardware does not support a DTS or if the initialization sequence failed.
ca_temp_hw_dts_init.notes: This function is hardware-dependent and acts as a wrapper for chip-specific implementations. It is not thread-safe and should be called during the system initialization phase before any temperature reading tasks are started. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. A common mistake is assuming that this function will always succeed; you must always check the return value, as many STM32 families (like F1, F4, F7) do not have a DTS and will always return false.
ca_temp_hw_dts_init.usage: This function is typically called once during the driver initialization sequence for the temperature sensor subsystem. It is usually paired with a generic initialization function (e.g., ca_temp_init) to ensure the hardware abstraction layer is ready. If it returns false, the application should handle the absence of the sensor gracefully, perhaps by disabling temperature-dependent features or logging a warning.

ca_temp_hw_dts_raw.brief: Converts a temperature in centi-degrees Celsius to the raw hardware counter value required by the DTS peripheral.

params.name: centi
params.desc: The target temperature in centi-degrees Celsius (e.g., 2500 for 25.00°C). Valid range depends on the specific hardware DTS calibration limits.

ca_temp_hw_dts_raw.returns: A u32 representing the raw counter value for the DTS hardware. Returns 0xFFFFU if the calculated value is out of range or if the hardware does not support DTS.
ca_temp_hw_dts_raw.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it performs a mathematical calculation based on hardware-specific calibration constants. It is safe to call from an ISR because it does not perform I/O or wait for locks. The function relies on the DTS peripheral being correctly calibrated at the factory; if the hardware does not support DTS (e.g., F1xx, F4xx, F7xx), it will return 0U or a dummy value. A common mistake is passing a temperature value that results in a negative frequency calculation, which the function handles by returning 0xFFFFU as an error indicator.
ca_temp_hw_dts_raw.usage: This function is primarily used to configure temperature alarm thresholds for the DTS peripheral. It is typically paired with ca_temp_set_alarm, where the raw values calculated by this function are passed as the 'hot' and 'cold' thresholds. Developers use this to translate human-readable temperature limits into the specific register-level counts the hardware expects for triggering interrupts.

ca_temp_hw_dts_sample.brief: Performs a single, fresh raw measurement from the internal Digital Temperature Sensor (DTS).
ca_temp_hw_dts_sample.returns: Returns the raw 32-bit sensor count on success. Returns 0U if the sensor fails to signal readiness within the internal timeout period or if the hardware does not support a DTS.
ca_temp_hw_dts_sample.notes: This function is blocking; it waits for the hardware to complete a conversion cycle, which may take several milliseconds. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR because it relies on polling the hardware status register. The function handles the complex state machine required to trigger a one-shot measurement even if the sensor was previously configured for continuous operation. A common mistake is calling this function too frequently in a tight loop without considering the sensor's conversion time, which can lead to unnecessary CPU overhead or timeout errors.
ca_temp_hw_dts_sample.usage: This function is typically used when you need a precise, non-averaged temperature reading. It is often paired with a loop to collect multiple samples for software-based averaging to improve signal stability. Before calling this, ensure the system has verified that the DTS hardware is present and initialized. It is usually called within a dedicated monitoring task that runs periodically, rather than in high-priority real-time control loops.

ca_temp_hw_init.brief: Low-level hardware initialization for the internal temperature sensor and reference voltage channel.
ca_temp_hw_init.returns: Returns true if the hardware was successfully configured and the ADC is ready; returns false if the initialization sequence failed (e.g., timeout waiting for ADC ready or LDO ready).
ca_temp_hw_init.notes: This function performs direct register manipulation to enable clocks, power up the ADC, calibrate it, and configure internal channels. It is NOT thread-safe and must be called before any attempt to read the temperature sensor. It is not intended to be called from an ISR as it contains blocking 'while' loops waiting for hardware flags. A common mistake is calling this function multiple times without checking the initialization state, which may trigger redundant calibration or reset the ADC state machine.
ca_temp_hw_init.usage: This function is the mandatory hardware-level setup step for the temperature sensing subsystem. It is typically called once during system startup or the first time a temperature reading is requested. It is designed to be wrapped by a higher-level function (like ca_temp_init) that manages a static initialization flag to ensure the hardware is configured only once. After this returns true, the system can safely use ca_temp_read or ca_temp_read_raw to retrieve sensor data.

ca_temp_hw_read_raw.brief: Reads the raw ADC value from the internal MCU temperature sensor.
ca_temp_hw_read_raw.returns: A 16-bit unsigned integer representing the raw ADC conversion result. The value range depends on the specific STM32 ADC resolution (typically 12-bit, 0-4095).
ca_temp_hw_read_raw.notes: This function is a low-level hardware abstraction layer (HAL) call. It is not thread-safe by itself and assumes the ADC peripheral has been correctly initialized and configured for the internal temperature channel. It is generally non-blocking, as it triggers or reads the ADC register directly, but it should not be called from an ISR unless the underlying ADC driver is specifically designed to handle concurrent access. The most common beginner mistake is calling this function before the temperature sensor or ADC peripheral has been initialized, which may result in reading garbage data or triggering a hardware fault.
ca_temp_hw_read_raw.usage: This function is used as the primary data acquisition step for temperature monitoring. It is typically paired with ca_temp_init to ensure the hardware is ready, and then used in conjunction with ca_temp_hw_read_vrefint to perform a calibrated conversion. In a typical application, a task will call this function periodically, pass the raw value to a conversion function, and then log or act upon the resulting temperature value.

ca_temp_hw_read_vrefint.brief: Reads the raw ADC value of the internal reference voltage (Vrefint) for temperature calculation.
ca_temp_hw_read_vrefint.returns: Returns a 16-bit unsigned integer representing the raw ADC conversion result of the internal reference channel. A value of 0 typically indicates an error or that the ADC peripheral is not properly initialized.
ca_temp_hw_read_vrefint.notes: This function is a low-level hardware abstraction layer (HAL) call. It is not thread-safe by itself and should only be called after the ADC peripheral has been initialized via the appropriate hardware driver. It is generally non-blocking, as it triggers a direct register read or a simple polling sequence depending on the MCU architecture. Do not call this from an ISR unless the underlying ADC driver is specifically designed to be re-entrant or protected by a spinlock, as concurrent access to the ADC hardware will cause data corruption or system instability. The most common beginner mistake is calling this function before the system clock or the ADC peripheral has been fully initialized, which will result in reading invalid or zero values.
ca_temp_hw_read_vrefint.usage: This function is used exclusively by the temperature sensor driver to perform calibration. It is typically paired with ca_temp_read_raw() to obtain both the sensor reading and the reference voltage reading simultaneously. These two raw values are then passed to a conversion function to calculate the actual temperature in degrees Celsius. The typical sequence is: ca_temp_init() -> ca_temp_read_raw() -> ca_temp_hw_read_vrefint() -> calculation. It is essential to use these values together because the internal reference voltage changes with the supply voltage, and using the raw sensor value alone without Vrefint compensation will lead to inaccurate temperature readings.

ca_temp_init.brief: Initializes the temperature sensor hardware and ensures it is ready for use.
ca_temp_init.returns: Returns true if the sensor is successfully initialized or was already initialized. Returns false if the hardware initialization fails.
ca_temp_init.notes: This function is a wrapper that ensures the temperature sensor hardware is only initialized once, preventing re-initialization conflicts. It is not thread-safe by itself, so it should be called during the system configuration phase before the RTOS scheduler starts. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. A common mistake is calling this function multiple times from different tasks without ensuring the system is in a stable state, or assuming it will re-initialize hardware if a previous attempt failed.
ca_temp_init.usage: This function is typically called once during the system startup sequence, specifically within the ca_os_configure() function. It acts as a prerequisite for any subsequent calls to ca_temp_read() or ca_temp_read_raw(). By placing it in the configuration phase, you ensure that the sensor hardware is ready before any application tasks attempt to access temperature data.

ca_temp_read.brief: Reads the internal MCU temperature sensor and returns the value in degrees Celsius.
ca_temp_read.returns: Returns the temperature as an i32 integer in degrees Celsius. Returns -999 if the sensor has not been initialized via ca_temp_init().
ca_temp_read.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a quick hardware read of the internal ADC channels for the temperature sensor and VREFINT. It is thread-safe as it only performs read operations on hardware registers, but it relies on the global initialization flag being set. It is generally safe to call from an ISR, provided the underlying ADC hardware is not being used by another high-priority task. The most common beginner mistake is calling this function before the system has completed the ca_temp_init() sequence, which will result in the error code -999.
ca_temp_read.usage: This function is typically used in periodic monitoring tasks or CLI commands to report system health. It is often paired with ca_temp_init() during system startup to prepare the hardware. In a typical application, you would call it inside a loop, perhaps combined with ca_os_sleep() to regulate the sampling frequency, and use the returned value to trigger safety logic or thermal throttling.

ca_temp_read_dts.brief: Reads the internal Digital Temperature Sensor (DTS) and returns the averaged temperature in centi-degrees Celsius.
ca_temp_read_dts.returns: Returns the temperature as a signed 32-bit integer (centi-degrees Celsius, e.g., 2550 for 25.50°C). Returns CA_TEMP_NO_DTS if the sensor is not present, not initialized, or if the hardware sampling fails.
ca_temp_read_dts.notes: This function is not thread-safe if called concurrently from multiple tasks without external synchronization, as it performs multiple hardware samples. It is not intended to be called from an ISR because it performs a loop of hardware samples which may take significant time, potentially violating real-time constraints. Before calling this, ensure the system has initialized the temperature hardware. A common mistake is ignoring the return value CA_TEMP_NO_DTS, which leads to using invalid temperature data in control logic.
ca_temp_read_dts.usage: This function is typically used in monitoring tasks or CLI interfaces to provide high-precision thermal data from the MCU core. It is often paired with ca_temp_dts_present() to verify hardware availability before attempting a read. In a typical lifecycle, the application calls ca_temp_init() during system startup, then periodically calls ca_temp_read_dts() to log thermal status or adjust cooling/performance parameters.

ca_temp_read_raw.brief: Reads the raw 12-bit ADC value from the internal temperature sensor.
ca_temp_read_raw.returns: Returns a 12-bit unsigned integer (0-4095) representing the raw ADC conversion. Returns 0 if the temperature sensor driver has not been initialized via ca_temp_init.
ca_temp_read_raw.notes: This function is a non-blocking, thread-safe wrapper that interacts with the hardware ADC peripheral. It is safe to call from both tasks and ISRs, provided the driver has been initialized. The most common mistake is calling this function before invoking ca_temp_init, which will result in a return value of 0, potentially leading to incorrect temperature calculations if the caller does not check for this error condition.
ca_temp_read_raw.usage: This function is typically used in a periodic monitoring task to fetch raw data before processing it into a human-readable format. The standard sequence is: first, call ca_temp_init during system startup to configure the ADC and internal references; then, periodically call ca_temp_read_raw within a loop or timer-triggered task; finally, use the returned value to perform calculations or pass it to other conversion functions.

ca_temp_retune.brief: Recalculates temperature alarm thresholds after a change in the system core clock frequency.
ca_temp_retune.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called only when the system scheduler is in a known state, typically immediately after a frequency change. It is not intended to be called from an ISR because it performs internal logic that may rely on system state consistency. The primary precondition is that the temperature sensor driver must have been initialized via ca_temp_init. A common beginner mistake is forgetting to call this after changing the clock frequency; if omitted, the temperature alarm thresholds will be mathematically incorrect (based on the old clock speed), leading to false positives or, worse, failing to trigger an alarm when the chip is actually overheating.
ca_temp_retune.usage: This function is used exclusively in the context of power management and clock scaling. Whenever the system frequency is modified using ca_pwr_set_freq or similar clock-adjusting functions, the hardware-dependent timing values (like DTS alarm thresholds) become invalid. You must call this function as part of the 'retuning' sequence, which typically includes calling ca_os_tick_retune, ca_uart_retune, and ca_can_retune to ensure all time-dependent peripherals remain synchronized with the new core clock.

ca_temp_set_alarm.signature: bool ca_temp_set_alarm(i32 cold_c, i32 hot_c, ca_temp_alarm_cb_t cb)
ca_temp_set_alarm.brief: Configures a temperature threshold alarm that triggers a callback when the DTS sensor crosses defined limits.

params.name: cold_c
params.desc: The temperature threshold in Celsius for the cold alarm. Must be strictly less than hot_c.

params.name: hot_c
params.desc: The temperature threshold in Celsius for the hot alarm. Must be strictly greater than cold_c.

params.name: cb
params.desc: A function pointer to the callback to execute when a threshold is crossed. Pass NULL to disable the alarm.

ca_temp_set_alarm.returns: Returns true if the alarm was successfully configured. Returns false if the DTS sensor is not initialized, if cold_c is not less than hot_c, or if the configuration failed.
ca_temp_set_alarm.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe. The callback provided runs directly within the context of the DTS (Digital Temperature Sensor) interrupt service routine (ISR). Because it runs in an ISR, the callback must be extremely fast, must not perform blocking operations (like waiting for a mutex or sleeping), and should avoid complex logic. A common mistake is to perform heavy processing or logging inside the callback, which can cause system instability or missed interrupts. Ensure the DTS hardware is initialized via ca_temp_init before calling this function.
ca_temp_set_alarm.usage: This function is used to monitor thermal conditions without polling the sensor continuously in a loop. It is typically used in a system initialization sequence after ca_temp_init is called. You define a callback function that handles the thermal event (e.g., triggering a fan or reducing CPU frequency via ca_os_clock_reduce_freq) and pass it to this function. Once a threshold is crossed, the callback fires once; to re-arm the alarm, you must call ca_temp_set_alarm again.

ca_tftp_get.signature: bool ca_tftp_get(const ca_tftp_cfg_t *cfg, ca_tftp_rx_block_t on_block, void *arg)
ca_tftp_get.brief: Downloads a file from a remote TFTP server using a callback-based mechanism.

params.name: cfg
params.desc: Pointer to configuration structure containing server IP, filename, timeout, and retry settings. Must not be NULL.

params.name: on_block
params.desc: Callback function invoked for every received data block. Must return true to continue or false to abort. Must not be NULL.

params.name: arg
params.desc: User-defined pointer passed directly to the on_block callback, useful for context (e.g., file handles or buffers).

ca_tftp_get.returns: Returns true if the file was successfully received in its entirety. Returns false if the transfer failed, timed out, was aborted by the callback, or if parameters were invalid.
ca_tftp_get.notes: This function is blocking and will suspend the calling task until the transfer completes or fails. It is NOT thread-safe for concurrent TFTP operations; it uses an internal mutex to ensure only one transfer occurs at a time. It must NOT be called from an ISR because it performs blocking network operations and mutex locking. A common mistake is providing a callback that takes too long to process, which can cause the TFTP block timeout to trigger and lead to unnecessary retransmissions.
ca_tftp_get.usage: Typically used in a dedicated background task to fetch configuration files or firmware updates from a server. It is usually paired with ca_tftp_service_init to ensure the network stack is ready. The sequence is: 1) Initialize network/TFTP service, 2) Define a callback function to handle incoming data (e.g., writing to flash), 3) Call ca_tftp_get with the configuration, 4) Check the boolean return value to verify success.

ca_tftp_put.signature: bool ca_tftp_put(const ca_tftp_cfg_t *cfg, const u8 *data, u32 total_len)
ca_tftp_put.brief: Uploads a data buffer to a remote TFTP server using the TFTP protocol.

params.name: cfg
params.desc: Pointer to a configuration structure containing server IP, filename, timeout, and retry settings. Must not be NULL.

params.name: data
params.desc: Pointer to the memory buffer containing the data to be uploaded. Must not be NULL.

params.name: total_len
params.desc: Total size of the data buffer in bytes.

ca_tftp_put.returns: Returns true if the file was successfully acknowledged by the server, false otherwise (e.g., invalid parameters, network timeout, or server error).
ca_tftp_put.notes: This function is blocking; it will suspend the calling task until the entire transfer completes or the retry limit is reached. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR because it uses mutexes for thread safety and performs network I/O. Before calling this, ensure the network stack is initialized and the TFTP service is ready. A common mistake is passing a pointer to a buffer that is modified by another task while the transfer is in progress, which will corrupt the uploaded data.
ca_tftp_put.usage: This function is typically used to push configuration files or firmware updates to a remote server. It is usually called after verifying network connectivity. It pairs with ca_tftp_service_init to ensure the underlying network buffers and state machines are ready. The sequence is: initialize the network, prepare the configuration struct, call ca_tftp_put, and then handle the boolean result to determine if the operation succeeded.

ca_tftp_receive.signature: bool ca_tftp_receive(const ca_tftp_srv_cfg_t *cfg, ca_tftp_wrq_t on_wrq, ca_tftp_rx_block_t on_block, void *arg, u32 wait_ms)
ca_tftp_receive.brief: Starts a blocking TFTP server listener to receive a single file transfer (WRQ) over UDP.

params.name: cfg
params.desc: Configuration structure containing local MAC, optional port, and error reporting pointer. Must not be NULL.

params.name: on_wrq
params.desc: Callback function invoked when a Write Request (WRQ) is received. Return 0 to accept, or a TFTP error code to refuse.

params.name: on_block
params.desc: Callback function invoked for every received data block. Must not be NULL.

params.name: arg
params.desc: User-defined pointer passed to the callbacks for context (e.g., file handles or status structures).

params.name: wait_ms
params.desc: Timeout in milliseconds to wait for an incoming WRQ. Use a large value or a specific constant for indefinite waiting.

ca_tftp_receive.returns: Returns true if the file was received successfully, false if a timeout occurred, the request was refused, or an error occurred during transfer.
ca_tftp_receive.notes: This function is blocking and must be called from a task context, never from an ISR. It is thread-safe regarding the internal service state, but only one task can listen for a WRQ at a time; subsequent calls will return false if the service is already waiting.
