It is typically called immediately after configuring the DMA channel with ca_dma_copy_target to ensure the hardware is ready to stream incoming bytes directly into memory. It is part of the standard initialization sequence: 1) Configure DMA, 2) Call ca_uart_hw_dma_rx_on, 3) Wait for completion using ca_uart_dma_wait.

ca_uart_hw_dma_tx_addr.brief: Returns the memory address of the UART Transmit Data Register (TDR/DR) for DMA operations.

params.name: inst
params.desc: Pointer to the specific UART hardware instance (e.g., USART1, USART2). Must be a valid, initialized peripheral pointer.

ca_uart_hw_dma_tx_addr.returns: A volatile void pointer to the hardware register where data must be written for transmission. Returns NULL if the provided instance pointer is invalid.
ca_uart_hw_dma_tx_addr.notes: This function is a low-level hardware abstraction layer (HAL) helper. It is non-blocking, thread-safe, and can be called from an ISR because it performs a simple pointer arithmetic operation based on the architecture. It is strictly intended to provide the destination address for DMA controllers. The most common mistake is passing a NULL or uninitialized peripheral pointer, which will cause a hard fault when the DMA controller attempts to access the address.
ca_uart_hw_dma_tx_addr.usage: This function is used exclusively when configuring DMA transfers for UART transmission. It is typically paired with ca_dma_copy_target to link a memory buffer to the UART hardware peripheral. The sequence is: first, identify the UART instance; second, retrieve the TDR address using this function; third, pass that address to the DMA configuration function to initiate the hardware-managed data transfer.

ca_uart_hw_init.signature: bool ca_uart_hw_init(u32 uart_num, u32 baudrate, USART_TypeDef **_instance)
ca_uart_hw_init.brief: Initializes a specific UART hardware peripheral, configures its baud rate, and enables its RX interrupt.

params.name: uart_num
params.desc: The hardware index of the UART peripheral (e.g., 1 for USART1, 2 for USART2). Must match the hardware mapping of the specific STM32 series.

params.name: baudrate
params.desc: The desired communication speed in bits per second (e.g., 115200).

params.name: _instance
params.desc: A pointer to a pointer that will be updated with the base address of the initialized hardware register block. Must not be NULL.

ca_uart_hw_init.returns: Returns true if the peripheral was successfully identified, clocked, and configured. Returns false if the uart_num is invalid or the hardware instance cannot be resolved.
ca_uart_hw_init.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should be called during system initialization before starting the OS scheduler. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. It performs low-level register manipulation, including enabling peripheral clocks in the RCC and configuring the NVIC for RX interrupts. A common mistake is passing an uninitialized pointer for _instance or attempting to re-initialize an already active UART without first ensuring no other tasks are using it. Note that this function does not configure GPIO pins; you must call ca_uart_configure_gpio separately to map the pins to the UART alternate function.
ca_uart_hw_init.usage: This function is the primary entry point for setting up serial communication. It is typically used in the board support package (BSP) initialization sequence. It is often paired with ca_uart_configure_gpio to set up the physical pins and ca_uart_retune if the system clock frequency changes dynamically. Once initialized, the returned instance pointer is used by other ca_uart_* functions to perform data transfers.

ca_uart_hw_put.brief: Transmits a string via UART using blocking polling mode.

params.name: _instance
params.desc: A pointer to the UART peripheral handle. Must not be NULL, and the dereferenced pointer must point to a valid initialized UART peripheral.

params.name: message
params.desc: A pointer to a structure containing the data buffer and its size. Must not be NULL.

ca_uart_hw_put.returns: Returns the number of bytes successfully sent (equal to message->size on success). Returns 0 if any input parameter is NULL or invalid.
ca_uart_hw_put.notes: This function is strictly blocking; it waits in a 'while' loop for the hardware registers to be ready for each byte and for the final transmission to complete. Because it uses busy-waiting, it is NOT thread-safe if multiple tasks attempt to write to the same UART simultaneously, and it must NEVER be called from an ISR as it will cause a system hang. Ensure the UART peripheral has been initialized via ca_uart_init before calling this. A common mistake is passing a message structure with an uninitialized or zero-length buffer, which results in no data being sent.
ca_uart_hw_put.usage: This function is typically used for low-level debugging or simple serial communication where DMA is not required or available. It is often paired with ca_uart_configure_gpio to set up the pins before the first transmission. In the caOS architecture, it serves as the fallback transmission method when DMA resources are exhausted or when the message size is too small to justify the overhead of a DMA transfer.

ca_uart_hw_recv_handler.brief: Low-level hardware handler to read a single byte from the UART receive register.

params.name: _instance
params.desc: Pointer to the UART peripheral instance handle. Must not be NULL and must point to a valid initialized UART peripheral.

params.name: rx_data
params.desc: Pointer to a memory location where the received byte will be stored. Must not be NULL.

ca_uart_hw_recv_handler.returns: Returns 0 if a byte was successfully read from the hardware register. Returns 1 if no data is available (RXNE flag not set) or if input pointers are invalid.
ca_uart_hw_recv_handler.notes: This function is designed to be called directly from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) or a high-priority polling loop. It is non-blocking and performs a direct register read, making it extremely fast but also dangerous if called without checking the hardware status first. It is not thread-safe by itself; it assumes the caller has already verified that the UART peripheral is initialized and that an interrupt or status flag indicates data is ready. A common mistake is calling this function without checking the UART status flags, which may result in reading stale or invalid data if the hardware buffer is empty.
ca_uart_hw_recv_handler.usage: This function is the lowest level of the UART receive chain. It is typically invoked by the UART interrupt handler (the ISR) when the hardware signals that a byte has arrived. After reading the byte, the ISR usually passes the data to higher-level functions like ca_cli_rx_byte for command processing or a queue-based buffer system to store the data for later consumption by a task. It is never used in isolation; it is always part of a sequence: check status -> call ca_uart_hw_recv_handler -> process byte.

ca_uart_init.signature: bool ca_uart_init(u32 uart_num, u32 baudrate, ca_uart_rx_cb_t on_rx, u8 alternate)
ca_uart_init.brief: Initializes a hardware UART peripheral, configures its GPIO pins, and registers an optional RX callback.

params.name: uart_num
params.desc: The hardware index of the UART peripheral (e.g., 1 for USART1). Must be within the range [1, CA_UART_MAX).

params.name: baudrate
params.desc: The desired communication speed in bits per second (e.g., 115200).

params.name: on_rx
params.desc: A function pointer to be called when data is received. Pass NULL if no callback is required.

params.name: alternate
params.desc: The alternate function mapping index for the GPIO pins. This determines which physical pins are assigned to the UART.

ca_uart_init.returns: Returns true if the UART and GPIO were successfully initialized, false otherwise (e.g., invalid uart_num or hardware configuration failure).
ca_uart_init.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should be called during system initialization before starting the OS scheduler. It performs hardware-level configuration, including GPIO setup, which is blocking and relies on underlying hardware registers. Do not call this function from an ISR, as it may perform operations that are not ISR-safe. A common mistake is passing an invalid uart_num or failing to ensure the peripheral clock is enabled, which will result in a false return value. Additionally, the 'alternate' parameter is critical; providing the wrong value can cause the UART to drive pins that are already in use by other board peripherals, potentially causing electrical conflicts.
ca_uart_init.usage: Use this function during the early boot phase to prepare communication interfaces. It is typically paired with other initialization functions like ca_os_tick_init. Once initialized, the UART can be used for data transmission or command-line interfaces. It is common to call this once at startup to set the hardware state, after which the driver maintains the configuration for subsequent use with functions like ca_uart_put or ca_uart_dma_send.

ca_uart_init_dma.signature: bool ca_uart_init_dma(u32 uart_num, u32 baudrate, ca_uart_rx_cb_t on_rx, u8 alternate)
ca_uart_init_dma.brief: Initializes a UART peripheral with DMA support for efficient, non-blocking data transmission and reception.

params.name: uart_num
params.desc: The hardware identifier for the UART peripheral (e.g., 1, 2, 3). Must not be 0.

params.name: baudrate
params.desc: The communication speed in bits per second (e.g., 115200).

params.name: on_rx
params.desc: A pointer to the callback function executed when data is received via DMA.

params.name: alternate
params.desc: Selects the alternate GPIO pin mapping for the UART peripheral. Use 0 for default mapping.

ca_uart_init_dma.returns: Returns true if the UART and DMA channels were successfully initialized and bound; returns false if the UART is already in use, no DMA channels are available, or hardware initialization fails.
ca_uart_init_dma.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should be called during system initialization before starting the scheduler. It is not callable from an ISR because it performs resource allocation and hardware configuration. A common mistake is failing to ensure that the DMA controller has been initialized via ca_dma_init() before calling this function, which will cause the internal binding process to fail. The function handles the complex task of mapping UART hardware requests to available DMA channels, so you do not need to manually configure DMA registers.
ca_uart_init_dma.usage: Use this function when you need high-performance serial communication that does not block the CPU during data transfers. It is typically called once during the system startup phase, immediately after ca_dma_init(). It is often paired with other DMA-based UART functions for actual data movement, and the provided callback will be triggered by the DMA interrupt once a transfer completes. Ensure the UART peripheral is not already initialized or in use by another task before calling this function.

ca_uart_put.brief: Transmits a message buffer over a specified UART peripheral.

params.name: uart_num
params.desc: The index of the UART peripheral to use. Must be a valid index within the range [1, CA_UART_MAX - 1]. Passing 0 or an index out of bounds will result in an immediate return of 0.

params.name: message
params.desc: A pointer to the message structure containing the data to send. Must not be NULL. The structure must have a valid size field.

ca_uart_put.returns: Returns a u16 value representing the status or number of bytes processed. Returns 0 if the UART index is invalid, the UART instance is not initialized, or the message pointer is NULL.
ca_uart_put.notes: This function acts as a high-level abstraction layer that automatically chooses between DMA-based transmission (if EN_UART_DMA is enabled and a DMA channel is found) or standard hardware-based transmission. It is not explicitly documented as thread-safe for concurrent access to the same UART instance, so ensure that multiple tasks do not attempt to write to the same UART simultaneously without external synchronization. It is generally not recommended to call this from an ISR unless the underlying driver implementation explicitly supports it, as it may involve blocking operations or resource contention. The most common beginner mistake is passing an uninitialized UART index or a NULL message pointer, which causes the function to fail silently by returning 0.
ca_uart_put.usage: This function is typically used for sending formatted data, logs, or communication packets to external devices or debug consoles. In a standard workflow, you would first initialize the UART peripheral using ca_uart_init, then prepare your data in a buffer, and finally call ca_uart_put to transmit it. It is often paired with ca_uart_dbg_put when you want to send data specifically to the system's designated debug UART. It is frequently used in communication loops where a message is constructed, its size is set, and then it is passed to this function for transmission.

ca_uart_recv_handler.brief: Processes incoming UART data by routing it to the CLI or a registered callback function.

params.name: uart_num
params.desc: The index of the UART peripheral. Must be a valid index within [1, CA_UART_MAX-1]. Values outside this range or 0 are ignored.

ca_uart_recv_handler.notes: This function is designed to be called from within a UART hardware interrupt service routine (ISR). It is not thread-safe in the sense that it relies on the hardware state being consistent at the time of the interrupt. The function performs a non-blocking check on the hardware buffer; if data is available, it either passes it to the CLI (if the UART is configured for debugging) or triggers a user-defined callback hook. A common mistake is failing to initialize the UART instance or the callback hook before the interrupt fires, which results in the function silently returning without processing data.
ca_uart_recv_handler.usage: This function is the core of the UART reception pipeline in caOS. It is typically invoked by the low-level hardware interrupt vector when a 'RXNE' (Receive Register Not Empty) event occurs. It pairs with ca_uart_init to set up the hardware and ca_cli_set_hook or a custom hook registration to define what happens to the received bytes. It acts as the bridge between raw hardware interrupts and the application-level logic.

ca_uart_retune.brief: Re-initializes all active UART peripherals to match the current system clock frequency.
ca_uart_retune.returns: This function returns void and does not provide a status code.
ca_uart_retune.notes: This function is intended to be called whenever the system clock configuration changes, such as during power-saving frequency scaling. It iterates through all registered UART instances and re-applies their baud rate settings using the current clock parameters. It is not thread-safe and should not be called from an ISR, as it performs hardware initialization which may involve blocking operations or shared resource access. A common mistake is calling this function before the UART hardware has been initialized at least once, which may lead to undefined behavior if the internal instance pointers are NULL.
ca_uart_retune.usage: This function is typically used within power management routines, specifically when the CPU frequency is scaled up or down to save energy. It is usually paired with ca_os_clock_reduce_freq or ca_os_clock_restore_freq to ensure that serial communication remains stable after the peripheral clock source changes. In a typical sequence, you would call ca_os_clock_reduce_freq to change the system speed, followed by ca_uart_retune to update the UART baud rate generators, and finally ca_os_tick_retune to adjust the OS heartbeat.

ca_udp_client_connect.brief: Initializes and registers a new UDP client instance to enable network communication.

params.name: cfg
params.desc: Pointer to a configuration structure containing server IP, ports, and callback functions. Must not be NULL.

ca_udp_client_connect.returns: Returns a 1-based handle (1 to UDPCLI_MAX_HANDLES) on success, or 0 if the connection fails or no slots are available.
ca_udp_client_connect.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses an internal mutex to manage slot allocation. It is NOT callable from an ISR because it performs blocking operations like mutex locking and potential network resolution (ARP). You must ensure the network stack is initialized before calling this. A common mistake is failing to check the return value; if it returns 0, the client was not created, and subsequent calls to send or receive using that handle will fail. The function also reserves a slot before performing network operations to prevent race conditions where two tasks might attempt to claim the same resource simultaneously.
ca_udp_client_connect.usage: This function is the entry point for UDP communication. It is typically called during system initialization or when a task needs to establish a connection to a remote server. It is used in a sequence: first, populate the configuration struct, then call this function to get a handle, use the handle for sending and receiving data, and finally call ca_udp_client_disconnect to release the slot when finished. It is often used in multi-tasking environments where multiple workers might need to open concurrent UDP streams.

ca_udp_client_disconnect.brief: Terminates an active UDP client session, releases associated network buffers, and unbinds the local port.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The unique identifier returned by ca_udp_client_connect. Valid range is 1 to UDPCLI_MAX_HANDLES. Passing 0 or an out-of-bounds value will result in a silent failure.

ca_udp_client_disconnect.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses an internal mutex to protect the client slot state. It is a blocking operation because it must acquire the mutex and potentially iterate through pending network buffers to free them. It must NOT be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because blocking calls are forbidden in interrupt context. A common mistake is to call this function without having previously initialized the UDP client system or using an invalid handle, which leads to memory leaks if buffers are not properly cleaned up or undefined behavior if the handle points to an uninitialized slot.
ca_udp_client_disconnect.usage: This function is used to gracefully shut down a UDP client when communication is no longer needed or when a connection error occurs. It is typically the final step in the lifecycle of a UDP client: ca_udp_client_connect -> ca_udp_client_recv/send -> ca_udp_client_disconnect. It ensures that the local port is released back to the system and that any memory allocated for queued packets is returned to the heap, preventing memory exhaustion. It is often called in a loop when cleaning up multiple client tasks during system shutdown or error recovery sequences.

ca_udp_client_reap.brief: Cleans up UDP client handles associated with tasks that are no longer running.
ca_udp_client_reap.notes: This function is a maintenance routine that scans the internal UDP client slot table. It checks if the task that owns a specific UDP handle is still alive using ca_os_owner_alive; if the task has terminated, it automatically releases the slot and frees the associated resources. It is thread-safe because it uses a mutex to protect the slot table during the scan. It is not intended to be called from an ISR because it performs blocking mutex operations. The most common mistake is calling this function too frequently in a high-priority loop, which can cause unnecessary CPU overhead; it should be triggered periodically by a system monitor or a background task.
ca_udp_client_reap.usage: This function is typically called by a system-level background task or a watchdog-like monitor that runs periodically to prevent resource leaks. It is used in conjunction with network initialization routines to ensure that if a task crashes or finishes its execution without explicitly closing its UDP connection, the network port and memory slots are reclaimed. It is usually paired with other 'reap' functions in the system's main maintenance loop to keep the OS resource table clean.

ca_udp_client_recv.signature: bool ca_udp_client_recv(u8 handle, u8 *buf, u16 buf_len, u16 *out_len, u32 timeout_ms)
ca_udp_client_recv.brief: Blocks the calling task until a UDP packet is received on the specified client handle or the timeout expires.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The unique ID of the UDP client session. Must be between 1 and UDPCLI_MAX_HANDLES.

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the destination buffer where the received payload will be copied.

params.name: buf_len
params.desc: Size of the destination buffer in bytes.

params.name: out_len
params.desc: Pointer to store the actual number of bytes copied. Can be NULL if not needed.

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time to wait in milliseconds. Use 0 for no wait or a large value for indefinite blocking.

ca_udp_client_recv.returns: Returns true if a packet was successfully received and copied to the buffer. Returns false if the handle is invalid, the client is inactive, the operation timed out, or the internal buffer is invalid.
ca_udp_client_recv.notes: This function is blocking; it puts the calling task into a waiting state until data arrives or the timeout occurs. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR because it performs blocking operations (semaphores and mutexes). Ensure the UDP client has been initialized and connected via ca_udp_client_connect before calling this. A common mistake is passing a buffer that is too small, which will result in truncated data without an error flag, or failing to check the return value, leading to processing uninitialized data.
ca_udp_client_recv.usage: This function is typically used in a dedicated network task loop to continuously poll for incoming UDP data. It is usually paired with ca_udp_client_connect to establish the session and ca_udp_client_send to transmit data. After receiving, the application processes the buffer and then waits for the next packet. It is the standard way to implement a request-response pattern where the client waits for a server reply.

ca_udp_client_recvfrom.signature: bool ca_udp_client_recvfrom(u8 handle, u8 *buf, u16 buf_len, u16 *out_len, ca_ipv4_t *src_ip, u16 *src_port, u32 timeout_ms)
ca_udp_client_recvfrom.brief: Receives a UDP packet from a specific client handle, optionally capturing the sender's IP and port.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The identifier of the UDP client socket. Must be between 1 and UDPCLI_MAX_HANDLES.

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the destination buffer where the received payload will be copied.

params.name: buf_len
params.desc: Size of the destination buffer in bytes.

params.name: out_len
params.desc: Pointer to store the actual number of bytes copied. Can be NULL if not needed.

params.name: src_ip
params.desc: Pointer to store the sender's IPv4 address. Can be NULL.

params.name: src_port
params.desc: Pointer to store the sender's UDP port. Can be NULL.

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time to wait for a packet in milliseconds. Use 0 for non-blocking or a large value for indefinite wait.

ca_udp_client_recvfrom.returns: Returns true if a packet was successfully received and copied to the buffer. Returns false if the handle is invalid, the socket is not active, the timeout expires, or the internal buffer is invalid.
ca_udp_client_recvfrom.notes: This function is blocking; it will suspend the calling task until a packet arrives or the timeout expires. It is thread-safe due to internal mutex protection, but it must NOT be called from an ISR because it performs blocking operations. A common mistake is passing an uninitialized handle or a buffer that is too small, which results in truncated data without an explicit error flag. Ensure the UDP client has been properly initialized and connected before calling this function.
ca_udp_client_recvfrom.usage: This function is typically used in a dedicated network task loop to process incoming UDP traffic. It is usually paired with ca_udp_client_connect to establish the communication channel and is called repeatedly until the application logic decides to close the connection. It is the primary mechanism for retrieving data from the network stack into the application layer, often used in conjunction with ca_os_delay_ms if a polling-based approach is preferred over a long timeout.

ca_udp_client_refresh_mac.brief: Forces an update of the cached MAC address for a specific UDP client handle by performing an ARP resolution.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The identifier of the UDP client slot. Must be between 1 and UDPCLI_MAX_HANDLES. Values outside this range will cause the function to return false.

params.name: arp_timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time in milliseconds to wait for the ARP resolution to complete. If the network is slow or the target is unreachable, the function will block for up to this duration.

ca_udp_client_refresh_mac.returns: Returns true if the MAC address was successfully resolved and updated in the client slot. Returns false if the handle is invalid, the client is not active, or the ARP resolution failed (e.g., timeout reached).
ca_udp_client_refresh_mac.notes: This function is blocking because it waits for the network stack to resolve the IP address via ARP. It is thread-safe as it uses internal mutexes to protect the client slot data, but it must NOT be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because blocking operations are forbidden in ISR context. A common mistake is to call this function with an extremely short timeout, which will cause it to fail frequently on busy networks. Ensure the UDP client has been initialized and is in an active state before calling this.
ca_udp_client_refresh_mac.usage: This function is typically used when a UDP client detects that communication with the server has failed or when the network topology has changed, requiring a fresh ARP lookup. It is usually called after a failed attempt to send data to the server. The typical sequence is: 1) Verify the client is active, 2) Call 'ca_udp_client_refresh_mac' to force an ARP update, 3) If successful, proceed with the next network operation. It is often used in recovery logic to ensure the hardware address mapping is current before retrying transmission.

ca_udp_client_send.signature: bool ca_udp_client_send(u8 handle, const u8 *payload, u16 len)
ca_udp_client_send.brief: Sends a UDP payload using a previously initialized and connected client handle.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The 1-based identifier returned by a successful connection function. Must be within the range [1, UDPCLI_MAX_HANDLES].

params.name: payload
params.desc: Pointer to the buffer containing the data to be transmitted.

params.name: len
params.desc: The number of bytes to send from the payload buffer.

ca_udp_client_send.returns: Returns true if the packet was successfully queued for transmission, false if the handle is invalid, the client is not active, or the transmission failed.
ca_udp_client_send.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses a mutex to verify the client's active status before proceeding. It is NOT callable from an ISR because it performs a mutex lock operation, which can cause the calling task to block; calling this from an ISR will likely trigger a system fault or kernel panic. The function assumes the client has been properly initialized and connected; calling this with an uninitialized handle will result in a false return. A common beginner mistake is failing to check the return value, assuming the packet was sent when it may have been dropped due to buffer congestion or an inactive client state.
ca_udp_client_send.usage: This function is used in the data transmission phase of a network application. It is typically paired with a connection function to establish the session and a disconnection function to clean up resources. In a typical workflow, the application initializes the client, connects to a remote endpoint, enters a loop to send data using this function, and finally disconnects when the communication is complete. If the function returns false, it often indicates that the network stack's internal buffers are full, requiring the application to wait briefly using ca_os_sleep before retrying.

ca_udp_client_sendto.signature: bool ca_udp_client_sendto(u8 handle, ca_ipv4_t dst_ip, u16 dst_port, const u8 *payload, u16 len, u32 arp_timeout_ms)
ca_udp_client_sendto.brief: Sends a UDP packet to a specific destination IP and port using an existing UDP client handle.

params.name: handle
params.desc: The identifier of the UDP client slot, obtained during initialization. Must be between 1 and UDPCLI_MAX_HANDLES.

params.name: dst_ip
params.desc: The destination IPv4 address structure. Cannot be 0.0.0.0.

params.name: dst_port
params.desc: The destination UDP port number.

params.name: payload
params.desc: Pointer to the data buffer to be sent.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the data in bytes.

params.name: arp_timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time to wait for ARP resolution if the MAC address is unknown.

ca_udp_client_sendto.returns: Returns true if the packet was successfully queued for transmission, false otherwise (e.g., invalid handle, inactive slot, ARP resolution failure, or null pointer).
ca_udp_client_sendto.notes: This function is blocking because it may trigger an ARP resolution process if the destination MAC address is not in the cache. It is thread-safe as it uses internal mutexes to protect the client slot state. It must NOT be called from an ISR because of the potential blocking behavior during ARP resolution. A common mistake is passing an uninitialized handle or a handle that has already been closed, which will result in an immediate false return.
ca_udp_client_sendto.usage: This function is used in network-enabled applications to send UDP datagrams to remote servers or peers. It is typically used after a UDP client slot has been opened and is used in a loop or event-driven task to transmit data. It is often paired with initialization functions that set up the network stack and the specific UDP client slot. Ensure the network interface is up and the ARP service is initialized before calling this, otherwise, the function will fail to resolve the destination MAC address.

ca_udp_server_bind.brief: Registers the UDP server port and assigns a callback function to handle incoming network packets.
ca_udp_server_bind.returns: Returns true if the port was successfully bound to the UDP handler, or false if the port configuration is invalid (e.g., port 0) or the binding process failed.
ca_udp_server_bind.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called during the system initialization phase before the network stack starts processing traffic. It is not intended to be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR). The function relies on a pre-configured static structure (s_srv_cfg) which must be initialized before calling this; failing to do so will result in a return value of false. A common beginner mistake is attempting to call this function before the network stack has been initialized via ca_net_proto_init, which will cause the binding to fail silently or return an error.
ca_udp_server_bind.usage: This function is typically used in the main initialization sequence of a network-enabled task. It is usually paired with ca_net_proto_init to prepare the stack, followed by ca_udp_server_bind to open the listening port. After binding, developers often call ca_eth_link_poll to ensure the physical link is active and ca_arp_send_garp to announce the device's presence on the network. It is essential to ensure the port is defined in the configuration before invocation.

ca_udp_server_client_count.brief: Returns the current number of active UDP server clients.
ca_udp_server_client_count.returns: Returns an unsigned 8-bit integer (u8) representing the count of currently assigned UDP clients. The value will always be between 0 and UDPSRV_MAX_CLIENTS.
ca_udp_server_client_count.notes: This function is thread-safe because it uses a mutex to protect the internal client list while iterating. It is a blocking call because it must wait for the mutex to be available; therefore, it must NEVER be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) or a critical section, as this would cause a system deadlock or crash. The UDP server must be initialized before calling this function. A common mistake is assuming the count remains constant after the function returns; in a multi-threaded environment, a client could disconnect or connect immediately after the function returns, so treat the result as a snapshot in time.
ca_udp_server_client_count.usage: This function is typically used for system monitoring, diagnostics, or telemetry reporting. It is often paired with CLI commands to display server status or included in periodic system health logs to track network load. Developers use it to verify if the server is reaching its maximum capacity or to detect if clients are failing to disconnect properly, which might indicate a memory or resource leak.

ca_udp_server_disconnect.brief: Forcefully disconnects a specific UDP client and clears its associated network buffers.

params.name: client_id
params.desc: The index of the client to disconnect. Must be less than UDPSRV_MAX_CLIENTS.

ca_udp_server_disconnect.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses a mutex to protect the client state during modification. It is a blocking operation because it must acquire the server mutex and iterate through the client's ring buffer to free pending packets. It must NOT be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because mutex locking is prohibited in interrupt context. A common mistake is passing an invalid client_id, which the function handles by returning early, but developers should always validate the ID before calling to ensure the intended client is actually the one being disconnected.
ca_udp_server_disconnect.usage: This function is typically used in network management tasks, such as a CLI command to 'kick' a misbehaving client or during a system shutdown sequence to clean up resources. It is often paired with ca_udp_server_get_client to verify the client exists before attempting to disconnect it. By clearing the ring buffer, it ensures that no stale data remains in memory, preventing potential memory leaks or processing of old packets if the same client slot is reused later.

ca_udp_server_get_client.brief: Retrieves connection details for a specific UDP server client slot.

params.name: client_id
params.desc: The index of the client slot to query. Must be less than UDPSRV_MAX_CLIENTS.

params.name: info
params.desc: Pointer to a structure where the client data will be copied. Must not be NULL.

ca_udp_server_get_client.returns: Returns true if the client slot is currently assigned (connected), false otherwise. Also returns false if the provided pointer is NULL or the client_id is out of range.
ca_udp_server_get_client.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses an internal mutex to protect the client table during the copy operation. It is a blocking function because it waits for the mutex; therefore, it must NEVER be called from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine). A common mistake is to assume the client remains connected after the function returns; since the network state can change asynchronously, always check the 'connected' field in the returned structure before using the IP or port data.
ca_udp_server_get_client.usage: This function is typically used in diagnostic tasks or CLI commands to iterate through all available client slots to display network status. It is usually paired with a loop that checks every index from 0 to UDPSRV_MAX_CLIENTS. It is the standard way to safely extract connection metadata (IP, port, and buffer usage) from the UDP server's internal state without causing race conditions.

ca_udp_server_send.signature: bool ca_udp_server_send(u8 client_id, const u8 *payload, u16 len)
ca_udp_server_send.brief: Sends a UDP packet to a specific client previously registered with the UDP server.

params.name: client_id
params.desc: The index of the client in the server's internal client table. Must be less than UDPSRV_MAX_CLIENTS.

params.name: payload
params.desc: Pointer to the data buffer to be sent.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the data in bytes.

ca_udp_server_send.returns: Returns true if the packet was successfully queued for transmission, false if the client_id is invalid, the client is not assigned, or the transmission failed.
ca_udp_server_send.notes: This function is thread-safe as it uses a mutex to protect access to the client table. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR because it performs a mutex lock, which can cause the system to hang or trigger a kernel panic if called from an interrupt context. Ensure the UDP server has been initialized and bound using ca_udp_server_bind before attempting to send data. A common mistake is passing an uninitialized or out-of-bounds client_id, which will immediately return false.
ca_udp_server_send.usage: This function is used to respond to clients that have previously sent data to the server. It is typically used in a request-response pattern where the server receives a packet, processes it, and then uses this function to send the reply back to the specific client identified by the index. It is usually paired with ca_udp_server_bind to set up the server and is called within the application logic after processing incoming data.

ca_udp_server_set_local_ip.brief: Updates the local IP address configuration for the UDP server module.

params.name: ip
params.desc: A structure containing the new IPv4 address to be assigned to the UDP server. Ensure the address is valid and formatted correctly before passing.

ca_udp_server_set_local_ip.notes: This function is a non-blocking, inline operation that directly updates the internal configuration structure of the UDP server. It is not thread-safe by itself; if multiple tasks attempt to modify network settings simultaneously, you must ensure external synchronization. It is safe to call from an ISR if the underlying memory access is atomic, but generally, network configuration changes should be performed in a task context. A common mistake is calling this before the UDP server has been properly initialized, which may lead to the configuration being overwritten or ignored.
ca_udp_server_set_local_ip.usage: This function is typically used during the network initialization sequence, specifically after a DHCP lease has been successfully acquired or a static IP has been assigned. It is usually paired with ca_net_proto_set_local_ip to update the global network stack and ca_arp_service_update_local_ip to ensure the ARP table reflects the new address. It is often wrapped in an EVAL_UDP_SRV macro to ensure the operation only executes if the UDP server module is enabled in the project configuration.

ca_udp_server_start.brief: Initializes and launches the UDP server background tasks based on the provided configuration.

params.name: cfg
params.desc: Pointer to a configuration structure. Must contain a valid callback function (on_rx) and a non-zero number of clients not exceeding UDPSRV_MAX_CLIENTS.

ca_udp_server_start.returns: Returns true if the server was successfully initialized and tasks were created; returns false if the configuration is invalid or NULL.
ca_udp_server_start.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called during system initialization, typically within ca_os_main, before the scheduler starts running tasks. It performs internal memory initialization for mutexes and semaphores for each client slot; therefore, it must not be called more than once. It is not callable from an ISR. A common mistake is passing a NULL pointer or a configuration where max_clients exceeds the hardcoded system limit, which will cause the function to fail silently by returning false.
ca_udp_server_start.usage: This function is used to set up the network infrastructure for UDP communication. It is typically called in the main initialization sequence alongside other network services like ca_arp_service_start or ca_dhcp_service_start. Once called, it spawns internal worker tasks that handle incoming UDP packets asynchronously. It should be invoked before any network-dependent tasks are created via ca_os_job to ensure the server is ready to process traffic.

ca_upy_adc_read.signature: int ca_upy_adc_read(int adc, int ch, uint32_t *v)
ca_upy_adc_read.brief: Reads a value from a specified ADC unit and channel, handling automatic initialization.

params.name: adc
params.desc: The ADC unit number (valid range: 1 to 3).

params.name: ch
params.desc: The ADC channel number (valid range: 0 to 19).

params.name: v
params.desc: Pointer to a variable where the read ADC value will be stored.

ca_upy_adc_read.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns UPY_EINVAL if the ADC unit or channel is out of range. Returns UPY_EIO if the ADC hardware initialization fails. Returns UPY_ENODEV if ADC support is disabled in the build configuration.
ca_upy_adc_read.notes: This function is not thread-safe because it uses a static variable to track initialization state across calls. It is intended for use in application-level tasks and should not be called from an ISR, as it performs hardware initialization which may involve blocking operations. The function automatically handles the initialization of the ADC peripheral the first time a specific unit is accessed, so you do not need to call an explicit init function beforehand. A common mistake is passing an invalid channel number for a specific STM32 pin, which will result in an error or undefined behavior at the hardware level.
ca_upy_adc_read.usage: This function is typically used in high-level language wrappers (like MicroPython) to expose hardware ADC functionality to user scripts. It is designed to be called whenever a sample is needed, abstracting away the complexity of peripheral setup. It pairs with the underlying hardware drivers to ensure the pin is configured correctly before the conversion starts. In a typical lifecycle, you would call this function repeatedly to poll sensor data, and the system handles the internal state management automatically.

ca_upy_aes_gcm.signature: int ca_upy_aes_gcm(int enc, int key_idx, const void *key, size_t klen, const uint8_t *iv12, const void *aad, size_t al, const void *in, void *out, size_t n, uint8_t *tag16)
ca_upy_aes_gcm.brief: Performs AES-GCM authenticated encryption or decryption using a managed key store.

params.name: enc
params.desc: Set to 1 for encryption, 0 for decryption.

params.name: key_idx
params.desc: Index of the key in the secure key store.

params.name: key
params.desc: Pointer to the key material or identifier.

params.name: klen
params.desc: Length of the key in bytes (must be 16, 24, or 32).

params.name: iv12
params.desc: Pointer to the 12-byte Initialization Vector (IV).

params.name: aad
params.desc: Pointer to Additional Authenticated Data (can be NULL).

params.name: al
params.desc: Length of the AAD in bytes.

params.name: in
params.desc: Pointer to input data (plaintext for encryption, ciphertext for decryption).

params.name: out
params.desc: Buffer to store output data.

params.name: n
params.desc: Length of the input/output data in bytes.

params.name: tag16
params.desc: Pointer to a 16-byte buffer for the authentication tag.

ca_upy_aes_gcm.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns UPY_ENOENT if the key is invalid, UPY_EINVAL for invalid key sizes, UPY_ENOMEM if memory allocation fails, UPY_EIO for encryption failure, or UPY_EBADMSG for decryption/authentication failure.
ca_upy_aes_gcm.notes: This function is blocking and performs dynamic memory allocation for the AES context; it is not safe to call from an ISR. It requires the caOS memory management system to be initialized. A common mistake is providing an incorrect IV length or failing to check the return value, which could lead to processing unauthenticated or corrupted data. If decryption fails, the function automatically clears the output buffer to prevent sensitive data leakage.
ca_upy_aes_gcm.usage: This function is typically used in secure communication modules or file encryption tasks. It is usually paired with key management functions to retrieve the key handle before processing. The typical sequence is: verify key availability, call this function to perform the cryptographic operation, and then handle the return code to determine if the data is authentic. It is often used in conjunction with buffer management functions to prepare input and output memory regions.

ca_upy_blake2s.signature: int ca_upy_blake2s(const void *key, size_t kl, const void *d, size_t n, uint8_t *out, size_t ol)
ca_upy_blake2s.brief: Computes a BLAKE2s cryptographic hash, optionally using a secret key.

params.name: key
params.desc: Pointer to the secret key buffer. Can be NULL if no key is used.

params.name: kl
params.desc: Length of the key in bytes. Must be 0 if key is NULL.

params.name: d
params.desc: Pointer to the input data buffer to be hashed.

params.name: n
params.desc: Length of the input data in bytes.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to the output buffer where the hash will be stored.

params.name: ol
params.desc: Desired length of the output hash in bytes (typically 1 to 32).

ca_upy_blake2s.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns UPY_ENOMEM if internal memory allocation fails, UPY_EINVAL if parameters are invalid, or UPY_ENODEV if the BLAKE2s feature is disabled in the build configuration.
ca_upy_blake2s.notes: This function performs a dynamic memory allocation internally to create a context object, which is then freed before returning. Because it uses dynamic memory, it is not suitable for use inside high-frequency Interrupt Service Routines (ISRs) where heap allocation is prohibited. It is thread-safe in the sense that it manages its own context, but ensure the input and output buffers remain valid for the duration of the call. A common mistake is providing an output length (ol) that exceeds the capacity of the output buffer or the maximum allowed by the algorithm (32 bytes).
ca_upy_blake2s.usage: This function is typically used in cryptographic applications to generate message digests or HMAC-like tags. It is often paired with memory management functions to prepare buffers before the call. In a typical workflow, you would allocate a buffer for the result, call this function to compute the hash, and then process or transmit the resulting bytes. If the system is low on memory, the function will return an error, so always check the return value before using the data in the output buffer.

ca_upy_chacha20poly1305.signature: int ca_upy_chacha20poly1305(int enc, int key_idx, const void *key, size_t klen, const uint8_t *nonce, size_t nlen, uint64_t nonce64, const void *aad, size_t al, const void *in, void *out, size_t n, uint8_t *tag16)
ca_upy_chacha20poly1305.brief: Performs authenticated encryption or decryption using the ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD algorithm.

params.name: enc
params.desc: Set to 1 for encryption, 0 for decryption.

params.name: key_idx
params.desc: Index of the key in the secure storage system.

params.name: key
params.desc: Pointer to the key buffer.

params.name: klen
params.desc: Length of the key in bytes.

params.name: nonce
params.desc: Pointer to the nonce buffer (ignored if nlen is 0).

params.name: nlen
params.desc: Nonce length: 0 for 64-bit (WireGuard), 12 for IETF, 24 for XChaCha.

params.name: nonce64
params.desc: 64-bit nonce value used when nlen is 0.

params.name: aad
params.desc: Pointer to Additional Authenticated Data.

params.name: al
params.desc: Length of the AAD in bytes.

params.name: in
params.desc: Input buffer (plaintext for encryption, ciphertext for decryption).

params.name: out
params.desc: Output buffer (ciphertext for encryption, plaintext for decryption).

params.name: n
params.desc: Length of the input data in bytes.

params.name: tag16
params.desc: 16-byte buffer for the authentication tag.

ca_upy_chacha20poly1305.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns UPY_EINVAL for invalid parameters, UPY_ENOENT if the key is not found, UPY_ENOMEM if heap allocation fails, or UPY_EBADMSG if decryption fails (authentication tag mismatch).
ca_upy_chacha20poly1305.notes: This function is blocking and performs heap allocations internally for the cryptographic context and processing buffers. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR because it uses heap management functions that may block or be non-reentrant. You must ensure the key storage is initialized before calling this. A common mistake is providing an incorrect nonce length or failing to check the return value, which leads to processing unauthenticated or corrupted data.
ca_upy_chacha20poly1305.usage: This function is typically used in secure communication protocols or file encryption tasks. It is usually paired with key management functions to retrieve a key handle, followed by this function to perform the cryptographic operation, and finally a key release function. In a typical sequence, you allocate output buffers, call this function to process the data, and then handle the returned status to verify if the decryption was successful before using the output data.

ca_upy_cli.signature: int ca_upy_cli(const char *cmd, char *out, size_t cap)
ca_upy_cli.brief: Executes a CLI command string and captures its output into a provided buffer.

params.name: cmd
params.desc: The command string to execute. Must not be NULL.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to the buffer where the command output will be stored. Must not be NULL.

params.name: cap
params.desc: Capacity of the output buffer. Must be at least 2 to accommodate the string and null terminator.

ca_upy_cli.returns: Returns the length of the captured output string (>= 0) on success, or -1 if the command failed, timed out, or if the CLI capture feature is disabled.
ca_upy_cli.notes: This function is blocking; it waits for the command to complete or for a timeout (5000ms) to occur. It is not safe to call from an ISR because it relies on internal RTOS synchronization primitives that may block. Ensure that the CLI subsystem is properly initialized before calling this. A common mistake is providing a buffer that is too small, which will cause the function to return -1 immediately if cap < 2.
ca_upy_cli.usage: This function is typically used to programmatically trigger system commands from within a MicroPython environment or another task. It acts as a bridge between high-level logic and the low-level CLI. It is often paired with memory management functions to allocate the output buffer dynamically, followed by a check of the return value to determine if the command output should be processed or if an error should be raised.

ca_upy_crc32.signature: int ca_upy_crc32(const void *d, size_t n, uint32_t *out)
ca_upy_crc32.brief: Calculates the CRC32 checksum of a data buffer for MicroPython integration.

params.name: d
params.desc: Pointer to the input data buffer. Must be a valid memory address.

params.name: n
params.desc: Length of the data buffer in bytes. Must be greater than 0.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to a 32-bit variable where the calculated CRC result will be stored.

ca_upy_crc32.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns UPY_ENODEV if the CRC hardware feature is disabled in the system configuration.
ca_upy_crc32.notes: This function is a wrapper designed for the MicroPython environment to interface with the underlying hardware CRC engine. It is thread-safe assuming the underlying hardware peripheral is properly managed by the OS. It is generally non-blocking, but performance depends on the size of the buffer 'n' as it processes data linearly. Do not call this from an ISR if the buffer is extremely large, as it may cause latency issues for the scheduler. The most common mistake is passing a NULL pointer for 'd' or 'out', which will lead to a hard fault.
ca_upy_crc32.usage: This function is used when you need to verify data integrity, such as checking a file or a network packet received via MicroPython. It is typically used in a sequence where you first obtain a buffer pointer (e.g., from a file or memory object), call this function to compute the checksum, and then compare the result against an expected value. It is often paired with memory management functions to ensure the buffer 'd' is valid before processing.

ca_upy_dac_write.brief: Writes a digital value to a DAC channel, automatically initializing the hardware if necessary.

params.name: ch
params.desc: The DAC channel number. Must be 1 or 2. Values outside this range will return an error.

params.name: v
params.desc: The digital value to convert. Must be in the range 0 to 4095 (12-bit resolution). Values > 4095 will return an error.

ca_upy_dac_write.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns UPY_EINVAL if parameters are out of range, UPY_EIO if hardware initialization fails, or UPY_ENODEV if the DAC feature is disabled in the build configuration.
ca_upy_dac_write.notes: This function is a high-level wrapper designed for MicroPython integration. It is not thread-safe because it uses a static variable to track initialization state; if called from multiple threads simultaneously, it could trigger redundant or conflicting initialization calls. It is not safe to call from an ISR because it performs hardware initialization which may involve blocking operations or resource allocation. The most common mistake is passing a value greater than 4095, which will cause the function to reject the request immediately.
ca_upy_dac_write.usage: This function is typically used in the context of a MicroPython machine module to expose DAC functionality to user scripts. It handles the 'lazy initialization' pattern: the first time a channel is accessed, the function calls the underlying hardware driver to configure the pins and registers. Subsequent calls reuse the initialized state, making it efficient for repeated writes. It is usually paired with user-level input validation to ensure the DAC output remains within the hardware's physical limits.

ca_upy_dns.signature: int ca_upy_dns(const char *host, uint32_t timeout_ms, uint8_t *ip4)
ca_upy_dns.brief: Resolves a hostname to an IPv4 address using the system DNS service.

params.name: host
params.desc: The null-terminated string containing the hostname to resolve (e.g., "google.com").

params.name: timeout_ms
params.desc: Maximum time in milliseconds to wait for the DNS server response. Must be greater than 0.

params.name: ip4
params.desc: Pointer to a buffer of at least 4 bytes where the resolved IPv4 address will be stored in network byte order.

ca_upy_dns.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns UPY_ETIMEDOUT (110) if the DNS query fails or times out. Returns UPY_ENODEV (defined by the wrapper) if the DNS service is disabled in the system configuration.
ca_upy_dns.notes: This function is a blocking call; it will suspend the calling task until the DNS resolution completes or the timeout expires. It is not safe to call this function from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it relies on the RTOS scheduler to manage the wait state. Before calling this, ensure the network stack is initialized and the DNS service is active. A common mistake is providing an insufficient buffer for the ip4 parameter or setting a timeout that is too short for the network latency, leading to frequent resolution failures.
ca_upy_dns.usage: This function is typically used in network-enabled applications to convert human-readable domain names into IP addresses required for socket connections. It is often paired with socket creation functions (like ca_upy_sock_open) and connection functions (like ca_upy_sock_connect). In a typical sequence, the developer calls this to resolve the address, checks the return value for errors, and then proceeds to use the resulting IP array to initiate communication with a remote server.

ca_upy_ecdsa_keygen.brief: Generates a new ECDSA P-256 private/public key pair for MicroPython.

params.name: priv32
params.desc: Pointer to a 32-byte buffer where the generated private key will be stored.

params.name: pub64

ca_upy_ecdsa_keygen.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns UPY_ENOMEM if memory allocation for the internal context fails, or UPY_EIO if the key generation process fails. Returns UPY_ENODEV if the ECDSA P256 feature is disabled in the build configuration.

ca_upy_ecdsa_keygen.usage: This function is typically used in high-level language bindings (like MicroPython) to generate cryptographic identities on-the-fly. It is usually paired with memory management functions to ensure the buffers are allocated before the call and processed (e.g., converted to bytes objects) immediately after. It is part of the initialization sequence for secure communication or signing tasks where a new key pair is required.

ca_upy_ecdsa_public.signature: int ca_upy_ecdsa_public(int key_idx, const uint8_t *priv32, uint8_t *pub64)

ca_upy_ecdsa_public.usage: This function is typically used in security-sensitive applications where a public key must be generated on-the-fly from a stored private key for identity verification or key exchange. It is often paired with MicroPython buffer management functions to allocate space for the output key. The typical sequence is: allocate a buffer for the 64-byte public key, call this function to populate it, and then use the resulting bytes for cryptographic operations.

ca_upy_ecdsa_sign.usage: This function is typically used in high-level application logic (like MicroPython wrappers or secure communication modules) to generate digital signatures for authentication or data integrity. It is used in a sequence where the application first retrieves the key handle, calls this function to sign the data, and then processes the resulting signature. It is often paired with ca_upy_ecdsa_verify for validation on the receiving end.

ca_upy_ecdsa_verify.notes: This function performs cryptographic operations which are computationally intensive and may take significant time to complete. ca_upy_ecdsa_verify.usage: This function is typically used in security-sensitive applications to verify the authenticity of data received over a network or from external storage. It is usually paired with message buffer retrieval functions (like those in MicroPython's buffer protocol) to prepare the data before verification. The typical sequence is: retrieve the public key, retrieve the message, retrieve the signature, call this function to verify, and finally handle the result to allow or deny access to the system.

ca_upy_ed25519_public.usage: This function is typically used in cryptographic applications where a public key must be generated on-the-fly from a stored secret seed. It is often paired with key management functions to retrieve the seed and memory management functions to handle the context. ca_upy_ed25519_sign.notes: This function is blocking and performs cryptographic operations that may take significant CPU time; do not call it from an ISR. ca_upy_ed25519_verify.usage: This function is typically used in security-sensitive applications to verify the authenticity of incoming data or firmware updates. It is often paired with buffer validation functions to ensure the input data is of the expected length. ca_upy_event_op.signature: uint32_t ca_upy_event_op(void *e, int op, uint32_t bits, uint32_t timeout_ms)
ca_upy_event_op.brief: A unified wrapper to perform set, clear, or wait operations on a caOS event group object.

params.name: e
params.desc: Pointer to the ca_event_group_t handle. Must be a valid, initialized event group.

params.desc: Operation code: 0=Set, 1=Clear, 2=Wait Any, 3=Wait All. Any other value returns the current state.

params.desc: Time in milliseconds to block if waiting. Use 0 for no wait or a large value for indefinite blocking.

ca_upy_event_op.returns: Returns the current state of the event group (as a bitmask) after the operation is performed. If a wait operation times out, it returns the state at the moment of timeout.
ca_upy_event_op.notes: This function acts as a bridge for MicroPython to interact with RTOS event groups. Ensure the event group handle is initialized via ca_event_init before passing it here. A common mistake is passing an uninitialized pointer or a NULL handle, which will lead to a hard fault.
ca_upy_event_op.usage: This function is typically used in synchronization logic where one task needs to signal another or wait for multiple conditions to be met. It is usually paired with ca_event_init during system setup. In a typical lifecycle, you initialize the event group, then use this function to set bits from a producer task (e.g., an interrupt handler or sensor task) and wait for those bits in a consumer task to trigger specific logic.

ca_upy_fatal.brief: Triggers an immediate, unrecoverable system halt for the MicroPython environment.

params.name: msg
params.desc: A descriptive string explaining the cause of the fatal error. This message is sent to the CLI before the system halts.

ca_upy_fatal.returns: This function never returns as it triggers a CPU trap.
ca_upy_fatal.notes: This function is a 'noreturn' routine that invokes __builtin_trap(). It is intended for catastrophic failures where the MicroPython state is corrupted beyond recovery. When called, the kernel will attempt to clean up the task's resources, including freeing its heap and releasing the CLI console. Do not use this for standard error handling; it is strictly for emergency situations where the only safe path is to stop execution immediately. It is not thread-safe in the sense that it stops the entire task context, and it should never be called from an ISR unless you are certain the system state is already compromised.
ca_upy_fatal.usage: Use this function only when the MicroPython interpreter encounters an internal inconsistency that cannot be caught by standard exception handling (e.g., a failed jump in the Non-Local Return mechanism). It is typically used in porting layers where the underlying C code detects that the interpreter's stack or heap is no longer valid. Once called, the system will effectively kill the task, so ensure all critical hardware states are handled or that a system reset is acceptable.

ca_upy_fs_close.brief: Closes a file handle previously opened via the MicroPython VFS layer in caOS.

params.name: h
params.desc: A pointer to the file handle object. Must be a valid handle previously returned by ca_upy_fs_open. Passing NULL or an invalid/already-closed handle will result in an error.

ca_upy_fs_close.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns a non-zero error code (e.g., UPY_EBADF) if the handle is invalid, not found in the active file table, or if the underlying filesystem close operation fails.
ca_upy_fs_close.notes: This function is part of the MicroPython VFS wrapper and is not intended for direct use in standard application logic unless you are extending the VFS layer. It is thread-safe regarding the internal file table management, but it is NOT safe to call from an ISR because it performs blocking filesystem operations. A common mistake is attempting to close a handle that has already been closed or invalidated by a system reset, which will trigger the UPY_EBADF error code. Always ensure the handle is set to NULL in your application logic immediately after calling this function to prevent dangling pointer access.
ca_upy_fs_close.usage: This function is used during the cleanup phase of file operations within the MicroPython environment. It is typically paired with ca_upy_fs_open to manage the lifecycle of a file. In the context of stream objects, it is invoked when the stream is closed (e.g., MP_STREAM_CLOSE request) to release the underlying filesystem resources and remove the handle from the internal tracking table.

ca_upy_fs_closedir.brief: Closes a directory handle previously opened by the MicroPython VFS layer.

params.name: d
params.desc: A pointer to the directory handle object. Must be a valid pointer previously returned by a directory opening operation; passing NULL or an invalid pointer will result in an error.

ca_upy_fs_closedir.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns UPY_EBADF if the provided handle is not found in the internal tracking table or is NULL. Other non-zero values represent filesystem-specific error codes mapped via fr_errno.
ca_upy_fs_closedir.notes: This function is part of the MicroPython VFS wrapper and is not intended for direct use in standard C application code unless you are extending the VFS layer. It is not thread-safe regarding the internal directory tracking table (s_upy_dirs), so ensure that directory operations are serialized if accessed from multiple tasks. It is not callable from an ISR. The function performs a lookup in a static array to validate the handle before calling the underlying filesystem close function. A common mistake is attempting to close a handle that has already been closed or passing a pointer that was never allocated by the VFS system, which will trigger the UPY_EBADF error.
ca_upy_fs_closedir.usage: This function is used during the cleanup phase of directory iteration or access. It is typically paired with a directory opening function (like ca_upy_fs_opendir, though not listed in the provided catalog, it is the logical counterpart). In the MicroPython VFS context, it is called when an iterator object is garbage collected or when the directory traversal is finished to ensure that system resources and file descriptors are released back to the OS.

ca_upy_fs_mkdir.brief: Creates a new directory at the specified path within the filesystem.

params.name: path
params.desc: A null-terminated string representing the full path of the directory to create. Must be a valid path format supported by the underlying FAT filesystem.

ca_upy_fs_mkdir.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns a non-zero error code (errno-style) if the operation fails, such as if the parent directory does not exist, the path is invalid, or the filesystem is read-only.
ca_upy_fs_mkdir.notes: This function is a wrapper for the underlying FAT filesystem driver. It is blocking, meaning the calling task will wait until the filesystem operation completes, which may involve multiple flash memory access cycles. It is not safe to call from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it performs blocking I/O operations. Ensure the filesystem is properly mounted using ca_upy_fs_mount before attempting to create directories. A common mistake is passing a relative path when the system expects an absolute path, or failing to check the return value, which leads to silent failures when the storage is full or write-protected.
ca_upy_fs_mkdir.usage: Used primarily in high-level application logic or MicroPython wrappers to organize data storage. It is typically used in a sequence: first, ensure the filesystem is mounted with ca_upy_fs_mount, then check for existing paths with ca_upy_fs_stat if necessary, and finally call ca_upy_fs_mkdir to create the directory structure. It is often paired with ca_upy_fs_open for subsequent file creation within the new directory.

ca_upy_fs_mount.brief: Mounts the filesystem for MicroPython access within the caOS environment.
ca_upy_fs_mount.returns: Returns 0 on success (already mounted or successfully mounted). Returns UPY_ENODEV if the underlying filesystem mount operation fails.
ca_upy_fs_mount.notes: This function is a wrapper that checks if the filesystem is already mounted using ca_fat_is_mounted before attempting to mount it via ca_fat_mount. It is not thread-safe by itself, so ensure that multiple tasks are not attempting to mount or unmount the filesystem simultaneously. It is intended to be called from task context; do not call this from an ISR as filesystem operations involve blocking I/O and potential mutex locks. A common beginner mistake is calling this function repeatedly without checking the return value or assuming it will always succeed even if the hardware (e.g., SD card) is not physically present.
ca_upy_fs_mount.usage: This function is typically used during the initialization phase of the MicroPython virtual filesystem (VFS) layer in caOS. It is paired with ca_upy_fs_reset or similar cleanup functions during system shutdown or VFS unmounting. Developers use this to ensure the storage medium is accessible before performing file operations like opening, reading, or writing files via the MicroPython interface.

ca_upy_fs_open.signature: int ca_upy_fs_open(void **h, const char *path, int mode)
ca_upy_fs_open.brief: Opens a file in the MicroPython VFS layer and assigns it to a file handle.

params.name: h
params.desc: Pointer to a void pointer that will store the file handle upon success. Must not be NULL.

params.name: path
params.desc: Null-terminated string representing the file path to open.

params.name: mode
params.desc: File access mode (e.g., read, write, append). Values must match the underlying FAT filesystem requirements.

ca_upy_fs_open.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns a negative error code (e.g., UPY_EMFILE) if the file cannot be opened, if the maximum number of open files is reached, or if the path is invalid.
ca_upy_fs_open.notes: This function is part of the MicroPython VFS wrapper and is not intended for direct use in standard RTOS tasks unless you are extending the MicroPython environment. It is not thread-safe by itself; it relies on the internal state of the MicroPython file table (s_upy_files). It is strictly forbidden to call this from an ISR because it performs filesystem operations which are blocking and non-deterministic. A common mistake is failing to check the return value, which leads to a NULL pointer dereference when attempting to use the uninitialized handle.
ca_upy_fs_open.usage: This function is used when integrating custom C modules with MicroPython to access the filesystem. It is typically called during the object initialization phase of a file-like object. It is always paired with ca_upy_fs_close to release the file handle and prevent resource leaks. The typical sequence is: call ca_upy_fs_open to get the handle, perform read/write operations using ca_upy_fs_read or ca_upy_fs_write, and finally call ca_upy_fs_close when the file is no longer needed.

ca_upy_fs_opendir.brief: Opens a directory on the filesystem for reading and returns a handle for subsequent directory operations.

params.name: d
params.desc: Pointer to a void pointer that will store the directory handle upon success. Must not be NULL.

params.name: path
params.desc: String containing the path of the directory to open. Must be a valid null-terminated string.

ca_upy_fs_opendir.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns UPY_EMFILE if the internal directory table is full, or a negative error code (mapped from the underlying FAT filesystem) if the directory cannot be opened (e.g., path not found).
ca_upy_fs_opendir.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should not be called from an ISR. It manages an internal static array of directory handles; if you open too many directories without closing them, you will exhaust the available slots (UPY_MAX_DIRS). Always ensure you pair this with a corresponding close function to prevent memory leaks and handle exhaustion. The function blocks while interacting with the underlying storage media, so it should not be called from high-priority real-time tasks that cannot tolerate latency.
ca_upy_fs_opendir.usage: Used when traversing a filesystem to list files or subdirectories. It is typically the first step in a sequence: open the directory with ca_upy_fs_opendir, iterate through entries using ca_upy_fs_readdir, and finally release the resources using ca_upy_fs_closedir. It is commonly used in MicroPython VFS implementations to support file listing commands.

ca_upy_fs_present.brief: Checks if the filesystem (typically SD card) is available and initialized for MicroPython.
ca_upy_fs_present.returns: Returns 1 if the filesystem is present and ready for use, 0 otherwise.
ca_upy_fs_present.notes: This function is a non-blocking, thread-safe check that queries the internal state of the caOS VFS (Virtual File System) layer. It does not perform any hardware I/O, so it is safe to call from any context, including ISRs, though it is primarily intended for application-level initialization logic. A common mistake is to assume that a return value of 1 guarantees that a specific file exists or that the SD card is physically inserted; it only confirms that the filesystem driver is registered and mounted in the system. Always verify the return value before attempting to mount or access files to prevent null pointer dereferences or system crashes.
ca_upy_fs_present.usage: This function is typically used during the system boot sequence or when a task initializes its storage requirements. It acts as a guard clause to ensure that filesystem-dependent features (like loading 'boot.py' or 'main.py' scripts) are only attempted if the underlying storage is actually available. It is usually paired with ca_upy_fs_mount or other ca_upy_fs_* functions to perform actual file operations once the presence is confirmed.

ca_upy_fs_read.signature: int ca_upy_fs_read(void *h, void *buf, size_t len, size_t *got)
ca_upy_fs_read.brief: Reads data from an open file handle into a provided buffer.

params.name: h
params.desc: A pointer to the file handle object, previously opened via ca_upy_fs_open.

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the memory buffer where the read data will be stored.

params.name: len
params.desc: The number of bytes to attempt to read.

params.name: got
params.desc: Pointer to a variable that will store the actual number of bytes successfully read.

ca_upy_fs_read.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns a non-zero error code (e.g., UPY_EBADF) if the file handle is invalid, closed, or if a hardware/filesystem error occurs.
ca_upy_fs_read.notes: This function is a blocking operation; it will wait for the underlying storage media (like SD card or Flash) to complete the read transaction before returning. It is not safe to call from an ISR (Interrupt Service Routine) because it relies on filesystem locks and potential thread-blocking mechanisms. Ensure the file handle 'h' is valid and not NULL before calling; passing a closed or uninitialized handle will result in an error. The most common mistake is failing to check the returned error code, which can lead to processing uninitialized or stale data in the buffer if the read operation failed.
ca_upy_fs_read.usage: This function is typically used within a file-processing loop where you open a file with ca_upy_fs_open, read chunks of data into a buffer, and finally close the file with ca_upy_fs_close. It is the standard way to stream data from the filesystem into application memory. In a typical sequence, you initialize the filesystem, open the file, perform one or more calls to this function to retrieve data, and then release the handle to free system resources.

ca_upy_fs_readdir.brief: Reads the next entry from an open directory handle in the filesystem.

params.name: d
params.desc: A pointer to the directory handle previously opened via ca_upy_fs_opendir. Must not be NULL.

params.name: st
params.desc: A pointer to a structure where the file/directory metadata will be stored. Must be pre-allocated.

ca_upy_fs_readdir.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns a non-zero error code (e.g., UPY_ENOMEM or filesystem-specific errors) if the operation fails. If the end of the directory is reached, the function typically returns 0 but populates the stat structure with an empty name string.
ca_upy_fs_readdir.notes: This function is blocking as it performs I/O operations on the storage medium. It is not safe to call from an ISR because it performs dynamic memory allocation using ca_memory_allocate. You must ensure the directory handle 'd' is valid and was successfully opened before calling this. A common mistake is failing to check the returned error code or the contents of the 'st' structure, which can lead to processing invalid file metadata or infinite loops when iterating through a directory.
ca_upy_fs_readdir.usage: This function is used to iterate through the contents of a directory, typically in a loop until no more entries are found. It is part of the standard filesystem traversal sequence: open the directory with ca_upy_fs_opendir, call ca_upy_fs_readdir repeatedly to fetch entries, and finally close the handle with ca_upy_fs_closedir. It is often paired with memory management functions to allocate the stat structure before the loop and free it afterwards.

ca_upy_fs_remove.brief: Deletes a file from the filesystem by its path.

params.name: path
params.desc: The null-terminated string representing the absolute or relative path to the file to be removed.

ca_upy_fs_remove.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns a non-zero error code (mapped via fr_errno) if the operation fails, such as when the file does not exist, the path is a directory, or the filesystem is read-only.
ca_upy_fs_remove.notes: This function is a wrapper around the FAT filesystem unlink operation. It is a blocking call, meaning the calling task will wait until the filesystem driver completes the disk I/O operation. It is not safe to call this function from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) because it performs blocking operations and potentially involves mutex locking within the filesystem driver. A common mistake is attempting to remove a directory using this function; for directories, you must use the appropriate directory-specific removal function instead.
ca_upy_fs_remove.usage: This function is typically used in application logic to manage file cleanup or user-requested deletions. It is often paired with file status checks (like checking if a file exists or verifying its type) before attempting the removal. In a typical lifecycle, you might use ca_upy_fs_stat to verify the target, then call ca_upy_fs_remove to delete it, and finally check the return value to confirm the operation succeeded before proceeding with further filesystem updates.

ca_upy_fs_rename.brief: Renames or moves a file or directory within the filesystem.

params.name: from
params.desc: The current path of the file or directory. Must be a valid, null-terminated string.

params.name: to
params.desc: The desired new path. If this path already exists, the operation may fail depending on the underlying filesystem implementation.

ca_upy_fs_rename.returns: Returns 0 on success. Returns a non-zero error code (e.g., MP_EEXIST, MP_ENOENT) if the operation fails, such as when the source does not exist or the destination is invalid.
ca_upy_fs_rename.notes: This function is a blocking call that interacts with the underlying storage driver; it should never be called from an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR). It is thread-safe provided the filesystem is properly initialized and mounted. A common mistake is passing relative paths without ensuring the current working directory is correctly set, or failing to check the return value, which leads to silent failures when the destination path is already occupied.
ca_upy_fs_rename.usage: This function is typically used in file management tasks, such as renaming configuration files or moving temporary files to their final destination. It is often paired with ca_upy_fs_remove if an existing file needs to be overwritten, as shown in the MicroPython VFS implementation.
