ca_usb_dbg_print.usage: Used primarily during development or troubleshooting to verify USB enumeration, endpoint activity, and interrupt performance. It is typically paired with CLI handlers to allow developers to dump the state of the USB stack on demand. In power management scenarios, it is used to verify that the USB peripheral has correctly resumed or re-enumerated after a low-power state transition by comparing the output before and after the sleep period. It is often used in a sequence: check status, perform an operation (like sleep or reset), and check status again to verify the state change.

ca_usb_dbg_reset.brief: Resets the internal USB debug counters and statistics for all enabled USB controllers.
ca_usb_dbg_reset.notes: This function is a wrapper that triggers a reset of the internal diagnostic counters for High-Speed (HS) and Full-Speed (FS) USB controllers, depending on the build configuration. It is not thread-safe in the sense that it modifies global state; if called while another task is reading statistics, the data might be inconsistent. It is generally safe to call from a task context, but you should avoid calling it from an ISR unless the underlying hardware-specific reset functions are explicitly documented as ISR-safe. The most common mistake is assuming this resets the USB hardware connection itself; it only clears the software-level debug counters used for performance monitoring.
ca_usb_dbg_reset.usage: This function is typically used during system maintenance or debugging sessions to clear accumulated statistics, such as interrupt counts or error flags, before starting a new test cycle. It is often paired with 'ca_usb_dbg_stat' to capture a baseline, followed by a period of USB activity, and then another 'ca_usb_dbg_stat' to analyze the delta. In a CLI environment, it is triggered by a user command to reset the performance metrics without requiring a full system reboot.

ca_usb_dbg_stat.brief: Retrieves real-time diagnostic statistics from the specified USB controller hardware.

params.name: out
params.desc: Pointer to a structure where the USB diagnostic data will be stored. Must not be NULL.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB controller to query (0 for primary, 1 for secondary). Valid values depend on hardware configuration.

ca_usb_dbg_stat.returns: This function returns void. If the provided pointer is NULL, the function safely does nothing (or clears the structure if supported).
ca_usb_dbg_stat.notes: This function is a dispatcher that routes the request to the appropriate low-level driver (HS or FS) based on your system configuration. It is non-blocking and executes quickly, making it safe to call from most contexts, though it is primarily intended for CLI or monitoring tasks. It is not thread-safe in the sense that it does not lock the USB hardware; if the USB controller is undergoing a reset or heavy re-initialization, the data returned might be inconsistent. The most common beginner mistake is passing an uninitialized pointer or assuming the data is updated in real-time without considering the overhead of the USB interrupt activity it measures.
ca_usb_dbg_stat.usage: This function is used for system health monitoring and debugging USB communication issues. It is typically called within a CLI command handler or a background monitoring task to inspect endpoint status, interrupt counts, and latency metrics. You would typically pair this with other diagnostic tools to print the gathered data to the console, allowing you to verify if endpoints are stalled or if the interrupt service routine is processing data as expected.

ca_usb_dev_mng_add.brief: Registers a new USB device configuration into the USB management system.

params.name: cfg
params.desc: Pointer to the USB device configuration structure. Must not be NULL, must contain valid operations, and must have a valid device type index.

ca_usb_dev_mng_add.returns: Returns true if the device was successfully registered, false if the configuration is invalid, the device type is already registered, or if there is an endpoint resource collision.
ca_usb_dev_mng_add.notes: This function is not thread-safe and is intended to be called during the system initialization phase before the USB stack is started. It performs a static check for endpoint (EP) collisions; if two different USB device types attempt to use the same hardware endpoint, the function will reject the second one. It is not callable from an ISR. A common mistake is attempting to add a device after calling ca_usb_dev_mng_start, which may lead to inconsistent USB enumeration states. Ensure the configuration structure is persistent (e.g., static or global) as the manager stores the pointer directly.
ca_usb_dev_mng_add.usage: This function is part of the USB initialization sequence. It is typically used after ca_usb_dev_mng_init and before ca_usb_dev_mng_start. You use it to register specific USB classes (like CDC or custom HID) into the management array. If you need to change device configurations at runtime, you must first call ca_usb_dev_mng_remove to free the endpoint resources before adding a new configuration.

ca_usb_dev_mng_cdc_cli.brief: Initializes and starts the USB CDC device manager for CLI communication.
ca_usb_dev_mng_cdc_cli.returns: Returns true if the USB device manager was successfully initialized, configured, and started; returns false if any step (init, add, or start) fails.
ca_usb_dev_mng_cdc_cli.notes: This function is intended to be called during system startup, specifically within ca_os_main before the RTOS scheduler is fully operational. It is not thread-safe and must never be called from an ISR. The function performs a blocking delay (ca_os_delay_ms) to allow the USB hardware and clock tree to stabilize after the D+ pull-up is enabled. A common mistake is calling this function after the scheduler has started or inside a task, which can lead to race conditions during USB enumeration or system instability due to the blocking nature of the internal delays.
ca_usb_dev_mng_cdc_cli.usage: This function is typically used in the main initialization sequence of an embedded application to enable a USB-based Command Line Interface (CLI). It is usually paired with ca_cli_create_thread and ca_cli_set_sender to establish the full CLI environment. The sequence is: 1) Initialize system peripherals, 2) Call ca_usb_dev_mng_cdc_cli to bring up the USB stack, 3) Configure the CLI hooks, and 4) Start the RTOS scheduler.

ca_usb_dev_mng_get_num.brief: Retrieves the internal identifier (index) of the currently active USB device.
ca_usb_dev_mng_get_num.returns: Returns a u32 representing the USB device index. This value is typically used as a handle for subsequent USB endpoint operations.
ca_usb_dev_mng_get_num.notes: This function is a simple getter for a static internal variable and is non-blocking. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs a read operation on a variable, but it does not provide synchronization guarantees if the USB device is being reconfigured or removed simultaneously. It is safe to call from an ISR, as it does not involve any OS primitives or blocking logic. The most common mistake is assuming the returned index is valid even when the USB stack is not initialized or has been stopped; always ensure the USB subsystem is in a valid state before using this index to open endpoints.
ca_usb_dev_mng_get_num.usage: This function is used as a prerequisite for almost all USB-related operations that require a device handle. In a typical lifecycle, it is called during the device configuration phase (e.g., inside an 'on_configure' callback) to obtain the index needed to open endpoints via 'ca_usb_ep_open'. It is also used in diagnostic contexts to identify which USB instance is being referenced when printing debug information or performing status checks. It is frequently paired with 'ca_usb_bulk_mps' to dynamically determine endpoint sizes based on the active device speed.

ca_usb_dev_mng_init.brief: Initializes the USB device management layer and prepares the hardware interface for a specific USB controller.

params.name: speed
params.desc: The desired USB operating speed (e.g., CA_USB_SPEED_FS for Full Speed). Must be a valid enum value supported by the hardware.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral to initialize (e.g., 0 or 1). Must be less than 8; values >= 8 are invalid and will cause initialization failure.

ca_usb_dev_mng_init.returns: Returns true if the USB management layer was successfully initialized. Returns false if the specified usb_num is already in use, if the hardware initialization fails, or if invalid parameters are provided.
ca_usb_dev_mng_init.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called during the system initialization phase before starting the RTOS scheduler or spawning USB-related tasks. It is strictly non-blocking and must NOT be called from an ISR, as it performs internal memory resets and hardware configuration that require a stable thread context. A common beginner mistake is calling this function multiple times without first calling a de-initialization or stop function, which will trigger the 'already in use' error. Ensure that the system clock and GPIOs associated with the USB peripheral are configured correctly before invoking this, as the underlying hardware init will fail otherwise.
ca_usb_dev_mng_init.usage: This function is the mandatory entry point for any USB-based application in caOS. It is typically used in the following sequence: first, call ca_usb_dev_mng_init to set up the management layer; second, call ca_usb_dev_mng_add to register specific USB device classes (like CDC or HID); and finally, call ca_usb_dev_mng_start to begin the enumeration process. It is paired with ca_usb_dev_mng_add to build the device descriptor tree before the host is allowed to connect.

ca_usb_dev_mng_remove.brief: Removes a registered USB device from the management system and frees its associated endpoint resources.

params.name: type
params.desc: The identifier of the USB device type to remove. Must be a valid enum value within the range (0, CA_USB_TYPE__MAX).

ca_usb_dev_mng_remove.returns: Returns true if the device was found and successfully removed. Returns false if the type is invalid, out of range, or if no device is currently registered for that type.
ca_usb_dev_mng_remove.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should be called within a controlled context where the USB management state is not being concurrently modified. It is not intended for use inside an ISR, as it performs internal management logic that assumes a stable environment. The most common mistake is attempting to remove a device that was never successfully added or has already been removed, which will result in a false return value. Ensure that any hardware-level USB activity associated with this device type is stopped or quiesced before calling this function to avoid dangling endpoint references.
ca_usb_dev_mng_remove.usage: This function is typically used during the teardown phase of a USB device lifecycle or when reconfiguring the USB stack at runtime. It is usually paired with the internal management functions that register devices to ensure the endpoint mask is updated and resources are reclaimed. In a CLI or configuration task, it is used to safely unregister a specific USB class (like DFU or a custom interface) so that the endpoint mask can be updated and the resources reclaimed for other purposes.

ca_usb_dev_mng_start.brief: Initializes USB descriptors and enables the D+ pull-up resistor to signal device presence to the host.
ca_usb_dev_mng_start.returns: Always returns true, indicating the USB stack has been instructed to start.
ca_usb_dev_mng_start.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should be called during the system initialization phase or from a dedicated management task. It is strictly non-blocking, meaning it triggers the hardware connection and returns immediately; however, the actual USB enumeration by the host happens asynchronously afterward. A common beginner mistake is to attempt to send data immediately after calling this function; you must wait for the host to complete enumeration (e.g., using ca_usb_cdc_wait_connected) before attempting any communication. Ensure that all USB device descriptors and endpoints have been configured via ca_usb_dev_mng_add before invoking this start function.
ca_usb_dev_mng_start.usage: This function is the final step in the USB initialization sequence. It is typically used after calling ca_usb_dev_mng_add to register specific device classes (like CDC or HID). Once started, the device pulls the D+ line high, which alerts the USB host that a device is connected. It is often paired with ca_usb_dev_mng_stop when the device needs to be logically disconnected from the bus, such as during a system reset or power-saving mode.

ca_usb_dev_mng_stop.brief: Stops the USB device management service and disconnects the device from the host.
ca_usb_dev_mng_stop.returns: Always returns true, indicating the stop command has been processed.
ca_usb_dev_mng_stop.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should be called from a single control task to avoid race conditions with the USB state machine. It is a non-blocking operation that immediately triggers a hardware disconnect. It must only be called after the USB management system has been successfully initialized via ca_usb_dev_mng_init. A common mistake is calling this function while a data transfer is still in progress, which may lead to unexpected behavior or incomplete packets on the host side. It is not safe to call this function from an ISR, as it interacts with the USB stack state machine which requires a task context.
ca_usb_dev_mng_stop.usage: This function is typically used in command-line interfaces or system state machines to gracefully shut down USB communication. It is the counterpart to ca_usb_dev_mng_start and is often paired with it to toggle USB connectivity. In a typical lifecycle, you would call this to release the USB bus before entering a low-power mode or when reconfiguring the USB device descriptors. It is often used in conjunction with ca_usb_dev_mng_add to manage the lifecycle of specific USB device classes.

ca_usb_dfu_poll.brief: Processes pending USB DFU (Device Firmware Upgrade) requests by waiting for a semaphore signal.

params.name: wait_ms
params.desc: Time in milliseconds to wait for a DFU job. Use CA_WAIT_FOREVER to block indefinitely until a job arrives.

ca_usb_dfu_poll.returns: Returns true if a DFU job was successfully processed, false if the timeout expired or the job type was invalid.
ca_usb_dfu_poll.notes: This function is blocking; it uses ca_sem_timedwait internally to suspend the calling task until the USB interrupt handler signals that a new DFU block or manifest command has arrived. It is NOT thread-safe for concurrent calls and must be called from a single dedicated task. It is not callable from an ISR. A common beginner mistake is calling this function from multiple tasks or failing to provide a valid configuration pointer (s_cfg) before the USB host starts sending data, which will cause the function to return false.
ca_usb_dfu_poll.usage: This function is the core of the DFU update loop. It is typically used in a dedicated background task that runs in an infinite loop. The sequence is: 1) Initialize the system, 2) Enter a while(1) loop, 3) Call ca_usb_dfu_poll with CA_WAIT_FOREVER, 4) Check the result and perform system actions like resetting the device via ca_os_reset once the update is complete. It pairs with the USB stack's interrupt-driven job posting mechanism.

ca_usb_disconnect.brief: Performs a soft disconnect of the USB device by signaling the host to drop the connection.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB controller to disconnect. Must be less than USB_MAX_CTRL and correspond to an initialized controller.

ca_usb_disconnect.returns: void. The function does not return a status code; it silently ignores invalid controller indices.
ca_usb_disconnect.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a 'soft' disconnect, meaning it pulls the D+ line low (or equivalent) to simulate a physical unplug event to the host. It is not inherently thread-safe if multiple tasks attempt to manipulate the same USB controller state simultaneously, so ensure proper synchronization if your application architecture allows concurrent access. It is generally safe to call from most contexts, but avoid calling it from high-priority ISRs if the underlying driver implementation performs complex operations or memory management. The most common beginner mistake is assuming this function physically powers down the USB peripheral; it only signals the host to stop communication, leaving the peripheral hardware in its current power state.
ca_usb_disconnect.usage: This function is typically used during system shutdown, device re-enumeration, or when the user explicitly requests a 'halt' or 'soft disconnect' via a CLI command. It is usually paired with ca_usb_connect to restore the link after a maintenance task or configuration change. In a typical lifecycle, you would call it as part of a teardown sequence (e.g., stopping the USB management service) to ensure the host does not attempt to send data to a device that is about to enter a low-power or idle state.

ca_usb_ep_clear_stall.brief: Clears the STALL condition on a specific USB endpoint to resume normal data communication.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB controller. Must be less than USB_MAX_CTRL and correspond to an initialized controller.

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The hardware address of the endpoint (e.g., 0x81 for IN endpoint 1, 0x02 for OUT endpoint 2).

ca_usb_ep_clear_stall.returns: Returns true if the stall was successfully cleared, false if the controller index is invalid or the operation failed.
ca_usb_ep_clear_stall.notes: This function is typically non-blocking and interacts directly with the USB hardware registers. It is not guaranteed to be thread-safe if called simultaneously from multiple tasks, so it should ideally be called from the USB management task or the USB ISR context. A common beginner mistake is calling this function without first verifying if the endpoint is actually stalled using ca_usb_ep_is_stalled, or failing to handle the subsequent USB protocol requirements (like sending a Zero Length Packet) after clearing the stall. Ensure the USB controller is initialized before calling this.
ca_usb_ep_clear_stall.usage: This function is used during USB enumeration or runtime when the host sends a CLEAR_FEATURE request to an endpoint. It is part of the standard USB control transfer sequence: the firmware receives a setup packet, identifies the request, calls ca_usb_ep_clear_stall to reset the endpoint's data toggle and stall bit, and then typically calls ca_usb_ep_write to send a status response (ZLP) back to the host. It is often paired with ca_usb_ep_stall when the device needs to signal an error to the host.

ca_usb_ep_close.brief: Closes a specific USB endpoint to stop data transmission and release associated resources.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB controller (e.g., 0 for FS, 1 for HS). Must be less than USB_MAX_CTRL.

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The address of the endpoint to close (e.g., 0x81 for IN endpoint 1, 0x02 for OUT endpoint 2).

ca_usb_ep_close.returns: Returns true if the endpoint was successfully closed, or false if the controller index is invalid or the operation failed.
ca_usb_ep_close.notes: This function is not thread-safe and should not be called from an ISR. It is a blocking operation that interacts with the low-level USB driver to disable the hardware endpoint. A common mistake is calling this function while a transfer is still active or without checking if the USB controller is actually initialized, which can lead to undefined behavior or system instability. Always ensure the USB stack is in a state where closing the endpoint is safe, such as during a device disconnect or a configuration change.
ca_usb_ep_close.usage: This function is typically used during USB device state transitions, such as moving from an 'configured' state to an 'idle' or 'disconnected' state. It is often paired with ca_usb_ep_open to manage dynamic endpoint allocation. In a typical sequence, you would call ca_usb_ep_close when the host requests a configuration change or when the device is unplugged, ensuring that no further data is processed on that specific endpoint. It is also used to clean up resources when a specific USB class driver (like NCM or CDC) decides to shut down its communication channels.

ca_usb_ep_is_stalled.brief: Checks if a specific USB endpoint is currently in a stalled state.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB controller. Must be less than USB_MAX_CTRL.

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The address of the endpoint to query (e.g., 0x81 for IN endpoint 1).

ca_usb_ep_is_stalled.returns: Returns true if the endpoint is stalled, false otherwise. Returns false if the usb_num is invalid or the driver is not initialized.
ca_usb_ep_is_stalled.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a direct read of the endpoint status register. It is generally thread-safe depending on the underlying driver implementation, but it is not intended to be called from an ISR unless the driver explicitly supports it. The most common mistake is passing an invalid endpoint address or an uninitialized USB controller index, which will silently return false without indicating an error. Always ensure the USB stack is fully initialized via ca_usb_init before calling this function.
ca_usb_ep_is_stalled.usage: This function is primarily used during USB enumeration or control transfers when the host requests the status of an endpoint via the GET_STATUS request. It is typically paired with ca_usb_ep_write to send the status back to the host. Developers use this to verify if a previous error condition (stall) has been cleared or to report the current state of the communication pipe to the USB host. It is part of the standard USB device management flow, often invoked within the USB event handler loop.

ca_usb_ep_open.signature: bool ca_usb_ep_open(u32 usb_num, u8 ep_addr, ca_usb_ep_type_t type, u16 mps)
ca_usb_ep_open.brief: Initializes and enables a specific USB endpoint for data transmission or reception.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB controller (e.g., 0 for FS, 1 for HS). Must be less than USB_MAX_CTRL.

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The endpoint address (e.g., 0x81 for IN endpoint 1, 0x02 for OUT endpoint 2). Bit 7 is set for IN endpoints.

params.name: type
params.desc: The transfer type: CA_USB_EP_TYPE_BULK, CA_USB_EP_TYPE_INTR, or CA_USB_EP_TYPE_ISOC.

params.name: mps
params.desc: Maximum Packet Size in bytes. Must match the descriptor requirements for the chosen endpoint type.

ca_usb_ep_open.returns: Returns true if the endpoint was successfully opened, false if the controller index is invalid, the controller is not initialized, or the hardware failed to configure the endpoint.
ca_usb_ep_open.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called during the USB configuration phase, typically triggered by the host's SET_CONFIGURATION request. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. The USB controller must be fully initialized via the driver's init sequence before calling this. A common mistake is providing an incorrect MPS value that does not align with the USB specification for the specific endpoint type, which will cause the host to reject the device or result in silent data corruption. Always ensure the endpoint address matches the descriptors provided to the host.
ca_usb_ep_open.usage: This function is used during the USB device enumeration process to prepare endpoints for data exchange. It is typically called inside a callback function (like an 'on_configure' handler) after the USB device has been assigned an address by the host. It is usually paired with ca_usb_ep_write or ca_usb_ep_read to perform actual data transfers once the endpoints are open. In complex classes like NCM, it may be called dynamically during interface changes.

ca_usb_ep_read.signature: u16 ca_usb_ep_read(u32 usb_num, u8 ep_addr, u8 *buf, u16 max_len)
ca_usb_ep_read.brief: Reads data from a specific USB endpoint into a provided buffer.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB controller. Must be less than USB_MAX_CTRL.

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The endpoint address (e.g., 0x00 for EP0, 0x81 for IN, 0x01 for OUT).

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the memory buffer where received data will be stored.

params.name: max_len
params.desc: The maximum number of bytes to read. Must not exceed the buffer size.

ca_usb_ep_read.returns: Returns the number of bytes actually read (u16). Returns 0 if the USB controller index is invalid, the controller is not initialized, or no data is available.
ca_usb_ep_read.notes: This function is a wrapper that delegates to the specific hardware driver implementation. It is generally non-blocking in the sense that it returns immediately with the data currently available in the endpoint buffer. It is not inherently thread-safe if multiple tasks access the same endpoint simultaneously, so ensure proper synchronization or task-exclusive access. Do not call this from an ISR unless the underlying driver implementation explicitly supports it, as it may involve complex buffer management or synchronization primitives that are unsafe in interrupt context. A common mistake is providing a buffer smaller than the actual incoming packet size, which can lead to memory corruption or truncated data.
ca_usb_ep_read.usage: This function is typically used within the USB stack's data processing loop or inside a callback triggered by a USB event. It is used to retrieve control requests (like SET_LINE_CODING in CDC) or bulk data (like CBW in MSC). It is usually paired with ca_usb_ep_write to send responses or status packets back to the host. In a typical sequence, you wait for a USB event, call this function to pull the data into a local buffer, process the data, and then potentially send an acknowledgment or the requested data back.

ca_usb_ep_stall.brief: Forces a USB endpoint into a STALL state to signal a protocol error or unsupported request to the host.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB controller. Must be less than USB_MAX_CTRL and correspond to an initialized controller.

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The address of the endpoint to stall (e.g., 0x80 for IN endpoint 0, 0x01 for OUT endpoint 1).

ca_usb_ep_stall.returns: void. If the parameters are invalid or the controller is not initialized, the function returns silently without performing any action.
ca_usb_ep_stall.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately by interacting with the USB peripheral registers. It is generally thread-safe, but calling it from an ISR is discouraged unless the specific hardware driver implementation guarantees atomicity for register access. The most common beginner mistake is calling this function on an endpoint that has not been opened via ca_usb_ep_open, or attempting to stall an endpoint that is already in a stalled state, which can lead to unexpected behavior in the USB host's error recovery logic. Always ensure the USB controller is active and the endpoint address is valid for the current configuration.
ca_usb_ep_stall.usage: This function is used during USB enumeration or data transfer to handle protocol violations, such as receiving an invalid Command Block Wrapper (CBW) in Mass Storage Class or an unsupported request during the SETUP phase. It is typically paired with ca_usb_ep_open during initialization and ca_usb_ep_clear_stall when the error condition is resolved. In a typical workflow, if a host sends a request that the device cannot fulfill, the device calls this function to inform the host that the endpoint is halted, effectively forcing the host to perform error recovery or reset the pipe.

ca_usb_ep_write.signature: bool ca_usb_ep_write(u32 usb_num, u8 ep_addr, const u8 *buf, u16 len)
ca_usb_ep_write.brief: Transmits data from the device to the USB host via a specific endpoint.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB controller instance. Must be less than USB_MAX_CTRL.

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The endpoint address (e.g., 0x80 for IN endpoint 0). Must be an endpoint previously opened with ca_usb_ep_open.

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the data buffer to send. Can be NULL if len is 0 (used for ZLP - Zero Length Packet).

params.name: len
params.desc: Number of bytes to transmit. Must not exceed the maximum packet size configured for the endpoint.

ca_usb_ep_write.returns: Returns true if the write request was successfully queued, false if the controller is invalid, the endpoint is not open, or the hardware is busy.
ca_usb_ep_write.notes: This function is non-blocking and typically queues the data for the USB hardware to transmit. It is not inherently thread-safe for concurrent access to the same endpoint, so ensure only one task or ISR manages a specific endpoint at a time. It is a mandatory precondition that the USB controller is initialized and the specific endpoint has been opened via ca_usb_ep_open. A common beginner mistake is passing a buffer that goes out of scope (e.g., a local stack variable) before the USB hardware has finished transmitting the data, which leads to memory corruption on the wire. Always ensure the buffer remains valid until the transmission is confirmed complete by the USB hardware.
ca_usb_ep_write.usage: This function is used in the USB stack to respond to host requests or send asynchronous data. It is typically paired with ca_usb_ep_open during initialization to prepare the endpoint. In control transfers, it is frequently used to send status packets or data descriptors, often with a NULL buffer and 0 length to signal a Zero Length Packet (ZLP) to the host, indicating the end of a control transaction. It is the standard way to finalize a response sequence after processing a setup packet.

ca_usb_ep_write_ref.signature: bool ca_usb_ep_write_ref(u32 usb_num, u8 ep_addr, const u8 *buf, u16 len, ca_usb_tx_release_cb_t release, u32 cookie)
ca_usb_ep_write_ref.brief: Queues a USB transmission buffer for zero-copy transfer, invoking a callback upon completion.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB controller to use. Must be less than USB_MAX_CTRL.

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The endpoint address (e.g., 0x81 for IN endpoint 1).

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the data buffer. Must be 4-byte aligned; otherwise, the function returns false.

params.name: len
params.desc: Length of the data in bytes. Must be greater than 0.

params.name: release
params.desc: Callback function executed by the USB stack when the buffer is no longer needed. Must not be NULL.

params.name: cookie
params.desc: User-defined value passed back to the release callback to identify the buffer or context.

ca_usb_ep_write_ref.returns: Returns true if the buffer was successfully queued for transmission. Returns false if the controller is invalid, the buffer is misaligned, the length is zero, the callback is NULL, or the driver cannot accept the buffer (e.g., ring buffer full).
ca_usb_ep_write_ref.notes: This function is designed for high-performance zero-copy transfers. It is non-blocking; it immediately returns after handing ownership of the buffer to the USB controller. You must ensure the buffer remains valid and untouched until the 'release' callback is triggered, as the hardware is reading directly from that memory address. The buffer must be 4-byte aligned, or the function will return false. This function is generally not safe to call from an ISR unless explicitly documented by the specific driver implementation; always check the driver's thread-safety requirements. A common mistake is to free the buffer immediately after the function returns true, which causes memory corruption because the USB hardware is still reading the data.
ca_usb_ep_write_ref.usage: Use this function when you need to send large amounts of data (like network packets in NCM mode) without copying them into internal driver buffers. It is typically used in a sequence: first, allocate memory (e.g., via ca_memory_allocate), then prepare the data, call ca_usb_ep_write_ref, and finally, the 'release' callback handles the memory cleanup (e.g., calling ca_memory_free). If this function returns false, the caller retains ownership of the buffer and must handle the error or free the memory manually. It is often paired with ca_os_sched_lock and ca_os_sched_unlock to ensure that the buffer handoff and any associated state updates (like incrementing packet counters) occur atomically.

ca_usb_fs_dev_clock_init.brief: Initializes the hardware clock and power supply requirements for the USB Full-Speed peripheral.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral to initialize (e.g., 0 for USB1, 1 for USB2). Value depends on the specific STM32 series hardware capabilities.

ca_usb_fs_dev_clock_init.notes: This function is hardware-specific and performs low-level register manipulation to enable the HSI48 oscillator, configure clock selection (CCIPR), and power up the USB transceiver. It is not thread-safe and must be called during the system initialization phase before any USB communication functions are invoked. It is strictly forbidden to call this from an ISR, as it contains blocking 'while' loops waiting for hardware ready flags (e.g., HSI48RDY). A common mistake is calling this function multiple times or after the USB stack has already started, which can cause clock instability or peripheral lockups. Always ensure the system clock is stable before calling this, as it relies on the RCC (Reset and Clock Control) subsystem being in a known state.
ca_usb_fs_dev_clock_init.usage: This function is the mandatory first step in the USB initialization sequence. It is typically called during the board support package (BSP) setup or early system boot. It must be followed by GPIO configuration (e.g., ca_usb_fs_dev_gpio_init) and the USB stack initialization (e.g., ca_usb_fs_dev_init) to ensure the peripheral is ready for enumeration. By isolating the clock and power setup, it ensures that the USB PHY is powered and clocked correctly before the digital logic attempts to access the peripheral registers, preventing bus faults.

ca_usb_fs_dev_connect.brief: Enables the USB device pull-up resistor to signal presence to the host.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral to connect. Must be a valid peripheral ID supported by the hardware.

ca_usb_fs_dev_connect.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a direct register write to the USB controller to release the 'Soft Disconnect' (SDIS) bit or enable the D+ pull-up. It is not thread-safe in the sense that it should only be called once the USB stack is fully initialized and ready to handle enumeration requests from the host. Calling this too early will cause the host to attempt enumeration before the device is ready, leading to failed connections or 'Device Descriptor Request Failed' errors. It is generally not intended to be called from an ISR, as it is part of the high-level device management sequence.
ca_usb_fs_dev_connect.usage: This function is the final step in the USB device initialization sequence. It is typically called by the USB management layer (e.g., ca_usb_dev_mng_start) only after the hardware has been clocked, GPIOs configured, and all required endpoints have been opened via ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_open. By keeping the pull-up disabled until this point, you ensure the host does not see the device until the firmware is prepared to respond to standard USB requests. If you call this before configuring your endpoints, the host will detect the device, but the subsequent enumeration process will time out or fail because the device cannot respond to the initial setup packets.

ca_usb_fs_dev_disconnect.brief: Disconnects the USB Full-Speed device from the host by pulling the D+ line low or setting the disconnect bit.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral to disconnect. Must be a valid peripheral index supported by the hardware (e.g., 0 or 1).

ca_usb_fs_dev_disconnect.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a direct register write to the USB peripheral's control register. It is generally thread-safe as it performs an atomic register modification, but it should not be called from an ISR unless the specific hardware implementation guarantees atomic access. The primary purpose is to simulate a physical cable unplug event to the host computer, forcing the host to re-enumerate the device. A common beginner mistake is calling this function while the USB stack is actively transmitting data, which can lead to undefined behavior or data loss in the USB buffers. Always ensure the USB stack is in a quiescent state before triggering a manual disconnect.
ca_usb_fs_dev_disconnect.usage: This function is typically used during device initialization sequences or when implementing a software-controlled USB reset. It is often paired with ca_usb_fs_dev_connect to toggle the connection state, allowing the device to 're-plug' itself to the host without physical intervention. In a typical lifecycle, you might call this during a system reset or when the application detects a critical USB error that requires a full re-enumeration. It is standard practice to use this in conjunction with a delay to ensure the host OS has sufficient time to process the disconnection event before the device attempts to reconnect.

ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_clear_stall.brief: Clears the STALL condition on a specific USB endpoint to resume normal communication.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral (e.g., 0 for FS, 1 for HS). Must be a valid peripheral index for the target MCU.

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The endpoint address (e.g., 0x81 for IN endpoint 1, 0x02 for OUT endpoint 2). Must be a valid endpoint index.

ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_clear_stall.returns: Returns true if the stall was successfully cleared, false if the endpoint address is invalid, the peripheral index is out of range, or the operation is not supported on the current hardware (e.g., f1xx).
ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_clear_stall.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs direct register manipulation on the USB OTG peripheral. It is generally not thread-safe if called concurrently from multiple tasks for the same endpoint, so ensure synchronization if necessary. It is typically safe to call from an ISR, but check specific hardware implementation constraints. A common beginner mistake is calling this function on an endpoint that has not been opened or initialized, which may lead to undefined behavior or system instability. Always ensure the endpoint is in a stalled state before attempting to clear it, as clearing a non-stalled endpoint may disrupt active data transfers by resetting the data toggle sequence.
ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_clear_stall.usage: This function is used during USB enumeration or error recovery when the host or device needs to reset the data toggle and clear the stall bit after a protocol error. It is typically paired with ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_stall to manage endpoint flow control. In a standard sequence, you would detect a stall condition, perform necessary cleanup or buffer resets, call this function to clear the hardware stall, and then resume data transmission or reception.

ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_close.brief: Safely disables and resets a specific USB device endpoint hardware configuration.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral (e.g., 0 for FS, 1 for HS). Must be a valid peripheral index.

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The endpoint address (e.g., 0x81 for IN endpoint 1, 0x02 for OUT endpoint 2). EP0 is not allowed.

ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_close.returns: Returns true if the endpoint was successfully closed, false if the endpoint was already closed, invalid (EP0), or if the peripheral index is out of range.
ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_close.notes: This function is blocking because it waits for hardware handshake signals (NAK/EPDISD) to ensure the endpoint is safely disabled before clearing registers. It is not thread-safe and must not be called from an ISR, as it performs busy-waiting loops that could hang the system if the hardware is unresponsive. A common mistake is attempting to close EP0, which is reserved for control transfers and managed by the stack; the function will return false immediately. Ensure the endpoint is no longer being accessed by the USB stack before calling this, as it clears internal state buffers and hardware masks.
ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_close.usage: This function is typically used during USB device re-enumeration or when a specific interface is being disabled to free up resources. It is the final step in the teardown sequence: first, stop data transmission/reception, then call this function to reset the hardware state, and finally update the application-level endpoint status. It is often paired with ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_open to re-initialize the endpoint with new parameters after a configuration change.

ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_is_stalled.brief: Checks if a specific USB endpoint is currently in a stalled state.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral. Must be within the hardware-supported range (typically 0 or 1).

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The endpoint address (e.g., 0x81 for IN endpoint 1, 0x02 for OUT endpoint 2). Must be a valid endpoint index.

ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_is_stalled.returns: Returns true if the endpoint is stalled, false otherwise. Returns false if the endpoint address is invalid, the peripheral index is out of range, or the hardware does not support this operation.
ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_is_stalled.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a direct register read from the USB hardware controller. It is thread-safe as it performs a read-only operation, but it does not provide synchronization against concurrent modifications of the endpoint state. It is safe to call from an ISR, as it does not involve OS primitives or blocking calls. A common beginner mistake is assuming that a 'false' return value implies the endpoint is ready for data; it only confirms the endpoint is not currently stalled. Always ensure the USB peripheral is initialized before calling this function, as accessing registers on an uninitialized peripheral may lead to undefined behavior.
ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_is_stalled.usage: This function is typically used during USB error handling or protocol recovery sequences. It is often paired with ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_clear_stall when a host requests a clear feature on a stalled endpoint. Developers use it to verify the current state of the hardware before attempting to send or receive data, ensuring that the endpoint is not in a 'halted' state that would cause data transfers to fail. It is part of the standard USB device management lifecycle, used to monitor endpoint health during active communication.

ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_open.signature: bool ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_open(u32 usb_num, u8 ep_addr, ca_usb_ep_type_t type, u16 mps)
ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_open.brief: Initializes and enables a specific USB endpoint for data transmission or reception.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral (e.g., 0 for FS, 1 for HS). Must be within valid hardware range.

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The endpoint address (e.g., 0x81 for IN endpoint 1, 0x02 for OUT endpoint 2). Bit 7 indicates direction.

params.name: type
params.desc: The transfer type (Control, Bulk, Interrupt, or Isochronous). Must match the descriptor.

params.name: mps
params.desc: Maximum Packet Size in bytes. Must not exceed the hardware buffer capacity.

ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_open.returns: Returns true if the endpoint was successfully configured and enabled, false if the endpoint index is invalid or the hardware failed to initialize.
ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_open.notes: This function is not thread-safe and must be called during the USB enumeration process or when reconfiguring an interface. It is typically not callable from an ISR as it performs direct hardware register manipulation. A common beginner mistake is providing an incorrect MPS value that exceeds the physical buffer size, which can lead to memory corruption or silent data loss. Ensure the USB peripheral clock and GPIOs are initialized via ca_usb_fs_dev_clock_init and ca_usb_fs_dev_gpio_init before calling this.
ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_open.usage: This function is used during the USB device setup phase, specifically after receiving a SET_CONFIGURATION or SET_INTERFACE request from the host. It is part of a sequence: first, initialize the USB core with ca_usb_fs_dev_init, then open the required endpoints using this function, and finally enable the device connection via ca_usb_fs_dev_connect. It is paired with ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_close when the interface is disabled or the device is disconnected.

ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_read.signature: u16 ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_read(u32 usb_num, u8 ep_addr, u8 *buf, u16 max_len)
ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_read.brief: Reads data from a specific USB device endpoint into a provided buffer.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral. Must be within the valid range for the specific hardware (e.g., 0 or 1).

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The endpoint address (e.g., 0x01 for EP1 OUT). Must be an OUT endpoint; IN endpoints will return 0.

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the destination buffer. Must not be NULL.

params.name: max_len
params.desc: Maximum number of bytes to copy. If the received packet is larger, only this amount is copied.

ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_read.returns: Returns the number of bytes actually copied into the buffer. Returns 0 if the endpoint is empty, invalid, or if an error occurs (e.g., NULL buffer or IN endpoint).
ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_read.notes: This function is non-blocking and retrieves data already present in the internal USB receive queues. It is thread-safe regarding the queue management, but it interacts with hardware registers that may be modified by the USB ISR; therefore, it uses critical sections internally to prevent race conditions during endpoint re-arming. It is NOT safe to call this function directly from an ISR, as it may perform complex queue operations or trigger hardware re-arming logic that expects a thread context. A common beginner mistake is calling this function in a tight loop without checking if data is actually available, which wastes CPU cycles; instead, wait for a signal or event indicating that data has arrived. Ensure the endpoint has been successfully opened with ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_open before attempting to read.
ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_read.usage: This function is typically used in a dedicated USB task or a callback triggered by a data-ready event. The standard sequence is: 1) Initialize the USB peripheral, 2) Open the desired endpoint using ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_open, 3) Wait for a notification (e.g., via ca_event_wait) that data is ready, 4) Call ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_read to copy the data into a local buffer, and 5) Process the data. It is often paired with ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_write to implement bidirectional communication. If the application requires high throughput, ensure the buffer provided is large enough to accommodate the maximum packet size expected for the endpoint.

ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_stall.brief: Forces a USB endpoint into the STALL state to signal a protocol error or lack of resources to the host.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral (e.g., 0 or 1). On single-controller chips, this is ignored.

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The endpoint address. Bit 7 is the direction (1 for IN, 0 for OUT). Bits 0-3 define the endpoint number.

ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_stall.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately by modifying hardware registers. It is generally safe to call from an ISR, as it performs simple register writes without waiting for external events. The most common mistake is passing an invalid endpoint address or forgetting that stalling an endpoint stops all communication on that pipe until the host sends a CLEAR_FEATURE request. Ensure the USB peripheral is properly initialized before calling this, otherwise, the register access may cause a hard fault.
ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_stall.usage: Use this function when your USB stack detects an invalid request or a buffer overflow condition that requires the host to stop sending data. It is typically paired with ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_clear_stall, which is used once the error condition is resolved and the host requests to resume communication. In a standard USB device implementation, you would call this inside your control transfer handler when a setup packet contains unsupported parameters.

ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_write.signature: bool ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_write(u32 usb_num, u8 ep_addr, const u8 *buf, u16 len)
ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_write.brief: Writes data to a specific USB device endpoint by queuing it for transmission.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral (usually 0 or 1).

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The endpoint address (e.g., 0x81 for IN endpoint 1). Must be an IN endpoint.

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the data buffer to be sent. Can be NULL if len is 0.

params.name: len
params.desc: Number of bytes to write. Must not exceed the endpoint's buffer capacity.

ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_write.returns: Returns true if the data was successfully queued for transmission, false otherwise (e.g., invalid endpoint, buffer full, or hardware busy).
ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_write.notes: This function is thread-safe and uses internal critical sections to protect the transmission ring buffer from concurrent access by multiple tasks or ISRs. It is non-blocking; if the internal queue is full, it returns false immediately, allowing the caller to decide whether to retry or yield. A common mistake is assuming the data is sent immediately; the function only copies data into the driver's internal queue. Ensure the endpoint has been properly opened with ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_open before calling this function. Misuse, such as passing an OUT endpoint address, will result in an immediate false return.
ca_usb_fs_dev_ep_write.usage: Used in USB device applications to send data to the host. It is typically called after the USB connection is established and the endpoint is configured. In a standard workflow, the application initializes the USB stack, opens the required endpoints, and then calls this function whenever data is ready to be transmitted. If the function returns false due to a full queue, the application should use ca_os_yield or a small delay before attempting to resend the data.

ca_usb_fs_dev_get_speed.brief: Retrieves the current operational speed of the specified USB Full-Speed device.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral to query. Valid values depend on the hardware configuration (usually 0 or 1 for multi-USB systems).

ca_usb_fs_dev_get_speed.returns: Returns a ca_usb_speed_t enum value (e.g., CA_USB_SPEED_FS). If the hardware does not support speed detection or the index is invalid, it typically defaults to CA_USB_SPEED_FS.
ca_usb_fs_dev_get_speed.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it typically reads from a cached state variable maintained by the USB driver. It is safe to call from an ISR because it performs a simple memory read without acquiring mutexes or waiting for hardware events. The most common mistake is assuming the speed can change dynamically without the USB stack re-enumerating; always ensure the USB peripheral has been initialized via the appropriate driver init function before calling this. On some platforms, the index is ignored if only one USB peripheral is supported, but you should always pass a valid index to maintain cross-platform compatibility.
ca_usb_fs_dev_get_speed.usage: This function is used during the USB enumeration process or when debugging connection issues to verify if the device has negotiated the expected speed. It is typically called after the USB stack has been initialized and the device is connected to a host. Developers often pair this with ca_usb_cdc_wait_connected to ensure the link is active before checking the speed, or use it in diagnostic logs to confirm hardware capabilities. It is part of the standard diagnostic sequence to verify that the hardware abstraction layer has correctly identified the link state.

ca_usb_fs_dev_gpio_init.brief: Configures the physical GPIO pins required for USB Full-Speed peripheral operation.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral to initialize (e.g., 0 for USB_OTG_FS1). Values depend on the specific MCU architecture.

ca_usb_fs_dev_gpio_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs direct register manipulation to set up GPIO pins in Alternate Function (AF) mode. It is not thread-safe and must be called during the system initialization phase before the USB peripheral is enabled. It is generally not intended to be called from an ISR. A common mistake is calling this function after the USB peripheral has already started, which can cause electrical contention or signal integrity issues on the data lines. On some architectures, this function may also perform manual pin toggling to force a bus reset, which is critical for re-enumeration on boards with fixed external pull-up resistors.
ca_usb_fs_dev_gpio_init.usage: This function is a mandatory step in the USB initialization sequence. It is typically called immediately after clock configuration and before the USB peripheral core is initialized via ca_usb_fs_dev_init. It ensures that the physical pins (D+, D-, and others like VBUS or ID) are correctly routed to the USB hardware block rather than acting as standard GPIOs. It is usually paired with ca_usb_fs_dev_clock_init to ensure the peripheral is powered before the pins are configured.

ca_usb_fs_dev_init.brief: Initializes the USB Full-Speed hardware peripheral and registers the application callback structure.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral to initialize (e.g., 0 for OTG_FS). Must be a valid hardware index for the specific MCU.

params.name: cb
params.desc: Pointer to a structure containing function pointers for USB events (e.g., reset, setup, data). Must not be NULL.

ca_usb_fs_dev_init.returns: Returns true if the hardware was successfully reset and configured, false if the initialization failed (e.g., invalid parameters or hardware timeout).
ca_usb_fs_dev_init.notes: This function performs low-level hardware initialization, including clock configuration, GPIO setup, and core reset. It is NOT thread-safe and must be called during the system startup phase before any USB communication begins. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. A common mistake is calling this function while the USB cable is already connected or before the required clocks are enabled, which can lead to hardware lockups or failed enumeration. Note that this function leaves the USB device in a disconnected state (D+ pull-up disabled); you must call ca_usb_fs_dev_connect later to signal presence to the host.
ca_usb_fs_dev_init.usage: This is the first step in the USB device lifecycle. It is typically called during system initialization after memory and clocks are configured. The sequence is: 1) ca_usb_fs_dev_init to prepare the hardware, 2) ca_usb_dev_mng_add to register endpoints, and 3) ca_usb_fs_dev_connect to physically signal the host that the device is ready for enumeration. It is paired with the callback structure that handles the USB protocol logic.

ca_usb_fs_dev_isr.brief: Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) for the USB Full-Speed device peripheral.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral to service. Use 0 for single-USB devices; for multi-USB devices, refer to the specific hardware manual.

ca_usb_fs_dev_isr.notes: This function is an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) and must be called exclusively from the hardware interrupt vector table associated with the USB peripheral. It is not thread-safe and must never be called from a standard task or thread context. Because it runs in interrupt context, it must execute as quickly as possible; avoid performing heavy processing or blocking operations inside this function. The most common mistake is attempting to use blocking caOS functions (like ca_os_delay or ca_mutex_lock) inside this ISR, which will cause system instability or deadlocks.
ca_usb_fs_dev_isr.usage: This function is the entry point for the USB hardware interrupt. It is typically registered in the startup vector table or the NVIC configuration. It handles low-level USB events such as bus resets, enumeration completion, and data packet reception by dispatching them to internal handler functions. It is the core of the USB stack's responsiveness; without it, the device will fail to communicate with the host or respond to enumeration requests.

ca_usb_fs_dev_set_address.brief: Updates the USB device address in the hardware configuration register.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral (e.g., 0 for FS, 1 for HS). Must be a valid peripheral index for the specific MCU.

params.name: addr
params.desc: The 7-bit USB address assigned by the host during enumeration. Valid range is 0 to 127.

ca_usb_fs_dev_set_address.notes: This function is a low-level hardware abstraction layer (HAL) call. It is not thread-safe and should only be called by the USB stack's control transfer handler. On some architectures (like H5xx), the address update is deferred until the status stage of the control transfer is complete; calling this manually outside the stack's state machine will likely break USB enumeration. Do not call this from an ISR unless the specific hardware implementation explicitly supports it, as it modifies shared peripheral registers.
ca_usb_fs_dev_set_address.usage: This function is used exclusively during the USB enumeration process when the host sends a 'Set Address' request. It is typically called by the USB stack after the device has successfully received the address from the host and is ready to switch to the new address. It is usually paired with other USB stack functions that manage the control endpoint (EP0) state machine to ensure the address change happens at the correct protocol timing. It is part of the low-level driver sequence: init -> enumeration -> set_address -> active communication.

ca_usb_get_speed.brief: Retrieves the current operational speed of the specified USB controller.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB controller to query. Must be less than USB_MAX_CTRL.

ca_usb_get_speed.returns: Returns a ca_usb_speed_t enum value (e.g., CA_USB_SPEED_FS, CA_USB_SPEED_HS). Returns CA_USB_SPEED_FS as a default fallback if the provided index is invalid or the controller is not initialized.
ca_usb_get_speed.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe, as it performs a simple lookup in the internal driver table. It is safe to call from an ISR because it does not perform any complex operations or wait for hardware responses. The most common mistake is passing an uninitialized or out-of-bounds index, which will silently return the default Full-Speed (FS) value rather than an error code, potentially leading to incorrect timing assumptions in your USB stack logic. Always ensure the USB controller has been properly initialized via the driver's internal setup before relying on this speed value.
ca_usb_get_speed.usage: This function is typically used during the USB enumeration process or when configuring endpoint buffers to determine if the hardware is operating at High-Speed (HS) or Full-Speed (FS). It is usually called after the USB hardware initialization sequence and before opening endpoints with ca_usb_ep_open. Developers use it to dynamically adjust packet sizes or polling intervals based on the negotiated bus speed, ensuring that the software stack matches the physical capabilities of the connected device.

ca_usb_hs_dev_clock_init.brief: Initializes the hardware clock and power configuration for the High-Speed USB peripheral.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral to initialize (e.g., 0 for USB_OTG_HS, 1 for USB_OTG_FS). Valid values are 0 or 1 depending on the specific STM32 hardware variant.

ca_usb_hs_dev_clock_init.notes: This function performs low-level register manipulation to enable the HSI48 oscillator and configure the USB clock source. It is a blocking function because it contains a busy-wait loop that polls the HSI48 ready flag; if the oscillator fails to start, the system will hang indefinitely. It is NOT thread-safe and must not be called from an ISR, as it performs hardware-level configuration that assumes exclusive access to RCC and PWR registers. The most common beginner mistake is calling this function multiple times or from different tasks simultaneously, which can corrupt the clock configuration or cause race conditions in the CRS (Clock Recovery System) settings.
ca_usb_hs_dev_clock_init.usage: This function is the mandatory first step in the USB hardware bring-up sequence, typically called during system initialization or before enabling a specific USB interface. It must be executed before any other USB-related functions, such as ca_usb_hs_dev_gpio_init or ca_usb_hs_dev_init, to ensure the peripheral's clock tree is stable. In a typical application, it is paired with GPIO configuration and peripheral-specific setup to prepare the hardware for the ca_usb_hs_dev_connect or similar connection routines.

ca_usb_hs_dev_connect.brief: Connects the USB High-Speed device to the host by enabling the D+ pull-up resistor.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral (e.g., 0 for USB_OTG_HS). Must be a valid index supported by the hardware.

ca_usb_hs_dev_connect.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a direct register write to the USB controller's Device Control Register (DCTL) to clear the Soft Disconnect (SDIS) bit. It is not thread-safe in the sense that it should only be called once the USB device stack is fully initialized and ready to handle enumeration requests from the host. Calling this too early will cause the host to detect the device before the firmware is ready, leading to enumeration failures or 'Device Descriptor Request Failed' errors. It is not intended to be called from an ISR, as it is part of the high-level device management sequence.
ca_usb_hs_dev_connect.usage: This function is the final step in the USB device initialization sequence. It is typically called after the USB hardware has been clocked, the GPIOs configured, and all endpoints have been opened using ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_open. It is usually invoked by the higher-level management function ca_usb_dev_mng_start to signal to the host that the device is ready to begin the enumeration process. Do not call this function until your application is prepared to handle the subsequent setup packets from the host.

ca_usb_hs_dev_disconnect.brief: Forces a USB High-Speed device to disconnect by setting the Soft Disconnect bit in the hardware controller.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB High-Speed peripheral (e.g., 0 or 1). Values outside the supported hardware range (typically >= 2) are ignored.

ca_usb_hs_dev_disconnect.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs a direct register write to the USB controller's DCTL register. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs an atomic register modification, but it does not provide synchronization with the USB stack state. It is safe to call from an ISR, as it does not involve any OS primitives or blocking waits. The most common mistake is calling this function while the USB stack is actively transmitting data, which can lead to unexpected behavior or incomplete transfers; ensure the stack is in a quiescent state before disconnecting.
ca_usb_hs_dev_disconnect.usage: This function is used to programmatically simulate a physical cable unplug event, which is useful for forcing a re-enumeration of the USB device by the host. It is typically paired with ca_usb_hs_dev_connect to reset the connection after a configuration change or a firmware-level reset. In a typical lifecycle, you would call this to drop the connection, perform necessary hardware re-initialization, and then call the connect function to signal the host to re-enumerate the device.

ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_clear_stall.brief: Clears the STALL condition on a specific USB High-Speed endpoint and resets its data toggle.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral (e.g., 0 for USB_OTG_HS). Must be less than 2.

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The endpoint address (e.g., 0x81 for IN endpoint 1, 0x02 for OUT endpoint 2). Must be a valid endpoint index.

ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_clear_stall.returns: Returns true if the stall was successfully cleared, false if the parameters were invalid or the hardware does not support this operation.
ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_clear_stall.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately by modifying hardware registers. It is thread-safe regarding the internal USB state structure, but it should be used carefully as it resets the data toggle (PID) to DATA0, which can cause synchronization issues if the host is not expecting a reset. It is not intended to be called from an ISR unless the specific hardware implementation guarantees atomicity, which is generally not the case for complex USB register sequences. The most common beginner mistake is calling this function when the endpoint is not actually stalled, which may force an unnecessary data toggle reset and lead to packet sequence errors.
ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_clear_stall.usage: This function is typically used in the USB device stack error recovery sequence. When a host sends a request that the device cannot process, the device may respond with a STALL; once the error condition is resolved, the host sends a 'Clear Feature' request, which triggers this function. It is usually paired with ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_stall to manage endpoint states and is called after the USB stack has successfully processed the control transfer that requested the stall clearance. It is part of the standard USB device lifecycle management, following the initial setup via ca_usb_hs_dev_init.

ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_close.brief: Safely disables and resets a specific USB device endpoint hardware and driver state.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral (e.g., 0 for USB_OTG_HS1).

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The endpoint address (e.g., 0x81 for IN endpoint 1, 0x02 for OUT endpoint 2). Must not be 0.

ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_close.returns: Returns true if the endpoint was successfully closed. Returns false if the endpoint was already closed, the address is invalid (including EP0), or the peripheral index is out of range.
ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_close.notes: This function is blocking because it waits for hardware handshake signals (like EPDISD or INEPNE) to ensure the endpoint is fully disabled before resetting registers. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR because of these internal wait loops. It is thread-safe only if the caller ensures no other task is simultaneously attempting to open or configure the same endpoint. A common mistake is attempting to close EP0, which is reserved for control transfers and managed by the stack; the function will correctly reject this request.
ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_close.usage: This function is typically used during USB configuration changes, such as when a host sends a SET_INTERFACE request or when a device is disconnected/reset. It is the counterpart to the endpoint opening process. You should call this to clean up resources when an endpoint is no longer needed, ensuring that the hardware FIFO is flushed and the driver's internal state (like busy flags or queue pointers) is reset to prevent stale data from affecting future transfers.

ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_is_stalled.brief: Checks if a specific USB High-Speed device endpoint is currently in a stalled state.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral (e.g., 0 or 1). Must be within the valid range for the specific MCU.

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The endpoint address (e.g., 0x81 for IN endpoint 1, 0x02 for OUT endpoint 2). Must be a valid endpoint number for the hardware.

ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_is_stalled.returns: Returns true if the endpoint is stalled, false if it is not stalled or if the parameters are invalid (e.g., out-of-bounds index).
ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_is_stalled.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it performs a direct register read. It is safe to call from an ISR because it does not involve OS primitives or waiting. The function relies on the underlying hardware registers (DWC2 on H7xx/H7rsxx); on many other STM32 series (F1, F4, F7, H5, U5), this function is currently unimplemented and will always return false. A common mistake is assuming this function will work on all STM32 platforms; always check the specific hardware implementation file for your target to ensure it is supported.
ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_is_stalled.usage: This function is typically used during USB error recovery or protocol debugging to determine why data transfers are failing. It is often paired with ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_clear_stall to reset an endpoint after a protocol error has been resolved. Developers use this to verify the state of the USB stack after receiving a stall condition from the host or after a local error event, ensuring the endpoint is ready for further communication.

ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_open.signature: bool ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_open(u32 usb_num, u8 ep_addr, ca_usb_ep_type_t type, u16 mps)
ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_open.brief: Configures and enables a specific USB High-Speed device endpoint for data transmission or reception.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral (0 or 1). Values >= 2 are invalid.

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The endpoint address (e.g., 0x81 for IN, 0x02 for OUT). Must be within valid hardware limits.

params.name: type
params.desc: The transfer type (Control, Bulk, Interrupt, or Isochronous).

params.name: mps
params.desc: Maximum Packet Size in bytes. Must match the descriptor requirements.

ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_open.returns: Returns true if the endpoint was successfully configured, false if the parameters are invalid or the hardware is not supported (e.g., on F1xx/F4xx/F7xx/H5xx/U5xx platforms).
ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_open.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs direct register manipulation on the USB OTG peripheral. It is not thread-safe; ensure that endpoint configuration is performed during the initialization phase or within a protected context to avoid race conditions. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. A common mistake is providing an endpoint address that exceeds the hardware's maximum endpoint count or failing to ensure the USB peripheral clock is initialized before calling this function. Note that this function is only implemented for H7 series hardware; calling it on other platforms will return false.
ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_open.usage: This function is typically used during the USB device enumeration process after the USB peripheral has been initialized via ca_usb_hs_dev_init. It is called for each endpoint defined in the device's configuration descriptor to prepare the hardware registers for data flow. It is usually paired with ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_write or ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_read to handle actual data transfers once the host has configured the device. Ensure the endpoint is only opened once per configuration cycle to prevent register corruption.

ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_read.signature: u16 ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_read(u32 usb_num, u8 ep_addr, u8 *buf, u16 max_len)
ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_read.brief: Reads received data from a specific USB High-Speed device endpoint into a provided buffer.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: Index of the USB peripheral (0 or 1). Must be valid for the hardware configuration.

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: Endpoint address (e.g., 0x01 for EP1 OUT). Must be an OUT endpoint; IN endpoints will return 0.

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the destination buffer where data will be copied. Must not be NULL.

params.name: max_len
params.desc: Maximum number of bytes to copy. If the received packet is larger, only this amount is copied.

ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_read.returns: Returns the number of bytes actually copied into the buffer. Returns 0 if the endpoint is empty, the parameters are invalid, or the endpoint is an IN type.
ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_read.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe for EP1+ as it uses a ring buffer mechanism. It is NOT safe to call from an ISR because it manages critical sections and internal state updates that must be synchronized with the main task context. A common mistake is passing an IN endpoint address or a NULL buffer, which will immediately return 0. Ensure the endpoint has been successfully opened via ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_open before attempting to read, otherwise the internal state will not be ready to receive data.
ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_read.usage: This function is typically used within a task loop or a callback triggered by a USB event. The standard sequence is: 1) Initialize the USB peripheral, 2) Open the desired endpoint using ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_open, 3) Periodically poll or wait for a signal indicating data availability, 4) Call ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_read to retrieve the data into a local buffer, and 5) Process the data. It is often paired with ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_write to send responses back to the host.

ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_stall.brief: Forces a USB endpoint into a STALL state to signal a protocol error or unsupported request to the host.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral (e.g., 0 for USB_OTG_HS). Must be a valid peripheral index supported by the hardware.

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The endpoint address. Bit 7 is the direction (1 for IN, 0 for OUT). Bits 0-3 represent the endpoint number.

ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_stall.notes: This function is non-blocking and executes immediately by modifying the hardware control registers. It is thread-safe in the sense that it performs atomic register writes, but it should be used carefully to avoid race conditions with the USB interrupt service routine. It is safe to call from an ISR, but typically it is called from the main USB stack logic when a request cannot be fulfilled. A common mistake is passing an invalid endpoint address or an endpoint number that has not been opened, which may lead to undefined behavior or ignored commands by the USB controller. Note that for Endpoint 0, this function internally triggers a re-arming of the OUT endpoint to ensure the control pipe remains responsive.
ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_stall.usage: This function is used during USB enumeration or data transfer phases when the device receives a request it cannot handle (e.g., an unsupported standard request or a buffer overflow condition). It is typically paired with 'ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_open' during initialization and 'ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_clear_stall' when the host clears the stall condition. In a standard USB stack flow, you would call this when the control transfer state machine enters an error state, signaling the host that the specific endpoint is temporarily unable to process further traffic.

ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_write.signature: bool ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_write(u32 usb_num, u8 ep_addr, const u8 *buf, u16 len)
ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_write.brief: Queues data for transmission on a specific USB High-Speed device endpoint.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral (e.g., 0 or 1).

params.name: ep_addr
params.desc: The endpoint address (e.g., 0x81 for IN endpoint 1). Must be an IN endpoint.

params.name: buf
params.desc: Pointer to the data buffer to be sent. Can be NULL if len is 0.

params.name: len
params.desc: Number of bytes to send. Must be within the limits of the endpoint buffer size.

ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_write.returns: Returns true if the data was successfully queued for transmission, false otherwise (e.g., invalid endpoint, buffer full, or peripheral not initialized).
ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_write.notes: This function is thread-safe and uses internal critical sections to protect the transmission ring buffer, allowing it to be called from multiple tasks or ISRs. It is non-blocking; if the internal queue is full, it immediately returns false rather than waiting for space. A common beginner mistake is assuming the data is sent immediately; this function only copies the data into the internal driver queue, and the actual USB transfer happens asynchronously in the background. Ensure the endpoint has been successfully opened with ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_open before attempting to write.
ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_write.usage: This function is used to send data to the USB host after the device has been initialized and the endpoint opened. It is typically called in a loop or event-driven task whenever there is data to transmit (e.g., CDC serial data or HID reports). The sequence is: ca_usb_hs_dev_init -> ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_open -> ca_usb_hs_dev_ep_write. If the function returns false, the application should implement a retry mechanism or wait for the next available slot in the queue.

ca_usb_hs_dev_get_speed.brief: Retrieves the current operational speed of the specified High-Speed USB device controller.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral to query (e.g., 0 for USB_HS1, 1 for USB_HS2). Must be within the valid range supported by the hardware.

ca_usb_hs_dev_get_speed.returns: Returns a ca_usb_speed_t enum value. Typically returns CA_USB_SPEED_HS (High Speed) or CA_USB_SPEED_FS (Full Speed).
ca_usb_hs_dev_get_speed.notes: This function is non-blocking and thread-safe as it typically reads a cached state or a hardware register directly. It is safe to call from an ISR, provided the USB peripheral has been properly initialized. A common mistake is passing an invalid usb_num index, which may lead to undefined behavior or return a default value depending on the specific hardware implementation. Always ensure the USB peripheral is initialized via the appropriate hardware-specific init function before querying its speed.
ca_usb_hs_dev_get_speed.usage: This function is used during the USB enumeration process or when diagnosing connection issues to verify if the device successfully negotiated High-Speed mode. It is typically called after the USB hardware has been initialized and the connection is established. It is often paired with ca_usb_hs_dev_init to set up the hardware and ca_usb_hs_dev_connect to initiate the bus activity.

ca_usb_hs_dev_gpio_init.brief: Configures the physical GPIO pins required for High-Speed USB peripheral operation.

params.name: usb_num
params.desc: The index of the USB peripheral (0 for the primary HS controller, 1 for the secondary). Invalid values may result in no pins being configured.

ca_usb_hs_dev_gpio_init.notes: This function is non-blocking and performs direct register manipulation to set GPIO modes, speeds, and alternate functions. It is not thread-safe and must be called during the system initialization phase before the USB peripheral is enabled. It is not intended to be called from an ISR. A common beginner mistake is calling this function multiple times or after the USB peripheral has already started, which can cause electrical contention or unexpected behavior on the USB data lines.
ca_usb_hs_dev_gpio_init.usage: This function is part of the hardware abstraction layer for USB initialization.
