CA_NOTIFY_ACTION_SET_IF_EMPTY.brief: Flag to set notification value only if no pending value exists
CA_NOTIFY_ACTION_SET_IF_EMPTY.notes: When enabled (value 5), the notification system will only write a new value to the notification structure if there is currently no pending value (indicated by value 0). If a value is already pending, the new value will be ignored. This prevents overwriting important pending notifications. The flag depends on proper initialization of notification structures and requires the notification system to be properly configured. Valid range is 0 (disabled) to 5 (enabled with specific behavior).
CA_NOTIFY_ACTION_SET_IF_EMPTY.usage: Enable this flag when you want to prevent notification value overwrites in critical applications where pending notifications must not be lost. Use only when the notification system is properly initialized and when you need to ensure that new values don't overwrite existing pending ones. Disable if you want to allow immediate value updates regardless of pending state. Warning: Setting this flag without proper notification structure initialization may cause unexpected behavior or missed notifications.

CA_NO_WAIT_TIME.brief: A configuration constant that disables wait time functionality in the caOS RTOS kernel
CA_NO_WAIT_TIME.notes: When CA_NO_WAIT_TIME is set to 0U (default), the RTOS kernel will not enforce wait time constraints for tasks. This flag typically depends on other timing-related configuration flags like CA_ENABLE_TIMERS. Setting this to 0U removes all wait time limitations, which may cause tasks to block indefinitely. Valid range is typically 0U (disabled) or 1U (enabled), though 0U is the standard default value. When enabled, it may affect task scheduling and system responsiveness.
CA_NO_WAIT_TIME.usage: Change this value to 1U only when you need to enable wait time functionality for specific task management requirements. Setting it to 0U (default) is recommended for most applications as it provides maximum flexibility in task scheduling. Warning: Enabling this flag without proper timer configuration may cause system instability or tasks that never complete execution. This flag should be used carefully in real-time applications where deterministic behavior is required.

CA_PI_MAX_CHAIN.brief: Defines the maximum number of nested priority inheritance locks allowed for a single task.
CA_PI_MAX_CHAIN.notes: This constant sets the depth of the internal stack used to track priority inheritance chains. Increasing this value consumes more RAM per task control block. It must be at least 1, but typical values range from 2 to 8 depending on the complexity of resource nesting in the application. If a task attempts to acquire more locks than this limit, the system may trigger a kernel panic or fail to grant the mutex.
CA_PI_MAX_CHAIN.usage: Increase this value if your application architecture involves tasks that hold multiple mutexes simultaneously in a nested fashion (e.g., Task A locks Mutex 1, then Mutex 2, then Mutex 3). If you encounter system instability or assertion failures during complex resource contention, verify if the nesting depth exceeds this constant. Keep it as low as possible to conserve memory.

CA_PWR_WAKE_LPTIM.brief: Enables the Low Power Timer (LPTIM) as a valid wake-up source for the system from low-power sleep modes.
CA_PWR_WAKE_LPTIM.notes: When enabled, the LPTIM peripheral is configured to trigger an interrupt that exits the CPU from Stop or Standby modes. This flag must be included in the wake-up mask passed to the power management API. It depends on the LPTIM peripheral clock being active during sleep, typically requiring the LSI or LSE clock source to be enabled.
CA_PWR_WAKE_LPTIM.usage: Enable this flag when your application requires periodic wake-ups or time-based events while the system is in a low-power state. Do not enable this if the LPTIM is not initialized, as it may cause the system to fail to wake up or trigger spurious interrupts.

CA_PWR_WAKE_LPUART.brief: Enables the LPUART peripheral as a valid wake-up source for the system from low-power sleep modes.
CA_PWR_WAKE_LPUART.notes: When enabled, the LPUART hardware is configured to trigger an interrupt that wakes the CPU from Stop or Standby modes upon receiving data. This flag must be used in conjunction with the system power management driver. If disabled, the LPUART will remain inactive during sleep, preventing serial communication from waking the device. The value is a bitmask intended for use with the CA_PWR_EnableWakeupSource() function.
CA_PWR_WAKE_LPUART.usage: Enable this flag when your application requires the device to remain in a low-power state while waiting for incoming serial commands or data. Ensure the LPUART clock is configured to remain active during sleep in the RCC settings, otherwise, the wake-up signal will not be detected. Do not enable this if the LPUART is not physically connected to an external device, as noise on the RX line could cause unintended wake-ups.

CA_PWR_WAKE_PIN.brief: Defines the specific GPIO pin index used to trigger a system wake-up event from low-power sleep modes.
CA_PWR_WAKE_PIN.notes: This constant represents a bitmask (1U << 1), targeting Pin 1 of the designated wake-up port. Enabling this flag allows the hardware to transition from standby or stop mode to active mode upon a signal change on this pin. It depends on the CA_PWR_WAKE_PORT configuration being correctly initialized. Valid values are bit-shifted integers corresponding to valid GPIO pins (0-15).
CA_PWR_WAKE_PIN.usage: Change this value when the hardware design requires a different physical pin to wake the MCU from sleep. Use this to solve issues where the system fails to resume operation after entering low-power states. Warning: Ensure the selected pin is physically connected to the wake-up source; using an incorrect pin will result in the system remaining permanently stuck in sleep mode.

CA_PWR_WAKE_RTC.brief: Enables the Real-Time Clock (RTC) alarm as a valid wake-up source for the system from low-power sleep modes.
CA_PWR_WAKE_RTC.notes: When enabled, the RTC peripheral is configured to trigger an interrupt that exits the CPU from sleep or stop modes. This flag must be used in conjunction with the system's power management API. If disabled, the RTC will continue to run but will not be capable of waking the processor, potentially causing the system to remain stuck in a low-power state indefinitely if no other wake-up sources are active.
CA_PWR_WAKE_RTC.usage: Enable this flag when your application requires periodic tasks or scheduled wake-ups based on time (e.g., waking up every hour to send sensor data). Ensure the RTC clock source (LSE or LSI) is correctly initialized before enabling this flag, otherwise, the system may fail to wake up as expected.

CA_PYTHON_NAME_MAX.brief: Defines the maximum allowed length (in bytes) for a Python-related identifier or name string within the caOS system.
CA_PYTHON_NAME_MAX.notes: This constant sets the buffer size for internal Python object naming or identification strings. If a name exceeds 16 characters, it will be truncated or rejected by the caOS Python integration layer. It is a fixed-size allocation to prevent dynamic memory fragmentation.
CA_PYTHON_NAME_MAX.usage: Increase this value only if your application requires longer identifiers for Python-exposed objects or tasks. Be aware that increasing this value consumes more static memory (RAM) for every internal structure that stores a name. Do not set this to an excessively high value to avoid wasting memory on embedded hardware.

CA_QSPI_DEV_NOR.brief: A configuration flag that enables or disables support for NOR-type flash memory devices on the QSPI peripheral.
CA_QSPI_DEV_NOR.notes: When set to 1U, the driver initializes the specific command sets and timing parameters required for NOR flash chips. When set to 0U, this support is excluded from the build to save code space. This flag depends on the QSPI peripheral being enabled in the system configuration. Valid values are 0U (disabled) or 1U (enabled).
CA_QSPI_DEV_NOR.usage: Change this value to 1U only if your hardware design includes a NOR flash memory connected to the QSPI bus. If you are using a different type of memory or no QSPI device at all, keep this at 0U to prevent compilation errors or unnecessary memory usage. Setting this to 1U without a physical NOR flash chip present may cause the driver initialization to hang or return errors.

CA_QSPI_DEV_RAM.brief: Enables or disables the use of internal RAM as a buffer for QSPI flash operations.
CA_QSPI_DEV_RAM.notes: When set to 1U, the driver allocates a dedicated memory buffer in internal SRAM for QSPI data transfers. Disabling this (0U) forces the driver to use direct memory-mapped access or external buffers, which may increase latency. This flag depends on having sufficient free SRAM; if enabled, ensure the linker script provides enough heap or static memory to accommodate the buffer size.
CA_QSPI_DEV_RAM.usage: Enable this when you need to improve read/write performance for QSPI flash operations by reducing bus contention. Change this to 0U if your application is running low on internal SRAM or if you are using a custom DMA implementation that manages its own memory buffers. Incorrectly enabling this on memory-constrained devices may lead to stack overflows or heap exhaustion.

CA_QSPI_DEV_RAW.brief: Defines the operating mode of the QSPI peripheral to use raw memory-mapped access instead of a file system or abstraction layer.
CA_QSPI_DEV_RAW.notes: When set to 2U, the QSPI driver bypasses high-level storage drivers and exposes the flash memory as a raw byte-addressable array. This flag is mutually exclusive with CA_QSPI_DEV_FS. Valid values are typically 0U (disabled), 1U (buffered), and 2U (raw).
CA_QSPI_DEV_RAW.usage: Change this to 2U when you need direct, low-latency access to the flash memory for custom data structures or bootloader operations. Warning: Using raw mode disables built-in wear leveling and file system safety features; ensure your application handles data integrity manually.

CA_QSPI_MMAP_BASE.brief: Defines the starting memory address where the external QSPI flash is mapped into the STM32 memory space.
CA_QSPI_MMAP_BASE.notes: This constant sets the base address for memory-mapped mode (XIP). Changing this value must strictly match the memory map defined in the STM32 reference manual for the specific QSPI peripheral instance. It is typically set to 0x90000000 for the first QSPI bank on most STM32 series. Incorrect values will result in hard faults or data corruption when attempting to read from flash memory.
CA_QSPI_MMAP_BASE.usage: Change this value only if you are porting the driver to a different STM32 microcontroller or if the hardware design uses a different memory bank mapping. Ensure that the linker script (.ld file) is updated to reflect this address if you intend to execute code or store constants directly from the QSPI flash.

CA_QSPI_SSHIFT_AUTO.brief: Enables or disables the automatic shifting of data samples for the Quad-SPI interface.
CA_QSPI_SSHIFT_AUTO.notes: When set to 1, the hardware automatically adjusts the sampling clock phase to compensate for signal propagation delays. When set to 0, the sampling phase is fixed. This flag depends on the specific QSPI peripheral clock frequency and PCB trace length. Valid values are 0 (disabled) or 1 (enabled).
CA_QSPI_SSHIFT_AUTO.usage: Enable this if you experience data corruption or CRC errors during high-speed QSPI read operations. Disable it if your hardware design uses a custom clock-delay circuit or if the peripheral is running at low frequencies where timing margins are naturally sufficient. Incorrect configuration may lead to intermittent read failures or complete communication loss.

CA_QSPI_SSHIFT_AUTO_HZ.brief: Defines the frequency threshold in Hz at which the QSPI driver automatically enables data sampling shift.
CA_QSPI_SSHIFT_AUTO_HZ.notes: When the QSPI clock frequency exceeds this value, the driver enables the internal delay line to compensate for signal propagation delays. If set too low, the system may experience data corruption at high speeds; if set too high, the system may fail to sample data correctly at lower speeds. The default value is 40MHz, which is standard for most QSPI flash memories on STM32 platforms.
CA_QSPI_SSHIFT_AUTO_HZ.usage: Adjust this value if you are using a specific QSPI flash chip that requires a different timing margin or if you are operating the QSPI bus at non-standard frequencies. Ensure this value is lower than the maximum clock frequency supported by your external flash memory to prevent read errors.

CA_QSPI_SSHIFT_OFF.brief: Defines the clock phase shift offset for the Quad-SPI (QSPI) peripheral interface.
CA_QSPI_SSHIFT_OFF.notes: This constant sets the internal delay cycles for the QSPI clock signal relative to the data sampling edge. Increasing this value shifts the clock phase forward, which is critical for maintaining signal integrity at high clock frequencies. It depends on the hardware trace length and the specific flash memory chip's timing requirements. Valid range is typically 0U to 3U, depending on the STM32 hardware revision.
CA_QSPI_SSHIFT_OFF.usage: Adjust this value if you encounter data corruption or CRC errors during high-speed QSPI read operations. If the system fails to read from external flash reliably, incrementing this value can compensate for propagation delays on the PCB. Warning: setting an incorrect value will cause communication failure or intermittent data bit-flips; always verify with an oscilloscope or logic analyzer when tuning.

CA_QSPI_SSHIFT_ON.brief: Enables the data sampling shift feature for the Quad-SPI peripheral to improve signal integrity.
CA_QSPI_SSHIFT_ON.notes: When set to 1U, the QSPI controller adds a half-cycle delay to the data sampling clock. This is critical for high-frequency QSPI operations where signal propagation delay might cause data to be sampled incorrectly. It depends on the hardware layout and the specific flash memory chip's timing requirements. Valid values are 0U (disabled) or 1U (enabled).
CA_QSPI_SSHIFT_ON.usage: Enable this flag if you encounter data corruption or CRC errors during QSPI read operations at high clock speeds. If the system fails to communicate with the external flash after enabling this, verify if your specific hardware design requires the shift or if the clock frequency is too high for the current trace length.

CA_RTC_ALARM_A.brief: Enables the RTC Alarm A interrupt functionality within the caOS driver layer.
CA_RTC_ALARM_A.notes: When set to 1u, the system initializes and enables the hardware interrupt for Alarm A. If set to 0u, the alarm hardware is ignored, and any associated callback functions will never trigger. This flag depends on the RTC peripheral clock being enabled in the system configuration.
CA_RTC_ALARM_A.usage: Set this to 1u when your application needs to trigger periodic tasks or wake the MCU from low-power modes at a specific time. Disable it (0u) to save code space if your project does not utilize RTC alarms, or to prevent interrupt conflicts if you are manually managing the RTC registers.

CA_RTC_ALARM_B.brief: Defines the hardware alarm channel index used for the RTC alarm interrupt.
CA_RTC_ALARM_B.notes: This constant specifies which of the available RTC alarm registers (e.g., Alarm A or Alarm B) the system driver will utilize. Setting this to 2u typically maps to Alarm B on STM32 hardware. It must be consistent with the hardware peripheral configuration and should not conflict with other drivers using the same alarm channel. Valid values are typically 1u or 2u depending on the specific STM32 series.
CA_RTC_ALARM_B.usage: Change this value if the system design requires a specific RTC alarm channel for task scheduling or periodic wake-ups. Use this when Alarm A is already reserved by another system component or peripheral. Incorrect values will result in the RTC interrupt failing to trigger, causing the RTOS to miss scheduled events or fail to wake from low-power modes.

CA_RWLOCK_MAP_WORDS.brief: Calculates the number of 32-bit words required to store a bitmask representing all tasks in the system for read-write lock tracking.
CA_RWLOCK_MAP_WORDS.notes: This constant determines the memory footprint of the internal bitmask used by the ca_rwlock_* API to track which tasks hold or are waiting for a lock. It depends directly on the MAX_TASK configuration. The value is calculated as (MAX_TASK + 31) / 32, effectively rounding up the number of tasks to the nearest multiple of 32 bits. If MAX_TASK is increased, this value scales linearly to ensure every task has a corresponding bit in the tracking map.
CA_RWLOCK_MAP_WORDS.usage: You should not manually change this value; it is automatically derived from the system-wide MAX_TASK definition. If you encounter a compilation error related to bitmask sizes or task indexing in synchronization primitives, verify that MAX_TASK is correctly defined for your project requirements. Ensure that MAX_TASK is not set unnecessarily high, as it increases the memory overhead for every read-write lock instance in the system.

CA_SAFEGUARD.brief: A macro-based dispatcher that validates the number of arguments passed to system-critical RTOS functions.
CA_SAFEGUARD.notes: This constant acts as a compile-time safety layer. When enabled, it ensures that the correct number of parameters is provided to kernel primitives. If the argument count is mismatched, the compiler will throw an error, preventing undefined behavior or stack corruption. It has no runtime overhead as it is resolved during the pre-processing stage.
CA_SAFEGUARD.usage: You should keep this enabled during development and debugging to catch API misuse early. It is typically disabled only in extreme memory-constrained production environments where every byte of pre-processed code size matters, though this is rarely recommended. Do not attempt to redefine this macro unless you are modifying the core kernel dispatch logic.

CA_SAFE_FAIL.brief: A macro used to trigger a system-wide safety halt or error recovery routine when a critical condition is not met.
CA_SAFE_FAIL.notes: When triggered, the system typically enters a locked state or resets to prevent undefined behavior. It depends on the CA_ENABLE_SAFEGUARD flag being set to 1. The first parameter is the error code, and the second is a descriptive string for debugging purposes.
CA_SAFE_FAIL.usage: Use this to wrap critical assertions or hardware state checks. Change this when you need to define custom error handling for specific modules. Warning: triggering this in a production environment will stop the application execution; ensure it is only used for truly unrecoverable system states.

CA_SAI_ERR_AFS.brief: Error flag indicating an Audio Frame Synchronization (AFS) error in the SAI peripheral.
CA_SAI_ERR_AFS.notes: This constant is a bitmask used within the ca_sai_errors() function to identify specific hardware-level synchronization failures. When this bit is set in the error status register, it means the SAI peripheral failed to align the audio frame correctly with the incoming clock signal. It is typically used in conjunction with other error flags in the ca_sai driver. The value 0x04U is specific to the SAI hardware abstraction layer in caOS.
CA_SAI_ERR_AFS.usage: Check this flag when debugging audio glitches, pops, or silence in your application. If ca_sai_errors() returns a value where (status & CA_SAI_ERR_AFS) is true, verify your external audio clock source (MCLK/BCLK) stability and ensure the SAI configuration matches the peripheral's expected frame format. Do not modify this value as it is defined by the hardware driver interface.

CA_SAI_ERR_LFS.brief: Error flag indicating a Low-Level Frame Synchronization (LFS) error in the SAI peripheral.
CA_SAI_ERR_LFS.notes: This constant represents a bitmask value (0x08U) used within the SAI error handling logic. When the SAI hardware detects a frame synchronization error, this bit is set in the error status register. It is typically checked by the ca_sai_errors function to determine if the audio stream has lost synchronization with the external codec or I2S device.
CA_SAI_ERR_LFS.usage: Use this constant when implementing custom error recovery routines or logging within the SAI interrupt service routine. If this error occurs frequently, check the physical clock signals (MCLK, SCK, WS) for noise or timing violations. Do not modify this value as it is mapped directly to the hardware status register bit.

CA_SAI_ERR_OVR.brief: Flag indicating a Serial Audio Interface (SAI) Overrun error.
CA_SAI_ERR_OVR.notes: This constant represents the bitmask for an overrun condition in the SAI peripheral, where the hardware receives data faster than the software can process it. It is typically used within the ca_sai_errors function to check the status register. When this bit is set, it indicates data loss in the audio stream. It is a hardware-level flag defined in the STM32 SAI peripheral registers.
CA_SAI_ERR_OVR.usage: Use this flag when debugging audio glitches or stuttering in your application. If ca_sai_errors returns a value containing CA_SAI_ERR_OVR, it means your task is not reading the SAI buffer fast enough. To solve this, ensure your audio processing task has a higher priority or optimize the code inside your audio callback to reduce execution time.

CA_SAI_ERR_UDR.brief: Flag representing a Serial Audio Interface (SAI) underrun error.
CA_SAI_ERR_UDR.notes: This constant is a bitmask value (0x01U) used within the ca_sai_errors function to identify if the SAI peripheral has failed to provide data to the audio buffer in time. When this bit is set in the error status, it indicates that the audio stream has been interrupted, typically resulting in audible clicks or pops. It is a hardware-level status flag dependent on the STM32 SAI peripheral configuration.
CA_SAI_ERR_UDR.usage: Use this flag when checking the return value of ca_sai_errors to diagnose audio playback issues. If this error occurs frequently, it suggests that the system is under heavy CPU load or that the DMA transfer is not keeping up with the audio sample rate. You should investigate task priorities or increase the audio buffer size if this flag is consistently detected.

CA_SAI_SPDIF_C.brief: Configuration flag to enable SPDIF input/output mode for the SAI peripheral.
CA_SAI_SPDIF_C.notes: This constant is a bitmask (1UL << 26) used within the ca_sai_init function to configure the SAI hardware interface for SPDIF protocol support. When enabled, the SAI peripheral switches from standard I2S/PCM framing to SPDIF mode. It is mutually exclusive with standard I2S configurations and requires the hardware pins to be physically connected to an SPDIF transceiver or optical module.
CA_SAI_SPDIF_C.usage: Use this flag when initializing the SAI peripheral specifically for digital audio transmission or reception via SPDIF. Do not enable this if you are using standard I2S or TDM audio protocols, as it will cause incorrect clocking and data framing, resulting in audio noise or complete signal loss.

CA_SAI_SPDIF_U.brief: A bitmask flag used to enable SPDIF input functionality on the SAI peripheral.
CA_SAI_SPDIF_U.notes: This constant represents the 25th bit of a configuration register. When enabled, it configures the Serial Audio Interface (SAI) to operate in SPDIF receiver mode rather than standard I2S/TDM mode. It is typically passed to the ca_sai_init function. Ensure the hardware pins are physically connected to an SPDIF source before enabling this flag.
CA_SAI_SPDIF_U.usage: Use this flag when your application needs to receive digital audio data via an SPDIF interface. Do not enable this if you are using the SAI peripheral for standard I2S communication, as it will misconfigure the clock and data framing logic, leading to invalid audio data or hardware errors.

CA_SAI_SPDIF_V.brief: A bitmask flag used to configure the SAI peripheral for S/PDIF protocol mode.
CA_SAI_SPDIF_V.notes: When enabled, this flag modifies the SAI peripheral's internal register configuration to support the S/PDIF (Sony/Philips Digital Interface) standard instead of standard I2S/PCM audio formats. It is typically passed as an argument to the ca_sai_init function. It depends on the underlying STM32 hardware supporting S/PDIF mode within the SAI block.
CA_SAI_SPDIF_V.usage: Use this flag when your application needs to interface with digital audio equipment via S/PDIF. Do not use this flag if you are connecting to standard I2S DACs or ADCs, as it will cause incorrect clocking and data framing. Ensure the hardware pins are correctly routed for S/PDIF signals before enabling this.

CA_SDIO_READ_TIMEOUT_MS.brief: SDIO read timeout value in milliseconds for caOS RTOS
CA_SDIO_READ_TIMEOUT_MS.notes: Controls how long the SDIO driver will wait for a read operation to complete before timing out. When enabled, this timeout prevents the system from hanging indefinitely during SD card operations. The value must be greater than 0 and typically ranges from 50-500ms. This flag is independent of other SDIO configuration parameters but affects the reliability of SD card communication. A value of 100ms is the default safe setting.
CA_SDIO_READ_TIMEOUT_MS.usage: Change this value when experiencing SD card read timeouts or slow performance. Increase to 200-500ms if SD card operations are failing due to slow card response, or decrease to 50-100ms if you need faster response times and know the SD card is performing well. Setting this value too low (below 20ms) may cause frequent timeouts, while setting it too high (above 1000ms) may cause unnecessary delays in error detection. The default value of 100ms provides a good balance between reliability and performance for most SD card applications.

CA_SDIO_WRITE_TIMEOUT_MS.brief: Configures the timeout duration for SDIO write operations in milliseconds
CA_SDIO_WRITE_TIMEOUT_MS.notes: This constant determines how long the system will wait for an SDIO write operation to complete before timing out. When increased, it allows more time for slow SD card operations or noisy electrical environments. When decreased, it makes the system more responsive but may cause timeouts on slower cards. This timeout directly affects the SDIO driver's reliability and performance. The value must be greater than 0 and typically ranges from 100-2000ms depending on SD card type and system requirements.
CA_SDIO_WRITE_TIMEOUT_MS.usage: Increase this value when experiencing SD card write timeouts, especially with slower SD cards or in noisy electrical environments. Decrease only when you need faster error detection and are certain about card performance. Setting it too low (below 100ms) may cause false timeouts, while setting it too high (above 2000ms) may delay system response times. Typical value of 500ms is suitable for most standard SD cards in normal operating conditions.

CA_SECRET_AREA_BASE.brief: Defines the starting memory address for the caOS secure storage area.
CA_SECRET_AREA_BASE.notes: This constant sets the base address in SRAM where sensitive data (like keys or secrets) is reserved. The value is hardware-dependent: 0x20040000UL for STM32H563 and 0x20030000UL for STM32U575. It is used by the ca_memory_reserve_secret function to ensure specific memory regions are protected from general allocation.
CA_SECRET_AREA_BASE.usage: Do not change this value manually unless porting to a new MCU variant. Ensure the address aligns with the specific SRAM bank layout defined in the MCU datasheet to avoid memory corruption or overlapping with the stack/heap. If you need to store sensitive data, use ca_memory_reserve_secret instead of accessing this address directly.

CA_SECRET_AREA_SIZE.brief: Defines the size of the protected memory region reserved for sensitive data storage.
CA_SECRET_AREA_SIZE.notes: This constant allocates a fixed block of memory (typically 64KB) used by the caOS security subsystem. It is used by functions like ca_memory_reserve_secret to isolate critical data from general application access. Increasing this value consumes more RAM, while decreasing it may cause allocation failures for secure objects. It must be aligned with the hardware-specific memory map of the STM32 H563 or U575.
CA_SECRET_AREA_SIZE.usage: Adjust this value only if your application requires more or less space for secure keys, certificates, or encrypted buffers. If you encounter errors during ca_memory_reserve_secret, verify if this area is exhausted. Ensure the value is a multiple of the memory page size for your specific MCU to avoid alignment issues.

CA_SECURE_PIPE_DECRYPT.brief: Defines the error code returned by the secure pipe service when a decryption operation fails.
CA_SECURE_PIPE_DECRYPT.notes: This constant is a negative integer (-3) used as a return value in the ca_secure_pipe_recv function. It indicates that the received data could not be decrypted, likely due to an invalid key, corrupted payload, or authentication failure. It is a specific error state within the secure pipe communication layer.
CA_SECURE_PIPE_DECRYPT.usage: Use this constant to check the return value of ca_secure_pipe_recv. If the function returns CA_SECURE_PIPE_DECRYPT, the application should discard the received buffer and potentially trigger a re-keying process or log a security event. Do not modify this value unless you are updating the entire error code mapping of the caOS crypto stack.

CA_SECURE_PIPE_ERR.brief: Error code returned by the secure pipe service when an operation fails.
CA_SECURE_PIPE_ERR.notes: This constant is defined as -1. It is used as a return value for functions like ca_secure_pipe_send or ca_secure_pipe_recv to indicate that the secure communication channel encountered an internal error, such as a timeout, decryption failure, or invalid packet structure. It does not depend on other flags but is specific to the secure pipe subsystem.
CA_SECURE_PIPE_ERR.usage: Use this constant to check the return status of secure pipe operations. If a function returns CA_SECURE_PIPE_ERR, you should handle the failure by logging the event or attempting to re-initialize the pipe using ca_secure_pipe_deinit and ca_secure_pipe_init. Do not attempt to process data buffers if this error code is returned, as the integrity of the pipe is no longer guaranteed.

CA_SECURE_PIPE_MAX_MSG.brief: Defines the maximum number of messages that can be queued in a secure pipe.
CA_SECURE_PIPE_MAX_MSG.notes: This constant sets the upper limit for the message buffer capacity within the secure pipe service. Increasing this value allows for higher throughput and better handling of burst traffic but consumes more RAM. The value 0xFFFFU (65535) is the maximum allowed, representing the total number of pending messages the system can track before rejecting new ones.
CA_SECURE_PIPE_MAX_MSG.usage: Adjust this value if you encounter 'buffer full' errors or dropped messages during high-frequency secure communication. If your system has limited RAM, consider reducing this value to save memory. Ensure that the memory allocated for the pipe is sufficient to hold the number of messages defined by this constant.

CA_SECURE_PIPE_NOT_UP.brief: Error code indicating that the secure communication pipe is not currently established.
CA_SECURE_PIPE_NOT_UP.notes: This constant is returned by secure pipe functions (e.g., ca_secure_pipe_send or ca_secure_pipe_recv) when the underlying link is not in an 'up' state. It is a negative integer (-6), consistent with other caOS error codes. It typically occurs if the handshake process has not completed or if the connection was dropped.
CA_SECURE_PIPE_NOT_UP.usage: Check for this return value when calling secure pipe functions. If received, the application should stop attempting to send or receive data and trigger the connection logic (e.g., ca_sp_link_open) to re-establish the secure channel. Do not ignore this error, as it indicates that data transmission is currently impossible.

CA_SECURE_PIPE_OK.brief: Enables or disables the secure pipe communication service in caOS.
CA_SECURE_PIPE_OK.notes: When set to 1, the system includes the secure pipe service logic, allowing for encrypted data transmission channels. When set to 0 (default), the service is disabled, reducing the binary footprint and removing dependencies on secure pipe internal buffers. This flag is a compile-time constant; changing it requires a full project rebuild.
CA_SECURE_PIPE_OK.usage: Change this value to 1 only if your application requires secure, encrypted inter-process or inter-device communication using ca_secure_pipe_init and related functions. If your project does not use secure pipes, keep it at 0 to save memory and processing overhead. Ensure that if enabled, you have sufficient heap memory allocated for the secure pipe buffers.

CA_SECURE_PIPE_REPLAY.brief: Defines the maximum number of allowed replay attempts or the error code for replay detection in the secure pipe service.
CA_SECURE_PIPE_REPLAY.notes: This constant is used by the secure pipe service to handle packet replay attacks. A value of -5 typically indicates a specific error state returned by the crypto layer when a sequence number mismatch or a replayed packet is detected. It is a signed integer; negative values are reserved for error signaling, while positive values would represent a threshold count.
CA_SECURE_PIPE_REPLAY.usage: Do not modify this value unless you are performing low-level debugging of the secure communication protocol. If you encounter this error code during development, it suggests that the device is receiving duplicate or out-of-order encrypted packets, which may indicate a network issue or an active security threat. Ensure that sequence numbers are correctly managed by the sender using ca_secure_pipe_send.

CA_SECURE_PIPE_REPLY.brief: Enables automatic reply generation for secure pipe communication.
CA_SECURE_PIPE_REPLY.notes: When set to 1, the caOS secure pipe service automatically handles acknowledgement or reply packets for incoming requests. Disabling this (0) requires the application layer to manually manage all response transmissions using ca_secure_pipe_send. This flag is a dependency for automated secure handshake protocols.
CA_SECURE_PIPE_REPLY.usage: Enable this when you want to reduce code complexity in your communication tasks by offloading reply logic to the OS. Disable it if your application requires custom, non-standard response timing or specific packet formatting that the automated service cannot provide. Ensure that if this is enabled, your task logic does not conflict with the automatic replies to avoid duplicate or malformed data on the pipe.

CA_SECURE_PIPE_SIZE.brief: Defines the internal buffer size for the secure communication pipe service.
CA_SECURE_PIPE_SIZE.notes: This constant determines the memory allocation for the secure pipe's internal data buffer. A value of -4 is a special configuration flag indicating that the buffer size is dynamically managed or derived from a specific hardware-dependent memory pool rather than a fixed static allocation. Modifying this value directly may cause memory corruption or initialization failures in the ca_secure_pipe_init service.
CA_SECURE_PIPE_SIZE.usage: Do not change this value unless instructed by the system architecture team. It is used to balance memory footprint against throughput for encrypted data streams. If you encounter 'buffer overflow' errors in secure communication, verify the memory pool availability using ca_memory_get_avail_memory before attempting to adjust system-wide buffer configurations.

CA_SECURE_PIPE_TIMEOUT.brief: Defines the default timeout duration for secure pipe communication operations.
CA_SECURE_PIPE_TIMEOUT.notes: This constant sets the wait time for secure pipe operations. A value of -2 typically indicates an infinite wait or a specific blocking behavior defined by the caOS secure pipe service. Changing this affects how long tasks block when calling ca_secure_pipe_send or ca_secure_pipe_recv. Ensure that the system architecture can handle blocking calls if this is set to a high value or infinite.
CA_SECURE_PIPE_TIMEOUT.usage: Modify this value if secure communication operations are timing out prematurely in high-latency environments or if you need to enforce stricter real-time constraints. Use caution: setting this too low may cause frequent communication failures, while setting it to infinite (if supported) may lead to task starvation if the remote peer becomes unresponsive.

CA_SLICE_MIN_TICKS.brief: Defines the minimum number of system ticks a task is guaranteed to run before being preempted by the scheduler.
CA_SLICE_MIN_TICKS.notes: This constant controls the granularity of the round-robin time-slicing mechanism. Increasing this value reduces the frequency of context switches, which lowers CPU overhead but increases latency for task responsiveness. It is typically set to 2U across all supported STM32 platforms to balance throughput and real-time performance. It depends on the system tick frequency configured via ca_os_tick_init.
CA_SLICE_MIN_TICKS.usage: Modify this value if you need to optimize for high-throughput background processing (increase the value) or if you require faster task switching for time-critical event handling (decrease the value). Warning: setting this to 0 or 1 may cause excessive context switching, leading to 'thrashing' where the CPU spends more time saving/restoring registers than executing application code.

CA_SPDIFRX_C.brief: A bitmask flag used to enable the SPDIFRX peripheral in caOS.
CA_SPDIFRX_C.notes: This constant represents the 27th bit of a configuration register. When enabled, it allows the caOS driver to initialize and interact with the hardware SPDIF receiver. It is typically used as an argument in the ca_spdifrx_init function. Ensure the hardware pins are correctly configured before setting this flag.
CA_SPDIFRX_C.usage: Use this flag when you need to initialize the SPDIFRX peripheral for digital audio input. If the peripheral is not required, keep this bit unset to save power and avoid unnecessary hardware initialization. Do not modify the bit position (1UL << 27) as it is hardcoded to match the STM32 hardware register mapping.

CA_SPDIFRX_CS_BYTES.brief: Defines the size in bytes of the S/PDIF Channel Status block buffer.
CA_SPDIFRX_CS_BYTES.notes: This constant sets the memory allocation size for storing the S/PDIF Channel Status data. The S/PDIF specification defines the Channel Status block as 192 bits (24 bytes). Changing this value will affect the memory footprint of the ca_spdifrx driver. It must be set to 24U to comply with the standard S/PDIF protocol.
CA_SPDIFRX_CS_BYTES.usage: Do not change this value unless you are implementing a non-standard S/PDIF protocol variant that uses a different Channel Status block size. Incorrect values will cause the ca_spdifrx_channel_status function to return incomplete or corrupted data, potentially leading to synchronization errors or misinterpretation of the audio stream metadata.

CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_FRM.brief: Flag indicating a framing error in the SPDIFRX peripheral.
CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_FRM.notes: This constant represents the 0x04 bit in the SPDIFRX error status register. It is triggered when the incoming SPDIF stream fails to adhere to the expected subframe structure. It is typically checked via the ca_spdifrx_errors() function. It does not have dependencies on other flags but is part of the broader error bitmask returned by the driver.
CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_FRM.usage: Use this flag when debugging audio signal integrity issues or synchronization problems. If ca_spdifrx_errors() returns a value where (errors & CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_FRM) is true, it indicates that the physical connection or the source clock is unstable. If this error persists, check the physical cable quality or the source device's sample rate stability.

CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_OVR.brief: Flag indicating an Overrun Error in the SPDIFRX peripheral.
CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_OVR.notes: This constant represents a bitmask (0x02U) used to identify when the SPDIFRX hardware buffer has been overwritten before the CPU could read the previous data. It is typically checked within the ca_spdifrx_errors function. If this bit is set, it means the application is not processing incoming audio data fast enough to keep up with the hardware sample rate.
CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_OVR.usage: Use this flag when debugging audio dropouts or glitches. If ca_spdifrx_errors returns a value containing this bit, you must optimize your data processing loop or increase the priority of the task handling the audio stream. Do not modify this value, as it is defined by the hardware register mapping.

CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_PAR.brief: Bitmask flag representing a parity error in the SPDIFRX peripheral.
CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_PAR.notes: This constant is used as a bitmask within the ca_spdifrx_errors() function. When the SPDIFRX hardware detects a parity error in the incoming stream, this bit is set in the error status register. It is typically checked alongside other error flags (like framing or overrun errors) to determine the health of the digital audio input signal.
CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_PAR.usage: Use this constant when implementing custom error handling logic for the SPDIFRX driver. If ca_spdifrx_errors() returns a value where (result & CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_PAR) is true, it indicates that the received audio data contains parity violations, which may result in audible noise or signal dropouts. Do not modify this value as it maps directly to the hardware register definition.

CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_SYNC.brief: Flag indicating a synchronization error in the S/PDIF receiver peripheral.
CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_SYNC.notes: This constant represents a bitmask (0x08U) used within the ca_spdifrx_errors() function to identify if the S/PDIF hardware has lost synchronization with the incoming audio stream. When this bit is set in the error status register, the receiver is unable to lock onto the incoming clock or data frame. It is typically checked alongside other error flags returned by the driver.
CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_SYNC.usage: Use this flag when implementing a callback or polling loop for the S/PDIF interface to detect signal loss. If ca_spdifrx_errors() returns a value where (result & CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_SYNC) is true, the application should trigger a re-synchronization routine or notify the user that the audio source is disconnected or unstable. Do not modify this value as it is mapped directly to the hardware register bit definition.

CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_TMO.brief: Defines the timeout threshold for SPDIFRX error detection.
CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_TMO.notes: This constant represents the number of cycles or internal ticks the SPDIFRX peripheral waits before flagging an error state. It is used by the ca_spdifrx driver to handle signal instability or synchronization loss. Typical values are small integers; 0x10U is the default configuration. Increasing this value makes the system more tolerant to jitter but slower to report actual signal loss.
CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_TMO.usage: Adjust this value if you experience frequent, false-positive error interrupts during SPDIF signal reception. If the signal is noisy, increasing the timeout can prevent unnecessary driver resets. If the system fails to detect a disconnected cable or a dead signal source promptly, consider decreasing this value.

CA_SPDIFRX_HW_SBD.brief: Defines the hardware synchronization bit mask for the SPDIFRX peripheral.
CA_SPDIFRX_HW_SBD.notes: This constant represents the bit field used to identify the Synchronization Block Detected (SBD) status within the SPDIFRX hardware registers. It is typically used by the ca_spdifrx_sync function to verify if the incoming audio stream has achieved frame and block synchronization. It is a hardware-specific constant and should not be modified unless the underlying STM32 hardware revision changes.
CA_SPDIFRX_HW_SBD.usage: Use this constant when checking the status of the SPDIFRX peripheral to ensure a valid audio signal is present before attempting to read data. If ca_spdifrx_sync returns a value that does not match this mask, the audio stream is not yet locked, and reading data will result in invalid samples or noise.

CA_SPDIFRX_HW_STOP.brief: Defines the set of SPDIFRX hardware error conditions that trigger an automatic stop of the receiver.
CA_SPDIFRX_HW_STOP.notes: This constant acts as a bitmask. When the hardware detects any of the included error flags (Frame error, Synchronization error, or Timeout error), the ca_spdifrx_stop() function is automatically invoked to halt the peripheral. It depends on the underlying STM32 SPDIFRX peripheral error registers. Typical values are a combination of CA_SPDIFRX_ERR_* flags.
CA_SPDIFRX_HW_STOP.usage: Modify this value if you need to change the error-handling policy of the SPDIFRX interface. For example, if you want the system to ignore specific errors (like minor frame errors) to maintain audio stream continuity, remove the corresponding flag from the mask. Warning: removing critical error flags may lead to the processing of corrupted data or system instability if the hardware enters an undefined state.

CA_SPDIFRX_HW_SYNCD.brief: Flag to enable hardware-level synchronization for the SPDIFRX peripheral.
CA_SPDIFRX_HW_SYNCD.notes: When enabled (0x100U), the driver forces the hardware to wait for a valid synchronization signal before reporting the stream as ready. If disabled, the driver may attempt to read data before the clock or frame alignment is stable. This flag is typically used in conjunction with ca_spdifrx_init and ca_spdifrx_sync. It is a bitmask value intended for use in the configuration structure of the SPDIFRX driver.
CA_SPDIFRX_HW_SYNCD.usage: Enable this flag if you experience noise, corrupted audio frames, or 'garbage' data at the start of an SPDIF stream. It solves synchronization issues caused by the peripheral starting before the external transmitter has fully locked onto the signal. Warning: Enabling this may increase the latency between calling ca_spdifrx_init and the first valid data read, as the system must wait for the hardware to achieve lock.

CA_SPDIFRX_PE.brief: Enables the Parity Error (PE) interrupt for the SPDIFRX peripheral.
CA_SPDIFRX_PE.notes: When this bit is set, the SPDIFRX hardware will trigger an interrupt if a parity error is detected in the incoming data stream. This flag is typically used in conjunction with the ca_spdifrx_init function. It is a bitmask value (1UL << 24) intended to be ORed with other configuration flags.
CA_SPDIFRX_PE.usage: Enable this flag when you need to monitor the integrity of the incoming SPDIF signal. If your application experiences data corruption or synchronization issues, enabling this interrupt allows you to catch parity errors in real-time via the ca_spdifrx_errors function. Do not enable this if your hardware source does not support parity or if you want to ignore transmission errors to prioritize continuous data flow.

CA_SPDIFRX_PT.brief: Extracts the 2-bit S/PDIF channel status information from a raw 32-bit register value.
CA_SPDIFRX_PT.notes: This macro performs a bitwise shift and mask operation on a 32-bit input word (w). It isolates bits 28 and 29, which typically represent specific channel status flags in the STM32 S/PDIF-RX peripheral. It is a low-level helper used internally by ca_spdifrx_channel_status.
CA_SPDIFRX_PT.usage: Use this macro when you need to parse raw register data from the S/PDIF-RX peripheral to determine channel status. Do not modify the shift or mask values unless the underlying hardware register mapping changes, as incorrect values will result in reading invalid status bits.

CA_SPDIFRX_PT_B.brief: Configures the SPDIFRX peripheral to use Port B for input signals.
CA_SPDIFRX_PT_B.notes: When set to 1U, the driver routes the SPDIFRX input pins to the STM32 Port B GPIO bank. If set to 0U, it typically defaults to Port A or another hardware-specific mapping depending on the MCU variant. This flag must be set before calling ca_spdifrx_init to ensure the hardware abstraction layer configures the correct GPIO alternate functions.
CA_SPDIFRX_PT_B.usage: Change this value if your hardware design connects the SPDIF input signal to pins located on Port B instead of the default port. Incorrect configuration will result in the peripheral failing to detect a valid signal, causing ca_spdifrx_sync to return an error or timeout.

CA_SPDIFRX_PT_M.brief: Defines the number of SPDIFRX peripheral channels available for concurrent use.
CA_SPDIFRX_PT_M.notes: This constant sets the hardware abstraction layer limit for the SPDIFRX driver. Increasing this value allows more simultaneous SPDIFRX instances to be initialized, but consumes more system memory for driver control blocks. It must be consistent with the actual number of SPDIFRX peripherals present on the specific STM32 MCU variant.
CA_SPDIFRX_PT_M.usage: Change this value only if the hardware design utilizes multiple SPDIFRX peripherals simultaneously. If you encounter initialization errors when attempting to open a second SPDIFRX channel, verify that this constant is set to at least 2. Do not set this value higher than the number of physical SPDIFRX interfaces supported by your target MCU.

CA_SPDIFRX_PT_W.brief: Configures the SPDIFRX peripheral input pin selection (multiplexing).
CA_SPDIFRX_PT_W.notes: This constant determines which physical GPIO pin is mapped to the SPDIFRX input. The value 3U corresponds to a specific hardware-defined input path on the STM32. Changing this value requires verifying the hardware schematic to ensure the correct pin is connected to the SPDIF source. It is a low-level hardware configuration constant and should not be modified unless the PCB layout changes.
CA_SPDIFRX_PT_W.usage: Change this value only if you are porting the code to a different hardware revision where the SPDIFRX signal is routed to a different pin. Using an incorrect value will result in the peripheral failing to receive any data (sync errors), as it will be listening to the wrong physical pin.

CA_SPDIFRX_SAMPLE.brief: A macro that performs sign-extension on a 24-bit SPDIF sample to a 32-bit signed integer.
CA_SPDIFRX_SAMPLE.notes: The macro shifts the input word left by 8 bits and then performs an arithmetic right shift by 8 bits. This effectively treats the 24-bit audio data as a signed value, preserving the sign bit (bit 23) across the upper 8 bits of the 32-bit container. It is intended for use with raw data retrieved from the SPDIFRX peripheral.
CA_SPDIFRX_SAMPLE.usage: Use this macro when processing raw audio samples from the SPDIFRX driver to ensure that negative values are correctly interpreted by the CPU. Do not use this on data that is already 32-bit or unsigned, as it will corrupt the bit pattern.

CA_SPDIFRX_U.brief: A bitmask flag used to enable the SPDIFRX peripheral in the caOS hardware abstraction layer.
CA_SPDIFRX_U.notes: This constant represents the 26th bit of a configuration register. When enabled, it allows the caOS driver to initialize and access the SPDIFRX hardware. It is typically used as an argument in hardware initialization functions. It has no direct dependencies on other flags but must be used only on STM32 microcontrollers that physically possess an SPDIFRX peripheral.
CA_SPDIFRX_U.usage: Use this flag when calling initialization routines for the SPDIFRX interface. If you are not using the SPDIFRX peripheral, do not include this flag to save system resources and avoid potential hardware conflicts. Warning: Enabling this on a device without the physical peripheral will result in undefined behavior or a system fault.

CA_SPDIFRX_V.brief: A bitmask flag used to identify or enable the SPDIFRX peripheral in caOS driver configurations.
CA_SPDIFRX_V.notes: This constant represents the 25th bit (value 0x02000000). It is typically used in bitwise operations to select the SPDIFRX hardware instance within the caOS driver initialization or resource management functions. It does not have dependencies on other flags but must be used in accordance with the specific STM32 hardware support for SPDIFRX.
CA_SPDIFRX_V.usage: Use this flag when calling ca_spdifrx_init or similar driver-level functions that require a peripheral identifier. Do not modify the bit position unless you are porting the driver to a different hardware architecture where the peripheral mapping has changed.

CA_SPINLOCK_COOP_INIT.brief: Initializes a cooperative spinlock structure to the 'free' state.
CA_SPINLOCK_COOP_INIT.notes: This constant sets the internal key of a spinlock to SPINLOCK_FREE, indicating that the resource is currently available. It is a static initializer used during the declaration of a spinlock variable. It has no dependencies on other flags but must be used only with variables of type ca_spinlock_t.
CA_SPINLOCK_COOP_INIT.usage: Use this when declaring a new spinlock in your global or static scope to ensure it starts in an unlocked state. Failure to initialize a spinlock before use will lead to undefined behavior, likely causing the system to hang or deadlock immediately upon the first attempt to acquire the lock.

CA_SPINLOCK_IRQ_INIT.brief: Initializes a spinlock structure to a safe, unlocked state with interrupts enabled.
CA_SPINLOCK_IRQ_INIT.notes: This constant sets the spinlock key to 'SPINLOCK_FREE' and resets the interrupt state tracker to 0. It is a static initializer used to define spinlock variables at compile time. It has no dependencies on other flags but must be used only for variables of type 'ca_spinlock_t'.
CA_SPINLOCK_IRQ_INIT.usage: Use this when declaring a new spinlock variable globally or within a struct. You should never manually assign these values at runtime; always use this initializer during declaration to ensure the lock starts in a known, valid state. Failure to initialize correctly will result in undefined behavior, likely causing system deadlocks or race conditions during the first attempt to acquire the lock.

CA_SPI_XFER_TIMEOUT_MS.brief: SPI transfer timeout value in milliseconds for the caOS RTOS
CA_SPI_XFER_TIMEOUT_MS.notes: This constant defines how long the SPI driver will wait for a transfer operation to complete before timing out. When enabled, it prevents the system from hanging indefinitely during SPI communication. The timeout value directly affects system responsiveness during SPI errors. Typical range is 100-10000ms, with 1000ms being the default. This flag is independent of other SPI configuration flags but requires proper error handling in the calling code.
CA_SPI_XFER_TIMEOUT_MS.usage: Change this value when experiencing SPI communication timeouts or when working with slow SPI devices. Increase to 2000-5000ms for devices with high latency or when debugging communication issues. Decrease to 100-500ms for time-critical applications or when using fast SPI peripherals. Setting this value too low (below 100ms) may cause false timeouts, while setting it too high (above 10000ms) may delay error detection and system recovery.

CA_SP_LINK_AAD_MAX.brief: Defines the maximum size in bytes for the Additional Authenticated Data (AAD) buffer in the secure pipe service.
CA_SP_LINK_AAD_MAX.notes: This constant sets the upper limit for the AAD field used during cryptographic operations in the secure pipe. Increasing this value allows for larger metadata headers in encrypted packets but consumes more static memory per secure pipe instance. It must be consistent across all communicating nodes to ensure successful packet decryption.
CA_SP_LINK_AAD_MAX.usage: Adjust this value only if you need to include larger authentication tags or metadata in your secure communication protocol. If you encounter 'buffer too small' errors during secure pipe transmission, verify if your AAD payload exceeds 48 bytes. Ensure that the memory allocated for the secure pipe context is sufficient to accommodate this buffer size.

CA_SP_LINK_DATA_HDR.brief: Defines the total size in bytes of the secure pipe link data header.
CA_SP_LINK_DATA_HDR.notes: The value (1U + 8U + 2U) = 11 bytes represents the fixed overhead for secure communication packets. This includes fields for protocol versioning, sequence numbers, and integrity metadata. It is a static constant used by the ca_secure_pipe_service to calculate buffer offsets and payload alignment. Modifying this value without updating the corresponding protocol implementation in the secure pipe service will cause packet corruption and communication failure.
CA_SP_LINK_DATA_HDR.usage: Do not change this value unless you are modifying the underlying secure pipe protocol specification. It is used internally by ca_secure_pipe_service to ensure that buffers allocated for transmission have enough space for the header. If you encounter 'buffer too small' errors during secure transmission, ensure your application-level buffers account for this header size plus the actual payload.

CA_SP_LINK_HELLO_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed byte size of the handshake 'HELLO' message in the caOS secure pipe service.
CA_SP_LINK_HELLO_SIZE.notes: The value is calculated as the sum of protocol fields: 1 (version) + 1 (flags) + 12 (nonce) + 32 (public key) + 16 (authentication tag). This constant determines the buffer allocation size for secure pipe link initialization. It must match the peer's expected message length exactly to prevent communication failures.
CA_SP_LINK_HELLO_SIZE.usage: Do not modify this value unless the secure pipe protocol specification is updated. Changing this value without updating the corresponding peer implementation will cause handshake rejection and connection failure. If you need to adjust the buffer size for custom extensions, ensure the peer is updated simultaneously.

CA_SP_LINK_OVERHEAD_MAX.brief: Defines the maximum buffer overhead required for secure pipe link communication.
CA_SP_LINK_OVERHEAD_MAX.notes: This constant represents the total byte overhead added to the payload, consisting of the link data header (CA_SP_LINK_DATA_HDR), a 15-byte padding/alignment buffer, and a 16-byte authentication tag. It is used to calculate buffer sizes for secure packet transmission. Changing this value affects memory allocation for secure pipe buffers; it must be large enough to accommodate the underlying cryptographic protocol requirements.
CA_SP_LINK_OVERHEAD_MAX.usage: Adjust this value only if the underlying cryptographic protocol (e.g., AES-GCM or similar) changes its authentication tag size or if the link header structure is modified. Incorrect values will lead to buffer overflows or decryption failures during secure pipe communication. Ensure that any buffer allocated using this constant is large enough to hold the payload plus this overhead.

CA_SP_LINK_PBKDF2_ITER.brief: Defines the number of iterations for the PBKDF2 key derivation function used in the secure pipe service.
CA_SP_LINK_PBKDF2_ITER.notes: This constant controls the computational cost of deriving a cryptographic key from a password. Increasing this value significantly improves resistance against brute-force attacks but increases the time required to establish a secure connection. It is a fixed integer value, typically set to 100,000. It is used internally by the ca_secure_pipe_service during the handshake process.
CA_SP_LINK_PBKDF2_ITER.usage: Increase this value if security requirements demand higher resistance to offline password cracking, provided the target STM32 hardware has sufficient CPU performance to handle the increased latency. Decrease it only if the connection handshake time exceeds the system's real-time constraints. Warning: setting this too low makes the system vulnerable to brute-force attacks; setting it too high may cause watchdog timeouts during the key derivation process.

CA_SP_LINK_REKEY_MS.brief: Defines the time interval in milliseconds after which the secure pipe session keys are automatically rotated.
CA_SP_LINK_REKEY_MS.notes: This constant determines the frequency of the rekeying process for secure communication channels. It is defined as 3,600,000 ms (1 hour). Reducing this value increases security by limiting the amount of data encrypted with the same key, but increases CPU overhead due to more frequent cryptographic operations. It is used by the secure pipe service to trigger key updates.
CA_SP_LINK_REKEY_MS.usage: Adjust this value if your security policy requires more frequent key rotation (e.g., for high-security environments) or less frequent rotation (e.g., to save power or reduce processing load on low-power STM32 devices). Ensure the value is set in milliseconds. Example: #define CA_SP_LINK_REKEY_MS (30UL * 60UL * 1000UL) // Rotate every 30 minutes.

CA_SP_LINK_REKEY_MSGS.brief: Defines the threshold for the number of messages sent over a secure pipe before triggering a key re-negotiation.
CA_SP_LINK_REKEY_MSGS.notes: This constant sets the maximum message count limit for a secure session. Once the number of messages sent exceeds this value, the system forces a re-keying process to maintain forward secrecy. The value (1UL << 20) equals 1,048,576 messages. Lowering this value increases security by rotating keys more frequently but introduces higher CPU overhead due to more frequent cryptographic handshakes.
CA_SP_LINK_REKEY_MSGS.usage: Adjust this value if your application requires stricter security policies or if you need to reduce the frequency of re-keying to save power/CPU cycles. Ensure the value is a power of two for optimal performance. If you notice performance drops during long-running sessions, verify if the re-keying frequency is too high for your specific throughput requirements.

CA_SP_LINK_SECRET_MAX.brief: Defines the maximum length in bytes allowed for the secret key used in the secure pipe service.
CA_SP_LINK_SECRET_MAX.notes: This constant sets the buffer size for cryptographic secrets. Increasing this value consumes more RAM per secure pipe instance. It must be large enough to accommodate the specific key exchange algorithm requirements (e.g., X25519). Typical value is 16U, which is sufficient for standard symmetric keys.
CA_SP_LINK_SECRET_MAX.usage: Change this value only if you are implementing a custom cryptographic protocol that requires longer keys. If you set this value too low, secure pipe connections will fail to initialize or authenticate. Ensure that the value is consistent across both ends of the communication link.

CA_SP_LINK_SECRET_MIN.brief: Defines the minimum required length in bytes for the secret key used in the secure pipe link.
CA_SP_LINK_SECRET_MIN.notes: This constant sets the security floor for key exchange operations. Increasing this value enhances security but requires both communication endpoints to support longer keys. It is used during the initialization of the secure pipe service. The default value is 8 bytes. Ensure that any custom key generation logic complies with this minimum to prevent connection rejection.
CA_SP_LINK_SECRET_MIN.usage: Modify this value only if your security policy requires a higher minimum entropy for link secrets. If you encounter 'link_init' failures, verify that the provided secret meets this length requirement. Do not set this value lower than 8, as it may weaken the cryptographic integrity of the secure pipe.

CA_ST_TH_BLOCKED.brief: A status flag indicating that a specific task is currently in the BLOCKED state.
CA_ST_TH_BLOCKED.notes: This flag is used by the scheduler to identify tasks waiting for an event, semaphore, or timer. When a task is in this state, it is removed from the ready list and will not be scheduled for execution until the blocking condition is resolved. It is a bitmask value typically used in conjunction with other status flags in the task control block (TCB).
CA_ST_TH_BLOCKED.usage: Do not manually modify this constant value as it is managed internally by the caOS kernel. Use this flag only when writing custom debugging tools or diagnostic functions that need to inspect the task state via the scheduler's API. Incorrectly interpreting this flag in custom code may lead to false assumptions about task availability.

CA_ST_TH_DIGEST_ERROR.brief: A specific error flag indicating that a thread's stack or control block digest verification has failed.
CA_ST_TH_DIGEST_ERROR.notes: This flag is set by the kernel's integrity monitor when a memory corruption or stack overflow is detected in a thread's metadata. It is typically used in conjunction with CA_ST_TH_ERROR. Enabling system-wide integrity checks will cause this flag to be raised if the calculated checksum of the thread structure does not match the stored value.
CA_ST_TH_DIGEST_ERROR.usage: Use this flag when debugging system crashes or unexpected task terminations to determine if the cause was memory corruption. Do not manually set this flag in application code; it is a read-only status indicator for the kernel. If you see this flag frequently, investigate your stack sizes and check for buffer overflows in your task functions.

CA_ST_TH_INIT.brief: Defines the initial stack pattern value used to fill task stacks during initialization.
CA_ST_TH_INIT.notes: This constant sets the byte value written to the entire stack memory area when a task is created. It is primarily used by the stack overflow detection mechanism to identify how much of the stack has been utilized. Typical values are 0x80 or 0xCC. Changing this does not affect system performance, but it is critical for debugging stack usage via the caOS stack watermarking tools.
CA_ST_TH_INIT.usage: Change this value if you need to distinguish between uninitialized stack memory and actual data during debugging. If you notice that your stack monitoring tools are reporting incorrect usage, ensure this value matches the pattern expected by your specific debugging configuration. Do not set this to 0x00, as it makes it impossible to differentiate between empty stack space and valid null-terminated strings or zero-initialized variables.

CA_ST_TH_REMOVE.brief: A bitmask flag used to identify and remove a specific thread from the scheduler's active task list.
CA_ST_TH_REMOVE.notes: This flag is typically used within the internal task control block (TCB) status field. When set, the scheduler ignores the thread during context switching. It is often used in conjunction with other status flags like CA_ST_TH_SUSPEND. It must not be manually toggled by application code unless using the provided caOS API functions to avoid memory corruption or scheduler deadlocks.
CA_ST_TH_REMOVE.usage: Change or use this flag when implementing custom thread management or debugging tools that require dynamic removal of tasks from the execution cycle. Incorrect usage can lead to a system hang if the scheduler attempts to context switch into a thread that has been improperly flagged as removed.

CA_ST_TH_RUN.brief: A bitmask flag representing the 'Running' state of a thread within the caOS scheduler.
CA_ST_TH_RUN.notes: This constant is used by the kernel to identify which thread is currently occupying the CPU. When this bit is set in a thread's status register, the scheduler recognizes it as the active task. It is typically used in conjunction with other status flags (like Ready, Blocked, or Suspended) and should not be manually modified by application code to avoid corrupting the scheduler's internal state.
CA_ST_TH_RUN.usage: This value is primarily used for debugging purposes or when implementing custom system monitors to check if a specific thread is currently executing. Do not change this value unless you are modifying the core kernel source code, as it is hardcoded into the scheduler's state machine logic.

CA_ST_TH_RUNNING.brief: A bitmask constant representing the internal state of a task when it is currently executing on the CPU.
CA_ST_TH_RUNNING.notes: This value is used by the caOS kernel scheduler to identify active tasks in the task control block (TCB). It is a read-only status flag for the system. Modifying this value manually will corrupt the scheduler's ability to track task execution, leading to kernel panics or system hangs. It is typically used in debugging tools or status monitoring functions to filter tasks that are currently running.
CA_ST_TH_RUNNING.usage: Do not modify this value. It is intended for internal kernel use only. If you are writing a custom task monitor or a system diagnostic tool, you may use this constant to compare against the task state field to determine if a specific task is currently occupying the processor.

CA_ST_TH_SIG_WDT.brief: Defines the bitmask flag used to signal that a thread has triggered a watchdog timeout event.
CA_ST_TH_SIG_WDT.notes: This constant represents a specific bit in the thread status register. When enabled, the scheduler identifies that the thread has exceeded its execution time budget. It depends on the system watchdog timer being active and the scheduler's monitoring task being enabled. The value 0x200 corresponds to the 9th bit position in the status word.
CA_ST_TH_SIG_WDT.usage: Use this flag when debugging thread starvation or infinite loops within a specific task. You should change this value only if you are remapping the internal status register bitmask for the entire RTOS kernel. Warning: modifying this value incorrectly will cause the scheduler to misinterpret thread states, leading to system instability or silent task failures.

CA_ST_TH_SLEEP.brief: A bitmask flag representing the thread state where a task is currently blocked or waiting for a timer/event.
CA_ST_TH_SLEEP.notes: This flag is used by the scheduler to identify threads that are not ready to run. When a thread is in this state, the scheduler skips it during the context switch process. It is a core internal state bit and should not be manually modified by application code. It is typically used in conjunction with other state flags like CA_ST_TH_READY.
CA_ST_TH_SLEEP.usage: Do not change this value as it is a hardcoded internal state identifier for the caOS kernel. If you are debugging and see this flag in the thread control block (TCB), it confirms the thread is correctly suspended and waiting for a resource or delay to expire.

CA_ST_TH_STACK_OVERFLOW.brief: A bitmask flag used to identify if a specific task has exceeded its allocated stack memory limit.
CA_ST_TH_STACK_OVERFLOW.notes: When this flag is set in the task status register, the kernel detects a stack overflow condition. It is typically checked by the kernel's memory protection unit (MPU) or software stack-check hooks. This flag is dependent on CA_CFG_STACK_CHECK being enabled. It is a read-only status bit for the user, managed internally by the scheduler.
CA_ST_TH_STACK_OVERFLOW.usage: Use this flag during debugging to verify if your task stack sizes are sufficient. If you encounter hard faults or erratic behavior, check if this bit is set in the task control block (TCB). Do not manually set this bit; it is intended for diagnostic purposes to identify memory corruption issues before they crash the system.

CA_ST_TH_STOP.brief: A status flag indicating that a specific thread has been explicitly stopped or suspended by the scheduler.
CA_ST_TH_STOP.notes: When this bit is set in the thread control block (TCB), the scheduler will skip this thread during context switching. It is typically used in conjunction with other status flags like CA_ST_TH_READY. If this flag is cleared, the thread becomes eligible for scheduling again, provided it is not blocked by other conditions.
CA_ST_TH_STOP.usage: Use this flag when you need to temporarily halt a task's execution without deleting it from memory. This is useful for power management or pausing non-essential background tasks. Do not manually modify this flag while the scheduler is running; always use the provided caOS API functions to suspend or resume threads to avoid race conditions or system instability.

CA_ST_TH_SUSPENDED.brief: A bitmask flag representing the suspended state of a task within the caOS scheduler.
CA_ST_TH_SUSPENDED.notes: When this bit is set in a task's status register, the scheduler will ignore the task during context switching, effectively pausing its execution. This flag is independent of the task's priority level. It is typically used in conjunction with other state flags (like CA_ST_TH_READY) to determine the task's lifecycle. Valid values are strictly defined by the bitmask 0x100.
CA_ST_TH_SUSPENDED.usage: Use this flag when you need to manually pause a background task (e.g., a data logger or communication handler) without deleting it from memory. You should change this value only when interacting directly with the task control block (TCB) status field. Warning: improperly setting this flag on a critical system task can lead to system deadlocks or watchdog resets if the task is responsible for clearing hardware interrupts.

CA_ST_TH_UNKNOW.brief: Represents the initial state of a task that has been created but not yet assigned a valid execution state by the scheduler.
CA_ST_TH_UNKNOW.notes: This constant is used as a placeholder in the Task Control Block (TCB). When a task is initialized, its state is set to CA_ST_TH_UNKNOW until the scheduler performs the first context switch or state transition. It is a reserved internal value and should not be manually assigned to a task state variable by the application code.
CA_ST_TH_UNKNOW.usage: This value is used internally by the caOS kernel during the task creation process. Do not modify this value or use it in your application logic, as it is intended for kernel-level state tracking. Changing this value will likely cause the scheduler to crash or behave unpredictably during task initialization.

CA_TASK_HANDLE_NONE.brief: A sentinel value representing an invalid or non-existent task handle.
CA_TASK_HANDLE_NONE.notes: This constant is used to initialize task handle variables before a task is created or to indicate that a lookup operation failed. It is defined as 0xFFFFFFFFU, which is an unsigned 32-bit integer representing all bits set to high. It is a system-wide constant and should not be modified, as internal kernel functions rely on this specific value to perform null-pointer-like checks for task objects.
CA_TASK_HANDLE_NONE.usage: Use this value to initialize your task handle variables (e.g., TaskHandle_t myTask = CA_TASK_HANDLE_NONE;) to ensure they do not point to valid memory before the task is actually created. Always compare your task handles against this constant after calling task creation functions to verify if the task was successfully initialized. Never assign this value to a running task, as it will cause the scheduler to lose track of the task's control block.

CA_TCP_GONE.brief: Return value of ca_tcp_send(): final failure, the handle is stale or the connection is not ESTABLISHED (value -1).
CA_TCP_GONE.notes: Also returned when len would need more than TCP_MAX_INFLIGHT segments. Because it is -1 it is truthy: 'if (!ca_tcp_send(...))' misses it. It is a ca_tcp_send() outcome, not a socket handle value (TCP handles are u8, 0 = invalid).
CA_TCP_GONE.usage: On CA_TCP_GONE stop sending on the handle and close it with ca_tcp_close().

CA_TCP_HDR_LEN.brief: Calculates the length of the TCP header in bytes based on the data offset field.
CA_TCP_HDR_LEN.notes: This macro extracts the 4-bit data offset field from the TCP header, which represents the number of 32-bit words in the header, and multiplies it by 4 to convert it into bytes. It depends on the 'tcp' pointer being valid and pointing to a structure containing the 'data_off' field. The result is typically between 20 and 60 bytes.
CA_TCP_HDR_LEN.usage: Use this macro when parsing incoming TCP packets to determine where the actual payload data begins. Do not modify the calculation logic unless the underlying TCP structure definition changes, as this follows standard RFC 793 header formatting.

CA_TCP_PAYLOAD.brief: A macro that calculates the memory address where the TCP payload data begins within a received packet buffer.
CA_TCP_PAYLOAD.notes: This constant performs pointer arithmetic by adding the TCP header length to the base address of the TCP segment. It depends on the CA_TCP_HDR_LEN macro, which parses the Data Offset field in the TCP header. It is used exclusively for accessing the application-layer data following the TCP header.
CA_TCP_PAYLOAD.usage: Use this macro whenever you need to extract or process the payload of a TCP packet. Do not manually calculate offsets, as TCP headers have variable lengths due to optional fields. Incorrect usage or passing a null pointer to this macro will result in a memory access violation or a hard fault on the STM32.

CA_TCP_RETRY.brief: Return value of ca_tcp_send(): transient refusal, nothing was sent (value 0).
CA_TCP_RETRY.notes: Not enough inflight slots or buffers for the whole buffer, so ca_tcp_send() queued none of it (all or nothing). The connection is still usable. It is not a retransmission count and has nothing to do with TCP retries on the wire.
CA_TCP_RETRY.usage: On CA_TCP_RETRY wait with ca_tcp_wait_writable(h, timeout_ms) and call ca_tcp_send() again with the same data.

CA_TCP_SENT.brief: Return value of ca_tcp_send(): the whole buffer was queued for transmission (value 1).
CA_TCP_SENT.notes: One of the three ca_tcp_send() outcomes, with CA_TCP_RETRY (0) and CA_TCP_GONE (-1). It is not a configuration flag. Always compare the result against CA_TCP_SENT explicitly: a boolean test treats CA_TCP_GONE (-1) as success.
CA_TCP_SENT.usage: if (ca_tcp_send(h, buf, len) != CA_TCP_SENT) { /* RETRY: send again later; GONE: close */ }

CA_TEMP_NO_DTS.brief: A sentinel value representing that the Digital Temperature Sensor (DTS) is not available or failed to provide a valid reading.
CA_TEMP_NO_DTS.notes: This constant is used by the ca_temp driver to indicate an error state or absence of hardware. It is set to -99900 (representing -999.00 degrees, assuming a fixed-point format with two decimal places). When ca_temp_read returns this value, it signifies that the sensor data is invalid or the sensor is disconnected. It is typically checked against the return value of ca_temp_read or ca_temp_read_dts.
CA_TEMP_NO_DTS.usage: Use this constant to validate temperature readings in your application logic. If your code calls ca_temp_read, always compare the result against CA_TEMP_NO_DTS before using the value for control loops or logging. Example: int16_t temp = ca_temp_read(); if (temp == CA_TEMP_NO_DTS) { /* Handle sensor error */ }.

CA_TFTP_NO_ERROR.brief: A sentinel value representing the absence of a TFTP error condition.
CA_TFTP_NO_ERROR.notes: This constant is used within the TFTP service layer to indicate that a packet or operation was processed successfully. It is typically returned by internal parsing or state-machine functions when no protocol-level error (like file not found or access violation) has occurred. It is not a standard TFTP error code defined by RFC 1350, but rather an internal caOS status flag.
CA_TFTP_NO_ERROR.usage: Use this constant when checking the return status of TFTP operations to verify success. Do not modify this value, as it is hardcoded to 0xFFFFU to avoid collision with standard TFTP error codes (0-7). If a function returns this value, it confirms the operation proceeded without protocol errors.
