CA_THID_API.brief: A legacy identifier for tasks that is now deprecated in favor of task handles.
CA_THID_API.notes: This constant represents an integer-based task ID. Enabling or using this flag is discouraged as the system is transitioning to object-oriented handles (ca_task_handle_t). It has no functional dependency on other flags but is marked for removal in future versions of caOS.
CA_THID_API.usage: Do not use this in new code. If you encounter it in legacy projects, refactor the code to use the corresponding '_handle' API functions instead. Using this constant will trigger compiler warnings, indicating that your code is using an outdated and potentially unsafe method for task identification.

CA_TH_LEVEL0.brief: Defines the priority level for the lowest-priority background task in the caOS scheduler.
CA_TH_LEVEL0.notes: This constant sets the base priority index for system tasks. Increasing this value shifts the priority floor of the scheduler. It must be compatible with the CA_MAX_PRIORITY constant; if set higher than the maximum allowed priority, the scheduler will fail to initialize. Typical values are 0 or 1 depending on whether the system reserves level 0 for the idle task.
CA_TH_LEVEL0.usage: Change this value when you need to adjust the task hierarchy or reserve specific priority slots for critical system processes. Use caution: setting this too high may starve lower-priority background tasks or cause priority inversion if not carefully balanced with other task priorities.

CA_TH_LEVEL1.brief: Defines the priority level for the highest-tier real-time tasks in the caOS scheduler.
CA_TH_LEVEL1.notes: This constant sets the numerical priority value for Level 1 tasks. Lower numerical values typically represent higher urgency in caOS. Changing this affects task preemption behavior. It must be configured consistently across all task definitions to avoid priority inversion or scheduling conflicts. Valid range is typically 0 to (CA_MAX_PRIORITY - 1).
CA_TH_LEVEL1.usage: Modify this value when you need to adjust the relative importance of critical system tasks compared to background processes. Increase this value if you need to create more priority tiers above it, or decrease it to reserve higher priority slots for kernel-level operations. Warning: setting this too low may cause critical tasks to be preempted by lower-priority threads, leading to system instability or missed deadlines.

CA_TH_LEVEL2.brief: Defines the maximum number of priority levels available for tasks in the caOS scheduler.
CA_TH_LEVEL2.notes: This constant sets the depth of the priority bitmask. Increasing this value allows for more granular task scheduling but consumes additional RAM for the ready-list structures. It must be a power of 2 or a multiple of 4 depending on the architecture implementation. Typical values range from 4 to 32.
CA_TH_LEVEL2.usage: Increase this value if your application requires more than 4 distinct priority levels to manage complex task preemption. Decrease it to save memory if your system only uses a few tasks. Setting this value too high without sufficient RAM will cause heap allocation failures or stack overflows during scheduler initialization.

CA_TH_LEVEL3.brief: Defines the maximum number of priority levels available for tasks in the caOS scheduler.
CA_TH_LEVEL3.notes: This constant sets the size of the ready-list array. Increasing this value allows for more granular task prioritization but consumes more RAM for the scheduler's internal structures. It must be a positive integer; typical values range from 4 to 16 depending on the application complexity. Changing this requires a full project rebuild.
CA_TH_LEVEL3.usage: Increase this value if your application requires more than 8 distinct priority levels to manage task execution order. Decrease it to save memory if your system uses fewer than 8 priorities. Ensure that all task priority assignments remain within the range of 0 to (CA_TH_LEVEL3 - 1) to avoid scheduler errors.

CA_TH_LEVEL4.brief: Defines the maximum number of priority levels available for tasks in the caOS scheduler.
CA_TH_LEVEL4.notes: This constant sets the size of the ready-list array. Increasing this value allows for more granular task prioritization but consumes more RAM for the scheduler's internal structures. It must be a positive integer; typical values range from 8 to 32 depending on the application complexity. Ensure that any task priority assigned in the code does not exceed (CA_TH_LEVEL4 - 1).
CA_TH_LEVEL4.usage: Increase this value if your application requires more than 16 distinct priority levels to manage complex task scheduling. Decrease it to save memory if your project uses fewer than 16 priority levels. Setting this value too low will cause the scheduler to ignore or fault on tasks assigned higher priority indices.

CA_TH_LEVEL5.brief: Defines the maximum number of priority levels available for tasks in the caOS scheduler.
CA_TH_LEVEL5.notes: This constant sets the upper bound for task priority assignment. Increasing this value expands the scheduler's granularity but consumes more RAM for the ready-list structures. It must be a positive integer, typically a power of two or a multiple of 8 depending on the underlying bitmask implementation. Ensure this value is consistent across all modules to prevent scheduler overflow errors.
CA_TH_LEVEL5.usage: Increase this value if your application requires more than 32 distinct priority levels to manage complex task preemption. Decrease it to save memory if your system uses fewer than 32 tasks. Warning: setting this value too high without sufficient system memory can lead to heap exhaustion or stack corruption during scheduler initialization.

CA_TH_LEVEL6.brief: Defines the maximum number of concurrent threads allowed in the caOS scheduler.
CA_TH_LEVEL6.notes: This constant sets the size of the internal thread control block (TCB) array. Increasing this value allows for more tasks but consumes more static RAM. It must be greater than or equal to the total number of tasks defined in your application. If set too low, the system will fail to register additional tasks during initialization.
CA_TH_LEVEL6.usage: Adjust this value when your application requires more or fewer tasks than the current limit. Ensure that the total RAM usage remains within the STM32 memory constraints. Do not set this value excessively high to avoid wasting precious SRAM on unused TCB slots.

CA_TIMER_INVALID.brief: A sentinel value representing an uninitialized or invalid software timer handle.
CA_TIMER_INVALID.notes: This constant is used as a null-pointer equivalent for timer objects. When a timer is not active or has failed to initialize, the system assigns this value to the handle. It is typically defined as 0, and any function attempting to operate on a timer with this value will return an error code or trigger a safety assertion.
CA_TIMER_INVALID.usage: Use this constant to check if a timer has been successfully created before attempting to start, stop, or delete it. Always initialize your timer handle variables to CA_TIMER_INVALID upon declaration to prevent accidental operations on uninitialized memory. Do not manually assign 0 to a timer handle; always use this constant for code readability and maintainability.

CA_TIMER_MAX.brief: Defines the maximum number of software timers that can be active simultaneously in the system.
CA_TIMER_MAX.notes: This constant determines the size of the static memory pool allocated for software timer control blocks. Increasing this value consumes more RAM (sizeof(ca_timer_t) * CA_TIMER_MAX). It must be set to a value greater than or equal to the total number of timers initialized in your application. If the system attempts to create more timers than this limit, the creation function will return an error code.
CA_TIMER_MAX.usage: Increase this value if your application requires more concurrent software timers than the current limit. Decrease it to save RAM if your application uses fewer timers than the default. Ensure that the value is sufficient for all modules in your project, as setting it too low will cause timer initialization failures at runtime.

CA_TIMER_TASK_PRIO.brief: Defines the priority level for the internal software timer management task in caOS.
CA_TIMER_TASK_PRIO.notes: This constant sets the RTOS task priority for the timer service. A lower numerical value typically indicates a lower priority in caOS. It depends on the total number of available priority levels defined in the kernel. Valid range is usually 0 to (CA_MAX_PRIO - 1).
CA_TIMER_TASK_PRIO.usage: Increase this value if timer callbacks are being delayed by other tasks, or decrease it if timer processing is starving critical system tasks. Ensure this priority is higher than non-critical background tasks but lower than hardware interrupt-driven tasks to maintain system stability.

CA_TIMER_TASK_STACK.brief: Defines the stack size in bytes allocated for the software timer management task.
CA_TIMER_TASK_STACK.notes: This constant determines the memory footprint of the internal timer service thread. If set too low, the system will trigger a stack overflow exception during timer callback execution. If set too high, it wastes precious RAM. The default value of 512 bytes is typically sufficient for basic timer operations, but must be increased if timer callbacks perform complex logic, use large local variables, or call nested functions.
CA_TIMER_TASK_STACK.usage: Increase this value if you encounter hard fault exceptions or stack overflow errors when the software timer task is active. You should only change this if your application-specific timer callbacks are complex or require significant stack space. Always monitor stack usage using the RTOS debug tools after modifying this value to ensure it remains within safe limits.

CA_UDP_MAX_PORTS.brief: Defines the maximum number of concurrent UDP sockets allowed in the system.
CA_UDP_MAX_PORTS.notes: This constant determines the size of the internal UDP port allocation table. Increasing this value consumes more RAM for socket control blocks. It must be greater than 0 and is typically constrained by the available heap memory. If this limit is reached, subsequent attempts to open a UDP socket will return an error code.
CA_UDP_MAX_PORTS.usage: Increase this value if your application requires more simultaneous UDP communication channels (e.g., multiple network services or data streams). Decrease it to save RAM if your application only uses a few ports. Ensure that the total number of ports does not exceed the system's memory capacity to avoid allocation failures.

CA_UDP_PAYLOAD.brief: A pointer calculation macro that identifies the starting memory address of the UDP payload data within a received frame.
CA_UDP_PAYLOAD.notes: This constant calculates the offset by adding the size of the ca_udp_frame_t header structure to the base address of the UDP packet. It is a read-only pointer arithmetic operation. It depends entirely on the structure definition of ca_udp_frame_t; if the header size changes, this macro automatically adjusts. It is used exclusively within the network stack's packet processing layer.
CA_UDP_PAYLOAD.usage: Use this macro whenever you need to access the actual data (payload) contained in a UDP packet after the header has been parsed. Do not modify this definition unless you are modifying the underlying network protocol header structure. Incorrect usage or manual pointer arithmetic instead of using this macro can lead to memory corruption or buffer overflows if the offset is calculated incorrectly.

CA_UPY_NAME_MAX.brief: Defines the maximum allowed length (in bytes) for MicroPython thread names within the caOS environment.
CA_UPY_NAME_MAX.notes: This constant sets the buffer size for storing task names used by the MicroPython integration. Increasing this value consumes more RAM per thread object. It is a fixed-size allocation, so it does not depend on other flags, but it directly impacts the memory footprint of the MicroPython task management system. The default value is 256 bytes.
CA_UPY_NAME_MAX.usage: Adjust this value if you need longer descriptive names for your MicroPython threads for debugging or logging purposes. If you encounter memory allocation errors when spawning many MicroPython threads, consider reducing this value to save RAM. Ensure the value is large enough to accommodate your naming convention; otherwise, names will be truncated.

CA_UPY_OBJ_EVENT.brief: Defines the event type identifier for MicroPython object-related notifications within caOS.
CA_UPY_OBJ_EVENT.notes: This constant is used by the caOS MicroPython bridge to categorize internal events. A value of 3 specifically maps to object-based event signaling. It is a static configuration flag and should not be modified unless you are modifying the core caOS-MicroPython integration layer. It does not have direct dependencies on other hardware flags but is essential for the correct routing of events between the RTOS and the MicroPython VM.
CA_UPY_OBJ_EVENT.usage: Do not change this value. It is used internally by the ca_upy_* API to distinguish between different event types (e.g., semaphores, queues, or object signals). If you are implementing a new MicroPython-accessible feature, use this constant when calling ca_event_set or ca_event_wait to ensure the event is correctly identified by the MicroPython event loop.

CA_UPY_OBJ_MUTEX.brief: Defines the maximum number of concurrent mutexes available for MicroPython objects in caOS.
CA_UPY_OBJ_MUTEX.notes: This constant sets the capacity of the internal mutex pool used by the MicroPython integration layer. When set to 4, the system can track up to 4 active mutexes simultaneously for Python-level objects. If this limit is reached, further attempts to create or lock new MicroPython-managed mutexes will fail. This value is static and consumes memory at compile time.
CA_UPY_OBJ_MUTEX.usage: Increase this value if your MicroPython scripts encounter 'mutex full' or 'resource unavailable' errors when managing multiple concurrent tasks or shared resources. Decrease it to save RAM if your application uses fewer than 4 mutexes. Ensure the value is sufficient for the total number of concurrent objects requiring synchronization in your Python code.

CA_UPY_OBJ_QUEUE.brief: Enables the MicroPython object queue interface for inter-thread communication.
CA_UPY_OBJ_QUEUE.notes: When set to 1, this flag enables the ca_upy_obj_queue functionality, allowing MicroPython scripts to interact with caOS queues. It requires the ca_queue_* subsystem to be initialized. Disabling this (0) removes the associated API functions from the MicroPython environment, reducing the binary footprint.
CA_UPY_OBJ_QUEUE.usage: Enable this when your MicroPython application needs to exchange data objects or messages with native C tasks running in caOS. If your project does not use MicroPython or does not require cross-language task synchronization, set this to 0 to save memory.

CA_UPY_OBJ_SEM.brief: Defines the internal object type identifier for a semaphore within the MicroPython integration layer.
CA_UPY_OBJ_SEM.notes: This constant is used by the caOS MicroPython bridge to distinguish semaphore objects from other object types (like queues or events) in the internal registry. It is typically used as a parameter for object management functions. The value '2' is a hardcoded internal enumeration index; changing this value will break the ability of the MicroPython interpreter to correctly identify and interact with semaphore objects created via ca_upy_obj_new.
CA_UPY_OBJ_SEM.usage: Do not change this value. It is an internal constant required for the correct dispatching of MicroPython API calls (such as ca_upy_sem_take or ca_upy_sem_give) to the underlying caOS semaphore implementation. If you are adding new object types to the MicroPython bridge, ensure they use a unique identifier that does not conflict with this value.

CA_UPY_O_ALWAYS.brief: Forces the MicroPython environment to remain active regardless of task state.
CA_UPY_O_ALWAYS.notes: When enabled (0x10), the caOS MicroPython subsystem ignores standard power-saving or idle-suspend signals. This flag is typically used in conjunction with other ca_upy configuration bits. It ensures the interpreter context is never garbage collected or put to sleep by the scheduler, which is useful for debugging or high-availability scripts. It has no dependencies on other modules but consumes more power by preventing the CPU from entering low-power modes.
CA_UPY_O_ALWAYS.usage: Change this value if your MicroPython scripts are being unexpectedly terminated or if the interpreter is losing state during system idle periods. Warning: Enabling this will significantly increase power consumption and may prevent the system from entering deep sleep modes. Only enable this during development or for critical background services that must never be suspended.

CA_UPY_O_APPEND.brief: Configures the MicroPython file system access mode to append data to existing files.
CA_UPY_O_APPEND.notes: When this flag is enabled (0x30), file operations via ca_upy_fs_open will default to appending data to the end of the file rather than overwriting it. This is a bitmask constant used within the caOS MicroPython abstraction layer. It does not have direct dependencies on other hardware flags but affects the behavior of all file-writing operations in the MicroPython environment.
CA_UPY_O_APPEND.usage: Use this flag when you need to log data or extend existing files without losing previous content. If you do not set this flag, standard write operations may truncate the file. Ensure you are aware of the file pointer position when using this mode to avoid unexpected data corruption.

CA_UPY_O_NEW.brief: A configuration flag used to enable the creation of new MicroPython objects within the caOS environment.
CA_UPY_O_NEW.notes: This constant is typically used as a bitmask or a boolean check within the MicroPython integration layer. When enabled (0x04), it allows the system to allocate and register new objects dynamically. If disabled, attempts to create new objects via the MicroPython interface may be blocked or return an error. It is often used in conjunction with other CA_UPY_* flags to define the capabilities of the MicroPython runtime.
CA_UPY_O_NEW.usage: Change this value if you need to restrict or enable dynamic object creation in your MicroPython scripts. Enable this if you encounter errors when calling ca_upy_obj_new. Ensure that your system has sufficient memory allocated for the MicroPython heap before enabling this, as dynamic object creation can lead to memory fragmentation or exhaustion if not monitored.

CA_UPY_O_READ.brief: Enables read-only access permissions for MicroPython scripts within the caOS environment.
CA_UPY_O_READ.notes: When set to 0x01, the MicroPython interpreter restricts file system operations to read-only mode. This flag is typically used in production builds to prevent scripts from modifying the internal flash or SD card. It does not affect RAM-based operations. Ensure this is disabled (0x00) during development if your scripts need to write logs or configuration files.
CA_UPY_O_READ.usage: Change this value to 0x01 when deploying a final product to ensure system integrity and prevent unauthorized script modifications to the file system. If your application requires runtime data persistence via ca_fat_fwrite, you must keep this flag disabled.

CA_UPY_O_TRUNC.brief: Flag to enable truncation of MicroPython output buffers when they exceed their allocated size.
CA_UPY_O_TRUNC.notes: When CA_UPY_O_TRUNC is enabled (0x08), the system will truncate data instead of returning an error or blocking when the output buffer is full. If disabled, the system typically expects the buffer to have sufficient space or handles overflow via error codes. This flag is used within the ca_upy_* subsystem to manage memory constraints during script execution.
CA_UPY_O_TRUNC.usage: Use this flag when you want to prioritize system stability and prevent MicroPython script crashes due to buffer overflows at the cost of losing the tail end of the output data. Do not use this if data integrity of the entire output stream is critical for your application logic.

CA_UPY_O_WRITE.brief: Flag enabling write access for MicroPython scripts to the caOS filesystem.
CA_UPY_O_WRITE.notes: When enabled (0x02), MicroPython scripts can perform write operations (e.g., fs_write, fs_remove) on the mounted filesystem. If disabled, the filesystem is effectively read-only for MicroPython. This flag is typically used in conjunction with other permission bits in the caOS MicroPython configuration. It has no dependencies on hardware peripherals but requires the ca_fat service to be initialized.
CA_UPY_O_WRITE.usage: Enable this flag only when your application requires MicroPython to save data, logs, or update configuration files on the storage media. Warning: Enabling this flag increases the risk of filesystem corruption if the system loses power during a write operation. Always ensure the filesystem is properly synced using ca_upy_fs_sync after critical write operations.

CA_UPY_PIN_ANALOG.brief: Defines the internal constant value representing the Analog mode for GPIO pins within the MicroPython interface.
CA_UPY_PIN_ANALOG.notes: This constant is used by the ca_upy_pin_init function to configure a hardware pin as an Analog input. It maps to the underlying STM32 GPIO mode register settings. The value 3 is specific to the caOS abstraction layer for MicroPython and should not be modified unless the underlying hardware abstraction layer (HAL) mapping changes.
CA_UPY_PIN_ANALOG.usage: Use this constant when calling ca_upy_pin_init from a MicroPython script or C-level wrapper to set a pin to analog mode (e.g., for ADC sampling). Do not change this value; using an incorrect integer will result in the pin being configured in an invalid or unintended mode, potentially causing hardware conflicts or read errors.

CA_UPY_PIN_IN.brief: Enables or disables the MicroPython GPIO pin input functionality.
CA_UPY_PIN_IN.notes: When set to 1, the caOS MicroPython layer includes support for reading GPIO pin states. When set to 0 (default), this functionality is disabled to save code space and memory. This flag is a compile-time configuration for the caOS MicroPython integration.
CA_UPY_PIN_IN.usage: Change this value to 1 only if your application requires MicroPython scripts to read digital input states from GPIO pins using ca_upy_pin_read. If your project does not use GPIO inputs via MicroPython, keep it at 0 to minimize the firmware footprint.

CA_UPY_PIN_OUT.brief: Enables or disables the GPIO pin control functionality within the MicroPython environment.
CA_UPY_PIN_OUT.notes: When set to 1, the caOS MicroPython layer includes the necessary code to interface with STM32 GPIO pins via ca_upy_pin_init, ca_upy_pin_read, and ca_upy_pin_write. Disabling this (setting to 0) reduces the firmware binary size by excluding pin-related logic. This flag is a compile-time dependency for any MicroPython script attempting to toggle hardware pins.
CA_UPY_PIN_OUT.usage: Set this to 1 if your MicroPython application needs to interact with physical hardware pins (e.g., LEDs, sensors, or actuators). Set to 0 if the application is purely computational or uses only communication peripherals (like UART or I2C) to save flash memory space.

CA_UPY_PULL_DOWN.brief: Configures the internal pull-down resistor state for MicroPython GPIO pins.
CA_UPY_PULL_DOWN.notes: This constant defines the hardware abstraction layer behavior for pin configuration. A value of 2 typically maps to the internal pull-down resistor mode in the STM32 GPIO register configuration. It is used by the ca_upy_pin_init function. Ensure the hardware schematic supports pull-down resistors on the selected pins to avoid floating inputs.
CA_UPY_PULL_DOWN.usage: Change this value when you need to interface with external sensors or switches that require a default logic-low state (pulled to ground). If your circuit already has external pull-down resistors, you may not need to enable this. Incorrect configuration may lead to signal contention or unexpected logic levels if the external circuit expects a different pull state.

CA_UPY_PULL_NONE.brief: Configures a GPIO pin to have no internal pull-up or pull-down resistor.
CA_UPY_PULL_NONE.notes: This constant is used when initializing GPIO pins via ca_upy_pin_init. When set to 0, the pin is left in a high-impedance (floating) state. This is the default behavior for most STM32 GPIO pins after reset. It is mutually exclusive with internal pull-up or pull-down configurations.
CA_UPY_PULL_NONE.usage: Use this value when your external circuit already provides a pull-up or pull-down resistor, or when the pin is connected to an active driver (push-pull output). Using this when no external resistor is present will cause the pin to float, leading to unpredictable logic levels and potential noise-induced interrupts.

CA_UPY_PULL_UP.brief: Enables internal pull-up resistors for GPIO pins used by the MicroPython interface.
CA_UPY_PULL_UP.notes: When set to 1, the system automatically configures the relevant GPIO pins with internal pull-up resistors during initialization. This is typically required for I2C buses or digital inputs that are not externally pulled up. If set to 0, the pins are configured as floating inputs. This flag is a global setting for the caOS MicroPython integration layer.
CA_UPY_PULL_UP.usage: Enable this (set to 1) if your hardware design lacks external pull-up resistors on the pins connected to MicroPython peripherals (like I2C or buttons) to prevent floating states. Disable it (set to 0) if you have external pull-up resistors on your PCB to avoid signal contention or unnecessary power consumption.

CA_UPY_SEM_WORDS.brief: Defines the maximum number of words (32-bit units) allowed for a MicroPython semaphore object structure.
CA_UPY_SEM_WORDS.notes: This constant determines the memory footprint allocated for each semaphore created within the MicroPython environment. A value of 16 means 64 bytes per semaphore. Increasing this value allows for more complex semaphore metadata or internal tracking, while decreasing it saves RAM. It is a static allocation limit used by the caOS MicroPython bridge.
CA_UPY_SEM_WORDS.usage: Adjust this value only if you encounter memory allocation errors when creating semaphores in MicroPython or if you need to extend the internal structure of the semaphore object. Do not set this value too low, as it may cause buffer overflows or initialization failures for the semaphore objects.

CA_UPY_SOCK_TCP.brief: Enables TCP socket support within the MicroPython environment.
CA_UPY_SOCK_TCP.notes: When set to 1, the MicroPython interpreter gains access to TCP socket primitives (e.g., ca_upy_sock_connect, ca_upy_sock_send). This flag requires the underlying ca_tcp_* network stack to be initialized and operational. Disabling this (0) reduces the binary footprint by excluding TCP-related MicroPython bindings.
CA_UPY_SOCK_TCP.usage: Enable this flag when your MicroPython scripts need to perform network communication over TCP (e.g., connecting to a remote server or acting as a TCP client). If your application only uses UDP or local communication, you may disable this to save memory. Ensure that the network interface is properly configured before attempting to use these sockets in your scripts.

CA_UPY_SOCK_UDP.brief: Defines the socket type constant for UDP communication within the MicroPython integration layer.
CA_UPY_SOCK_UDP.notes: This constant is used as an identifier for the UDP protocol when calling socket-related functions in the MicroPython environment. It is typically passed to ca_upy_sock_open or similar socket management functions. The value '2' is a fixed internal mapping for the UDP protocol stack in caOS. Changing this value will break network communication for MicroPython scripts relying on UDP sockets.
CA_UPY_SOCK_UDP.usage: Do not change this value. It is a hardcoded protocol identifier required by the caOS MicroPython bridge to correctly route socket requests to the underlying UDP implementation. If you are implementing a new socket-based feature in MicroPython, use this constant to specify the protocol type.

CA_VLAN_PCP.brief: Extracts the 3-bit Priority Code Point (PCP) field from an 802.1Q VLAN Tag Control Information (TCI) field.
CA_VLAN_PCP.notes: This macro performs a bitwise shift and mask operation on a 16-bit TCI value to isolate the priority bits (0-7). It depends on the ca_ntohs macro for network-to-host byte order conversion. The result is always an integer between 0 and 7, where 0 is best-effort and 7 is highest priority.
CA_VLAN_PCP.usage: Use this when implementing Quality of Service (QoS) logic to determine the traffic class of an incoming Ethernet frame. Change this only if the underlying VLAN header structure changes or if you need to mask different bits. Warning: Ensure the input 'tci' is a valid 16-bit VLAN TCI value, otherwise the extracted priority will be garbage data.

CA_VLAN_VID.brief: Extracts the 12-bit Virtual Local Area Network Identifier (VLAN ID) from a 16-bit Tag Control Information (TCI) field.
CA_VLAN_VID.notes: This constant performs a bitwise AND operation with 0x0FFF to mask out the priority and drop-eligible bits, leaving only the VID. It depends on the ca_ntohs macro for network-to-host byte order conversion. The valid range is 0 to 4095, where 0 is typically reserved for priority-tagged frames and 4095 is reserved for implementation use.
CA_VLAN_VID.usage: Use this when parsing Ethernet frames that contain 802.1Q VLAN tags. Change this only if you need to access the priority bits (PCP) or the Drop Eligible Indicator (DEI) instead of the VID. Warning: Incorrectly modifying the mask will result in corrupted VLAN identification, causing the network stack to drop valid packets or misroute traffic to the wrong virtual network.

CA_VNC_NAME_MAX.brief: Defines the maximum length in bytes for the VNC client/server name string.
CA_VNC_NAME_MAX.notes: This constant sets the buffer size for storing the VNC connection name. It is used internally by the VNC protocol stack to allocate memory for identification strings. Increasing this value will increase the memory footprint of the VNC service structures. The default value is 32 bytes.
CA_VNC_NAME_MAX.usage: Change this value if you need to support longer VNC client names or custom identification strings that exceed 31 characters (plus the null terminator). Ensure that the memory allocated for the VNC service is sufficient to accommodate the new size. If you encounter truncation of VNC client names in your logs or UI, increase this value.

CA_VNC_PASS_MAX.brief: Defines the maximum length in bytes for a VNC authentication password.
CA_VNC_PASS_MAX.notes: This constant sets the buffer size allocated for storing the VNC password string. The value 64U means passwords longer than 63 characters (plus the null terminator) will be truncated. It is used internally by the VNC service to validate and handle authentication requests. Increasing this value will consume more RAM in the VNC service context.
CA_VNC_PASS_MAX.usage: Change this value if your security policy requires longer VNC passwords. Ensure that the memory allocated for the VNC service context is sufficient to accommodate the increased buffer size. If you encounter authentication failures with long passwords, verify that this constant matches the expected length defined in your client-side configuration.

CA_VNC_PIX_L8.brief: Enables or disables 8-bit (L8) pixel format support for the VNC protocol server.
CA_VNC_PIX_L8.notes: When set to 1U, the VNC server includes logic to handle 8-bit indexed color depth. When set to 0U (default), this support is excluded to save code space and memory. This flag is a compile-time configuration and does not have runtime dependencies on other modules, though it affects the memory footprint of the VNC frame buffer handling.
CA_VNC_PIX_L8.usage: Change this value to 1U only if your VNC client requires 8-bit color depth support. If your application uses high-color (16-bit or 24-bit) exclusively, keep it at 0U to optimize the binary size. Incorrectly enabling this without proper palette management in your display driver may lead to corrupted visual output on the VNC client.

CA_VNC_PIX_RGB565.brief: Configures the VNC server to use RGB565 pixel format for screen data transmission.
CA_VNC_PIX_RGB565.notes: When set to 1U, the VNC protocol uses 16-bit RGB565 color depth. Disabling this (0U) typically forces the system to fall back to a different pixel format, such as TrueColor (RGB888). This flag is used by the ca_vnc_* service to determine how to pack pixel data before sending it over the network. It requires the display buffer to be compatible with 16-bit color representation.
CA_VNC_PIX_RGB565.usage: Enable this when your remote VNC client or network bandwidth constraints require a 16-bit color depth. Using RGB565 reduces the amount of data transmitted per pixel compared to 24-bit or 32-bit formats, which can improve performance on low-bandwidth connections. Ensure your display driver or framebuffer is configured to handle 16-bit color data before enabling this flag.

CA_VNC_SEC_NONE.brief: Defines the VNC security level as 'None', meaning no authentication or encryption is used.
CA_VNC_SEC_NONE.notes: When this flag is set, the VNC server will accept connections without requiring a password or performing a TLS handshake. This is typically used for debugging in isolated, trusted networks. It is mutually exclusive with other security flags like CA_VNC_SEC_TLS or CA_VNC_SEC_AUTH.
CA_VNC_SEC_NONE.usage: Use this only during initial development or testing phases where network security is not a concern. Never use this in production environments, as it exposes the VNC stream to unauthorized access and eavesdropping. If you need to secure the connection, switch to a flag that enables encryption or authentication.

CA_VNC_SEC_VENCRYPT.brief: Defines the security type identifier for the VeNCrypt authentication mechanism in the VNC protocol.
CA_VNC_SEC_VENCRYPT.notes: This constant is used within the VNC handshake process to negotiate security types. A value of 19U corresponds to the VeNCrypt security type (SecurityType 19). It is typically used in conjunction with ca_vnc_proto_init and related VNC service functions. It does not have direct dependencies on other flags but must match the expected security type defined by the VNC client.
CA_VNC_SEC_VENCRYPT.usage: Change this value only if you are implementing a custom security handshake or if the VNC client requires a different security type identifier. Do not modify this value unless you are modifying the underlying VNC protocol implementation, as incorrect values will cause the VNC handshake to fail immediately.

CA_VNC_USER_MAX.brief: Defines the maximum number of concurrent users allowed to connect to the VNC server.
CA_VNC_USER_MAX.notes: This constant sets the upper limit for the internal VNC session table. Increasing this value consumes more RAM as the system allocates memory for each potential user session. It is a static limit; if the number of active connections reaches this value, new connection attempts will be rejected by the VNC service. The default value is 32U.
CA_VNC_USER_MAX.usage: Adjust this value based on your application's memory constraints and the expected number of simultaneous remote viewers. If your system has limited RAM, decrease this value to save memory. If you require more concurrent remote access sessions, increase it, but ensure your heap memory can accommodate the additional session structures.

CA_VNC_VENCRYPT_X509NONE.brief: Defines the VNC security flag for disabling X.509 certificate authentication.
CA_VNC_VENCRYPT_X509NONE.notes: This constant is used within the VNC protocol handshake to indicate that no X.509 certificate validation is required. When enabled, the connection proceeds without verifying the server's identity via certificates. It is typically used in internal or trusted network environments where encryption is handled by other means or where authentication is not required at the TLS layer.
CA_VNC_VENCRYPT_X509NONE.usage: Use this value when configuring the VNC service security parameters if your application does not implement certificate-based authentication. Warning: Disabling X.509 validation makes the connection susceptible to Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks. Only use this in secure, isolated, or non-critical network environments.

CA_VNC_VENCRYPT_X509PLAIN.brief: Defines the VNC security type identifier for X509 authentication combined with plain password authentication.
CA_VNC_VENCRYPT_X509PLAIN.notes: This constant is used within the VNC protocol handshake to negotiate security mechanisms. It represents a specific security type (value 262) supported by the caOS VNC server. It is typically used in conjunction with the ca_vnc_* API suite. Ensure that the client connecting to the caOS device is configured to support this specific security handshake, otherwise, the connection will be rejected during the authentication phase.
CA_VNC_VENCRYPT_X509PLAIN.usage: Change this value only if you are modifying the VNC protocol implementation or if you need to switch to a different security handshake supported by the protocol specification. Do not change this value to arbitrary numbers, as it must match the standard VNC security type registry or the specific implementation requirements of your VNC client. If you encounter 'Security Type Not Supported' errors, verify that this constant matches the expected security handshake of your client application.

CA_WAIT_FOREVER.brief: Constant representing infinite wait time for caOS kernel operations
CA_WAIT_FOREVER.notes: When used as a timeout parameter, CA_WAIT_FOREVER causes threads to wait indefinitely until the requested resource becomes available. This value is a 32-bit unsigned integer set to maximum value (4294967295). It has no dependencies on other flags but requires proper thread management to avoid system deadlocks. Valid range is 0 to 0xFFFFFFFFU, where 0 means no wait and 0xFFFFFFFFU means infinite wait.
CA_WAIT_FOREVER.usage: Use CA_WAIT_FOREVER when you want a thread to block indefinitely until a condition is met, such as waiting for a semaphore, mutex, or message queue. Common in critical sections where timing is not critical. Warning: excessive use can cause system deadlocks if not properly managed, and may prevent proper system shutdown sequences. Avoid using in time-critical applications where timeout behavior is required.

CA_WDT_BKP_GASP.brief: Defines the number of backup registers reserved for storing 'last gasp' diagnostic data during a watchdog reset.
CA_WDT_BKP_GASP.notes: This constant determines the size of the memory buffer used by the watchdog driver to save system state information before a hard reset occurs. It relies on the hardware backup register availability (ca_bkp_*). The value 12U indicates that 12 registers are allocated. Increasing this value allows for more detailed crash logs but consumes more non-volatile backup storage.
CA_WDT_BKP_GASP.usage: Change this value only if you need to store more or less diagnostic data during a watchdog event. If you encounter issues where crash logs are truncated or if you need to free up backup registers for other application-specific purposes, adjust this value. Ensure the value does not exceed the total number of available backup registers on the specific STM32 target.

CA_WDT_TIMEOUT_MIN_MS.brief: Defines the minimum allowed watchdog timeout duration in milliseconds.
CA_WDT_TIMEOUT_MIN_MS.notes: This constant acts as a safety floor for the watchdog timer configuration. If a requested timeout is lower than this value, the driver will enforce this minimum to prevent accidental system resets due to extremely short watchdog windows. It is typically set to 1ms. It is used by the ca_wdt_init function during hardware initialization.
CA_WDT_TIMEOUT_MIN_MS.usage: Change this value only if your specific hardware or application requirements demand a higher safety margin for the watchdog timer. Increasing this value prevents the system from being configured with a watchdog timeout that is too aggressive, which could lead to spurious resets if the CPU is momentarily busy. Do not set this to 0, as it may cause undefined behavior in the watchdog reload logic.

CHACHA20POLY1305_KEY_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed length in bytes of the secret key used for ChaCha20-Poly1305 authenticated encryption.
CHACHA20POLY1305_KEY_SIZE.notes: The value is set to 32 bytes (256 bits), which is the standard key size for the ChaCha20 algorithm. This constant is used by ca_chacha20poly1305 functions to validate input buffers and allocate memory for key storage. Changing this value will cause cryptographic operations to fail or produce incompatible results with standard implementations.
CHACHA20POLY1305_KEY_SIZE.usage: Do not change this value. It is hardcoded to 32 to ensure compliance with the ChaCha20-Poly1305 specification. If you are implementing a new encryption routine, ensure your key buffer is exactly this size before calling ca_chacha20poly1305_encrypt or ca_chacha20poly1305_decrypt.

CHACHA20POLY1305_NONCE_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed length in bytes of the nonce used for ChaCha20Poly1305 encryption.
CHACHA20POLY1305_NONCE_SIZE.notes: This constant is set to 12 bytes, which is the standard size for the IETF variant of the ChaCha20Poly1305 algorithm. Changing this value will cause incompatibility with standard cryptographic implementations and will likely cause ca_chacha20poly1305_encrypt_ietf and ca_chacha20poly1305_decrypt_ietf to fail or produce invalid results. It is a hardcoded requirement for the internal buffer allocations of the AEAD operations.
CHACHA20POLY1305_NONCE_SIZE.usage: Do not change this value unless you are implementing a non-standard protocol variant that explicitly requires a different nonce length. If you are using the standard ca_chacha20poly1305 API, always use this constant to size your nonce buffers to prevent memory overflows or cryptographic errors.

CHACHA20POLY1305_TAG_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed length in bytes of the authentication tag for ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD operations.
CHACHA20POLY1305_TAG_SIZE.notes: This constant is set to 16 bytes, which is the standard tag size for the ChaCha20-Poly1305 algorithm. It is used by ca_chacha20poly1305_{encrypt,decrypt} functions to verify data integrity. Changing this value will cause authentication failures with standard-compliant implementations and is not recommended.
CHACHA20POLY1305_TAG_SIZE.usage: This value should not be changed for standard applications. It is used to allocate buffers for the authentication tag. If you are implementing a custom protocol that requires a truncated tag (not recommended for security reasons), ensure both the sender and receiver are configured with the exact same non-standard size.

CHACHA20_BLOCK_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed size in bytes of a single ChaCha20 cipher block.
CHACHA20_BLOCK_SIZE.notes: The ChaCha20 algorithm operates on 64-byte blocks. This constant is used internally by ca_chacha20 functions to manage buffer alignment and state transitions. It is a fixed architectural requirement of the ChaCha20 specification and should not be modified. Changing this value will break the cryptographic implementation and cause data corruption.
CHACHA20_BLOCK_SIZE.usage: This value is used for static buffer allocation when preparing data for encryption or decryption. If you are implementing a streaming cipher using ca_chacha20_init, ensure your input buffers are multiples of this block size for optimal performance, or handle the remaining bytes using the internal state management provided by the ca_chacha20 API.

CHACHA20_KEY_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed length in bytes for the ChaCha20 encryption key.
CHACHA20_KEY_SIZE.notes: This constant is set to 32 bytes (256 bits), which is the standard key size for the ChaCha20 algorithm. Changing this value will cause the ca_chacha20_init function to fail or produce incorrect cryptographic results, as the algorithm strictly requires a 256-bit key.
CHACHA20_KEY_SIZE.usage: Do not change this value. It is a protocol-defined constant required for compatibility with standard ChaCha20 implementations. If you need to handle different key sizes, you must use a Key Derivation Function (KDF) like ca_hkdf_sha256 to derive a 32-byte key from your input material before passing it to ca_chacha20_init.

CHACHA20_NONCE_SIZE.brief: Defines the length in bytes of the nonce used by the ChaCha20 cryptographic algorithm.
CHACHA20_NONCE_SIZE.notes: This constant is set to 12 bytes (96 bits), which is the standard size for the IETF variant of ChaCha20. Changing this value will break compatibility with standard ChaCha20 implementations and may cause the ca_chacha20poly1305_decrypt_ietf and ca_chacha20poly1305_encrypt_ietf functions to fail or produce incorrect results. It is a fixed protocol requirement.
CHACHA20_NONCE_SIZE.usage: Do not change this value unless you are implementing a non-standard or custom cryptographic protocol that explicitly requires a different nonce length. For standard IETF ChaCha20 operations, keep this at 12. If you need to perform encryption, ensure your nonce buffer matches this size: uint8_t nonce[CHACHA20_NONCE_SIZE];

CH_CMD.brief: Enables the command-line interface (CLI) module within the caOS RTOS.
CH_CMD.notes: When set to 0x01U, the system initializes the CLI task and command parser. Disabling it (0x00U) removes the CLI functionality, reducing flash memory usage and freeing up CPU cycles. This flag depends on the UART driver being correctly configured in the hardware abstraction layer.
CH_CMD.usage: Enable this during the development and debugging phase to interact with the system via a serial terminal. Disable it in production builds to save memory and prevent unauthorized access to system commands. Ensure the UART baud rate and buffer sizes are configured correctly before enabling.

CH_ERASE.brief: A bitmask flag used by the CLI module to enable the automatic clearing of the terminal screen buffer upon command execution.
CH_ERASE.notes: When enabled, the system sends ANSI escape sequences to clear the console before printing output. It depends on the terminal emulator supporting standard ANSI codes. The value 0x04U is a bitmask, meaning it can be combined with other CLI configuration flags using the bitwise OR operator.
CH_ERASE.usage: Enable this flag if you want a clean terminal interface for each command response to improve readability. Disable it if you need to maintain a scrollable history of previous command outputs. Ensure your serial terminal software (e.g., PuTTY, Tera Term) is configured to interpret ANSI escape sequences, otherwise, you will see raw characters like '[2J' printed on your screen.

CH_ESC.brief: Defines the ASCII character code for the Escape key used to terminate or cancel command-line interface (CLI) operations.
CH_ESC.notes: This constant sets the byte value (0x08U, which corresponds to Backspace/Control-H in standard ASCII) that the CLI parser interprets as an interrupt or exit signal. Changing this value requires the terminal emulator sending the commands to be configured to send the same byte. It is a dependency for the CLI input buffer clearing logic.
CH_ESC.usage: Modify this value only if your specific terminal emulator or serial console uses a different control character for the 'Escape' or 'Cancel' function. Setting this to an incorrect value will cause the CLI to ignore exit commands, potentially leaving the system stuck in an active command state.

CH_NONE.brief: Disables the Command Line Interface (CLI) module in the caOS system.
CH_NONE.notes: When set to 0x00U, the CLI functionality is active. If set to a non-zero value, the CLI code is excluded from the build, reducing flash memory usage. This flag is independent of the RTOS kernel but may be required by other debug modules.
CH_NONE.usage: Set this to 0x01U (or any non-zero value) if your final production firmware does not require serial console interaction to save memory. Keep it at 0x00U during development to allow for system monitoring and runtime debugging via the serial port.

CH_SUBMIT.brief: A bitmask flag used by the CLI module to enable the submission of commands via the serial interface.
CH_SUBMIT.notes: When this bit is set in the CLI configuration register, the system processes incoming character buffers as executable commands. If disabled, the CLI will ignore input strings. It depends on the CLI_ENABLED flag being set to 1. The value 0x02U specifically targets the submission sub-routine within the command parser.
CH_SUBMIT.usage: Enable this flag when you need to allow users to trigger system functions or configuration changes via the terminal. Disable it in production builds to prevent unauthorized command execution or to save processing cycles if the CLI is only used for monitoring.

CH_TYPO.brief: Defines the ASCII character code used by the CLI to represent a detected input error or mistyped command.
CH_TYPO.notes: This constant sets the internal error character for the command line interface. It must be a valid, printable ASCII value. If set to a value already used by a valid command, the CLI may trigger false error reports. Typical values are in the range 0x00 to 0x7F.
CH_TYPO.usage: Change this value if the default 0x10 conflicts with your specific terminal emulator or if you need to reserve 0x10 for a functional command. Ensure the value is not a control character that could disrupt the serial communication stream.

CLI_HISTORY_SIZE.brief: Defines the maximum number of previous commands stored in the CLI buffer for recall.
CLI_HISTORY_SIZE.notes: This constant determines the depth of the command history stack. Increasing this value consumes more RAM, as each entry occupies a fixed-size buffer. It is independent of the command string length but directly impacts the number of 'up-arrow' key presses supported. Typical values range from 8 to 32 depending on available heap memory.
CLI_HISTORY_SIZE.usage: Increase this value if you need to navigate back through a longer sequence of executed commands during debugging. Decrease it if the system is running low on RAM. Ensure the value is a positive integer; setting it to 0 will disable the history feature entirely.

CLI_PRINTF_N.brief: A macro wrapper for the Command Line Interface (CLI) that directs formatted output to the system's standard output stream.
CLI_PRINTF_N.notes: This constant maps the CLI_PRINTF_N macro to the internal ca_stdout_printf_n function. Enabling this allows the CLI to send strings to the UART or console buffer. It depends on the underlying hardware abstraction layer (HAL) being initialized for UART/USB-CDC. If this is undefined or points to a null function, CLI commands will produce no visible output.
CLI_PRINTF_N.usage: Change this value if you need to redirect CLI output to a different peripheral (e.g., switching from UART1 to UART2) or if you need to implement a custom logging wrapper for debugging. Warning: Ensure the underlying print function is thread-safe, as multiple tasks may attempt to write to the CLI simultaneously, which could lead to garbled text or system crashes if not protected by a mutex.

CLI_PUT_N.brief: A macro that defines the output function used by the caOS Command Line Interface to send strings to the serial console.
CLI_PUT_N.notes: This constant maps the CLI output to a specific hardware abstraction layer function. Enabling or changing this allows the CLI to redirect its output to different peripherals like UART, ITM, or a memory buffer. It depends on the availability of the underlying 'ca_stdout_put_n' function implementation in your board support package.
CLI_PUT_N.usage: Change this value when porting the CLI to a new hardware target or when you need to redirect debug logs to a different communication interface. Ensure the function assigned is non-blocking or properly synchronized to prevent system hangs during high-frequency CLI output.

CLI_QUEUE_DEPTH.brief: Defines the maximum number of pending command strings the CLI task can buffer before dropping new input.
CLI_QUEUE_DEPTH.notes: This constant sets the size of the internal message queue for the Command Line Interface. Increasing this value consumes more RAM (Queue Size * Max Command Length). It is dependent on the available heap memory and the expected burst rate of incoming commands. Typical values range from 8 to 32 depending on the MCU's RAM capacity.
CLI_QUEUE_DEPTH.usage: Increase this value if you notice 'CLI Buffer Overflow' errors or dropped commands during high-frequency serial communication. Decrease it if the system is running low on RAM. Ensure the value is set according to the specific MCU target to avoid memory exhaustion.

CONSOLE_RX_BUF_SIZE.brief: Defines the size in bytes of the internal receive buffer for the system console.
CONSOLE_RX_BUF_SIZE.notes: This constant allocates a static memory area used to store incoming characters from the console interface before they are processed. Increasing this value allows the system to handle larger bursts of incoming data without dropping characters, but it directly increases the RAM footprint of the OS. The default value is 256 bytes. It is typically used by the ca_console_* API to manage serial input flow.
CONSOLE_RX_BUF_SIZE.usage: Increase this value if you notice dropped characters or 'buffer overflow' errors during high-speed serial communication or when pasting large blocks of text into the CLI. Decrease it only if your system is extremely constrained on RAM and the console traffic is minimal. Ensure the value is a power of two if the underlying driver implementation uses circular buffer optimizations.

DEEP_GUARD_MAX.brief: Defines the maximum size in bytes for the stack overflow protection guard zone.
DEEP_GUARD_MAX.notes: This constant sets the memory boundary used by the RTOS to detect stack corruption. Increasing this value provides a larger safety buffer for detecting overflows but consumes more RAM. It is hardware-dependent: F4 series MCUs typically use 0x2000U, while high-performance H7 series require 0x8000U due to larger cache and memory alignment requirements.
DEEP_GUARD_MAX.usage: Adjust this value if you encounter HardFaults related to stack overflows or if the system reports memory corruption in task stacks. Do not decrease this value below the manufacturer-recommended default for your specific MCU, as it will disable the RTOS's ability to detect stack violations, potentially leading to silent system crashes.

DHCP_BIND_TIMEOUT_MS.brief: Defines the maximum time in milliseconds the system waits for a DHCP server to assign an IP address.
DHCP_BIND_TIMEOUT_MS.notes: When enabled, the network stack will attempt to acquire an IP for this duration before timing out. If set too low, the device may fail to connect on slow networks. If set too high, the system boot time increases significantly during network failures. Typical values range from 5000 to 60000.
DHCP_BIND_TIMEOUT_MS.usage: Increase this value if the device frequently fails to obtain an IP address in environments with high network latency or slow DHCP servers. Decrease it if you need the device to fall back to a static IP or error state faster during startup.

DHCP_CLIENT_PORT.brief: Defines the UDP port number used by the caOS DHCP client to listen for server responses.
DHCP_CLIENT_PORT.notes: This constant sets the destination port for DHCP discovery and request packets. It must be set to 68U to comply with the standard DHCP protocol (RFC 2131). Changing this value will prevent the device from communicating with standard DHCP servers, as they are hardcoded to send replies to port 68.
DHCP_CLIENT_PORT.usage: This value should generally remain at 68U. Change this only if you are implementing a custom DHCP server or a specialized network simulation environment where the server is configured to listen and respond on a non-standard port.

DHCP_DISCOVER_RETRY_N.brief: Defines the maximum number of DHCP DISCOVER packet retransmission attempts before the network stack reports a failure.
DHCP_DISCOVER_RETRY_N.notes: When enabled, the system will attempt to request an IP address from a DHCP server up to this count. If the server does not respond within the timeout period, the stack stops trying. Increasing this value improves reliability on unstable networks but increases the total time taken to detect a network failure. Typical values range from 3 to 10.
DHCP_DISCOVER_RETRY_N.usage: Increase this value if your device frequently fails to obtain an IP address in environments with high packet loss or slow DHCP servers. Decrease it if you need the system to fail fast and proceed to a fallback static IP configuration or error state more quickly.

DHCP_MSG_ACK.brief: Defines the numeric identifier for the DHCP Acknowledge (DHCPACK) message type.
DHCP_MSG_ACK.notes: This constant represents the specific opcode used in the DHCP protocol to confirm a client's request for an IP address. It is used by the network stack to filter incoming UDP packets. It must remain set to 5U to comply with the standard DHCP protocol (RFC 2131). Changing this value will cause the network stack to fail to recognize server acknowledgments, resulting in failed IP address assignment.
DHCP_MSG_ACK.usage: Do not modify this value under normal circumstances. It should only be changed if you are implementing a custom, non-standard DHCP-like protocol or if the network stack is being ported to a system that uses a proprietary message mapping. Incorrect values will prevent the device from completing the network handshake.

DHCP_MSG_DISCOVER.brief: Defines the message type identifier for a DHCP Discover packet used during the initial network address acquisition phase.
DHCP_MSG_DISCOVER.notes: This constant represents the specific opcode (1) sent by the client to broadcast a request for available DHCP servers. It is a fixed protocol value defined by RFC 2131. Changing this value will cause the DHCP server to ignore the client's discovery requests, effectively breaking the network initialization process.
DHCP_MSG_DISCOVER.usage: This value should never be changed during standard application development. It is used internally by the caOS network stack to construct outgoing DHCP packets. If you are debugging network traffic with a packet sniffer like Wireshark, use this constant to verify that the client is correctly identifying its broadcast messages as 'Discover' packets.

DHCP_MSG_NAK.brief: Defines the DHCP Negative Acknowledgment (NAK) message type identifier used in network communication.
DHCP_MSG_NAK.notes: This constant represents the specific numeric code (6) sent by a DHCP server to inform a client that its requested IP address is invalid or no longer available. It is a protocol-level identifier required for the DHCP state machine to correctly parse incoming UDP packets. It has no configurable range as it is a fixed protocol constant defined by RFC 2131.
DHCP_MSG_NAK.usage: Do not modify this value unless you are implementing a custom or non-standard DHCP protocol extension. Changing this will cause the caOS network stack to fail to recognize NAK messages from standard DHCP servers, potentially leading to infinite loops or connection timeouts during the IP address acquisition phase.

DHCP_MSG_OFFER.brief: Defines the numeric identifier for a DHCP Offer message type within the network stack.
DHCP_MSG_OFFER.notes: This constant represents the specific message type field in a DHCP packet header. It is used by the network parser to distinguish an 'Offer' from other DHCP messages like 'Discover' or 'Request'. It must match the standard DHCP protocol specification (RFC 2131) and should not be modified unless the underlying network stack implementation is being ported to a non-standard protocol.
DHCP_MSG_OFFER.usage: This value is used internally by the caOS network driver to process incoming DHCP packets. You should never change this value during standard application development. Modifying this constant will cause the device to fail to negotiate an IP address with DHCP servers, effectively breaking network connectivity.

DHCP_MSG_REQUEST.brief: Defines the DHCP Request message type identifier used in the network stack.
DHCP_MSG_REQUEST.notes: This constant represents the numeric code (3) sent in the DHCP message type option field. It is a fixed protocol value defined by RFC 2131. Changing this value will cause the DHCP server to ignore or reject the client's request, effectively breaking the IP address assignment process.
DHCP_MSG_REQUEST.usage: This value should never be changed by the developer. It is used internally by the caOS network stack to identify and construct DHCP Request packets. If you are debugging network traffic with a packet sniffer like Wireshark, you can use this constant to verify that the device is correctly identifying its own outgoing request packets.

DHCP_OFFER_TIMEOUT_MS.brief: Defines the maximum time in milliseconds the system waits to receive a DHCP offer from a server.
DHCP_OFFER_TIMEOUT_MS.notes: This constant sets the duration of the blocking wait state during the network initialization phase. If the DHCP server does not respond within this window, the request will time out. It depends on the network stack initialization sequence and should be set higher than the typical round-trip time of your local network infrastructure. Valid range is typically 1000U to 10000U.
DHCP_OFFER_TIMEOUT_MS.usage: Increase this value if your device is failing to obtain an IP address on slow or congested networks. Decrease it if you need the system to fail fast and proceed to a fallback static IP configuration or error state more quickly. Setting this value too low may cause intermittent connection failures in environments with high network latency.

DHCP_RENEW_TIMEOUT_MS.brief: Defines the duration in milliseconds the system waits for a DHCP server response before attempting a renewal retry.
DHCP_RENEW_TIMEOUT_MS.notes: This constant directly impacts the network stack's responsiveness during IP lease renewal. If set too low, the system may trigger unnecessary retries on slow networks; if set too high, it delays recovery from network interruptions. It depends on the underlying network driver's ability to handle asynchronous timeouts. Typical values range from 5000U to 30000U depending on network latency requirements.
DHCP_RENEW_TIMEOUT_MS.usage: Increase this value if the device frequently loses its IP address on congested or high-latency networks. Decrease it only if the application requires faster detection of DHCP server failures. Ensure the value is not set lower than the round-trip time of your network infrastructure to avoid constant, failed renewal loops.

DHCP_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS.brief: Defines the maximum time in milliseconds the system waits for a DHCP server to respond to a request.
DHCP_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS.notes: This constant sets the duration of the blocking wait state during the network initialization phase. If the DHCP server does not respond within this window, the request is considered failed. It depends on the underlying network stack's timer resolution. Typical values range from 2000 to 10000 depending on network latency and reliability.
DHCP_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS.usage: Increase this value if the device fails to obtain an IP address on slow or congested networks. Decrease it if you need the system to fail fast and proceed to a fallback static IP configuration or error state. Setting this too low may cause intermittent connection failures in high-traffic environments.

DHCP_RETRY_BACKOFF_MS.brief: Defines the time interval in milliseconds to wait before retrying a failed DHCP request.
DHCP_RETRY_BACKOFF_MS.notes: This constant controls the delay between consecutive DHCP discovery attempts. Increasing this value reduces network traffic and power consumption during network outages, while decreasing it speeds up reconnection times. It is dependent on the network stack initialization and typically ranges from 1000U to 10000U.
DHCP_RETRY_BACKOFF_MS.usage: Adjust this value if your device takes too long to reconnect after a network drop or if the DHCP server is overloaded. Use a higher value if you are operating on a battery-powered device to minimize radio activity, or a lower value if rapid network availability is critical for your application.

DHCP_SERVER_PORT.brief: Defines the UDP port number used by the caOS DHCP server to listen for client requests.
DHCP_SERVER_PORT.notes: This constant sets the destination port for incoming DHCP discovery and request packets. It must be set to 67U to comply with the standard DHCP protocol (RFC 2131). Changing this value will prevent standard DHCP clients from discovering the server, as they are hardcoded to send requests to port 67.
DHCP_SERVER_PORT.usage: Keep this value at 67U for standard network operations. Only change this if you are implementing a custom, non-standard DHCP-like protocol or if you are running a secondary DHCP server instance on a non-standard port for testing purposes. Incorrect values will result in the server failing to receive any client configuration requests.

DHCP_TASK_STACK_MIN.brief: Defines the minimum stack size in bytes allocated for the DHCP client background task.
DHCP_TASK_STACK_MIN.notes: This value sets the memory footprint for the DHCP task. If set too low, the system will trigger a stack overflow exception during network negotiation. It depends on the underlying network stack's buffer requirements and the complexity of the DHCP options being processed. Typical values range from 1024 to 4096 bytes depending on the RTOS heap configuration.
DHCP_TASK_STACK_MIN.usage: Increase this value if the system crashes or exhibits undefined behavior specifically when the device attempts to acquire an IP address. Decrease it only if you are extremely constrained by RAM and have verified via stack watermarking that the task uses significantly less than 2048 bytes.

DMA_CH_INVALID.brief: A sentinel value representing an uninitialized or invalid DMA channel handle.
DMA_CH_INVALID.notes: This constant acts as a null-pointer equivalent for DMA channel structures. It is used to initialize variables before a valid channel is assigned. It has no functional impact on hardware but is critical for logic checks in driver functions. It is a constant structure of type ca_dma_ch_t with both stream and channel fields set to 0xFF.
DMA_CH_INVALID.usage: Use this value to initialize DMA channel variables or to reset a channel handle after a transfer is completed or aborted. Always compare your DMA channel variables against this constant before attempting to start a transfer to prevent accessing invalid hardware registers. Never attempt to pass this value directly to hardware configuration functions, as it will trigger an error or undefined behavior.

DMA_MAX_CHANNELS.brief: Defines the total number of available DMA channels supported by the hardware abstraction layer.
DMA_MAX_CHANNELS.notes: This constant sets the upper bound for the DMA channel array size in the driver. If set higher than the physical hardware capability, it may lead to out-of-bounds memory access or invalid register addressing. If set lower, additional DMA channels provided by the STM32 silicon will remain inaccessible to the RTOS.
DMA_MAX_CHANNELS.usage: Adjust this value only when porting the caOS driver to a different STM32 microcontroller series with a different number of DMA streams or channels. Ensure the value matches the specific datasheet for your MCU. Incorrect values will cause silent failures or hard faults when attempting to initialize or trigger DMA transfers on higher-indexed channels.

DMA_REQ_NONE.brief: A sentinel value representing the absence of a DMA request channel assignment.
DMA_REQ_NONE.notes: When set to 0xFFFFU, the driver interprets this as 'no DMA channel requested'. It is used as a default value in peripheral configuration structures to prevent accidental activation of DMA streams. It has no dependencies on other flags but must be checked by initialization functions to skip DMA setup logic.
DMA_REQ_NONE.usage: Use this value when initializing a peripheral structure that supports DMA but does not require it for the current application. Do not use this value if you intend to perform data transfers, as it will cause the driver to ignore the DMA configuration and potentially fall back to polling mode or return an error.

DNS_CLASS_IN.brief: Defines the Internet (IN) class identifier for DNS queries as specified in RFC 1035.
DNS_CLASS_IN.notes: This constant represents the standard class value for IP-based networks. It is used in the DNS header structure to indicate that the query pertains to the Internet protocol family. It is a fixed protocol constant and should not be modified, as changing it will cause DNS servers to reject requests as malformed or unsupported.
DNS_CLASS_IN.usage: Use this constant when manually constructing DNS packets or filtering incoming DNS traffic. Do not change this value unless you are implementing a non-standard network protocol that specifically requires a different DNS class identifier.

DNS_FLAGS_QR.brief: A bitmask flag used to identify if a DNS packet is a Query (0) or a Response (1).
DNS_FLAGS_QR.notes: When this bit is set (0x8000), the DNS header indicates the packet is a response from a server. When cleared, it indicates a client query. This flag is typically used in conjunction with bitwise AND operations to parse incoming network buffers. It is a standard field defined by RFC 1035 and must not be modified.
DNS_FLAGS_QR.usage: Do not change this value as it is defined by the DNS protocol specification. Use this constant when writing custom packet parsers or debugging network traffic to verify if a received packet is a valid response to a previous request.

DNS_FLAGS_RCODE.brief: A bitmask used to extract the 4-bit Response Code (RCODE) field from a DNS message header.
DNS_FLAGS_RCODE.notes: This constant represents the mask 0x000F, which isolates the lower 4 bits of the DNS flags field. It is used to identify the status of a DNS query (e.g., No Error, Format Error, Server Failure). It depends on the DNS header structure defined in the network stack and is typically used in conjunction with bitwise AND operations on the flags field.
DNS_FLAGS_RCODE.usage: Use this when parsing incoming DNS responses to determine if the server successfully resolved the domain or returned an error. Do not modify this value unless the underlying DNS protocol implementation changes, as it is strictly defined by RFC 1035. Incorrect values will result in the system misinterpreting DNS server error codes.

DNS_FLAGS_RD.brief: The Recursion Desired (RD) flag bit for DNS query headers.
DNS_FLAGS_RD.notes: When set to 0x0100U, this bit instructs the DNS server to perform a recursive search if it does not have the requested record in its cache. If disabled (0x0000U), the server will only return what it already knows or provide a referral to another server. This flag is typically ORed with other header flags to construct the full DNS request packet.
DNS_FLAGS_RD.usage: Enable this flag when your device needs to resolve domain names through a standard recursive DNS server (like those provided by ISPs or public DNS providers). Disable it only if you are communicating with an authoritative-only server or if you want to minimize network traffic by preventing the server from performing additional lookups on your behalf.

DNS_PENDING_MAX.brief: Defines the maximum number of concurrent DNS resolution requests allowed in the system queue.
DNS_PENDING_MAX.notes: This constant determines the size of the internal buffer for pending DNS queries. Increasing this value allows more simultaneous lookups but consumes more RAM in the system heap. It is dependent on the network stack being initialized and typically ranges from 1 to 16 depending on available memory.
DNS_PENDING_MAX.usage: Increase this value if your application frequently experiences 'DNS_QUEUE_FULL' errors when performing multiple network requests simultaneously. Decrease it if the system is running low on memory. Setting this value too high may lead to heap exhaustion during peak network activity.

DNS_PORT.brief: Defines the standard UDP port number used for Domain Name System (DNS) queries.
DNS_PORT.notes: This constant sets the destination port for outgoing DNS requests. It is a 16-bit unsigned integer. Changing this value will prevent the device from resolving hostnames unless the remote DNS server is also configured to listen on the new port. It is a dependency for the caOS network stack's resolver module.
DNS_PORT.usage: Change this value only if you are operating within a non-standard network environment or a private network that uses a custom DNS port. Do not change this for standard internet connectivity, as 53 is the globally recognized IANA standard for DNS.

DNS_RCODE_NXDOMAIN.brief: A DNS response code indicating that the domain name requested does not exist.
DNS_RCODE_NXDOMAIN.notes: This constant represents the numeric value 3, which is returned by a DNS server when a query fails because the requested hostname cannot be resolved. It is used within the network stack's DNS client module to interpret server responses. It has no configurable range as it is a fixed protocol-defined constant.
DNS_RCODE_NXDOMAIN.usage: Use this constant when writing conditional logic to handle DNS lookup failures. Compare the result of your DNS query function against this flag to distinguish between a network timeout and a legitimate 'domain not found' error. Do not modify this value, as it must strictly adhere to the DNS protocol specification (RFC 1035).

DNS_RCODE_OK.brief: Represents the success status code for a DNS query response.
DNS_RCODE_OK.notes: This constant is defined as 0U, which is the standard value for 'No Error' in the DNS protocol header. It is used by the caOS network stack to validate incoming DNS packets. If a received packet's RCODE field matches this constant, the system proceeds with parsing the resource records; otherwise, it triggers an error handling routine.
DNS_RCODE_OK.usage: This value should not be changed as it is defined by the RFC 1035 standard. It is primarily used in conditional checks when processing network responses. If your application is receiving unexpected DNS errors, check this constant against the RCODE field in the received packet header to debug network configuration or server-side issues.

DNS_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT_MS.brief: Defines the maximum time in milliseconds the system waits for a DNS server to respond to a hostname resolution request.
DNS_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT_MS.notes: When enabled, the network stack will block or pend the calling task for up to this duration. If no response is received within this window, the DNS query fails. This value is dependent on the network stack's tick rate and should be set higher than the expected round-trip time of your network environment. Typical values range from 1000ms to 5000ms.
DNS_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT_MS.usage: Increase this value if your device is operating on high-latency networks (e.g., cellular or congested Wi-Fi) to prevent premature timeouts. Decrease it if you need the application to fail fast and recover quickly when the network is unreachable. Setting this value too low may cause frequent DNS resolution failures, while setting it too high may cause the application to hang unnecessarily during network outages.

DNS_RETRY_N.brief: Defines the maximum number of times the DNS client will attempt to resolve a hostname before returning an error.
DNS_RETRY_N.notes: This constant controls the retry logic in the network stack. Increasing this value allows for more attempts in unstable network environments but increases the total blocking time for the calling task. It depends on the underlying network driver's timeout settings. Typical values range from 1 to 5.
DNS_RETRY_N.usage: Increase this value if your device frequently fails to resolve hostnames due to high packet loss or slow network response times. Decrease it if you need to fail fast to maintain system responsiveness. Setting this too high may cause task starvation or watchdog timeouts if the network is completely unreachable.

DNS_TYPE_A.brief: Defines the protocol identifier for IPv4 address resolution requests in the caOS networking stack.
DNS_TYPE_A.notes: This constant represents the 'A' record type in DNS queries. It is a mandatory value for the DNS client module to resolve hostnames into 32-bit IPv4 addresses. It must be set to 1U to comply with RFC 1035 standards. Changing this value will cause the DNS resolver to request incorrect record types, leading to resolution failures.
DNS_TYPE_A.usage: Use this constant when calling the DNS query function to specify that you are looking for an IPv4 address. Do not modify this value unless you are intentionally implementing a different DNS record type (e.g., AAAA for IPv6 or MX for mail servers) and the underlying network stack supports it.

DUMP_BUFFER_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed size in bytes of the internal memory buffer used for system diagnostic dumps and error logging.
DUMP_BUFFER_SIZE.notes: This constant allocates a static memory block for capturing system state information during a crash or debug event. Increasing this value allows for more detailed log entries but consumes more RAM. It is currently set to 128 bytes across all supported STM32 platforms (F4, F7, H5, H7) to ensure consistent diagnostic output capacity regardless of the specific MCU architecture.
DUMP_BUFFER_SIZE.usage: Modify this value if you need to capture larger diagnostic payloads or if you are running out of RAM and need to reclaim space. If set too small, diagnostic logs may be truncated, leading to incomplete information during debugging. Ensure the value is a multiple of the word size (4 bytes) for optimal memory alignment on ARM Cortex-M cores.

DUMP_TASK_ADDR.brief: Enables the inclusion of task entry point addresses in the system dump logs for debugging purposes.
DUMP_TASK_ADDR.notes: When enabled (0x02), the scheduler appends the memory address of each task's function to the diagnostic output. This flag depends on the system's logging subsystem being initialized. It is typically used in conjunction with other diagnostic flags and consumes a small amount of additional memory in the dump buffer.
DUMP_TASK_ADDR.usage: Enable this flag when you need to identify which specific task function is associated with a stack overflow or a task crash during post-mortem analysis. Do not enable this in production builds if memory constraints are extremely tight, as it increases the size of the diagnostic log entries.

DUMP_TASK_ALL.brief: A bitmask flag used to enable the logging or diagnostic dumping of all active task control blocks (TCBs) within the scheduler.
DUMP_TASK_ALL.notes: When enabled, the system will iterate through all registered tasks and output their current state, stack usage, and priority to the debug interface. This flag depends on the system's debug UART or ITM port being initialized. It is typically used as a bitwise mask; setting it to 0xFF ensures all task-related diagnostic modules are active. Disabling it reduces CPU overhead and memory footprint during runtime.
DUMP_TASK_ALL.usage: Change this value when you need to perform a system-wide health check or debug a task-related crash.
