FF_MIN_GPT.usage: Change this value only if you encounter file system corruption or DMA transfer errors when reading/writing to storage media. It is used to solve alignment-related issues where the hardware requires buffers to start at specific memory boundaries. Warning: Setting an incorrect value may lead to system crashes, data corruption, or failed file operations if the underlying hardware cannot handle the specified alignment.

FF_MIN_SS.brief: Defines the minimum sector size in bytes for the FATFS file system.
FF_MIN_SS.notes: This constant sets the lower bound for sector size supported by the file system driver. Typical values are 512, 1024, 2048, or 4096. It must be a power of 2. Increasing this value may improve performance on certain storage media but will increase memory usage for internal buffers.
FF_MIN_SS.usage: Change this value only if you are interfacing with storage media that requires a specific sector size (e.g., some high-capacity SD cards or specific flash memory chips). If you set this incorrectly, the file system will fail to mount or return read/write errors. For standard SD cards, 512 is the industry-standard default.

FF_NORTC_MDAY.brief: Disables the storage of the day-of-month field in the FAT file system timestamps.
FF_NORTC_MDAY.notes: When set to 1, the FAT file system driver ignores the day-of-month field in file timestamps. This is typically used in embedded systems where the RTC (Real-Time Clock) might not be fully implemented or where precise file modification dates are not required. It reduces the complexity of timestamp calculations during file operations.
FF_NORTC_MDAY.usage: Set this to 1 if your application does not require accurate file modification dates or if you are experiencing issues with RTC synchronization affecting file system metadata. Keep it enabled to save minor processing overhead. If your application requires accurate file timestamps for logging or data management, set this to 0 and ensure the RTC is properly initialized using ca_rtc_init.

FF_NORTC_MON.brief: Disables the requirement for a Real-Time Clock (RTC) when handling file timestamps in the FATFS file system.
FF_NORTC_MON.notes: When set to 1, the file system ignores the system RTC for file modification times, typically defaulting to a fixed timestamp or zero. This removes the dependency on ca_rtc_* functions for file operations. If set to 0, the system expects a valid RTC to provide accurate timestamps for file creation and modification.
FF_NORTC_MON.usage: Enable this (set to 1) if your hardware lacks an RTC or if you do not need accurate file timestamps, which saves code space and avoids potential initialization errors related to the RTC peripheral. Disable this (set to 0) only if your application requires accurate file metadata for logging or synchronization purposes.

FF_NORTC_YEAR.brief: Sets the base year for FATFS timestamps when no Real-Time Clock (RTC) is available.
FF_NORTC_YEAR.notes: This constant defines the starting year used by the FAT filesystem driver to calculate file modification dates when the system lacks a hardware RTC or the RTC is uninitialized. It is a static integer value. If your system has a valid RTC, this value is ignored by the file system logic, but it remains a required configuration for the FATFS layer in caOS.
FF_NORTC_YEAR.usage: Update this value annually or to match the deployment year of your firmware. It ensures that files created on systems without a battery-backed RTC have a sensible, non-zero timestamp. If you set this to an incorrect value, files created without an RTC will appear to have been modified in the wrong year, which can cause issues with file synchronization or log sorting.

FF_PATH_DEPTH.brief: Defines the maximum depth of the directory path string supported by the FAT filesystem.
FF_PATH_DEPTH.notes: This constant limits the number of subdirectories allowed in a path (e.g., /dir1/dir2/dir3/file.txt has a depth of 3). Increasing this value consumes more stack memory during path parsing operations. The default value is 10, which is sufficient for most embedded applications. It must be a positive integer.
FF_PATH_DEPTH.usage: Increase this value if your application needs to navigate deeper directory structures than the current limit. Decrease it if you are experiencing stack overflows during file operations and your directory structure is shallow. Ensure your stack size is adjusted accordingly if you significantly increase this value.

FF_PRINT_FLOAT.brief: Enables or disables support for floating-point number formatting in FatFS printf-style functions.
FF_PRINT_FLOAT.notes: When set to 1, the FatFS library includes code to parse and format floating-point numbers (e.g., %f). When set to 0 (default), this support is disabled to save significant code space (Flash memory). This flag is specific to the FatFS module and does not affect the global ca_printf or ca_snprintf functions.
FF_PRINT_FLOAT.usage: Change this to 1 only if your application specifically requires writing floating-point values to files using FatFS formatting functions. If you are only logging integers or strings, keep it at 0 to minimize the binary size of your firmware.

FF_STRF_ENCODE.brief: Enables or disables support for character encoding conversion (e.g., OEM code pages) in the FATFS file system.
FF_STRF_ENCODE.notes: When set to 0 (disabled), the file system uses standard ASCII/UTF-8 character handling. Enabling this (setting to 1) allows for non-English character support but increases the memory footprint of the FATFS module and requires additional configuration tables. It is typically disabled in resource-constrained embedded systems to save Flash and RAM.
FF_STRF_ENCODE.usage: Change this value to 1 only if your application specifically requires support for non-ASCII file names or specific international character sets. If you are only using standard alphanumeric file names, keep it at 0 to minimize code size and memory usage. If enabled, ensure you have sufficient heap memory available for the FATFS work buffer.

FF_STR_VOLUME_ID.brief: Enables or disables the support for volume identification strings in the FATFS file system.
FF_STR_VOLUME_ID.notes: When set to 1, the system allows the use of volume labels/IDs. When set to 0 (default), this feature is disabled, saving a small amount of memory and code space. This flag is part of the FatFs configuration and does not have direct dependencies on other caOS modules, but it affects how volume information is retrieved via ca_fat functions.
FF_STR_VOLUME_ID.usage: Change this value to 1 only if your application specifically requires reading or setting volume labels on storage media. If you are just performing standard file I/O operations (like ca_fat_fopen or ca_fat_fread), keep it at 0 to minimize the memory footprint of the file system driver.

FF_USE_EXPAND.brief: Enables or disables the f_expand function in the FatFs file system layer.
FF_USE_EXPAND.notes: When set to 1, the f_expand function is included, allowing pre-allocation of contiguous disk space for a file. When set to 0 (default), this feature is disabled to save code space. This flag has no direct dependencies on other caOS modules but requires sufficient underlying storage driver support to handle file allocation effectively.
FF_USE_EXPAND.usage: Change this to 1 only if your application requires pre-allocating large files to ensure contiguous storage, which helps prevent fragmentation and guarantees write performance for high-speed data logging. If your application does not perform pre-allocation, keep it at 0 to minimize the firmware footprint.

FF_USE_FASTSEEK.brief: Enables or disables the Fast Seek feature in FatFs to speed up file seeking operations.
FF_USE_FASTSEEK.notes: When enabled (1), FatFs creates a cluster-to-offset link map in memory, allowing O(1) seek operations instead of O(n). This increases RAM usage proportional to the file size. When disabled (0), seeking requires scanning the FAT table, which is slower for large files but memory-efficient. It depends on FF_USE_FATFS being enabled.
FF_USE_FASTSEEK.usage: Enable this only if your application performs frequent, random-access reads/writes on large files and you have sufficient heap memory to store the link map. If your system is memory-constrained or you only perform sequential file access, keep this set to 0 to save RAM.

FF_USE_FORWARD.brief: Enables or disables the forward seek functionality in the FatFs file system.
FF_USE_FORWARD.notes: When set to 0 (disabled), the file system does not support seeking forward beyond the current file pointer position using fseek. This reduces the code footprint of the FatFs library. If set to 1, it allows the application to jump ahead in a file, which requires additional internal logic in the file system driver. This flag is independent of backward seeking.
FF_USE_FORWARD.usage: Keep this at 0 to save memory and code space if your application only reads files sequentially or performs simple rewinds. Change this to 1 only if your application logic requires jumping to arbitrary future offsets within a file (e.g., skipping headers in large binary files). If you attempt to use fseek to move forward while this is 0, the operation will fail.

FF_USE_LFN.brief: Enables support for Long File Names (LFN) in the FAT filesystem.
FF_USE_LFN.notes: Setting this to 3 enables LFN support using a heap-allocated buffer. This requires the system to have sufficient memory available for the FAT work buffer. If set to 0, only 8.3 short filenames are supported. Enabling LFN increases the memory footprint of the filesystem operations.
FF_USE_LFN.usage: Change this value to 3 when your application needs to handle files with names longer than 8 characters or containing special characters. Ensure that ca_memory_init has been called and sufficient heap is available, otherwise file operations may fail. Do not use LFN if your system is extremely memory-constrained.

FF_USE_MKFS.brief: Enables the ability to format a storage volume (create a new filesystem) at runtime.
FF_USE_MKFS.notes: When set to 1, the ca_fat_mkfs function is compiled into the system, allowing you to initialize empty storage media. If set to 0, this function is excluded to save flash memory space. This flag is a dependency for any application that needs to perform initial setup of SD cards or internal flash partitions from within the firmware.
FF_USE_MKFS.usage: Enable this (1) during the initial production or maintenance phase if your device needs to format new, uninitialized storage media. Disable it (0) in final production builds to reduce binary size if the filesystem is pre-formatted or if runtime formatting is not required by the end-user.

FF_USE_STRFUNC.brief: Enables or disables string manipulation functions (like printf, sprintf, etc.) within the FatFS module.
FF_USE_STRFUNC.notes: When set to 1, FatFS includes internal string formatting functions. This increases the code size (Flash usage) but allows the use of formatted output functions within the file system layer. If set to 0, these functions are excluded to save space. This flag is independent of the main caOS ca_printf functions.
FF_USE_STRFUNC.usage: Set to 1 if your application requires formatted string output or logging directly through FatFS-related operations. Set to 0 if you are strictly constrained by Flash memory and do not use string formatting features in your file system logic. Example: if you need to log file names or status strings using ca_printf, ensure this is enabled if the underlying FatFS logic requires it.

FF_USE_TRIM.brief: Enables or disables the TRIM command support for ATA/SD/eMMC storage devices in FatFs.
FF_USE_TRIM.notes: When set to 1, the file system will issue TRIM commands to the storage device when files are deleted or truncated, informing the controller that the blocks are no longer in use. This helps improve write performance and wear leveling on flash-based media. Setting this to 0 (default) disables this feature, which is safer if the underlying hardware or driver does not correctly implement or support the TRIM command.
FF_USE_TRIM.usage: Enable this (set to 1) only if your storage hardware (e.g., specific SD cards or eMMC chips) explicitly supports TRIM and you notice performance degradation after frequent file deletions. If you are unsure, keep it at 0 to avoid potential compatibility issues or data corruption on unsupported storage media.

FF_VOLUMES.brief: Defines the maximum number of logical volumes (drives) supported by the FatFs file system.
FF_VOLUMES.notes: This constant determines the size of the internal volume table. Valid range is 1 to 10. Increasing this value allows mounting multiple physical or logical drives (e.g., SD card, internal Flash, USB mass storage) simultaneously. It directly impacts the memory footprint of the FatFs module.
FF_VOLUMES.usage: Change this value only if your application needs to access more than one storage device at the same time. For a single SD card setup, keep it at 1 to save RAM. If you need to support both an SD card and an internal flash partition, increase this to 2 or more.

FF_VOLUME_STRS.brief: Defines the logical volume name used to identify the SD card in the file system.
FF_VOLUME_STRS.notes: This constant sets the string identifier for the FatFs volume. When using ca_fat_mount, this string is used to reference the SD card drive. Changing this value requires updating all code paths that reference the volume by name. It must be a non-empty string.
FF_VOLUME_STRS.usage: Change this value if you need to support multiple storage devices or if the project naming convention requires a specific identifier (e.g., '0', 'SD', 'FLASH'). Ensure that the string matches the identifier expected by your application logic when calling ca_fat_mount.

HASH_CTX_INIT_CAP.brief: Defines the initial memory allocation size in bytes for the hashing context buffer.
HASH_CTX_INIT_CAP.notes: This constant determines the static memory footprint of the hash driver's internal state. Increasing this value allows for larger internal buffers or more complex hashing algorithms, while decreasing it saves RAM. It must be large enough to accommodate the context structure of the specific hardware peripheral or software algorithm being used; otherwise, the driver will trigger a buffer overflow or memory corruption.
HASH_CTX_INIT_CAP.usage: Adjust this value if you encounter memory allocation errors during hash initialization or if you switch to a hashing algorithm that requires a larger state structure. Do not set this value lower than the size of the largest context structure required by your enabled algorithms, as this will lead to undefined behavior or system crashes.

HASH_MAX_DIGEST_SIZE.brief: Defines the maximum buffer size in bytes allocated for storing cryptographic hash results.
HASH_MAX_DIGEST_SIZE.notes: This constant sets the static memory allocation for hash output buffers. If set too low, hashing algorithms requiring larger outputs (like SHA-256) will trigger buffer overflows or truncation errors. It must be at least 32 to support SHA-256. Increasing this value consumes more RAM in the driver's internal state structures.
HASH_MAX_DIGEST_SIZE.usage: Change this value only if you need to support newer or stronger hashing algorithms that produce digests larger than 32 bytes (e.g., SHA-512). Ensure that all application-level buffers receiving hash outputs are sized according to this constant to prevent memory corruption.

HASH_SHA1_DIGEST_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed output length in bytes for the SHA-1 cryptographic hash algorithm.
HASH_SHA1_DIGEST_SIZE.notes: The value is set to 20 bytes (160 bits) as per the SHA-1 standard specification. This constant is used to allocate buffers for hash results. Changing this value will cause the SHA-1 hardware peripheral or software implementation to produce incorrect results or trigger buffer overflows in dependent code.
HASH_SHA1_DIGEST_SIZE.usage: This value should not be changed as it is strictly defined by the SHA-1 algorithm. It is used primarily for static memory allocation in security modules and communication protocols that require SHA-1 integrity checks. If you need a different digest size, you must switch to a different algorithm (e.g., SHA-256) rather than modifying this constant.

HASH_SHA256_DIGEST_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed output length in bytes for the SHA-256 cryptographic hash algorithm.
HASH_SHA256_DIGEST_SIZE.notes: This constant is set to 32 bytes (256 bits) as per the SHA-256 standard. Changing this value will break compatibility with standard cryptographic libraries and hardware acceleration drivers. It is a read-only configuration used to allocate buffers for hash results.
HASH_SHA256_DIGEST_SIZE.usage: Do not modify this value unless you are implementing a custom variant of the algorithm. It is used to size arrays that store the final digest; setting it incorrectly will lead to buffer overflows or truncated hash outputs.

HCHACHA20_NONCE_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed length in bytes for the HCHACHA20 nonce.
HCHACHA20_NONCE_SIZE.notes: This constant is set to 16 bytes, which is the standard requirement for the HCHACHA20 algorithm. It is used by the ca_hchacha20 function to ensure the input buffer for the nonce is correctly sized. Changing this value will cause cryptographic failures or buffer overflows in the underlying implementation.
HCHACHA20_NONCE_SIZE.usage: Do not change this value. It is a protocol-defined constant for the HCHACHA20 primitive. If you are implementing a new cryptographic protocol using ca_hchacha20, ensure your nonce buffers are exactly 16 bytes long to match this constant.

HCHACHA20_OUT_SIZE.brief: Defines the output size in bytes for the HCHACHA20 cryptographic function.
HCHACHA20_OUT_SIZE.notes: This constant sets the length of the derived key/output block generated by the HCHACHA20 algorithm. In caOS, it is fixed to 32 bytes, which corresponds to the standard 256-bit output required for subsequent ChaCha20 operations. Modifying this value will break compatibility with standard cryptographic implementations and may cause buffer overflows if the underlying buffers are not sized accordingly.
HCHACHA20_OUT_SIZE.usage: This value is used internally by the ca_hchacha20 function. You should not change this value unless you are implementing a non-standard variant of the protocol. If you need to perform a key derivation, use it as follows: uint8_t output[HCHACHA20_OUT_SIZE]; ca_hchacha20(key, nonce, output); // Ensure output buffer matches HCHACHA20_OUT_SIZE

HCLK_FREQ_HZ.brief: Defines the AHB bus clock frequency (HCLK) in Hertz for the system timer and peripheral timing calculations.
HCLK_FREQ_HZ.notes: This constant is used by the RTOS kernel to calibrate the system tick timer (SysTick) and ensure accurate task scheduling. If this value does not match the actual hardware clock configuration set in the RCC registers, timing-dependent functions like vTaskDelay() or hardware timeouts will run at the wrong speed. It must be set to the exact frequency resulting from your PLL and prescaler settings.
HCLK_FREQ_HZ.usage: Change this value whenever you modify the system clock tree configuration (e.g., changing the crystal frequency or PLL multipliers). If your tasks are running faster or slower than expected, or if communication peripherals like UART/I2C have baud rate errors, verify that this constant matches the actual HCLK frequency output by the MCU clock tree.

HKDF_SHA256_MAX_OUT.brief: Defines the maximum output length in bytes for the HKDF-SHA256 key derivation function.
HKDF_SHA256_MAX_OUT.notes: This constant sets the upper limit for the key material generated by the HKDF process. It is calculated as 255 times the SHA256 digest size (32 bytes), resulting in a maximum of 8160 bytes. Increasing this value consumes more stack or heap memory during the derivation process, while decreasing it limits the amount of key material you can extract in a single call.
HKDF_SHA256_MAX_OUT.usage: Modify this value only if your application requires a specific, smaller buffer size to save RAM, or if you need to generate larger amounts of key material than the default allows. Ensure that the buffer passed to ca_hkdf_sha256 does not exceed this limit to prevent buffer overflows.

HMAC_BLAKE2S_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed output size in bytes for the BLAKE2s HMAC implementation.
HMAC_BLAKE2S_SIZE.notes: This constant sets the buffer size required for HMAC-BLAKE2s operations. A value of 32 bytes corresponds to a 256-bit hash output. Changing this value affects the memory allocation requirements for any buffers passed to ca_hmac_blake2s_final. It is a static configuration and should not be modified unless the underlying cryptographic protocol requirements change.
HMAC_BLAKE2S_SIZE.usage: Use this constant when allocating buffers for HMAC results to ensure compatibility with the ca_hmac_blake2s API. Example: uint8_t mac[HMAC_BLAKE2S_SIZE]; ca_hmac_blake2s_final(&ctx, mac);. Do not change this value to arbitrary numbers, as the BLAKE2s algorithm expects specific output lengths for security integrity.

HMAC_SHA256_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed byte length of the HMAC-SHA256 output digest.
HMAC_SHA256_SIZE.notes: This constant is set to SHA256_DIGEST_SIZE (32 bytes). It determines the buffer size required for storing HMAC-SHA256 results. Changing this value will break compatibility with standard HMAC-SHA256 implementations and cause buffer overflows or truncated data if the underlying ca_hmac_sha256 functions expect the standard 32-byte output.
HMAC_SHA256_SIZE.usage: Do not change this value under normal circumstances. It is used by the ca_hmac_sha256 family of functions to allocate memory for cryptographic operations. If you are implementing a custom protocol that requires a truncated HMAC, perform the truncation manually after the calculation rather than modifying this constant.

HTTPS_DEFAULT_PORT.brief: Defines the default TCP port number used for HTTPS communication services.
HTTPS_DEFAULT_PORT.notes: This constant sets the listening or connection port for the ca_https service. The value 443U is the IANA standard for HTTPS. Changing this value will prevent the device from connecting to standard web servers unless they are specifically configured to listen on a non-standard port. It is a 16-bit unsigned integer.
HTTPS_DEFAULT_PORT.usage: Modify this value only if your application must communicate with an HTTPS server running on a non-standard port (e.g., 8443). Do not change this for standard web traffic. Ensure the server side is configured to match this port, otherwise, the connection will be rejected by the remote host.

HTTP_DEFAULT_PORT.brief: Defines the default TCP port number used by the caOS HTTP server when no specific port is provided.
HTTP_DEFAULT_PORT.notes: This constant sets the listening port for the HTTP stack. Changing this value affects all incoming HTTP connections. It must be a valid 16-bit unsigned integer (1-65535). Ensure that the chosen port does not conflict with other network services running on the STM32, such as DHCP or MQTT.
HTTP_DEFAULT_PORT.usage: Change this value if your application needs to run on a non-standard port (e.g., 8080 for development or 443 for HTTPS). Note that ports below 1024 are typically reserved for system services; using them may require specific network privileges or configurations.

HTTP_METHOD_GET.brief: A bitmask flag representing the HTTP GET request method used by the caOS network service.
HTTP_METHOD_GET.notes: This constant is used to identify or filter HTTP GET requests within the service stack. It is typically used in conjunction with other method flags (e.g., POST, PUT) as part of a bitwise field. The value 0x01U is a fixed identifier and should not be modified to ensure compatibility with the internal HTTP parser.
HTTP_METHOD_GET.usage: Use this flag when configuring request handlers or defining allowed methods for a specific endpoint. Do not change this value, as it is hardcoded to match the HTTP protocol specification expected by the caOS network stack. If you are implementing a custom callback, check the incoming request method against this constant using a bitwise AND operation.

HTTP_METHOD_HEAD.brief: A constant representing the HTTP HEAD method identifier used by the caOS network stack.
HTTP_METHOD_HEAD.notes: This value is used internally by the HTTP service to identify requests that ask for header information only, without the response body. It must match the value expected by the server-side parser. It is a static identifier and does not affect system memory or task scheduling.
HTTP_METHOD_HEAD.usage: Use this constant when implementing custom HTTP request handlers or filtering incoming traffic. Do not modify this value unless you are updating the entire network stack to a different protocol specification, as changing it will cause the HTTP service to fail to recognize HEAD requests.

HTTP_METHOD_OPTIONS.brief: A bitmask flag used to enable or disable support for the HTTP OPTIONS method in the caOS web server.
HTTP_METHOD_OPTIONS.notes: When enabled, the HTTP service will process and respond to OPTIONS requests, typically used for CORS preflight checks. If disabled, the server will return a 405 Method Not Allowed error for these requests. This flag is part of a bitmask configuration; it must be ORed with other method flags (e.g., GET, POST) to define the full set of supported HTTP verbs.
HTTP_METHOD_OPTIONS.usage: Enable this flag if your web application requires CORS support or if a client needs to query the server's capabilities. Disable it to reduce the memory footprint and attack surface if your application only performs simple data retrieval or submission.

HTTP_METHOD_POST.brief: A constant representing the HTTP POST request method identifier used by the caOS networking stack.
HTTP_METHOD_POST.notes: This value is used internally by the HTTP service to distinguish POST requests from other methods like GET (0x01) or PUT (0x03). It is typically passed as an argument to the http_send_request function. It has no direct impact on system memory or scheduling, but must match the protocol definition expected by the remote server.
HTTP_METHOD_POST.usage: Use this constant when you need to send data to a server, such as submitting a form or uploading sensor readings. Do not change this value unless you are modifying the core HTTP protocol implementation, as changing it will cause the server to reject the request or misinterpret the data payload.

HTTP_QUERY_MAX.brief: Defines the maximum character length allowed for an incoming HTTP query string.
HTTP_QUERY_MAX.notes: This constant sets the buffer size for parsing URL parameters. If the incoming query exceeds 128 bytes, the HTTP service will truncate the data or return a 414 Request-URI Too Long error. It must be large enough to accommodate your longest expected URL parameters but should be kept small to conserve RAM in the heap or stack.
HTTP_QUERY_MAX.usage: Increase this value if your application requires processing long URL query strings or complex API parameters. Decrease it if you are running low on system memory and your application only uses short, simple query strings. Ensure that the buffer allocated in the HTTP task is sufficient to hold this value plus any necessary headers.

HTTP_RECV_TIMEOUT_MS.brief: Defines the maximum time in milliseconds the HTTP service waits for incoming data packets before aborting the request.
HTTP_RECV_TIMEOUT_MS.notes: Increasing this value allows for slower network connections but consumes more memory and blocks the task for longer periods. Decreasing it improves responsiveness but may cause premature timeouts on high-latency networks. It is dependent on the underlying TCP stack timeout settings and should generally be greater than the round-trip time of the network.
HTTP_RECV_TIMEOUT_MS.usage: Adjust this value if you encounter frequent 'HTTP Timeout' errors during data reception. Increase it if the device is operating on a slow or congested network. Decrease it if you need the system to fail fast to maintain real-time performance. Ensure the value is not set too low, or valid data transfers will be interrupted.

HTTP_REQ_BUF_SIZE.brief: Defines the maximum size in bytes for the internal buffer used to store incoming HTTP request data.
HTTP_REQ_BUF_SIZE.notes: Increasing this value allows the system to handle larger HTTP headers or payloads but directly consumes more RAM from the heap. It must be large enough to accommodate the longest expected request header; if the request exceeds this size, the parser will return an error. Typical values range from 512 to 4096 depending on available memory.
HTTP_REQ_BUF_SIZE.usage: Increase this value if you encounter 'HTTP 414 Request-URI Too Long' or '400 Bad Request' errors when sending complex requests. Decrease it if the system is running low on heap memory and you are only handling small, simple API calls.

HTTP_RESP_BUF_SIZE.brief: Defines the maximum size in bytes of the buffer used to store incoming HTTP response payloads.
HTTP_RESP_BUF_SIZE.notes: This constant allocates a static memory block for HTTP data processing. Increasing this value allows the system to handle larger HTTP responses but directly increases the static RAM footprint of the application. It must be large enough to hold the expected response body; if the response exceeds this size, the HTTP client will truncate the data or return an overflow error. Ensure that the total RAM usage does not exceed the STM32 device's available heap and stack limits.
HTTP_RESP_BUF_SIZE.usage: Adjust this value when your application needs to fetch larger JSON objects or files from a web server. If you encounter 'Buffer Overflow' or 'Incomplete Data' errors during HTTP GET requests, increase this value. Conversely, if your device is running low on RAM, decrease this value to the smallest size that still accommodates your largest expected response.

HTTP_URI_MAX.brief: Defines the maximum character length allowed for an HTTP request URI string.
HTTP_URI_MAX.notes: This constant sets the size of the static buffer used to store incoming URI paths. If the incoming URI exceeds 128 bytes, the HTTP service will return a 414 Request-URI Too Long error. It directly impacts the memory footprint of the HTTP task stack or heap allocation. Valid range is typically 32 to 1024 depending on available RAM.
HTTP_URI_MAX.usage: Increase this value if your application requires complex REST API endpoints with long query parameters or deep directory structures. Decrease it to save RAM if your device only handles simple, short resource requests. Ensure the value is large enough to accommodate the longest expected URI plus the null terminator.

I2C_EN_IRQ.brief: Enables interrupt-driven mode for the I2C peripheral driver.
I2C_EN_IRQ.notes: When enabled, the driver uses hardware interrupts to handle data transfer instead of blocking the CPU in a polling loop. This requires the corresponding I2C interrupt vector to be enabled in the NVIC. If disabled, the driver defaults to a blocking polling mechanism. The value 0x0102 acts as a bitmask configuration for the I2C peripheral control register.
I2C_EN_IRQ.usage: Enable this flag to improve system efficiency and allow the CPU to perform other tasks while waiting for I2C data transfers to complete. Change this to disabled only if you are debugging timing-sensitive issues or if the system lacks sufficient interrupt priority resources. Ensure that the I2C interrupt handler is correctly implemented in your project before enabling this flag to prevent system hangs.

IPERF_DEFAULT_DURATION_MS.brief: Defines the default execution time in milliseconds for the built-in iPerf network performance test.
IPERF_DEFAULT_DURATION_MS.notes: This constant sets the duration for which the network stack will transmit or receive data during a test session. It is used as the fallback value when no specific duration is provided by the user command. The value must be a positive integer representing milliseconds; typical values range from 1000U to 60000U depending on the desired test granularity.
IPERF_DEFAULT_DURATION_MS.usage: Adjust this value if your network performance tests are too short to provide a stable average or too long, causing system unresponsiveness. Increase this value if you need to observe long-term network stability or throughput trends. Be aware that setting an excessively high value may block other low-priority tasks if the iPerf task is not properly preempted.

IPERF_DEFAULT_PORT.brief: Defines the default TCP/UDP port number used by the caOS built-in iPerf network performance testing utility.
IPERF_DEFAULT_PORT.notes: This constant sets the listening port for the iPerf server task. It must be a valid 16-bit unsigned integer (1-65535). Changing this value requires a recompile of the firmware. Ensure the chosen port does not conflict with other network services like HTTP (80) or MQTT (1883).
IPERF_DEFAULT_PORT.usage: Change this value if your network environment or firewall policies restrict the use of port 5001, or if you need to run multiple iPerf instances simultaneously on different ports. Always ensure the client-side testing tool is configured to match this port number, otherwise, the connection will be refused.

IPERF_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS.brief: Defines the maximum duration in milliseconds the system waits for network activity before entering an idle state during iPerf testing.
IPERF_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS.notes: When enabled, the system monitors incoming packets; if no data is received within this window, the test session is terminated. This value is dependent on the network stack's tick rate. Typical values range from 1000U to 10000U depending on the expected latency of the network environment.
IPERF_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS.usage: Increase this value if you experience premature test termination due to high network jitter or slow link initialization. Decrease it if you need the system to recover faster from dropped connections. Setting this value too low may cause valid tests to fail, while setting it too high may prevent the system from freeing up resources after a genuine connection loss.

IP_DEFRAG_MAX_PAYLOAD.brief: Defines the maximum size in bytes of the reassembled IP packet payload that the system can buffer.
IP_DEFRAG_MAX_PAYLOAD.notes: This constant sets the memory limit for the IP fragmentation reassembly buffer. If set too low, fragmented packets larger than this value will be dropped. If set too high, it increases static RAM consumption. The value must be a multiple of the MTU and is typically set to 1480 to accommodate standard Ethernet frames minus the IP header.
IP_DEFRAG_MAX_PAYLOAD.usage: Increase this value if your application receives large fragmented IP packets that are currently being discarded. Decrease it to save RAM if your network environment guarantees that packets will not exceed a smaller size. Ensure the value does not exceed the total available heap or static buffer allocation defined in the network stack configuration.

IP_DEFRAG_MAX_SESSIONS.brief: Defines the maximum number of concurrent IP fragments the system can track for reassembly.
IP_DEFRAG_MAX_SESSIONS.notes: This constant determines the size of the internal buffer pool for fragmented packets. Increasing this value consumes more RAM but allows the system to handle more simultaneous fragmented network streams. It must be set based on available heap memory and expected network traffic patterns. Typical values range from 4 to 16 depending on the STM32 memory footprint.
IP_DEFRAG_MAX_SESSIONS.usage: Increase this value if your application experiences dropped packets or network communication failures when receiving large data frames over UDP or TCP. Decrease it if the system is running low on RAM. Setting this value too high may lead to heap exhaustion, while setting it too low will cause the network stack to discard incoming fragments.

IP_DEFRAG_TIMEOUT_MS.brief: Defines the maximum time in milliseconds to wait for all fragments of an IP packet to arrive before discarding them.
IP_DEFRAG_TIMEOUT_MS.notes: When enabled, the system buffers incoming IP fragments until the full packet is reassembled or this timer expires. If set too low, fragmented packets will be dropped, causing network communication failures. If set too high, it consumes more system memory by holding incomplete packets longer. Typical values range from 5000 to 30000 depending on network latency.
IP_DEFRAG_TIMEOUT_MS.usage: Increase this value if you observe packet loss or incomplete data reception in environments with high network latency or congested links. Decrease it if you are running low on heap memory and need to free up buffers faster. Ensure this value is consistent with the expected round-trip time of your network infrastructure.

IP_FLAG_DF.brief: A bitmask flag representing the 'Don't Fragment' (DF) option in the IPv4 header.
IP_FLAG_DF.notes: When this bit is set in the IP header flags field, it instructs routers not to fragment the packet. If the packet size exceeds the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) of the next hop, the router will drop the packet and send an ICMP 'Destination Unreachable' message. This flag is typically used in Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) mechanisms. It has no dependencies on other flags but requires the network stack to handle ICMP error responses correctly.
IP_FLAG_DF.usage: Enable this flag when you need to prevent packet fragmentation to improve network efficiency or to perform Path MTU Discovery. Use it with caution: if the path between your STM32 device and the destination contains a link with a smaller MTU than your packet size, the communication will fail. Ensure your application layer is prepared to handle dropped packets or reduced payload sizes if this flag is active.

IP_FLAG_MF.brief: A bitmask flag representing the 'More Fragments' bit in an IPv4 header.
IP_FLAG_MF.notes: When this bit is set (1), it indicates that the current IP packet is not the last fragment of a larger datagram. When cleared (0), it signifies the last fragment. This flag is used by the network stack's reassembly logic. It is a standard protocol constant defined by RFC 791 and should not be modified manually.
IP_FLAG_MF.usage: Do not change this value as it is defined by the IPv4 protocol specification. It is used internally by the caOS network stack when parsing incoming fragmented packets or constructing outgoing ones. Modifying this will break network compatibility and cause packet reassembly failures.

IP_FRAG_IN_DEPTH.brief: Defines the maximum number of concurrent IP packet fragments the system can track for reassembly.
IP_FRAG_IN_DEPTH.notes: This constant controls the memory allocation for the IP defragmentation buffer. Increasing this value allows the system to handle more fragmented packets simultaneously but consumes more RAM. If the system receives more fragments than this value, incoming fragments will be dropped. Typical values range from 2 to 8 depending on available heap memory.
IP_FRAG_IN_DEPTH.usage: Increase this value if your device experiences packet loss or fails to reassemble large IP packets when receiving traffic from networks with small MTUs. Decrease it if you are running low on system memory and the network traffic is mostly non-fragmented.

IP_FRAG_OFF_MASK.brief: A bitmask used to extract the 13-bit fragment offset field from an IPv4 header.
IP_FRAG_OFF_MASK.notes: The value 0x1FFF represents the 13 bits allocated for the fragment offset in the IP header. This constant is used during packet reassembly to identify the position of a data fragment within the original datagram. It is a fixed protocol constant defined by RFC 791 and should not be modified unless implementing a non-standard IP stack.
IP_FRAG_OFF_MASK.usage: Use this constant when parsing incoming IP packets to isolate the offset value from the flags field. Do not change this value; modifying it will cause the network stack to incorrectly calculate fragment positions, leading to corrupted data reassembly and dropped packets.

IP_FRAG_QUEUE_DEPTH.brief: Defines the maximum number of concurrent IP packet fragments that can be held in the reassembly queue.
IP_FRAG_QUEUE_DEPTH.notes: This constant controls the memory footprint of the IP defragmentation module. Each slot in the queue stores metadata for an incomplete packet. If the queue is full, incoming fragments for new packets will be dropped until existing ones are reassembled or timed out. Typical values range from 8 to 32 depending on available RAM and expected network traffic patterns.
IP_FRAG_QUEUE_DEPTH.usage: Increase this value if your device receives fragmented IP packets from multiple sources simultaneously and you observe packet loss in the IP layer. Decrease this value to save RAM if your device is memory-constrained and only handles minimal fragmentation. Ensure that the system memory pool is sufficient to accommodate the memory overhead associated with this depth.

IP_PROTO_ICMP.brief: Enables or disables the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) stack within the caOS networking layer.
IP_PROTO_ICMP.notes: When set to 1U, the system includes code to process ICMP packets, such as Echo Requests (ping). Disabling it (0U) reduces the firmware binary size and memory footprint by removing ICMP handling logic. This flag is a prerequisite for network diagnostic tools and requires the base IP stack to be enabled.
IP_PROTO_ICMP.usage: Set this to 1U if your device needs to respond to 'ping' requests for network connectivity testing. Disable it (0U) in production environments where you want to minimize the attack surface or save flash memory on resource-constrained STM32 devices.

IP_PROTO_TCP.brief: Defines the protocol number for TCP as specified in the IPv4 header.
IP_PROTO_TCP.notes: This constant is set to 6, which is the IANA-assigned protocol number for TCP. It is used by the network stack to identify incoming packets as TCP segments. Changing this value will cause the stack to fail to recognize TCP traffic, effectively disabling all TCP-based communication.
IP_PROTO_TCP.usage: This value should generally not be changed as it is defined by the Internet Protocol standard. It is used when constructing raw IP packets or filtering incoming traffic. Ensure this matches the standard value of 6 to maintain compatibility with external network devices and standard protocol stacks.

IP_PROTO_UDP.brief: Defines the protocol identifier for the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) within the caOS network stack.
IP_PROTO_UDP.notes: This constant is set to 17U, which is the standard IANA-assigned protocol number for UDP. It is used by the network layer to identify incoming packets and to populate the protocol field in outgoing IP headers. It has no dependencies on other flags but must match the value expected by the underlying hardware abstraction layer (HAL) for packet filtering.
IP_PROTO_UDP.usage: You should never change this value as it is defined by the IPv4 protocol standard. It is used primarily when creating new socket structures or debugging packet headers in the network stack. If you are implementing a custom protocol, do not modify this constant; instead, define a new constant for your specific protocol ID.

IP_TX_MTU_DEFAULT.brief: Defines the default Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) in bytes for outgoing IP packets.
IP_TX_MTU_DEFAULT.notes: This value sets the upper limit for the payload size of an IP packet before fragmentation occurs. It must be less than or equal to the physical interface's maximum frame size (e.g., 1500 for standard Ethernet). Reducing this value can decrease memory usage per buffer but may increase CPU overhead due to packet fragmentation.
IP_TX_MTU_DEFAULT.usage: Adjust this value if your network hardware or specific protocol requirements (such as VPN tunnels or specific link-layer constraints) mandate a smaller MTU. Ensure that the system's memory pool for network buffers is large enough to accommodate this size plus protocol headers; setting this too high without sufficient RAM will lead to buffer overflows or allocation failures.

ITM_BAUDRATE.brief: Defines the transmission speed in bits per second for the Instrumentation Trace Macrocell (ITM) debug output.
ITM_BAUDRATE.notes: This value sets the clock frequency for the SWO (Serial Wire Output) pin. It must match the baud rate configured in your debugger software (e.g., STM32CubeIDE or ST-Link Utility). If the value is too high for your hardware probe or trace clock settings, you will see garbled text or no output in the console. Typical values range from 115200 to 2000000.
ITM_BAUDRATE.usage: Adjust this value if you are experiencing data corruption in your debug logs or if your specific hardware probe requires a lower speed for stability. Ensure that the system core clock (HCLK) is high enough to support the requested baud rate, as the ITM clock is derived from the CPU frequency.

KSTORE_DATE_DAY.brief: Extracts the day component from a packed date value used in the key storage system.
KSTORE_DATE_DAY.notes: This macro performs a bitwise AND operation with 0xFF to isolate the lower 8 bits of a provided date variable. It assumes the date is stored in a packed format where the day occupies the least significant byte. It has no dependencies on other RTOS flags but relies on the input 'v' being a valid packed date integer.
KSTORE_DATE_DAY.usage: Use this macro when retrieving or parsing key metadata from the secure storage. Change this only if the underlying packed date structure changes its bit-field layout. Incorrect usage will result in corrupted date values being returned, potentially causing key expiration logic to fail.

KSTORE_DATE_MONTH.brief: Extracts the month component from a packed 16-bit date value stored in the key management system.
KSTORE_DATE_MONTH.notes: This macro performs a bitwise right shift by 8 bits followed by a mask of 0xFF to isolate the month field. It assumes the input 'v' is a 16-bit integer where the month is stored in the second byte. It has no dependencies on other flags but requires the input data to follow the specific caOS packed date format (typically bits 8-15).
KSTORE_DATE_MONTH.usage: Use this macro when retrieving or validating the expiration date of cryptographic keys stored in the system. Do not modify this macro unless the underlying packed date structure in the key store is redefined. Providing an incorrectly formatted input will result in an invalid month value, potentially causing key validation logic to fail.

KSTORE_DATE_PACK.brief: A macro used to pack a calendar date (year, month, day) into a single 32-bit unsigned integer for efficient storage.
KSTORE_DATE_PACK.notes: The macro performs bit-shifting to place the year in the upper 16 bits, the month in the middle 8 bits, and the day in the lower 8 bits. It requires three arguments (y, m, d). It is typically used in the key management system to timestamp cryptographic keys. Ensure the year value does not exceed 65535 to avoid overflow into other bit fields.
KSTORE_DATE_PACK.usage: Use this macro when you need to store or compare key expiration dates within the caOS key store. It is essential for maintaining a compact memory footprint in the key database. Do not use this for general-purpose date arithmetic, as it is strictly a formatting tool for storage.

KSTORE_DATE_YEAR.brief: Extracts the year component from a packed 32-bit date representation used in the key storage system.
KSTORE_DATE_YEAR.notes: This macro performs a bitwise right shift by 16 bits followed by a mask of 0xFF to isolate the year byte. It assumes the input 'v' is a 32-bit integer where the year is stored in bits 16-23. It is a dependency for any function that validates key expiration dates or performs time-based key rotation logic.
KSTORE_DATE_YEAR.usage: Use this macro when you need to read or verify the year of a key stored in the secure vault. Do not modify the shift or mask values unless the underlying data structure of the key metadata is updated, as incorrect values will result in corrupted date parsing and potential security validation failures.

KSTORE_SVC_IV_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed byte size of the Initialization Vector (IV) used for cryptographic operations within the Keystore Service.
KSTORE_SVC_IV_SIZE.notes: This constant sets the buffer size for IVs in AES-based encryption/decryption routines. Changing this value requires a full recompile of the crypto module and all dependent services. It must match the requirements of the underlying hardware acceleration (e.g., STM32 AES peripheral) or software library implementation. Typical value is 16 bytes for AES-128/256 in CBC or GCM modes.
KSTORE_SVC_IV_SIZE.usage: Modify this only if the security protocol or the underlying cryptographic algorithm requires a different IV length. Setting an incorrect value will cause cryptographic operations to fail with invalid parameter errors or result in corrupted data during decryption. Ensure that the hardware crypto engine supports the new length before changing this constant.

KSTORE_SVC_KEY_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed byte length for cryptographic keys managed by the caOS Keystore Service.
KSTORE_SVC_KEY_SIZE.notes: This constant sets the buffer size for key storage operations. Enabling this ensures memory alignment for AES-256 keys. It must be consistent across all modules accessing the keystore; changing this value requires a full system recompile and may invalidate existing stored keys in non-volatile memory.
KSTORE_SVC_KEY_SIZE.usage: Change this value only if your security requirements dictate a different key length (e.g., 16 for AES-128). Ensure the hardware crypto peripheral supports the new size. Setting this too low will cause truncation errors, while setting it too high will waste precious SRAM and Flash resources.

KSTORE_SVC_LABEL_SIZE.brief: Defines the maximum character length allowed for labels assigned to cryptographic keys in the caOS keystore.
KSTORE_SVC_LABEL_SIZE.notes: This constant sets the fixed-size buffer allocation for key identifiers. Increasing this value will increase the memory footprint of every keystore entry. It must be consistent across all modules that interface with the keystore service to prevent buffer overflows or truncation errors. The default value is 6 bytes.
KSTORE_SVC_LABEL_SIZE.usage: Increase this value if your application requires more descriptive or longer unique names for cryptographic keys. Decrease it only if you are extremely constrained by RAM and your naming convention allows for shorter identifiers. Ensure that any external storage or communication protocols expecting this specific size are updated accordingly to avoid data corruption.

KSTORE_SVC_NONCE_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed byte length of the cryptographic nonce used by the Keystore Service.
KSTORE_SVC_NONCE_SIZE.notes: This constant sets the size of the initialization vector (IV) or nonce for encryption operations. Changing this value affects the memory allocation of internal buffers and the compatibility with external cryptographic standards. It must match the requirements of the underlying cipher suite (e.g., AES-GCM). Typical values are 12 bytes for GCM mode, though it may vary based on the specific security protocol implemented.
KSTORE_SVC_NONCE_SIZE.usage: Modify this value only if the security protocol or the hardware-accelerated cryptographic engine requires a different nonce length. Setting an incorrect value will cause cryptographic operations to fail or result in invalid ciphertext. Ensure that any change is synchronized with the peer devices or backend systems that expect a specific nonce size.

KSTORE_SVC_P1_SIZE.brief: Defines the size in bytes of the primary partition buffer used by the keystore service.
KSTORE_SVC_P1_SIZE.notes: This constant determines the memory allocation for the primary keystore storage slot. Increasing this value allows for larger cryptographic keys or more metadata but directly increases the static RAM footprint of the keystore service. It must be a multiple of the underlying flash page size if the service performs direct hardware writes. Typical values range from 16 to 256 depending on the security module requirements.
KSTORE_SVC_P1_SIZE.usage: Adjust this value when you need to store larger keys (e.g., moving from AES-128 to RSA-2048) or when the keystore service reports buffer overflow errors. Warning: setting this value too low will cause key storage operations to fail, while setting it too high may lead to stack or heap exhaustion in memory-constrained STM32 devices.

KSTORE_SVC_P2_SIZE.brief: Defines the size of the secondary buffer (P2) used by the keystore service for cryptographic operations.
KSTORE_SVC_P2_SIZE.notes: This constant sets the memory allocation in bytes for the secondary keystore processing stage. Increasing this value allows for larger cryptographic payloads or more complex key derivation functions but directly consumes more RAM from the system heap. It must be large enough to accommodate the maximum expected output size of the configured hash or encryption algorithms. Typical values range from 16 to 128 depending on the security requirements.
KSTORE_SVC_P2_SIZE.usage: Adjust this value if you encounter buffer overflow errors or 'insufficient memory' faults during cryptographic operations. Increase it if you switch to stronger encryption standards that require larger intermediate buffers. Do not set this value unnecessarily high to avoid wasting precious RAM on resource-constrained STM32 devices.

KSTORE_SVC_TAG_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed byte size for the authentication tag used in the keystore service cryptographic operations.
KSTORE_SVC_TAG_SIZE.notes: This constant sets the length of the Message Authentication Code (MAC) or tag appended to encrypted data. Changing this value directly affects the memory layout of the keystore storage structures. It must match the tag size expected by the underlying hardware cryptographic peripheral or software library. Typical values are 16 bytes for AES-GCM or similar standards; values other than 16 may cause decryption failures or buffer overflows if the storage buffers are not sized accordingly.
KSTORE_SVC_TAG_SIZE.usage: Change this value only if the security protocol or the cryptographic algorithm used by the keystore service is updated to require a different tag length. Ensure that all existing stored keys are re-encrypted or cleared before changing this value, as a mismatch will render stored data unreadable. Incorrect values will lead to integrity check failures during key retrieval.

LPUART_STD_BAUD.brief: Defines the default baud rate for the Low Power UART (LPUART) peripheral in the caOS RTOS.
LPUART_STD_BAUD.notes: This constant sets the communication speed in bits per second. It directly affects the clock prescaler calculation for the LPUART hardware. Ensure this value matches the baud rate configured on your terminal emulator (e.g., PuTTY or Tera Term). It is typically set to 115200U, but valid ranges depend on the specific STM32 LPUART clock source frequency.
LPUART_STD_BAUD.usage: Change this value if your hardware interface requires a different communication speed (e.g., 9600 or 921600). If you set this incorrectly, you will see garbage characters or no output at all on your serial console. Always verify that the system clock configuration supports the requested baud rate to avoid framing errors.

LPUART_STD_WAKE.brief: Enables the Low-Power UART (LPUART) wake-up capability for the system.
LPUART_STD_WAKE.notes: When set to 1, the LPUART peripheral is configured to trigger an interrupt that wakes the MCU from Stop or Standby power modes upon receiving data. This requires the LPUART clock source to be set to HSI or LSE to remain active during low-power states. If set to 0, the LPUART will not wake the system, potentially causing data loss if the MCU is in a deep sleep state.
LPUART_STD_WAKE.usage: Enable this flag when your application needs to remain in a low-power state while waiting for incoming serial commands. Change this to 0 if you are not using LPUART or if you want to prevent serial traffic from waking the device to save power. Ensure your hardware design supports LPUART wake-up pins before enabling.

LV_BUILD_DEMOS.brief: Enables or disables the compilation of LVGL demonstration widgets and example code.
LV_BUILD_DEMOS.notes: When set to 1, the system includes pre-built LVGL demo applications in the binary. When set to 0 (default), these demos are excluded, significantly reducing the flash memory footprint. This flag does not affect the core LVGL library functionality, only the inclusion of optional sample UI code.
LV_BUILD_DEMOS.usage: Set this to 0 for production builds to save flash space. Set to 1 only during the initial development phase if you need to verify the display driver and LVGL integration using standard reference widgets. Ensure your flash memory partition is large enough before enabling this, as demo code can be quite large.

LV_BUILD_EXAMPLES.brief: Enables or disables the compilation of LVGL demonstration examples.
LV_BUILD_EXAMPLES.notes: When set to 1, the LVGL library includes built-in demo widgets and example code. When set to 0 (default), these examples are excluded, significantly reducing the final binary size and flash memory usage. This flag does not affect the core functionality of the LVGL library itself.
LV_BUILD_EXAMPLES.usage: Set to 0 for production builds to save flash space. Set to 1 only during the initial development phase if you need to verify the display driver or GUI rendering capabilities using pre-built LVGL test screens. Ensure your flash memory budget can accommodate the extra code before enabling.

LV_COLOR_FORMAT_DEFAULT.brief: Defines the default pixel color format used by the LVGL graphics library in caOS.
LV_COLOR_FORMAT_DEFAULT.notes: This constant determines how colors are stored in memory (e.g., 16-bit RGB565). Changing this affects the memory footprint of framebuffers and the performance of pixel-drawing operations. It must match the hardware display controller's capabilities. Valid values include standard LVGL color formats like LV_COLOR_FORMAT_RGB565, LV_COLOR_FORMAT_ARGB8888, etc.
LV_COLOR_FORMAT_DEFAULT.usage: Change this value only if you are porting the system to a new display panel that requires a different color depth or pixel layout. Incorrect values will result in distorted colors or corrupted screen rendering. Ensure that any custom framebuffers allocated via ca_fb_create are compatible with the format defined here.

LV_DEF_REFR_PERIOD.brief: Defines the refresh period in milliseconds for the LVGL graphical interface.
LV_DEF_REFR_PERIOD.notes: This constant determines how often the LVGL task triggers a screen refresh. A value of 33ms corresponds to approximately 30 frames per second (FPS). Lowering this value increases the refresh rate, which makes animations smoother but consumes more CPU cycles and power. Increasing it reduces CPU load but may result in choppy UI updates. It is typically used by the internal LVGL task loop managed by caOS.
LV_DEF_REFR_PERIOD.usage: Adjust this value if you notice screen flickering or if the UI feels sluggish. If the system is under heavy CPU load, increasing this value (e.g., to 50ms) can help free up resources for other tasks. Ensure the value is not set too low, as it may starve other threads of processing time. Use this in conjunction with ca_os_delay if manual task timing is required elsewhere.

LV_DPI_DEF.brief: Defines the default Dots Per Inch (DPI) value for the LVGL graphics library to scale UI elements.
LV_DPI_DEF.notes: This constant determines the physical size of UI components on the display. A value of 130 is typical for medium-density screens. Increasing this value makes UI elements (buttons, text, icons) appear larger, while decreasing it makes them smaller. It is used by LVGL to calculate pixel dimensions from physical measurements. It does not affect the hardware resolution, only the rendering scale.
LV_DPI_DEF.usage: Adjust this value if your UI elements appear too small or too large for the physical screen size. If you change the display hardware to one with a different pixel density, you must recalibrate this value to maintain consistent UI proportions. Incorrect values may cause elements to overlap or become illegible.

LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_A8.brief: Enables software rendering support for 8-bit alpha (A8) color format in LVGL.
LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_A8.notes: When enabled (1), the LVGL library can process and render images or objects using 8-bit alpha channels in software. This increases the binary size and CPU usage during rendering. If disabled (0), A8 support is removed, which saves memory but will cause A8-formatted assets to render incorrectly or not at all. This flag is typically used in conjunction with hardware acceleration (like ca_dma2d) to determine if the software fallback is required.
LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_A8.usage: Enable this if your UI design requires anti-aliased fonts, rounded corners, or semi-transparent images that rely on A8 alpha blending. Disable it only if you are strictly memory-constrained and your UI assets do not use 8-bit alpha transparency, as this will reduce the flash footprint of the graphics stack.

LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_AL88.brief: Enables software-based rendering support for the AL88 (8-bit Alpha, 8-bit Red, 8-bit Green, 8-bit Blue) pixel format in LVGL.
LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_AL88.notes: When set to 1, the system includes code to process AL88 color formats using the CPU. When set to 0 (default), this support is excluded to save flash memory. This flag is specific to the LVGL graphics library integration within caOS. It does not depend on hardware acceleration flags but may increase binary size if enabled.
LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_AL88.usage: Change this to 1 only if your UI design specifically requires the use of AL88 color format images or widgets. If your application does not use AL88, keep it at 0 to minimize the firmware footprint. Warning: Enabling this without a specific need wastes precious flash space on STM32 targets.

LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_ARGB8888.brief: Enables software-based rendering support for 32-bit ARGB8888 color format in LVGL.
LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_ARGB8888.notes: When set to 1, the LVGL library includes code to process and render images or buffers using the 32-bit ARGB8888 pixel format (8 bits each for Alpha, Red, Green, and Blue). This is a software-fallback mechanism. If your STM32 hardware has a dedicated DMA2D peripheral, you should ideally use hardware acceleration via ca_dma2d_blend or ca_dma2d_copy instead of relying on this software support to save CPU cycles. Enabling this increases the binary size (Flash usage).
LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_ARGB8888.usage: Enable this flag if your GUI requires displaying 32-bit color images or using ARGB8888 buffers and you do not have a hardware-accelerated path configured for this specific format. Disable it to reduce code size if your application only uses simpler formats like RGB565 or if all rendering is handled by the ca_dma2d_* API.

LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_I1.brief: Enables software-based support for indexed (I1) color formats in the LVGL graphics library.
LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_I1.notes: When set to 0, the system relies on hardware acceleration (e.g., DMA2D) or assumes the display driver handles indexed color conversion. Enabling this (setting to 1) increases code size as it adds software routines to process 1-bit indexed pixel data. This flag is typically disabled in caOS to prioritize performance and memory efficiency on STM32 targets.
LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_I1.usage: Change this to 1 only if your display driver or specific UI elements require rendering 1-bit indexed images and you lack hardware support for this format. If your application uses standard 16-bit or 32-bit color depths, keep this at 0 to save flash memory.

LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_RGB565.brief: Enables software-based rendering support for the RGB565 color format in the LVGL graphics library.
LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_RGB565.notes: When set to 1, the LVGL engine includes the necessary code to process and render pixels in 16-bit RGB565 format using the CPU. This is required if your display hardware or framebuffer expects this specific color depth. If disabled (0), the system will not be able to render to RGB565 buffers, which may cause graphical artifacts or rendering failures. This flag is typically used in conjunction with ca_dma2d_* functions for hardware-accelerated transfers if the display controller supports it.
LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_RGB565.usage: Set this to 1 if your display module is configured for 16-bit color depth (RGB565). You should only change this if you are porting the application to a new display hardware that uses a different color format (e.g., ARGB8888), in which case you would disable this and enable the corresponding support flag for that format. Ensure your framebuffer allocation in ca_memory_* is sized correctly for 16-bit pixels when this is enabled.

LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_RGB565_SWAPPED.brief: Configures byte-swapping for RGB565 color data in the LVGL software renderer.
LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_RGB565_SWAPPED.notes: When set to 1, the software renderer swaps the high and low bytes of each 16-bit RGB565 pixel. This is typically required when the display controller expects Little-Endian byte order but the frame buffer is stored in Big-Endian (or vice versa). It has no effect if hardware acceleration (DMA2D) is used for rendering. Valid values are 0 (disabled) or 1 (enabled).
LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_RGB565_SWAPPED.usage: Change this value to 1 if your display shows incorrect colors (e.g., red and blue channels appear swapped or colors look inverted) despite the display driver being correctly initialized. If the colors are correct, leave this at 0 to avoid unnecessary CPU overhead during pixel processing.

LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_RGB888.brief: Enables or disables software rendering support for the RGB888 color format in the LVGL graphics library.
LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_RGB888.notes: When set to 1, the system includes software routines to process 24-bit RGB888 colors. When set to 0 (default), this support is excluded to save flash memory. This flag is specific to the LVGL integration within caOS. If your display driver or UI requires RGB888 and hardware acceleration (e.g., ca_dma2d) is not configured to handle this format, you must enable this flag to avoid rendering artifacts or blank screens.
LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_RGB888.usage: Change this to 1 only if you are using a display buffer configured for 24-bit color depth and you notice that UI elements are not rendering correctly. Warning: Enabling this increases the binary size significantly. If you are constrained by flash memory, keep this at 0 and ensure your display is configured for a supported format like RGB565.

LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_XRGB8888.brief: Enables software-based rendering support for XRGB8888 pixel format in LVGL.
LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_XRGB8888.notes: When set to 1, the LVGL library includes code to process 32-bit XRGB8888 color data using the CPU. When set to 0 (default), this support is disabled to save code space. This flag is independent of hardware acceleration (like ca_dma2d) but may be required if your display driver or frame buffer expects this specific color depth and you are not using hardware-accelerated blitting.
LV_DRAW_SW_SUPPORT_XRGB8888.usage: Enable this (set to 1) only if your application specifically requires rendering or manipulating XRGB8888 images in software and you are experiencing missing colors or rendering artifacts. Keep it disabled (0) for most STM32 projects to minimize the binary size, especially if you rely on ca_dma2d for pixel operations.

LV_FONT_DEFAULT.brief: Sets the default font used by the LVGL graphics library in caOS.
LV_FONT_DEFAULT.notes: This constant defines the global font pointer used by LVGL widgets when no specific font is assigned. It must point to a valid lv_font_t structure defined in the LVGL font library. Changing this affects the memory footprint of the application, as larger fonts consume more Flash memory and RAM for glyph caching. Ensure the selected font is enabled in your LVGL configuration.
LV_FONT_DEFAULT.usage: Change this value when you need to adjust the UI readability or optimize memory usage. Use a smaller font (e.g., lv_font_montserrat_10) if you are running low on Flash memory or need to fit more text on a small display. Use a larger font if the display resolution is high or if the text is difficult to read. Always verify that the new font pointer is correctly linked and available in the project build.

LV_FONT_MONTSERRAT_14.brief: Enables the inclusion of the Montserrat 14-point font in the LVGL graphics library.
LV_FONT_MONTSERRAT_14.notes: When set to 1, the font data is compiled into the binary, increasing the flash memory footprint. This flag is a dependency for UI elements configured to use this specific font size. If disabled (0), any UI component attempting to use this font will fail to render text correctly or may cause a runtime error in the LVGL rendering engine.
LV_FONT_MONTSERRAT_14.usage: Enable this flag when your GUI design requires a 14px Montserrat font. If your application is running low on flash memory and you do not use this specific font size, set this to 0 to save space. Ensure that your LVGL style definitions match the enabled fonts to avoid rendering issues.

LV_FONT_MONTSERRAT_16.brief: Enables the inclusion of the 16-point Montserrat font in the LVGL graphics library.
LV_FONT_MONTSERRAT_16.notes: When set to 1, the font data is compiled into the firmware binary, increasing the flash memory footprint. This flag is a dependency for UI elements that require this specific font size. If disabled (0), any attempt to use this font in an LVGL style will result in a rendering error or a fallback to a default font.
LV_FONT_MONTSERRAT_16.usage: Enable this when your UI design requires a 16px Montserrat font for labels or text areas. If your application is running low on flash memory, consider disabling unused font sizes to save space. Ensure that your LVGL style definitions are updated to reference this font only when this flag is enabled.

LV_FONT_MONTSERRAT_20.brief: Enables the inclusion of the Montserrat 20pt font in the LVGL library.
LV_FONT_MONTSERRAT_20.notes: When set to 1, the Montserrat 20 font data is compiled into the firmware, increasing the flash memory footprint. If set to 0, this font will not be available for UI rendering. This flag is a dependency for any UI elements configured to use this specific font size.
LV_FONT_MONTSERRAT_20.usage: Enable this flag when your graphical interface requires a 20pt Montserrat font for text display. If your application is running low on flash memory and you do not use this font size, set it to 0 to save space. Ensure that your LVGL style definitions match the enabled fonts to avoid rendering errors.

LV_MEM_POOL_ALLOC.brief: Configures the memory allocation function used by the LVGL graphics library within caOS.
LV_MEM_POOL_ALLOC.notes: This constant defines the function pointer or macro that LVGL calls to allocate memory. By setting this to 'caos_lvgl_pool_alloc', you redirect LVGL's internal memory requests to the caOS memory pool manager. This ensures that graphics memory is tracked and managed by the caOS kernel rather than the standard C library heap. It requires that the caOS memory pool is properly initialized before the LVGL library is started.
LV_MEM_POOL_ALLOC.usage: Change this value when you need to switch between different memory allocation strategies (e.g., using a dedicated static pool vs. dynamic system heap). Use this to solve 'out of memory' errors in the GUI or to prevent heap fragmentation. Warning: ensure the pool size is sufficient for your UI complexity; if the allocation fails, the GUI may fail to render or the system may trigger a fault.

LV_MEM_POOL_INCLUDE.brief: Specifies the header file containing custom memory pool configurations for the LVGL graphics library.
LV_MEM_POOL_INCLUDE.notes: This constant defines the path to a header file that overrides default LVGL memory allocation settings. It is essential for integrating LVGL with the caOS memory management system (e.g., ca_memory_allocate). If this file is missing or incorrectly named, the build will fail during the LVGL compilation phase. It typically points to 'caos_lvgl_port.h' where custom macros for LV_MEM_CUSTOM are defined.
LV_MEM_POOL_INCLUDE.usage: Change this value only if you are porting LVGL to a new hardware target or changing the memory management strategy for the GUI. Ensure the file specified exists in the include path. Incorrect values will cause the graphics library to fail to initialize its memory heap, leading to hard faults or undefined behavior when creating UI widgets.

LV_MEM_SIZE.brief: Defines the total amount of RAM (in bytes) allocated for the LVGL graphics library heap.
LV_MEM_SIZE.notes: This constant reserves a static block of memory from the system heap for LVGL objects (widgets, styles, buffers). If this value is too small, LVGL will fail to allocate memory for new UI elements, potentially causing the UI to freeze or crash. It is independent of the general caOS system heap but consumes a portion of the total available RAM on the STM32.
LV_MEM_SIZE.usage: Increase this value if your UI becomes complex (many widgets, large images, or animations) and you encounter memory allocation errors. Decrease it if your application is running low on total system RAM and the UI is simple. Ensure the value is a multiple of 4 to maintain memory alignment. Monitor usage using ca_top or by checking the return values of UI creation functions.

LV_USE_ASSERT_MALLOC.brief: Enables runtime assertions for memory allocation operations within the LVGL library.
LV_USE_ASSERT_MALLOC.notes: When set to 1, the system will trigger a hard fault or a controlled system halt if an LVGL memory allocation (malloc) returns a NULL pointer. This is a debugging feature that helps catch out-of-memory conditions immediately. It has no dependencies on other flags but relies on the underlying ca_memory_* system. Typical value is 1 during development and 0 for production builds to save code space and avoid unnecessary halts.
LV_USE_ASSERT_MALLOC.usage: Enable this during the development phase to detect memory exhaustion or heap fragmentation issues early. If your application crashes with this enabled, use ca_memory_info() or ca_memory_dump() to inspect the heap state. Disable this in final production firmware to prevent the system from halting if a non-critical UI component fails to allocate memory.

LV_USE_ASSERT_NULL.brief: Enables assertion checks for null pointers within the LVGL graphics library integration.
LV_USE_ASSERT_NULL.notes: When set to 1, the system will trigger an assertion if a null pointer is passed to an LVGL function. This helps catch bugs early during development. It has no dependencies on other flags but relies on the underlying caOS assertion handling mechanism. Typical value is 1 for debug builds and 0 for production builds to save code space and execution time.
LV_USE_ASSERT_NULL.usage: Enable this during the development and testing phase to identify invalid memory access or uninitialized object pointers before they cause hard faults. Disable it in final production firmware to optimize performance and reduce binary size, provided that your application logic is verified to be stable.

LV_USE_FLOAT.brief: Enables or disables floating-point number support in the LVGL graphics library.
LV_USE_FLOAT.notes: When set to 0 (disabled), LVGL will use fixed-point arithmetic for calculations. Enabling this (set to 1) allows the use of float types in UI elements, which increases code size and requires the FPU (Floating Point Unit) to be enabled on the STM32 for optimal performance. If your hardware lacks an FPU, enabling this will significantly slow down UI rendering.
LV_USE_FLOAT.usage: Change this to 1 only if your UI design specifically requires floating-point precision for animations, complex coordinate calculations, or data visualization. For most standard embedded UIs, keep it at 0 to save flash memory and CPU cycles. If you encounter compilation errors related to 'float' or 'double' types within LVGL widgets, verify this flag is enabled.

LV_USE_OS.brief: Configures the OS abstraction layer for the LVGL graphics library.
LV_USE_OS.notes: When set to LV_OS_NONE, LVGL runs in a single-threaded, non-preemptive mode. This means LVGL functions are not thread-safe and must be called from a single task or within a critical section using ca_enter_critical and ca_exit_critical. If you need to call LVGL functions from multiple caOS tasks, you must change this to a value that supports OS synchronization primitives.
LV_USE_OS.usage: Change this value if you are implementing a multi-threaded GUI where different tasks need to update the display or handle input events simultaneously. If you change this from LV_OS_NONE, ensure you have configured the corresponding OS-specific hooks in lv_conf.h to allow LVGL to use ca_mutex or ca_sem for internal resource protection.

LV_USE_PERF_MONITOR.brief: Enables or disables the LVGL performance monitor overlay on the display.
LV_USE_PERF_MONITOR.notes: When set to 1, LVGL renders a small box showing CPU usage and frame rate (FPS) on the screen. This feature consumes additional CPU cycles and memory bandwidth. It is typically disabled (0) in production builds to save resources and improve aesthetics. It has no direct dependencies on other caOS modules but requires an active display driver initialized via ca_fb_* functions.
LV_USE_PERF_MONITOR.usage: Change this to 1 during the development and debugging phase to monitor UI responsiveness and identify performance bottlenecks. Always set it back to 0 before deploying the firmware to the end user to ensure optimal performance and a clean user interface.

LV_USE_STDLIB_SPRINTF.brief: Configures the standard library implementation used by LVGL for string formatting functions like sprintf.
LV_USE_STDLIB_SPRINTF.notes: When set to LV_STDLIB_BUILTIN, LVGL uses its own internal, lightweight implementation of sprintf. This avoids dependencies on the C standard library (libc) provided by the compiler, which is often larger and may not be thread-safe in embedded environments. This flag is independent of caOS core functions like ca_printf, but ensures LVGL remains self-contained.
LV_USE_STDLIB_SPRINTF.usage: Keep this set to LV_STDLIB_BUILTIN for most STM32 projects to minimize binary size and avoid potential linker conflicts with the system's libc. Change this only if you specifically need advanced formatting features (like floating-point support) not provided by the built-in version, and ensure your project is configured to handle the resulting increase in memory usage.

LV_USE_STDLIB_STRING.brief: Configures whether LVGL uses the standard C library or caOS internal functions for string operations.
LV_USE_STDLIB_STRING.notes: When set to LV_STDLIB_BUILTIN, LVGL will use caOS-provided functions (e.g., ca_memcpy, ca_strlen, ca_strcmp) instead of standard <string.h> functions. This is mandatory in caOS to ensure memory safety and compatibility with the RTOS memory management system. Do not change this to LV_STDLIB_CLIB unless specifically instructed, as it may cause memory corruption or linker errors.
LV_USE_STDLIB_STRING.usage: Keep this set to LV_STDLIB_BUILTIN for all caOS projects. If you encounter 'undefined reference' errors for standard string functions during compilation, verify this flag is set correctly in lv_conf.h.
