Changing this value is only necessary if you are porting external libraries that strictly require standard C library behavior, which is generally discouraged in this environment.

MAX.brief: A macro that returns the greater of two provided values.
MAX.notes: This is a standard ternary-based comparison macro. It evaluates both arguments, so avoid passing expressions with side effects (e.g., 'MAX(x++, y)') as they will be executed twice. It is type-agnostic but relies on the compiler to handle implicit type promotion between the two arguments.
MAX.usage: Use this for calculating buffer sizes, timeout durations, or threshold comparisons. Always ensure the arguments are of compatible types to prevent unexpected compiler warnings or truncation errors. Avoid using this with function calls that modify global state.

MAX_SECURE_KEYS.brief: Defines the maximum number of cryptographic keys that can be stored in the caOS secure key vault.
MAX_SECURE_KEYS.notes: This constant determines the size of the static array allocated in RAM for key management. Increasing this value consumes more memory (sizeof(key_t) * MAX_SECURE_KEYS). It must be greater than or equal to the total number of unique keys required by your application tasks. If set too low, key registration functions will return an error code (ERR_KEY_STORAGE_FULL).
MAX_SECURE_KEYS.usage: Increase this value if your application needs to handle more concurrent encrypted connections or secure storage slots than the default 20. Ensure that your STM32 device has sufficient RAM before increasing this limit, as it directly impacts the heap/static memory footprint.

MAX_TASK.brief: Defines the maximum number of concurrent tasks allowed in the caOS scheduler.
MAX_TASK.notes: This constant determines the size of the internal Task Control Block (TCB) array. Increasing this value consumes more static RAM, as each task requires a dedicated memory slot regardless of whether it is currently active. It must be set to a value greater than or equal to the total number of tasks created in your application. If you attempt to create more tasks than this limit, the system will trigger an assertion or return an error code during initialization.
MAX_TASK.usage: Adjust this value when adding or removing tasks from your project. Set it to the exact number of tasks you intend to run plus a small buffer for future expansion. Do not set this value excessively high, as it will waste precious RAM on your STM32 microcontroller. Always verify that your total RAM usage remains within the limits of your specific MCU model after increasing this constant.

MAX_TIMER.brief: Defines the maximum number of software timers that can be active simultaneously in the caOS system.
MAX_TIMER.notes: This constant allocates a static array in memory to track timer control blocks. Increasing this value consumes more RAM (sizeof(Timer_t) * MAX_TIMER). It is hardware-dependent; higher-performance MCUs like the H7 series support more timers due to larger memory availability. Ensure this value is greater than or equal to the total number of unique software timers initialized in your application code.
MAX_TIMER.usage: Increase this value if your application requires more concurrent software timers and you encounter 'Timer Allocation Failed' errors during runtime. Decrease it if you need to optimize RAM usage on memory-constrained devices like the F103. Do not set this value arbitrarily high, as it wastes static memory.

MAX_TOTAL_KEY_STORAGE.brief: Defines the maximum total memory in bytes allocated for storing cryptographic keys within the system.
MAX_TOTAL_KEY_STORAGE.notes: This constant determines the static buffer size for the key management module. Increasing this value consumes more RAM from the heap or static data segment. It must be large enough to accommodate the sum of all individual key sizes plus internal metadata overhead. If set too low, key registration functions will return an 'out of memory' error.
MAX_TOTAL_KEY_STORAGE.usage: Adjust this value when your application needs to store more keys or larger key types (e.g., switching from AES-128 to RSA-2048). Ensure the total size does not exceed the available RAM on your STM32 target. Always verify that the system heap remains sufficient for other RTOS tasks after increasing this constant.

MCU_HAS_ETH.brief: A boolean flag indicating whether the target microcontroller hardware includes an integrated Ethernet MAC peripheral.
MCU_HAS_ETH.notes: When set to 1U, the caOS network stack and hardware abstraction layer (HAL) will initialize Ethernet-related registers and interrupt vectors. When set to 0U, these features are disabled to save memory and prevent illegal memory access. This flag must match the specific STM32 part number; enabling it on a chip without an Ethernet controller will cause a hard fault during system initialization.
MCU_HAS_ETH.usage: Change this value only when porting the project to a different STM32 MCU variant. If your application requires network connectivity, ensure this is set to 1U for supported chips (e.g., F407, H7 series). If you are using a chip without Ethernet (e.g., F103, F446), this must remain 0U, or the build will fail during the linking stage due to missing peripheral definitions.

MCU_HAS_GPDMA.brief: A boolean flag indicating if the target microcontroller includes a General Purpose Direct Memory Access (GPDMA) controller.
MCU_HAS_GPDMA.notes: When set to 1U, the caOS kernel enables support for the GPDMA peripheral, which is distinct from the older DMA controllers found in F4/F7 series. Enabling this requires the hardware to support the GPDMA architecture (e.g., STM32H5 series). If set to 0U, the system will use standard DMA or polling methods. This flag is hardware-dependent and must match the specific MCU datasheet.
MCU_HAS_GPDMA.usage: Change this value only when porting caOS to a new STM32 series. Set to 1U if your MCU features the newer GPDMA block to allow the OS to offload data transfers efficiently. Setting this to 1U on an MCU that lacks GPDMA will result in compilation errors or hard faults during peripheral initialization.

MCU_HAS_QSPI.brief: A boolean flag indicating if the target STM32 microcontroller features a hardware Quad-SPI (QSPI) peripheral.
MCU_HAS_QSPI.notes: When set to 1U, the caOS kernel enables drivers and memory-mapped access routines for external QSPI flash memory. When set to 0U, these features are disabled to save code space and prevent compilation errors on MCUs lacking the peripheral. This flag must match the specific hardware capabilities of the selected MCU; enabling it on an unsupported chip will cause linker errors or hard faults.
MCU_HAS_QSPI.usage: Set this to 1U only if your specific STM32 model includes a QSPI controller and you intend to interface with external flash memory. If you are using an F103 or F407 series chip, this must remain 0U. Always verify your MCU datasheet's peripheral list before changing this value to avoid undefined behavior.

MCU_HAS_RNG.brief: A boolean flag indicating whether the target STM32 microcontroller has a built-in hardware Random Number Generator (RNG) peripheral.
MCU_HAS_RNG.notes: When set to 1U, the caOS kernel will utilize the hardware RNG for entropy-based features such as secure task stack canaries or cryptographic seeding. If set to 0U, the system will fall back to a software-based pseudo-random number generator or disable RNG-dependent features. This flag must match the specific hardware capabilities of the MCU defined in the datasheet; enabling it on an MCU without an RNG peripheral will cause a hard fault or undefined behavior during peripheral initialization.
MCU_HAS_RNG.usage: Set this value based on the specific STM32 series being used. You should change this only when porting the project to a different MCU model. If you are unsure, check the 'Reference Manual' for your specific STM32 part under the 'RNG' section. Incorrect configuration will lead to initialization errors or failure of security-related features.

MCU_HAS_USB.brief: A hardware abstraction flag that indicates whether the target STM32 microcontroller includes a built-in USB peripheral.
MCU_HAS_USB.notes: When set to 1U, the caOS kernel enables USB-related drivers and memory allocation for USB stacks. When set to 0U, all USB-related code is excluded from the build to save flash memory. This flag is strictly dependent on the specific MCU part number; enabling it on an MCU without USB hardware will cause compilation errors or hard faults during peripheral initialization.
MCU_HAS_USB.usage: Change this value only when porting caOS to a new STM32 chip. You must set this to 1U if your application requires USB communication (e.g., CDC, HID, or MSC). If you are working on a chip like the F103, ensure this is set to 0U to prevent the compiler from attempting to access non-existent USB registers.

MCU_NO_ETH.brief: A configuration flag that disables the Ethernet peripheral driver and stack within the caOS RTOS.
MCU_NO_ETH.notes: When set to 1, the Ethernet hardware abstraction layer and associated network buffers are excluded from the build. This reduces the memory footprint (RAM and Flash) and prevents the RTOS from attempting to initialize non-existent or unused network hardware. It is independent of other peripherals but must be set to 1 for STM32 models like F103 and F446 that lack integrated Ethernet MAC controllers.
MCU_NO_ETH.usage: Set this to 1 for any STM32 target that does not have a built-in Ethernet peripheral to avoid compilation errors or runtime faults. You should only set this to 0 if you are using a specific MCU variant that supports Ethernet and you intend to use the networking stack. Setting this to 0 on an unsupported MCU will lead to undefined behavior or hard faults during system initialization.

MDNS_CACHE_FLUSH.brief: Defines the bitmask flag used to trigger an immediate flush of the mDNS resource record cache.
MDNS_CACHE_FLUSH.notes: When this flag is set in the mDNS control register, the system clears all cached mDNS entries to force a re-discovery of network services. It is a bitwise constant (0x8000U) and should be used in conjunction with the mDNS command interface. It has no dependencies on other flags but requires the mDNS stack to be initialized.
MDNS_CACHE_FLUSH.usage: Use this flag when you need to resolve stale network service information or after a significant network topology change. Do not set this flag continuously in a loop, as it will cause excessive network traffic and CPU overhead due to constant re-querying of the local network.

MDNS_DST_IP.brief: Defines the IPv4 multicast destination address used for mDNS (Multicast DNS) service discovery packets.
MDNS_DST_IP.notes: The value represents the standard mDNS multicast address 224.0.0.251 in an array format. Modifying this will cause the device to stop responding to or sending mDNS queries on the standard network, effectively isolating it from local service discovery. It must remain as {224U, 0U, 0U, 251U} for standard network compatibility.
MDNS_DST_IP.usage: Change this only if you are operating on a non-standard, isolated network that requires a custom multicast group for service discovery. Incorrect values will result in the device being invisible to other network nodes using standard mDNS protocols.

MDNS_DST_MAC.brief: Defines the standard IPv4 multicast MAC address used for mDNS discovery packets.
MDNS_DST_MAC.notes: This constant represents the IEEE 802.3 multicast address 01:00:5E:00:00:FB. It is required by the network stack to filter incoming mDNS traffic at the hardware level. Changing this value will cause the device to stop receiving mDNS queries and announcements, effectively making the device invisible to network discovery services.
MDNS_DST_MAC.usage: Do not modify this value unless you are implementing a custom or non-standard multicast protocol. It is used by the caOS network driver to configure the Ethernet MAC address filter. Ensure that the hardware peripheral is initialized to accept this multicast group, otherwise, the stack will not process mDNS packets.

MDNS_PORT.brief: Defines the UDP port number used for mDNS (Multicast DNS) service discovery.
MDNS_PORT.notes: This constant sets the destination port for mDNS packets. It must be set to 5353 to comply with the RFC 6762 standard. Changing this value will prevent the device from being discovered by standard mDNS clients like Bonjour or Avahi. It is a dependency for the caOS network stack's zero-configuration networking module.
MDNS_PORT.usage: Keep this value at 5353U for standard network interoperability. Only change this value if you are operating in a private, isolated network environment that requires a non-standard port for custom service discovery protocols. Incorrect values will result in the device becoming invisible to network discovery tools.

MDNS_TTL.brief: Defines the Time-To-Live (TTL) value in seconds for mDNS resource records.
MDNS_TTL.notes: This constant determines how long network peers should cache the mDNS service information before re-querying. The value is an unsigned integer, typically set to 120 seconds. Lowering this value increases network traffic due to more frequent queries, while increasing it reduces traffic but may cause stale service information if the device IP or status changes.
MDNS_TTL.usage: Adjust this value if your device frequently changes its network configuration or if you notice other devices on the network failing to discover your service after a reconnection. A value of 120 is a standard balance for most local networks; avoid setting this to extremely low values (e.g., < 10) to prevent network congestion.

MICROPY_ALLOC_PATH_MAX.brief: Defines the maximum length in bytes for file system paths used by the MicroPython interpreter.
MICROPY_ALLOC_PATH_MAX.notes: This constant sets the buffer size for path strings (e.g., '/flash/main.py'). Increasing this value consumes more stack memory during file operations. It is typically set to 128 bytes, which is sufficient for most embedded file system structures. If you encounter 'OSError: [Errno 2] ENOENT' or path truncation errors when accessing deeply nested directories, you may need to increase this value, provided your task stack size can accommodate the larger buffer.
MICROPY_ALLOC_PATH_MAX.usage: Change this value only if your application requires deep directory nesting or long filenames that exceed the current 128-character limit. Always verify that your task stack (configured via ca_os_*) is large enough to handle the increased memory usage before increasing this constant.

MICROPY_CONFIG_ROM_LEVEL.brief: Defines the level of MicroPython features included in the caOS build.
MICROPY_CONFIG_ROM_LEVEL.notes: This constant controls the size and capability of the MicroPython interpreter. 'MICROPY_CONFIG_ROM_LEVEL_CORE_FEATURES' is the standard setting, providing essential language features. Increasing this level adds more advanced modules and built-in functions, which increases the memory footprint (Flash and RAM). Decreasing it may remove standard library support.
MICROPY_CONFIG_ROM_LEVEL.usage: Change this value when you need to optimize memory usage or require specific advanced Python features. If your application runs out of memory, consider reducing this level. If you are missing standard Python modules, you may need to increase it. Ensure your hardware has sufficient Flash/RAM before increasing the level.

MICROPY_ENABLE_EXTERNAL_IMPORT.brief: Enables the ability to import external Python modules from the filesystem within the MicroPython environment.
MICROPY_ENABLE_EXTERNAL_IMPORT.notes: When enabled (1), MicroPython can load .py or .mpy files from the storage mounted via ca_fat. When disabled (0), only built-in modules are available. This flag requires the ca_fat service to be initialized and mounted to function correctly. Enabling this increases the memory footprint of the MicroPython interpreter.
MICROPY_ENABLE_EXTERNAL_IMPORT.usage: Set to 1 if your application needs to load scripts dynamically from an SD card or internal flash storage. Set to 0 to save memory and reduce the attack surface if your application only uses pre-compiled, built-in Python code.

MICROPY_ENABLE_GC.brief: Enables or disables the MicroPython Garbage Collector (GC) within the caOS environment.
MICROPY_ENABLE_GC.notes: When set to (1), the system automatically reclaims memory occupied by unreachable Python objects. Disabling this (0) forces manual memory management or results in memory exhaustion over time. This flag is a core dependency for MicroPython functionality; disabling it may cause runtime errors in scripts that allocate objects. Typical value is (1).
MICROPY_ENABLE_GC.usage: Enable this to allow dynamic memory allocation in Python scripts. Disable it only in highly constrained, deterministic systems where you perform all allocations at startup and never create new objects during runtime to avoid non-deterministic GC pauses. Warning: If disabled, ensure your code does not trigger any allocation, or the system will crash.

MICROPY_ENABLE_SCHEDULER.brief: Enables the MicroPython scheduler integration within the caOS RTOS environment.
MICROPY_ENABLE_SCHEDULER.notes: When set to (1), the MicroPython VM can defer execution of tasks or callbacks to the caOS scheduler. This is essential for handling asynchronous events (like interrupts or network callbacks) safely within the MicroPython interpreter. Disabling it (0) will prevent MicroPython from using the RTOS task-switching mechanisms, which may lead to race conditions or missed events in complex applications.
MICROPY_ENABLE_SCHEDULER.usage: Keep this enabled (1) for any project using MicroPython on caOS. Only disable it if you are running a strictly single-threaded, non-interrupt-driven MicroPython script and need to save a small amount of memory or CPU cycles. If you encounter 'RuntimeError: scheduler not enabled' or similar issues when using callbacks, ensure this flag is set to (1).

MICROPY_ENABLE_SOURCE_LINE.brief: Enables the inclusion of source file line numbers in MicroPython error tracebacks.
MICROPY_ENABLE_SOURCE_LINE.notes: When enabled (1), MicroPython stores line number information for bytecode, which increases the memory footprint of the compiled scripts. When disabled (0), this information is omitted, saving RAM and Flash space. This flag is a standard MicroPython configuration option used within the caOS port.
MICROPY_ENABLE_SOURCE_LINE.usage: Enable this during development and debugging to easily identify the exact location of runtime errors in your Python scripts. Disable it in production environments if you are running low on memory and do not require detailed error reporting.

MICROPY_ERROR_REPORTING.brief: Controls the level of detail provided in MicroPython error messages.
MICROPY_ERROR_REPORTING.notes: This flag determines how much information is printed when a Python script encounters an error. MICROPY_ERROR_REPORTING_NORMAL provides basic error information, while higher levels (like _TERSE or _FULL) adjust the verbosity. It affects the memory footprint of the MicroPython engine, as more descriptive error strings consume more flash memory.
MICROPY_ERROR_REPORTING.usage: Change this value during development to debug complex script failures by setting it to a more verbose level. In production environments with limited flash space, keep it at MICROPY_ERROR_REPORTING_NORMAL or lower to save memory. Do not use higher levels in production if the device has strict memory constraints.

MICROPY_FLOAT_IMPL.brief: Defines the implementation method for floating-point numbers in the MicroPython environment.
MICROPY_FLOAT_IMPL.notes: This constant determines whether MicroPython uses hardware-accelerated floating-point (MICROPY_FLOAT_IMPL_FLOAT) or software emulation. Setting this to MICROPY_FLOAT_IMPL_FLOAT enables the use of the STM32 FPU (Floating Point Unit). It is typically set to MICROPY_FLOAT_IMPL_FLOAT for performance-critical applications on STM32 chips that include a hardware FPU.
MICROPY_FLOAT_IMPL.usage: Change this value if you need to switch between hardware-accelerated math (for speed) and software-based math (for compatibility or if the specific STM32 model lacks an FPU). Incorrect values may lead to compilation errors or significant performance degradation in floating-point calculations. Use MICROPY_FLOAT_IMPL_FLOAT when the target hardware supports it to ensure efficient execution of ca_upy_* functions that involve math.

MICROPY_GCREGS_SETJMP.brief: Configures whether MicroPython uses setjmp/longjmp for garbage collection register preservation.
MICROPY_GCREGS_SETJMP.notes: When set to 0 (disabled), MicroPython uses architecture-specific assembly to save registers during GC. When set to 1 (enabled), it uses the standard C library setjmp/longjmp functions. This flag is typically 0 on STM32 ports to avoid overhead and dependency on libc implementation details. It does not require other flags but affects how the stack is scanned for root pointers.
MICROPY_GCREGS_SETJMP.usage: Keep this at 0 for standard STM32 caOS deployments. Only change to 1 if you encounter specific issues with register state corruption during garbage collection that cannot be resolved by stack alignment or compiler optimization settings. Warning: enabling this may increase code size and slightly degrade performance due to the overhead of setjmp.

MICROPY_HELPER_REPL.brief: Enables the interactive MicroPython REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) interface.
MICROPY_HELPER_REPL.notes: When set to 1, the system initializes the MicroPython command-line interface, allowing real-time code execution and debugging via the console. Disabling it (0) removes the REPL overhead, saving flash memory and RAM. This flag is a prerequisite for using the ca_upy_* API functions effectively in an interactive environment.
MICROPY_HELPER_REPL.usage: Enable this during the development and debugging phase to interact with the system via the serial console. Disable it in production firmware to reduce the attack surface and reclaim memory resources. Ensure that your console communication (e.g., ca_uart_*) is properly initialized before enabling this flag.

MICROPY_HW_BOARD_NAME.brief: Defines the human-readable name of the hardware board for the MicroPython environment.
MICROPY_HW_BOARD_NAME.notes: This string is used by the MicroPython REPL and system information commands to identify the specific hardware platform. It does not affect the underlying RTOS kernel or hardware drivers, but it is critical for identifying the board in logs and remote management tools. Typical value is a string literal representing the board model.
MICROPY_HW_BOARD_NAME.usage: Change this value when porting the caOS firmware to a new hardware revision or a different STM32 board. Ensure the string is descriptive enough to distinguish between different hardware configurations in your fleet. Example: #define MICROPY_HW_BOARD_NAME "STM32F4-Discovery-v2"

MICROPY_HW_MCU_NAME.brief: Defines the hardware platform name string for the MicroPython port.
MICROPY_HW_MCU_NAME.notes: This constant is a string literal used by the MicroPython environment to identify the underlying MCU architecture. It does not affect the low-level RTOS kernel behavior, but it is used for system identification and reporting. It is typically set to 'STM32' for all STM32-based caOS targets.
MICROPY_HW_MCU_NAME.usage: Change this value only if you are porting caOS to a different hardware architecture (e.g., 'ESP32' or 'RP2040'). Do not modify this for standard STM32 development as it may break platform-specific identification logic in the MicroPython REPL or system diagnostic tools.

MICROPY_KBD_EXCEPTION.brief: Enables the ability to interrupt a running MicroPython script using a keyboard interrupt signal (Ctrl+C).
MICROPY_KBD_EXCEPTION.notes: When enabled (1), the MicroPython interpreter checks for a keyboard interrupt character in the input stream. If detected, it raises a KeyboardInterrupt exception within the script. This flag is typically used in interactive REPL environments. Disabling it (0) saves a small amount of processing overhead and prevents users from stopping scripts via the console.
MICROPY_KBD_EXCEPTION.usage: Set this to 1 during development to allow easy termination of infinite loops or hung scripts in the MicroPython REPL. Set to 0 in production firmware to prevent accidental or malicious interruption of critical background tasks running via MicroPython.

MICROPY_LONGINT_IMPL.brief: Configures the implementation method for arbitrary-precision integers in MicroPython.
MICROPY_LONGINT_IMPL.notes: When set to MICROPY_LONGINT_IMPL_MPZ, MicroPython uses the MPZ library to handle integers of arbitrary size. This is the most flexible option but consumes more heap memory and CPU cycles compared to fixed-size integer implementations. It is a dependency for scripts requiring large number arithmetic (e.g., cryptography or complex math).
MICROPY_LONGINT_IMPL.usage: Change this value only if you need to optimize memory usage for a system that strictly uses small integers (e.g., changing to MICROPY_LONGINT_IMPL_NONE or _LONGLONG). Warning: switching away from MPZ will cause runtime errors if your Python scripts attempt to perform operations resulting in integers larger than the native machine word size.

MICROPY_PY_BUILTINS_BYTES_HEX.brief: Enables the bytes.fromhex() and bytes.hex() methods in the MicroPython environment.
MICROPY_PY_BUILTINS_BYTES_HEX.notes: When set to (1), the MicroPython interpreter includes built-in support for converting between byte strings and their hexadecimal string representations. This feature consumes a small amount of additional flash memory. It has no direct dependencies on other caOS hardware drivers but is a standard component of the MicroPython core library.
MICROPY_PY_BUILTINS_BYTES_HEX.usage: Enable this flag if your application needs to parse hex-encoded configuration strings or format binary data for transmission over protocols like UART or MQTT. If your application is strictly memory-constrained and does not perform hex-to-binary conversions, you may set this to (0) to save a small amount of flash space.

MICROPY_PY_GC.brief: Enables the MicroPython Garbage Collector (GC) within the caOS environment.
MICROPY_PY_GC.notes: When set to 1, the system automatically reclaims memory used by unreachable Python objects. Disabling this (0) will cause the system to leak memory until it runs out, leading to crashes. This flag is a core dependency for the MicroPython interpreter; it should almost always remain enabled in production firmware.
MICROPY_PY_GC.usage: Keep this enabled (1) for all standard MicroPython applications. You might only disable it (0) during low-level debugging of memory allocation issues or if you are running a strictly static, non-allocating script, though this is highly discouraged for junior developers.

MICROPY_PY_JSON.brief: Enables or disables the built-in JSON parsing and generation module in MicroPython.
MICROPY_PY_JSON.notes: When set to (1), the 'ujson' module is included in the MicroPython environment, allowing scripts to use json.loads() and json.dumps(). Enabling this increases the firmware binary size significantly due to the inclusion of the JSON parsing logic. It has no direct dependencies on other caOS flags, but requires sufficient heap memory to handle large JSON objects.
MICROPY_PY_JSON.usage: Enable this if your MicroPython scripts need to exchange data with web services or parse configuration files in JSON format. If your application is memory-constrained or does not use JSON, set this to (0) to save flash space and reduce the memory footprint of the MicroPython interpreter.

MICROPY_PY_OS_URANDOM.brief: Enables the MicroPython os.urandom() function to provide cryptographically secure random bytes.
MICROPY_PY_OS_URANDOM.notes: When set to 1, this flag integrates the caOS hardware random number generator (ca_rng) into the MicroPython environment. It requires the ca_rng module to be initialized and functional on the STM32 hardware. If disabled (0), os.urandom() will be unavailable or return an error, potentially breaking scripts that rely on secure entropy for cryptographic operations.
MICROPY_PY_OS_URANDOM.usage: Enable this when your MicroPython scripts require secure random numbers for tasks like generating session keys, nonces, or salts. Ensure that the underlying hardware RNG is properly configured in your system initialization. If you are running in a resource-constrained environment where security is not a requirement, you may disable it to save a small amount of code space.

MICROPY_PY_RANDOM.brief: Enables the MicroPython 'random' module for generating pseudo-random numbers.
MICROPY_PY_RANDOM.notes: When set to 1, the MicroPython environment includes the 'random' module, allowing scripts to call functions like random.random() or random.randint(). This flag depends on the underlying MicroPython port configuration. It consumes a small amount of additional flash memory for the module's implementation code.
MICROPY_PY_RANDOM.usage: Enable this if your MicroPython scripts require random number generation for logic, simulations, or security-related tasks (though for high-security cryptographic needs, use ca_rng_get instead). Disable it to save flash space if your application does not use random numbers.

MICROPY_PY_RANDOM_SEED_INIT_FUNC.brief: Defines the function used to initialize the MicroPython random number generator seed.
MICROPY_PY_RANDOM_SEED_INIT_FUNC.notes: This constant maps to the ca_upy_random_seed() function. It ensures that the MicroPython environment receives a non-deterministic seed value upon startup, typically leveraging the hardware RNG capabilities of the STM32. It is a dependency for any MicroPython script relying on the 'random' module.
MICROPY_PY_RANDOM_SEED_INIT_FUNC.usage: Change this only if you need to provide a custom entropy source for MicroPython. Ensure the replacement function returns a valid 32-bit unsigned integer. If you remove or change this, MicroPython's random number sequences may become predictable, which is a security risk for cryptographic operations.

MICROPY_PY_RE.brief: Enables the MicroPython regular expression (re) module support.
MICROPY_PY_RE.notes: When enabled (1), the 're' module is included in the MicroPython build, allowing for regex pattern matching and string manipulation. This increases the flash memory footprint significantly. It has no direct dependencies on other caOS flags but requires sufficient heap memory to perform complex pattern matching operations.
MICROPY_PY_RE.usage: Enable this if your Python scripts need to perform advanced text parsing or pattern searching. Disable it if you are constrained by flash memory or if your application does not require regex functionality to save space.

MICROPY_PY_SYS_EXIT.brief: Enables the sys.exit() function within the MicroPython environment.
MICROPY_PY_SYS_EXIT.notes: When set to (1), the MicroPython interpreter includes the sys.exit() function, allowing scripts to terminate execution gracefully. If set to (0), the function is excluded to save flash memory. This flag is a standard MicroPython configuration constant and does not depend on other caOS-specific flags, though it requires the sys module to be enabled in the build.
MICROPY_PY_SYS_EXIT.usage: Enable this if your MicroPython scripts need to programmatically stop execution or return control to the caOS task manager. Disable it in production environments where you want to prevent scripts from exiting unexpectedly or to minimize the binary footprint.

MICROPY_PY_THREAD.brief: Enables multi-threading support within the MicroPython interpreter environment.
MICROPY_PY_THREAD.notes: When enabled (1), MicroPython can spawn and manage multiple concurrent threads using the 'ca_upy_thread_start' API. This requires the underlying caOS scheduler to handle task switching for Python threads. Disabling this (0) reduces the memory footprint and simplifies the interpreter, but prevents the use of concurrent Python tasks.
MICROPY_PY_THREAD.usage: Enable this flag if your application requires running multiple independent Python scripts or background tasks simultaneously. If your application is single-threaded and memory-constrained, set this to 0 to save RAM. Ensure that your stack sizes for Python threads are sufficient, as enabling this adds overhead to the task context switching.

MICROPY_PY_THREAD_GIL.brief: Enables the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) for MicroPython threads within caOS.
MICROPY_PY_THREAD_GIL.notes: When enabled (1), the GIL ensures that only one MicroPython thread executes bytecode at a time, preventing data corruption in the MicroPython heap. Disabling it (0) is generally not supported in this port as it would require thread-safe modifications to the MicroPython core which are not implemented. This flag is a dependency for using multiple MicroPython threads via ca_upy_thread_start.
MICROPY_PY_THREAD_GIL.usage: Keep this set to (1) for all standard applications. Only change this if you are performing advanced debugging of the MicroPython interpreter core. Disabling this without implementing external locking mechanisms will lead to unpredictable system crashes and memory corruption.

MICROPY_PY_TIME.brief: Enables the MicroPython 'time' module within the caOS environment.
MICROPY_PY_TIME.notes: When set to (1), the MicroPython interpreter includes standard time-related functions (e.g., time.sleep, time.ticks_ms). Disabling this (0) reduces the firmware footprint by excluding these functions. It depends on the underlying ca_os_tick and ca_os_sleep_ms services to provide accurate timing data.
MICROPY_PY_TIME.usage: Enable this flag when your Python scripts require time-based delays, periodic execution, or timestamping. If your application is strictly event-driven or does not use Python-level timing, you may disable it to save flash memory. Ensure that ca_os_tick_init has been called during system startup for these functions to operate correctly.

MICROPY_PY_TIME_GMTIME_LOCALTIME_MKTIME.brief: Enables MicroPython time conversion functions (gmtime, localtime, mktime).
MICROPY_PY_TIME_GMTIME_LOCALTIME_MKTIME.notes: When set to 1, the MicroPython environment includes standard C-like time manipulation functions. This flag depends on the underlying caOS RTC implementation (ca_rtc_get/ca_rtc_set) to provide the actual time data. It consumes a small amount of additional flash memory for the conversion logic.
MICROPY_PY_TIME_GMTIME_LOCALTIME_MKTIME.usage: Enable this when your Python scripts need to handle calendar dates or convert between Unix timestamps and human-readable time structures. If your application does not use time-related Python modules, you can set this to 0 to save code space.

MICROPY_PY_TIME_INCLUDEFILE.brief: Specifies the header file containing the MicroPython time module implementation for caOS.
MICROPY_PY_TIME_INCLUDEFILE.notes: This constant tells the MicroPython build system which file to include to map standard time functions to caOS-specific hardware abstractions. It must point to a valid header file within the project structure that defines the necessary time-related structures and function prototypes. Changing this value requires a full rebuild of the MicroPython component.
MICROPY_PY_TIME_INCLUDEFILE.usage: Change this value only if you are porting MicroPython to a new hardware configuration or creating a custom time-handling module for caOS. Ensure the file 'modtime_caos.h' exists and correctly interfaces with ca_os_tick_ms or ca_rtc_get to provide accurate timekeeping to the Python environment. Incorrect values will result in compilation errors during the MicroPython build process.

MICROPY_PY_TIME_TIME_TIME_NS.brief: Enables the time.time_ns() function in the MicroPython environment.
MICROPY_PY_TIME_TIME_TIME_NS.notes: When set to (1), the MicroPython interpreter exposes the time_ns() method, which returns the current time in nanoseconds as an integer. This requires the underlying caOS system to have a high-resolution timer source available. Disabling it (0) reduces the MicroPython binary footprint slightly.
MICROPY_PY_TIME_TIME_TIME_NS.usage: Enable this flag if your MicroPython scripts require high-precision timing or timestamping that exceeds the resolution of standard millisecond-based functions. Ensure your hardware clock configuration is stable, as nanosecond precision is sensitive to system tick jitter.

MICROPY_READER_VFS.brief: Enables the MicroPython Virtual File System (VFS) support within the caOS environment.
MICROPY_READER_VFS.notes: When set to (1), MicroPython can mount and interact with file systems (like FAT or LittleFS) using standard Python file I/O commands. This flag requires the ca_fat_* API to be initialized and available in the system. Disabling this (0) will reduce the binary footprint but will prevent MicroPython scripts from accessing external storage or internal flash filesystems.
MICROPY_READER_VFS.usage: Enable this when your MicroPython application needs to read scripts, configuration files, or log data from storage. If you encounter 'OSError: [Errno 19] ENODEV' when attempting to open files in MicroPython, ensure this flag is set to (1) and that ca_fat_mount has been called successfully during system initialization.

MICROPY_REPL_AUTO_INDENT.brief: Enables automatic indentation in the MicroPython REPL when typing code.
MICROPY_REPL_AUTO_INDENT.notes: When set to (1), the MicroPython REPL will automatically insert spaces or tabs to match the indentation level of the previous line after pressing Enter. This is a convenience feature for interactive coding. It does not affect the compiled bytecode or the execution logic of the scripts. It is typically enabled by default in caOS builds to improve the developer experience in the console.
MICROPY_REPL_AUTO_INDENT.usage: Change this value to (0) if you are pasting large blocks of pre-formatted code into the REPL and experience issues with double-indentation or unexpected formatting. Keep it at (1) for standard manual coding sessions to save time and reduce syntax errors related to indentation.

MICROPY_STACK_CHECK.brief: Enables runtime stack overflow detection for the MicroPython interpreter.
MICROPY_STACK_CHECK.notes: When enabled (1), the system performs a check on the stack pointer during MicroPython execution to prevent memory corruption. This adds a small overhead to function calls within the interpreter. It is highly recommended to keep this enabled during development and debugging. If disabled (0), the system will not detect stack overflows, which can lead to silent, hard-to-debug crashes or unpredictable behavior.
MICROPY_STACK_CHECK.usage: Keep this enabled (1) for all standard applications to ensure system stability. You should only consider disabling it (0) if you are performing extreme performance profiling and have verified that your MicroPython scripts do not exceed the allocated stack size, though this is generally discouraged in production environments.

MICROPY_STACK_CHECK_MARGIN.brief: Defines the safety buffer size (in bytes) for MicroPython stack overflow detection.
MICROPY_STACK_CHECK_MARGIN.notes: This constant reserves a portion of the task stack that the MicroPython interpreter will not use for its own execution. If the stack pointer enters this margin, the system triggers a stack overflow fault. It depends on the total stack size allocated to the MicroPython task. Typical values range from 512 to 2048 bytes depending on the complexity of the Python scripts and the depth of C-level calls.
MICROPY_STACK_CHECK_MARGIN.usage: Increase this value if you encounter random hard faults or stack overflow errors during complex Python execution or deep recursion. Decrease it only if you are extremely constrained by RAM and have verified that your application's stack usage is well-behaved and does not approach the limit. Always ensure the total task stack size is significantly larger than this margin.

MICROPY_USE_INTERNAL_ERRNO.brief: Enables the use of a private, internal error number (errno) variable within the MicroPython port.
MICROPY_USE_INTERNAL_ERRNO.notes: When set to 1, MicroPython uses its own internal storage for error codes instead of relying on the standard C library's global errno. This is critical in RTOS environments to ensure thread safety, as a global errno would be shared across all tasks, leading to race conditions. Typical value is 1 for caOS ports.
MICROPY_USE_INTERNAL_ERRNO.usage: Keep this enabled (1) for all standard caOS MicroPython builds. Disable it only if you are integrating a specific external library that strictly requires the standard C library's errno and you have implemented a thread-local storage mechanism for it. If disabled, expect unpredictable behavior in multi-threaded Python scripts when multiple tasks perform I/O operations simultaneously.

MICROPY_USE_INTERNAL_PRINTF.brief: Determines whether MicroPython uses its own internal printf implementation or the caOS system-wide printf.
MICROPY_USE_INTERNAL_PRINTF.notes: When set to (0), MicroPython is configured to use the caOS-provided ca_printf function. This ensures consistent output formatting and routing across the entire system. If set to (1), MicroPython would use its own internal, often larger, implementation. In caOS, this is typically disabled (0) to save flash memory and unify console output through the ca_stdout service.
MICROPY_USE_INTERNAL_PRINTF.usage: Keep this value at (0) for standard caOS projects. Only change this to (1) if you are debugging MicroPython's internal string formatting independently of the caOS kernel or if you encounter specific issues with MicroPython's output buffer handling that cannot be resolved via ca_stdout.

MICROPY_VFS.brief: Enables the Virtual File System (VFS) support within the MicroPython environment.
MICROPY_VFS.notes: When set to 1, MicroPython can interface with the caOS file system (ca_fat_* API). This allows Python scripts to perform file operations like open, read, write, and directory listing on storage media. Disabling this (0) removes file system capabilities from the Python interpreter, reducing the binary footprint but preventing scripts from accessing persistent storage.
MICROPY_VFS.usage: Enable this flag when your MicroPython application needs to read configuration files, log data to storage, or execute scripts stored on an SD card or internal flash. Ensure that the ca_fat_mount service is initialized in your main application code before attempting to access files from Python.

MIN.brief: A macro that returns the smaller of two provided values.
MIN.notes: This is a functional macro that performs a comparison between two inputs. It is side-effect prone if the arguments contain increment or decrement operators (e.g., MIN(a++, b)), as the chosen argument will be evaluated twice. It has no dependencies on other RTOS flags and works with any comparable data type.
MIN.usage: Use this macro to safely determine the minimum of two variables without writing manual if-else blocks. Warning: Avoid passing expressions with side effects as arguments to prevent unexpected behavior, such as double-incrementing a counter.

MIN_KEY_SIZE.brief: Defines the minimum allowed length in bytes for cryptographic keys stored in the system.
MIN_KEY_SIZE.notes: This constant enforces a security floor for key generation and storage. Setting this value higher increases security but may cause key generation functions to fail if the requested entropy or algorithm requires smaller keys. It is typically set to 16 (128 bits) to comply with AES standards. Ensure that all hardware-accelerated crypto peripherals support the chosen minimum size.
MIN_KEY_SIZE.usage: Increase this value if your security policy requires stronger encryption (e.g., 32 for 256-bit keys). Decrease it only if you are using legacy algorithms that explicitly require shorter keys. Warning: setting this too low may expose the system to brute-force attacks, while setting it too high may cause runtime errors in modules that expect smaller key buffers.

MODBUS_RX_BUF_SIZE.brief: Defines the maximum size in bytes for the Modbus reception buffer.
MODBUS_RX_BUF_SIZE.notes: This constant determines the memory allocation for incoming Modbus frames. The value must be large enough to accommodate the maximum expected PDU size plus any protocol overhead. It is typically set to 270 to support the Modbus standard maximum frame size of 256 bytes plus additional framing bytes. Increasing this value consumes more RAM, while setting it too low will cause frame truncation and CRC errors.
MODBUS_RX_BUF_SIZE.usage: Adjust this value if your application needs to handle larger custom Modbus frames or if you need to optimize RAM usage on memory-constrained devices. Ensure the value is at least 256. If you encounter 'Buffer Overflow' or 'Invalid Frame' errors during communication, verify that this size is sufficient for the specific Modbus function codes being used.

MODBUS_TIMEOUT_MS.brief: Defines the maximum duration in milliseconds to wait for a response from a Modbus slave device.
MODBUS_TIMEOUT_MS.notes: This constant sets the timeout threshold for the Modbus master state machine. If no valid response is received within this period, the transaction is marked as failed. It depends on the underlying UART baud rate and the physical latency of the bus. Typical values range from 100ms to 2000ms depending on the network topology.
MODBUS_TIMEOUT_MS.usage: Increase this value if you experience frequent 'timeout' errors on long or noisy communication lines. Decrease it if you need faster error recovery in high-speed, reliable networks. Setting this value too low will cause valid responses to be discarded, while setting it too high will make the system unresponsive during communication failures.

MPU_ACCESS_NONE.brief: A configuration constant representing a memory region with no read, write, or execute permissions.
MPU_ACCESS_NONE.notes: When applied to an MPU region, this setting triggers a MemManage fault if the CPU attempts to access the memory address. It is the default state for uninitialized or restricted memory segments. It has no dependencies on other flags but acts as the base security level for the MPU configuration.
MPU_ACCESS_NONE.usage: Use this value when defining MPU regions that should be completely inaccessible to tasks to prevent buffer overflows or unauthorized memory access. Do not use this for memory regions where your application code or data resides, as it will cause the system to crash immediately upon access.

MPU_ACCESS_RDONLY.brief: Defines the memory protection unit (MPU) attribute for read-only memory regions.
MPU_ACCESS_RDONLY.notes: When enabled, this flag configures the hardware MPU to trigger a memory management fault if a write operation is attempted on the associated memory region. It is typically used in conjunction with memory region definition structures. It depends on the hardware support for MPU on the specific STM32 series being used.
MPU_ACCESS_RDONLY.usage: Use this flag when defining memory regions for constants, flash-based code, or read-only lookup tables to prevent accidental data corruption. Ensure that the memory region is not intended to be modified at runtime; setting this on a RAM region that requires updates will cause the system to crash with a MemManage fault.

MPU_ACCESS_RDWR.brief: Defines the Memory Protection Unit (MPU) access permission level for Read and Write operations.
MPU_ACCESS_RDWR.notes: When set to 2, this constant configures the MPU region to allow both read and write access to the associated memory block. It is typically used in conjunction with other MPU configuration flags to define memory attributes. Disabling or changing this value incorrectly will trigger a MemManage fault if the CPU attempts to write to a region restricted to read-only or no-access.
MPU_ACCESS_RDWR.usage: Change this value when you need to grant or restrict write permissions to specific memory regions, such as shared buffers or peripheral registers. Use this when you encounter hard faults during memory access operations. Ensure that the memory region is properly aligned and sized according to the STM32 MPU hardware requirements before applying this flag.

MPU_CANARY_REGION_MSP.brief: Enables or disables the MPU memory protection region specifically for the Main Stack Pointer (MSP) stack overflow detection.
MPU_CANARY_REGION_MSP.notes: When set to 1, the MPU configures a hardware-enforced guard zone at the end of the MSP stack; any write access to this region triggers a MemManage fault. When set to 0, this hardware protection is disabled. This flag depends on MPU_ENABLED being set to 1. Valid values are 0 (disabled) or 1 (enabled).
MPU_CANARY_REGION_MSP.usage: Enable this (set to 1) during development and debugging to catch stack overflows immediately via hardware exceptions. Disable it (set to 0) only if you need to reclaim the MPU region for other memory mapping purposes or if you are running on hardware that does not support sufficient MPU regions. Warning: disabling this removes a critical safety mechanism that prevents silent memory corruption.

MPU_CANARY_REGION_PSP_END.brief: Defines the MPU region index used to protect the end of the Process Stack Pointer (PSP) memory area.
MPU_CANARY_REGION_PSP_END.notes: This constant sets the specific hardware MPU slot (0-7) reserved for stack overflow detection. Enabling this requires the MPU to be active and the stack memory to be aligned to the MPU region size requirements. If set to an index already used by another memory region, it will cause a configuration conflict or system fault.
MPU_CANARY_REGION_PSP_END.usage: Change this value only if the hardware memory map or the MPU region allocation scheme is modified. It is used to solve stack overflow issues by triggering a MemManage fault when the stack pointer exceeds the defined boundary. Ensure the chosen index does not overlap with Flash, RAM, or peripheral regions defined elsewhere in the system.

MPU_CANARY_REGION_PSP_START.brief: Enables the MPU memory protection region for the Process Stack Pointer (PSP) start address to detect stack overflows.
MPU_CANARY_REGION_PSP_START.notes: When enabled, the MPU configures a hardware-enforced boundary at the beginning of the task stack. If the stack pointer moves below this address, a MemManage fault is triggered. This flag depends on MPU_ENABLED being set to 1. Typical value is 1 for production builds and 0 only for specific low-memory debugging scenarios.
MPU_CANARY_REGION_PSP_START.usage: Enable this to prevent silent memory corruption caused by stack overflows. Change this to 0 only if you are performing advanced memory mapping that conflicts with the default stack placement, though this is strongly discouraged as it removes a critical safety mechanism.

MPU_REGION_COUNT.brief: Defines the total number of hardware memory protection regions available on the specific STM32 microcontroller.
MPU_REGION_COUNT.notes: This constant sets the limit for the Memory Protection Unit (MPU) configuration. Enabling this allows the RTOS to isolate tasks and protect memory areas. The value is hardware-dependent: F1/F4/F7 series typically support 8 regions, while H5/H7 series support 16. Setting this value higher than the hardware capability will cause MPU configuration errors or hard faults.
MPU_REGION_COUNT.usage: You should change this value only when porting the RTOS to a different STM32 family. It is used by the kernel to allocate memory protection tables. Ensure the value matches the datasheet specification for your specific MCU part number; an incorrect value will lead to unpredictable system behavior or immediate crashes during kernel initialization.

MP_STATE_PORT.brief: Defines the scope and storage location for MicroPython virtual machine state variables.
MP_STATE_PORT.notes: This constant determines how the MicroPython VM manages its internal state (e.g., global variables, heap pointers). Setting it to MP_STATE_VM ensures that the VM state is stored within the virtual machine's own context structure rather than as global C variables. This is critical for thread safety in caOS, allowing multiple MicroPython instances to run concurrently without interfering with each other's memory space.
MP_STATE_PORT.usage: This value should generally remain set to MP_STATE_VM in caOS to support multi-threaded MicroPython environments. Do not change this unless you are performing low-level porting of the MicroPython core. Incorrect configuration here will lead to memory corruption or crashes when multiple tasks attempt to execute Python code simultaneously.

MQTT_KEEPALIVE_SEC.brief: Defines the interval in seconds at which the MQTT client sends a PINGREQ packet to the broker to maintain the connection.
MQTT_KEEPALIVE_SEC.notes: This value determines the timeout period for the broker to consider the client disconnected. If set too low, it increases network traffic and power consumption; if set too high, the system may take longer to detect a dropped connection. It must be less than the broker's maximum allowed keep-alive threshold. Typical values range from 30 to 300 seconds.
MQTT_KEEPALIVE_SEC.usage: Adjust this value if the broker frequently disconnects the device or if you need to optimize for low-power battery operation. Ensure the value is synchronized with the broker's configuration to prevent unexpected session termination.

MQTT_RX_BUF_SIZE.brief: Defines the maximum size in bytes of the buffer used to store incoming MQTT messages.
MQTT_RX_BUF_SIZE.notes: This value determines the memory footprint of the MQTT task. If set too low, incoming packets exceeding this size will be truncated or dropped. It must be large enough to accommodate the largest expected MQTT payload plus protocol headers. Typical values range from 256 to 2048 depending on available RAM and application requirements.
MQTT_RX_BUF_SIZE.usage: Increase this value if you observe incomplete message reception or errors when receiving large MQTT payloads. Decrease it if your system is running low on heap memory and you are only handling small control messages. Ensure the value is a multiple of 4 for optimal memory alignment on STM32 architectures.

NET_BUF_COUNT.brief: Defines the total number of network packet buffers available in the system memory pool.
NET_BUF_COUNT.notes: This constant determines the maximum number of concurrent network packets the stack can hold. Increasing this value consumes more RAM (each buffer is typically 1536 bytes). If set to 0, networking features are disabled. Values must be chosen based on available SRAM; for example, F7/H7 series support higher counts due to larger memory capacity, while F103 lacks sufficient resources for network buffering.
NET_BUF_COUNT.usage: Increase this value if the system experiences 'packet dropped' errors or fails to handle high-traffic bursts. Decrease it if the application encounters hard faults or memory allocation failures during startup. Ensure the value is sufficient for your application's throughput requirements, but do not exceed available heap space.

NET_BUF_DATA_SIZE.brief: Defines the actual payload capacity in bytes for a network buffer by subtracting the header overhead from the total buffer size.
NET_BUF_DATA_SIZE.notes: This constant is derived from NET_BUF_SIZE and NET_BUF_HDR_SIZE. It represents the maximum amount of application data that can fit into a single network packet. If NET_BUF_SIZE is too small, this value may become negative or insufficient for standard MTU requirements, potentially causing memory corruption or packet fragmentation issues.
NET_BUF_DATA_SIZE.usage: Adjust this value only if you need to change the total buffer size (NET_BUF_SIZE) to accommodate larger network packets. Ensure that the resulting size is sufficient for your protocol's MTU (e.g., 1500 bytes for Ethernet). Always verify that the total memory allocated for buffers does not exceed the available RAM on the STM32.

NET_BUF_F_IN_USE.brief: A bitmask flag indicating that a specific network buffer is currently allocated and being used by the system.
NET_BUF_F_IN_USE.notes: When this bit is set in the buffer's status field, the memory manager considers the buffer busy and will not reallocate it. If cleared, the buffer is marked as free for reuse. This flag is typically checked by the network stack's allocation functions to prevent memory leaks or data corruption. It is a fundamental flag for the buffer management lifecycle.
NET_BUF_F_IN_USE.usage: You should never manually toggle this flag in your application code; it is managed internally by the caOS network stack. If you notice that network buffers are not being freed, check if your code is correctly passing buffers back to the stack after processing. Modifying this flag directly will lead to memory leaks or system crashes due to double-allocation of the same memory block.

NET_BUF_F_RAW.brief: Flag to disable automatic checksum calculation for a network buffer.
NET_BUF_F_RAW.notes: When this flag is set in the buffer flags, the caOS network stack skips the automatic insertion of checksums (e.g., TCP/UDP/IP checksums) before transmission. This is typically used when the application layer or a hardware offload engine is responsible for calculating the checksum, or when sending raw packets that do not require standard protocol checksums. It is a bitmask value (1U << 2).
NET_BUF_F_RAW.usage: Use this flag when you are manually constructing a packet and have already calculated the checksum, or when you are sending custom protocol frames that do not follow standard checksum requirements. Warning: If you enable this flag without providing a valid checksum, the receiving device will likely drop the packet as corrupted.

NET_BUF_F_REASM.brief: Flag indicating that a network buffer contains a datagram reassembled by the IP defragmentation module.
NET_BUF_F_REASM.notes: This flag is set by the IP defragmentation service (ca_ip_defrag_*) when multiple fragmented IP packets are merged into a single complete datagram. It informs the network stack that the buffer now contains a full L4 payload (e.g., TCP or UDP segment) ready for processing. It is typically used internally by the stack and should not be manually toggled by application code.
NET_BUF_F_REASM.usage: Do not modify this flag manually. It is used by the network stack to distinguish between raw fragments and fully reassembled packets. If you are inspecting network buffers using ca_net_buf_ptr or similar, you can check this bit to determine if the buffer represents a complete datagram or a partial fragment.

NET_BUF_F_TX.brief: A bitmask flag indicating that the network buffer is currently designated for transmission (TX) operations.
NET_BUF_F_TX.notes: This flag is used by the network stack to distinguish between incoming (RX) and outgoing (TX) buffers. When set, the buffer is managed by the transmission logic and should not be modified by the RX interrupt service routines. It is typically used in conjunction with buffer allocation functions and must be cleared once the transmission is complete to allow the buffer to be recycled.
NET_BUF_F_TX.usage: Use this flag when manually allocating or inspecting buffers within the network stack to ensure the buffer is correctly routed to the hardware DMA or MAC peripheral. Do not manually toggle this bit unless you are implementing custom network drivers, as incorrect state management will lead to memory leaks or buffer corruption in the network pool.

NET_BUF_HDR_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed size in bytes reserved for the network buffer header metadata.
NET_BUF_HDR_SIZE.notes: This value determines the memory offset where the actual payload data begins within a network buffer. Increasing this value consumes more RAM per buffer but allows for larger protocol headers (e.g., adding custom tunneling or encryption headers). It must be large enough to accommodate the stack's internal headers; otherwise, packet corruption will occur. Typical values are powers of 2 to ensure memory alignment.
NET_BUF_HDR_SIZE.usage: Adjust this value if you are implementing custom network protocols that require additional metadata space before the payload. Do not decrease this value below the default unless you are certain the underlying network stack requires less header space, as doing so will cause buffer overflows and system instability.

NET_BUF_HEADROOM.brief: Defines the number of bytes reserved at the beginning of a network buffer for protocol headers.
NET_BUF_HEADROOM.notes: This value sets the offset where the actual payload data begins within a network packet buffer. Increasing this value allows for more layers of encapsulation (e.g., adding VLAN tags or tunneling headers) without reallocating the buffer. It must be large enough to accommodate the maximum expected stack of headers (Ethernet + IP + TCP/UDP + custom headers). Typical values are powers of 2, and it must be less than the total buffer size.
NET_BUF_HEADROOM.usage: Increase this value if you encounter buffer overflow errors or kernel panics when adding new protocol layers or tunneling protocols. Decrease it only if memory is extremely constrained and you are certain the header stack will never exceed the new limit. Setting this too low will cause memory corruption or packet drops when headers are prepended.

NET_BUF_INVALID.brief: A sentinel value representing an uninitialized or invalid network buffer handle.
NET_BUF_INVALID.notes: This constant is used as a null-pointer equivalent for network buffer descriptors. When a function returns this value, it indicates that the requested buffer allocation failed or the buffer reference is no longer valid. It is defined as 0xFFFFU to ensure it falls outside the range of valid memory-mapped buffer indices.
NET_BUF_INVALID.usage: Use this constant to check the success of network buffer allocation functions. Always compare the returned handle against NET_BUF_INVALID before attempting to access buffer data to prevent memory corruption or system crashes. Do not modify this value unless the underlying buffer pool architecture is redefined.

NET_BUF_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed size in bytes for each network packet buffer allocated by the caOS networking stack.
NET_BUF_SIZE.notes: This value determines the maximum payload size a single network buffer can hold. Increasing this value consumes more RAM from the heap for every allocated buffer, which can lead to memory exhaustion if the pool size is not adjusted accordingly. It must be large enough to accommodate the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) of the underlying network interface, typically 1500 bytes for Ethernet plus protocol headers.
NET_BUF_SIZE.usage: Increase this value if you encounter packet fragmentation or if your application needs to handle jumbo frames. Decrease it only if you are extremely constrained by RAM and are certain that your network traffic will never exceed the smaller limit. Setting this value too low will cause incoming packets to be dropped or truncated, leading to communication failures.

NET_HANDLER_MAX.brief: Defines the maximum number of concurrent network socket handlers allowed in the system.
NET_HANDLER_MAX.notes: This constant determines the size of the internal static array used to track active network connections. Increasing this value consumes more RAM in the .bss section. It must be greater than or equal to the number of simultaneous TCP/UDP sockets your application intends to open. If set too low, new connection attempts will be rejected by the network stack.
NET_HANDLER_MAX.usage: Adjust this value based on your application's memory constraints and communication requirements. Increase it if your application needs to handle more simultaneous connections (e.g., a web server with multiple clients). Decrease it to save RAM if your device only communicates with a single server. Ensure that the total memory usage does not exceed the STM32's available SRAM.

NET_IFACE_INVALID.brief: A sentinel value representing an uninitialized or non-existent network interface handle.
NET_IFACE_INVALID.notes: This constant is used as a null-equivalent for network interface pointers or IDs. When a function returns this value, it indicates that the requested interface could not be found or is not currently active. It is typically used in comparison checks against interface handles returned by the network stack.
NET_IFACE_INVALID.usage: Use this constant to validate interface handles before performing operations like sending or receiving packets. Always check if your interface handle equals NET_IFACE_INVALID to prevent null pointer dereferences or accessing invalid memory regions. Do not use this value as a valid interface index in your application code.

NET_IFACE_MAX.brief: Defines the maximum number of network interfaces that can be registered simultaneously in the caOS network stack.
NET_IFACE_MAX.notes: This constant determines the size of the internal interface registry array. Increasing this value consumes more static RAM for the interface control blocks. It must be set to at least 1, and it is typically constrained by the available memory and the number of physical or virtual hardware peripherals (e.g., Ethernet, Wi-Fi, or PPP) present in the system.
NET_IFACE_MAX.usage: Increase this value if your application needs to support multiple network connections simultaneously, such as a dual-homed gateway or a system with both Ethernet and Wi-Fi. If you set this value higher than the number of actual hardware drivers initialized, you will waste RAM; if set too low, additional interfaces will fail to register during system startup.

NET_MAC_FILTER_MAX.brief: Defines the maximum number of MAC addresses that can be stored in the network hardware filter list.
NET_MAC_FILTER_MAX.notes: This constant determines the size of the internal array used by the network stack to manage MAC address filtering. Increasing this value consumes more static RAM. It is typically used in conjunction with ca_net_filter_mac_set to whitelist specific devices. The default value is 2U, which is sufficient for simple point-to-point or gateway configurations.
NET_MAC_FILTER_MAX.usage: Increase this value if your application needs to filter or whitelist more than two specific MAC addresses simultaneously. If you set this too high, you will waste memory; if you set it too low, calls to ca_net_filter_mac_set will fail once the limit is reached. Ensure you have enough RAM before increasing this constant.

NET_MPU_REGION.brief: Defines the specific MPU memory region index reserved for network buffer operations.
NET_MPU_REGION.notes: This constant sets the hardware MPU slot used to enforce memory protection on network packet buffers. It must be a valid MPU region index supported by the STM32 hardware (typically 0-7). Changing this value requires ensuring that the corresponding MPU configuration in the system startup code is updated to match, otherwise, the system will trigger a MemManage fault when accessing network buffers.
NET_MPU_REGION.usage: Change this value only if the default MPU region conflicts with other system-critical memory protections or if the hardware abstraction layer requires a specific region for DMA-capable network memory. Ensure that the chosen region is not already assigned to the RTOS kernel stack or peripheral memory maps to avoid system instability.

NET_PROTO_ARP.brief: Enables or disables the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) support in the caOS network stack.
NET_PROTO_ARP.notes: When set to 0x01U, the system includes the logic to resolve IP addresses to MAC addresses. Disabling this (0x00U) will prevent the device from communicating with other nodes on a local Ethernet network unless static ARP entries are manually configured. This flag is a dependency for IPv4 networking modules.
NET_PROTO_ARP.usage: Enable this flag when your application needs to communicate over an Ethernet network using IPv4. Disable it only if you are implementing a custom, non-ARP based protocol or if you are operating in a point-to-point environment where ARP is explicitly not required to save memory and code space.

NET_PROTO_IP4.brief: Enables IPv4 protocol support within the caOS networking stack.
NET_PROTO_IP4.notes: When set to 0x02U, the system includes the IPv4 header processing logic and routing tables. Disabling this flag will remove IPv4 functionality, reducing the binary footprint but preventing communication over standard IPv4 networks. This flag is often a dependency for higher-level protocols like TCP or UDP if they are configured to run over IPv4.
NET_PROTO_IP4.usage: Enable this flag when your application needs to communicate over an IPv4 network. Change this value only if you are strictly using IPv6 or a custom non-IP protocol to save memory. Ensure that your network interface driver is compatible with IPv4 before enabling this, otherwise, the stack may attempt to process unsupported packets.

NET_PROTO_IP6.brief: Enables IPv6 protocol support within the caOS network stack.
NET_PROTO_IP6.notes: When set to 0x03U, the system allocates memory structures and enables logic for IPv6 packet processing. This flag is a dependency for any network services requiring IPv6 addressing. It must be consistent across all network modules to prevent memory alignment issues or stack overflows. Valid values are 0x00U (disabled) or 0x03U (enabled).
NET_PROTO_IP6.usage: Enable this flag when your application needs to communicate over IPv6 networks. Change this value if you are migrating from an IPv4-only environment to a dual-stack or IPv6-only setup. Warning: Enabling this increases the static memory footprint of the network buffer pool; ensure your heap size is sufficient before activation.

NET_PROTO_NONE.brief: A configuration flag indicating that no network protocol stack is currently initialized or active.
NET_PROTO_NONE.notes: When set to 0x00U, the network buffer management system bypasses all protocol-specific processing. This flag is typically used as a default state or a sentinel value in the network stack initialization sequence. It has no dependencies on other flags but must be checked before attempting to access protocol-specific headers or payload structures.
NET_PROTO_NONE.usage: Use this value during system initialization or when the network interface is explicitly disabled to prevent the stack from attempting to process incoming or outgoing packets. Changing this value incorrectly can lead to null pointer dereferences or memory corruption if the system expects a valid protocol handler to be present.

NET_QUEUE_DEPTH.brief: Defines the maximum number of network packets that can be buffered in the internal queue before dropping new incoming data.
NET_QUEUE_DEPTH.notes: Increasing this value consumes more RAM from the heap, as each slot reserves space for a packet descriptor. It must be a power of two if the underlying implementation uses bitwise masking for circular buffer indexing. Typical values range from 16 to 256 depending on available memory and traffic burst intensity.
NET_QUEUE_DEPTH.usage: Increase this value if the system experiences packet loss during high-traffic bursts or when the processing task is temporarily preempted by higher-priority threads. Decrease it if the system is running low on heap memory and network throughput requirements are low.

NET_ROUTE_MAX.brief: Defines the maximum number of entries allowed in the network routing table.
NET_ROUTE_MAX.notes: This constant determines the size of the static array used to store routing paths. Increasing this value consumes more RAM but allows the device to manage more complex network topologies or subnets. It must be a positive integer, typically ranging from 4 to 32 depending on available heap/stack memory.
NET_ROUTE_MAX.usage: Increase this value if your device needs to communicate with multiple gateways or subnets and you encounter 'route not found' errors. Decrease it to save RAM if your device only communicates with a single local gateway.

NTP_EPOCH_DELTA.brief: The constant representing the number of seconds between the NTP epoch (January 1, 1900) and the Unix epoch (January 1, 1970).
NTP_EPOCH_DELTA.notes: This value is used to convert NTP timestamps into standard Unix timestamps used by the system clock. It is a fixed constant of 2208988800 seconds. Changing this value will cause incorrect system time synchronization and will break all time-dependent network protocols like TLS/SSL certificate validation.
NTP_EPOCH_DELTA.usage: This value should generally not be changed. It is used internally by the caOS network stack when parsing NTP packets. You only need to verify this value if you are porting the stack to a non-standard time reference or if you encounter significant time offsets during network synchronization.

NTP_POLL_MS.brief: Defines the time interval in milliseconds between consecutive NTP server synchronization requests.
NTP_POLL_MS.notes: This value determines the frequency of network time updates. Increasing this value reduces network traffic and CPU overhead but may lead to larger clock drift between syncs. It depends on the network stack being initialized and the NTP client task being active. The value is an unsigned integer (U), typically set to 64000ms (64 seconds).
NTP_POLL_MS.usage: Adjust this value if your application requires higher time precision (lower the value) or if you need to minimize bandwidth consumption (increase the value). Warning: Setting this value too low may flood the network or cause the NTP server to block your device; setting it too high may cause the system clock to drift significantly beyond acceptable tolerances for your application.

NTP_PORT.brief: Defines the UDP port number used for Network Time Protocol (NTP) synchronization.
NTP_PORT.notes: This constant sets the destination port for outgoing time sync requests and the listening port for incoming server responses. It must match the standard NTP port (123) to communicate with public or local time servers. Changing this value will prevent the system from synchronizing with standard NTP servers unless the server is specifically configured to listen on a non-standard port.
NTP_PORT.usage: Change this value only if your network architecture requires NTP traffic to be routed through a custom port or a proxy server. Ensure that your firewall settings and the target NTP server configuration are updated to match this value, otherwise, the system clock will fail to synchronize.

NTP_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT_MS.brief: Defines the maximum duration in milliseconds to wait for an NTP server response before timing out.
NTP_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT_MS.notes: This constant determines the blocking duration for the network stack during time synchronization. If set too low, the system may fail to sync on high-latency networks. If set too high, it may delay system startup or task execution. The value is an unsigned integer, typically ranging from 1000 to 10000 depending on network stability.
NTP_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT_MS.usage: Increase this value if the device frequently fails to synchronize time due to poor network conditions or high latency. Decrease it if the system startup time is too slow and you are operating on a reliable, low-latency local network. Ensure the value is sufficient to account for round-trip time (RTT) plus server processing time.

NTP_RETRY_BACKOFF_MS.brief: Defines the base time interval in milliseconds for the exponential backoff mechanism during NTP synchronization failures.
NTP_RETRY_BACKOFF_MS.notes: This value acts as the multiplier for the retry delay. When NTP requests fail, the system waits for (NTP_RETRY_BACKOFF_MS * 2^n) milliseconds before the next attempt, where 'n' is the number of consecutive failures. It must be a positive unsigned integer. Setting this too low may flood the network or the NTP server, while setting it too high increases the time required to recover from transient network outages.
NTP_RETRY_BACKOFF_MS.usage: Adjust this value if your device operates on high-latency networks or if the NTP server enforces strict rate-limiting. Increase this value if you observe 'NTP sync failed' errors due to network congestion. Ensure this value is not set to zero to avoid immediate, rapid-fire retry loops that could crash the network stack.

NTP_RETRY_N.brief: Defines the maximum number of attempts the system will make to synchronize time with an NTP server before failing.
NTP_RETRY_N.notes: When enabled, the system attempts to reach the NTP server up to this count. If the value is set to 0, the system will not attempt any retries. Increasing this value improves reliability in unstable network environments but increases the total boot or sync time if the server is unreachable. Typical values range from 1 to 5.
NTP_RETRY_N.usage: Increase this value if your device frequently logs 'NTP Sync Failed' errors during startup or periodic updates due to poor network connectivity. Decrease it if you need the system to fail fast and proceed to other tasks without waiting for network timeouts.

NTP_SERVER_N.brief: Defines the maximum number of NTP server addresses stored in the system configuration.
NTP_SERVER_N.notes: This constant determines the size of the internal array used to hold NTP server hostnames or IP addresses. Increasing this value allows the system to attempt synchronization with multiple time servers for redundancy. It must be a positive integer. If set to 0, NTP functionality may be disabled or restricted to a hardcoded default.
NTP_SERVER_N.usage: Change this value when you need to add more fallback NTP servers to improve time synchronization reliability. Ensure that the memory allocated for the NTP client task is sufficient to handle the increased array size. Setting this value too high may lead to unnecessary memory consumption in the heap or static data section.

OS_TICK_US.brief: Defines the duration of a single system tick in microseconds, determining the OS heartbeat frequency.
OS_TICK_US.notes: This constant sets the resolution of the RTOS scheduler and software timers. Lower values (e.g., 100US) provide higher precision for task scheduling and timeouts but increase CPU overhead due to more frequent interrupt handling. It must be compatible with the hardware timer configuration. Typical values range from 100 to 2000 microseconds depending on the MCU performance class.
OS_TICK_US.usage: Adjust this value to balance timing precision against CPU load. Increase the value if the system is overloaded by too many context switches. Decrease it only if your application requires high-resolution task execution or faster response times for software timers. Ensure all time-based logic in your application is scaled relative to this tick rate.

PACKET_TRACER_RING_SIZE.brief: Defines the total number of slots available in the circular buffer used for packet tracing.
PACKET_TRACER_RING_SIZE.notes: This constant determines the depth of the internal trace log. Increasing this value allows for a longer history of captured packets but consumes more RAM. It must be a power of two for optimal performance in the ring buffer logic. Typical values range from 4 to 64 depending on available heap memory.
PACKET_TRACER_RING_SIZE.usage: Increase this value if you are losing trace data during high-frequency communication bursts. Decrease it if the system is running low on static RAM. Ensure that the value is not set too high, as it may lead to stack overflow or memory exhaustion in resource-constrained STM32 devices.

PCLK1_FREQ_HZ.brief: Defines the operating frequency of the Peripheral Clock 1 (PCLK1) bus in Hertz.
