PCLK1_FREQ_HZ.notes: This constant is used by the RTOS kernel and peripheral drivers to calculate timing-dependent parameters such as baud rates, timer prescalers, and watchdog timeouts. It must match the actual hardware clock configuration set in the RCC registers. Incorrect values will cause communication errors (e.g., wrong UART baud rate) or incorrect timing intervals.
PCLK1_FREQ_HZ.usage: Update this value whenever the system clock tree configuration (RCC) is modified. It is critical for ensuring that peripherals like UART, SPI, and Timers operate at the intended speeds. Always verify this value against the STM32 CubeMX clock configuration tab for your specific target MCU.

PCLK2_FREQ_HZ.brief: Defines the operating frequency of the Peripheral Clock 2 (PCLK2) bus in Hertz.
PCLK2_FREQ_HZ.notes: This constant informs the RTOS kernel and peripheral drivers of the exact clock speed of the APB2 bus. It is critical for calculating baud rates for UART, SPI, and timer prescalers. Values must match the actual hardware clock tree configuration set in the RCC registers. Incorrect values will lead to incorrect peripheral timing, such as garbled serial communication or wrong PWM frequencies.
PCLK2_FREQ_HZ.usage: Update this value whenever the system clock tree (RCC) is modified in the hardware abstraction layer or startup files. If you change the PLL settings or the APB2 prescaler, you must recalculate and update this constant. Failure to keep this in sync with the hardware will cause peripheral drivers to malfunction, even if the CPU core itself appears to be running correctly.

PCLK3_FREQ_HZ.brief: Defines the operating frequency in Hertz of the Peripheral Clock 3 (PCLK3) bus for the specific STM32 microcontroller.
PCLK3_FREQ_HZ.notes: This constant is used by the RTOS kernel and peripheral drivers to calculate timing-dependent parameters such as baud rates, timer intervals, and watchdog timeouts. Enabling this ensures hardware peripherals attached to the APB3 bus operate at the correct speed. Values must match the actual hardware clock tree configuration defined in the System Clock Configuration (RCC). Typical values range from 50MHz to 250MHz depending on the specific STM32 series and PLL settings.
PCLK3_FREQ_HZ.usage: Change this value only when modifying the system clock tree (e.g., changing the PLL multipliers or dividers in the RCC configuration). If this value is incorrect, peripheral communication (like UART, SPI, or I2C) will fail due to incorrect timing calculations, and RTOS software timers may drift significantly. Always verify this value against the STM32CubeMX clock configuration tool output.

PCLK4_FREQ_HZ.brief: Defines the operating frequency in Hertz of the Peripheral Clock 4 (PCLK4) bus for the STM32 MCU.
PCLK4_FREQ_HZ.notes: This constant is used by the caOS hardware abstraction layer to calculate baud rates and timing intervals for peripherals connected to the APB4 bus. Enabling or changing this value directly affects the accuracy of communication interfaces like I2C, SPI, or timers mapped to this clock domain. It must match the actual clock tree configuration set in the System Clock Configuration (RCC) registers. Typical values are 100MHz for H747 and 120MHz for H753.
PCLK4_FREQ_HZ.usage: Change this value only when modifying the system clock tree (e.g., changing the PLL settings or clock dividers). If this value is incorrect, peripherals on the APB4 bus will operate at the wrong speed, leading to communication errors, frame corruption, or timeout failures. Always verify this value against the STM32CubeMX clock configuration tool output.

PCLK5_FREQ_HZ.brief: Defines the clock frequency in Hertz for the PCLK5 peripheral bus.
PCLK5_FREQ_HZ.notes: This constant is used by the caOS kernel and hardware abstraction layers to calculate timing-dependent operations, such as baud rate generation or peripheral timeouts. It must match the actual hardware clock configuration of the STM32 H773. If set incorrectly, peripheral communication (like UART or SPI) will operate at the wrong speed, leading to data corruption or framing errors. Typical values are determined by the RCC (Reset and Clock Control) configuration of the MCU.
PCLK5_FREQ_HZ.usage: Change this value only when modifying the system clock tree (e.g., changing PLL settings or prescalers in the clock configuration). Ensure the value matches the output of the RCC clock tree for the specific bus. Using an incorrect value will cause timing-sensitive drivers to fail. Always verify this against the STM32 CubeMX clock configuration or the hardware reference manual.

POLY1305_BLOCK_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed block size in bytes for the Poly1305 authenticator algorithm.
POLY1305_BLOCK_SIZE.notes: The value is set to 16 bytes (128 bits), which is the standard block size required by the Poly1305 specification. This constant is used by the ca_poly1305 and ca_chacha20poly1305 modules to manage internal buffers and process data chunks. It is a fixed architectural requirement of the algorithm and should not be modified.
POLY1305_BLOCK_SIZE.usage: This constant is used internally by the crypto stack. You should never change this value, as doing so will cause the Poly1305 authentication to fail and result in invalid MAC (Message Authentication Code) calculations. If you are implementing a custom buffer for data processing, use this constant to ensure your buffer alignment matches the algorithm's requirements.

POLY1305_TAG_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed length of the Poly1305 authentication tag in bytes.
POLY1305_TAG_SIZE.notes: The value is set to 16 bytes (128 bits), which is the standard output size for the Poly1305 authenticator. This constant is used by the ca_chacha20poly1305 and ca_poly1305 APIs to allocate buffers and verify message integrity. It is a fixed protocol requirement and should not be modified.
POLY1305_TAG_SIZE.usage: Do not change this value. It is used internally by ca_chacha20poly1305_encrypt and ca_chacha20poly1305_decrypt to ensure that the authentication tag matches the expected cryptographic standard. Modifying this will cause authentication failures and protocol incompatibility.

POOL_QUEUE_SIZE.brief: Defines the maximum number of message slots available in the system memory pool for inter-task communication.
POOL_QUEUE_SIZE.notes: This constant determines the total capacity of the global message queue. Increasing this value consumes more RAM from the heap. It must be greater than zero and is typically set to a power of two for optimal performance. If the queue fills up, tasks attempting to send messages will be blocked or return an error depending on the API call.
POOL_QUEUE_SIZE.usage: Increase this value if your application experiences 'Queue Full' errors during high-traffic periods or when multiple tasks send messages simultaneously. Decrease it if your system is running low on RAM and you have verified that the current queue depth is never fully utilized.

PRINTF.brief: Enables or disables the system-wide formatted output logging functionality via the ca_printf macro.
PRINTF.notes: When enabled, this constant maps the standard printf-style calls to the caOS internal serial output driver. Disabling this flag removes the overhead of string formatting and buffer management, significantly reducing flash memory usage and CPU cycles. It depends on the UART/USART peripheral being initialized in the hardware abstraction layer.
PRINTF.usage: Enable this during development and debugging to monitor system state and task execution via a serial terminal. Disable this in production builds to save memory and prevent blocking the CPU with slow serial transmission. Ensure the buffer size (BUFF) is large enough to accommodate your longest log message, otherwise, output will be truncated.

PRINTF_N.brief: Defines the macro used for system-wide formatted output logging.
PRINTF_N.notes: This constant maps the standard printf functionality to the specific caOS output driver. Enabling or modifying this allows redirection of logs to UART, ITM, or memory buffers. It depends on the underlying hardware abstraction layer (HAL) being initialized. Typical values are function pointers or macros that wrap the hardware-specific transmit function.
PRINTF_N.usage: Change this value when porting the RTOS to new hardware or when switching the debug output interface (e.g., from UART to SWO). Ensure the provided function signature matches the expected arguments (STDOUT, buffer, length, and variadic arguments) to prevent memory corruption or hard faults during runtime logging.

PSP_CHECK_TOP.brief: Enables or disables the stack overflow detection mechanism for the Process Stack Pointer (PSP).
PSP_CHECK_TOP.notes: When set to 1, the MPU (Memory Protection Unit) monitors the stack limit to trigger a fault if the stack pointer exceeds the defined boundary. When set to 0, this hardware-based protection is disabled. This flag requires the MPU to be initialized and configured in the system startup code. Typical values are 0 (disabled) or 1 (enabled).
PSP_CHECK_TOP.usage: Enable this flag (set to 1) during development and debugging to catch stack overflow errors early, which otherwise cause silent memory corruption or hard faults. Disable it (set to 0) only if you need to save a negligible amount of CPU cycles or if your specific hardware configuration does not support MPU-based stack monitoring. Warning: disabling this makes the system vulnerable to undetected stack overflows.

PUT.brief: A macro function used to send formatted debug messages or system logs to the standard output (STDOUT) interface.
PUT.notes: This function acts as a wrapper for the system's serial or logging peripheral. Enabling it allows real-time monitoring of task execution and error reporting. It depends on the hardware abstraction layer (HAL) being initialized for the UART or ITM port. Typical usage involves passing a string literal or a formatted buffer. It is non-blocking in some configurations but may introduce latency if the output buffer is full.
PUT.usage: Use this during development to trace task transitions, interrupt triggers, or variable states. Change this value when switching between different debug interfaces (e.g., UART to SWO). Warning: Excessive use of ca_put within high-frequency tasks or critical sections can significantly degrade system performance and timing determinism; always remove or wrap in debug-only macros before deploying to production.

PUT_N.brief: A macro used to output a specific message string to a designated system output stream.
PUT_N.notes: This constant defines the interface for system logging or console output. When enabled, it routes messages to the hardware peripheral defined by STDOUT (e.g., UART or ITM). It depends on the underlying hardware abstraction layer (HAL) being initialized. Typical values are the macro definition itself, which wraps the system's low-level character transmission function.
PUT_N.usage: Change this value when redirecting system logs to a different peripheral, such as switching from UART1 to UART2 for debugging. Use this to solve issues where system status messages are not appearing on your terminal. Warning: Ensure the baud rate and hardware pins for the new STDOUT are correctly configured, or the system may hang while waiting for the transmission buffer to clear.

RO_MPU_REGION.brief: Defines the total number of hardware Memory Protection Unit (MPU) regions available for the caOS kernel to manage.
RO_MPU_REGION.notes: This constant directly maps to the physical MPU hardware capabilities of the STM32H563. Setting this value higher than the hardware limit (15) will cause memory access faults or kernel initialization errors. It is a static configuration that dictates how many memory segments (e.g., Flash, RAM, Peripheral space) the RTOS can protect simultaneously.
RO_MPU_REGION.usage: You should only change this value if you are porting the RTOS to a different STM32 chip with a different MPU architecture. For the H563, it must remain at 15U. Do not modify this value to 'solve' memory access errors; if you encounter a MemManage fault, check your task stack sizes or memory region definitions instead.

SHA256_BLOCK_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed byte length of a single data block processed by the SHA-256 hashing algorithm.
SHA256_BLOCK_SIZE.notes: This constant is set to 64 bytes (512 bits) as per the FIPS 180-4 standard. It is a hard-coded requirement for the internal buffer size of the SHA-256 state machine. Changing this value will cause the cryptographic functions to produce incorrect hashes or trigger memory access violations.
SHA256_BLOCK_SIZE.usage: Do not modify this value under any circumstances. It is defined by the SHA-256 specification. If you are implementing a custom crypto driver or buffer management, use this constant instead of hard-coding the number 64 to ensure code maintainability and compliance with the algorithm's requirements.

SHA256_DIGEST_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed output length in bytes for the SHA-256 cryptographic hash algorithm.
SHA256_DIGEST_SIZE.notes: This constant is set to 32 bytes (256 bits) as per the SHA-256 standard. Changing this value will break the cryptographic implementation and cause buffer overflows or incorrect hash calculations. It is a read-only constant used for memory allocation in hash context structures.
SHA256_DIGEST_SIZE.usage: Do not modify this value. It is used to allocate static buffers for storing digest results. If you are implementing a function that handles SHA-256 outputs, always use this constant instead of hardcoding the number 32 to ensure code maintainability and prevent errors if the algorithm is ever swapped.

SHA384_DIGEST_SIZE.brief: Defines the output size in bytes for the SHA-384 cryptographic hash algorithm.
SHA384_DIGEST_SIZE.notes: This constant represents the 384-bit digest length (384 bits / 8 = 48 bytes). It is used by the ca_sha384_* family of functions to allocate buffers and validate input/output sizes. Changing this value will break the SHA-384 implementation and cause cryptographic mismatches.
SHA384_DIGEST_SIZE.usage: Do not change this value. It is a fixed standard defined by FIPS PUB 180-4. If you need a different digest size, use the appropriate constant for SHA-256 (32 bytes) or SHA-512 (64 bytes) instead.

SHA512_BLOCK_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed byte length of a single data block processed by the SHA-512 hashing algorithm.
SHA512_BLOCK_SIZE.notes: This constant is set to 128 bytes (1024 bits) as per the FIPS 180-4 standard for SHA-512. It is a hard-coded architectural requirement for the internal buffer size of the hashing engine. Changing this value will cause compilation errors or runtime memory corruption in the crypto stack, as it is tightly coupled with the SHA-512 state machine and padding logic.
SHA512_BLOCK_SIZE.usage: Do not modify this value. It is defined by the cryptographic standard and is not a tunable parameter. If you are implementing a custom crypto driver or buffer management system, use this constant to ensure your buffers are correctly sized to hold exactly one SHA-512 block.

SHA512_DIGEST_SIZE.brief: Defines the fixed output length of the SHA-512 hashing algorithm in bytes.
SHA512_DIGEST_SIZE.notes: This constant is set to 64 bytes (512 bits). It is a hard-coded requirement of the SHA-512 standard. Modifying this value will cause cryptographic signature verification failures and buffer overflows in functions expecting a 64-byte digest array.
SHA512_DIGEST_SIZE.usage: Do not change this value. It is used to allocate buffers for hash results. If you are writing code that stores SHA-512 hashes, always use this constant to define your array size (e.g., uint8_t hash[SHA512_DIGEST_SIZE]) to ensure compatibility and prevent memory corruption.

SPINLOCK_FREE.brief: A configuration flag that determines whether the kernel uses hardware-based spinlocks for atomic operations.
SPINLOCK_FREE.notes: When set to 0, the system enforces the use of hardware spinlocks to ensure thread safety during atomic operations. If set to 1, spinlocks are disabled, which may lead to race conditions in multi-core or preemptive environments. This flag is typically dependent on the underlying architecture's support for atomic instructions (e.g., LDREX/STREX on ARM Cortex-M).
SPINLOCK_FREE.usage: Set this to 0 in multi-threaded or multi-core applications to prevent data corruption. Only set this to 1 if you are running on a single-core system with interrupts disabled or if you are implementing a custom, non-blocking synchronization mechanism, as disabling it without proper alternatives will cause system instability.

SPINLOCK_TAKEN.brief: A unique magic number used to identify the state of a spinlock as currently held by a processor core.
SPINLOCK_TAKEN.notes: This constant is used as a sentinel value in atomic memory operations to verify lock ownership. It must be a unique 32-bit pattern that does not conflict with valid memory addresses or other status flags. Changing this value requires updating all assembly-level atomic primitives and the spinlock acquisition logic across the entire kernel.
SPINLOCK_TAKEN.usage: This value should generally not be changed. It is used for debugging and memory integrity checks during spinlock operations. If you are porting the RTOS to a new architecture or suspect memory corruption in the spinlock state, ensure this constant matches the value expected by the hardware-specific atomic instructions.

SPI_DEF_PKT_SIZE.brief: Defines the default size in bytes for SPI data packets when no specific length is provided.
SPI_DEF_PKT_SIZE.notes: This constant sets the buffer allocation size for SPI transactions. Increasing this value consumes more RAM in the SPI driver's internal buffers. It must be large enough to accommodate the largest expected data frame in your application. Typical values range from 16 to 256 depending on available heap memory.
SPI_DEF_PKT_SIZE.usage: Adjust this value if you encounter buffer overflow errors during SPI transfers or if your peripheral requires larger data chunks. Ensure that the value does not exceed the available RAM allocated for the SPI driver, otherwise, the system may experience memory corruption or hard faults.

SSH_LISTEN_PORT.brief: Defines the TCP port number on which the caOS SSH server listens for incoming remote connections.
SSH_LISTEN_PORT.notes: This constant sets the listening socket port for the SSH daemon. The default value is 22, which is the standard IANA port for SSH. Valid values range from 1 to 65535. Ensure the chosen port does not conflict with other network services running on the STM32, such as HTTP (80) or Telnet (23).
SSH_LISTEN_PORT.usage: Change this value if you need to run the SSH server on a non-standard port for security through obscurity or to avoid port collisions in a specific network environment. Warning: Changing this to a port below 1024 may require specific privileges in some environments, and remote clients must be updated to connect to the new port number.

STACK_CANARY_SIZE.brief: Defines the size in bytes of the memory protection guard zone added to each task stack to detect overflows.
STACK_CANARY_SIZE.notes: When enabled, the RTOS places a specific pattern at the end of the stack. If the stack pointer exceeds this boundary, the MPU triggers a fault. Increasing this value provides a larger buffer but consumes more RAM per task. It is typically set to 32 bytes, but must be a multiple of the MPU region alignment requirements (usually 32 or 64 bytes depending on the STM32 architecture).
STACK_CANARY_SIZE.usage: Increase this value if you suspect stack corruption or intermittent hard faults during heavy task execution. Decrease it only if you are extremely constrained by RAM and have verified stack usage via static analysis or runtime monitoring. Setting this to 0 disables stack overflow protection, which is strongly discouraged for production firmware.

STACK_CANARY_VALUE.brief: A unique 64-bit pattern placed at the end of each task stack to detect memory corruption.
STACK_CANARY_VALUE.notes: When enabled, the kernel writes this specific hex value to the stack boundary. If the value is overwritten, the system triggers a stack overflow exception. It requires the MPU (Memory Protection Unit) to be active. The value must be a 64-bit constant to ensure alignment and uniqueness.
STACK_CANARY_VALUE.usage: Change this value only if you suspect a collision with legitimate data patterns in your application memory. Use this to debug 'HardFault' errors caused by stack overflows. Do not disable this in production, as it is a critical safety mechanism for detecting buffer overruns.

STACK_FILL_PATTERN.brief: The hexadecimal byte pattern used to initialize task stack memory areas upon creation.
STACK_FILL_PATTERN.notes: When a task is created, the RTOS fills its allocated stack space with this specific pattern. This allows the system to track stack usage by checking how much of this pattern has been overwritten by function calls and local variables. It has no functional impact on task execution but is critical for debugging stack overflows. The value must be a 32-bit word.
STACK_FILL_PATTERN.usage: Change this value if you need to distinguish stack memory from other initialized data in your debugger's memory view. It is primarily used during development to identify stack depth; if you see the pattern at the very bottom of the stack, you are at risk of a stack overflow. Do not change this value unless you have a specific reason to track memory patterns differently in your IDE.

STACK_MIN.brief: Defines the absolute minimum stack size in bytes allowed for any task created within the caOS RTOS.
STACK_MIN.notes: This constant acts as a safety floor for task memory allocation. If a task is created with a stack size smaller than STACK_MIN, the kernel will either reject the task creation or force the size to this value. Higher values are required for architectures with larger register sets or deeper interrupt nesting (e.g., H7 series). It is strictly dependent on the specific MCU architecture's memory footprint and stack frame requirements.
STACK_MIN.usage: Increase this value if you encounter stack overflow errors or hard faults during task initialization. Do not decrease this value below the recommended architecture default, as it will lead to unpredictable system crashes and memory corruption. Ensure that your task stack sizes are always a multiple of 8 bytes to maintain proper alignment on ARM Cortex-M processors.

STACK_SLICE.brief: Defines the default memory size in bytes allocated for each task's stack.
STACK_SLICE.notes: This constant determines the stack depth for tasks created without a custom stack size. Increasing this value consumes more RAM globally. It is hardware-dependent: STM32F103 uses 1024 bytes, while higher-performance series (F4, F7, H7, U5) typically use 2048 bytes. Ensure this value is sufficient to prevent stack overflow, which can be monitored using ca_scheduler_stack_report.
STACK_SLICE.usage: Adjust this value if your tasks trigger stack overflow faults or if you are running out of RAM. If you have tasks with deep recursion or large local buffers, you may need to increase this value or manually specify a larger stack size during task creation. Warning: setting this too low will cause unpredictable system crashes or hard faults.

STACK_WARN_PERMILLE.brief: Defines the threshold (in per-mille) of stack usage that triggers a warning in the caOS scheduler.
STACK_WARN_PERMILLE.notes: This constant sets the limit at which the system considers a task's stack to be dangerously full. A value of 750U means that if a task consumes more than 75% of its allocated stack space, the system will flag it. This value is used by the ca_scheduler_update_all_stack_usage function. It is a global configuration constant and does not depend on other flags, but it should be tuned based on the memory safety requirements of your application.
STACK_WARN_PERMILLE.usage: Increase this value if you are receiving false-positive stack overflow warnings in tasks with high but safe memory usage. Decrease it if you need to detect potential stack overflows earlier to prevent memory corruption. Ensure that your task stack sizes are large enough to accommodate the worst-case execution path before adjusting this threshold.

STDOUT_ON_ITM.brief: Enables or disables the redirection of standard output (printf) to the ARM Cortex-M ITM (Instrumentation Trace Macrocell) peripheral.
STDOUT_ON_ITM.notes: When set to 1, the system routes stdout data through the ITM stimulus port 0, allowing real-time logging via an external debugger like ST-LINK. When set to 0, this feature is disabled, and stdout will not produce output via ITM. This requires the debugger's SWO pin to be connected and configured in your IDE's debug settings.
STDOUT_ON_ITM.usage: Enable this (set to 1) during development when you need to monitor system logs or debug messages without using a physical UART peripheral. Disable it (set to 0) for production builds to save CPU cycles and avoid potential blocking behavior if the debugger is not connected.

STDOUT_ON_LPUART.brief: Enables or disables the redirection of standard output (printf) to the LPUART peripheral.
STDOUT_ON_LPUART.notes: When set to 1, the system initializes the LPUART hardware and routes all standard output streams to it. When set to 0, standard output is disabled or redirected to a null device. This flag depends on the LPUART peripheral being correctly configured in the hardware abstraction layer. Typical values are 0 (disabled) or 1 (enabled).
STDOUT_ON_LPUART.usage: Set this to 1 during development to enable serial debugging and log messages via the LPUART interface. Set to 0 in production builds to save power and reduce CPU overhead caused by string formatting and UART transmission. Ensure the baud rate and GPIO pins are correctly initialized before enabling this flag to avoid system hangs during initialization.

STDOUT_ON_UART.brief: Enables or disables the redirection of standard output (printf) to the hardware UART peripheral.
STDOUT_ON_UART.notes: When set to 1, the system routes stdout to the configured UART port; when 0, stdout is disabled or redirected to a null device. This flag depends on the UART driver being initialized in the board support package. Typical values are 0 (disabled) or 1 (enabled).
STDOUT_ON_UART.usage: Enable this during development to view debug logs via a serial terminal. Disable it in production builds to save CPU cycles and reduce power consumption, or if the UART pins are required for other communication protocols.

STDOUT_ON_USB_CDC.brief: Enables or disables the redirection of standard output (printf) to the USB CDC virtual COM port.
STDOUT_ON_USB_CDC.notes: When set to 1, the system initializes the USB peripheral and routes stdout to the host PC via USB. When set to 0, stdout is disabled or routed to the default UART peripheral. This flag requires the USB_DEVICE_ENABLED flag to be set to 1. Valid values are 0 (disabled) or 1 (enabled).
STDOUT_ON_USB_CDC.usage: Change this to 1 when you need to debug your application using a terminal emulator on your PC via USB. Set it to 0 if you are using UART for logging or if you need to save power by disabling the USB stack. Ensure your USB hardware is connected and the driver is installed on the host PC before enabling.

STDOUT_QUEUE_DEPTH.brief: Defines the maximum number of characters that can be buffered in the STDOUT output queue before blocking or dropping data.
STDOUT_QUEUE_DEPTH.notes: This constant sets the size of the circular buffer used by the system's standard output stream. If the buffer fills up faster than the hardware peripheral (e.g., UART) can transmit, subsequent print calls may block or lose data depending on the driver implementation. It must be a positive integer, typically a power of two for optimal performance. Increasing this value consumes more RAM but reduces the likelihood of output stalls during high-frequency logging.
STDOUT_QUEUE_DEPTH.usage: Increase this value if you notice truncated log messages or if your application performs heavy logging that causes the system to hang. Decrease this value if your device is running low on SRAM. Ensure that the value is large enough to hold the longest single log message you intend to print to avoid partial output.

SVC_OS_END.brief: A magic constant used by the caOS kernel to identify the end of a Supervisor Call (SVC) sequence.
SVC_OS_END.notes: This value is typically used in the context of system call handling or kernel-level state transitions. It acts as a sentinel or marker in the stack frame or register set during an SVC exception. It is a fixed internal constant (0xFD) and should not be modified by application code. It is tightly coupled with the low-level assembly implementation of the caOS context switcher.
SVC_OS_END.usage: This constant is for internal kernel use only. Do not change this value. Modifying it will break the kernel's ability to correctly identify and return from system calls, likely resulting in a hard fault or system hang. If you are debugging and see this value in a register or stack dump, it indicates the processor is currently processing an OS-level service request.

SVC_SAFEGUARD.brief: A magic constant used to verify the integrity of the Supervisor Call (SVC) stack frame during context switches.
SVC_SAFEGUARD.notes: When enabled, the kernel checks this value at the base of the stack to detect stack overflows or memory corruption. If the value does not match 0xFE, the system triggers a kernel panic. This flag must be consistent across all task stack initializations and is dependent on the architecture-specific SVC handler implementation.
SVC_SAFEGUARD.usage: Change this value only if you are porting caOS to a new architecture or if you need to avoid a collision with specific hardware-reserved memory patterns. Do not modify this value during runtime; incorrect values will cause the system to enter a hard fault or kernel panic immediately upon the first task switch.

SYSCLK_FREQ_HZ.brief: Defines the target system clock frequency in Hertz for the MCU core.
SYSCLK_FREQ_HZ.notes: This constant is used by the RTOS kernel to calculate timing intervals, tick rates, and peripheral baud rates. It must match the actual hardware clock configuration set in the RCC registers. Setting this value incorrectly will cause all time-dependent functions (like delays, timeouts, and UART communication) to run at the wrong speed. Valid values are strictly determined by the specific STM32 model's maximum operating frequency.
SYSCLK_FREQ_HZ.usage: Change this value only when modifying the system clock tree (e.g., changing the PLL settings or external crystal frequency). Always ensure this value matches the frequency calculated in your clock configuration code. If your system timing seems 'slow' or 'fast' compared to real-time, verify this constant first.

SYSLOG_FAC_KERN.brief: Defines the facility code for kernel-level messages in the system logging protocol.
SYSLOG_FAC_KERN.notes: This constant sets the 'facility' field in syslog packets to 0, identifying the source as the kernel. It is used by the network logging stack to categorize messages. Changing this value will cause log aggregators to misclassify kernel events as coming from other system components (e.g., mail or user processes). It must remain 0 to comply with standard RFC 5424 logging conventions for kernel logs.
SYSLOG_FAC_KERN.usage: Do not modify this value unless you are implementing a custom logging protocol that requires non-standard facility mapping. Changing this will break log filtering and severity analysis on remote syslog servers.

SYSLOG_FAC_LOCAL0.brief: Defines the syslog facility identifier for local use 0, used to categorize network log messages.
SYSLOG_FAC_LOCAL0.notes: This constant sets the facility field in the syslog header to 16. It is used by the network stack to tag outgoing log packets. It has no direct impact on system performance but requires the remote syslog server to be configured to accept messages from the 'local0' facility.
SYSLOG_FAC_LOCAL0.usage: Change this value only if your network infrastructure requires a specific syslog facility code (e.g., local1 through local7) to route logs to different files or servers. Ensure the value matches the standard syslog facility definitions (0-23) to avoid malformed log headers.

SYSLOG_FAC_LOCAL7.brief: Defines the syslog facility code for local use 7 (value 23) used in network logging protocols.
SYSLOG_FAC_LOCAL7.notes: This constant maps to the standard Syslog facility 'local7' as defined in RFC 5424. It is used to categorize log messages sent over the network. Changing this value will cause log collectors (like rsyslog or syslog-ng) to misclassify or ignore incoming logs from the device. It has no direct impact on RTOS scheduling or memory, but it must match the configuration of your remote logging server.
SYSLOG_FAC_LOCAL7.usage: Change this value only if your network infrastructure requires a specific facility code for log filtering or routing. Use this when you need to separate device logs from other system logs on a centralized server. Ensure the value remains within the valid syslog facility range (0-23) to avoid protocol violations.

SYSLOG_FAC_USER.brief: Defines the facility code for user-level messages in the system logging protocol.
SYSLOG_FAC_USER.notes: This constant sets the 'facility' field in a syslog packet to the 'USER' category (value 1). It is used by the network stack to categorize logs generated by application-level tasks. It must be a valid integer defined by the RFC 5424 standard; changing this value may cause log servers to misclassify or ignore incoming messages.
SYSLOG_FAC_USER.usage: Change this value only if your network logging infrastructure requires a specific facility code other than the standard 'USER' category. Ensure that your remote syslog server is configured to accept and process the facility code you assign here, otherwise, your application logs may be filtered out or lost.

SYSLOG_MSG_MAX.brief: Defines the maximum character length allowed for a single system log message.
SYSLOG_MSG_MAX.notes: This constant sets the buffer size for the internal logging queue. If a message exceeds 128 bytes, it will be truncated. Increasing this value consumes more RAM from the system heap, while decreasing it saves memory but risks losing data in long diagnostic strings.
SYSLOG_MSG_MAX.usage: Increase this value if you notice your debug logs are being cut off mid-sentence. Decrease it only if your STM32 device is running extremely low on RAM. Ensure that the buffer size is large enough to accommodate your longest 'printf' style debug statements.

SYSLOG_PORT.brief: Defines the UDP port number used for transmitting system log messages over the network.
SYSLOG_PORT.notes: This constant sets the destination port for the caOS logging subsystem. It typically defaults to 514, which is the standard port for the Syslog protocol (RFC 5424). Changing this value requires the receiving log server to be configured to listen on the new port. It is a dependency for the network logging module; if the network stack is disabled, this value is ignored.
SYSLOG_PORT.usage: Change this value only if your network infrastructure requires logs to be sent to a non-standard port or if there is a port conflict with other network services. Ensure the value is a valid 16-bit unsigned integer (1-65535). Setting this to an invalid or occupied port will result in log packets being dropped or rejected by the network stack.

SYSLOG_QUEUE_SIZE.brief: Defines the maximum number of log messages that can be stored in the system log queue before new messages are dropped.
SYSLOG_QUEUE_SIZE.notes: This value determines the depth of the internal message buffer for the system logger. Increasing this value consumes more RAM but prevents log loss during high-frequency bursts. It must be a positive integer, typically a power of two for optimal performance. If set too low, the system may experience 'log overflow' errors when multiple tasks attempt to write logs simultaneously.
SYSLOG_QUEUE_SIZE.usage: Increase this value if you notice missing log entries during high-load scenarios or complex interrupt sequences. Decrease it if your application is running low on heap memory. Ensure that the task processing the log queue is fast enough to keep up with the rate of incoming messages to avoid filling the buffer.

SYSLOG_SEV_ALERT.brief: Defines the severity level for system alert messages within the caOS network logging subsystem.
SYSLOG_SEV_ALERT.notes: This constant represents the numerical priority level for 'Alert' events. It is used by the logging filter to determine if a message should be recorded or transmitted. It typically ranges from 0 to 7, where lower values indicate higher urgency. It depends on the global SYSLOG_LEVEL_THRESHOLD setting; if the system threshold is set higher than 1, these alerts may be suppressed.
SYSLOG_SEV_ALERT.usage: Change this value only if you are modifying the core network protocol logging architecture. It is used to categorize critical network failures that require immediate attention. Do not change this value to filter logs; instead, adjust the system-wide logging threshold to avoid missing critical system alerts.

SYSLOG_SEV_CRIT.brief: Defines the numerical severity level for critical system log messages within the caOS networking stack.
SYSLOG_SEV_CRIT.notes: This constant sets the threshold for logging; when enabled, only messages with a severity level equal to or greater than 2 are recorded. It is typically used in conjunction with the global logging verbosity filter. Valid values are integers, where lower numbers represent higher urgency.
SYSLOG_SEV_CRIT.usage: Change this value if you need to filter out non-critical network logs to save memory or reduce UART/buffer traffic. Do not set this value too high during debugging, as you may lose visibility into critical system failures or stack overflows occurring within the network protocol layer.

SYSLOG_SEV_DEBUG.brief: Sets the minimum severity level for system log messages to include debug-level information.
SYSLOG_SEV_DEBUG.notes: When enabled, the system logs all messages with a severity level of 7 or lower. Disabling or increasing this value reduces memory usage and CPU overhead by filtering out verbose debug logs. It depends on the global logging subsystem being initialized and requires sufficient buffer space in the log queue.
SYSLOG_SEV_DEBUG.usage: Change this value during development to troubleshoot network protocol issues by enabling detailed trace logs. Set it to a lower value (e.g., 3 for errors only) in production environments to prevent log buffer overflows and minimize performance impact.

SYSLOG_SEV_EMERG.brief: Defines the numerical severity level for emergency system logs, representing the highest priority error state.
SYSLOG_SEV_EMERG.notes: This constant is used as a filter or identifier in the caOS logging subsystem. Setting this to 0U indicates that the message is critical and the system is likely unusable. It is typically used in conjunction with a bitmask or threshold check; if the system log level is set to 0, only emergency messages will be recorded.
SYSLOG_SEV_EMERG.usage: Do not change this value as it is part of the standard syslog protocol definition (RFC 5424). Use this constant when calling the logging API to report catastrophic hardware failures or kernel panics that require immediate attention.

SYSLOG_SEV_ERR.brief: Defines the severity level threshold for system error logging in the network stack.
SYSLOG_SEV_ERR.notes: This constant sets the minimum severity level required for a network event to be recorded in the system log. A value of 3U typically corresponds to 'Error' level messages. Decreasing this value increases log verbosity, while increasing it filters out less critical warnings. It depends on the global logging subsystem being initialized.
SYSLOG_SEV_ERR.usage: Change this value during debugging to capture more granular network diagnostic information. Set it to a higher value in production environments to reduce memory usage and CPU overhead caused by excessive logging. Ensure the value remains within the range defined by the system's logging enumeration to avoid undefined behavior.

SYSLOG_SEV_INFO.brief: Defines the severity level threshold for system logging, specifically set to informational messages.
SYSLOG_SEV_INFO.notes: This constant sets the logging filter level to 6. When enabled, the system will record all messages with a severity level of 6 (INFO) or higher (more critical). Decreasing this value increases the volume of logs, while increasing it filters out less critical information. It depends on the global logging subsystem being initialized.
SYSLOG_SEV_INFO.usage: Change this value when you need to debug network protocol behavior without flooding the log buffer with low-level debug data. Use it during integration testing to monitor standard operational events. Warning: setting this value too low in a production environment may cause performance degradation due to excessive UART or flash memory write operations.

SYSLOG_SEV_NOTICE.brief: Defines the severity level for 'Notice' messages in the caOS system logging framework.
SYSLOG_SEV_NOTICE.notes: This constant represents a numerical severity level of 5. It is used by the logging subsystem to filter messages; only logs with a severity equal to or higher than the configured system threshold will be processed or transmitted. It is typically used in conjunction with other severity constants like SYSLOG_SEV_ERROR or SYSLOG_SEV_DEBUG.
SYSLOG_SEV_NOTICE.usage: Change this value only if you are modifying the core logging protocol definitions. It is used as a reference point for log filtering logic. Do not change this value if you are simply trying to adjust the verbosity of your application logs; instead, adjust the global system log level threshold in your configuration header.

SYSLOG_SEV_WARN.brief: Defines the severity level threshold for system logging, specifically targeting warning-level events.
SYSLOG_SEV_WARN.notes: This constant sets the filter level for the caOS logging subsystem. When enabled, the system will record events with a severity of 4 or higher. Lowering this value increases log verbosity, while raising it filters out less critical messages. It depends on the global SYSLOG_LEVEL configuration and typically ranges from 0 (Emergency) to 7 (Debug).
SYSLOG_SEV_WARN.usage: Change this value when you need to debug network protocol issues without flooding the log buffer with informational messages. Increase the threshold (e.g., to 5 or 6) in production environments to reduce memory usage and CPU overhead caused by excessive logging, or decrease it during development to capture potential warning signs before they escalate into system errors.

SYSTICK_ERROR.brief: A sentinel value representing a failure in the system timer initialization or operation.
SYSTICK_ERROR.notes: This constant is typically returned by the caOS kernel initialization functions when the hardware timer fails to start. It is not a configurable setting but a status code. It depends on the HAL_SYSTICK_Config function success. The value -1 is used to indicate an error state in signed integer return types.
SYSTICK_ERROR.usage: Use this constant to check the return value of system initialization functions. If a function returns SYSTICK_ERROR, the RTOS kernel cannot guarantee timing accuracy, and the system should enter a safe state or trigger a hardware reset. Do not modify this value as it is a reserved error code.

SYSTICK_OK.brief: A configuration flag that enables or disables the internal caOS System Tick timer driver.
SYSTICK_OK.notes: When set to 1, the RTOS initializes the hardware timer to generate periodic interrupts for task scheduling. When set to 0, the Systick driver is disabled, meaning the kernel will not have a time base for preemptive multitasking or delay functions. This flag must be enabled for any RTOS features requiring time-slicing or blocking delays.
SYSTICK_OK.usage: Set this to 1 for standard RTOS operation. Set to 0 only if you are implementing a custom time-base driver or if you are running the system in a bare-metal mode where the RTOS scheduler is not required. Disabling this while using RTOS primitives like vTaskDelay will cause the system to hang or behave unpredictably.

TASK_CANARY_VALUE_SAFE.brief: A unique 32-bit pattern used to detect stack overflows by filling unused stack memory.
TASK_CANARY_VALUE_SAFE.notes: When enabled, the kernel writes this value to the entire stack area during task creation. The system periodically checks if this value has been overwritten, indicating a stack overflow. It requires sufficient RAM to store the canary pattern and depends on the stack monitoring feature being active in the kernel configuration.
TASK_CANARY_VALUE_SAFE.usage: Change this value only if it conflicts with specific memory patterns used by your application code. Use this to debug hard faults caused by stack corruption. Warning: Do not set this to 0x00000000 or 0xFFFFFFFF, as these are common values in uninitialized memory and will lead to false negatives in overflow detection.

TASK_CANARY_VALUE_SAFE_FP.brief: The specific 32-bit pattern used to detect stack overflows in task memory regions.
TASK_CANARY_VALUE_SAFE_FP.notes: When enabled, the kernel writes this value to the entire stack area of a task upon creation. During context switches, the scheduler checks if the top of the stack still contains this value. If the value is corrupted, the system triggers a stack overflow fault. This constant must be a 32-bit word aligned with the architecture's word size. It has no direct dependencies on other flags but requires sufficient stack space to be allocated to avoid false positives.
TASK_CANARY_VALUE_SAFE_FP.usage: Change this value only if you suspect memory corruption patterns are conflicting with the default constant. It is primarily used for debugging stack usage; if your system crashes with a stack overflow error, verify that your task stack sizes are large enough. Do not set this to a value that is likely to appear naturally in your application's data, as it will mask potential stack overflows.

TASK_CANARY_VALUE_STD.brief: The default 32-bit pattern used to fill task stacks to detect stack overflows.
TASK_CANARY_VALUE_STD.notes: When enabled, the kernel writes this specific hex value across the entire stack memory area of a task during creation. If the stack pointer exceeds the allocated bounds, the kernel checks if this pattern has been overwritten. It requires the stack monitoring feature to be enabled in the kernel configuration. The value 0xCACAFEF8 is chosen because it is unlikely to occur naturally in program data.
TASK_CANARY_VALUE_STD.usage: Change this value only if you need to avoid specific memory patterns that might conflict with your application's data or if you are performing advanced debugging. Ensure the value is a 32-bit word aligned with the architecture. If you change this, you must also update the corresponding check logic in the kernel's stack overflow handler.

TASK_CANARY_VALUE_STD_FP.brief: The default 32-bit pattern used to fill task stacks to detect stack overflows.
TASK_CANARY_VALUE_STD_FP.notes: When enabled, the kernel writes this specific hex value across the entire stack memory area of a task during creation. If the stack pointer exceeds the allocated bounds, the kernel checks if this pattern has been overwritten. This constant must be a 32-bit word aligned value. Changing this value requires a full project rebuild to ensure all stack initialization routines use the new pattern.
TASK_CANARY_VALUE_STD_FP.usage: Change this value if you suspect the default pattern (0xCACAFEF9) is accidentally appearing in your application data, causing false-positive stack overflow detections. Use a unique, non-zero value that is unlikely to occur naturally in your program's variables. Ensure the value is defined as a 32-bit unsigned integer to maintain memory alignment and prevent bus faults during stack initialization.

TASK_NAME_LEN.brief: Defines the maximum number of characters allowed for a task name string.
TASK_NAME_LEN.notes: This constant sets the fixed size of the character array used to store task identifiers in the Task Control Block (TCB). If set to 12, names longer than 11 characters (plus the null terminator) will be truncated. Increasing this value increases the memory footprint of every task created in the system.
TASK_NAME_LEN.usage: Adjust this value if your project requires more descriptive task names for debugging or logging purposes. Ensure that the value is large enough to accommodate your naming convention, but keep it as small as possible to conserve RAM, especially in systems with a high number of concurrent tasks.

TCP_ARP_TIMEOUT_MS.brief: Defines the duration in milliseconds that the system waits for an ARP response before timing out.
TCP_ARP_TIMEOUT_MS.notes: This constant determines the lifespan of an ARP request packet. If set too low, the system may fail to resolve IP addresses to MAC addresses on busy networks. If set too high, it increases latency when communicating with new devices. The value is typically set between 1000 and 5000 milliseconds depending on network stability.
TCP_ARP_TIMEOUT_MS.usage: Increase this value if you experience frequent 'Host Unreachable' errors or connection timeouts on high-latency or congested networks. Decrease it only if your application requires rapid failure detection for non-responsive network nodes. Ensure this value is consistent with the overall network stack timeout settings to avoid race conditions.

TCP_CLOSE_WAIT_MS.brief: Defines the timeout duration in milliseconds for a TCP connection to remain in the CLOSE_WAIT state.
TCP_CLOSE_WAIT_MS.notes: This constant determines how long the stack waits for the application to acknowledge a connection closure before forcing a reset. It is dependent on the system tick frequency. Typical values range from 5000U to 30000U depending on network latency requirements.
TCP_CLOSE_WAIT_MS.usage: Increase this value if you experience premature connection resets during slow application processing. Decrease it if you need to free up socket resources faster in high-traffic environments. Setting this too low may cause active connections to drop unexpectedly.

TCP_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS.brief: Defines the maximum time in milliseconds the system waits for a TCP connection to be established.
TCP_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS.notes: This constant sets the timeout duration for the socket connect operation. If the connection is not completed within this period, the function returns a timeout error. It depends on the underlying network stack's tick rate. Typical values range from 1000U to 10000U depending on network latency requirements.
TCP_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MS.usage: Increase this value if you are connecting to remote servers over high-latency networks or unstable connections to prevent premature timeouts. Decrease it if you need the application to fail fast when a server is unreachable to maintain system responsiveness. Setting this too low may cause connection failures on busy networks.

TCP_FLAG_ACK.brief: A bitmask flag representing the Acknowledgment (ACK) field in a TCP packet header.
TCP_FLAG_ACK.notes: When set, this flag indicates that the Acknowledgment Number field in the TCP header is valid. It is a fundamental component of the TCP state machine, used to confirm receipt of data segments. This constant is typically used in conjunction with bitwise OR operations to construct or parse TCP headers. It has no direct dependencies on other flags but must be used in accordance with the TCP protocol specification (RFC 793).
TCP_FLAG_ACK.usage: Use this flag when manually constructing TCP packets or when inspecting incoming packet headers to determine if the segment is an acknowledgment. Do not modify the value 0x10U, as it is defined by the TCP protocol standard. Incorrect usage or failure to set this flag when required will result in dropped connections or retransmission loops.

TCP_FLAG_FIN.brief: A bitmask flag representing the TCP FIN (Finish) control bit used to signal the graceful termination of a connection.
TCP_FLAG_FIN.notes: This flag is set in the TCP header control field. When enabled, it indicates that the sender has no more data to transmit. It is typically used in conjunction with the TCP state machine to transition from ESTABLISHED to FIN_WAIT_1 or CLOSE_WAIT states. It has no dependencies on other flags but must be handled by the TCP stack's state transition logic.
TCP_FLAG_FIN.usage: Change this value only if you are modifying the low-level TCP/IP stack implementation or debugging packet headers. Do not modify this constant for application-level code. Using an incorrect value will cause the TCP stack to misinterpret connection termination requests, leading to hung sockets or broken network communication.

TCP_FLAG_PSH.brief: Defines the PUSH flag in the TCP header to force immediate data delivery to the application layer.
TCP_FLAG_PSH.notes: When set, this flag instructs the receiving TCP stack to push buffered data to the application immediately rather than waiting for the buffer to fill. It is a single-bit flag within the TCP control byte. It has no direct dependencies on other flags but must be used in conjunction with valid sequence numbers.
TCP_FLAG_PSH.usage: Enable this flag when sending time-sensitive control packets or the final segment of a data stream to reduce latency. Do not set this flag on every single packet in a high-throughput stream, as it can cause excessive interrupt overhead and degrade network performance by preventing efficient packet coalescing.

TCP_FLAG_RST.brief: A control flag used in the TCP header to indicate an immediate connection reset.
TCP_FLAG_RST.notes: When this flag is set in a TCP packet, the receiving stack must immediately abort the connection and discard all associated buffers. It is a bitmask value (0x04U) typically combined with other TCP flags. It has no dependencies on other RTOS flags but requires the network stack to be in a valid state to process the reset signal.
TCP_FLAG_RST.usage: Use this flag when you need to force-close a connection due to an error, a timeout, or an invalid packet sequence. Do not set this flag manually unless you are implementing custom low-level socket handling, as incorrect usage will cause unexpected connection drops and potential data loss for the peer.

TCP_FLAG_SYN.brief: A bitmask flag representing the Synchronize sequence number control bit in a TCP packet header.
TCP_FLAG_SYN.notes: This flag is used during the TCP three-way handshake to initiate a connection. When set to 0x02, the TCP stack interprets the segment as a connection request. It is typically used in conjunction with other flags like ACK or FIN. It must be defined as 0x02 to comply with RFC 793 standards for TCP header formatting.
TCP_FLAG_SYN.usage: Change this value only if you are implementing a custom or non-standard TCP stack variant. For standard network communication, this value should remain unchanged. Incorrect values will cause the remote host to reject connection attempts or fail to recognize the packet type, leading to silent connection timeouts.

TCP_FLAG_URG.brief: A bitmask flag representing the Urgent pointer field in a TCP packet header.
TCP_FLAG_URG.notes: When set in the TCP control bits, this flag indicates that the Urgent Pointer field in the TCP header is valid and contains data that should be processed with higher priority. It is typically used in conjunction with the TCP_URG_PTR field. This flag is a standard part of the TCP protocol stack and should not be modified unless implementing custom protocol extensions.
TCP_FLAG_URG.usage: Use this flag when inspecting or constructing TCP segments that require out-of-band data signaling. It is primarily used for urgent data transmission, such as interrupting a remote process. Do not manually set this flag unless you are handling specific legacy protocols or specialized network traffic, as incorrect usage can lead to unexpected behavior in standard TCP/IP stacks.

TCP_MAX_CONN.brief: Defines the maximum number of concurrent TCP connections allowed by the caOS network stack.
TCP_MAX_CONN.notes: This constant determines the size of the internal connection control block (CCB) table. Increasing this value consumes more RAM (each connection requires a fixed memory buffer for state tracking). It must be greater than 0 and is typically limited by the available heap memory. If set too low, new connection requests will be rejected by the stack.
TCP_MAX_CONN.usage: Adjust this value based on your application's memory constraints and the expected number of simultaneous clients. Increase it if your device acts as a server handling multiple concurrent requests; decrease it to save RAM if the device only communicates with a single master node.

TCP_MAX_INFLIGHT.brief: Defines the maximum number of unacknowledged TCP segments allowed in the network buffer.
TCP_MAX_INFLIGHT.notes: This constant controls the TCP sliding window size at the transport layer. Increasing this value allows higher throughput on high-latency links but consumes more RAM per socket. It must be balanced against the total available heap memory and the number of concurrent active connections. Typical values range from 4 to 32.
TCP_MAX_INFLIGHT.usage: Increase this value if you observe slow data transfer speeds or high packet loss on high-bandwidth networks. Decrease this value if the system experiences memory allocation failures (heap exhaustion) during heavy network traffic. Ensure that the total memory allocated for all sockets does not exceed the system's available RAM.

TCP_MAX_LISTEN.brief: Defines the maximum number of pending TCP connection requests that can be queued for a listening socket.
TCP_MAX_LISTEN.notes: This constant determines the size of the backlog queue for the TCP stack. Increasing this value allows the system to handle more simultaneous incoming connection attempts before rejecting new ones. It consumes additional RAM for each slot in the queue. Valid range is typically 1 to 16, depending on available heap memory.
TCP_MAX_LISTEN.usage: Increase this value if your application experiences 'Connection Refused' errors during high-traffic periods or when multiple clients attempt to connect simultaneously. Decrease it if the system is running low on memory. Setting this too high may lead to memory exhaustion if many clients attempt to connect at once.

TCP_MAX_RETRIES.brief: Defines the maximum number of times the TCP stack will attempt to retransmit a packet before declaring a connection failure.
TCP_MAX_RETRIES.notes: When enabled, the stack will retry sending unacknowledged segments up to this count. Increasing this value improves reliability on lossy networks but increases the time taken to detect a broken connection. It depends on the TCP_RETRANSMIT_TIMEOUT setting. Typical values range from 3 to 10; setting this too high may cause the application to hang while waiting for a timeout.
TCP_MAX_RETRIES.usage: Increase this value if your device experiences frequent packet loss or intermittent connectivity issues that cause premature socket closures. Decrease it if you need the system to detect and recover from network failures faster. Ensure this value is balanced with your application's latency requirements.

TCP_MSS_DEFAULT.brief: Defines the Maximum Segment Size (MSS) in bytes for TCP connections, representing the largest amount of data that can be received in a single TCP segment.
TCP_MSS_DEFAULT.notes: This value directly impacts the TCP payload size. Enabling a larger value increases throughput by reducing header overhead, while a smaller value may be required for networks with specific MTU constraints. It is typically set to 1460 to fit within a standard 1500-byte Ethernet MTU after accounting for IP and TCP headers. It must be less than or equal to the network interface MTU minus 40 bytes.
TCP_MSS_DEFAULT.usage: Adjust this value if your device communicates over networks with restricted MTU sizes (e.g., VPNs, tunnels, or specific cellular links) to prevent packet fragmentation. Setting this value too high relative to the network path MTU will cause packet loss or performance degradation due to fragmentation; setting it too low will unnecessarily increase protocol overhead.

TCP_MSS_MIN.brief: Defines the minimum Maximum Segment Size (MSS) allowed for TCP connections.
TCP_MSS_MIN.notes: This constant sets the lower bound for the TCP MSS negotiation. If a remote peer requests an MSS smaller than this value, the stack will reject the connection or force the minimum. It is typically set to 64 bytes to ensure that TCP segments are large enough to carry meaningful data without excessive header overhead. It is used by the TCP state machine during the SYN/SYN-ACK handshake.
TCP_MSS_MIN.usage: Increase this value if you need to enforce a higher minimum payload size to optimize throughput on high-latency links. Decrease it only if you are working with extremely constrained memory buffers or specialized low-bandwidth protocols that require very small packets. Warning: setting this too low may lead to inefficient network utilization due to the high ratio of TCP/IP headers to actual data payload.

TCP_REAP_MS.brief: Defines the timeout duration in milliseconds for cleaning up inactive or closed TCP connections.
TCP_REAP_MS.notes: This constant controls the 'reaping' process of the TCP stack. When a connection enters a closed or timed-out state, the system waits for this duration before freeing the associated memory and control blocks. A value of 1000U means 1 second. Lower values free memory faster but may prematurely drop connections under high latency; higher values keep resources occupied longer.
TCP_REAP_MS.usage: Adjust this value if you observe memory exhaustion (e.g., ca_net_buf_pressure) during high TCP traffic or frequent connection cycles. If your application handles many short-lived connections, you might decrease this value to reclaim memory buffers more aggressively. Ensure you do not set it too low, as it may interfere with the TCP state machine's ability to handle delayed packets.

TCP_RTO_INITIAL_MS.brief: Defines the initial Retransmission Timeout (RTO) value in milliseconds for new TCP connections.
TCP_RTO_INITIAL_MS.notes: This value sets the duration the stack waits for an acknowledgment before retransmitting the first SYN packet. Increasing this value helps in high-latency networks, while decreasing it speeds up connection failure detection. It must be a positive integer, typically ranging from 200 to 3000 depending on the expected network stability.
TCP_RTO_INITIAL_MS.usage: Adjust this value if you experience frequent connection timeouts on slow or congested networks. If set too low, the system may trigger unnecessary retransmissions, wasting bandwidth; if set too high, the system will be slow to recover from dropped packets during the initial handshake.

TCP_RTO_MAX_MS.brief: Defines the maximum timeout duration in milliseconds for a TCP retransmission attempt.
TCP_RTO_MAX_MS.notes: This constant sets the upper bound for the exponential backoff algorithm used during packet loss. If the system fails to receive an ACK within this period, the connection is typically dropped. It depends on the TCP_MAX_RETRIES setting; increasing this value allows for more robust connections on high-latency or unstable networks but increases the time taken to detect a dead link.
TCP_RTO_MAX_MS.usage: Increase this value if your device operates on high-latency networks (e.g., satellite or congested cellular links) to prevent premature connection termination. Decrease it only if your application requires rapid detection of broken connections. Setting this value too low may cause frequent, unnecessary connection drops on busy networks.

TCP_RX_RING_DEPTH.brief: Defines the number of packet slots available in the TCP receive buffer ring.
TCP_RX_RING_DEPTH.notes: This value determines how many incoming TCP segments can be queued before the stack begins dropping packets or applying backpressure. Increasing this value consumes more RAM (each slot is fixed-size based on MTU). It must be a power of two for optimal performance in the circular buffer implementation. Typical range is 2 to 16 depending on available heap memory.
TCP_RX_RING_DEPTH.usage: Increase this value if you observe packet loss or 'TCP receive buffer overflow' errors during high-throughput network bursts. Decrease this value if the system is running low on RAM and the network traffic is low-frequency or strictly request-response based.

TCP_TCP_ACCEPT_TIMEOUT_MS.brief: Defines the maximum time in milliseconds the system waits for an incoming TCP connection request before aborting.
TCP_TCP_ACCEPT_TIMEOUT_MS.notes: This constant controls the blocking duration of the accept() function. If set to 0, the system waits indefinitely. If the value is too low, legitimate clients may fail to connect during network congestion. It depends on the underlying TCP/IP stack's tick rate and memory availability for socket buffers.
TCP_TCP_ACCEPT_TIMEOUT_MS.usage: Increase this value if your application experiences frequent 'connection timeout' errors in high-latency network environments. Decrease it if you need the system to remain responsive and quickly free up resources when a client fails to initiate a handshake. Ensure the value is sufficient to cover the round-trip time of your network infrastructure.

TCP_TIMER_TICK_MS.brief: Defines the time interval in milliseconds for the TCP/IP stack's internal timer heartbeat.
TCP_TIMER_TICK_MS.notes: This constant determines the resolution of TCP retransmissions, keep-alive probes, and connection timeouts. Decreasing this value increases the frequency of stack processing, which improves responsiveness but consumes more CPU cycles. It must be a multiple of the system tick period. Typical values range from 50ms to 500ms.
TCP_TIMER_TICK_MS.usage: Adjust this value if you experience slow connection recovery or delayed timeouts. Use a smaller value for high-speed networks requiring fast retransmission, or a larger value to reduce CPU overhead in low-power applications. Setting this too low may cause the stack to starve other tasks of processing time.

TCP_TIME_WAIT_MS.brief: Defines the duration in milliseconds that a TCP connection remains in the TIME_WAIT state after closure.
TCP_TIME_WAIT_MS.notes: This constant controls how long the socket remains reserved after a connection is closed to ensure delayed packets are handled. Increasing this value consumes more memory resources as the socket control block cannot be reused until the timer expires. The default value is 4000ms (4 seconds).
TCP_TIME_WAIT_MS.usage: Increase this value if you experience data corruption or connection errors due to late-arriving packets from a previous session. Decrease it only if your system is running out of available sockets and you are certain that network latency is low enough to avoid packet collisions.

TFTP_BLOCK_SIZE.brief: Defines the size in bytes of a single data packet transferred during a TFTP operation.
TFTP_BLOCK_SIZE.notes: This value directly impacts the payload size of UDP packets sent over the network. While 512 bytes is the standard defined by RFC 1350, increasing this value can improve throughput on high-speed networks, provided the underlying network stack and hardware buffers support larger MTUs. Decreasing it may be necessary for memory-constrained systems or unstable links, but values larger than 512 may cause compatibility issues with standard TFTP clients.
TFTP_BLOCK_SIZE.usage: Adjust this value if you encounter packet fragmentation issues or if you need to optimize file transfer speeds. Ensure that your network buffer size (defined elsewhere in the stack) is large enough to accommodate this value plus the UDP/IP/Ethernet header overhead. Do not change this unless you have verified that both the client and server support the chosen block size.

TFTP_BLOCK_TIMEOUT_MS.brief: Defines the maximum time in milliseconds the system waits for a response during a TFTP data block transfer.
TFTP_BLOCK_TIMEOUT_MS.notes: This constant sets the timeout duration for the TFTP client state machine. If no acknowledgment is received from the server within this period, the transfer is aborted. It depends on the network latency and the reliability of the connection. Typical values range from 1000ms to 10000ms depending on the network environment.
TFTP_BLOCK_TIMEOUT_MS.usage: Increase this value if you experience frequent 'timeout' errors on high-latency or congested networks. Decrease it if you need the system to fail fast and recover quickly during a network disconnection. Setting this value too low may cause premature termination of valid transfers on slow links.

TFTP_ERR_ACCESS.brief: An error code indicating that the TFTP server has denied access to the requested file or directory.
TFTP_ERR_ACCESS.notes: This constant is returned by the TFTP service layer when a client attempts to read or write a file that violates security permissions or is outside the allowed root directory. It is a standard TFTP error code (Error Code 2) defined in RFC 1350. It does not depend on other flags but requires the file system abstraction layer to be correctly initialized.
TFTP_ERR_ACCESS.usage: Use this value when implementing custom file access control logic within the TFTP callback functions. Do not modify this value, as it must remain compliant with the TFTP protocol specification to ensure compatibility with standard TFTP clients.

TFTP_ERR_DISKFULL.brief: Error code indicating that the TFTP server cannot write data because the storage medium is full.
TFTP_ERR_DISKFULL.notes: This constant is returned by the TFTP service layer when a file write operation fails due to insufficient disk space. It is a specific error enumeration used in the TFTP packet response. It depends on the underlying filesystem driver reporting a 'disk full' status to the network stack.
TFTP_ERR_DISKFULL.usage: Use this value when implementing custom error handling or logging for TFTP file transfers. Do not modify this value as it must remain compliant with the TFTP protocol error code definitions (RFC 1350). If you see this error frequently, check the filesystem capacity or the file size limits of the storage partition.

TFTP_ERR_EXISTS.brief: Error code indicating that the file requested for creation already exists on the server.
TFTP_ERR_EXISTS.notes: This constant is returned by the TFTP service layer when a write request (WRQ) is received for a filename that is already present in the file system. It is a standard TFTP error code (Error Code 6) as defined in RFC 1350. It does not require configuration but must be handled by the client-side logic to prevent accidental overwriting of existing data.
TFTP_ERR_EXISTS.usage: Use this constant in your application-level error handling switch-case blocks when implementing TFTP file transfer clients. If you receive this error, you should prompt the user or the automated system to either choose a different filename or explicitly delete the existing file before attempting the upload again.

TFTP_ERR_ILLEGAL.brief: An error code indicating that the TFTP request received by the server is not supported or violates the protocol format.
TFTP_ERR_ILLEGAL.notes: This constant represents the 'Illegal TFTP Operation' error defined in RFC 1350. When returned, the TFTP service will send an error packet to the client and terminate the current transfer session. It is a read-only status code used internally by the caOS network stack and should not be modified by the user.
TFTP_ERR_ILLEGAL.usage: This value is used for debugging network communication issues. If you see this error in your logs, it typically means the TFTP client is sending malformed packets, using an unsupported transfer mode (e.g., requesting 'mail' mode instead of 'octet'), or attempting an operation that the caOS TFTP server does not implement.

TFTP_ERR_NOTFOUND.brief: Error code returned by the TFTP service when a requested file does not exist on the storage medium.
TFTP_ERR_NOTFOUND.notes: This constant is used as a return value in the TFTP protocol handler. It indicates that the server successfully processed the request but could not locate the specified filename. It is typically used in conjunction with the TFTP error packet mechanism (Error Code 1).
TFTP_ERR_NOTFOUND.usage: Do not modify this value as it is defined by the TFTP protocol specification (RFC 1350). Use this constant in your application logic when checking the return status of file system read operations to distinguish between 'file not found' and other hardware or permission errors.

TFTP_ERR_NOUSER.brief: Error code indicating that the requested TFTP user or account does not exist on the server.
TFTP_ERR_NOUSER.notes: This is a constant value (7U) used within the TFTP protocol stack to signal an authentication or authorization failure. It is returned by the TFTP service layer when a client attempts to access a resource associated with a non-existent user. It does not affect system memory or scheduling, but acts as a return status for error handling logic.
TFTP_ERR_NOUSER.usage: This value should not be changed as it is defined by the TFTP protocol specification (RFC 1350). Use this constant in your application code when implementing custom file access control or user validation logic to ensure compatibility with standard TFTP clients. If you receive this error, verify the user credentials or the file path mapping configured in the TFTP service.

TFTP_ERR_TID.brief: Defines the specific error code returned by the TFTP service when an unexpected Transfer Identifier (TID) is received.
TFTP_ERR_TID.notes: This constant is used to identify packets originating from an unknown or unauthorized source port during an active TFTP session. When enabled, the stack compares the incoming packet's TID against the session's expected TID. If they do not match, the system triggers this error code. It is a standard protocol requirement for security and session integrity. The value 5U is the protocol-defined error code for 'Unknown transfer ID'.
TFTP_ERR_TID.usage: Do not change this value unless you are implementing a custom, non-standard TFTP variant. Changing this constant will cause the TFTP client to fail to recognize the error, potentially leading to session hangs or security vulnerabilities where unauthorized packets could interfere with an active file transfer.

TFTP_ERR_UNDEF.brief: Represents a generic or undefined error condition within the TFTP service state machine.
TFTP_ERR_UNDEF.notes: This constant is used as a fallback error code when a specific protocol violation or network failure does not map to a defined TFTP error type. It is typically returned by the TFTP server task when an unexpected packet structure or internal state mismatch occurs. It does not require specific dependencies but should be handled by the client-side error logging mechanism.
TFTP_ERR_UNDEF.usage: This value should not be modified as it is part of the standard TFTP error enumeration. It is used by developers to identify 'catch-all' failure scenarios during debugging. If you encounter this error frequently, check for network packet corruption or incomplete TFTP request frames.

TFTP_MAX_XFER.brief: Defines the maximum number of concurrent TFTP transfer sessions allowed by the caOS TFTP service.
TFTP_MAX_XFER.notes: This constant controls the memory allocation for the TFTP server's internal session table. Increasing this value allows more simultaneous file transfers but consumes more RAM. It is typically set to a small integer (e.g., 2U to 4U) to conserve resources on embedded STM32 targets. It must be defined before initializing the TFTP service via ca_tftp_service_init.
TFTP_MAX_XFER.usage: Increase this value if your application requires multiple simultaneous TFTP clients to upload or download files. Decrease it if you encounter memory allocation failures or if the system has very limited RAM. Ensure that the total memory footprint of all concurrent sessions does not exceed the available heap.

TFTP_PORT.brief: Defines the UDP port number used by the caOS TFTP server for file transfer operations.
TFTP_PORT.notes: This constant sets the listening port for incoming TFTP requests. The default value is 69, which is the IANA-registered port for TFTP. Changing this value requires all TFTP clients to be configured to connect to the new port. It must be a valid 16-bit unsigned integer (1-65535).
TFTP_PORT.usage: Change this value only if your network environment requires a non-standard port to avoid conflicts with other services or to bypass specific firewall restrictions. Ensure that the new port is not already reserved by other system services or protocols to prevent binding failures.

TFTP_RETRY_N.brief: Defines the maximum number of times the TFTP client will attempt to retransmit a packet before declaring a timeout error.
TFTP_RETRY_N.notes: Increasing this value allows the system to tolerate more packet loss on unstable networks but increases the total time taken to report a failed transfer. It depends on the TFTP_TIMEOUT_MS setting; if the timeout is too short, high retry counts may still fail. Typical values range from 3 to 10 depending on network reliability.
TFTP_RETRY_N.usage: Increase this value if you experience frequent 'Transfer Failed' errors during firmware updates over lossy or congested Ethernet links. Do not set this value to 0, as it will disable retransmission entirely, causing the transfer to fail on the first dropped packet.

TLS_HASH_MAX.brief: Defines the maximum buffer size in bytes allocated for storing hash values during TLS handshake operations.
TLS_HASH_MAX.notes: This constant determines the memory footprint of the TLS stack's internal hash buffers. A value of 48U is sufficient to accommodate SHA-384 hashes. If you are using stronger algorithms or custom extensions requiring larger digests, this value must be increased. It is a static allocation, so increasing it directly impacts the RAM usage of every TLS context.
TLS_HASH_MAX.usage: Adjust this value only if you encounter buffer overflow errors during TLS handshake or if you need to support cryptographic algorithms with larger output sizes than SHA-384. Ensure the value is always large enough to hold the largest hash digest used in your TLS configuration; otherwise, the system will fail to verify handshake integrity.

TLS_HS_BUF_SIZE.brief: Defines the size in bytes of the internal buffer used for TLS handshake operations.
TLS_HS_BUF_SIZE.notes: This constant allocates a static memory block for the TLS handshake state machine. Increasing this value allows for larger certificate chains or more complex handshake parameters, but consumes more RAM. Decreasing it may cause handshake failures if the peer sends large certificate chains that exceed the buffer capacity. Typical value is 4096 bytes, which is generally sufficient for standard TLS 1.2/1.3 handshakes.
TLS_HS_BUF_SIZE.usage: Adjust this value if you encounter 'TLS handshake failed' errors when connecting to servers with large certificate chains. Ensure the value is a multiple of the system's memory alignment requirements. If your system is low on RAM, you may attempt to reduce this value, but be aware that it will limit the maximum size of the handshake messages the device can process.
