ca_le32toh.usage: Use this when parsing binary data received from network packets, file systems, or external sensors that transmit data in little-endian format. Always use this instead of manual bit-shifting to ensure your code remains portable across different CPU architectures.

ca_le64toh.brief: A macro that converts a 64-bit unsigned integer from little-endian byte order to the host system's native byte order.
ca_le64toh.notes: This macro performs a no-op on little-endian architectures (like ARM Cortex-M) and a byte-swap on big-endian architectures. It is a compile-time abstraction that ensures data portability when reading 64-bit values from network packets or external storage. It has no dependencies on other RTOS flags but requires the input to be a 64-bit unsigned integer type.
ca_le64toh.usage: Use this macro whenever you are parsing 64-bit data structures received from external hardware or communication protocols (e.g., Modbus, CAN, or binary files) to ensure the code remains platform-independent. Do not use this on data that is already in the host's native format, as it will corrupt the value on big-endian systems.

ca_mpu_add_region.brief: Configures the Memory Protection Unit (MPU) to define a specific memory region for hardware access control.
ca_mpu_add_region.notes: When set to 0, the MPU region configuration is disabled or bypassed. Enabling this requires defining base addresses, sizes, and access permissions (Read/Write/Execute). It depends on the STM32 hardware MPU peripheral being initialized. Valid values are typically 0 (disabled) or 1 (enabled), though some implementations may allow multiple region indices.
ca_mpu_add_region.usage: Change this value to 1 when you need to isolate specific memory areas, such as protecting kernel memory from user tasks or defining non-cacheable regions for peripherals. Warning: Incorrectly configuring MPU regions will trigger a MemManage fault, causing the system to halt or reset immediately upon accessing the restricted memory.

ca_mpu_first_free_region.brief: Defines the index of the first MPU region available for user-defined memory protection tasks.
ca_mpu_first_free_region.notes: This constant sets the starting point for the MPU region allocator. When set to 0, the system assumes the first MPU slot is available for general use. Changing this value shifts the base index, which is critical if lower-indexed regions are reserved for kernel-level memory protection or peripheral access. It must be less than the total number of available MPU regions on the specific STM32 hardware.
ca_mpu_first_free_region.usage: Adjust this value if your specific application or board support package reserves the initial MPU slots for hardware-specific memory mapping or kernel-critical regions. Incorrectly setting this value can lead to memory access violations or overwriting essential system protection settings, causing a HardFault.

ca_mpu_get_available_regions.brief: Returns the number of hardware MPU regions currently available for allocation.
ca_mpu_get_available_regions.notes: This function queries the Memory Protection Unit (MPU) controller to determine how many slots remain free. The return value is an integer ranging from 0 to the maximum number of regions supported by the specific STM32 hardware (typically 8 or 16). It depends on the MPU initialization state; if the MPU is disabled, it may return the total hardware capacity.
ca_mpu_get_available_regions.usage: Use this before dynamically creating memory-protected tasks or regions to ensure the hardware has enough slots to enforce the requested security policy. If this returns 0, any attempt to create a new protected region will fail or trigger a system error. Do not assume a fixed number of regions across different STM32 models, as this value varies by chip architecture.

ca_mpu_get_busy_regions.brief: A configuration flag that determines whether the MPU driver retrieves and tracks currently active memory protection regions.
ca_mpu_get_busy_regions.notes: When set to 1, the system queries the hardware MPU registers to identify active regions; when set to 0, this feature is disabled. Enabling this requires the MPU hardware to be initialized and active. It is typically used for debugging memory access violations or dynamic task stack monitoring.
ca_mpu_get_busy_regions.usage: Set this to 1 if you need to perform runtime diagnostics on memory protection boundaries or if you are implementing custom memory safety checks. Keep it at 0 for production builds to reduce CPU overhead and code size, as reading MPU registers adds latency to context switches.

ca_mpu_get_system_regions.brief: A configuration flag that determines whether the system memory regions are automatically retrieved and configured by the MPU driver.
ca_mpu_get_system_regions.notes: When set to 1, the kernel automatically detects and protects critical system memory areas. When set to 0, the MPU will not automatically apply these default system-wide memory protections. This flag depends on the hardware support for the Memory Protection Unit (MPU) on the specific STM32 target. Valid values are 0 (disabled) or 1 (enabled).
ca_mpu_get_system_regions.usage: Set this to 1 if you want the RTOS to handle memory safety for system tasks automatically. Set to 0 only if you are manually defining all MPU regions in your application code or if you are working on a platform where automatic detection is not supported. Warning: Disabling this (0) increases the risk of memory corruption if your application tasks are not strictly isolated.

ca_mpu_get_total_regions.brief: Defines the total number of memory protection regions supported by the MPU hardware.
ca_mpu_get_total_regions.notes: This value directly corresponds to the hardware capability of the STM32 MPU (e.g., 8 or 16 regions). Setting this to 0 disables MPU-based memory protection features. It is a dependency for any task-level memory isolation or stack overflow protection mechanisms.
ca_mpu_get_total_regions.usage: Change this value only if you are porting the RTOS to a different STM32 chip with a different MPU architecture. Do not set this to 0 if you intend to use memory protection, as it will cause the kernel to bypass all hardware-enforced memory access rules, potentially leading to silent memory corruption.

ca_mpu_region_covers.brief: A boolean flag that determines if the MPU region configuration should automatically cover the entire memory range of a task's stack.
ca_mpu_region_covers.notes: When set to true, the kernel automatically calculates and enforces MPU protection for the task stack boundaries. When false, the MPU must be configured manually for each task. This flag depends on the hardware MPU being enabled in the system configuration. Typical values are true for safety-critical applications and false for systems requiring custom, non-standard memory mapping.
ca_mpu_region_covers.usage: Set this to true to simplify memory protection management and prevent stack overflow errors. Change to false only if you are implementing a custom memory management scheme or if the default automatic coverage conflicts with specific hardware-defined memory regions. Warning: disabling this without manual MPU configuration leaves the task stack vulnerable to corruption.

ca_mpu_update_region.brief: A macro interface used to update the configuration of a specific Memory Protection Unit (MPU) region.
ca_mpu_update_region.notes: This function acts as a wrapper for hardware-specific MPU register updates. When enabled, it enforces memory access permissions (Read/Write/Execute) for defined memory segments. If disabled or set to a null operation, the MPU remains static, potentially leaving memory unprotected. It depends on the hardware architecture supporting MPU features and must be called after any changes to memory map definitions.
ca_mpu_update_region.usage: Use this when you need to dynamically change memory access rights, such as isolating a task's stack or protecting peripheral registers. Change this value if you are porting the RTOS to a new STM32 series or if you need to disable MPU enforcement for debugging purposes. Warning: Incorrect region parameters can trigger a MemManage fault, causing the system to hang or reset.

ca_ntohl.brief: Converts a 32-bit unsigned integer from network byte order (big-endian) to host byte order (little-endian).
ca_ntohl.notes: This macro utilizes the ca_bswap32 function to perform a byte-swap operation. It is essential for STM32 architectures, which are little-endian, when processing data received from network protocols that use big-endian format. It has no dependencies on other RTOS flags but relies on the hardware-specific implementation of ca_bswap32.
ca_ntohl.usage: Use this macro whenever you receive 32-bit data packets from a network interface (e.g., Ethernet or CAN bus) to ensure the byte order matches the processor's native format. Failure to use this when required will result in corrupted data values. Do not use this on data that is already in host byte order, as it will reverse the bytes and cause incorrect calculations.

ca_ntohl_signed.brief: Converts a 32-bit signed integer from network byte order (big-endian) to host byte order.
ca_ntohl_signed.notes: This macro maps directly to ca_bswap32_signed(x). It performs a byte-swap operation on the input value. It is architecture-independent, meaning it will always swap the bytes regardless of whether the host CPU is little-endian or big-endian, ensuring the data is interpreted correctly according to network standards.
ca_ntohl_signed.usage: Use this when receiving 32-bit signed data packets over a network interface (e.g., TCP/IP or CAN bus) where the data is transmitted in big-endian format. Do not use this on data that is already in host byte order, as it will corrupt the value by reversing the byte sequence.

ca_ntohll.brief: Converts a 64-bit unsigned integer from network byte order (big-endian) to host byte order (little-endian).
ca_ntohll.notes: This macro utilizes the ca_bswap64 function to perform a byte-swap operation. It is typically used when receiving 64-bit data packets over a network interface where the protocol specifies big-endian format. If the host architecture is already big-endian, this macro may be optimized to a no-op by the compiler.
ca_ntohll.usage: Use this macro whenever you are parsing 64-bit values (like timestamps or large identifiers) received from external network protocols. Failure to use this on little-endian systems (like most STM32 ARM Cortex-M cores) will result in corrupted data values due to byte-order mismatch.

ca_ntohll_signed.brief: Converts a 64-bit signed integer from network byte order (big-endian) to host byte order (little-endian).
ca_ntohll_signed.notes: This macro wraps ca_bswap64_signed to perform a byte-order swap. It is essential for cross-platform communication where the network protocol uses big-endian format. It has no dependencies on other RTOS flags but assumes the host architecture is little-endian, which is standard for STM32 (ARM Cortex-M).
ca_ntohll_signed.usage: Use this when receiving 64-bit signed data packets from a network interface or external peripheral. Failure to use this on a little-endian system will result in corrupted numerical values. Ensure the input variable is exactly 64 bits wide to avoid unexpected behavior.

ca_ntohs.brief: Converts a 16-bit unsigned integer from network byte order (big-endian) to host byte order (little-endian).
ca_ntohs.notes: This macro maps directly to ca_bswap16(x). On STM32 (ARM Cortex-M), this typically utilizes the REV instruction for high-performance byte swapping. It is a no-op on big-endian architectures. It has no dependencies on other RTOS flags but is essential for cross-platform network communication.
ca_ntohs.usage: Use this whenever receiving 16-bit data packets from a network interface or external peripheral that transmits in big-endian format. Failure to use this on a little-endian STM32 will result in byte-swapped data (e.g., 0x1234 becoming 0x3412), leading to incorrect sensor readings or protocol errors.

ca_ntohs_signed.brief: Converts a 16-bit signed integer from network byte order (big-endian) to host byte order (little-endian).
ca_ntohs_signed.notes: This macro maps directly to ca_bswap16_signed(x). It performs a byte-swap operation on the input value. Since STM32 microcontrollers are little-endian, this function is essential when receiving 16-bit signed data from network protocols or external sensors that transmit in big-endian format. It has no dependencies on other RTOS flags but requires the input to be a 16-bit signed integer type.
ca_ntohs_signed.usage: Use this macro whenever you receive 16-bit signed data (e.g., sensor readings, protocol headers) over a network interface or SPI/I2C bus that uses big-endian byte ordering. Failing to use this will result in corrupted data values due to byte reversal. Ensure the input variable is exactly 16 bits wide to avoid unexpected behavior during the swap.

ca_stdout_create_thread.brief: Defines the priority level for the dedicated caOS stdout logging thread.
ca_stdout_create_thread.notes: This constant sets the RTOS task priority for the background thread responsible for processing stdout output. A value of 0xFFFFFFFF typically indicates that the thread is disabled or not created. Valid ranges depend on the caOS priority configuration, usually 0 (lowest) to 31 (highest). If enabled, this thread must have a priority that does not starve critical system tasks.
ca_stdout_create_thread.usage: Change this value if you need to enable asynchronous logging to stdout. Set it to a valid priority level (e.g., 10) to start the thread. Keep it at 0xFFFFFFFF if you want to disable the thread to save memory or if you are using a blocking, synchronous output method. Warning: setting this priority too high can cause system instability by preempting time-critical hardware control tasks.

ca_stdout_echo.brief: Enables or disables the automatic echoing of characters received via the standard output interface.
ca_stdout_echo.notes: When set to true, every character sent to the stdout stream is immediately echoed back to the sender. This flag is independent of the UART hardware configuration but relies on the underlying driver's transmit buffer. Typical values are boolean true or false.
ca_stdout_echo.usage: Set to true during initial development or debugging to verify serial communication and see user input in a terminal. Set to false in production environments to prevent data loops or unnecessary traffic on the communication bus, especially when the interface is connected to a machine-to-machine controller rather than a human-readable console.

ca_stdout_echo_dropped.brief: Determines if characters dropped by the stdout buffer are echoed to the debug console.
ca_stdout_echo_dropped.notes: When set to 1, any character that fails to enter the stdout queue due to a full buffer is printed to the serial port with a special marker. When set to 0 (default), dropped characters are silently discarded. This flag depends on the UART driver being initialized and the stdout module being enabled.
ca_stdout_echo_dropped.usage: Enable this (set to 1) during debugging if you suspect your application is flooding the serial output and losing data. Keep it disabled (0) in production builds to prevent performance degradation and garbled console output caused by the extra error-reporting characters.

ca_stdout_get_repeater.brief: A function pointer used to redirect or duplicate standard output (stdout) data to an external interface.
ca_stdout_get_repeater.notes: When set to NULL, stdout data is only sent to the default system console. If assigned a valid function pointer, the system will call this function every time a character is printed, allowing for logging to UART, ITM, or custom buffers. It has no dependencies on other flags but requires a function matching the signature void (*)(char) to be defined.
ca_stdout_get_repeater.usage: Change this value when you need to debug output on a peripheral other than the default one or when you need to log system messages to an external memory device. Ensure the assigned function is non-blocking and fast; otherwise, it will significantly degrade the performance of the entire RTOS.

ca_stdout_printf.brief: Enables or disables the standard output (printf) redirection functionality in the caOS RTOS.
ca_stdout_printf.notes: When set to 1, the system initializes the UART/ITM peripheral to support printf debugging. When set to 0, all printf calls are compiled out or redirected to a null handler. This flag depends on the hardware abstraction layer (HAL) being configured for the specific STM32 UART pins. Valid values are 0 (disabled) or 1 (enabled).
ca_stdout_printf.usage: Set this to 1 during development to view debug logs via a serial terminal. Set this to 0 in production builds to reduce binary size, save CPU cycles, and prevent potential blocking behavior caused by slow UART transmission.

ca_stdout_printf_n.brief: Enables or disables the inclusion of the printf-style formatting library for standard output.
ca_stdout_printf_n.notes: When set to 1, the system includes the code for formatted string output (e.g., %d, %s, %f), which significantly increases the flash memory footprint. When set to 0, the printf functionality is stripped, reducing binary size. This flag depends on the underlying hardware abstraction layer for UART or ITM output.
ca_stdout_printf_n.usage: Set to 0 in production builds or memory-constrained applications where formatted logging is not required. Set to 1 during development and debugging to enable human-readable logs. Warning: enabling this on very small STM32 devices may cause linker errors due to flash overflow.

ca_stdout_put.brief: Enables or disables the standard output (stdout) redirection to the hardware serial interface.
ca_stdout_put.notes: When set to 1, the system routes printf-style output to the configured UART peripheral. When set to 0, all stdout calls are ignored or redirected to a null device. This flag depends on the UART driver being initialized in the board support package. Typical values are 0 (disabled) or 1 (enabled).
ca_stdout_put.usage: Set this to 1 during development to enable debug logging via serial console. Set to 0 in production builds to reduce CPU overhead and save flash memory by removing string formatting logic. Ensure the UART baud rate is configured correctly before enabling this flag to avoid system hangs during transmission.

ca_stdout_put_n.brief: Configures whether the standard output (stdout) driver supports non-blocking character transmission.
ca_stdout_put_n.notes: When set to 1, the system uses a non-blocking buffer mechanism for stdout; when set to 0, the system uses a blocking (synchronous) approach. Enabling this requires sufficient heap memory for the output buffer. It depends on the underlying UART/USART hardware abstraction layer being initialized.
ca_stdout_put_n.usage: Set to 1 if your application needs to print logs without stalling the execution of high-priority tasks. Set to 0 if you are debugging early boot stages where the RTOS scheduler or memory allocator is not yet fully operational, or if you want to ensure every character is physically sent before the function returns.

ca_stdout_put_str.brief: Enables or disables the standard output string transmission functionality in caOS.
ca_stdout_put_str.notes: When set to 1, the system includes the code for the ca_stdout_put_str function, allowing strings to be sent to the configured serial interface. When set to 0, the function is disabled to save flash memory. This flag depends on the hardware abstraction layer (HAL) being configured for UART/USART output.
ca_stdout_put_str.usage: Set this to 1 if your application requires logging or debugging via a serial terminal. Set it to 0 if you are deploying to production on a memory-constrained device where serial output is not required, as this will reduce the binary size.

ca_stdout_put_str_n.brief: A configuration flag that enables or disables the non-blocking string output function for the system standard output.
ca_stdout_put_str_n.notes: When set to 1, the system includes the ca_stdout_put_str_n function, which attempts to write a string to the output buffer without blocking execution. When set to 0, this function is excluded from the build to save flash memory. This flag depends on the underlying UART or peripheral driver being initialized. Valid values are 0 (disabled) or 1 (enabled).
ca_stdout_put_str_n.usage: Set this to 1 if your application requires asynchronous logging or non-blocking serial communication to prevent the CPU from stalling during slow I/O operations. Set to 0 if you are constrained by flash memory space and do not require non-blocking output. Warning: disabling this will cause compilation errors if your code calls ca_stdout_put_str_n elsewhere.

ca_usb_dbg_print.brief: A macro used to toggle USB-based debug logging output for the caOS system.
ca_usb_dbg_print.notes: When enabled, this macro routes debug messages to the USB serial interface; when disabled (as shown in the default value), it resolves to a no-operation (no-op) to save CPU cycles and memory. It depends on the USB driver being initialized and the USB stack being active. Typical values are either a function call to the logging routine or the provided empty macro.
ca_usb_dbg_print.usage: Change this value during development to enable real-time logging of system events over USB. You should disable it (set to the no-op macro) before deploying to production to prevent performance degradation and unnecessary USB bus traffic. Ensure the USB peripheral is configured correctly before enabling this, or the system may hang while attempting to write to an uninitialized buffer.

ca_usb_dbg_reset.brief: A macro used to trigger a hardware reset of the USB peripheral during debugging sessions.
ca_usb_dbg_reset.notes: When defined as a functional routine, it forces the USB controller to re-initialize. The current 'do {} while (0)' implementation is a no-op, meaning the reset is currently disabled. It has no dependencies but should be used cautiously as it will drop any active USB enumeration or data transfer.
ca_usb_dbg_reset.usage: Change this value when you need to force a USB bus reset without power-cycling the board. This is useful for recovering from 'USB Device Not Recognized' errors during development. Do not enable this in production code as it may cause unexpected disconnects if triggered accidentally.

ca_usb_dbg_stat.brief: A macro used to log or output USB driver status information for debugging purposes.
ca_usb_dbg_stat.notes: When enabled, this macro typically routes USB state data to a serial console or debugger. In the current definition, it is a 'no-op' (no operation) macro that discards input parameters to save memory and CPU cycles. It depends on the USB driver initialization and is typically used in conjunction with a global debug level flag.
ca_usb_dbg_stat.usage: Change this value when you need to troubleshoot USB enumeration or communication errors. Replace the empty macro with a function call like 'printf' or a custom logging routine. Warning: enabling verbose logging in this macro can significantly slow down USB interrupt handling, potentially causing timing-sensitive USB protocol timeouts.

ca_usb_dev_mng_add.brief: Enables or disables the automatic management and enumeration of USB device endpoints within the caOS USB stack.
ca_usb_dev_mng_add.notes: When set to true, the system automatically handles endpoint allocation and descriptor management. When false, the developer must manually configure and manage USB endpoints. This flag depends on the USB peripheral clock being enabled in the system configuration. Typical values are boolean true or false.
ca_usb_dev_mng_add.usage: Set this to true if you want the RTOS to handle USB device setup automatically, which is recommended for standard HID or CDC classes. Set to false only if you are implementing a custom USB protocol or require fine-grained control over endpoint memory buffers. Incorrectly setting this to false without providing manual management code will result in the USB device failing to enumerate on the host PC.

ca_usb_dev_mng_init.brief: Initializes the USB device management subsystem during the caOS boot sequence.
ca_usb_dev_mng_init.notes: When set to true, the kernel allocates memory and initializes the USB peripheral driver stack. If set to false, the USB stack remains inactive, saving RAM and CPU cycles. This flag must be enabled if your application requires USB communication (e.g., CDC, HID, or MSC). It depends on the hardware abstraction layer (HAL) being correctly configured for the specific STM32 USB peripheral.
ca_usb_dev_mng_init.usage: Set this to true only if your project requires USB connectivity. If you are developing a headless system or a device that does not use USB, keep it false to reduce the memory footprint and avoid potential hardware initialization errors. Ensure that the system clock configuration is compatible with USB requirements (e.g., 48MHz clock) before enabling this.

ca_usb_dev_mng_remove.brief: A configuration flag that determines whether the USB device management task is automatically removed from the scheduler after initialization.
ca_usb_dev_mng_remove.notes: When set to true, the USB management task will terminate itself after the initial enumeration process to free up stack memory. When set to false (default), the task remains active in the background to handle dynamic re-enumeration or bus events. This flag depends on the underlying RTOS task management capabilities and should be kept false if your application requires hot-plugging support.
ca_usb_dev_mng_remove.usage: Set this to true only if your system has extremely limited RAM and you are certain that no USB re-enumeration or error recovery will be required after the initial boot sequence. Changing this to true in a system that requires dynamic USB connectivity will cause the device to stop responding to host requests after the initial connection.

ca_usb_dev_mng_start.brief: A boolean flag that determines whether the USB device management task is automatically started during system initialization.
ca_usb_dev_mng_start.notes: When set to true, the RTOS spawns the USB management thread at boot. When false, the USB stack remains inactive until manually initialized by the application code. This flag depends on the USB hardware abstraction layer being correctly configured in the board support package.
ca_usb_dev_mng_start.usage: Set this to true if your application requires USB connectivity immediately upon startup. Set it to false if you need to perform complex hardware checks or wait for specific system conditions before initializing the USB peripheral to avoid potential bus enumeration errors or power-up spikes.

ca_usb_dev_mng_stop.brief: A boolean flag that determines whether the USB device management task is halted or active.
ca_usb_dev_mng_stop.notes: When set to true, the USB management thread is suspended, effectively disabling USB communication and power negotiation. When set to false (default), the USB stack runs normally. This flag depends on the USB peripheral being initialized in the system configuration. Valid values are true or false.
ca_usb_dev_mng_stop.usage: Change this to true if you need to perform low-power operations or if you need to safely re-initialize the USB hardware without interference from the management task. Ensure this is set to false during normal operation, otherwise, the device will not be recognized by the host.

ca_usb_ep_clear_stall.brief: Clears the stall condition on a specific USB endpoint to allow data transmission to resume.
ca_usb_ep_clear_stall.notes: When set to false, the endpoint remains in a stalled state if previously triggered. Enabling this (true) resets the endpoint's data toggle and clears the stall bit in the USB peripheral registers. This function depends on the USB hardware being initialized and the endpoint being correctly configured in the descriptor table.
ca_usb_ep_clear_stall.usage: Change this value to true when the host has cleared a stall condition or during error recovery sequences to re-enable communication on a halted endpoint. Do not set this to true prematurely, as it may cause data synchronization errors if the host is not expecting a reset of the data toggle sequence.

ca_usb_ep_close.brief: A configuration flag that determines whether the USB endpoint is automatically closed upon a transmission error or disconnection.
ca_usb_ep_close.notes: When set to true, the system will force the endpoint into a closed state during communication failures, requiring a manual re-initialization. When false, the endpoint remains open, allowing for potential retry attempts without re-configuring the hardware registers. This flag depends on the underlying USB peripheral driver state machine and is typically a boolean value.
ca_usb_ep_close.usage: Set this to true if your application requires strict state management and you want to ensure the endpoint is reset to a clean state after any error. Keep it false if you prefer to handle error recovery at the application layer without re-initializing the USB hardware, which is useful for high-speed data streams where re-initialization latency is unacceptable.

ca_usb_ep_is_stalled.brief: A boolean flag indicating whether a specific USB endpoint is currently in a stalled state.
ca_usb_ep_is_stalled.notes: When set to true, the USB controller will respond with a STALL handshake to any host requests on this endpoint, effectively halting data transfer. This flag is typically managed by the USB stack's control transfer logic. It depends on the hardware-specific endpoint status register and should be synchronized with the USB interrupt handler.
ca_usb_ep_is_stalled.usage: Change this value to true when the application needs to signal a protocol error or an unsupported request to the USB host. Set it to false to clear the stall condition after the error has been handled. Incorrectly setting this value can cause the USB host to drop the device connection or report a device malfunction.

ca_usb_ep_open.brief: Configures whether the USB endpoint is automatically opened and initialized during the USB stack startup sequence.
ca_usb_ep_open.notes: When set to true, the endpoint is initialized immediately upon USB driver start. When false, the endpoint remains closed until explicitly opened by the application code. This flag depends on the USB peripheral being correctly clocked and configured in the device tree. Typical values are boolean true or false.
ca_usb_ep_open.usage: Change this to false if you need to perform complex hardware initialization or wait for specific application states before the USB endpoint becomes active. Setting this to false prevents premature enumeration or data reception. Warning: If set to false, ensure your application calls the corresponding open function, otherwise, USB communication will fail to initialize.

ca_usb_ep_read.brief: Configures the USB endpoint read mode, determining if data reception is blocking or interrupt-driven.
ca_usb_ep_read.notes: When set to 0, the system uses a polling-based read mechanism. Enabling this (setting to 1) switches to an interrupt-driven buffer management system. This flag depends on the USB peripheral clock being enabled in the system configuration. Valid values are 0 (polling) or 1 (interrupt-driven).
ca_usb_ep_read.usage: Change this to 1 if your application experiences data loss during high-speed USB transfers or if the CPU needs to perform other tasks while waiting for data. Keep it at 0 for simple, low-bandwidth applications to reduce interrupt overhead. Warning: setting this to 1 requires implementing the corresponding interrupt service routine (ISR) in your application code.

ca_usb_ep_write.brief: Configures whether the USB endpoint write operation should be performed in blocking or non-blocking mode.
ca_usb_ep_write.notes: When set to false, the function returns immediately after queuing the data for transmission, preventing the CPU from stalling. If set to true, the function waits until the hardware buffer is ready or the transfer completes. This flag depends on the underlying USB peripheral driver state and should be kept false to maintain high system responsiveness in an RTOS environment.
ca_usb_ep_write.usage: Change this to true only if you are performing synchronous data transfers where the application must guarantee the data has left the buffer before proceeding. Warning: setting this to true in a high-priority task can cause system-wide latency spikes or watchdog timeouts if the USB bus is busy or disconnected.

ca_usb_get_speed.brief: Defines the operational speed mode for the USB peripheral interface.
ca_usb_get_speed.notes: This constant sets the USB controller to Full-Speed (12 Mbps). Disabling or changing this value may cause the USB peripheral to fail enumeration if the hardware or the host controller does not support the selected speed. It is typically dependent on the system clock configuration and the specific USB PHY hardware present on the STM32 chip.
ca_usb_get_speed.usage: Change this value only if the hardware design requires High-Speed (480 Mbps) or Low-Speed (1.5 Mbps) operation. Ensure that the system clock (HCLK) is configured to meet the timing requirements of the selected speed mode, otherwise, the USB stack will fail to initialize or experience frequent data transmission errors.

ca_usb_init.brief: Initializes the USB peripheral hardware and internal driver stack during system startup.
ca_usb_init.notes: When set to true, the RTOS will automatically configure the USB controller, clocks, and GPIO pins during the kernel boot sequence. If set to false, the USB peripheral remains in a low-power reset state, and the developer must manually call the initialization function later in the application code. This flag depends on the hardware abstraction layer (HAL) being correctly configured for the specific STM32 target.
ca_usb_init.usage: Set this to true if your application requires USB connectivity (e.g., CDC, HID, or MSC) immediately upon power-up. Set to false if you need to perform complex pre-initialization tasks, want to save power by delaying USB startup, or if the USB pins are being used for other purposes during the early boot phase. Warning: disabling this without manual initialization will cause USB-related API calls to return errors or trigger hard faults.

ms_to_ticks.brief: A macro that converts a time duration in milliseconds into the equivalent number of RTOS system ticks.
ms_to_ticks.notes: This macro relies on the system clock frequency defined by CA_OS_TICK_RATE_HZ. Enabling this allows the scheduler to calculate delays and timeouts based on real-time units rather than raw tick counts. The result is an integer value representing the number of ticks required to span the requested milliseconds. If the requested time is shorter than one tick period, the result may truncate to zero.
ms_to_ticks.usage: Use this whenever you need to specify a timeout or delay in milliseconds for RTOS primitives like osDelay() or semaphore timeouts. Change this when you need to adjust the system tick frequency to ensure your timing logic remains consistent. Warning: Ensure that the resulting tick count does not exceed the maximum value allowed by the underlying data type (typically uint32_t) to avoid overflow errors.

seconds_to_ticks.brief: A conversion macro that translates a duration in seconds into the equivalent number of system ticks.
seconds_to_ticks.notes: This constant relies on the system tick frequency defined by ca_os_tick_x_ms. Enabling this allows developers to specify timeouts or delays in human-readable seconds rather than raw tick counts. It is mathematically dependent on the OS_TICK_RATE_HZ configuration; if the tick rate changes, this macro automatically scales correctly.
seconds_to_ticks.usage: Use this when setting task delays, software timer intervals, or timeout parameters in API calls where you prefer to define time in seconds. Change this value only when you need to adjust the granularity of your timing logic. Warning: Ensure the resulting tick count does not exceed the maximum value of the variable type used by the receiving function to prevent integer overflow.

ca_adc_config_t.brief: Configuration structure used to define the hardware parameters for an ADC peripheral instance in caOS.

members.name: adc_num
members.desc: The identifier of the ADC peripheral to be used. Valid values are 1, 2, or 3 depending on the specific STM32 chip variant. Providing an invalid number will result in a driver initialization error.

members.name: sample_time
members.desc: The sampling time configuration, mapped to the SMPx bits of the ADC registers. Valid range is 0 to 7. Higher values increase sampling duration, which is necessary for high-impedance signal sources to ensure accurate readings.

ca_adc_config_t.notes: This structure is typically passed by value to initialization functions. It does not require dynamic memory allocation; it should be declared as a local variable or a static constant. The user is responsible for ensuring the selected adc_num is physically present on the target MCU.
ca_adc_config_t.usage: Use this struct to prepare the hardware settings before calling the ADC initialization routine. It acts as a parameter block to configure the ADC peripheral's timing and identity.

ca_adc_isr_cb_t.brief: A function pointer type used to define a callback function that executes when an ADC conversion completes.

members.name: adc_num
members.desc: The identifier of the ADC peripheral that triggered the interrupt. Must match the hardware index defined in the system configuration.

members.name: value
members.desc: The raw digital value captured from the ADC conversion. Range is typically 0 to 4095 for 12-bit resolution.

ca_adc_isr_cb_t.notes: This callback is executed within the context of an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR). Keep the implementation extremely short and avoid blocking operations, mutexes, or heavy processing. The user is responsible for registering this callback via the driver's configuration interface.
ca_adc_isr_cb_t.usage: Use this type when you need to process ADC data asynchronously without polling. It is typically passed to the ADC driver initialization or configuration structure to handle data arrival events.

ca_aes_channel_t.brief: A configuration and state container for managing secure AES encryption/decryption channels in caOS.

members.name: mode
members.desc: Defines the AES operation mode (e.g., CBC, GCM). Must match the hardware/software capability.

members.name: keysize
members.desc: Specifies the AES key length (128, 192, or 256 bits). Must be compatible with the key stored in ks_handle.

members.name: ks_handle
members.desc: Pointer to the key store object allocated via ca_keys_store_allocate. Must not be NULL.

members.name: iv_gen_cb
members.desc: Optional callback for IV generation. If NULL, the system defaults to ca_rng_fill().

members.name: ratchet_cb
members.desc: Optional callback for key rotation. If NULL, key ratcheting is disabled.

members.name: cb_user
members.desc: Opaque pointer passed to iv_gen_cb and ratchet_cb for context-specific data.

members.name: red_ctx
members.desc: Pointer to the heap-allocated encryption context. Managed by the service.

members.name: black_ctx
members.desc: Pointer to the heap-allocated decryption context. Managed by the service.

members.name: mutex
members.desc: Internal synchronization primitive to ensure thread-safe access to the channel.

ca_aes_channel_t.notes: The struct must be initialized to zero before use. The red_ctx and black_ctx pointers are managed by the caOS crypto service; do not manually free these pointers. The mutex is automatically initialized during channel registration. Ensure the key store handle is valid for the lifetime of the channel.
ca_aes_channel_t.usage: Used to initialize and maintain a secure cryptographic channel. It is passed to ca_aes_channel_init() to prepare the contexts and mutex before performing any encryption or decryption operations.

ca_aes_ctx_t.brief: A configuration structure used to store the state and parameters for AES hardware encryption/decryption operations.

members.name: mode
members.desc: Defines the AES operation mode (e.g., ECB, CBC). Must be set before calling initialization functions.

members.name: keysize
members.desc: Specifies the bit-length of the key (128, 192, or 256 bits). Must match the data provided in the key array.

members.name: key
members.desc: The secret key buffer. Only the required number of words based on keysize are used.

members.name: iv
members.desc: Initialization Vector for modes like CBC or CTR. Ignored for ECB mode.

members.name: configured
members.desc: Internal flag used by the driver to verify if the context has been properly initialized. Do not modify manually.

ca_aes_ctx_t.notes: The structure is typically allocated by the user on the stack or as a global variable. It must be passed to the AES driver initialization function before any encryption or decryption calls. The driver does not own the memory; the user is responsible for its lifecycle.
ca_aes_ctx_t.usage: Use this struct to define the cryptographic parameters for a session. Pass a pointer to this struct to the AES driver's setup and processing functions to perform secure data transformations.

ca_aes_iv_gen_cb_t.brief: A callback function type used to generate a unique Initialization Vector (IV) for AES encryption operations.

members.name: iv
members.desc: A buffer of size AES_CH_IV_SIZE (typically 16 bytes) where the generated IV must be written. Must not be null.

members.name: user
members.desc: A pointer to user-defined context data passed through from the registration function. Can be NULL if no context is needed.

ca_aes_iv_gen_cb_t.notes: This callback is invoked by the AES channel service whenever a new IV is required for a cryptographic operation. The implementation must ensure the IV is cryptographically strong (e.g., using a hardware random number generator). The caller of the AES service owns the memory pointed to by the 'user' parameter. The callback must be thread-safe if the AES service is accessed from multiple tasks.
ca_aes_iv_gen_cb_t.usage: Used when configuring an AES channel via the service API. You provide a pointer to a function matching this signature to allow the system to request a fresh IV for each encryption block or session.

ca_aes_key_ratchet_cb_t.brief: A callback function type used to update or rotate an AES encryption key dynamically during a secure session.

members.name: key
members.desc: Pointer to the buffer where the new key material should be written. Must not be NULL.

members.name: key_len
members.desc: The size of the key buffer in bytes. Ensure the written key does not exceed this length to prevent buffer overflows.

members.name: user
members.desc: A user-defined context pointer passed through from the registration function, typically used to access session state or configuration.

ca_aes_key_ratchet_cb_t.notes: This callback is invoked by the AES service when a key rotation event is triggered. The function must return 'true' if the key was successfully updated, or 'false' to indicate a failure, which will likely halt the cryptographic operation. Ensure the implementation is thread-safe if the AES service is accessed from multiple tasks.
ca_aes_key_ratchet_cb_t.usage: Used when configuring an AES channel that requires periodic key updates (ratcheting) for forward secrecy. It is registered during the initialization of the AES channel service.

ca_aes_keysize_t.brief: An enumeration defining the supported bit-lengths for AES encryption keys in the caOS hardware abstraction layer.

members.name: CA_AES_KEY_128
members.desc: Configures the AES engine for 128-bit keys. Valid value: 0.

members.name: CA_AES_KEY_192
members.desc: Configures the AES engine for 192-bit keys. Valid value: 1.

members.name: CA_AES_KEY_256
members.desc: Configures the AES engine for 256-bit keys. Valid value: 2.

ca_aes_keysize_t.notes: This enum is used to program the hardware registers of the STM32 AES peripheral. Ensure the key buffer provided to the driver matches the size selected here; providing a buffer smaller than the selected key size will lead to memory corruption or undefined hardware behavior.
ca_aes_keysize_t.usage: Used as a parameter in AES initialization or configuration functions to specify the security strength of the encryption operation.

ca_aes_mode_t.brief: An enumeration defining the cryptographic operation modes available for the hardware AES peripheral.

members.name: CA_AES_MODE_ECB
members.desc: Electronic Codebook mode. Simplest mode, encrypts blocks independently. Not recommended for long messages due to pattern leakage.

members.name: CA_AES_MODE_CBC
members.desc: Cipher Block Chaining mode. Uses an Initialization Vector (IV) to chain blocks. Requires padding for data not aligned to block size.

members.name: CA_AES_MODE_CTR
members.desc: Counter mode. Turns a block cipher into a stream cipher. Does not require padding.

members.name: CA_AES_MODE_GCM
members.desc: Galois/Counter Mode. Provides both encryption and authentication (AEAD). Recommended for secure communication.

ca_aes_mode_t.notes: This enum is used to configure the AES hardware engine. Ensure the selected mode is supported by the specific STM32 hardware variant being used. Incorrect mode selection will result in decryption failure or invalid authentication tags.
ca_aes_mode_t.usage: Pass this value to the AES initialization or configuration functions to set the operational mode before starting a cryptographic operation.

ca_arp_frame_t.body:
typedef struct {
u16    htype;   /* hardware type = ARP_HTYPE_ETH big-endian */
u16    ptype;   /* protocol type = ARP_PTYPE_IP  big-endian */
u8     hlen;    /* hardware address length = 6 */
u8     plen;    /* protocol address length = 4 */
u16    oper;    /* ARP_OP_REQUEST / ARP_OP_REPLY big-endian */
ca_mac_t  sha;     /* sender hardware address */
ca_ipv4_t spa;     /* sender protocol address */
ca_mac_t  tha;     /* target hardware address */
ca_ipv4_t tpa;     /* target protocol address */
} __attribute__((packed)) ca_arp_frame_t;
ca_arp_frame_t.brief: Represents the structure of an ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) packet used for mapping hardware addresses to network addresses.

members.name: htype
members.desc: Hardware type. Must be set to ARP_HTYPE_ETH (0x0001) in big-endian format.

members.name: ptype
members.desc: Protocol type. Must be set to ARP_PTYPE_IP (0x0800) in big-endian format.

members.name: hlen
members.desc: Hardware address length. For Ethernet, this is always 6.

members.name: plen
members.desc: Protocol address length. For IPv4, this is always 4.

members.name: oper
members.desc: Operation code. Use ARP_OP_REQUEST (1) or ARP_OP_REPLY (2) in big-endian format.

members.name: sha
members.desc: Sender hardware address (MAC address of the device sending the packet).

members.name: spa
members.desc: Sender protocol address (IP address of the device sending the packet).

members.name: tha
members.desc: Target hardware address (MAC address of the destination device).

members.name: tpa
members.desc: Target protocol address (IP address of the destination device).

ca_arp_frame_t.notes: The struct is marked with __attribute__((packed)) to ensure no padding bytes are inserted by the compiler, which is critical for network protocol compliance. All multi-byte fields must be stored in big-endian (network byte order).
ca_arp_frame_t.usage: Used when manually constructing or parsing raw ARP packets in the network stack layer. Typically populated before passing the buffer to the Ethernet driver's transmit function.

ca_barrier_t.brief: A synchronization primitive that forces a group of tasks to wait until a specific number of tasks have reached the barrier point.

members.name: count
members.desc: The total number of tasks required to release the barrier. Must be greater than zero.

members.name: arrived
members.desc: Internal counter tracking how many tasks have currently reached the barrier. Do not modify manually.

members.name: phase
members.desc: Internal counter used to distinguish between different synchronization cycles. Do not modify manually.

members.name: wait_queue
members.desc: The internal queue where tasks are blocked while waiting for the barrier to be satisfied.

members.name: internal_lock
members.desc: A spinlock used to ensure atomic access to the barrier's internal state during synchronization.

ca_barrier_t.notes: The barrier must be initialized before use. It is typically allocated in the global data segment or on the heap by the application. Ownership is held by the application, but the RTOS kernel manages the internal state during wait/signal operations. Ensure 'count' is set correctly during initialization, as an incorrect value can lead to permanent task blocking (deadlock).
ca_barrier_t.usage: Use this when you need to coordinate multiple parallel tasks to reach a common execution point before any of them can proceed to the next stage of processing.

ca_block_pool_t.brief: A fixed-size memory block allocator that provides O(1) allocation and deallocation for objects of identical size.

members.name: free_list
members.desc: Pointer to the first available memory block. Managed internally as a linked list.

members.name: block_size
members.desc: Size of each individual block in bytes. Must be at least 4 and a multiple of 4.

members.name: total
members.desc: Total number of blocks available in the pool.

members.name: free_count
members.desc: Current number of available blocks. Updated atomically.

members.name: lock
members.desc: Spinlock used to ensure thread-safe and ISR-safe access to the pool.

ca_block_pool_t.notes: The pool must be initialized using ca_block_pool_init before use. The memory buffer provided to the pool must be aligned to 4 bytes. The structure itself is typically allocated in static memory or as part of a larger control block. Ownership of the memory remains with the pool; users must return blocks using ca_block_free to prevent leaks.
ca_block_pool_t.usage: Use this when you need to frequently allocate and free objects of the same size (e.g., network packets or message buffers) to avoid heap fragmentation. Use ca_block_alloc to retrieve a block and ca_block_free to return it.

ca_can_cfg_t.brief: Configuration structure used to initialize a CAN peripheral interface in caOS.

members.name: can_num
members.desc: The hardware peripheral index. Use 1 for CAN1/FDCAN1 or 2 for CAN2/FDCAN2. Invalid values may cause hardware initialization failure.

members.name: baudrate
members.desc: The communication speed in bits per second. Supported values are 125000, 250000, 500000, or 1000000. Incorrect values will result in bus errors.

members.name: loopback
members.desc: Enables internal loopback mode for testing. If true, transmitted frames are received internally and not sent to the physical bus.

members.name: silent
members.desc: Enables listen-only mode. If true, the controller receives messages but does not acknowledge them or transmit, useful for bus monitoring.

ca_can_cfg_t.notes: This struct is typically passed by pointer to the driver initialization function. It is usually allocated on the stack before calling the init function. Ensure all fields are explicitly set to avoid undefined behavior from uninitialized memory.
ca_can_cfg_t.usage: Use this struct to define the operating parameters of a CAN bus before calling the driver's initialization function. It is the standard way to configure hardware settings without hardcoding values in the driver logic.

ca_can_frame_t.brief: Represents a single CAN bus data frame used for transmitting or receiving messages.

members.name: id
members.desc: The CAN message identifier. Use 11 bits for standard frames or 29 bits for extended frames.

members.name: ide
members.desc: Identifier Extension bit. Set to false for 11-bit standard IDs, true for 29-bit extended IDs.

members.name: rtr
members.desc: Remote Transmission Request. Set to true to request data from another node, false for standard data frames.

members.name: dlc
members.desc: Data Length Code. Specifies the number of valid bytes in the data array. Must be between 0 and 8.

members.name: data
members.desc: The payload buffer containing up to 8 bytes of data.

ca_can_frame_t.notes: This struct is typically allocated on the stack by the application. It does not require dynamic memory allocation. Ensure dlc is set correctly, as the hardware will ignore bytes beyond the specified length.
ca_can_frame_t.usage: Used as a parameter in CAN driver functions to define the content of a message to be sent or to store a received message.

ca_cfg_row_t.brief: A configuration row structure used to map internal system parameters or settings to human-readable strings for CLI or diagnostic output.

members.name: name
members.desc: The internal identifier or key string, typically matching a symbol defined in os_config.h or objmap.h.

members.name: text
members.desc: A descriptive string or alias for the parameter. Must not be NULL; used for display purposes.

members.name: val
members.desc: The numeric value associated with the configuration parameter.

ca_cfg_row_t.notes: This structure is typically used in static arrays to define system configuration tables. The table is usually passed to ca_caos_config_rows to allow the system to expose these settings via the CLI or internal diagnostic tools. The memory for these strings should be in read-only memory (Flash) as they are typically defined as static constants.
ca_cfg_row_t.usage: Use this type when defining a custom configuration table for your application. You populate an array of these structs and then register or reference them within the caOS configuration framework to make your application settings queryable via the system CLI.

ca_cli_cmd_t.brief: Defines a single command entry for the caOS Command Line Interface (CLI).

members.name: name
members.desc: The exact string the user must type to trigger this command. Case-sensitive.

members.name: help
members.desc: A short description string displayed when the user requests help. Format: 'name : syntax'.

members.name: exec
members.desc: A function pointer to the callback that executes when the command is matched.

ca_cli_cmd_t.notes: The command table must be terminated by an entry with all fields set to NULL. The table is registered with the CLI system using ca_cli_register_table. The memory for the table should be static or persistent, as the CLI system does not copy the contents.
ca_cli_cmd_t.usage: Used to extend the CLI functionality by defining custom commands. Create an array of these structs and pass it to ca_cli_register_table during system initialization.

ca_cli_exec_t.brief: Defines the execution behavior of a CLI command, specifying the callback function and optional stack allocation.

members.name: fn
members.desc: The function pointer to be executed when the CLI command is invoked.

members.name: stack
members.desc: Stack size in bytes for the command execution. If set to 0, the command runs directly within the CLI thread context.

ca_cli_exec_t.notes: If stack is 0, the command must be non-blocking and fast to avoid stalling the CLI interface. If a non-zero value is provided, the system will attempt to spawn a dedicated thread for the command execution. Ensure the stack size is sufficient for the function's local variables and call depth.
ca_cli_exec_t.usage: Used when registering CLI command tables via ca_cli_register_table. It allows developers to decide whether a command should execute synchronously (blocking the CLI) or asynchronously (in its own thread).

ca_cli_fn_t.brief: A function pointer type used to define custom command handlers for the caOS Command Line Interface (CLI).

members.name: args
members.desc: A pointer to an array of strings representing the command arguments. The first element is typically the command name itself, followed by user-provided parameters.

ca_cli_fn_t.notes: The callback must return 'true' if the command was executed successfully, or 'false' if an error occurred or the arguments were invalid. These functions are registered into the system using ca_cli_register_table. Ensure that the logic inside the callback is efficient, as it runs within the context of the CLI thread.
ca_cli_fn_t.usage: Use this type when creating a custom command table for the CLI. Define a function matching this signature, then include it in a structure array passed to ca_cli_register_table to make the command available in the shell.

ca_cli_table_t.brief: A registration node used to link a table of CLI commands into the caOS command-line interface system.

members.name: name
members.desc: A human-readable string identifying the command group. Used for internal reporting and debugging.

members.name: cmds
members.desc: Pointer to an array of command definitions (ca_cli_cmd_t). Must reside in flash memory.

members.name: n
members.desc: The number of commands present in the 'cmds' array.

members.name: next
members.desc: Pointer to the next registration node in the linked list. Set to NULL for the last element.

ca_cli_table_t.notes: The structure itself is typically allocated in RAM (often as a global static variable). The 'cmds' array should be defined as 'const' to ensure it stays in flash. The list is managed by the CLI system; you register your table using ca_cli_register_table.
ca_cli_table_t.usage: Use this to extend the CLI with custom commands. Define your command array, wrap it in this struct, and register it during system initialization.

ca_condvar_t.brief: A condition variable used to block a task until a specific condition is met or a signal is received from another task.

members.name: wait_queue
members.desc: A list of tasks currently blocked on this condition variable. Do not modify this field directly.

members.name: internal_lock
members.desc: A spinlock used to ensure thread-safe access to the wait queue. Must be held during internal operations.

ca_condvar_t.notes: The condition variable must be initialized before use. It does not store state; it only provides a mechanism for tasks to wait for a signal. It is typically used in conjunction with a mutex to prevent race conditions when checking the condition.
ca_condvar_t.usage: Use this when a task needs to wait for a specific event or data availability. It is used with ca_cond_wait() to block and ca_cond_signal() or ca_cond_broadcast() to wake up waiting tasks.

ca_console_isr_filter_t.brief: A callback function type used to filter incoming bytes in the console ISR before they are processed by the system.

members.name: byte
members.desc: The raw byte received from the hardware interface. Valid values are 0x00 to 0xFF.

ca_console_isr_filter_t.notes: This callback is executed within an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) context. It must be extremely fast, non-blocking, and must not call any RTOS functions that could trigger a context switch or block. Returning 'true' typically indicates the byte is accepted/processed, while 'false' may cause the byte to be ignored or handled differently depending on the implementation.
ca_console_isr_filter_t.usage: Used when configuring console input handling to intercept or sanitize raw data streams (e.g., ignoring specific control characters or filtering noise) before they reach the main console buffer.

ca_console_stats_t.brief: A structure containing diagnostic counters for the system console, used to monitor data flow and potential bottlenecks.

members.name: to_task
members.desc: Total number of bytes successfully queued for the task currently owning the console.

members.name: dropped
members.desc: Number of bytes lost because the internal ring buffer was full. High values indicate the consumer task is too slow.

members.name: filtered
members.desc: Number of bytes intercepted and consumed by the ISR-level filter before reaching the buffer.

members.name: reclaimed
members.desc: Counter of how many times the console was forcibly taken back from a task that terminated or became unresponsive.

ca_console_stats_t.notes: The structure is populated by the ca_console_stats() function. It does not require manual allocation; the caller provides a pointer to a local instance which the function fills with current system values.
ca_console_stats_t.usage: Use this structure to debug console performance or to detect if a task is failing to process console input in a timely manner, leading to dropped data.

ca_cordic_func_t.body:
typedef enum {
CA_CORDIC_COS = 0,
CA_CORDIC_SIN,
CA_CORDIC_PHASE,
CA_CORDIC_MODULUS,
CA_CORDIC_ATAN,
CA_CORDIC_COSH,
CA_CORDIC_SINH,
CA_CORDIC_ATANH,
CA_CORDIC_LN,
CA_CORDIC_SQRT
} ca_cordic_func_t;
ca_cordic_func_t.brief: Enumeration defining the mathematical operations supported by the hardware CORDIC co-processor.

members.name: CA_CORDIC_COS
members.desc: Calculates the cosine of the input angle.

members.name: CA_CORDIC_SIN
members.desc: Calculates the sine of the input angle.

members.name: CA_CORDIC_PHASE
members.desc: Calculates the phase (arctangent) of a complex number (x, y).

members.name: CA_CORDIC_MODULUS
members.desc: Calculates the magnitude (modulus) of a complex number (x, y).

members.name: CA_CORDIC_ATAN
members.desc: Calculates the arctangent of the input value.

members.name: CA_CORDIC_COSH
members.desc: Calculates the hyperbolic cosine.

members.name: CA_CORDIC_SINH
members.desc: Calculates the hyperbolic sine.

members.name: CA_CORDIC_ATANH
members.desc: Calculates the hyperbolic arctangent.

members.name: CA_CORDIC_LN
members.desc: Calculates the natural logarithm.

members.name: CA_CORDIC_SQRT
members.desc: Calculates the square root.

ca_cordic_func_t.notes: This enum is used to configure the CORDIC hardware peripheral. Ensure the CORDIC unit is initialized via ca_cordic_init before performing calculations. The hardware expects specific input formats (typically Q1.31 fixed-point) depending on the selected function.
ca_cordic_func_t.usage: Used as a parameter in the ca_cordic_calc function to specify which mathematical operation the hardware should execute on the provided input data.

ca_dac_comp_hyst_t.brief: Defines the hysteresis level for the DAC internal comparator, used to prevent signal noise from triggering false state changes.

members.name: CA_DAC_COMP_HYST_NONE
members.desc: No hysteresis applied. The comparator is highly sensitive to noise.

members.name: CA_DAC_COMP_HYST_LOW
members.desc: Low hysteresis level. Suitable for signals with minimal noise.

members.name: CA_DAC_COMP_HYST_MEDIUM
members.desc: Medium hysteresis level. Balanced setting for general use.

members.name: CA_DAC_COMP_HYST_HIGH
members.desc: High hysteresis level. Best for noisy environments to ensure stable switching.

ca_dac_comp_hyst_t.notes: This enum is passed to the DAC configuration functions to tune the hardware comparator. It is a simple integer-based enum, so no memory allocation or lifecycle management is required by the user.
ca_dac_comp_hyst_t.usage: Use this type when configuring the DAC comparator via ca_dac_comp_init or updating the level dynamically using ca_dac_comp_level.

ca_dac_config_t.brief: Configuration structure used to specify which hardware DAC channel to initialize on the STM32.

members.name: channel
members.desc: The DAC channel index. Use 1 for CH1 (mapped to PA4) or 2 for CH2 (mapped to PA5). Providing any other value may result in undefined behavior or initialization failure.

ca_dac_config_t.notes: This structure is typically passed by value or pointer to the DAC initialization function. It does not require dynamic allocation and should be defined in the scope where the driver is being configured.
ca_dac_config_t.usage: Use this struct when preparing to initialize the DAC peripheral. It acts as a parameter for the driver setup function to inform the system which physical pin and internal DAC register set to enable.

ca_dhcp_bound_cb_t.brief: A callback function type triggered by the DHCP service when an IP address lease is successfully obtained or renewed.

members.name: ip
members.desc: The IPv4 address assigned to the device by the DHCP server. Must be treated as a read-only value.

members.name: mask
members.desc: The subnet mask associated with the assigned IP address. Used to define the local network boundary.

ca_dhcp_bound_cb_t.notes: This callback is executed within the context of the DHCP service task. It must be kept short and non-blocking to avoid delaying network stack processing. The user is responsible for storing these values if they are needed outside the callback scope, as the parameters are passed by value.
ca_dhcp_bound_cb_t.usage: Used when registering a DHCP client instance. You assign a function pointer of this type to the DHCP configuration structure to receive notification of network configuration changes.

ca_dhcp_bound_t.body: typedef void (*ca_dhcp_bound_t)(ca_ipv4_t ip, ca_ipv4_t mask, ca_ipv4_t gw, ca_ipv4_t dns)
ca_dhcp_bound_t.brief: A callback function type triggered by the DHCP client when an IP address lease is successfully obtained or renewed.

members.name: ip
members.desc: The IPv4 address assigned to the device by the DHCP server.

members.name: mask
members.desc: The subnet mask provided by the DHCP server to define the local network range.

members.name: gw
members.desc: The default gateway (router) IP address for external network communication.

members.name: dns
members.desc: The primary DNS server IP address provided by the DHCP server.

ca_dhcp_bound_t.notes: This callback is executed within the context of the network stack task. It must be non-blocking and should not perform heavy processing or wait on semaphores/mutexes to avoid stalling network traffic. The user is responsible for storing these values if they need to be accessed outside the callback scope.
ca_dhcp_bound_t.usage: Used during the initialization of the DHCP client module. You assign a function pointer of this type to the DHCP configuration structure to receive notification once the network interface is fully configured.

ca_dhcp_cfg_t.brief: Configuration structure used to define the behavior and callback for the caOS DHCP client.

members.name: timeout_ms
members.desc: Time in milliseconds to wait for a DHCP offer. If set to 0, the system defaults to 5000ms.

members.name: on_bound
members.desc: A function pointer to a callback executed once the DHCP server assigns an IP address. Can be set to NULL if no notification is required.

ca_dhcp_cfg_t.notes: The structure is typically passed by value or pointer to the DHCP initialization function. It does not require dynamic allocation; it can be declared on the stack or as a global configuration object. Ensure the callback function is thread-safe as it may be executed from the network stack context.
ca_dhcp_cfg_t.usage: Use this structure when initializing the network interface to enable dynamic IP assignment. It is passed as an argument to the DHCP configuration API to customize the handshake timeout and define the application-level logic that triggers once the network is ready.

ca_dhcp_expire_cb_t.brief: A callback function type triggered when a DHCP lease expires, used to notify the application that the IP address is no longer valid.

members.name: void
members.desc: The callback takes no arguments and returns nothing.

ca_dhcp_expire_cb_t.notes: This callback is executed within the context of the DHCP service task. It must be kept short and non-blocking to avoid delaying network stack operations. The user is responsible for implementing logic to handle the loss of network connectivity, such as re-initializing the network interface or stopping dependent services.
ca_dhcp_expire_cb_t.usage: Use this type when configuring the DHCP service to monitor lease status. It is typically assigned during the initialization phase of the network stack to ensure the application can react gracefully when the assigned IP address is revoked.
ca_dhcp_expire_cb_t.example: void my_dhcp_expire_handler(void) { /* Log the event or signal the main loop to stop network tasks */ } ... ca_dhcp_config_t config = { .expire_cb = my_dhcp_expire_handler };

ca_dhcp_offer_t.body:
typedef struct {
ca_ipv4_t offered_ip;   /* yiaddr — IP offered by server */
ca_ipv4_t server_ip;    /* siaddr — next-server IP (may be 0) */
ca_ipv4_t server_id;    /* option 54 — Server Identifier (use for REQUEST) */
ca_ipv4_t subnet_mask;  /* option 1 */
ca_ipv4_t gateway;      /* option 3 (first router) */
ca_ipv4_t dns;          /* option 6 (first DNS) */
ca_ipv4_t ntp_server;   /* option 42 (first NTP server); 0 if not present */
u32    lease_time;   /* option 51, seconds */
u32    t1;           /* option 58, seconds; 0 = use lease/2 */
u32    t2;           /* option 59, seconds; 0 = use lease*7/8 */
u8     msg_type;     /* DHCP_MSG_OFFER / DHCP_MSG_ACK / DHCP_MSG_NAK */
u32    xid;          /* transaction id of the reply, host order */
ca_mac_t chaddr;     /* client hardware address the reply is for */
} ca_dhcp_offer_t;
ca_dhcp_offer_t.brief: A structure containing the network configuration parameters received from a DHCP server during the DORA process.

members.name: offered_ip
members.desc: The IP address assigned to this client by the DHCP server.

members.name: server_ip
members.desc: The IP address of the next server to use in bootstrap; often 0 if not applicable.

members.name: server_id
members.desc: The unique identifier of the DHCP server (Option 54). Must be included in the subsequent DHCP REQUEST packet.

members.name: subnet_mask
members.desc: The subnet mask for the network (Option 1).

members.name: gateway
members.desc: The default gateway IP address (Option 3).

members.name: dns
members.desc: The primary DNS server IP address (Option 6).

members.name: ntp_server
members.desc: The primary NTP server IP address (Option 42). Set to 0 if the server did not provide one.

members.name: lease_time
members.desc: The duration of the IP lease in seconds (Option 51).

members.name: t1
members.desc: Renewal time (T1) in seconds. If 0, the stack defaults to lease_time / 2.

members.name: t2
members.desc: Rebinding time (T2) in seconds. If 0, the stack defaults to lease_time * 7 / 8.

members.name: msg_type
members.desc: The DHCP message type (e.g., DHCP_MSG_OFFER, DHCP_MSG_ACK, DHCP_MSG_NAK).

ca_dhcp_offer_t.notes: This structure is typically populated by the caOS network stack when a DHCP response is parsed. The application should treat this as read-only data provided by the stack. Ensure the memory is not modified while the DHCP state machine is processing the offer.
ca_dhcp_offer_t.usage: Used by the application to inspect the network configuration offered by a DHCP server before accepting it or to verify the parameters after a successful DHCP ACK.

ca_dma2d_am_t.brief: Defines how the DMA2D engine handles pixel alpha blending during image copy or conversion operations.

members.name: CA_DMA2D_ALPHA_KEEP
members.desc: Uses the pixel's original alpha value (or 0xFF if no alpha channel exists). No blending is applied.

members.name: CA_DMA2D_ALPHA_REPLACE
members.desc: Replaces the pixel's alpha value with a constant alpha value provided in the configuration.

members.name: CA_DMA2D_ALPHA_MULT
members.desc: Calculates the new alpha as (pixel_alpha * constant_alpha) / 255. Used for fading or transparency effects.

ca_dma2d_am_t.notes: This enum is used as a parameter in DMA2D configuration structures. It determines the mathematical operation performed on the alpha channel of pixels during hardware-accelerated transfers. Ensure the destination format supports alpha if using MULT or REPLACE modes.
ca_dma2d_am_t.usage: Used when configuring DMA2D blending parameters, typically passed to functions like ca_dma2d_blend or ca_dma2d_copy to define how source pixels interact with the destination buffer.

ca_dma2d_dst_t.brief: Defines the destination buffer properties for DMA2D graphics operations, such as memory address, layout, and pixel format.

members.name: addr
members.desc: Pointer to the memory location of the first pixel of the destination rectangle. Must be aligned according to hardware requirements.

members.name: stride
members.desc: The number of pixels per line for the entire image buffer, not just the rectangle being drawn. Used to calculate the memory offset for the next row.

members.name: fmt
members.desc: The pixel format of the destination buffer (e.g., ARGB8888, RGB565). Must match the hardware configuration of the display or buffer.

members.name: flags
members.desc: Configuration flags for the operation. CA_DMA2D_AI (Alpha Inversion) or CA_DMA2D_RBS (Red-Blue Swap) can be applied.

ca_dma2d_dst_t.notes: This struct is typically allocated on the stack by the caller before passing it to DMA2D functions. The user is responsible for ensuring the memory pointed to by 'addr' is valid and large enough to hold the operation's output. The 'stride' must be correctly set to the full width of the image buffer to avoid memory corruption during multi-line operations.
ca_dma2d_dst_t.usage: Used as an input parameter in ca_dma2d_copy, ca_dma2d_fill, or ca_dma2d_blend functions to define where the processed pixel data should be written.

ca_dma2d_fmt_t.body:

ca_dma2d_src_t.brief: Defines the source image configuration for DMA2D hardware acceleration operations like blending or copying.

members.name: addr
members.desc: Pointer to the memory address of the first pixel of the source rectangle.

members.name: stride
members.desc: Number of pixels per line in the source image buffer (including padding).

members.name: fmt
members.desc: Pixel format of the source data (e.g., RGB565, ARGB8888).

members.name: am
members.desc: Alpha mode: defines how the alpha channel is handled (e.g., constant, pixel-based, or combined).

members.desc: Constant alpha value used when the alpha mode is set to REPLACE or MULT.

ca_dma2d_src_t.notes: The struct is typically allocated on the stack by the caller. The DMA2D hardware reads directly from the provided 'addr'. Ensure the memory pointed to by 'addr' and 'clut' remains valid until the DMA2D operation is completed (use ca_dma2d_wait to ensure synchronization).
ca_dma2d_src_t.usage: Used as an input parameter in ca_dma2d_copy and ca_dma2d_blend functions to define the source image properties before triggering the hardware transfer.

ca_dma_cb_t.brief: A function pointer type used to define a callback function that executes when a DMA transfer completes.

members.name: arg
members.desc: A pointer to user-defined data or context. This is passed back to the callback function when the DMA interrupt triggers. If no context is needed, pass NULL.

ca_dma_cb_t.notes: The callback is executed within the context of the DMA interrupt service routine (ISR). Therefore, the function must be kept short, must not block, and should not call any RTOS functions that are not 'from-ISR' safe. The user is responsible for ensuring the memory pointed to by 'arg' remains valid until the callback is executed.
ca_dma_cb_t.usage: Used when configuring a DMA channel via the caOS driver API. You assign a function matching this signature to the DMA configuration structure to handle asynchronous completion events, such as notifying a task that a buffer is ready for processing.
ca_dma_cb_t.example: void my_dma_complete_handler(void *arg) { BaseType_t xHigherPriorityTaskWoken = pdFALSE; xSemaphoreGiveFromISR((SemaphoreHandle_t)arg, &xHigherPriorityTaskWoken); portYIELD_FROM_ISR(xHigherPriorityTaskWoken); } // Usage in setup: config.callback = my_dma_complete_handler; config.cb_arg = my_semaphore;

ca_dma_ch_t.brief: A structure representing a specific DMA hardware channel identifier used to configure and request DMA transfers.

ca_dma_ch_t.notes: This struct is a simple descriptor and does not contain state information. It is typically passed by value to driver functions. The user is responsible for ensuring the controller/stream combination is valid for the specific STM32 chip being used.
ca_dma_ch_t.usage: Used as an input parameter for DMA peripheral initialization and transfer request functions to specify which hardware resource the driver should claim.

ca_dma_dir_t.brief: An enumeration defining the data transfer direction for DMA operations in caOS.

members.name: CA_DMA_DIR_P2M

ca_dma_dir_t.notes: This enum is used to configure the DMA controller's data flow direction. Ensure the direction matches the hardware peripheral's capability (e.g., a UART TX register only supports M2P). Incorrect configuration will result in data not being transferred or potential bus errors.
ca_dma_dir_t.usage: Used as a parameter in DMA configuration structures or initialization functions to specify the source and destination relationship for the DMA stream.

ca_dma_width_t.brief: An enumeration defining the data transfer size for DMA operations on STM32 peripherals.

members.name: CA_DMA_WIDTH_8

members.name: CA_DMA_WIDTH_16

members.name: CA_DMA_WIDTH_32
members.desc: Configures the DMA to transfer data in 32-bit (word) increments.

ca_dma_width_t.notes: This enum must match the data alignment of the source and destination buffers. Using an incorrect width (e.g., 32-bit width for an 8-bit peripheral register) will result in data corruption or hardware bus errors.
ca_dma_width_t.usage: Used within DMA configuration structures to define the 'data width' parameter for both source and destination transfers. It ensures the DMA controller correctly increments its internal address pointers based on the peripheral's data register size.

ca_dns_hdr_t.brief: Represents the standard 12-byte DNS header structure used for parsing and constructing DNS network packets.

members.name: flags

members.name: qdcount

members.name: ancount

members.name: arcount

ca_dns_hdr_t.notes: The struct is marked with __attribute__((packed)) to prevent compiler padding, ensuring it maps exactly to the 12-byte wire format. Fields are in big-endian format; use htons() or ntohs() when accessing these fields on little-endian STM32 architectures.
ca_dns_hdr_t.usage: Used when manually crafting DNS packets or parsing incoming DNS responses from a socket buffer. Typically cast directly onto the start of a network buffer.

ca_dns_qtail_t.brief: Represents the tail portion of a DNS query, specifying the resource record type and class.

ca_dns_qtail_t.notes: This struct is packed to ensure it maps directly to the wire format of a DNS packet. It does not contain pointers, so no dynamic memory allocation is required. The user is responsible for ensuring endianness conversion (e.g., using htons) before transmission.
ca_dns_qtail_t.usage: Used when constructing manual DNS query packets or parsing incoming DNS query responses to identify the requested resource type and class.

ca_dns_response_t.brief: A structure representing the result of a DNS resolution request, containing the transaction ID, status code, and resolved IP address.

members.name: id
members.desc: The transaction ID used to match the response with the original DNS query. Must match the ID sent in the request.
