ca_vnc_proto_t.notes: The struct must be zero-initialized before passing to ca_vnc_proto_init. The user is responsible for allocating memory for 'tile_hash' and 'line' buffers based on the dimensions provided. The struct maintains internal state and should not be modified directly while the VNC service is active.
ca_vnc_proto_t.usage: Used as the primary handle for a VNC session. Initialize it with ca_vnc_proto_init, then pass it to ca_vnc_proto_rx to process incoming network packets or ca_vnc_proto_update to push framebuffer changes.

ca_vnc_security_t.brief: Defines the security policy for VNC connections, determining whether to use TLS encryption or plain text.

members.name: CA_VNC_SECURITY_AUTO
members.desc: Automatically selects TLS if hardware AES acceleration is available, otherwise falls back to unencrypted view-only mode.

members.name: CA_VNC_SECURITY_TLS
members.desc: Forces the use of TLS encryption for the VNC session.

members.name: CA_VNC_SECURITY_NONE
members.desc: Uses plain RFB protocol without any encryption.

ca_vnc_security_t.notes: This enum is used as a configuration parameter when initializing the VNC service. It does not require manual allocation as it is a simple enumeration type.
ca_vnc_security_t.usage: Pass this value to the VNC service initialization function to define the security requirements for incoming remote desktop connections.

ca_vnc_src_t.brief: An enumeration defining the origin of input data for the VNC service, used to determine how the system processes incoming events.

members.name: CA_VNC_SRC_CLIENT
members.desc: Input originates from the standard VNC client connection defined in the service configuration.

members.name: CA_VNC_SRC_LOCAL
members.desc: Input originates from local hardware peripherals (e.g., physical touch or mouse).

members.name: CA_VNC_SRC_REMOTE
members.desc: Input originates from another trusted remote connection.

ca_vnc_src_t.notes: This enum is used to categorize the source of input events. It is typically passed to VNC service functions to ensure the system applies the correct security and routing logic for the specific input stream.
ca_vnc_src_t.usage: Used primarily when configuring or interacting with the VNC service, specifically when setting up client input handlers or processing incoming VNC protocol packets.

ca_vnc_state_t.body:
typedef enum {
CA_VNC_ST_VERSION = 0,      /* waiting for the client's version line */
CA_VNC_ST_SECURITY,         /* 3.7/3.8: waiting for the chosen type */
CA_VNC_ST_VENC_VERSION,     /* VeNCrypt: waiting for the client's version */
CA_VNC_ST_VENC_SUBTYPE,     /* VeNCrypt: waiting for the chosen subtype */
CA_VNC_ST_TLS_START,        /* paused: the caller runs the TLS handshake */
CA_VNC_ST_PLAIN_LEN,        /* X509Plain: waiting for the two lengths */
CA_VNC_ST_PLAIN_DATA,       /* X509Plain: waiting for user + password */
CA_VNC_ST_CLIENT_INIT,      /* waiting for the shared flag */
CA_VNC_ST_MSG,              /* normal operation */
CA_VNC_ST_CLOSED
} ca_vnc_state_t;
ca_vnc_state_t.brief: Represents the current connection state of a VNC protocol session, used to track the handshake and operational progress.

members.name: CA_VNC_ST_VERSION
members.desc: Initial state: waiting for the client to send the protocol version string.

members.name: CA_VNC_ST_SECURITY
members.desc: Waiting for the client to select a security type (VNC 3.7/3.8).

members.name: CA_VNC_ST_VENC_VERSION
members.desc: VeNCrypt specific: waiting for the client's version.

members.name: CA_VNC_ST_VENC_SUBTYPE
members.desc: VeNCrypt specific: waiting for the client to select a security subtype.

members.name: CA_VNC_ST_TLS_START
members.desc: Paused state: the system waits for the application to perform the TLS handshake.

members.name: CA_VNC_ST_CLIENT_INIT
members.desc: Waiting for the client's shared-flag initialization message.

members.name: CA_VNC_ST_MSG
members.desc: Normal operation: the session is established and processing VNC messages.

members.name: CA_VNC_ST_CLOSED
members.desc: The session is terminated.

ca_vnc_state_t.notes: This enum is managed internally by the caOS VNC protocol stack. It is typically stored within a VNC session context structure. Do not manually modify this state unless you are implementing custom protocol extensions, as it is updated automatically by ca_vnc_proto_rx and related functions.
ca_vnc_state_t.usage: Used by the VNC service to determine which protocol phase is currently active. It is checked during packet processing to ensure the incoming data matches the expected handshake or operational stage.

ca_vnc_stats_t.body:
typedef struct {
bool     running;           /* task alive and listening */
bool     connected;         /* a client is in session */
u32      sessions;          /* clients served */
u32      refused;           /* second clients closed */
u32      updates, rects, pixels;
u32      bytes_tx;
u32      keys, pointers;    /* client events received (dropped or not) */
u32      auth_ok, auth_fail;  /* X509Plain logins */
u32      auth_backoff;      /* clients closed during the wait after a failure */
u32      auth_ms;           /* time of the last password check (PBKDF2) */
u8       bpp;               /* client's format, 0 = no client */
bool     tls;               /* sessions run over TLS (decided at init) */
u16      suite;             /* last negotiated TLS suite, 0 = none */
u32      tls_ok, tls_fail;  /* TLS handshakes */
u8       tls_alert;         /* alert of the last failed handshake */
const char *last_close;     /* why the last session ended */
} ca_vnc_stats_t;
ca_vnc_stats_t.brief: A structure containing diagnostic and operational metrics for the VNC service.

members.name: running
members.desc: Indicates if the VNC task is active and listening for connections.

members.name: connected
members.desc: Indicates if a VNC client is currently in an active session.

members.name: sessions
members.desc: Total number of client sessions served since startup.

members.name: refused
members.desc: Number of connection attempts rejected (e.g., when a session is already active).

members.name: updates
members.desc: Total number of framebuffer updates sent to the client.

members.name: rects
members.desc: Total number of rectangles transmitted.

members.name: pixels
members.desc: Total number of pixels transmitted.

members.name: bytes_tx
members.desc: Total bytes transmitted to the client.

members.name: keys
members.desc: Count of keyboard events received from the client.

members.name: pointers
members.desc: Count of pointer (mouse) events received from the client.

members.name: bpp
members.desc: Bits per pixel format of the current client; 0 if no client is connected.

members.name: tls
members.desc: Indicates if the service is configured to use TLS.

members.name: suite
members.desc: The TLS cipher suite ID negotiated for the last session; 0 if none.

members.name: tls_ok
members.desc: Count of successful TLS handshakes.

members.name: tls_fail
members.desc: Count of failed TLS handshakes.

members.name: tls_alert
members.desc: The specific TLS alert code from the last failed handshake.

members.name: last_close
members.desc: A string describing the reason for the termination of the last session.

ca_vnc_stats_t.notes: This structure is populated by the caOS VNC service. The user does not allocate this memory; it is retrieved via the service API. The fields are updated asynchronously by the VNC task, so treat the data as a snapshot.
ca_vnc_stats_t.usage: Use this structure to monitor VNC service health, debug connection issues, or display performance statistics in a CLI or UI. It is typically passed to ca_vnc_service_stats to fill the structure with current values.

ca_wait_queue_t.brief: A wait queue structure used to manage a list of threads that are blocked waiting for a specific resource or event.

members.name: head
members.desc: Pointer to the first thread in the waiting list. If NULL, the queue is empty.

members.name: tail
members.desc: Pointer to the last thread in the waiting list. Used to efficiently append new threads to the end of the queue.

ca_wait_queue_t.notes: This structure must be initialized to {NULL, NULL} before use. It is typically managed by the kernel's synchronization primitives (like semaphores or mutexes). Do not manually modify these pointers unless you are implementing custom synchronization logic, as it may lead to kernel instability or thread starvation.
ca_wait_queue_t.usage: Used internally by caOS synchronization objects to track threads that are in the BLOCKED state. You will encounter this when inspecting kernel objects or implementing custom blocking mechanisms.

ca_wdt_early_cb_t.brief: A callback function type triggered by the Watchdog Timer (WDT) shortly before the system reset occurs.

members.name: arg
members.desc: A user-defined pointer passed to the callback when it is executed. It is typically used to pass context data or state information.

ca_wdt_early_cb_t.notes: This callback is executed in an interrupt context (ISR) or a high-priority system context depending on the hardware implementation. It must be extremely fast, non-blocking, and must not perform complex operations like memory allocation or heavy I/O. The callback is registered using ca_wdt_on_early.
ca_wdt_early_cb_t.usage: Use this to perform emergency logging, save critical state to non-volatile memory, or signal other tasks that a system reset is imminent due to a watchdog timeout.

ca_wdt_mode_t.brief: Defines the behavior of the Watchdog Timer (WDT) when a timeout occurs.

members.name: CA_WDT_MODE_RESET
members.desc: The system will trigger a hardware MCU reset upon timeout. Supported by all STM32 families.

members.name: CA_WDT_MODE_INTERRUPT
members.desc: The system triggers an early warning interrupt before the reset. If the interrupt is not cleared or the WDT is not refreshed, a reset follows. Only available on specific hardware.

ca_wdt_mode_t.notes: This enum is used during the initialization phase of the WDT driver. Ensure the hardware supports the interrupt mode before selecting CA_WDT_MODE_INTERRUPT, otherwise, the driver may default to reset or return an error.
ca_wdt_mode_t.usage: Pass this value to the WDT initialization function to configure the watchdog's recovery strategy. Use RESET for critical safety applications and INTERRUPT for debugging or logging purposes.

ca_wdt_reset_t.brief: An enumeration representing the cause of the last system reset, specifically identifying if a watchdog triggered it.

members.name: CA_WDT_RESET_NONE
members.desc: The system did not reset due to a watchdog; it was likely a power-on, manual reset, or software reset.

members.name: CA_WDT_RESET_IWDG
members.desc: The system reset was triggered by the Independent Watchdog (IWDG).

members.name: CA_WDT_RESET_WWDG
members.desc: The system reset was triggered by the Window Watchdog (WWDG).

ca_wdt_reset_t.notes: This value is typically populated by the hardware abstraction layer during the boot process. It is read-only for the application. You should check this value early in your main() function to log or handle unexpected watchdog resets.
ca_wdt_reset_t.usage: Use this enum with the ca_wdt_reset_cause() function to determine why the system restarted after a crash or hang.

ca_wdt_type_t.brief: An enumeration defining the hardware watchdog timer peripheral type available on the STM32.

members.name: CA_WDT_TYPE_IWDG
members.desc: Independent Watchdog. Uses the internal LSI clock. Remains active even if the main system clock fails.

members.name: CA_WDT_TYPE_WWDG
members.desc: Window Watchdog. Uses the APB clock. Requires the application to refresh within a specific time window.

ca_wdt_type_t.notes: This enum is used to select the hardware peripheral during the initialization phase of the watchdog driver. It does not require manual allocation as it is a simple integer-based enumeration.
ca_wdt_type_t.usage: Used as a parameter in the ca_wdt_init() function to specify which hardware watchdog peripheral the driver should configure and manage.

ca_x25519_ctx_t.brief: A structure holding the internal state and working buffers for X25519 elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman key exchange operations.

members.name: e
members.desc: The clamped scalar (private key). Must be 32 bytes. Incorrect clamping or invalid scalar values will result in an insecure or invalid shared secret.

members.name: x1, x2, z2, x3, z3, tmp0, tmp1
members.desc: Internal working buffers for field elements used during the Montgomery ladder calculation. These are managed by the library and should not be modified manually.

ca_x25519_ctx_t.notes: This structure is allocated by the user (e.g., on the stack or as a static variable). It does not require explicit initialization functions, but it must be passed to the X25519 calculation routines to perform key agreement. The memory is owned by the caller.
ca_x25519_ctx_t.usage: Used as the primary context object for X25519 operations. It is passed to ca_x25519_base to compute a public key from a private scalar.

values.name: CA_AES_KEY_128
values.desc: 128-bit key length. Use for standard security requirements; offers the best performance and lowest power consumption.

values.name: CA_AES_KEY_192
values.desc: 192-bit key length. Provides a balance between security and performance.

values.name: CA_AES_KEY_256
values.desc: 256-bit key length. Use for high-security applications requiring maximum resistance against brute-force attacks.

ca_aes_keysize_t.brief: Defines the supported AES key lengths for cryptographic operations in the ca_aes_* API.
ca_aes_keysize_t.notes: The chosen key size must match the length of the key buffer provided to the ca_aes_ctx_setup function. Using an incorrect size will lead to undefined cryptographic behavior or hardware errors in the STM32 AES peripheral.
ca_aes_keysize_t.usage: This enum is passed as an argument to ca_aes_ctx_setup to configure the AES context before calling ca_aes_encrypt or ca_aes_decrypt.

values.name: CA_DMA_DIR_M2P
values.desc: Memory-to-Peripheral transfer. Use this when sending data from a buffer in RAM to a hardware peripheral (e.g., UART TX, SPI TX, DAC).

values.name: CA_DMA_DIR_P2M
values.desc: Peripheral-to-Memory transfer. Use this when receiving data from a hardware peripheral into a buffer in RAM (e.g., UART RX, SPI RX, ADC).

ca_dma_dir_t.brief: Defines the direction of data transfer for DMA operations in caOS drivers.
ca_dma_dir_t.notes: This enum is used to configure the DMA controller's flow direction. Choosing the wrong direction will result in data not being transferred or hardware errors. Ensure the memory address provided is valid for the chosen direction (e.g., source buffer for M2P, destination buffer for P2M).
ca_dma_dir_t.usage: This type is used in ca_dma_set_request and related DMA initialization functions to define the data flow path for a specific DMA channel.

values.name: CA_DMA_WIDTH_8
values.desc: 8-bit data width (byte). Use for peripheral registers or memory buffers containing char or uint8_t data.

values.name: CA_DMA_WIDTH_16
values.desc: 16-bit data width (half-word). Use for 16-bit ADC samples or audio data buffers.

values.name: CA_DMA_WIDTH_32
values.desc: 32-bit data width (word). Use for high-speed memory-to-memory transfers or 32-bit peripheral registers.

ca_dma_width_t.brief: Defines the data width for DMA transfer operations, used in caOS DMA configuration structures.
ca_dma_width_t.notes: The width must match the destination/source register size. Mismatched widths between source and destination can lead to data corruption or hardware-level alignment faults. Ensure the memory address is aligned to the chosen width (e.g., 4-byte alignment for 32-bit transfers).
ca_dma_width_t.usage: Used in the ca_dma_config_t struct passed to ca_dma_init(). Choose the value that matches the data type of the buffer or the peripheral register being accessed.

values.name: CA_EXTI_EDGE_RISING
values.desc: Triggers the interrupt when the signal transitions from low to high (0 to 1). Use this for buttons pulled to ground or sensors that output a high pulse.

values.name: CA_EXTI_EDGE_FALLING
values.desc: Triggers the interrupt when the signal transitions from high to low (1 to 0). This is the most common setting for active-low buttons or switches.

values.name: CA_EXTI_EDGE_BOTH
values.desc: Triggers the interrupt on both rising and falling edges. Use this for rotary encoders or monitoring signal state changes where both transitions are significant.

ca_exti_edge_t.brief: Defines the signal transition trigger condition for external interrupts (EXTI) in the caOS driver API.
ca_exti_edge_t.notes: The hardware configuration depends on the specific STM32 EXTI line capabilities. Ensure the GPIO pin is correctly configured with internal pull-up or pull-down resistors if no external hardware resistor is present, otherwise the pin will float and trigger spurious interrupts.
ca_exti_edge_t.usage: This enum is passed to the 'ca_exti_config' function during peripheral initialization. Choose the value based on the electrical characteristics of your input signal and the desired logic state change.

values.name: CA_GPIO_MODE_INPUT
values.desc: Configures the pin as a high-impedance input. Use this for reading external digital signals like buttons or sensors.

values.name: CA_GPIO_MODE_OUTPUT
values.desc: Configures the pin as a push-pull or open-drain output. Use this for driving LEDs, relays, or communication lines.

values.name: CA_GPIO_MODE_ANALOG
values.desc: Configures the pin for analog mode. Essential for ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter) or DAC (Digital-to-Analog Converter) operations to prevent digital input buffer leakage.

ca_gpio_mode_t.brief: Defines the operational mode of an STM32 GPIO pin, used in the caOS GPIO configuration API.
ca_gpio_mode_t.notes: The default value is typically CA_GPIO_MODE_INPUT to ensure safety upon reset. Ensure the pin is not configured as an output if it is connected to an external voltage source to avoid short circuits. On some STM32 families, AF mode requires an additional register configuration (AFR) to select the specific peripheral mapping.
ca_gpio_mode_t.usage: This enum is passed to the 'gpio_init()' function. Choose the mode based on the hardware schematic: use INPUT for sensors, OUTPUT for actuators, AF for communication peripherals, and ANALOG for voltage measurement.

values.name: CA_GPIO_OTYPE_PP
values.desc: Push-Pull configuration. The pin actively drives the line to both VCC and GND. Use this for standard digital signals like SPI, UART, or driving LEDs.

values.name: CA_GPIO_OTYPE_OD
values.desc: Open-Drain configuration. The pin can only drive the line to GND or remain in a high-impedance state. Requires an external pull-up resistor to reach VCC. Essential for I2C buses or shared-bus architectures where multiple devices pull the line low.

ca_gpio_otype_t.brief: Defines the output type configuration for STM32 GPIO pins, used in the GPIO initialization API.
ca_gpio_otype_t.notes: CA_GPIO_OTYPE_PP is the default state for most GPIO pins after reset. Choosing Open-Drain without an external pull-up will result in the signal floating, which can cause unpredictable logic levels. Ensure the hardware schematic supports the chosen mode, especially for communication protocols.
ca_gpio_otype_t.usage: This enum is passed to the 'gpio_init' function within the GPIO configuration structure. Choose PP for general-purpose outputs and OD for communication buses or scenarios requiring wired-OR logic.

values.name: CA_GPIO_PIN_0
values.desc: Pin 0 of the selected port. Use for standard I/O or peripheral alternate functions.

values.name: CA_GPIO_PIN_1
values.desc: Pin 1 of the selected port.

values.name: CA_GPIO_PIN_3
values.desc: Pin 3 of the selected port.

values.name: CA_GPIO_PIN_5
values.desc: Pin 5 of the selected port. Often used for SPI SCK or LED indicators.

values.name: CA_GPIO_PIN_7
values.desc: Pin 7 of the selected port.

values.name: CA_GPIO_PIN_9
values.desc: Pin 9 of the selected port.

values.name: CA_GPIO_PIN_11
values.desc: Pin 11 of the selected port.

values.name: CA_GPIO_PIN_13
values.desc: Pin 13 of the selected port. Note: Often reserved for onboard user LEDs or JTAG/SWD pins.

values.name: CA_GPIO_PIN_15
values.desc: Pin 15 of the selected port.

ca_gpio_pin_t.brief: Represents the specific physical pin index (0-15) on a GPIO port, used in all caOS GPIO configuration and control APIs.
ca_gpio_pin_t.notes: These values correspond directly to the bit position in the STM32 GPIO IDR/ODR registers. Ensure the physical pin is not being used by the debugger (e.g., PA13/PA14) before assigning it to general logic, or you may lose connection to the board.
ca_gpio_pin_t.usage: Used in functions like gpio_init(), gpio_write(), and gpio_read(). Select the value based on the schematic pinout of your specific STM32 target board.

values.name: CA_GPIO_PORT_A
values.desc: Port A. Typically used for primary peripherals like USART1 or SPI1. Ensure the RCC clock for Port A is enabled before use.

values.name: CA_GPIO_PORT_B
values.desc: Port B. Often used for I2C peripherals and general-purpose I/O.

values.name: CA_GPIO_PORT_D
values.desc: Port D. Common on larger STM32 packages for external memory interfaces or additional communication pins.

values.name: CA_GPIO_PORT_F
values.desc: Port F. Often used for specialized hardware features or system-level pins.

values.name: CA_GPIO_PORT_H
values.desc: Port H. Typically associated with high-performance STM32 series (e.g., F4/F7/H7).

values.name: CA_GPIO_PORT_J
values.desc: Port J. Used in very high-pin-count packages; rarely present on entry-level STM32 chips.

ca_gpio_port_t.brief: Represents the physical GPIO port identifier on the STM32 microcontroller, used in all caOS GPIO configuration and control functions.
ca_gpio_port_t.notes: Not all ports are available on every STM32 chip. Attempting to configure a port that does not exist on your specific MCU will result in undefined behavior or a hard fault. Always consult the datasheet for your specific part number to confirm port availability.
ca_gpio_port_t.usage: Used as the first argument in functions like caos_gpio_init(), caos_gpio_write(), and caos_gpio_read(). Choose the port based on the physical pin label found on the schematic (e.g., PA5 corresponds to CA_GPIO_PORT_A).

values.name: CA_GPIO_NOPULL
values.desc: Disables both pull-up and pull-down resistors. Use this for push-pull outputs or when an external resistor is already present on the PCB.

values.name: CA_GPIO_PULLUP
values.desc: Connects an internal resistor to VDD. Use this for input pins (like buttons or I2C lines) that must default to a logic HIGH state when the external circuit is floating.

ca_gpio_pull_t.brief: Defines the internal resistor configuration for STM32 GPIO pins, used in GPIO initialization and configuration APIs.
ca_gpio_pull_t.notes: The internal pull resistors are typically weak (approx 40k ohms). They are not a substitute for strong external resistors in high-speed communication or noisy environments. Do not enable both pull-up and pull-down simultaneously on the same pin as it may cause unexpected behavior or increased power consumption.
ca_gpio_pull_t.usage: This enum is passed to the 'caos_gpio_init' function within the 'GPIO_InitTypeDef' structure. Choose 'CA_GPIO_NOPULL' for standard outputs, 'CA_GPIO_PULLUP' for active-low inputs (e.g., buttons connected to GND), and 'GPIO_PULLDOWN' for active-high inputs.

values.name: CA_GPIO_SPEED_LOW
values.desc: Lowest slew rate. Use for low-frequency signals (e.g., status LEDs, buttons). Minimizes EMI and power consumption.

values.name: CA_GPIO_SPEED_MED
values.desc: Medium slew rate. Suitable for moderate frequency signals where signal integrity is not critical but noise must be controlled.

values.name: CA_GPIO_SPEED_VERY_HIGH
values.desc: Maximum slew rate. Use only for high-speed peripherals (e.g., high-speed SPI, external memory interfaces). Increases EMI significantly.

ca_gpio_speed_t.brief: Defines the output slew rate of a GPIO pin, used in the GPIO configuration API to balance signal integrity against electromagnetic interference (EMI).
ca_gpio_speed_t.notes: Higher speeds increase the risk of signal ringing and ground bounce. Always choose the lowest speed that meets your timing requirements to ensure system stability and compliance with EMC standards. The default value is typically CA_GPIO_SPEED_LOW.
ca_gpio_speed_t.usage: Used in the 'gpio_init_t' structure passed to 'gpio_init()'. Choose the speed based on the maximum toggle frequency of the specific pin function.

values.name: CA_HASH_ALGO_SHA1
values.desc: Selects the SHA-1 algorithm. Produces a 160-bit hash value. Use only for legacy compatibility as it is considered cryptographically broken and vulnerable to collision attacks.

values.name: CA_HASH_ALGO_SHA256
values.desc: Selects the SHA-256 algorithm. Produces a 256-bit hash value. This is the industry standard for secure data integrity and should be the default choice for all new designs.

ca_hash_algo_t.brief: Defines the cryptographic hashing algorithm to be used by the caOS hardware abstraction layer for the STM32 HASH peripheral.
ca_hash_algo_t.notes: The hardware peripheral must be initialized before selecting an algorithm. Switching algorithms mid-operation without resetting the HASH peripheral will result in undefined behavior. SHA-256 is significantly more computationally intensive than SHA-1, though the STM32 hardware accelerator minimizes this impact.
ca_hash_algo_t.usage: This enum is passed as an argument to 'ca_hash_init()' to configure the hardware engine. Choose CA_HASH_ALGO_SHA256 for security-critical applications or CA_HASH_ALGO_SHA1 only when interfacing with existing legacy systems.

values.name: CA_I2C_SPEED_STANDARD
values.desc: Sets the I2C bus speed to 100 kHz. Use this for maximum compatibility with older sensors and long PCB traces.

values.name: CA_I2C_SPEED_FAST
values.desc: Sets the I2C bus speed to 400 kHz. Use this for high-throughput data transfers, provided the hardware pull-up resistors are strong enough to maintain signal integrity at this frequency.

ca_i2c_speed_t.brief: Defines the operating clock frequency mode for the I2C peripheral in the caOS I2C driver API.
ca_i2c_speed_t.notes: The actual timing parameters (rise/fall times) are calculated by the driver based on the peripheral clock frequency. Ensure your pull-up resistors are sized correctly; 400 kHz requires lower resistance values than 100 kHz to avoid signal rounding.
ca_i2c_speed_t.usage: This enum is passed as a parameter to the ca_i2c_init() function during peripheral configuration. Choose STANDARD for general-purpose communication and FAST when the slave device supports it and bus speed is a bottleneck.

values.name: CA_JOB_STD
values.desc: Standard task without FPU support or extra safety overhead. Use this for simple logic, I/O handling, or integer-only calculations to minimize context switch latency.

values.name: JOB_SAFE
values.desc: A standard task with additional stack overflow protection and memory isolation checks. Use this for critical system tasks where stability is prioritized over raw performance.

values.name: JOB_FLOAT_POINT
values.desc: Enables the FPU (Floating Point Unit) context saving for the task. Use this if your task performs floating-point arithmetic to prevent data corruption during context switches.

values.name: CA_JOB_SAFE_FLOAT_POINT
values.desc: Combines FPU context saving with enhanced safety checks. Use this for critical control loops that require floating-point math.

ca_job_type.brief: Defines the execution context and hardware resource requirements for a task, used in the ca_scheduler_add_job API.
ca_job_type.notes: Choosing a FLOAT_POINT type on an MCU without a hardware FPU will trigger a software emulation overhead, significantly slowing down the task. JOB_SAFE types consume more RAM due to the inclusion of stack guard zones. Do not use CA_JOB_STD if the task uses float variables, as the FPU registers will not be saved, leading to non-deterministic behavior.
ca_job_type.usage: This enum is passed as the second argument to ca_scheduler_add_job. Choose CA_JOB_STD by default for performance, and upgrade to JOB_FLOAT_POINT only if the compiler flags indicate floating-point usage.

values.name: CA_KEYS_STORE_NO_ACCESS
values.desc: The key is completely inaccessible. Use this to disable a key slot or revoke access to a sensitive key.

values.name: CA_KEYS_STORE_READ_ONLY
values.desc: The key can be read by the crypto engine for operations but cannot be modified or overwritten. Use this for production keys that should remain immutable.

values.name: CA_KEYS_STORE_READ_WRITE
values.desc: The key can be read and updated. Use this for session keys or keys that need to be rotated frequently during runtime.

values.name: CA_KEYS_STORE_EXEC_ONLY
values.desc: The key is used by the hardware crypto accelerator but cannot be read back by the CPU. Use this for high-security keys (e.g., master keys) to prevent extraction via memory dumping.

ca_keys_store_access_mode_t.brief: Defines the permission levels for accessing cryptographic keys stored in the caOS secure key store, used in key management APIs.
ca_keys_store_access_mode_t.notes: The default value is typically CA_KEYS_STORE_NO_ACCESS for security reasons. Once a key is set to CA_KEYS_STORE_EXEC_ONLY, it cannot be read back, meaning you must keep a secure backup if the key needs to be restored later. Changing access modes may require a system reset or specific privilege levels depending on the STM32 hardware security module (HSM) configuration.
ca_keys_store_access_mode_t.usage: This enum is passed to 'keys_store_set_access()' and 'keys_store_init()' functions. Choose the most restrictive mode possible (Principle of Least Privilege) to minimize the impact of potential software vulnerabilities.

values.name: CA_L2_ACCEPT_UNICAST
values.desc: Accepts only packets addressed specifically to the device's MAC address. This is the standard operational mode for point-to-point communication.

values.name: CA_L2_ACCEPT_BROADCAST
values.desc: Accepts packets sent to the broadcast address (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF). Required for protocols like DHCP or ARP discovery.

values.name: CA_L2_ACCEPT_MULTICAST
values.desc: Accepts packets sent to multicast groups. Necessary for mDNS, IGMP, or specific group-based communication.

values.name: CA_L2_DROP
values.desc: Silently discards the incoming packet at the L2 layer. Used to implement firewall-like behavior or to ignore specific traffic types.

ca_l2_result_t.brief: Defines the packet filtering or acceptance policy for the network layer (L2) in caOS, used primarily in ca_net_proto_l2.
ca_l2_result_t.notes: The default behavior depends on the network interface configuration. These values are typically used to configure hardware filters or software hooks in the network stack. Choosing CA_L2_DROP is useful for security or to reduce CPU load by ignoring irrelevant traffic early in the processing pipeline.
ca_l2_result_t.usage: This enum is used within the ca_net_proto_l2 function to determine how the network stack should handle incoming frames. When implementing a custom network filter or configuring the Ethernet controller, pass one of these values to define the acceptance policy.

values.name: CA_LPTIM_MODE_PERIODIC
values.desc: The timer automatically reloads and restarts after reaching the compare value. Use this for recurring tasks like periodic sensor polling or heartbeat signals.

values.name: CA_LPTIM_MODE_ONESHOT
values.desc: The timer stops automatically after reaching the compare value. Use this for single-shot delays or one-time event triggers to save power.

ca_lptim_mode_t.brief: Defines the operational behavior of the Low Power Timer (LPTIM) peripheral within the caOS hardware abstraction layer.
ca_lptim_mode_t.notes: The default value is CA_LPTIM_MODE_PERIODIC. Ensure the LPTIM clock source is configured correctly in the RCC before initialization, as some modes may not be supported depending on the specific STM32 series (e.g., L0 vs U5). A common mistake is using ONESHOT mode when a continuous timebase is required for RTOS scheduling.
ca_lptim_mode_t.usage: This enum is passed to the ca_lptim_init() function during peripheral configuration. Choose PERIODIC for continuous background tasks and ONESHOT for transient, event-driven operations.

values.name: CA_PWR_MODE_SLEEP
values.desc: CPU clock is off, but peripherals remain active. Wakeup is near-instant via interrupts.

values.name: CA_PWR_MODE_STOP
values.desc: CPU and most clocks are stopped. SRAM is retained. Wakeup takes longer due to clock stabilization.

values.name: PWR_MODE_STANDBY
values.desc: Deepest power saving. SRAM and CPU state are lost. Wakeup triggers a system reset.

ca_pwr_mode_t.brief: Defines the power consumption state for the MCU, used in the ca_pwr_enter API.
ca_pwr_mode_t.notes: The power modes are mutually exclusive. Choosing the wrong mode can lead to unexpected system resets (Standby) or failure to wake up if the interrupt source is disabled in that specific mode. Always ensure the required wakeup interrupt is configured before entering low power.
ca_pwr_mode_t.usage: This enum is passed to the ca_pwr_enter(ca_pwr_mode_t mode) function. Select the mode based on the required balance between power consumption and wakeup latency.

values.name: CA_RTC_CLK_LSE
values.desc: Uses the Low-Speed External 32.768 kHz crystal. This is the recommended choice for battery-backed RTC operation as it provides high accuracy and low power consumption.

values.name: CA_RTC_CLK_LSI
values.desc: Uses the Low-Speed Internal RC oscillator. Use this when no external crystal is present; note that LSI frequency varies significantly with temperature and voltage, making it unsuitable for high-precision timekeeping.

values.name: CA_RTC_CLK_HSE
values.desc: Uses the High-Speed External oscillator (divided). Use this if high precision is required but LSE is unavailable; note that this consumes more power and requires the HSE to be running constantly.

ca_rtc_clk_src_t.brief: Defines the clock source for the RTC peripheral in the caOS RTC driver API.
ca_rtc_clk_src_t.notes: The clock source must be configured before the RTC is initialized. Changing the clock source while the RTC is running may lead to undefined behavior or loss of time data. Ensure the corresponding oscillator is enabled in the system clock configuration before selecting it here.
ca_rtc_clk_src_t.usage: This enum is passed to the ca_rtc_init() function. Choose CA_RTC_CLK_LSE for production devices requiring accurate timekeeping, and CA_RTC_CLK_LSI for low-cost prototypes without an external crystal.

values.name: CA_TH_INFO_DEFAULT
values.desc: The standard information mode. Returns basic task metadata such as priority, state, and task handle. Use this for general monitoring.

values.name: CA_TH_INFO_FLAG
values.desc: Returns the current status of task-specific event flags. Use this when debugging inter-task synchronization or waiting mechanisms.

values.name: TH_INFO_RUNTIME
values.desc: Returns CPU usage statistics and execution time metrics. Use this for performance profiling and identifying tasks that consume excessive CPU cycles.

values.name: CA_TH_INFO_MEM
values.desc: Provides memory usage statistics for the task, specifically stack high-water mark. Use this to optimize stack sizes and prevent stack overflows.

values.name: TH_INFO_ASSERT
values.desc: Retrieves information related to task assertion failures. Use this during debugging to identify which task triggered a system halt or assertion.

ca_scheduler_tasks_info_mode.brief: Defines the level of detail and data source for task information retrieval in the caOS scheduler API.
ca_scheduler_tasks_info_mode.notes: CA_TH_INFO_DEFAULT is the fallback mode if an invalid value is passed. These modes are mutually exclusive; you can only request one type of information per function call. Note that TH_INFO_RUNTIME requires the scheduler's runtime statistics feature to be enabled in the configuration file, otherwise it may return zeroed data.
ca_scheduler_tasks_info_mode.usage: This enum is used as an argument in the 'ca_scheduler_get_task_info' function. Choose the mode based on the specific diagnostic data required: use DEFAULT for general status, MEM for stack analysis, or RUNTIME for performance tuning.

values.name: CA_SPI_BR_DIV2
values.desc: Sets the baud rate to fPCLK/2. Use for high-speed communication when signal integrity is guaranteed.

values.name: CA_SPI_BR_DIV4
values.desc: Sets the baud rate to fPCLK/4. A balanced choice for standard SPI peripherals.

values.name: CA_SPI_BR_DIV8
values.desc: Sets the baud rate to fPCLK/8. Recommended for moderate distances or slightly noisy environments.

values.name: CA_SPI_BR_DIV16
values.desc: Sets the baud rate to fPCLK/16. Good for general-purpose sensors with lower clock requirements.

values.name: CA_SPI_BR_DIV32
values.desc: Sets the baud rate to fPCLK/32. Use when the slave device has strict timing constraints or slow response times.

values.name: CA_SPI_BR_DIV64
values.desc: Sets the baud rate to fPCLK/64. Suitable for low-speed peripherals or long cable runs.

values.name: CA_SPI_BR_DIV128
values.desc: Sets the baud rate to fPCLK/128. Use for debugging or very slow legacy SPI devices.

values.name: CA_SPI_BR_DIV256
values.desc: Sets the baud rate to fPCLK/256. The slowest possible speed; use only if the slave device requires extremely low clock frequencies.

ca_spi_br_t.brief: Defines the SPI baud rate prescaler relative to the peripheral clock, used in ca_spi_init() to configure communication speed.
ca_spi_br_t.notes: The actual frequency depends on the clock source of the specific SPI bus (e.g., APB1 or APB2). Ensure the resulting frequency does not exceed the maximum clock speed specified in the datasheet of the connected slave device. Choosing a value that is too high will result in data corruption or failed communication.
ca_spi_br_t.usage: This enum is passed as a member of the configuration structure to the ca_spi_init() function. Select the highest value that remains within the slave device's maximum clock frequency specification.

values.name: STACK_SMALL
values.desc: Standard size for basic tasks. Suitable for simple logic, minimal local variables, and shallow call stacks.

values.name: STACK_MEDIUM
values.desc: The balanced choice for most application tasks. Provides enough headroom for standard middleware and moderate local variable usage.

values.name: STACK_LARGE
values.desc: Alias for STACK_MEDIUM. Used to improve code readability when a task requires more than a small stack.

values.name: STACK_XLARGE
values.desc: Alias for STACK_MEDIUM. Intended for tasks performing complex operations or using large local arrays, though it currently maps to the same size as STACK_MEDIUM.

values.name: STACK_KERNEL
values.desc: Alias for STACK_MEDIUM. Reserved for internal system tasks or high-priority background processes.

ca_stack_size_t.brief: Defines predefined memory allocation sizes for task stacks within the caOS RTOS, used during task creation APIs.
ca_stack_size_t.notes: On the STM32F103, stack sizes are defined in bytes. Note that STACK_LARGE, STACK_KERNEL, and STACK_XLARGE are currently aliases for STACK_MEDIUM. Choosing a size too small will result in a stack overflow, which typically triggers a HardFault exception. Always monitor stack usage using the caOS debug tools.
ca_stack_size_t.usage: Used as an argument in task creation functions like 'caos_task_create()'. Choose based on the task's complexity: start with STACK_MEDIUM and reduce to STACK_SMALL if memory is tight, or increase if you encounter stack overflow errors.

values.name: CA_TIMER_ONE_SHOT
values.desc: The timer triggers its callback exactly once after the initial delay expires. It then enters an inactive state and must be manually restarted if needed.

values.name: CA_TIMER_PERIODIC
values.desc: The timer automatically reloads its period after each expiration, triggering the callback repeatedly at fixed intervals until explicitly stopped or deleted.

ca_sw_timer_mode_t.brief: Defines the execution behavior of a software timer within the caOS RTOS timer management API.
ca_sw_timer_mode_t.notes: The timer mode is set during the creation phase and cannot be changed while the timer is running. Choosing CA_TIMER_PERIODIC requires careful management of the callback execution time to ensure it does not exceed the timer period, which could lead to missed intervals or system instability.
ca_sw_timer_mode_t.usage: This enum is used as an argument in the ca_sw_timer_create() function. Choose CA_TIMER_ONE_SHOT for tasks like delayed power-off or debouncing, and CA_TIMER_PERIODIC for recurring tasks like status polling or heartbeat signals.

values.name: CA_TIMER_STOPPED
values.desc: The timer is inactive and not currently counting. It will not trigger any callbacks until explicitly started.

values.name: CA_TIMER_RUNNING
values.desc: The timer is active and decrementing its tick count. It will execute its associated callback function upon reaching zero.

values.name: CA_TIMER_EXPIRED
values.desc: The timer has reached its terminal count. This state is typically transient before the timer either stops or auto-reloads.

ca_sw_timer_state_t.brief: Represents the current operational state of a software timer within the caOS RTOS timer management API.
ca_sw_timer_state_t.notes: The state is managed internally by the caOS kernel. Manually forcing these values via pointers is discouraged as it may lead to race conditions or inconsistent timer queue processing. CA_TIMER_STOPPED is the default state upon timer initialization.
ca_sw_timer_state_t.usage: Used in ca_sw_timer_get_state() to query the status of a timer handle and internally by the scheduler to determine if a timer callback should be executed.

values.name: CA_TICK_SPEED_100US
values.desc: 100 microsecond tick. High resolution, but increases CPU overhead due to frequent interrupt handling.

values.name: CA_TICK_SPEED_200US
values.desc: 200 microsecond tick. Balanced for applications requiring sub-millisecond precision without excessive context switching.

values.name: CA_TICK_SPEED_250US
values.desc: 250 microsecond tick. Useful for timing loops that need to align with 4kHz frequency requirements.

values.name: CA_TICK_SPEED_500US
values.desc: 500 microsecond tick. Standard high-resolution setting for most real-time control tasks.

values.name: CA_TICK_SPEED_1MS
values.desc: 1 millisecond tick. The industry standard for general-purpose RTOS applications.

values.name: CA_TICK_SPEED_2MS
values.desc: 2 millisecond tick. Reduces CPU load compared to 1ms, suitable for slower background tasks.

values.name: CA_TICK_SPEED_5MS
values.desc: 5 millisecond tick. Low power consumption, recommended for battery-operated devices with low timing requirements.

values.name: CA_TICK_SPEED_10MS
values.desc: 10 millisecond tick. Lowest CPU overhead, but limits the granularity of task delays and timeouts.

ca_tick_speed_t.brief: Defines the system tick interval in microseconds, used in the caOS initialization API to configure the SysTick timer frequency.
ca_tick_speed_t.notes: The tick speed determines the resolution of all OS delays and timeouts. Choosing a value that is too small (e.g., 100us) on low-clock-speed MCUs can lead to 'tick starvation' where the CPU spends most of its time in the SysTick ISR. This value must be set once during system boot and cannot be changed at runtime.
ca_tick_speed_t.usage: Passed as an argument to the 'caos_init()' or 'caos_systick_config()' functions. Choose the largest value that still satisfies the timing requirements of your most time-critical task.

values.name: CA_TIMER_MODE_PERIODIC
values.desc: The default mode. The timer continuously reloads and triggers events at a fixed frequency. Use this for standard system heartbeats or periodic task scheduling.

values.name: CA_TIMER_MODE_ONESHOT
values.desc: The timer counts once until the compare match is reached and then stops. Ideal for generating single-pulse delays or timeout triggers.

values.name: TIMER_MODE_COUNTER
values.desc: Configures the timer as a simple up/down counter. Useful for measuring external pulses or counting events without triggering interrupts.

values.name: CA_TIMER_MODE_ENCODER
values.desc: Configures the timer to interface with quadrature encoders. It automatically handles phase A/B signals to track position and direction.

values.name: TIMER_MODE_COUNTER_IRQ
values.desc: Similar to TIMER_MODE_COUNTER but enables hardware interrupts on overflow or update events. Use this when you need to track high-frequency events that require CPU intervention.

values.name: CA_TIMER_MODE_PWM
values.desc: Configures the timer to generate Pulse Width Modulation signals on output compare channels. Used for motor control, LED dimming, or DAC-like signal generation.

ca_timer_mode_t.brief: Defines the operational mode of a hardware timer peripheral within the caOS timer driver API.
ca_timer_mode_t.notes: CA_TIMER_MODE_PERIODIC is the default value. Ensure the timer peripheral supports the selected mode, as some basic timers (e.g., TIM6/TIM7 on STM32) do not support PWM or Encoder modes. Avoid changing modes while the timer is running; always stop the timer before reconfiguring.
ca_timer_mode_t.usage: Used in the ca_timer_init() function. Choose the mode based on your hardware requirement: use PERIODIC for timing, PWM for power control, and ENCODER for motion feedback.

values.name: CA_UART_BAUD_9600
values.desc: Standard low-speed baud rate. Use for legacy devices or long-distance cabling where signal integrity is a concern.

values.name: CA_UART_BAUD_19200
values.desc: Common low-speed rate for industrial sensors and serial debug consoles.

values.name: CA_UART_BAUD_38400
values.desc: Intermediate speed for moderate data throughput requirements.

values.name: CA_UART_BAUD_57600
values.desc: Higher speed for applications requiring faster response times than standard 38400.

values.name: CA_UART_BAUD_115200
values.desc: The industry standard for most serial communication. Recommended default for general-purpose debugging and logging.

values.name: CA_UART_BAUD_230400
values.desc: High-speed rate for faster data logging; requires shorter cable lengths to avoid bit errors.

values.name: CA_UART_BAUD_460800
values.desc: High-speed rate; ensure the system clock frequency is sufficient to maintain low jitter.

values.name: CA_UART_BAUD_921600
values.desc: Very high speed; requires careful PCB layout and short traces to maintain signal integrity.

values.name: CA_UART_BAUD_1000000
values.desc: 1 Mbps rate. Useful for high-speed data transfer between microcontrollers.

values.name: CA_UART_BAUD_2000000
values.desc: 2 Mbps rate. Requires high-performance UART hardware and DMA usage to prevent buffer overruns.

values.name: CA_UART_BAUD_3000000
values.desc: 3 Mbps rate. Only recommended for short-range, point-to-point communication on the same PCB.

values.name: CA_UART_BAUD_4000000
values.desc: 4 Mbps rate. Verify that the STM32 peripheral clock (PCLK) can support this baud rate with minimal error.

values.name: CA_UART_BAUD_4500000
values.desc: 4.5 Mbps rate. Extremely high speed; ensure the receiver is capable of handling this throughput.

values.name: CA_UART_BAUD_5000000
values.desc: 5 Mbps rate. Maximum supported speed. Use only when strictly necessary and with high-quality signal paths.

ca_uart_baud_rate_t.brief: Defines the supported communication speeds for UART peripherals in the caOS driver API.
ca_uart_baud_rate_t.notes: The actual baud rate error depends on the STM32 peripheral clock frequency. Always check the calculated baud rate error in the datasheet for your specific MCU. High baud rates (>1 Mbps) are highly sensitive to cable length and capacitance. DMA is strongly recommended for baud rates above 115200 to avoid CPU starvation.
ca_uart_baud_rate_t.usage: Used in the uart_init() function to configure the hardware baud rate generator. Select the value based on the requirements of the connected peripheral device.

values.name: CA_USB_SPEED_FS
values.desc: Full-Speed mode (12 Mbps). Use this for standard USB 2.0 devices or when hardware constraints prevent High-Speed operation. It is the most compatible and stable mode.

values.name: CA_USB_SPEED_HS
values.desc: High-Speed mode (480 Mbps). Use this for data-intensive applications. Requires an external PHY on many STM32 series; ensure your hardware design supports the necessary clocking and signal integrity for HS.

ca_usb_speed_t.brief: Defines the operational speed mode for the USB peripheral, used in the caOS USB initialization and configuration API.
ca_usb_speed_t.notes: The default value is typically CA_USB_SPEED_FS. Not all STM32 MCUs support High-Speed; attempting to set CA_USB_SPEED_HS on a device without an integrated or external HS PHY will result in initialization failure. Ensure the system clock configuration (HSE/PLL) is sufficient to support the chosen speed, especially for HS.
ca_usb_speed_t.usage: This enum is passed to the ca_usb_init() function. Choose CA_USB_SPEED_FS for general-purpose connectivity or CA_USB_SPEED_HS only if your hardware design explicitly includes a High-Speed PHY and you require higher throughput.

values.name: CA_USB_TYPE_NONE
values.desc: USB functionality is disabled. Use this to save power or when the USB peripheral is not required by the application.

values.name: CA_USB_TYPE_CDC
values.desc: Communications Device Class. Configures the device as a Virtual COM Port (VCP) for serial communication with a host.

values.name: CA_USB_TYPE_MSC
values.desc: Mass Storage Class. Allows the device to appear as a USB flash drive to the host, typically for file system access.

values.name: CA_USB_TYPE_NCM
values.desc: Network Control Model. Configures the device as a network interface (Ethernet over USB) for high-speed data transfer.

values.name: CA_USB_TYPE_DFU
values.desc: Device Firmware Upgrade. Enables the built-in bootloader mode for updating the device firmware via USB.

values.name: CA_USB_TYPE_CUSTOM
values.desc: Custom class. Used for proprietary protocols or HID devices where the user provides a custom descriptor and callback handlers.

values.name: CA_USB_TYPE__MAX
values.desc: Sentinel value representing the upper bound of the enum. Do not use this as a valid configuration.

ca_usb_type_t.brief: Defines the USB device class configuration for the caOS USB management stack, used during initialization to determine the device's functional role.
ca_usb_type_t.notes: The default value is CA_USB_TYPE_NONE. These values are mutually exclusive; only one USB class can be active per instance. Ensure the hardware descriptors match the selected type, as selecting an incorrect type will cause enumeration failure on the host PC.
ca_usb_type_t.usage: This enum is passed to the ca_usb_init() function. Choose the value based on the desired communication protocol required by your project specifications.

values.name: CA_WDT_MODE_RESET
values.desc: Forces a hardware system reset when the watchdog expires. This is the standard production mode to ensure system recovery from hangs or infinite loops.

values.name: CA_WDT_MODE_INTERRUPT
values.desc: Triggers a callback function when the watchdog expires instead of resetting the MCU. Use this for debugging or logging purposes where you need to capture state before a manual reset.

ca_wdt_mode_t.brief: Defines the watchdog timer behavior upon timeout, used in the caOS WDT driver initialization API.
ca_wdt_mode_t.notes: CA_WDT_MODE_RESET is the default and safest choice for production firmware. CA_WDT_MODE_INTERRUPT should be used with caution as it does not guarantee system recovery if the CPU is stuck in a hard fault or critical error state. Ensure the watchdog is refreshed (kicked) frequently enough to avoid unintended resets.
ca_wdt_mode_t.usage: This enum is passed to the 'ca_wdt_init()' function. Choose CA_WDT_MODE_RESET for standard watchdog functionality. Choose CA_WDT_MODE_INTERRUPT only during development phases when you need to inspect the system state via a breakpoint or log before the watchdog forces a reset.

values.name: CA_WDT_TYPE_IWDG
values.desc: Independent Watchdog. Uses a dedicated low-speed internal clock (LSI). It remains active even if the main system clock fails, making it ideal for critical system recovery.

values.name: CA_WDT_TYPE_WWDG
values.desc: Window Watchdog. Driven by the main system clock (APB). It requires the application to refresh the counter within a specific time window, making it suitable for detecting software execution timing errors.

ca_wdt_type_t.brief: Defines the hardware watchdog timer peripheral type used in the caOS WDT driver API.
ca_wdt_type_t.notes: IWDG is independent of the system clock and is the safest choice for general system hang recovery. WWDG is more precise but will stop if the system clock fails or enters certain low-power modes. Do not attempt to refresh a WWDG too early, as it will trigger a reset if the counter is above the window threshold.
ca_wdt_type_t.usage: Used in 'ca_wdt_init()' to configure the hardware peripheral. Choose IWDG for long-term system stability and WWDG for strict timing-sensitive task monitoring.
